1.q: The Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) is considering whether it is bound by one of its own previous decisions in a case where following it might result in an individual being wrongly imprisoned. Counsel argues the criminal division has a degree of flexibility not available in civil appeals. The case concerns the liberty of the subject. The court weighs following its own precedent. The earlier decision is directly in point and, if followed, would leave the appellant convicted and imprisoned on a basis the court now doubts, and counsel presses that the division dealing with criminal appeals is not shackled to its own precedent quite as tightly as the civil side, precisely because a person's liberty is at stake. Which of the following best describes the position of the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division)?
o: It may depart from its own decisions only with the consent of the parties.
It is never bound by any of its own previous decisions in any circumstances.
It is bound only by decisions of the Court of Appeal (Civil Division).
It may depart from its own previous decision with rather more flexibility where following it would cause injustice to the subject.
It is absolutely bound by its own previous decisions with no exceptions whatsoever on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
1.w: The Court of Appeal is generally bound by its own previous decisions (subject to the Young v Bristol Aeroplane exceptions), but the Criminal Division has somewhat greater flexibility to depart from its own precedent where following it would cause injustice, because the liberty of the subject is at stake.

n.0: Departure does not depend on the parties' consent.
n.1: It is generally bound by its own decisions subject to exceptions, so 'never bound' is wrong.
n.2: It is not bound by the Civil Division; each division generally follows its own decisions.
n.4: It is not absolutely bound with no exceptions; it has some added flexibility in criminal cases.

1.q: A joiner agrees to build and fit a complete bespoke staircase for a fixed lump sum of £8,000, payable on completion of the whole job. After doing a substantial part of the work, the joiner abandons the project entirely and never returns, leaving the staircase unusable and unfinished. The client has to engage another joiner to finish it. The original joiner now claims to be paid a proportion of the £8,000 for the work he did carry out. The client refuses to pay him anything. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The joiner cannot recover any of the price, as it was payable only on complete performance.
The joiner may recover the price, because the client will benefit from the finished staircase.
The joiner may recover the full £8,000, because he did the greater part of the work involved.
The joiner may recover the price in full, subject only to a small deduction for the unfinished part.
The joiner may recover a fair proportion of the price for the work he actually did before abandoning it.
1.w: Where payment is due only on completion of an entire obligation, a party who fails to complete cannot recover the price, or any part of it, for incomplete performance (Cutter v Powell; Sumpter v Hedges). The joiner, having abandoned the job, cannot claim the lump sum or a proportion of it.

n.1: The client's eventual benefit from another joiner's work does not entitle the defaulting joiner to payment.
n.2: Doing the greater part does not entitle him to the full price where the obligation is entire and unfinished.
n.3: He is not entitled to the price less a deduction, because he did not substantially perform.
n.4: An entire obligation must be completed before the price is earned; part performance earns nothing.

1.q: A claimant is injured as a result of the combined negligence of two different defendants, each of whom contributed to causing the same damage. The claimant sues and recovers the whole of their damages from the first defendant, who was the easier to pursue. The first defendant, having paid the full amount, considers that the second defendant should bear a fair share of the liability, since both were responsible for the harm. The first defendant seeks advice on recovering a contribution from the second defendant. Both defendants had been careless in different ways, and together they brought about the single injury. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The first defendant must recover exactly half from the second defendant in every case.
The first defendant may recover a contribution only if the two defendants had a contract between them on these facts.
The first defendant has no remedy, because a defendant who pays a claim cannot pursue anyone else.
The first defendant can recover nothing, because it has already paid the claimant in full.
The first defendant may recover a contribution from the second, assessed as just and equitable to their responsibility.
1.w: Under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978, a person liable for damage may recover a contribution from any other person also liable for the same damage. The amount is such as the court finds just and equitable having regard to each party's responsibility.

n.0: Contribution is apportioned according to responsibility, not fixed at half.
n.1: A contribution claim under the Act does not require a contract between the defendants.
n.2: A defendant who has paid may pursue others liable for the same damage for a contribution.
n.3: Paying the claimant in full does not prevent a contribution claim against another tortfeasor.

1.q: A young child lawfully visits a park run by a local authority and is injured by an attractive but dangerous feature which drew the child in but which an adult would have recognised and avoided. The authority argues it took the care that would keep an ordinary adult visitor safe, and that this should be enough. The child's parents sue under the occupiers' liability legislation, arguing a higher standard applied because the visitor was a child. The feature was brightly coloured and obviously tempting to a young child exploring the park with little supervision. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An occupier owes children exactly the same standard as adults, with no allowance for their age.
An occupier discharges its duty to children simply by displaying a warning notice that adults could read on these facts.
An occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults, so a greater standard of care may be required.
An occupier owes no duty at all to child visitors, who are the responsibility of their parents alone.
An occupier's duty to children arises only where the child paid to enter the premises.
1.w: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, an occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults. A danger that is not a trap to an adult may be an allurement to a child, so a higher standard of care may be needed to keep child visitors reasonably safe.

n.0: The Act expressly requires allowance for children being less careful than adults.
n.1: A notice an adult could read may not discharge the duty owed to a young child.
n.3: An occupier does owe duties to child visitors under the 1957 Act.
n.4: The duty to child visitors does not depend on payment of an entry fee.

1.q: A defendant is charged with an offence requiring intention or recklessness as to a particular circumstance. The defendant made a genuine mistake of fact, so that they did not have the state of mind the offence requires as to that circumstance. The offence requires a particular mens rea as to the circumstance. The defendant's mistake meant they lacked that mens rea. The offence the defendant faces is one built around a particular state of mind as to a circumstance, and the defendant genuinely got that circumstance wrong, so that on their own understanding of the facts they simply did not have the awareness the offence demands. Which of the following best describes the effect of the mistake of fact?
o: A mistake of fact provides a general defence to all offences automatically.
A mistake of fact is relevant only to sentencing, not to guilt.
A mistake of fact excuses liability only if it was reasonable, whatever the offence requires on these facts.
A mistake of fact is never relevant to criminal liability in any circumstances.
A genuine mistake of fact may mean the defendant lacked the required mens rea, so the offence is not made out.
1.w: Where an offence requires proof of a particular mens rea, a genuine mistake of fact that means the defendant did not have that state of mind can negate the mens rea, so the offence is not made out. For crimes requiring intention or subjective recklessness, the mistake need not be reasonable, though reasonableness may be required for some defences or strict liability offences.

n.0: It is not an automatic general defence to all offences; it operates by negating mens rea.
n.1: A mistake going to mens rea affects guilt, not merely sentence.
n.2: For subjective mens rea offences the mistake need not be reasonable to negate mens rea.
n.3: A mistake of fact can be relevant where it negates the required mens rea.

1.q: A defended money claim proceeds and the court must allocate it to a case management track. The claim is for a sum of around £8,000, is factually straightforward, and does not involve any complex issues or a long trial. The parties want to know which track the claim is likely to be allocated to, and the general features of that track. The court considers allocation to the small claims track under the Civil Procedure Rules. The dispute was a simple unpaid consumer bill with no wider complications at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim will be allocated to the small claims track only if both parties are litigants in person on these facts.
The claim cannot be allocated to any track until the trial has already taken place.
The claim must be allocated to the multi-track, because all money claims go to the multi-track.
The claim is likely to be allocated to the small claims track, which has a limited costs regime and a simplified procedure.
The claim will be allocated to the fast track, because the small claims track no longer exists.
1.w: The small claims track is the normal track for straightforward claims with a value of not more than £10,000 (with lower limits for some claim types). It uses a simplified procedure and a restricted costs regime under which recoverable costs are very limited.

n.0: Allocation to the small claims track does not depend on the parties being unrepresented.
n.1: Allocation happens before trial, as part of case management.
n.2: Low-value straightforward claims go to the small claims track, not automatically the multi-track.
n.4: The small claims track still exists; the fast track is for higher-value claims.

1.q: A solicitor is representing the defendant in a contested civil trial due to be heard next week. Shortly before the defendant is due to give evidence, the client tells the solicitor privately that they intend to lie under oath about a central factual issue in the case, in order to improve their chances of winning, and instructs the solicitor to carry on regardless and to put that false account to the court in cross-examination and submissions. The solicitor is quite certain, from the documents, that the account is untrue. The solicitor considers how they must respond to the client's stated intention to give false evidence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must not put forward evidence they know to be false, and must cease acting if the client insists on giving it.
The solicitor may present the client's account as instructed, because the solicitor must always follow the client's instructions.
The solicitor must immediately inform the judge that the client intends to lie about the central factual issue.
The solicitor may present the account, provided the solicitor privately warns the client that lying is a criminal offence.
The solicitor may continue to act and simply avoid asking the client any question about the disputed issue.
1.w: A solicitor must not knowingly or recklessly mislead the court, and must not adduce evidence they know to be false. If the client insists on giving false evidence, the solicitor cannot participate and must cease to act; they cannot, however, breach privilege by telling the court why.

n.1: The duty to follow instructions does not extend to helping the client deceive the court.
n.2: The solicitor must not disclose the client's privileged confidence to the judge.
n.3: A private warning does not make it proper to put forward evidence known to be false.
n.4: Carrying on while steering around the issue still misleads the court and is not permitted.

1.q: A fee-earner working on a transaction at a firm forms a genuine suspicion that a client may be engaged in money laundering. The fee-earner is unsure of the correct first step to take, and wonders whether they should personally telephone the National Crime Agency straight away, or perhaps put the concern directly to the client, or simply do nothing at all for the time being. The firm, like most firms of its size, has appointed a nominated officer to handle exactly these matters internally. The fee-earner considers what they are actually required to do first. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The fee-earner must make an internal report to the firm's nominated officer, who then decides whether to report to the NCA.
The fee-earner should first put the concern to the client, to give them a chance to explain matters.
The fee-earner should simply record the suspicion on the file and take no further action of any kind.
The fee-earner must personally report the suspicion directly to the National Crime Agency without telling anyone at the firm.
The fee-earner need do nothing at all unless and until the nominated officer specifically asks them about it.
1.w: Within a firm that has a nominated officer (MLRO), an individual who suspects money laundering discharges their obligation by making an internal report to that nominated officer, who then considers whether an external suspicious activity report to the NCA is required. The fee-earner must not tip off the client.

n.1: Putting the concern to the client risks the offence of tipping off.
n.2: Merely noting the suspicion on the file, without an internal report, does not discharge the duty.
n.3: In a firm with a nominated officer, the internal report goes to that officer, not directly and secretly to the NCA.
n.4: The fee-earner has a positive duty to report the suspicion internally, not to wait to be asked.

1.q: A local planning authority discovers that a building operation was carried out some years ago without the required planning permission. The authority is considering whether it may still take enforcement action against the breach. A period of time has elapsed since the unauthorised building operation was substantially completed. The authority is considering enforcement. During the buyer's investigations it comes to light that an extension was built some years back without the planning permission it needed, and the parties are now weighing whether, given the time that has passed, the local authority could still take steps against the unauthorised work. Which of the following best describes the position on time limits for enforcement?
o: Enforcement may be time-barred once the relevant statutory period since the breach has expired.
There is no time limit, so enforcement can always be taken however long ago the breach occurred.
Enforcement depends solely on whether the neighbours object.
Enforcement is possible only within 6 months of the breach in every case.
Enforcement is barred as soon as the building is occupied.
1.w: Planning enforcement is subject to time limits: after the relevant statutory period has elapsed since the breach (historically four years for building operations and certain changes of use to a single dwelling, and ten years for other breaches, though these limits have been reformed), the development generally becomes immune from enforcement and lawful. A buyer's solicitor should check for immunity or a certificate of lawfulness.

n.1: There is a time limit; enforcement is not always available regardless of when the breach occurred.
n.2: Time limits, not merely neighbour objections, determine whether enforcement can be taken.
n.3: The limitation period is measured in years, not a flat six months.
n.4: Enforcement is not barred simply by occupation; the statutory period governs.

1.q: A person, at another's request, carries out substantial services for that other in circumstances where both understood the services were to be paid for, but no price was ever fixed or agreed between them. When the work is complete, the parties fall out over payment, and it emerges that there was never a concluded agreement as to the amount to be paid. The person who did the work wishes to be paid a fair sum for the work actually done and requested. Which of the following best describes the basis of the claim?
o: The person may claim nothing, because no price for the services was ever agreed between the parties.
The person may claim only if the services were provided under a fully concluded written contract.
The person may claim only the amount they personally hoped to be paid for the work.
The person may claim a quantum meruit — a reasonable sum for the value of the services requested and provided.
The person may claim the highest price that any provider could conceivably have charged.
1.w: Where services are requested and provided on the understanding that they will be paid for, but no price is agreed, the provider may recover a quantum meruit — a reasonable sum for the value of the work done — under the law of restitution or an implied term as to reasonable remuneration.

n.0: The absence of an agreed price does not defeat the claim; a reasonable sum is recoverable.
n.1: A quantum meruit can arise without a concluded written contract fixing the price.
n.2: The measure is an objectively reasonable sum, not the claimant's private hopes.
n.4: The claim is for a reasonable sum, not the highest conceivable charge.

1.q: A person is buying an existing leasehold flat from the current leaseholder, taking over the remainder of an existing long lease rather than being granted a brand new lease by the landlord. The buyer's solicitor must appreciate the nature of the transaction and the additional matters that arise because the interest is leasehold. The buyer asks how taking over an existing lease differs from being granted a new one. The solicitor considers the distinction between the assignment and the grant of a lease. The flat was held on a long lease with many years still left to run at a modest ground rent. Which of the following best describes it?
o: There is no legal difference between taking over an existing lease and being granted a new one on these facts as a general rule.
This is a freehold purchase, because the buyer is paying a capital sum for the flat.
This cannot be done at all, because existing leases can never be transferred to a new person.
This is an assignment of the existing lease, transferring the current leaseholder's interest, rather than the grant of a new lease.
This is the grant of a new lease directly by the landlord to the buyer.
1.w: Where a buyer takes over the unexpired term of an existing lease from the current tenant, this is an assignment of the lease (the assignor transfers their leasehold interest to the assignee). It is distinct from the grant of a new lease, where the landlord creates a fresh leasehold estate in favour of the tenant.

n.0: Assignment and grant differ significantly in their legal mechanics and consequences.
n.1: A leasehold flat is a leasehold, not a freehold, interest.
n.2: Existing leases can be assigned to a new person, subject to the lease terms.
n.4: The landlord is not granting a new lease; the existing lease is being assigned.

1.q: During pre-contract discussions to sell a car, the seller tells the buyer that the car has 'done only 20,000 miles', which the seller genuinely believes. The parties later sign a detailed written contract for the sale which contains a clause stating that it constitutes the entire agreement between them and that no statement made during negotiations forms part of the contract. The mileage statement turns out to be wrong. The buyer wishes to sue for breach of contract, treating the mileage statement as a contractual term. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The mileage statement is a term, because the entire agreement clause is automatically void.
The mileage statement is unlikely to be a term, given the entire agreement clause.
The mileage statement is automatically a term, because it was important to the buyer's decision.
The mileage statement is a term, because any statement made before a contract becomes part of it.
The mileage statement is a term, because the seller genuinely believed that it was true.
1.w: An 'entire agreement' clause is designed to confine the contract to its written terms and to exclude prior statements from forming part of the contract. Its presence makes it unlikely that the pre-contract mileage statement is a contractual term, though it may still found a misrepresentation claim.

n.0: Entire agreement clauses are generally effective and are not automatically void.
n.2: Importance to the buyer does not make a statement a term where an entire agreement clause excludes prior statements.
n.3: Not every pre-contract statement becomes a term; many are representations only.
n.4: The seller's honest belief goes to whether any misrepresentation was innocent, not to whether the statement is a term.

1.q: A borrower has defaulted on a legal mortgage over registered land, and the lender wishes to sell the property to recover the debt. The lender is considering how it may sell and what duty it owes in doing so. The lender's power of sale has arisen and become exercisable following the borrower's default. The lender proposes to sell the mortgaged property. The borrower has fallen badly into arrears, the lender wants to realise its security by selling the house, and it is weighing up how it may go about the sale and, in particular, what obligation if any it owes to the borrower when it comes to the price it achieves. Which of the following best describes the lender's position on sale?
o: The lender may keep any surplus proceeds of sale over the debt for itself.
The lender must always sell the property at a public auction and never by private treaty on these facts as a general rule.
The lender may sell under its power of sale but must take reasonable care to obtain a proper price for the property.
The lender cannot sell without first obtaining a court order in every case.
The lender may sell at any price it chooses, owing no duty at all to the borrower.
1.w: A mortgagee exercising its power of sale must take reasonable care to obtain the true market value (a proper price) for the property. It need not necessarily obtain a court order to sell (though possession may require one), it cannot sell at an undervalue with impunity, and any surplus after discharging the debt and prior charges is held for the borrower or subsequent chargees.

n.0: Surplus proceeds are held for the borrower/subsequent chargees, not kept by the lender.
n.1: The lender may sell by private treaty; auction is not compulsory.
n.3: A court order is not invariably required to exercise the power of sale.
n.4: The lender owes a duty to obtain a proper price; it cannot sell at any price with impunity.

1.q: A defendant's solicitor is advising on where a case will be tried, which depends on how the offence is classified. Offences in England and Wales fall into different categories that determine the court of trial. The offence in question is one that can be tried in either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court depending on various factors. The solicitor considers the classification of criminal offences. The offence carried a range of possible sentences and could be dealt with at different levels. Which of the following best describes the classification of an offence that may be tried in either court?
o: It is an offence that can only ever be dealt with by a fixed penalty notice on these facts.
It is an indictable-only offence, triable only in the Crown Court.
It is an either-way offence, triable either in the magistrates' court or in the Crown Court.
It is an offence that is not triable in any court in England and Wales.
It is a summary-only offence, triable only in the magistrates' court.
1.w: Criminal offences are classified as summary-only (tried in the magistrates' court), indictable-only (tried in the Crown Court), or either-way. An either-way offence may be tried in either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court, depending on the plea-before-venue and allocation decisions.

n.0: An either-way offence is not dealt with merely by a fixed penalty.
n.1: An indictable-only offence is tried only in the Crown Court.
n.3: The offence is triable; the question is which court.
n.4: A summary-only offence is tried only in the magistrates' court.

1.q: A firm of solicitors that is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority wishes to give its clients a certain amount of advice on investments as part of the wider legal services it provides, for example when winding up deceased persons' estates or advising on the division of assets in matrimonial settlements. A partner simply assumes that, because the firm is a firm of solicitors, it must be free to carry on any investment work it likes as an ordinary part of its practice. The firm seeks advice on the basis, if any, on which such activities may lawfully be carried on. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may carry on any investment activities it wishes, simply because it is a firm of solicitors.
The firm is completely barred from any investment activity unless it becomes authorised by the FCA.
The firm may carry on investment activities freely, provided it does not charge a separate fee for them.
The firm may do such work only if it is incidental to its legal services and SRA-compliant.
The firm may carry on investment activities, provided each client signs a waiver of FCA protection.
1.w: A firm without FCA authorisation may only carry on 'exempt regulated activities' under Part 20 FSMA where they arise out of, or are complementary to, the provision of legal services, and it complies with the SRA's financial services rules as a profession supervised by a designated professional body.

n.0: Being a firm of solicitors does not permit unrestricted investment work.
n.1: The firm is not wholly barred; the exempt regime allows incidental activities.
n.2: Not charging separately does not remove the need to fall within the exempt regime.
n.4: A client waiver cannot substitute for the statutory and regulatory basis required.

1.q: A defendant becomes voluntarily intoxicated by alcohol and, while intoxicated, commits an offence of basic intent (one that can be committed recklessly), such as a basic assault. The defendant says they were too drunk to form any mens rea. The offence charged is a basic intent offence. The intoxication was voluntary. Having chosen to drink heavily, the defendant went on while intoxicated to commit an everyday offence of the kind that can be committed recklessly, and now protests that the drink had left them incapable of forming any guilty state of mind at the moment they acted. Which of the following best describes the effect of the voluntary intoxication?
o: Voluntary intoxication negates the mens rea of a basic intent offence and excuses the defendant.
Voluntary intoxication is a complete defence to any offence committed while drunk.
Voluntary intoxication is relevant only to offences of specific intent, never affecting the analysis of basic intent offences at all.
Voluntary intoxication reduces every offence to a lesser one automatically.
Voluntary intoxication is not a defence to a basic intent offence, as becoming intoxicated is itself reckless.
1.w: Under the rule in Majewski, voluntary intoxication is not a defence to a crime of basic intent: getting voluntarily intoxicated is itself regarded as a reckless course of conduct, supplying the recklessness needed. It may, however, negate the specific intent required for a specific intent offence (often leaving a basic intent fallback offence).

n.0: It does not excuse a basic intent offence; the recklessness in getting drunk suffices.
n.1: Voluntary intoxication is not a complete defence to any offence.
n.2: It is precisely for basic intent offences that voluntary intoxication provides no defence, so it is not irrelevant to their analysis.
n.3: It does not automatically reduce every offence to a lesser one.

1.q: A firm takes on a new corporate client, a private limited company, on a substantial commercial property purchase, and must complete customer due diligence before it starts work. The fee-earner obtains and verifies the identity of the single director who is giving the firm its instructions, and treats that as sufficient to satisfy the firm's obligations. In fact the company is owned and ultimately controlled, behind the scenes, by several other individuals whose identities the fee-earner has not checked or even asked about. The firm's money laundering reporting officer reviews the file. Which of the following best describes what due diligence requires here?
o: Beneficial owners need only be identified if the company is based in another country entirely.
Due diligence on a company client requires identifying and verifying its beneficial owners.
No due diligence is needed on a company at all, because only individual clients present a money laundering risk.
Verifying the director who gives instructions is always enough, because a company acts only through its directors.
It is enough to note the company's registered number, without identifying any of the individuals behind it.
1.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require, for a corporate client, that the firm identifies and takes reasonable measures to verify the company's beneficial owners — broadly, individuals who ultimately own or control it — as well as the person giving instructions.

n.0: The duty to identify beneficial owners is not confined to overseas companies.
n.2: Companies are within the money laundering regime; corporate clients are not exempt.
n.3: Verifying the instructing director does not satisfy the requirement to identify the beneficial owners.
n.4: Noting the registered number does not identify the individuals who own or control the company.

1.q: A trustee, in breach of trust, makes an unauthorised investment which loses a substantial part of the trust fund's value, causing loss to the beneficiaries. The beneficiaries wish to hold the trustee personally responsible for the loss the breach has caused to the trust. The trustee accepts the investment was unauthorised but argues that they should not have to make good the loss out of their own pocket. The beneficiaries seek advice on the remedy available against the trustee. The unauthorised investment had been a large part of the fund and its collapse left the beneficiaries much worse off. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The trustee's only obligation is to apologise and to act more carefully in the future.
The trustee is liable only if the beneficiaries can prove the trustee acted dishonestly.
The trustee has no personal liability, because the loss was caused by a fall in the market.
The trustee is personally liable to compensate the trust for the loss caused by the breach.
The trustee is liable only up to the amount of any fee they received for acting.
1.w: A trustee who commits a breach of trust is personally liable to restore the trust fund to the position it would have been in but for the breach, by way of equitable compensation for the loss caused. Liability does not depend on dishonesty.

n.0: An apology is no substitute for restoring the loss to the trust.
n.1: Liability for breach of trust does not require proof of dishonesty.
n.2: The trustee cannot escape liability by attributing the loss to the market where the investment was an unauthorised breach.
n.4: Liability is measured by the loss caused, not capped at any fee received.

1.q: In a genuine national emergency threatening the life of the nation, a state wishes to take measures that would otherwise breach certain Convention rights, and considers whether it may formally suspend some of its obligations. The measures respond to a public emergency threatening the life of the nation. Only certain rights are involved. Facing a grave crisis said to threaten the life of the nation, the state wants to take emergency measures that would otherwise cut across some Convention guarantees, and it is considering whether it can formally suspend a measure of its obligations to do so, and within what limits. Which of the following best describes the position on derogation under the European Convention on Human Rights?
o: Derogation is permitted only with the consent of every other Convention state.
Derogation automatically repeals the Human Rights Act 1998 during the emergency.
A state may derogate from all Convention rights without limit during any emergency on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A state may never derogate from any Convention right in any circumstances.
A state may derogate from certain Convention rights in a public emergency, to the extent strictly required, but not from non-derogable rights.
1.w: Article 15 of the Convention permits a state, in time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation, to derogate from certain Convention obligations to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation. However, some rights are non-derogable (for example, the prohibition of torture), and derogations are subject to conditions and scrutiny.

n.0: Derogation does not require the consent of every other state.
n.1: Derogation does not repeal the Human Rights Act; it concerns specific obligations.
n.2: Derogation is limited to what is strictly required and excludes non-derogable rights, not unlimited.
n.3: Derogation is possible in a qualifying emergency, so 'never' is wrong.

1.q: A company circulates to the public a notice promising a stated sum to anyone who uses its product as directed and still suffers a particular illness, stating that it has deposited money in a bank to show its sincerity. A member of the public buys and uses the product exactly as directed but still falls ill, and claims the sum. The company argues the notice was a mere advertising puff. The notice specified conduct that would earn the sum. The notice was widely circulated, framed in definite terms about exactly what a user had to do to qualify, and backed by the statement about money set aside to meet claims, and the claimant followed the directions to the letter and still contracted the illness the product was said to prevent. Which of the following best describes the notice's legal character?
o: It was a statement of opinion that could never give rise to contractual liability.
It was void for uncertainty because it was addressed to the public at large.
It was a bilateral offer requiring the claimant to communicate acceptance in advance.
It was a unilateral offer that could be accepted by performing the specified conditions.
It was only an invitation to treat, incapable of forming a contract when acted upon.
1.w: An advertisement promising payment to anyone who performs specified conditions can be a unilateral offer, distinguishable from a mere invitation to treat, especially where (as here) the promisor shows an intention to be bound (the deposited money). It is accepted by performing the conditions, and prior communication of acceptance is not required.

n.0: The evidence of a deposited fund shows intention to be bound, so it is not a mere opinion or puff.
n.1: An offer to the world at large is not void for uncertainty; it can be accepted by anyone who performs.
n.2: A unilateral offer of this kind does not require acceptance to be communicated in advance of performance.
n.4: Unlike a shop display, this promise of payment on conditions is an offer, not a mere invitation to treat.

1.q: During a reconciliation a firm discovers £100 in its general client account that it cannot attribute to any client or matter, having been paid in some time ago with no identifying reference. The bookkeeper wants to deal with it correctly and asks whether the firm can simply transfer it to the office account to tidy the ledgers. The firm has records of its receipts. The payment carried no client name, matter reference or narrative when it reached the bank, none of the firm's fee-earners recognises it, and it has been sitting unallocated in the general client account, so the cashier wants to know how to treat it while its true owner is investigated. Which of the following best describes the correct approach to the unidentified funds under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm may keep the money in a suspense office ledger and treat it as profit on these facts as a general rule.
The firm may ignore the money because it is a small sum below any threshold.
The firm must pay the money to the SRA as soon as it is discovered.
The firm may transfer the money to the office account immediately as unclaimed.
The firm must take reasonable steps to identify the owner and, meanwhile, keep the money in the client account.
1.w: Unidentified money received into the client account is treated as client money until its owner is established. The firm must take reasonable steps to identify the correct recipient and, in the meantime, keep the money safe in the client account. It cannot simply be swept into the office account or treated as the firm's profit.

n.0: The money is not the firm's profit and must be kept as client money.
n.1: There is no threshold that allows unidentified client money simply to be ignored.
n.2: The money is kept in the client account while its owner is sought, not paid to the SRA on discovery.
n.3: Unidentified funds cannot be transferred to the office account as unclaimed.

1.q: A devolved legislature passes an Act dealing with a matter, and a question arises whether the Act is within the legislature's legislative competence, given that certain matters are reserved to the Westminster Parliament. The Act may stray into a reserved matter outside the devolved legislature's competence. Its validity is challenged. The devolved legislature has passed an Act that arguably strays into territory reserved to Westminster and so beyond its own powers, and a party affected by it is asking the courts to rule on whether the measure is within competence or must be struck down. Which of the following best describes how such a challenge is determined?
o: Devolved legislation always overrides Acts of the Westminster Parliament.
A devolved Act is valid provided the devolved legislature intended it to be.
Only the Westminster Parliament, not the courts, may rule on devolved competence on these facts as a general rule.
Devolved legislation is immune from challenge in the courts in all circumstances.
The courts may determine whether the devolved Act is within legislative competence and, if it is outside it, hold it invalid.
1.w: Devolved legislatures have limited legislative competence: they cannot legislate on reserved matters or outside their defined powers. Unlike Acts of the sovereign Westminster Parliament, a devolved Act can be challenged in the courts, which may determine whether it is within competence and, if not, hold the provision to be not law (invalid).

n.0: Devolved legislation does not override Westminster Acts; Westminster remains sovereign.
n.1: The legislature's intention does not cure an Act that is outside its competence.
n.2: The courts, not only Parliament, rule on devolved competence.
n.3: Devolved legislation is not immune from challenge; competence can be tested in the courts.

1.q: A firm acting for the seller in a conveyancing transaction receives a deposit of £4,000 from the buyer's solicitor, expressed to be held by the firm as stakeholder pending completion. Before completion, the seller asks the firm to release the deposit to the seller straight away. The firm holds the money as stakeholder. The transaction has exchanged but not yet completed, the seller is keen to get its hands on the money early, and the firm must weigh the seller's request against the terms on which the deposit was handed over and the protections those terms are designed to give the other side. Which of the following best describes how the firm may deal with the deposit under the SRA Accounts Rules and its stakeholder role?
o: The firm may release the deposit to the seller on the seller's instruction alone on these facts as a general rule.
The firm may keep the deposit as security for its own costs on the sale.
The firm may release the deposit to the buyer at any time before completion.
As stakeholder the firm must hold the deposit and not release it before completion without both parties' authority.
The firm may pay the deposit into the office account as it acts for the seller.
1.w: A deposit held as stakeholder is client money held for both parties: the firm holds it in the client account and may only release it in accordance with the stakeholder terms, generally on completion. It cannot pay it out on the seller's instruction alone, treat it as office money, or apply it to its own costs.

n.0: As stakeholder the firm cannot release it on the seller's instruction alone.
n.1: The firm cannot apply a stakeholder deposit to its own costs.
n.2: It cannot simply be released to the buyer before completion either; the stakeholder terms govern.
n.4: A stakeholder deposit is client money and must not go into the office account.

1.q: A borrower took out a mortgage over her home to fund her business. A term of the mortgage provides that the borrower may not redeem the mortgage — that is, repay the loan and have the charge removed from the title — for a period of 40 years, effectively tying her to this particular lender, on onerous terms, for the entire likely life of the loan. The borrower's financial circumstances have since improved and she wishes to repay the loan early and remortgage elsewhere on much better terms, but the lender insists that she is bound by the 40-year restriction on redemption. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The borrower may redeem early only by paying the lender all the interest that would have accrued over 40 years.
The postponement is fully binding, because parties are free to agree any redemption date they choose.
The mortgage is entirely void, so the borrower owes nothing and keeps the property free of charge.
The postponement is likely void as a clog on the equity of redemption, so the borrower may redeem.
The borrower may redeem only if the lender is shown to have acted dishonestly in taking the mortgage.
1.w: Equity protects the borrower's right to redeem. A term that postpones or fetters redemption so as to render the equity of redemption illusory or is otherwise oppressive is void as a clog on the equity, allowing the borrower to redeem.

n.0: Redemption on such an onerous fetter does not require paying all future interest.
n.1: A postponement that makes the right to redeem illusory is not simply binding as agreed.
n.2: Only the offending term is struck down; the mortgage debt itself remains.
n.4: Dishonesty is not required; the clog doctrine invalidates oppressive fetters on redemption.

1.q: By a deed made some years ago, the owner of Plot A was granted a legal easement, a right of way, to use a driveway over the neighbouring Plot B in order to reach the road. Plot A has since been sold and transferred to a new owner, who now wishes to use the driveway to get to and from their property in the ordinary way. The owner of Plot B refuses to allow this, arguing that the right of way was personal to the original owner of Plot A in whose favour it was granted, and did not pass to the new owner when Plot A was sold. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The new owner may use the driveway only if a fresh deed of grant is executed.
The new owner may use the driveway only with the express consent of Plot B's owner.
The easement benefits Plot A, so it passes to the new owner and can be used by them.
The easement lapsed when Plot A changed hands and must be re-created to continue.
The easement was personal to the original grantee and did not pass on the sale of Plot A.
1.w: An easement is a property right attached to the dominant land, not a personal right. The benefit runs with Plot A automatically on a transfer, so the new owner of Plot A takes the benefit of the easement over Plot B.

n.0: No fresh deed is needed; the benefit passes with the dominant land.
n.1: The new owner does not need Plot B owner's consent to exercise an existing easement.
n.3: The easement does not lapse on a sale of the dominant land.
n.4: A validly granted easement is proprietary, not personal to the first grantee.

1.q: A firm's bank levies charges relating to the operation of the general client account, and the firm also incurs charges on its office account. The cashier is unsure how the bank charges on the client account should be met and recorded, and asks whether they can be deducted from the client money in the account. No client has agreed to bear the firm's bank charges. The bank has debited the charges directly, and the cashier is deciding which side of the firm's books should bear them and from which pot of money they should ultimately be met, conscious that anything taken from client money would leave the clients' funds short. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the client account bank charges?
o: The bank charges may be left as a debit on the client cash account until year end.
The firm's bank charges are the firm's own expense and must be met from office money.
The bank charges must be paid to the SRA rather than the bank.
The bank charges may be deducted proportionately from the client money held.
The bank charges may be deducted from the ledger of the client last paid in.
1.w: Bank charges on the operation of the firm's accounts are the firm's own running costs and are office money expenses. They must be met from office money and must not be deducted from client money, which would reduce the funds held for clients and create a shortfall on the client account.

n.0: Leaving a debit on the client cash account would mean client money bears the firm's costs.
n.2: Bank charges are paid to the bank, not the SRA; the point is that they are office money.
n.3: Client money must not be reduced to pay the firm's bank charges.
n.4: The charges cannot be taken from an individual client's ledger.

1.q: A defendant commits an offence while voluntarily intoxicated through drink or drugs, and argues that, because of the intoxication, they did not form the mens rea for the offence. The offence is one of specific intent, and in the alternative the prosecution can prove a lesser offence of basic intent on the same facts. The court considers the effect of voluntary intoxication on liability. The defendant had drunk heavily before the incident and claimed to remember almost nothing of it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Voluntary intoxication automatically reduces every offence to a lesser included offence.
Voluntary intoxication may negate the mens rea of a specific intent offence, but is no defence to a basic intent offence.
Voluntary intoxication is a complete defence to any offence, whether of specific or basic intent.
Voluntary intoxication is never relevant to criminal liability in any circumstances at all.
Voluntary intoxication is a defence only to offences of basic intent, and never to specific intent on these facts.
1.w: Voluntary intoxication may be relevant to whether the defendant formed the mens rea of a specific intent offence (and so may reduce, e.g., murder to manslaughter). It is not a defence to offences of basic intent, because becoming voluntarily intoxicated is itself regarded as reckless (DPP v Majewski).

n.0: It does not automatically reduce every offence; the specific/basic distinction governs.
n.2: It is not a complete defence to all offences; basic intent offences remain.
n.3: It can be relevant to specific intent offences, so it is not always irrelevant.
n.4: The position is reversed: it may assist for specific intent, not for basic intent.

1.q: A restrictive covenant imposed in 1965 restricts a plot of land to use for a single dwelling only. The covenant has never been formally discharged or modified, and it remains registered against the burdened land. The current owner of the plot now wishes to build a second house on it, and a neighbouring owner who has the benefit of the covenant objects to the proposal. The plot owner argues that the covenant is by now so old, dating back some sixty years, that it can no longer be relied upon or enforced against them. The neighbour seeks advice on the position. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The covenant is automatically discharged once the plot owner decides to build.
The covenant is unenforceable, because covenants made before 1970 are no longer valid.
The covenant remains enforceable, because a restrictive covenant is not lost by mere age.
The covenant is enforceable, but only for damages and never by injunction after so long.
The covenant is unenforceable, because restrictive covenants expire after a fixed number of years.
1.w: A restrictive covenant does not lapse merely through the passage of time. It remains enforceable unless discharged or modified (for example by the Upper Tribunal under s.84 LPA 1925) or defeated by conduct such as acquiescence.

n.0: A covenant is not discharged simply because the burdened owner wishes to breach it.
n.1: Covenants made before 1970 are not automatically invalid.
n.3: Age alone does not confine the claimant to damages instead of an injunction.
n.4: There is no fixed expiry period for restrictive covenants.

1.q: A buyer's solicitor is investigating title to registered land before exchange. The solicitor needs to obtain evidence of the seller's ownership and of the entries affecting the title. The land is registered at the Land Registry. The solicitor is deducing and investigating title. Ahead of exchange the buyer's solicitor needs to satisfy itself that the seller really owns what is being sold and to see every entry that burdens or benefits the title, and since the land is registered it must obtain the right form of official evidence from the Land Registry rather than sifting old deeds. Which of the following best describes how title to registered land is deduced?
o: By carrying out a full-title indemnity insurance policy in place of investigation.
By providing official copies of the register and title plan (and any referred-to documents).
By handing over the original paper title deeds going back 30 years.
By providing an epitome of title with a good root of title at least 15 years old.
By obtaining a statutory declaration of ownership from the seller.
1.w: Title to registered land is deduced by supplying official copies of the register (showing the property, proprietorship and charges registers) and the title plan, together with copies of any documents referred to. This differs from unregistered land, where title is deduced by an epitome of title tracing ownership from a good root of title at least 15 years old.

n.0: Indemnity insurance does not replace deducing title; it addresses specific defects.
n.2: Registered title is deduced from official copies, not by handing over old paper deeds.
n.3: An epitome and good root of title are used for unregistered, not registered, land.
n.4: A statutory declaration is not the ordinary means of deducing registered title.

1.q: A neighbour built a garage that encroaches slightly onto the adjoining landowner's land. The neighbour did so openly, over several weeks, while the landowner stood by and, by both words and conduct, actively encouraged the neighbour to believe that they would be allowed to keep the garage where it was. Relying on that encouragement, the neighbour spent substantial sums of money completing the garage. The landowner has since fallen out with the neighbour, changed position, and now demands that the garage be removed. The neighbour seeks advice on the basis on which they might resist removal and assert a right. Which of the following is that basis?
o: Adverse possession, because building the garage gave them immediate title to the strip.
A resulting trust, because the money spent on building the garage is treated as a contribution to the purchase of the land.
A restrictive covenant, because the landowner impliedly promised not to object.
An easement, because the garage now needs access over the landowner's remaining land.
Proprietary estoppel, because they relied to their detriment on the landowner's encouragement.
1.w: Where an owner encourages or acquiesces in another's detrimental reliance such that it would be unconscionable to deny them a right, proprietary estoppel arises. The court then satisfies the equity, which may allow the encroachment to remain or require compensation.

n.0: Building the garage does not give instant title by adverse possession.
n.1: Spending on the garage does not create a resulting trust of the neighbour's land.
n.2: There is no restrictive covenant; the neighbour's protection, if any, is estoppel.
n.3: The issue is the encroachment itself, not a need for access amounting to an easement.

1.q: A firm holds money for many clients in its general client account. During a compliance review it emerges that the firm has not carried out any reconciliation comparing its client cash account, the client ledger balances and the bank statement for several months. The COFA is asked how often such a reconciliation must be performed under the SRA Accounts Rules. The compliance review has already flagged that client ledger totals have not been checked against the bank statements for some time, and the COFA is anxious to put a proper timetable in place so that any discrepancy between the firm's records and the bank would be caught and investigated quickly. Which of the following best describes the requirement for reconciling the client account?
o: The firm need only reconcile the client account when a discrepancy is suspected.
The firm must reconcile the client account at least every five weeks.
There is no set frequency, provided reconciliations are done from time to time.
The firm must reconcile the client account at least every six months.
The firm must reconcile the client account only once each financial year.
1.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require a firm, at least every five weeks, to obtain statements for all client accounts, reconcile the bank balance with the client cash account and the total of the client ledger balances, and to promptly investigate and resolve any differences. The reconciliation must be signed off by the COFA or a manager.

n.0: Reconciliations must be regular, not only when a discrepancy is suspected.
n.2: There is a specific maximum interval of five weeks.
n.3: Six-monthly reconciliation does not meet the five-week requirement.
n.4: Annual reconciliation is far less frequent than the rules require.

1.q: A firm holds £900 in the client account for a client's disbursement. The fee-earner needs to pay a disbursement of £1,100 on that client's behalf and asks the cashier to pay the full amount from the client account. Only £900 of client money is held for this client. The cashier considers how the payment may properly be made under the SRA Accounts Rules. The disbursement is due to a third party and cannot be delayed without prejudicing the client's matter, yet the client has provided only part of the sum required, so the cashier must find a way to make the full payment without allowing this client's ledger to fall into a debit balance. Which of the following best describes the correct approach?
o: The firm may pay the £1,100 and correct the resulting debit balance within five weeks.
The firm may pay £900 from the client's funds and must fund the £200 excess from office money.
The firm may pay the whole £1,100 from the client account despite holding only £900.
The firm may pay the whole £1,100 by using another client's money in the account.
The firm must refuse to pay the disbursement until the client provides more money.
1.w: A firm must not make a payment from the client account that exceeds the money held for that client, as that would overdraw the client's ledger and use other clients' money. It may pay out the £900 held and must meet the £200 excess from office money (or wait for further client funds), keeping the client ledger from going into debit.

n.0: An overdrawn client ledger is a breach even if corrected within five weeks.
n.2: Paying the whole £1,100 from client funds would overdraw the client's ledger.
n.3: Using another client's money for this payment is prohibited.
n.4: The firm can lawfully pay by funding the excess from office money, so outright refusal is not required.

1.q: A man lives with his partner in a house of which she is the sole registered owner. On several occasions she expressly assured him that 'half of this is yours'. Relying on those repeated assurances, he paid for and personally project-managed a large two-storey extension to the house, and he gave up the tenancy of his own flat in order to move in and commit fully to the relationship. The couple have now separated, and the partner denies that he has acquired any beneficial interest in the house at all. On which basis is he most likely to establish a beneficial share?
o: A resulting trust, measured strictly and only by the amount of his direct financial contribution to the original purchase price.
An easement over the home, arising from the money he spent on the extension.
No interest, because the assurance was not put into a signed written declaration of trust.
A licence, revocable by the legal owner on giving him reasonable notice to leave.
A common intention constructive trust, based on the express assurance and his detrimental reliance.
1.w: An express assurance of a share, coupled with detrimental reliance (paying for the extension and giving up his flat), gives rise to a common intention constructive trust (Grant v Edwards; Stack v Dowden).

n.0: His interest is not confined to purchase-price contributions once a common intention trust is shown.
n.1: Spending on the property founds a trust interest, not an easement.
n.2: A constructive trust does not require a signed written declaration.
n.3: He has a beneficial interest, not a mere revocable licence.

1.q: A defendant occupies a position in which they are expected to safeguard, or not to act against, the financial interests of another person — for example as an employee or agent handling that person's affairs. The defendant dishonestly abuses that position, intending to make a gain for themselves or cause loss to the other, for example by secretly diverting the other's funds. The defendant is charged under the Fraud Act 2006. The court considers fraud by abuse of position. The defendant, an employee trusted with the accounts, quietly diverted company funds to themselves. Which of the following best describes the offence?
o: The offence can only be committed by a company director and by no one else.
The offence requires the defendant to have made an express false representation to the victim on these facts as a general rule.
The offence is committed only where the defendant used force against the victim.
Under s.4, the offence is committed by dishonestly abusing a position of financial trust, intending to gain or cause loss.
The offence requires the victim to have actually suffered a financial loss as a result.
1.w: Under s.4 Fraud Act 2006, fraud by abuse of position is committed where a person occupies a position in which they are expected to safeguard, or not act against, another's financial interests, and dishonestly abuses that position intending to make a gain or cause loss. No false representation or actual loss is required.

n.0: It is not limited to company directors; many relationships qualify.
n.1: This form of fraud does not require an express false representation.
n.2: Force is not an element of the offence.
n.4: Actual loss to the victim is not required.

1.q: A trust holds a fund for a minor beneficiary who is not yet entitled to the capital, and which produces income. The minor needs money for their education and maintenance. The trustees wish to apply some of the trust income for the minor's benefit but are unsure of their power to do so where the beneficiary is under age and not yet entitled to income as of right. The trustees seek advice on their statutory power to apply income for a minor beneficiary. The minor's school fees and living costs were mounting, and there was ample income available in the trust. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustees may never apply any trust money for a minor until the minor comes of age.
The trustees must accumulate all income and can never use it for the minor's benefit.
The trustees may apply income only with the prior approval of the court in every case.
The trustees may apply income only if the minor's parents formally consent in writing.
The trustees have a statutory power of maintenance to apply income for the minor's benefit.
1.w: Under s.31 of the Trustee Act 1925, trustees have a statutory power of maintenance to apply income (as they think fit) for the maintenance, education or benefit of a minor beneficiary, accumulating any surplus income, unless the trust instrument excludes or varies the power.

n.0: Trustees are not barred from applying money for a minor until majority.
n.1: Trustees need not accumulate all income; they may apply it for the minor's benefit.
n.2: Prior court approval is not required to exercise the statutory power of maintenance.
n.3: Parental written consent is not the statutory precondition.

1.q: A defendant acquires property in circumstances where the owner appears to have consented to the transfer, but the defendant then assumes the rights of an owner over that property. A question arises as to whether there can be an 'appropriation' for the purposes of theft where the owner consented to the defendant taking the property. The defence argues that consent by the owner prevents any appropriation. The court considers the meaning of appropriation under the Theft Act 1968. The owner had handed the property over, but the defendant then dealt with it entirely as their own. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There can be an appropriation even where the owner consented, as any assumption of an owner's rights suffices.
There can be no appropriation where the owner consented to the defendant taking the property.
Appropriation requires the owner to have been completely unaware that the property had been taken on these facts.
Appropriation occurs only where the defendant physically removes the property from the premises.
Appropriation requires the defendant to have used force to take the property from the owner.
1.w: Appropriation under s.3 Theft Act 1968 is any assumption of the rights of an owner. It can occur even where the owner has consented to the transfer of the property, so consent does not prevent an appropriation (R v Gomez; R v Hinks).

n.1: Owner consent does not prevent an appropriation.
n.2: The owner's awareness or otherwise is not the test for appropriation.
n.3: Appropriation does not require physical removal of the property.
n.4: Appropriation does not require force; that is robbery.

1.q: After the end of the implementation period, a court is dealing with a body of EU-derived law that was preserved in domestic law, and must decide how to treat pre-exit case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union when interpreting it. The rules concern assimilated (formerly retained) EU law. The court is considering the status of retained EU case law. The dispute turns on a slice of EU-derived law carried over into domestic law after the implementation period ended, and the judge has to work out how much weight to give to rulings the Court of Justice handed down before exit when construing that preserved body of law today. Which of the following best describes the position of the higher courts?
o: Retained EU case law has been entirely abolished and may never be referred to.
All UK courts remain absolutely bound by CJEU case law exactly as before Brexit.
Only the Court of Justice of the European Union may interpret retained EU law.
UK courts must refer all questions of retained EU law to the CJEU for a ruling.
Certain higher courts may depart from retained EU case law where it appears right to do so.
1.w: Following the UK's departure from the EU, retained (now assimilated) EU case law continues to be relevant to interpreting retained EU law, but certain higher courts (such as the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal) are empowered to depart from it, applying a test similar to that for departing from their own precedent, rather than being bound by it as before.

n.0: Retained EU case law is not abolished; it remains relevant to interpretation.
n.1: UK courts are not absolutely bound by CJEU case law as before; higher courts may depart.
n.2: UK courts, not only the CJEU, interpret retained/assimilated EU law after Brexit.
n.3: UK courts no longer make references to the CJEU for such rulings.

1.q: A partner in a trading partnership, without the actual authority of the other partners, orders goods of a kind the firm usually buys from a supplier who deals with the firm and is unaware of any restriction on that partner's authority. The other partners refuse to pay, saying the partner had no authority. The transaction was in the ordinary course of the firm's business and the supplier did not know of any limit on authority. The partner placed a routine order of the sort the firm regularly makes, the supplier had dealt with the firm before and had no inkling of any private arrangement between the partners limiting who could order what, and only after delivery did the remaining partners try to disown the purchase. Which of the following best describes whether the firm is bound?
o: The firm is bound only if the supplier had made specific enquiries about authority.
The firm is bound because the partner had apparent authority to bind it in the firm's usual business.
The firm is bound only if the other partners later ratify the order in writing.
The firm is not bound because a partner never has authority without the others' express consent.
The firm is not bound because internal restrictions always defeat a third party's claim.
1.w: Under the Partnership Act 1890, the acts of a partner carrying on in the usual way the business of the kind carried on by the firm bind the firm and the other partners, unless the partner had no authority and the third party knew this or did not believe them to be a partner. Here the transaction was usual business and the supplier had no notice of any restriction, so the firm is bound.

n.0: A third party dealing in the usual course need not make specific enquiries about authority.
n.2: The firm is already bound by apparent authority; ratification is not required.
n.3: A partner has apparent authority in the firm's usual business without needing express consent each time.
n.4: Internal restrictions do not defeat a third party without notice of them.

1.q: A claimant brings a substantial contract claim in the High Court. After trial, judgment is given against the claimant, who believes the judge made an error of law and wishes to challenge the decision. The claim was heard at first instance in the High Court. The claimant's solicitor considers to which court a first appeal against the High Court's decision would ordinarily lie. The claim was worth several hundred thousand pounds and was tried by a High Court judge in the King's Bench Division, and the claimant, having lost, is now taking advice on where and how a challenge to the judgment on a point of law would have to be brought and whether permission would be needed. Which of the following best identifies the appropriate appeal court?
o: The County Court, as the court with general civil jurisdiction.
The Crown Court, exercising its civil appellate jurisdiction.
The Court of Appeal (Civil Division).
A different judge of the High Court sitting alone.
The Supreme Court, as the next court above the High Court.
1.w: An appeal from a decision of the High Court at first instance ordinarily lies to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division), usually with permission. The Supreme Court hears appeals from the Court of Appeal (and occasionally by the leapfrog procedure), not routine first appeals from the High Court.

n.0: The County Court is a lower civil court and does not hear appeals from the High Court.
n.1: The Crown Court has no civil appellate jurisdiction over the High Court.
n.3: An appeal is not reheard by another High Court judge at the same level.
n.4: The Supreme Court is not the ordinary first appeal court from the High Court.

1.q: A buyer of a property intends to carry out significant works, including building an extension and changing the use of part of the property. The buyer's solicitor advises that certain permissions may be needed before the works can lawfully go ahead, to avoid enforcement action. The buyer asks what permission is generally required for development of land. The solicitor considers the requirement for planning permission. The proposed extension was large and the change of use was likely to attract the council's attention. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Planning permission is needed only for commercial and never for residential property on these facts as a general rule.
No permission is ever required to build on or change the use of one's own land.
Planning permission is granted automatically once the buyer completes the purchase.
Planning permission is generally required for development, which includes building works and material changes of use.
Planning permission is required only where the property is a listed building.
1.w: Under planning legislation, planning permission is generally required to carry out 'development', which includes building, engineering and other operations, and material changes in the use of land or buildings (subject to permitted development rights and exceptions). Carrying out development without permission may lead to enforcement action.

n.0: Planning control applies to residential as well as commercial development.
n.1: Development generally needs permission; owners cannot always build or change use freely.
n.2: Permission is not granted automatically on completion of a purchase.
n.4: Planning control is not limited to listed buildings (which have additional controls).

1.q: A company stores a large quantity of a hazardous chemical in tanks on its industrial site as part of an unusual and high-risk operation, an activity not regarded as an ordinary use of land in the area. The chemical unexpectedly escapes from the site and causes damage to neighbouring land of a kind that was a foreseeable consequence of such an escape. The neighbour sues, seeking to rely on strict liability rather than having to prove negligence. The company argues that it took all reasonable care and so should not be liable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The company is not liable, because strict liability has no place in the modern law of tort.
The company is liable for the escape only if the damage caused was entirely unforeseeable.
The company is liable only if it intended the chemical to escape from its site.
The company is liable only if the neighbour can prove that the company was actually negligent on these facts.
The company may be strictly liable under Rylands v Fletcher for the escape from its non-natural use of land.
1.w: Under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher, a person who, for their own purposes, brings and keeps on their land something likely to do mischief if it escapes, in a non-natural use of the land, is strictly liable for foreseeable damage caused by its escape, without the need to prove negligence (Cambridge Water requires foreseeability of the type of damage).

n.0: Rylands v Fletcher strict liability remains part of English law.
n.1: Liability requires that the type of damage was foreseeable, not that it was unforeseeable.
n.2: Intention to cause the escape is not required for liability.
n.3: The rule imposes strict liability, so proof of negligence is not required.

1.q: A claimant seeks an interim injunction to restrain the defendant from doing something until trial, arguing that damages would not adequately compensate the harm. The court must decide whether to grant the interim injunction before the merits have been fully determined. The court considers the principles governing the grant of an interim (interlocutory) injunction. The claimant wanted to stop the defendant acting until the dispute could be tried in full. Which of the following best describes the approach?
o: The court can never grant any injunction before the trial of the action.
The court asks whether there is a serious issue to be tried, whether damages are an adequate remedy, and where the balance of convenience lies.
The court grants an interim injunction only where the claimant has already won at trial.
The court grants an interim injunction automatically whenever a claimant asks for one.
The court decides the full merits of the claim at the interim stage before granting relief on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
1.w: Under the guidelines in American Cyanamid v Ethicon, in deciding whether to grant an interim injunction the court asks whether there is a serious question to be tried, whether damages would be an adequate remedy for either side, and where the balance of convenience lies, together with the usual cross-undertaking in damages.

n.0: Interim injunctions can be granted before trial; that is their purpose.
n.2: An interim injunction is by definition granted before, not after, trial.
n.3: Interim injunctions are not granted automatically on request.
n.4: The court does not decide the full merits at the interim stage.

1.q: A claimant develops an industrial disease after being exposed to a harmful substance by several different employers over the years, each of whom was in breach of duty. Because of the nature of the disease, it is scientifically impossible to say which particular exposure actually triggered it, so the claimant cannot satisfy the ordinary 'but for' test against any single defendant. The claimant argues they should not be left without a remedy simply because of this scientific uncertainty. The court considers how to approach causation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim fails entirely, because the claimant cannot prove which exposure caused the disease.
Only the last employer to expose the claimant can be held liable for the disease.
Only the first employer to expose the claimant can ever be held liable for the disease.
The claim succeeds only if the claimant can identify the exact exposure that caused the disease.
Each employer that materially increased the risk of the disease may be held liable.
1.w: Where scientific uncertainty makes the 'but for' test impossible to satisfy in certain cases (such as mesothelioma from asbestos), a defendant who materially increased the risk of the claimant's harm may be held liable (McGhee; Fairchild). The claimant is not left remediless because of the impossibility of pinpointing the exposure.

n.0: The claim does not automatically fail; the material-increase-in-risk approach may apply.
n.1: Liability is not confined to the last exposing employer.
n.2: Liability is not confined to the first exposing employer.
n.3: The claimant need not identify the exact causative exposure in these special cases.

1.q: Shortly before going into insolvent liquidation, a company paid one particular unsecured creditor in full, putting that creditor in a better position than it would have been in the liquidation, and did so influenced by a desire to prefer that creditor. The creditor was a connected person. The payment was made within the relevant period and the company wished to improve that creditor's position. The liquidator seeks to challenge the payment. In the run-up to insolvency the company singled out one creditor, connected to it, and paid that creditor off in full while others went unpaid, apparently wanting to put that creditor ahead of the rest, and the liquidator is examining whether the payment can now be reversed. Which of the following best describes the basis of challenge?
o: The liquidator cannot challenge payments made to genuine creditors in any circumstances.
The liquidator may challenge it as a preference, the relevant period being two years for a connected person.
The liquidator may challenge it as a preference, but only if made within one month of insolvency.
The liquidator may challenge it only as a transaction at an undervalue.
The liquidator may challenge it only if the creditor knew the company was insolvent.
1.w: Under s.239 of the Insolvency Act 1986, a preference arises where a company, influenced by a desire to prefer, puts a creditor in a better position on insolvency than they would otherwise have been. The relevant look-back period is six months, extended to two years where the creditor is a connected person, and a desire to prefer is presumed for connected persons.

n.0: Preferential payments can be challenged; genuine creditors are not immune where a preference is shown.
n.2: The connected-person period is two years, not one month.
n.3: This is a preference, distinct from a transaction at an undervalue.
n.4: The creditor's knowledge of insolvency is not the test; the company's desire to prefer is.

1.q: The parties to litigation reach a settlement of their dispute and wish to record the agreed terms in a way that stays the proceedings but allows either party to return to court to enforce the settlement terms if the other defaults, without those terms all being set out in a public court order. The court considers the use of a Tomlin order to record a settlement. The parties had negotiated hard and wanted the agreed terms of their settlement to stay confidential. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A Tomlin order is available only in claims worth more than the multi-track threshold.
A Tomlin order stays the proceedings on agreed terms set out in a schedule, with liberty to apply to enforce them.
A Tomlin order requires all the confidential settlement terms to be read out in open court.
A Tomlin order can only be made after a full trial on the merits has taken place.
A Tomlin order brings the proceedings to a permanent end with no means of enforcing the settlement on these facts.
1.w: A Tomlin order is a form of consent order that stays the proceedings on the terms set out in a schedule to the order (which can remain confidential), while giving the parties liberty to apply to the court to enforce those terms without needing to start fresh proceedings.

n.0: There is no such value threshold for a Tomlin order.
