n.2: The confidential terms are in the schedule, not read out in open court.
n.3: A Tomlin order records a settlement; it does not require a prior trial.
n.4: It preserves a means of enforcement through the liberty to apply.

1.q: A person dies intestate and is survived by their spouse, but they had no children or other issue, and no other closer relatives who take priority. The estate is substantial. The spouse and more distant relatives dispute how the estate is distributed. The court considers the entitlement of a surviving spouse on intestacy where the intestate leaves no issue. The intestate had never had children and had outlived most of their wider family. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The estate is shared equally between the spouse and the intestate's parents and siblings.
The surviving spouse takes the whole of the estate absolutely where the intestate leaves no issue.
The spouse takes only a statutory legacy, with the rest passing to more distant relatives.
The whole estate passes to the intestate's parents, and the spouse receives nothing.
The estate passes to the Crown because the intestate left no children.
1.w: Under the current intestacy rules, where an intestate is survived by a spouse or civil partner but leaves no issue, the spouse takes the whole of the estate absolutely (the previous entitlement of parents and siblings in that situation having been removed).

n.0: The estate is not shared with parents and siblings where there is a spouse and no issue.
n.2: The spouse takes the whole estate, not just a statutory legacy.
n.3: The estate does not pass to the parents ahead of the spouse.
n.4: The estate does not pass to the Crown where there is a surviving spouse.

1.q: A claimant establishes that a public authority acted unlawfully by breaching their Convention rights, and wishes to know what remedy the court may grant, including whether financial compensation is available. A solicitor is asked about the remedies a court may give for a breach of Convention rights. The solicitor considers section 8 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The claimant had suffered real harm and wanted to know what the court could actually do for them. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Damages for a breach of Convention rights are available as of right in every case.
The court may only make a declaration and can never grant any other form of relief.
The court may grant such relief as it considers just and appropriate, and may award damages where necessary to afford just satisfaction.
The court must always award substantial damages for any breach of a Convention right on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court has no power to grant any remedy for a breach of Convention rights.
1.w: Under s.8 of the Human Rights Act 1998, where a court finds that a public authority has acted unlawfully under s.6, it may grant such relief or remedy within its powers as it considers just and appropriate, and may award damages, but only where necessary to afford 'just satisfaction' — so damages are not automatic.

n.0: HRA damages are not available as of right in every case.
n.1: The court may grant a range of remedies, not only a declaration.
n.3: Damages are not always awarded; they are discretionary and subject to the just satisfaction test.
n.4: The court does have remedial powers under s.8.

1.q: A testator wishes to appoint a partner in a firm of solicitors as their executor, and intends that the solicitor should be able to charge the estate for the professional work of administering it. The will is being drafted. The testator wants the professional executor to be paid for their services. The executor is a professional acting in the course of their profession. The testator is keen to appoint an experienced solicitor to shoulder the administration and expects that professional to be paid for the work involved, so the person drafting the will needs to know what has to be included if the solicitor is lawfully to charge the estate for their time. Which of the following best describes what is required for the professional executor to be remunerated?
o: The executor may charge whatever they wish without any authority, as executors are always paid on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The executor may charge only if appointed by the court rather than by the will.
The executor can never be paid for administering an estate in any circumstances.
The will should contain a charging clause (or statutory provision must apply) authorising the professional executor to charge for their services.
The executor may charge only if the residuary beneficiaries later agree in writing.
1.w: An executor is not automatically entitled to remuneration for time and trouble; authority is needed. This is usually given by a charging clause in the will permitting a professional executor to charge for their services, and there is also statutory provision allowing a trust corporation or professional PR to charge reasonable remuneration where others consent, subject to conditions.

n.0: Executors are not automatically entitled to be paid; authority such as a charging clause is required.
n.1: Court appointment is not the basis for a professional executor's charging entitlement.
n.2: A professional executor can be paid where properly authorised, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: Remuneration usually rests on a charging clause, not merely on later beneficiary agreement.

1.q: A general partnership incurs a substantial debt to a supplier in the ordinary course of its business. The partnership assets are insufficient to pay the debt in full, and the supplier wishes to recover the balance. The partners argue about the extent to which each of them is responsible for the firm's debts. The supplier seeks advice on the liability of the individual partners for the debts of the firm under the Partnership Act 1890. The debt had been run up buying stock for the firm in the ordinary course of its trading. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The partners have no personal liability, because the firm is a separate legal person.
The partners are liable only up to the amount of capital they each contributed to the firm.
Each partner is liable only for the share of the debt equal to their share of the profits.
Only the partner who incurred the particular debt is liable to the creditor for it.
The partners are jointly liable for the debts of the firm, and personally so without limit.
1.w: Under the Partnership Act 1890, partners are jointly liable for the debts and obligations of the firm incurred while they are partners, and that liability is personal and unlimited, so a creditor may pursue the partners' personal assets.

n.0: An ordinary partnership is not a separate legal person; partners are personally liable.
n.1: Liability is not capped at capital contributed.
n.2: Liability is not limited to each partner's profit share.
n.3: Liability is not confined to the partner who incurred the debt; partners are jointly liable.

1.q: A lender is exercising its power of sale over a defaulting borrower's home. Rather than marketing and selling the property on the open market, the lender wishes to sell it directly to a company that the lender itself owns and controls. The borrower has heard of the proposed sale and is worried that the price paid by the connected company will be well below what the home is really worth, leaving a large shortfall for which the borrower would remain personally liable. The borrower seeks advice on whether the lender is entitled to sell the home to its own company at all, and on what terms. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The lender may sell to a connected company only if it proves it took reasonable care to obtain the true market value.
The sale to a connected company is automatically void and cannot be completed.
The lender cannot sell the property at all while it has any connection with the buyer.
The lender owes no duty as to price once it has decided to sell to a connected buyer.
The lender may sell to its own company on any terms, because it controls the power of sale, on the facts described above.
1.w: A mortgagee cannot sell to itself, and a sale to a connected company is closely scrutinised: the burden is on the mortgagee to show it took reasonable care to obtain the true market value (Tse Kwong Lam v Wong Chit Sen). If it cannot, it is liable for any shortfall.

n.1: Such a sale is not automatically void; the issue is whether a proper price was obtained.
n.2: A sale to a connected buyer is permitted but heavily scrutinised, not outright prohibited.
n.3: The duty as to price applies with particular force where the buyer is connected to the lender.
n.4: Control of the power of sale does not free the lender from the duty to obtain a proper price.

1.q: At a Crown Court trial the prosecution case depends significantly on the identification of the defendant by an eyewitness, and there is a recognised risk that even an honest witness may be mistaken about identity. The defence is concerned that the jury should be warned about the dangers of identification evidence. The defendant's solicitor considers the direction required where identification is disputed. The solicitor considers the Turnbull direction. The witness had seen the offender only briefly and in poor light on the night in question. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The judge must direct the jury to accept identification evidence without question on these facts as a general rule.
The judge should give a Turnbull warning about the special need for caution before convicting on identification evidence.
The jury alone decides whether any warning about identification is necessary.
No warning about identification evidence is ever required in a criminal trial.
Identification evidence is automatically inadmissible whenever it is disputed.
1.w: Where the case against a defendant depends wholly or substantially on disputed identification evidence, the judge must give the jury a Turnbull warning: to exercise special caution before convicting on such evidence, explaining why mistakes can occur, and directing the jury to examine the circumstances of the identification.

n.0: The jury should be warned to be cautious, not to accept identification without question.
n.2: The requirement to warn is a matter of law for the judge, not the jury's choice.
n.3: A Turnbull warning is required in disputed-identification cases.
n.4: Disputed identification evidence is not automatically inadmissible; it is subject to the warning.

1.q: A prospective client telephones a firm to ask it to act on a perfectly straightforward matter that is well within the firm's ordinary expertise and capacity. On working out the prospective client's religion from their name and their manner of speaking, the fee-earner tells them, quite untruthfully, that the firm is simply too busy to be able to help them, when in reality the fee-earner has decided that they do not wish to act for someone of that particular religion. The prospective client suspects the real reason for the refusal and complains to the firm. The firm considers its position. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The firm must not refuse to act, or provide a worse service, because of a client's protected characteristic.
The firm may refuse on this basis, provided it does not tell the client the real reason for the refusal.
The firm may refuse to act for anyone it chooses, for any reason, because it is a private business.
The firm may refuse on this basis, provided another local firm is available to take the client on.
The firm has no obligations to a mere prospective client who has not yet been formally taken on.
1.w: Under the Equality Act 2010 and the SRA's requirements, a firm must not discriminate against a person because of a protected characteristic (such as religion), including by refusing to act or by offering a lesser service. This applies to prospective clients as well as existing ones.

n.1: Concealing the real reason does not make discriminatory refusal lawful.
n.2: A firm's freedom to choose clients does not extend to unlawful discrimination.
n.3: The availability of another firm does not excuse discriminatory treatment.
n.4: Anti-discrimination duties apply to prospective clients, not only those already retained.

1.q: A mortgage of a commercial property contains a term giving the lender an option to purchase the mortgaged property itself, at a fixed price set at the outset, exercisable at the lender's choice at any time during the mortgage. The borrower has since repaid, or now wishes to repay, the loan in full and to recover the property free of the mortgage; but the lender says it intends to exercise the option and take the property at the fixed price instead. The borrower seeks advice on whether the option is valid and enforceable against them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The option binds the borrower only after the borrower has first defaulted on the loan.
The option is fully valid, because a lender may always negotiate an option to buy as part of its security. on these facts
The option is void, because an option for the lender to buy the mortgaged property is a clog on the equity of redemption.
The whole mortgage is void, so the borrower keeps the property free of any charge.
The option is valid only if the borrower had independent legal advice before signing.
1.w: An option granted to the mortgagee to purchase the mortgaged property is repugnant to the equity of redemption and void as a clog: the borrower must be able to get the property back on redemption, free of any right in the lender to acquire it (Samuel v Jarrah Timber).

n.0: Default does not validate the option; it is void as a clog whenever exercisable.
n.1: Such an option is not simply valid; it is struck down as inconsistent with redemption.
n.3: Only the offending option is void; the mortgage and debt remain.
n.4: Independent advice does not save an option that clogs the equity of redemption.

1.q: A claimant wishes to bring a single set of proceedings against two defendants who are both said to be liable in respect of the same damage, and to include two related claims arising out of the same facts. The claimant wants to know whether multiple parties and claims can be dealt with together in one action. The court considers the joinder of parties and claims under the Civil Procedure Rules. Both potential defendants were said to have contributed to the same loss the claimant had suffered. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Claims can only be joined if the defendants expressly consent to being sued together.
Each claim and each defendant must always be pursued in an entirely separate set of proceedings.
Multiple claims and parties may be joined in one set of proceedings where it is convenient to dispose of them together.
Multiple claims may be joined only where they exceed the multi-track value threshold.
A claimant may never sue more than one defendant in the same proceedings under any circumstances on these facts.
1.w: The CPR permit a claimant to use a single claim form to start all claims which can be conveniently disposed of in the same proceedings, and multiple parties may be joined where there is a common question of law or fact or the claims arise out of the same transaction, so long as it is desirable to deal with them together.

n.0: Joinder does not require the defendants' consent.
n.1: Separate proceedings for every claim and defendant are not required.
n.3: Joinder is not gated behind the multi-track value threshold.
n.4: Multiple defendants can be sued together in appropriate cases.

1.q: An occupier of commercial premises engages an apparently reputable and suitably qualified specialist contractor to carry out electrical work. The occupier checks the contractor's competence and, so far as it reasonably can, that the work has been done properly. A visitor is later injured because of a latent defect in the contractor's work that the occupier could not reasonably have detected. The visitor sues the occupier under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957. The occupier acted reasonably in selecting the contractor and in checking the work. Which of the following best describes the occupier's likely liability?
o: The occupier is strictly liable for any injury caused by a contractor's work on the premises.
The occupier is liable unless the visitor was expressly warned about the electrical work.
The occupier is liable because a contractor's negligence is always attributed to the occupier.
The occupier is likely not liable, having acted reasonably in entrusting the work to a competent contractor and checking it.
The occupier is liable because the common duty of care can never be discharged through a contractor on these facts.
1.w: Under s.2(4)(b) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, where damage is caused by the faulty work of an independent contractor, the occupier is not liable if it acted reasonably in entrusting the work to a contractor and took reasonable steps to satisfy itself that the contractor was competent and (where appropriate) that the work had been properly done. Those conditions are met here.

n.0: The occupier is not strictly liable for a contractor's faulty work.
n.1: Discharge turns on the reasonableness of entrusting and checking the work, not on warning the visitor.
n.2: A competent independent contractor's negligence is not automatically attributed to the occupier.
n.4: The common duty of care can be discharged by reasonably entrusting specialist work to a contractor.

1.q: Trustees are ready to distribute the estate but are unsure whether a particular potential beneficiary is still alive or has died, having made reasonable enquiries without resolving the question. They are anxious to distribute without risk of personal liability if the missing person later appears. The trustees cannot be certain whether a beneficiary is alive or dead despite reasonable enquiry. They wish to protect themselves before distributing. The trustees have chased every lead to establish whether the potential beneficiary is alive but drawn a blank, they are ready to wind up the estate and pay out to the others, and they are looking for a way to do so that will not leave them personally answerable if the missing person later surfaces. Which of the following best describes a step the trustees can take for protection?
o: Retain the entire fund indefinitely and never distribute to anyone.
Pay the whole fund to the Crown as if it were ownerless property.
Distribute the fund on their own assumption without any protection, accepting personal liability.
Apply to the court for a Benjamin order permitting distribution on a stated assumption about the missing beneficiary.
Distribute equally among the known beneficiaries and ignore the missing person entirely without any order.
1.w: Where trustees cannot establish whether a beneficiary is alive or dead, they may apply to the court for a Benjamin order, authorising distribution on a specified assumption (for example that the missing person predeceased). This protects the trustees from personal liability if the assumption later proves wrong, while the missing beneficiary's claim (if any) survives against the recipients.

n.0: Retaining the fund indefinitely is not a proper discharge of the trustees' duties.
n.1: The fund is not paid to the Crown merely because one beneficiary cannot be traced.
n.2: Distributing on their own assumption without protection leaves the trustees personally exposed.
n.4: Simply ignoring the missing person without an order or other protection risks personal liability.

1.q: A well-known performer agrees in a contract that, for a period, they will sing exclusively for one venue and will not perform for any competitor. The performer then proposes to breach that negative undertaking by performing for a rival venue. The original venue does not seek to force the performer to sing for it, but does want to stop the performer singing for the competitor in breach of the exclusivity promise. The venue seeks advice on the remedy available. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court will order the performer to sing for the original venue by way of specific performance.
The court can grant no remedy at all, because promises about personal services are unenforceable.
The court may grant a prohibitory injunction to restrain the performer from breaching the negative undertaking.
The court will refuse any injunction, because that would indirectly compel personal service.
The court will grant an injunction only if the performer has already begun performing for the rival.
1.w: A court will not order specific performance of a contract for personal services, but it may grant a prohibitory injunction to enforce a negative undertaking (such as a promise not to perform for competitors), provided this does not in substance compel the personal service (Lumley v Wagner; Warner Bros v Nelson).

n.0: The court will not order the performer to sing for the venue; that is specific performance of personal service.
n.1: Negative undertakings in personal-service contracts can be enforced by injunction, so a remedy exists.
n.3: An injunction restraining the negative promise is permissible where it does not compel the service itself.
n.4: An injunction may be granted to prevent a threatened breach, not only after it starts.

1.q: A court is applying a provision of an Act of Parliament that, read in its natural sense, would operate in a way that interferes with a person's rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. Counsel argues the provision can reasonably be read in a different, Convention-compatible way. The court is considering its duty under the Human Rights Act 1998. The provision was drafted before the point now in issue arose, its ordinary meaning would cut across a right the claimant enjoys under the Convention, and counsel maintains that a perfectly natural alternative reading exists that would respect that right, so the court must be clear about how far its interpretive duty stretches. Which of the following best describes the court's obligation under section 3 of the Act?
o: It must refer the legislation to the European Court of Human Rights for a ruling.
It must suspend the legislation until Parliament amends it.
It must strike down the legislation as invalid because it interferes with Convention rights on these facts.
It must apply the natural meaning and disregard the Convention entirely.
It must read and give effect to the legislation compatibly with Convention rights so far as it is possible to do so.
1.w: Section 3 of the Human Rights Act 1998 requires courts, so far as it is possible to do so, to read and give effect to primary and subordinate legislation in a way that is compatible with Convention rights. This is a strong interpretive obligation, but it does not permit the court to strike down primary legislation.

n.0: Domestic courts do not refer legislation to the European Court of Human Rights for rulings.
n.1: The court has no power to suspend an Act of Parliament pending amendment.
n.2: Courts cannot strike down primary legislation for incompatibility; section 3 is interpretive.
n.3: The court cannot simply disregard the Convention; section 3 imposes a positive duty.

1.q: A consumer brings a straightforward County Court claim against a trader for £6,000 in respect of faulty goods. The claim raises no complex issues of law or fact and is defended. When directions are given the court must allocate the claim to a case management track. The claim is a modest, uncomplicated money claim. The goods were a household appliance that failed shortly after purchase, the consumer wants a refund plus a modest sum for consequential expense, the trader disputes liability, and the sums and issues involved are exactly the kind the civil rules channel into a streamlined, low-cost procedure with limited costs recovery. Which of the following best identifies the track to which the claim would ordinarily be allocated?
o: The multi-track.
The fast track.
The Crown Court list.
The intermediate track.
The small claims track.
1.w: The small claims track is the normal track for straightforward claims with a value not exceeding £10,000. A defended, uncomplicated claim for £6,000 falls within it, providing a streamlined and low-cost procedure with limited recovery of costs.

n.0: The multi-track is for the highest value or most complex claims.
n.1: The fast track is generally for claims above £10,000 up to £25,000.
n.2: The Crown Court is a criminal court and has no role in allocating a civil money claim.
n.3: The intermediate track is for certain claims above £25,000 up to £100,000.

1.q: A defendant is convicted after a trial in the magistrates' court and wishes to challenge both the conviction and the sentence. The defendant's solicitor advises on the route of appeal available against a decision of the magistrates' court on the facts and merits. The solicitor considers an appeal from the magistrates' court to the Crown Court. The defendant felt the magistrates had got both the verdict and the sentence badly wrong. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An appeal from the magistrates' court is decided by a different bench of magistrates.
A defendant convicted in the magistrates' court may appeal to the Crown Court against conviction and/or sentence, by way of a rehearing.
An appeal from the magistrates' court is available only against sentence and never conviction on these facts as a general rule.
An appeal from the magistrates' court lies directly to the Supreme Court.
There is no right of appeal from the magistrates' court to any other court.
1.w: A defendant convicted in the magistrates' court may appeal to the Crown Court against conviction (if they pleaded not guilty) and/or sentence. The appeal takes the form of a complete rehearing before a judge and (usually) two magistrates.

n.0: The appeal is heard in the Crown Court, not by a fresh magistrates' bench.
n.2: Appeal to the Crown Court can be against conviction as well as sentence.
n.3: The appeal lies to the Crown Court, not directly to the Supreme Court.
n.4: There is a right of appeal from the magistrates' court to the Crown Court.

1.q: A body that is not a core organ of government, but which exercises certain functions of a public nature (alongside private activities), acts in a way said to be incompatible with a Convention right when performing one of those public functions. A claimant wishes to rely on the Human Rights Act 1998. The body is a hybrid body performing some public functions. The act complained of relates to a public function. The body sits somewhere between the public and private spheres, running some genuinely public functions alongside its ordinary commercial activities, and the act complained of arose in the course of one of those public functions, so the claimant must show the body counts as a public authority for that purpose. Which of the following best describes when such a body is bound by the Human Rights Act?
o: It is bound by the Act in respect of all its activities, public and private alike.
It can never be bound by the Human Rights Act because it is not a core public authority on these facts as a general rule.
It is a public authority in respect of its functions of a public nature, and is bound when performing those functions.
It is bound only where it consents to be treated as a public authority.
It is bound only if it is wholly owned by central government.
1.w: Under s.6 of the Human Rights Act 1998, 'public authority' includes any person certain of whose functions are functions of a public nature (a 'hybrid' or functional public authority). Such a body is bound by the Act when exercising its public functions, but not in relation to acts of a private nature.

n.0: It is bound only for its public functions, not its private acts.
n.1: A hybrid body can be bound in respect of its public functions, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Its status does not depend on its consent; it turns on the nature of its functions.
n.4: Being bound does not depend on being wholly owned by central government.

1.q: A person dies intestate, leaving no will and therefore no appointed executor. A close relative wishes to take on the administration of the estate and obtain formal authority to deal with the assets and distribute them under the intestacy rules. The relative asks what grant of representation is appropriate where the deceased left no valid will. The court considers the appropriate grant on intestacy. The deceased had left no will at all, and a son wished to sort out the estate for the family. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The estate passes automatically to the Crown because there is no will.
No grant is required on intestacy, and any relative may distribute the estate freely.
The relative must be appointed as an executor by the court before administering the estate.
A grant of probate is obtained, as for a person who left a valid will and executor.
A grant of letters of administration is obtained by an entitled applicant under the intestacy rules.
1.w: Where there is no valid will (or no proving executor), the appropriate grant is a grant of letters of administration, obtained by a person entitled to apply under the rules of priority (broadly following the order of those entitled to the estate on intestacy).

n.0: The estate does not pass to the Crown merely because there is no will, if there are relatives.
n.1: A grant is generally required; relatives cannot simply distribute freely.
n.2: On intestacy an administrator is appointed via letters of administration, not an executor.
n.3: A grant of probate applies where there is a will and a proving executor, not on intestacy.

1.q: A 17-year-old, who is not yet an adult, orders a quantity of basic clothing suitable to their actual needs from a retailer, but then refuses to pay, arguing that as a minor they cannot be bound by the contract. The goods supplied were necessaries appropriate to the minor's condition in life and actual requirements. The minor has taken delivery of the clothing. The retailer supplied everyday items genuinely suited to the young person's needs and station in life rather than extravagant luxuries, the goods were delivered and used, and the young person is now attempting to avoid paying anything at all by relying simply on being under age. Which of the following best describes the minor's liability?
o: The minor is liable to pay the full contract price regardless of whether it was reasonable.
The minor is liable only if a parent or guardian countersigned the order.
The minor is liable to pay a reasonable price for necessaries actually sold and delivered.
The minor is liable only if the goods were luxuries rather than basic items.
The minor is not liable at all, because contracts with minors are always entirely void.
1.w: Contracts with minors for necessaries (goods suitable to the minor's condition in life and to their actual requirements at the time) are binding, but the minor is liable only to pay a reasonable price, not necessarily the agreed price. Basic clothing suitable to the minor's needs can be necessaries, so the minor must pay a reasonable price for what was delivered.

n.0: Liability for necessaries is to pay a reasonable price, which may differ from the contract price.
n.1: A parent's countersignature is not required to make a minor liable for necessaries.
n.3: Liability arises precisely because the items were necessaries, not luxuries.
n.4: Contracts with minors are not all void; those for necessaries bind the minor.

1.q: At the end of a short interim application hearing lasting less than a day, the successful party asks the court to determine the amount of costs payable by the losing party there and then, rather than leaving the amount to be worked out in separate later proceedings. The hearing has lasted less than one day. The court is asked to fix the amount of costs immediately. The interim application took well under a day, the winning party has a schedule of its costs ready, and rather than putting everyone to the trouble and delay of a separate assessment process later, it asks the judge to fix the sum the loser must pay right there at the end of the hearing. Which of the following best describes the usual approach to assessing the costs of such a hearing?
o: The court cannot assess costs until the whole claim has concluded.
The court will refer the costs to be agreed by the parties without any assessment.
The court will order each party to bear its own costs of the hearing.
The court must always order a detailed assessment to be carried out later.
The court will usually assess the costs of the hearing summarily at the end of it.
1.w: For a hearing lasting not more than one day, the court will generally undertake a summary assessment of costs at the conclusion of the hearing, fixing the amount payable immediately (aided by the parties' statements of costs). Detailed assessment, conducted later by a costs officer, is generally reserved for larger or more complex costs, such as those of a whole trial.

n.0: The court can and usually does assess the costs of the interim hearing immediately.
n.1: The court assesses rather than simply leaving costs to the parties to agree.
n.2: There is a successful party entitled to costs; the court does not simply order each side to bear its own.
n.3: Detailed assessment is not always required; short hearings are usually assessed summarily.

1.q: A company wishes to pay a dividend to its shareholders. The finance director is concerned about whether the company is legally permitted to make the distribution, given the company's accumulated financial position. A dividend can only lawfully be paid from a particular source. The court considers the rules on the payment of dividends and distributions under the Companies Act 2006. The company had built up losses in earlier years that exceeded its more recent trading profits. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A dividend may be paid out of any of the company's assets, whether or not it has any profits on these facts.
A dividend may always be paid out of the company's share capital to reward shareholders.
A dividend may only be paid out of profits available for distribution (accumulated realised profits less losses).
A dividend may be paid whenever the directors decide it would please the shareholders.
A dividend may be paid only if every creditor of the company first consents to it.
1.w: Under the Companies Act 2006, a company may only make a distribution (such as a dividend) out of profits available for the purpose — broadly, its accumulated realised profits less its accumulated realised losses. Paying dividends otherwise contravenes the capital maintenance rules.

n.0: A dividend cannot be paid where there are no distributable profits.
n.1: Dividends cannot be paid out of share capital.
n.3: The directors' wish to please shareholders does not make a distribution lawful without profits.
n.4: Creditor consent is not the test; availability of distributable profits is.

1.q: The buyer's and seller's solicitors have agreed all the terms and are ready to make the contract legally binding. They intend to exchange contracts by telephone using a recognised Law Society formula rather than meeting in person. The buyer asks at what point the parties become legally committed to the transaction, and what exchange achieves. The solicitor considers the effect of exchange of contracts in a conveyancing transaction. Both parties had been treating the deal as provisional and could still have walked away until now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Exchange transfers legal ownership of the property to the buyer immediately.
The parties are legally bound from the moment terms are first agreed, long before exchange.
Exchange of contracts has no legal effect, and either party may still withdraw freely afterwards on these facts.
On exchange the parties become legally bound to complete, and neither can withdraw without being in breach of contract.
The parties become bound only once completion has actually taken place, not on exchange.
1.w: Before exchange, either party may withdraw without liability ('subject to contract'). On exchange of contracts, a binding contract comes into existence and both parties are committed to completing on the agreed date; a party who then fails to complete is in breach.

n.0: Exchange does not transfer legal ownership; that happens on completion and registration.
n.1: The parties are not bound merely by agreeing terms subject to contract before exchange.
n.2: Exchange is precisely what makes the contract binding; it is not without effect.
n.4: The binding commitment arises on exchange, before completion.

1.q: A defendant has been convicted following a trial in the Crown Court and wishes to appeal against the conviction, arguing that it is unsafe. The defendant's solicitor advises on the court to which such an appeal lies and what is required to bring it. The solicitor considers an appeal against conviction from the Crown Court. The defendant believed the jury had been misdirected and that the conviction could not stand. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An appeal against a Crown Court conviction succeeds only if the defendant is factually innocent on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
An appeal against conviction lies to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally with permission, and succeeds if the conviction is unsafe.
An appeal against a Crown Court conviction lies to the magistrates' court for a rehearing.
There is no right of appeal against a conviction in the Crown Court.
An appeal against a Crown Court conviction may be brought at any time without permission.
1.w: A defendant convicted in the Crown Court may appeal against conviction to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally requiring leave (permission). The Court of Appeal will allow the appeal if it thinks the conviction is unsafe.

n.0: The test is whether the conviction is unsafe, not proof of factual innocence.
n.2: The appeal lies to the Court of Appeal, not down to the magistrates' court.
n.3: There is a right of appeal against Crown Court conviction to the Court of Appeal.
n.4: Permission (leave) is generally required, and there are time limits.

1.q: A father transfers property into the sole name of his young child, or a husband transfers property into his wife's sole name, without any express declaration of trust and without any evidence one way or the other about his intention. A dispute later arises as to whether the child or wife holds the property on resulting trust for the transferor, or takes it beneficially. The transferor argues a resulting trust arises in his favour. The property was valuable, and years later the transferor sought to recover it from the transferee. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A presumption of advancement may apply, so the transfer is presumed to be a gift, though this can be rebutted.
The property passes to the Crown, because the intention behind the transfer is unclear.
A resulting trust automatically arises in the transferor's favour and cannot be displaced on these facts.
The transferee always holds on trust for the transferor, whatever their relationship.
The transfer is always an outright gift, and no presumption can ever be rebutted.
1.w: In certain relationships (such as father to child, or husband to wife) equity presumes advancement — that a gift was intended — which displaces the ordinary presumption of a resulting trust. The presumption of advancement is itself rebuttable by evidence of a contrary intention.

n.1: The property does not pass to the Crown for uncertainty of intention.
n.2: A resulting trust does not automatically arise where the presumption of advancement applies, and presumptions can be rebutted.
n.3: The transferee does not hold on trust in every case; advancement may apply.
n.4: The presumption of advancement is rebuttable, not conclusive.

1.q: A partner retires from a general partnership which continues in business with the remaining partners. After the retirement, the firm incurs new debts to an existing supplier who had dealt with the firm before, and who was never told that the partner had left. The supplier seeks to hold the retired partner liable for the new debts. The retired partner argues they are no longer a partner and so cannot be liable. The court considers the position of a retired partner under the Partnership Act 1890. The contract was an everyday purchase of the sort the firm routinely made in its line of work. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The retired partner remains liable for all the firm's future debts forever, whatever notice is given on these facts.
The retired partner may remain liable to existing customers for new debts unless proper notice of retirement was given.
The retired partner is liable only for debts that existed at the exact date of retirement.
The retired partner is liable only if their name still appeared on the firm's bank account.
The retired partner is automatically free of all liability the moment they retire from the firm.
1.w: A retiring partner remains liable to existing customers of the firm for debts incurred after retirement unless those customers are given actual notice of the retirement (and notice to the wider world requires publication, e.g. in the London Gazette) (s.36 Partnership Act 1890).

n.0: Proper notice can bring liability for future debts to an end, so it is not forever.
n.2: Liability can extend to post-retirement debts to existing customers absent notice, not only pre-existing debts.
n.3: Liability turns on notice to customers, not on the bank account details.
n.4: Retirement does not automatically end liability to those who dealt with the firm without notice.

1.q: A testator executed a will which, on its face, was properly signed and witnessed. After the testator's death a beneficiary under an earlier will alleges that the testator did not actually know and approve the contents of the later will — for example because it was prepared by someone who benefited and there are suspicious circumstances. The court must decide whether the testator knew and approved the will's contents. The court considers the requirement of knowledge and approval. The later will had been drawn up by a relative who took the largest share under it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Knowledge and approval are irrelevant once a will has been signed and witnessed.
The testator is always presumed to know and approve the contents, and this can never be challenged on these facts as a general rule.
The testator must have known and approved the contents of the will, and suspicious circumstances may require the propounder to prove this.
The will fails automatically wherever the person who drafted it takes any benefit under it.
Knowledge and approval need only be shown where the testator could not read the will themselves.
1.w: A valid will requires that the testator knew and approved its contents. Normally this is presumed where the will was duly executed by a capable testator, but where there are circumstances exciting suspicion (such as the preparation of the will by a substantial beneficiary), the burden is on the person propounding the will to prove positive knowledge and approval.

n.0: Knowledge and approval remain a requirement even where the will is signed and witnessed.
n.1: The presumption can be displaced where suspicious circumstances arise.
n.3: A benefit to the drafter raises suspicion but does not automatically invalidate the will.
n.4: Knowledge and approval must be shown generally, not only where the testator cannot read.

1.q: A firm receives settlement funds on behalf of a client following the conclusion of a hard-fought dispute. A paralegal, dealing with the incoming payment, mistakenly pays the money into the firm's office account rather than into the separate client account. The error is not spotted at the time and is only discovered several weeks later, during a routine internal audit of the firm's accounts. The money has not been spent or otherwise touched and remains fully available. The firm's compliance officer is asked to explain exactly what rule has been breached and why. Which of the following best states the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The settlement funds became the firm's own office money the moment they were received, so paying them into that account was correct.
Client money may be mixed with the firm's own money, provided the two are properly separated again at the end of the retainer.
Client money must be held in a separate client account, so paying it into the office account was a breach to correct promptly.
Discovery of the error on the internal audit retrospectively excuses the breach, provided the money is later moved across.
Only a qualified solicitor, and never a paralegal, may handle client money, so the payment had no legal effect at all.
1.w: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, client money (which includes settlement monies held for a client) must be kept in a client account, separate from the firm's own money, and any breach must be remedied promptly on discovery.

n.0: Settlement monies held on behalf of the client are client money, not the firm's office money.
n.1: Client money must be kept separate from office money at all times, not merely reconciled at the end.
n.3: Discovery on audit does not excuse the breach; it triggers the duty to put it right promptly.
n.4: Staff may handle client money under proper supervision; the rule breached concerns the account it is held in.

1.q: Two people run a business together and hold certain assets that are used in the business. A dispute arises as to whether particular assets are partnership property (belonging to the firm) or the personal property of one of the partners, which matters for how they are dealt with on dissolution. The assets were bought with the firm's money and used exclusively for the firm's business. The court considers what counts as partnership property under the Partnership Act 1890. The assets in question were vehicles bought entirely out of the firm's own bank account. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: All property used by the business automatically belongs personally to the senior partner on these facts.
Property bought with the firm's money belongs to whichever partner physically holds it.
There is no such thing as partnership property; all assets are always owned personally.
Property bought with the firm's money for the firm's purposes is presumed to be partnership property.
Property is partnership property only if the partnership agreement lists it by name.
1.w: Under the Partnership Act 1890, property bought with money belonging to the firm is presumed, unless a contrary intention appears, to have been bought on account of the firm and is partnership property. Such property must be held and applied by the partners exclusively for the purposes of the partnership.

n.0: Firm assets do not automatically belong to a senior partner personally.
n.1: Physical possession does not determine ownership of firm-bought assets.
n.2: Partnership property does exist as a distinct category.
n.4: Property need not be individually listed to be partnership property.

1.q: A professionally drafted trust instrument contains a clause purporting to exempt the trustees from liability for loss to the trust caused by their own negligence, however serious, but not for loss caused by their own fraud or dishonesty. A beneficiary who has suffered loss through the trustees' careless (but honest) administration challenges the clause, arguing that a trustee can never exclude liability for failing to take proper care. The clause had been drawn carefully to cover even serious carelessness, but stopped short of dishonesty. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A trustee exemption clause may validly exclude liability for fraud as well as for negligence.
A trustee exemption clause may validly exclude liability for negligence, but not for fraud or dishonesty.
A trustee exemption clause is valid only in trusts administered by lay, unpaid trustees.
A trustee exemption clause is always void, because trustees can never limit their liability at all.
A trustee exemption clause is valid only where every beneficiary consented to it in writing.
1.w: A trustee exemption clause can validly exclude liability for breaches of trust committed negligently, and even with gross negligence, but cannot exclude liability for the trustee's own fraud or dishonesty (Armitage v Nurse).

n.0: Liability for fraud or dishonesty cannot be excluded.
n.2: Such clauses are not confined to lay or unpaid trustees.
n.3: Such clauses are not always void; they can exclude liability for negligence.
n.4: Validity does not depend on every beneficiary's written consent.

1.q: In their will, a testator leaves all their property to their spouse absolutely, adding the words that they do so 'in the full confidence that she will do what is right' as regards the testator's children. After the testator's death, the children argue that these words created a binding trust in their favour over the property, so that the spouse holds it on trust for them rather than taking it outright. The spouse contends that the words were merely an expression of hope. The estate was large, and the spouse and children each held a very different understanding of what the words meant. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The words create a charitable trust for the benefit of the family.
The words create a trust because the testator expressed confidence in the spouse.
The words create a trust because they refer specifically to the testator's children on these facts.
The words are likely precatory only, so no trust arises and the spouse takes the property absolutely.
The words automatically create a binding trust in favour of the children.
1.w: Certainty of intention requires an intention to impose a binding trust obligation. Precatory words expressing a hope, wish or 'confidence' generally do not create a trust (Lambe v Eames; Re Adams and the Kensington Vestry), so the spouse takes absolutely.

n.0: No charitable purpose is involved; this concerns a private gift.
n.1: Expressing confidence is a hope, not the imposition of a trust obligation.
n.2: Merely referring to the children does not turn precatory words into a trust.
n.4: Precatory words do not automatically create a binding trust.

1.q: A company wishes to change its articles of association to alter the way directors are appointed. The directors ask what type of members' decision is required to amend the articles under the Companies Act 2006. The proposal is to amend the company's existing articles. The company wishes to act validly. The company has decided to overhaul the way its directors are appointed and that means changing the wording of its existing articles, so the board needs to be clear about the level of member support the law requires before an amendment to the constitution can take effect. Which of the following best describes the resolution required to alter the articles?
o: A resolution of the board of directors alone.
The prior approval of the Registrar of Companies.
A special resolution of the members (at least 75%).
An ordinary resolution of the members (a simple majority).
A unanimous decision of all the members.
1.w: Under s.21 of the Companies Act 2006, a company may amend its articles by special resolution, which requires a majority of at least 75%. A copy of the amended articles and the resolution must then be filed at Companies House. The board alone cannot alter the articles.

n.0: The board alone cannot amend the articles.
n.1: The Registrar's prior approval is not required; the resolution is filed after being passed.
n.3: An ordinary resolution is insufficient to alter the articles; a special resolution is required.
n.4: Unanimity is not required; a 75% special resolution suffices.

1.q: A judge in the County Court is considering an earlier judgment of a higher court. Part of that judgment sets out the legal principle essential to the earlier decision on its facts, and another part consists of the judge's general observations on a hypothetical situation that did not arise. The County Court judge must decide which part binds the court. The earlier judgment ran to many pages, weaving together the reasoning that decided the actual dispute with wider commentary on situations that were not before the court, and the County Court judge must separate the part that governs the present case from the part that does not. Which of the following best describes what is binding under the doctrine of precedent?
o: Neither the ratio nor obiter is binding on a lower court in any circumstances.
The ratio decidendi of the earlier decision is binding, while obiter remarks are only persuasive.
Both the ratio decidendi and the obiter remarks are equally binding.
Only the final order of the earlier court is binding, not any reasoning.
The obiter remarks are binding, while the ratio decidendi is merely persuasive on these facts.
1.w: The binding element of a precedent is the ratio decidendi: the legal reasoning necessary to the decision on its material facts. Obiter dicta, such as observations on hypothetical situations not essential to the decision, are persuasive only and do not bind a later court.

n.0: The ratio of a higher court's decision does bind a lower court.
n.2: Obiter remarks are not binding; only the ratio binds.
n.3: It is the ratio (the reasoning), not merely the order, that binds.
n.4: This reverses the position; obiter is persuasive, not binding.

1.q: A defendant who has been sued wishes not only to defend the claim but also to bring their own claim against the claimant arising out of the same matter, and to bring a claim against a third party for a contribution towards any liability. The defendant asks how such additional claims are made within the existing proceedings. The court considers counterclaims and additional (Part 20) claims under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant said the claimant in fact owed them money arising out of the very same dealings. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A defendant may bring a counterclaim only if it is for exactly the same amount as the claim.
A defendant can only ever defend the claim and may never bring any claim of their own.
A defendant must start entirely separate proceedings to make any claim against the claimant on these facts.
A defendant may never bring a third party into existing proceedings under any circumstances.
A defendant may bring a counterclaim against the claimant and, by an additional claim, bring in a third party.
1.w: Under Part 20 CPR, a defendant may make a counterclaim against the claimant and may bring additional claims (for example for a contribution or indemnity, or a related claim) against a third party, so that connected disputes can be resolved in the same proceedings.

n.0: A counterclaim need not match the amount of the claim.
n.1: A defendant can bring claims of their own, not merely defend.
n.2: Separate proceedings are not required; a counterclaim can be made in the same action.
n.3: Third parties can be brought in by additional (Part 20) claims.

1.q: After a testator's death, it becomes clear that the will, owing to a clerical error or a failure to understand the testator's instructions, does not carry out the testator's actual intentions — for example a figure or name was mistyped. A beneficiary wishes to have the will corrected to reflect what the testator truly intended. The court considers the power to rectify a will under the Administration of Justice Act 1982. A legacy figure had plainly been mistyped, giving a result the testator could never have intended. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court may rewrite the will freely to achieve whatever result seems fairest to the family on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may rectify a will only if every beneficiary consents to the change.
A will can never be corrected once the testator has died, whatever the error.
Rectification is available only where the whole will was forged or fraudulently made.
The court may rectify the will where it fails to carry out the testator's intentions due to a clerical error or a failure to understand instructions.
1.w: Under s.20 Administration of Justice Act 1982, the court may order rectification of a will if satisfied that it fails to carry out the testator's intentions in consequence of a clerical error, or a failure to understand the testator's instructions. Applications are generally subject to a time limit from the grant.

n.0: Rectification corrects specific errors; it does not permit free rewriting for fairness.
n.1: Rectification does not require every beneficiary's consent.
n.2: A will can be rectified in the defined circumstances after death.
n.3: Rectification is not confined to forgery or fraud.

1.q: A restrictive covenant benefits Plot A and burdens Plot B, restricting building on Plot B. Plot A has since been sold, and in the conveyance to the buyer the seller expressly assigned to the buyer the benefit of the restrictive covenant, at the same time as transferring the land itself. The owner of Plot B has now begun building work in clear breach of the covenant. The new owner of Plot A, relying on the express assignment of the benefit contained in their own conveyance, wishes to enforce the covenant against the owner of Plot B and bring the building work to a halt. Which of the following best describes the new owner of Plot A's position?
o: The new owner of Plot A cannot enforce it, because the benefit of a covenant can never be assigned.
The new owner of Plot A can enforce the covenant. in the circumstances
The new owner can enforce it only by first obtaining the burdened owner's agreement.
Only the original covenantee can enforce the covenant, whatever the conveyance said.
The covenant lapsed on the sale of Plot A and can no longer be enforced by anyone.
1.w: The benefit of a restrictive covenant can pass to a successor by express assignment (as well as by annexation or under a building scheme). Here the conveyance assigned the benefit, so the new owner of the benefited land can enforce it against the burdened owner.

n.0: The benefit of a restrictive covenant can be assigned, so enforcement is not confined to the original parties.
n.2: Enforcement does not require fresh agreement from the burdened owner.
n.3: Successors can enforce where the benefit has passed to them by assignment or annexation.
n.4: The covenant did not lapse; its benefit was carried to the new owner by assignment.

1.q: A court is considering a claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 and must decide whether the will (or intestacy) makes reasonable financial provision for the applicant, and if not, what provision to order. The court is directed to weigh a range of matters. The court must exercise its discretion by reference to statutory guidelines. The applicant qualifies to claim. The court has accepted that the applicant is entitled to bring the claim and must now decide whether the estate makes reasonable provision for them and, if not, what to award, weighing the competing interests of the applicant and the beneficiaries rather than looking at any single consideration in isolation. Which of the following best describes the matters the court takes into account?
o: Only the size of the estate, regardless of anyone's needs.
A range of statutory factors, including the needs and resources of the applicant and beneficiaries, the deceased obligations, and the estate size.
Only the applicant's conduct towards the deceased during their lifetime.
Only the express wishes stated by the deceased in the will, and nothing else on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances on these facts.
Only whether the applicant is a blood relative of the deceased.
1.w: Section 3 of the 1975 Act sets out the factors the court must consider, including the financial needs and resources of the applicant and of any beneficiary, any obligations the deceased had towards them, the size and nature of the estate, any disability, and the conduct of the parties. The deceased's wishes are relevant but not decisive.

n.0: The estate's size is one factor among many, not the sole consideration.
n.2: Conduct is only one of several statutory factors.
n.3: The deceased's wishes are one factor, not the only consideration.
n.4: Being a blood relative is not the sole factor; needs and resources are central.

1.q: Three siblings own a house together, holding it as beneficial joint tenants. Over a number of years they came to a clear understanding among themselves, and consistently acted on the basis, that each of them owned a distinct one-third share which they were each free to dispose of by will. No formal written notice of severance was ever served by any of them on the others. One of the siblings has now died, having left a will purporting to deal with their share of the house. The question arises how the beneficial interest in the house is now held. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The joint tenancy was severed by their mutual conduct. on the facts of this case
The joint tenancy is intact, so the deceased's share passes by survivorship to the other two.
The beneficial ownership reverted to the person who originally provided the purchase money.
The deceased's third passes to the state, because informal severance is legally ineffective.
Severance is impossible without a signed written notice served on all the other joint tenants.
1.w: A beneficial joint tenancy can be severed not only by written notice under s.36(2) LPA 1925 but also by mutual agreement or a course of dealing showing all treat their shares as held in common (Williams v Hensman). Severance defeats survivorship, so the deceased's share passes under their estate.

n.1: Survivorship does not apply once the joint tenancy has been severed by mutual conduct.
n.2: Severance does not send the interest back to whoever paid the purchase money.
n.3: Informal severance by agreement or course of dealing is effective in equity.
n.4: Written notice is one method; mutual agreement or a course of dealing also severs.

1.q: A statute makes it an offence to sell a particular regulated product to an underage buyer. A trader is charged after a sale to an underage buyer, even though the trader honestly and reasonably believed the buyer was of age. The offence is one that, on its proper construction, imposes liability without proof of mens rea as to the age element. The defendant was not at fault as to age. The trader made the sale in good faith, having checked as best they could and honestly and reasonably concluding the customer was old enough, yet the customer was in fact underage, and the offence as drafted says nothing about the seller needing to know or suspect the buyer's true age. Which of the following best describes the trader's liability?
o: The trader is liable only if the prosecution proves dishonesty.
The trader cannot be liable without proof of intention or recklessness as to the buyer's age on these facts.
The trader is liable only if they intended to break the law.
The trader may be liable because the offence is one of strict liability as to that element, requiring no mens rea.
The trader can never be convicted of an offence without full mens rea for every element.
1.w: Some statutory offences are offences of strict liability, requiring no mens rea as to one or more elements of the actus reus. Where, on its proper construction, an offence imposes strict liability (often regulatory offences protecting the public), the defendant may be convicted despite an honest and reasonable mistake, so the trader can be liable notwithstanding the belief as to age.

n.0: Dishonesty is not an element of such regulatory strict liability offences.
n.1: Strict liability offences do not require intention or recklessness as to the relevant element.
n.2: Liability does not depend on an intention to break the law.
n.4: Not every offence requires full mens rea; strict liability offences exist.

1.q: Part way through a retainer, a solicitor wishes to stop acting for a client. The solicitor is aware that they cannot simply abandon the client without justification. The retainer is ongoing and the client still needs representation. The solicitor is considering when and how they may cease to act. Midway through the matter the solicitor would prefer to bow out, but is conscious that the client still needs representation and that simply dropping the client could leave them badly exposed, so the solicitor needs to know on what basis and with what notice they may properly stop acting. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may cease to act only where there is good reason and on reasonable notice to the client.
The solicitor may cease to act only with the permission of the court in every case on these facts.
The solicitor may never cease to act once a retainer has begun.
The solicitor may cease to act only if the client has failed to pay any fee at all.
The solicitor may cease to act at any time for any reason without notice.
1.w: A solicitor should not cease acting for a client without good reason and without giving reasonable notice, so as not to prejudice the client. Good reasons may include a conflict of interest, the client's failure to give proper instructions or to pay, or being asked to act improperly. The solicitor must still protect the client's position when withdrawing.

n.1: Court permission is not required in every case to cease acting.
n.2: A solicitor can cease acting for good reason, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Non-payment is one possible good reason, but not the only one.
n.4: A solicitor cannot simply cease acting at any time without reason or notice.

1.q: A woman is not present at a disaster but later learns that her adult child was caught up in it. She attends the hospital some hours afterwards, sees her injured child, and subsequently develops a recognised psychiatric illness. She was never herself in any physical danger. She claims damages for her psychiatric injury as a secondary victim. The defendant argues that she cannot satisfy the requirements the law imposes on such claims. By the time she reached the hospital the immediate rescue was long over and her child had already been treated. Which of the following best describes the requirements she must meet?
o: She may recover provided she learned of the event from a reliable third party or the media.
She must show a close tie of love and affection, closeness in time and space to the event or its aftermath, and perception by her own senses.
She may recover on the same basis as if she had been in physical danger herself.
She need only show that her psychiatric illness was in fact caused by the defendant's negligence on these facts as a general rule.
She may recover simply because she is a parent of the person who was injured in the disaster.
1.w: A secondary victim must satisfy the control mechanisms in Alcock: a close tie of love and affection with the immediate victim, proximity in time and space to the incident or its immediate aftermath, and perception of the event through their own unaided senses. Mere causation is not enough.

n.0: Being told by a third party or via the media does not satisfy the perception requirement.
n.2: A secondary victim is not treated the same as a primary victim in physical danger.
n.3: Causation alone is insufficient for a secondary victim; the control mechanisms must be met.
n.4: Being a parent creates the tie, but the other Alcock requirements must also be satisfied.

1.q: A buyer is induced to enter a contract by a statement of fact which was false but which the maker honestly and reasonably believed to be true when it was made — an innocent misrepresentation. The buyer, on discovering the truth, wishes to set the contract aside. The court, however, considers that rescission would be a disproportionate response given the minor nature of the matter, and that it would be more appropriate to keep the contract on foot and compensate the buyer instead. Which of the following best describes the court's power?
o: The court may award damages as of right, in addition to rescission, for an innocent misrepresentation.
The court has a discretion to award damages in lieu of rescission for an innocent misrepresentation.
The court can do nothing, because an innocent misrepresentation gives rise to no remedy at all.
The court may only refer the parties to renegotiate the contract between themselves.
The court must always grant rescission for an innocent misrepresentation if the buyer asks for it.
1.w: Under section 2(2) of the Misrepresentation Act 1967, where a person would be entitled to rescind for a non-fraudulent (including innocent) misrepresentation, the court has a discretion to declare the contract subsisting and award damages in lieu of rescission where it is equitable to do so.

n.0: Damages under s.2(2) are in lieu of rescission, not an additional as-of-right award.
n.2: An innocent misrepresentation is not remediless; rescission or damages in lieu may follow.
n.3: The court has its own statutory remedy; it is not confined to sending the parties back to negotiate.
n.4: Rescission for innocent misrepresentation is not an absolute right; s.2(2) allows damages in lieu.

1.q: A solicitor is running a matter for a client on an hourly-rate basis, and the fees are steadily mounting month by month. The solicitor privately forms the clear and settled view that the client's claim now has very poor prospects of success and is really no longer worth continuing, but deliberately says nothing to the client about any of this. Instead the solicitor continues to encourage the client to press on, and keeps on billing, precisely because the ongoing work is profitable for the firm. The client later discovers just how weak the claim always was. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's regulatory position?
o: The solicitor breached only the rules on client money by continuing to render bills for the work.
The solicitor acted properly, because a solicitor is entitled to keep earning fees for as long as a client will pay them.
The solicitor did nothing wrong, provided the work that was actually billed was genuinely carried out.
The solicitor breached the duties of honesty and best interests by concealing the poor prospects while continuing to bill.
The solicitor acted properly, because it is always for the client alone to decide whether to continue a claim.
1.w: A solicitor must act with honesty and integrity and in the client's best interests. Deliberately withholding advice about the poor prospects of the claim, so as to keep generating fees, breaches those duties, whatever the client would ultimately have decided.

n.0: The core failing is the dishonest withholding of advice, not merely a client-money matter.
n.1: The entitlement to charge does not permit keeping the client in the dark to generate fees.
n.2: That the billed work was done does not excuse concealing the claim's true prospects.
n.4: Although the decision is the client's, it must be an informed one; the solicitor must give the advice.

1.q: In a Crown Court case, the defence serves a defence statement. At trial, the defence advances a positive case that was not mentioned in that statement, departing from it without explanation. The defence statement did not set out the case now run at trial. The departure is unexplained. The defence had served a statement setting out its case, but at trial counsel runs a positive account that the earlier statement never mentioned, departing from it without any explanation, and the judge must consider what, if anything, may flow from that discrepancy. Which of the following best describes the consequence of a fault in the defence statement?
o: The defence statement fault has no consequences of any kind.
The prosecution is barred from cross-examining the defendant on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant automatically loses the right to give evidence.
The defendant's trial must be stopped and the case dismissed.
The court or jury may draw such inferences as appear proper from the fault in the defence statement.
1.w: Under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996, faults in a defence statement, such as failing to disclose a defence later relied on, or departing from the statement at trial, may allow the court or jury to draw such inferences as appear proper. It does not automatically end the trial or bar the defence, but it can damage the defendant's credibility.

n.0: There are potential consequences (adverse inferences), so it is not consequence-free.
n.1: The prosecution is not barred from cross-examining; indeed the fault may be explored.
n.2: The defendant does not automatically lose the right to give evidence.
n.3: A defence statement fault does not require the case to be dismissed.

1.q: A decision affecting a party is taken by an adjudicator who has a direct personal financial interest in the outcome of the very matter being decided. The party challenges the decision on the ground of bias, without needing to show a real possibility of bias. A solicitor is asked about the position where the decision-maker has a direct interest in the outcome. The solicitor considers automatic disqualification for bias. The adjudicator stood to gain financially from the very decision they were being asked to make. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Automatic disqualification applies only to full-time salaried judges.
A direct financial interest in the outcome is irrelevant unless actual bias is proved.
A decision-maker may always decide a case in which they have a financial interest.
A decision-maker with a direct personal interest in the outcome is automatically disqualified, without proof of bias.
A direct interest disqualifies the decision-maker only if the losing party objects in advance on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
1.w: Where a decision-maker has a direct personal interest in the outcome — classically a direct pecuniary interest — they are automatically disqualified from acting, and the decision is liable to be set aside without any need to investigate whether there was a real possibility of bias (Dimes v Grand Junction Canal).

n.0: Automatic disqualification is not confined to salaried judges.
n.1: A direct interest disqualifies automatically; proof of actual bias is not needed.
n.2: A decision-maker may not decide a case in which they have such an interest.
n.4: Automatic disqualification does not depend on an advance objection.

1.q: A statute lists specific items followed by general words, for example 'cats, dogs and other animals'. A court must decide whether the general words ('other animals') are limited by the class of the specific items that precede them. The general words follow a list of specific items of the same kind. The court applies a rule of language. The section sets out a run of specific examples and then tacks on a sweeping general phrase, and the argument is about whether that catch-all phrase should be read at large or cut down to cover only more things of the same character as the specific items that came before it. Which of the following best identifies the rule the court is applying?
o: The ejusdem generis rule, by which general words following a list are limited to the same class as the specific items.
The literal rule, giving the general words their widest possible meaning.
The expressio unius principle, meaning the express mention of one excludes others on these facts as a general rule.
The golden rule, modifying the words to avoid absurdity.
The mischief rule, focusing on the defect in the earlier law.
1.w: The ejusdem generis ('of the same kind') rule is a rule of language: where general words follow a list of specific words forming a class, the general words are read as limited to things of the same class. So 'other animals' following 'cats, dogs' might be read as limited to domestic animals of that kind.

n.1: The literal rule concerns ordinary meaning generally, not this list-and-general-words situation.
n.2: Expressio unius is a different maxim (express mention of one excludes others), not the class-limiting rule here.
n.3: The golden rule addresses absurdity, not the limiting of general words by a preceding class.
n.4: The mischief rule looks at the defect in the old law, not rules of language.

1.q: A defendant is remanded in custody awaiting Crown Court trial. The applicable custody time limit is about to expire, but the trial cannot start in time. The prosecution wishes the defendant to remain in custody and applies to extend the custody time limit. The custody time limit is close to expiry before trial. The prosecution seeks an extension. The defendant has been held in custody awaiting his Crown Court trial, the maximum period he can lawfully be kept there before trial is about to run out, but the trial simply cannot be got on in time, and the prosecution, wanting him to stay in custody, applies to push the limit back. Which of the following best describes when the court may extend the custody time limit?
o: The custody time limit can never be extended in any circumstances.
The limit may be extended only with the defendant's consent.
The court must extend the limit automatically on the prosecution's request on these facts as a general rule.
The limit may be extended for any reason the prosecution chooses.
Where the prosecution shows good and sufficient cause and that it has acted with due diligence and expedition.
1.w: Custody time limits cap how long a defendant may be held in custody awaiting trial. The court may extend a limit only if satisfied there is good and sufficient cause to do so and that the prosecution has acted with all due diligence and expedition. If the limit expires without extension, the defendant is entitled to bail.

n.0: Custody time limits can be extended where the statutory test is met.
n.1: The defendant's consent is not required to extend the limit.
n.2: Extension is not automatic on request; the court must be satisfied of the test.
n.3: Extension requires good and sufficient cause and due diligence, not any reason at all.

2.q: A party wishes to rely at trial on the evidence of a witness of fact as to what that witness saw and heard. The court has given directions for the exchange of witness statements. The party asks about the function of a witness statement and what happens if it is not served in time. The court considers witness statements under the Civil Procedure Rules. The witness had seen the key events and their account was central to the party's case at trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A witness statement generally stands as the witness's evidence in chief, and a party who fails to serve one may need permission to call the witness.
Witness statements have no role, and all factual evidence must be given entirely orally without notice on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A witness statement is served only after the trial has concluded, as a record of the evidence.
A party may call any witness at trial without ever serving a witness statement in advance.
