Witness statements are required only from the parties themselves, never from other witnesses.
2.w: Parties must exchange witness statements of the factual witnesses they intend to call, in accordance with the court's directions. At trial the statement generally stands as the witness's evidence in chief. If a party fails to serve a statement, they may not call that witness without the court's permission.

n.1: Witness statements have a central role; evidence is not given wholly orally without notice.
n.2: Statements are exchanged before trial, not served afterwards.
n.3: Calling a witness without a served statement generally needs the court's permission.
n.4: Statements are required from the factual witnesses generally, not only the parties.

2.q: A trustee of a private trust wishes to retire from the trusteeship. There will remain, after the retirement, two trustees who will continue to administer the trust, and all the other trustees consent to the retirement by deed. The retiring trustee wants to be properly discharged without a new appointment being made. At least two trustees will remain and all co-trustees consent by deed. The trustee has grown elderly and wishes to step back, the remaining trustees are content to carry on between them and are willing to formalise matters, and everyone wants the departure handled in a way that leaves the retiring trustee properly discharged rather than exposed to lingering responsibility. Which of the following best describes how the trustee may retire under the Trustee Act 1925?
o: The trustee may retire only if all the beneficiaries consent in writing.
The trustee may retire simply by informing the beneficiaries orally.
The trustee may retire only if a new trustee is appointed to replace them on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The trustee cannot retire without a court order in any circumstances.
The trustee may retire by deed, provided at least two trustees (or a trust corporation) remain and the co-trustees consent.
2.w: Under s.39 of the Trustee Act 1925, a trustee may retire without a replacement being appointed if, after the retirement, there will remain at least two trustees or a trust corporation, the retirement is by deed, and the co-trustees (and anyone empowered to appoint trustees) consent by deed. Those conditions are met here.

n.0: It is the co-trustees' consent by deed that is required, not that of all beneficiaries.
n.1: Retirement requires a deed and consents, not merely oral notice to beneficiaries.
n.2: A replacement need not be appointed if two trustees will remain (s.39).
n.3: A court order is not required where the s.39 conditions are satisfied.

2.q: A bank, at the request of a customer's supplier, gives the supplier a reference about the customer's creditworthiness. The bank does so carelessly and the reference is inaccurate. The supplier, reasonably relying on the reference, extends credit to the customer and loses a large sum when the customer cannot pay. The supplier sues the bank in negligence for the purely financial loss. The bank argues that it owed the supplier no duty of care for a careless statement causing only financial loss. The supplier had no other means of assessing the customer's finances and took the reference at face value. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A duty arises automatically whenever one party gives another any information at all.
A duty arises only where the maker of the statement acted dishonestly rather than merely carelessly.
A duty may arise for a negligent statement where the maker assumes responsibility and the claimant reasonably relies on it.
No duty can ever arise for a careless statement that causes only financial rather than physical loss on these facts.
A duty arises only where there was a contract between the maker of the statement and the claimant.
2.w: A duty of care can arise for negligent misstatement causing pure economic loss where there is a special relationship: the maker of the statement, having relevant skill, assumes responsibility for it and the claimant reasonably relies on it to their detriment (Hedley Byrne v Heller).

n.0: A duty does not arise for every statement; a special relationship is required.
n.1: Liability can arise for careless statements, not only dishonest ones.
n.3: Pure economic loss from a negligent statement can be recoverable via the Hedley Byrne principle.
n.4: A contract is not required; the assumption of responsibility can arise without one.

2.q: A company borrows money from a lender and grants security over its assets. The lender is considering whether to take a fixed charge over specific identified assets, or a floating charge over a class of assets that changes from time to time (such as stock in trade). The company wishes to understand the essential difference between the two, particularly the company's freedom to deal with the charged assets. The court considers the distinction between fixed and floating charges. The lender was weighing which form of security would best protect it if the company later failed. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A fixed charge attaches to specific assets restricting dealings, while a floating charge hovers over a class of assets the company may deal with until crystallisation.
A floating charge attaches to specific assets and prevents any dealing with them at all.
A fixed charge allows the company to deal freely with the assets until the lender intervenes.
Only a floating charge can ever be taken over a company's property; fixed charges are not permitted on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
There is no practical difference between a fixed charge and a floating charge.
2.w: A fixed charge attaches to specific, identified assets and the company cannot dispose of them free of the charge without consent. A floating charge 'floats' over a fluctuating class of assets (such as stock), allowing the company to deal with them in the ordinary course of business until the charge crystallises and attaches to the assets then within the class.

n.1: The description is reversed; it is the fixed charge that attaches to specific assets restricting dealings.
n.2: A fixed charge restricts dealings; the freedom to deal is a feature of the floating charge before crystallisation.
n.3: Both fixed and floating charges may be taken over company property.
n.4: There are significant practical differences between the two.

2.q: A person who has never qualified as a solicitor, and who is not on the roll of solicitors or the holder of any practising certificate, sets up in business advising members of the public on their legal problems for a fee. In marketing that business, the person repeatedly describes themselves to clients and prominently on their website as a 'solicitor', genuinely believing that, because they give legal advice for a living, they are entitled to use the title. A qualified solicitor is asked whether an unqualified person may lawfully describe themselves as a solicitor in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The person may use the title 'solicitor', provided they make clear that they are not regulated by the SRA.
The person may use the title 'solicitor', provided their clients do not object to their doing so.
Only a person on the roll with a current practising certificate may practise as, or hold themselves out as, a solicitor.
Anyone who gives legal advice to the public may lawfully describe themselves as a solicitor to their clients.
The person may use the title 'solicitor', provided they do not carry out any court work for their clients.
2.w: The title 'solicitor' is protected. It is an offence for an unqualified person wilfully to pretend to be, or to take or use any name or title implying that they are, a solicitor. Only those on the roll with a practising certificate may practise as, or hold out as, solicitors.

n.0: A disclaimer about SRA regulation does not permit an unqualified person to use the title.
n.1: The clients' lack of objection does not legitimise holding out as a solicitor.
n.3: Giving legal advice does not entitle a person to the protected title of solicitor.
n.4: Avoiding court work does not make the misuse of the title lawful.

2.q: A defendant is convicted of a specified violent offence and is assessed as posing a significant risk of serious harm to the public from further such offences. The court is considering a sentence that provides for a longer period of protection than a standard determinate sentence. The defendant meets the dangerousness criteria for a specified offence. The court seeks to protect the public. The defendant has been convicted of a specified violent offence and the reports paint him as a continuing and significant danger of causing serious harm to others, so the judge is looking beyond an ordinary fixed term to a sentence that keeps the public protected for longer than a standard determinate sentence would. Which of the following best describes a sentence available for such a dangerous offender?
o: The court must impose a community order regardless of the risk posed.
Only a standard fine may be imposed on a dangerous offender.
The court must impose a suspended sentence in every case of dangerousness on these facts.
The court has no power to impose any longer or protective sentence.
An extended sentence, comprising a custodial term plus an extended licence period, may be imposed.
2.w: Where a defendant is convicted of a specified offence and found to be a dangerous offender (posing a significant risk of serious harm from further specified offences), the court may impose an extended sentence, comprising an appropriate custodial term plus an extended period of licence, to provide additional public protection (with a life sentence available in the most serious cases).

n.0: A community order is not mandated for a dangerous offender; protective custodial sentences are available.
n.1: A fine is plainly inadequate and not the protective sentence for a dangerous offender.
n.2: A suspended sentence is not required; extended (or life) sentences address dangerousness.
n.3: The court does have powers to impose longer, protective sentences for dangerous offenders.

2.q: An adult child of the deceased, who was not adequately provided for by the deceased's will, wishes to claim against the estate. The child is not a spouse or civil partner of the deceased and was financially independent as an adult, though now in some need. The applicant is an adult child, not a surviving spouse. The claim is under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975. The claimant is a grown-up child of the deceased who was left little or nothing by the will and, though long financially independent, is now facing real need, and the court must decide what yardstick applies to a claim of this kind brought by someone who is not the deceased's surviving spouse. Which of the following best describes the standard of provision the court may order for such an applicant?
o: No provision at all, because only spouses may claim under the Act.
Such financial provision as would be reasonable for the applicant's maintenance.
Such financial provision as would be reasonable in all the circumstances, whether or not for maintenance.
An equal share of the estate with all other children of the deceased.
Whatever sum the applicant requests, provided the estate can afford it.
2.w: Under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, for applicants other than a surviving spouse or civil partner, the standard is such financial provision as it would be reasonable for the applicant to receive for their maintenance. The higher 'reasonable in all the circumstances' standard, not limited to maintenance, applies only to a surviving spouse or civil partner.

n.0: Children, cohabitants and others may claim, not only spouses.
n.2: The non-maintenance standard is reserved for surviving spouses/civil partners, not an adult child.
n.3: There is no automatic equal share among children; the court assesses maintenance provision.
n.4: The court does not simply award whatever the applicant requests; it applies the maintenance standard and the statutory factors.

2.q: A defendant, during an argument, shouts a threat at the victim who is standing close by, causing the victim to fear that unlawful force will be used against them then and there, although the defendant does not touch the victim. The victim apprehended immediate unlawful personal violence as a result of the words and situation. No physical contact occurred. Tempers flared and the defendant, standing only a pace or two from the victim, snarled a threat of immediate violence that left the victim genuinely fearing they were about to be struck, even though in the event the defendant never actually laid a finger on them. Which of the following best describes the offence of assault (technical assault) in these circumstances?
o: Assault is committed where the defendant causes the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful personal violence, which words alone can do.
Assault requires the defendant to intend to kill the victim.
Assault requires actual physical contact with the victim in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Assault requires the victim to suffer some physical injury.
Assault cannot be committed by words alone under any circumstances.
2.w: A technical assault is committed where the defendant intentionally or recklessly causes the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful personal violence. Physical contact is not required (that would be battery), and words alone (and even, in some cases, silence) can constitute an assault if they cause the requisite apprehension of immediate violence.

n.1: Assault does not require an intention to kill.
n.2: Physical contact is battery; assault requires apprehension of force, not contact.
n.3: Assault does not require actual injury; apprehension of force suffices.
n.4: Words alone can amount to assault if they cause apprehension of immediate violence.

2.q: A firm holds a sum of money in the client account on behalf of a client, out of which the firm intends to take payment of its own professional fees for the work it has carried out on the matter to date. A fee-earner, keen to get the firm paid without delay, proposes simply transferring the amount of the firm's costs straight out of the client account and into the firm's own office account, without first sending the client any bill or other written notification of the costs being charged. The firm's compliance officer questions whether this may be done. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Money may be moved from the client account to the office account for costs only after a bill has been delivered to the client.
The firm may take its costs from the client account first and deliver a bill to the client at some later date.
The firm may never take its own costs from money held in the client account in any circumstances at all.
The firm may take its costs from the client account without a bill, provided the amount taken is reasonable.
The firm may transfer its costs from the client account at any time, since the money is held for that client anyway.
2.w: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, money held for a client may be transferred to the office account in respect of the firm's costs only once a bill of costs or other written notification of the costs incurred has been given to the client.

n.1: The bill must precede the transfer, not follow it.
n.2: The firm may properly take costs from client money, but only after delivering a bill.
n.3: Reasonableness of the amount does not dispense with the requirement for a bill first.
n.4: Holding the money for the client does not permit taking costs before a bill is delivered.

2.q: A landowner claims to have an easement over neighbouring land. To be capable of existing as an easement at all, the right must satisfy the essential characteristics of an easement. There is a dominant and a servient piece of land. The court applies the established test. The owner insists they enjoy an easement over the neighbouring land, and, with a benefited plot and a burdened plot in the picture, the court must test the claimed right against the established requirements before it can be recognised as an easement rather than some lesser or invalid right. Which of the following best describes the characteristics required for a right to be an easement?
o: There must be a dominant and servient tenement in different ownership, the right must accommodate the dominant land, and be capable of grant.
The dominant and servient land must always be owned by the same person.
The right must be registered as a company charge to be valid.
The right must give the dominant owner exclusive possession of the servient land on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
There need only be a dominant tenement, with no servient land required.
2.w: Under Re Ellenborough Park, a right can be an easement only if: there is a dominant and a servient tenement; the right accommodates (benefits) the dominant tenement; the dominant and servient tenements are owned or occupied by different persons; and the right is capable of forming the subject matter of a grant (sufficiently definite, within the general nature of easements, and not amounting to exclusive possession).

n.1: The tenements must be owned/occupied by different persons, not the same person.
n.2: Registration as a company charge is not a characteristic of an easement.
n.3: An easement must not give exclusive possession of the servient land.
n.4: Both a dominant and a servient tenement are required.

2.q: A testator made a first will, then revoked it by making a second will, and later destroyed the second will intending to bring back the first. The testator believes the original first will is automatically restored. After death, a dispute arises about which will (if any) is effective. The court considers the revival of a revoked will under the Wills Act 1837. The testator had believed, wrongly, that tearing up the second will would bring the first back to life. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A revoked will can be revived only by re-execution or by a codicil showing an intention to revive it, not merely by destroying the later will.
Both the first and second wills take effect together once the second is destroyed.
Destroying the later will automatically revives the earlier will in every case.
The earlier will revives provided the testator tells someone they wish to revive it on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A revoked will can never be revived under any circumstances at all.
2.w: Under s.22 Wills Act 1837, a will once revoked is not revived merely by revoking the instrument that revoked it. It can be revived only by re-executing it with will formalities, or by a duly executed codicil showing an intention to revive it.

n.1: The two wills do not both take effect; revival requires the proper steps.
n.2: Destroying the later will does not automatically revive the earlier one.
n.3: An oral statement of intention does not revive a revoked will.
n.4: A revoked will can be revived by re-execution or codicil, so 'never' is wrong.

2.q: A firm receives a sum of money from a client on account of costs for future work, which is client money under the SRA Accounts Rules. The bookkeeper must decide where this money should be held. The firm operates a general client account. The bookkeeper considers the requirement as to where client money must be kept under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm has a single general client account at its bank and no separate designated deposit account for this client, and the fee-earner asks the bookkeeper for confirmation of where the money should sit while the work is carried out over the coming weeks. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Client money may be kept in the personal account of the fee-earner handling the matter.
Client money may be kept in the firm's office account with its own money.
Client money must be kept in cash in the firm's safe rather than in any bank account.
Client money need not be kept in any particular account, so long as it is spent on the client.
Client money must be kept in a client account, separate from the firm's own money.
2.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require client money to be kept in a client account (an account at a bank or building society in the firm's name that includes the word 'client'), separate from the firm's own (office) money.

n.0: Client money must not be held in a fee-earner's personal account.
n.1: Client money must not be kept in the office account.
n.2: Client money is held in a client bank account, not as cash in a safe.
n.3: Client money must be held in a client account, not merely spent appropriately.

2.q: A tenant of a commercial lease (a new tenancy) wishes to assign the lease, and the landlord, as a condition of giving consent, requires the outgoing tenant to guarantee the performance of the incoming assignee. The outgoing tenant asks whether such a guarantee is lawful and what it involves, given that they would otherwise be released on assignment. The solicitor considers the authorised guarantee agreement under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995. The landlord was cautious about the assignee and wanted the outgoing tenant to stand behind them. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The landlord can require the outgoing tenant to guarantee every future assignee indefinitely down the chain on these facts as a general rule.
An authorised guarantee agreement makes the outgoing tenant liable even after a lawful further assignment.
The landlord may require an authorised guarantee agreement, under which the outgoing tenant guarantees the immediate assignee's performance.
The outgoing tenant remains automatically liable for the whole term regardless of any guarantee.
No guarantee of any kind may lawfully be required from an outgoing tenant on assignment.
2.w: Under the LTCA 1995, although an outgoing tenant of a new tenancy is released on a lawful assignment, the landlord may (where reasonable or required by the lease) require the outgoing tenant to enter an authorised guarantee agreement (AGA), guaranteeing the performance of the immediate assignee only, until that assignee itself lawfully assigns.

n.0: An AGA can guarantee only the immediate assignee, not every future assignee.
n.1: AGA liability ends when the assignee lawfully assigns onward.
n.3: The outgoing tenant is released on lawful assignment, subject only to an AGA; it is not automatically liable for the whole term.
n.4: A guarantee (AGA) can lawfully be required in appropriate circumstances.

2.q: A party has obtained permission to appeal a first-instance decision and must identify the basis on which the appeal court may interfere. The appellant contends the judge below reached the wrong conclusion, or alternatively that the process was so flawed as to make the decision unjust. The appeal is against a decision of a lower court. The appellant must frame proper grounds. The would-be appellant needs to pin its complaint to a recognised basis for appellate intervention, arguing either that the judge below simply got the decision wrong or that the way the hearing was conducted was so seriously flawed that the resulting decision cannot stand as just. Which of the following best describes the grounds on which an appeal will be allowed?
o: Where new evidence is available, which is always admitted on appeal as of right.
Where the appeal court would prefer to substitute its own view on the facts in every case on these facts as a general rule.
Where the decision was wrong, or unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity in the proceedings below.
Where any minor procedural error occurred, regardless of its effect on the outcome.
Where the appellant simply disagrees with the outcome and would have decided differently.
2.w: An appeal will be allowed where the decision of the lower court was wrong (in law, fact or the exercise of discretion) or unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity in the proceedings. Mere disagreement, or a trivial irregularity with no effect on the outcome, is insufficient, and appeals are generally reviews rather than rehearings.

n.0: New evidence is not admitted as of right on appeal; strict conditions apply.
n.1: An appeal is generally a review, not an occasion to re-decide the facts afresh at will.
n.3: The irregularity must be serious and render the decision unjust, not any minor error.
n.4: Mere disagreement with the outcome is not a ground of appeal.

2.q: A property owner wishes to carry out a modest development, such as a small extension, that falls within the categories the general planning legislation treats as permitted without a specific application. The owner asks whether express planning permission is needed. The works fall within the scope of permitted development rights and any conditions and limits are met. The owner wants to avoid an unnecessary application. The owner wants only a modest addition to the house, the sort of works the general development order treats as already permitted so long as the stated limits and conditions are respected, and is keen not to spend time and money on a formal application if none is actually needed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Express planning permission is always required for any works to a building without exception on these facts.
The works require permission only if they cost above a fixed monetary threshold.
Permitted development rights remove the need for building regulations approval as well.
Express planning permission may not be required because the works fall within permitted development rights.
Planning permission is never required for works to residential property.
2.w: Certain classes of development are granted planning permission by a general development order (permitted development rights), so that no express application is needed provided the works fall within the specified classes and comply with the relevant conditions and limitations. Where the works exceed those limits, express permission is required.

n.0: Express permission is not always required; permitted development rights can apply.
n.1: The test is the class and limits of development, not a monetary cost threshold.
n.2: Permitted development addresses planning permission, not building regulations, which are separate.
n.4: Permission can be required for residential works that exceed permitted development limits.

2.q: A developer wishes to grant a would-be buyer the right, exercisable in the future, to buy a plot of land at a set price if the buyer chooses to do so within a stated period. The buyer wants to be sure this right will bind the land even if the developer sells to someone else first. The buyer asks how such a right can be protected against third parties. The solicitor considers the protection of an option to purchase over registered land. The developer was actively marketing the surrounding land and might sell before the option was used. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An option to purchase cannot be protected on the register and can never bind a later buyer.
An option to purchase must be registered as a local land charge with the local authority.
An option to purchase binds all future owners automatically without any need to protect it.
An option to purchase is protected only by the buyer taking physical possession of the land on these facts.
An option to purchase is an estate contract which should be protected by entering a notice on the register.
2.w: An option to purchase land is an estate contract (an interest in land). To bind a later purchaser of registered land, it should be protected by entering a notice on the charges register of the burdened title; if not protected, it may be lost against a subsequent registered disposition for value.

n.0: An option can be protected by a notice; it is not incapable of binding a later buyer.
n.1: An option over registered land is protected at the Land Registry, not as a local land charge.
n.2: An option does not bind future owners automatically; it needs protection.
n.3: Protection is by a register notice, not merely by taking possession.

2.q: Personal representatives are pressed by residuary beneficiaries to distribute the estate very soon after the death, before the PRs have been able to ascertain the full extent of the assets and liabilities. The PRs are concerned about distributing too early. Only a few months have passed since the death. The PRs wish to know whether they are obliged to distribute so soon. Barely a few months after the death the residuary beneficiaries are pressing hard to be paid out, but the personal representatives have not yet pinned down all the assets and liabilities, and they want to know whether they can be forced to distribute so soon or whether they are entitled to more time. Which of the following best describes the 'executor's year'?
o: The PRs must distribute the entire estate within 28 days of the death.
The PRs must distribute as soon as the grant is issued, whatever the state of the estate.
The PRs are not bound to distribute the estate before the expiry of one year from the death.
The PRs may never distribute until at least six years have passed.
The PRs must distribute immediately on demand by any residuary beneficiary.
2.w: By the 'executor's year', personal representatives are not bound to distribute the estate before the expiry of one year from the death. They may need longer where the estate is complex, and distributing prematurely risks personal liability if further liabilities emerge, but beneficiaries generally cannot compel distribution within the first year.

n.0: There is no 28-day distribution requirement.
n.1: PRs need not distribute the moment the grant issues, regardless of the estate's state.
n.3: The executor's year is one year, not a six-year bar on distribution.
n.4: PRs are not compelled to distribute immediately on a beneficiary's demand within the year.

2.q: A settlor purports to create a discretionary trust for the benefit of an enormous, effectively boundless class, such as 'all the residents of a large region', so vast that any sensible exercise of the trustees' discretion would be impossible even though the class concept is clear. A beneficiary challenges the trust's validity. Conceptually the class is certain, but it is so large that the trust cannot sensibly be carried out. The drafting is clear enough in the abstract, but the sheer number of potential objects runs into the millions, so the trustees protest that they could not begin to survey the class or make any rational choice between its members however hard they tried. Which of the following best describes why the trust may nonetheless fail?
o: It must be valid because the class concept is conceptually certain.
It fails for uncertainty of subject matter rather than of objects.
It fails only because the trustees have not yet been appointed.
It fails because discretionary trusts are not recognised in English law on these facts as a general rule.
It may fail for administrative unworkability, the class being so wide that the trust cannot be executed.
2.w: Even where a class is conceptually certain, a discretionary trust may be void for administrative unworkability if the class is so hopelessly wide (for example, all the residents of a large area) that the trust cannot sensibly be executed. This is a distinct ground of invalidity from conceptual uncertainty.

n.0: Conceptual certainty does not guarantee validity; administrative unworkability can still defeat the trust.
n.1: The issue is the objects being unworkably wide, not uncertainty of subject matter.
n.2: The problem is the width of the class, not the absence of appointed trustees.
n.3: Discretionary trusts are recognised; the issue is the unworkable width of this class.

2.q: A defendant receives goods from a friend, knowing or believing them to have been stolen, and dishonestly assists in disposing of them for the thief's benefit. The defendant was not the original thief. The goods were stolen and the defendant knew or believed this. The defendant dishonestly received or dealt with them. The defendant took no part in the original theft but later took delivery of the goods from the thief well aware that they were stolen, and then dishonestly lent a hand in getting rid of them so that the thief could turn them into cash. Which of the following best identifies the offence under the Theft Act 1968?
o: Burglary under section 9.
Handling stolen goods under section 22.
No offence, because the defendant did not steal the goods.
Robbery under section 8.
Theft of the goods under section 1.
2.w: Handling stolen goods (s.22 Theft Act 1968) is committed where a person, otherwise than in the course of stealing, dishonestly receives stolen goods, or dishonestly undertakes or assists in their retention, removal, disposal or realisation by or for another, knowing or believing them to be stolen. The defendant's dishonest dealing with goods known to be stolen fits this offence.

n.0: There is no entry as a trespasser to a building, so it is not burglary.
n.2: Not being the original thief does not exonerate the defendant; handling is a distinct offence.
n.3: There is no use of force, so it is not robbery.
n.4: Theft is committed by the original appropriation; this defendant handled goods already stolen.

2.q: A rogue, pretending in a face-to-face meeting to be a wealthy and creditworthy individual, persuades a private seller to sell them goods and to accept a cheque in payment. The seller deals with the rogue in person and, although mistaken about the rogue's creditworthiness and honesty, intends to sell to the individual physically present. The cheque bounces, and the rogue sells the goods on to an innocent third party. The seller argues there was never any contract with the rogue because of the mistake as to identity. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is void, because identity is always a fundamental matter in any face-to-face sale.
The contract is fully valid and unaffected, because the seller received a cheque in payment.
There is a presumption the seller intended to deal with the person present, so the contract is voidable, not void.
The contract is void, because a seller is always mistaken when dealing with a dishonest rogue.
The contract is automatically void for mistake as to identity, so no title could pass to the third party.
2.w: In a face-to-face dealing there is a strong presumption that a party intends to contract with the person physically present, whatever their assumed identity. The contract is therefore voidable for fraudulent misrepresentation, not void for mistake, so an innocent third party who buys before rescission can acquire good title (Phillips v Brooks; Lewis v Averay).

n.0: Identity is not automatically fundamental in a face-to-face sale; the presumption is the opposite.
n.1: Payment by cheque does not render the contract unaffected; the fraud makes it voidable.
n.3: The mere fact the rogue was dishonest does not make the contract void for mistake.
n.4: Face-to-face identity mistakes generally render the contract voidable, not automatically void.

2.q: A director learns, through their position, of a valuable business opportunity in which the company would be interested, and then takes that opportunity for themselves personally, without the company's informed consent, profiting from it. The company complains that the director has breached a general duty. The director argues that the company might not have pursued the opportunity anyway. The court considers the relevant directors' duty under the Companies Act 2006. The opportunity had come to the director's attention only because of their role within the company. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The duty to declare an interest in an existing transaction with the company (s.182) on these facts.
The duty to avoid a situation in which the director's interests conflict with the company's (s.175).
The duty to exercise independent judgement in performing the role (s.173).
The duty to act within the company's constitution and for proper purposes (s.171).
The duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the role (s.174).
2.w: Under s.175 Companies Act 2006, a director must avoid situations in which they have, or can have, a direct or indirect interest that conflicts, or may conflict, with the interests of the company — including the exploitation of property, information or opportunity — regardless of whether the company could have taken advantage of it.

n.0: Section 182 concerns declaring interests in existing transactions.
n.2: Section 173 concerns independent judgement.
n.3: Section 171 concerns constitutional limits.
n.4: Section 174 concerns care and skill, not conflicts.

2.q: A public body proposes to make a decision that will adversely affect an individual's interests, but does so without telling the individual what is being considered or giving them any chance to respond before the decision is taken. The individual challenges the decision. A solicitor is asked about the individual's entitlement to be heard before an adverse decision is made. The solicitor considers the right to a fair hearing in procedural fairness. The person only learned of the decision after it had already been taken against them. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A person is entitled to a full court trial before any administrative decision is made.
A person may be heard only after the decision has already been made against them.
The right to be heard applies only in criminal proceedings, never in administrative decisions on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A person has no right to be heard before a public body makes a decision affecting them.
Fairness generally requires that a person affected be given notice and a fair opportunity to make representations before an adverse decision.
2.w: The common-law rules of natural justice require procedural fairness, including that a person whose interests are adversely affected should generally be given notice of what is proposed and a fair opportunity to make representations before the decision is made. What fairness requires varies with the context.

n.0: Fairness requires a fair opportunity to be heard, not necessarily a full court trial.
n.1: The opportunity to be heard should come before, not only after, the decision.
n.2: Fairness applies to administrative decisions, not only criminal proceedings.
n.3: There is generally a right to be heard before an adverse decision.

2.q: A district judge is case managing a civil claim and must apply the guiding principle that underpins the Civil Procedure Rules when giving directions and making case management decisions. Counsel refers the judge to the fundamental principle stated at the very start of the rules. The judge is exercising case management powers. The parties are pressing competing applications and each accuses the other of running up disproportionate costs, and the judge, before ruling, wants to anchor the decision in the guiding principle the rule-makers placed at the very front of the Civil Procedure Rules to govern how the court manages litigation. Which of the following best describes the overriding objective of the Civil Procedure Rules?
o: To ensure the claimant always succeeds if a claim is issued on these facts.
To decide cases as slowly as necessary to avoid any error.
To resolve every case by a full trial regardless of cost.
To enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost.
To give priority to the wealthier party's convenience.
2.w: The overriding objective of the Civil Procedure Rules is to enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost. This includes ensuring the parties are on an equal footing, saving expense, dealing with cases proportionately, expeditiously and fairly, and allotting an appropriate share of the court's resources.

n.0: The objective is to deal with cases justly, not to guarantee the claimant's success.
n.1: Cases are to be dealt with expeditiously, not as slowly as possible.
n.2: Proportionality is central; not every case requires a full trial regardless of cost.
n.4: The objective promotes equal footing, not the wealthier party's convenience.

2.q: A defendant negligently causes a claimant a leg injury which leaves the claimant with a slightly weakened leg. Some time later, the claimant, well aware of the weakness, chooses to descend a steep staircase that has no handrail, in an unreasonable way and without any need to do so, and falls, suffering a much more serious injury. The original defendant accepts responsibility for the first injury but denies responsibility for the second. The claimant argues the whole chain of loss flows from the original negligence. The defendant says the claimant's own conduct broke the chain. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The original defendant is liable for all later injuries, whatever the claimant subsequently chooses to do.
The chain of causation can only ever be broken by the act of a third party, and never by the claimant.
The claimant's own unreasonable conduct may break the chain of causation for the later, more serious injury.
The claimant's conduct is irrelevant, because the defendant's original negligence started the sequence of events.
The defendant is liable for the second injury only if it was more serious than the first injury.
2.w: The chain of causation may be broken by the claimant's own conduct where that conduct is so unreasonable as to be regarded as a new intervening cause (McKew v Holland). The claimant's unreasonable act in descending the staircase may relieve the defendant of liability for the later injury.

n.0: The defendant is not automatically liable for all subsequent injuries.
n.1: The claimant's own act can break the chain, not only a third party's act.
n.3: The claimant's own unreasonable conduct is very relevant to legal causation.
n.4: The break in causation does not turn on which injury was more serious.

2.q: A solicitor is found, following a full investigation and a contested hearing, to have deliberately taken money from the client account for their own personal use and to have created a series of false ledger entries over many months in order to conceal what they had been doing. The matter comes before the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal, which finds as a fact that the solicitor acted dishonestly. In mitigation, the solicitor points to their previously unblemished record, the severe personal financial pressures they were under at the time, and the fact that the money has since been repaid in full. The tribunal considers the appropriate sanction. Which of the following best describes the likely outcome?
o: The tribunal has no power to strike off a solicitor and can only refer the matter back to the firm.
The solicitor will receive no more than a written rebuke, given their previously unblemished record.
A finding of dishonesty will ordinarily lead to the solicitor being struck off, save in exceptional circumstances.
The solicitor will simply be fined, because repaying the money in full cures the dishonesty entirely.
The solicitor cannot be struck off unless a criminal court has first convicted them of theft.
2.w: Proven dishonesty is treated with the utmost seriousness. Following the approach in Bolton v Law Society, a solicitor who has acted dishonestly will almost invariably be struck off the roll, save in exceptional circumstances, to maintain public confidence in the profession.

n.0: The SDT does have power to strike a solicitor off the roll.
n.1: A rebuke is not an adequate response to proven dishonesty of this kind.
n.3: Repayment mitigates loss but does not undo the dishonesty or avoid striking off.
n.4: The tribunal's jurisdiction does not depend on a prior criminal conviction.

2.q: A new client instructs a firm on the purchase of a residential property and, on the very first attendance, offers to pay £5,000 towards the firm's fees in cash. The fee-earner, keen to get the matter moving, accepts the cash without carrying out any check on the client's identity and without making any enquiry at all into the source of the funds, and the transaction then proceeds towards exchange. Some weeks later the firm's money laundering reporting officer reviews the file and questions the way in which the retainer was set up. Which of the following best explains the breach under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017?
o: Customer due diligence under the Regulations is only required where the client is a company rather than an individual person.
Due diligence checks are optional in any case where the firm expects a long-standing relationship with the client.
A solicitor is entitled to assume that a new client is honest and so need not carry out any identity checks on them.
Customer due diligence, including identity checks, is mandatory here for conveyancing, so accepting the funds without them was a breach.
Cash payments below £10,000 are exempt, so no customer due diligence was required before accepting the money on these facts.
2.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require customer due diligence, including identity verification, when a business relationship is established in a relevant activity such as conveyancing. There is no blanket cash threshold that removes the obligation on these facts.

n.0: Customer due diligence applies to individual clients as well as to companies.
n.1: An expected long relationship does not dispense with due diligence at the outset.
n.2: A solicitor may not simply assume honesty; the Regulations require positive verification.
n.4: There is no general exemption for cash under £10,000 that removes the CDD obligation here.

2.q: A member of the public asks a solicitor about the composition of the UK Parliament and how the members of the principal, elected chamber come to hold their seats. They understand that this chamber is central to the democratic legitimacy of law-making. The solicitor considers the composition of the House of Commons and general elections. They were curious about how the people in the main chamber actually came to sit there. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The House of Commons is composed of judges chosen by the government.
The House of Commons is composed of Members of Parliament elected from constituencies at general elections.
The House of Commons is composed entirely of hereditary peers.
The House of Commons is composed of members appointed for life by the monarch.
The House of Commons is composed of members selected at random from the electorate on these facts.
2.w: The House of Commons is the elected chamber of Parliament, made up of Members of Parliament each returned for a constituency at a general election under the first-past-the-post system. Its elected character underpins the democratic legitimacy of the legislature.

n.0: The Commons is not composed of government-chosen judges.
n.2: Hereditary peers sit (in limited numbers) in the Lords, not the Commons.
n.3: MPs are elected, not appointed for life by the monarch.
n.4: MPs are elected, not selected at random.

2.q: On a company's insolvent liquidation the liquidator discovers that, before the liquidation, the business had been carried on with the actual intention of defrauding creditors, and that a particular person was knowingly a party to carrying on the business in that way. The liquidator wishes to hold that person personally liable. The court considers fraudulent trading under the Insolvency Act 1986. Money and assets had been siphoned out of the company while its creditors went unpaid. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Only the company itself, and never any individual, can be liable for fraudulent trading.
Fraudulent trading liability arises only where the company was in fact solvent throughout on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Fraudulent trading is a purely civil matter and can never give rise to criminal liability.
Fraudulent trading requires no intention to defraud and is the same as wrongful trading.
A person knowingly party to carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors may be made personally liable for fraudulent trading.
2.w: Under s.213 Insolvency Act 1986, if in the course of winding up it appears that the business was carried on with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, the court may order those knowingly party to it to contribute to the assets. There is also a related criminal offence of fraudulent trading.

n.0: Individuals knowingly party to it can be personally liable.
n.1: It arises in the context of insolvency/winding up, not where the company was solvent throughout.
n.2: Fraudulent trading can also be a criminal offence, not purely civil.
n.3: Fraudulent trading requires intent to defraud, unlike wrongful trading.

2.q: A defendant is charged with an either-way offence and appears in the magistrates' court. The court must go through a particular process to determine whether the case will be dealt with in the magistrates' court or the Crown Court, starting with the defendant indicating their plea. The defendant's solicitor explains the procedure. The solicitor considers plea before venue and allocation for an either-way offence. The defendant wanted to understand whether the case would stay in the magistrates' court or go higher. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The magistrates alone decide the court of trial and the defendant has no say at all.
The defendant must be tried in the magistrates' court whatever the circumstances.
The prosecution alone chooses the court of trial for an either-way offence.
An either-way offence is automatically sent to the Crown Court without any plea or allocation on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The defendant indicates a plea; if not guilty, the court decides allocation, and the defendant may elect Crown Court trial if the magistrates accept jurisdiction.
2.w: For an either-way offence, there is first a plea before venue: the defendant indicates plea. If they indicate not guilty (or no plea), the court conducts allocation, deciding whether the case is suitable for summary trial; if the magistrates accept jurisdiction, the defendant may consent to summary trial or elect trial by jury in the Crown Court.

n.0: The defendant has a say (electing Crown Court trial), so the magistrates do not decide alone.
n.1: The defendant may elect Crown Court trial, so magistrates' trial is not compulsory.
n.2: The choice is not the prosecution's alone.
n.3: An either-way offence is not automatically sent up without plea and allocation.

2.q: An offender has been convicted of an offence and the court is considering whether to impose a custodial sentence. The defendant's solicitor argues that imprisonment is not justified in this case. The court must apply the correct test before it can impose a prison sentence. The solicitor considers the custody threshold for an adult offender. The offending was on the borderline between a community penalty and a short custodial term. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A custodial sentence may be imposed only where the offence is so serious that neither a fine nor a community sentence can be justified.
A custodial sentence must be imposed for every offence of which a defendant is convicted.
There is no threshold for custody, and the judge may imprison for any offence at will.
A custodial sentence may be imposed only where the offender has previous convictions.
A custodial sentence may be imposed whenever the victim asks the court to imprison the offender on these facts as a general rule.
2.w: The custody threshold provides that a court must not pass a custodial sentence unless it is of the opinion that the offence (or the combination of the offence and associated offences) was so serious that neither a fine alone nor a community sentence can be justified for it.

n.1: Custody is not mandatory for every conviction.
n.2: There is a custody threshold; the judge cannot imprison for any offence at will.
n.3: The threshold turns on seriousness, not solely on previous convictions.
n.4: The victim's wishes do not determine whether the threshold is met.

2.q: A firm's bookkeeper is classifying the various receipts of the firm and needs to identify which money counts as the firm's own 'office money', as distinct from client money, because office money is handled differently under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm has billed some clients for its fees. The bookkeeper considers the meaning of office money. The firm has delivered bills to several clients for completed work, holds sums to meet its own office overheads such as rent and salaries, and also holds money for ongoing matters, and the bookkeeper needs to isolate which of these belongs to the firm itself. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Office money is the firm's own money, such as money to pay the firm's own expenses or billed profit costs.
Office money means any money held for a client on account of future costs.
Office money means client money that has not yet been paid into the client account on these facts.
Office money means money held for a third party in a transaction.
Office money means money held by the firm as trustee for a beneficiary.
2.w: Office money is money that belongs to the firm itself — for example money to meet the firm's own running costs, and money the firm is entitled to for costs once a bill has been delivered. It is kept in the office account, separate from client money.

n.1: Money held on account of a client's future costs is client money, not office money.
n.2: Client money remains client money even before it is banked.
n.3: Money held for a third party is client money.
n.4: Money held as trustee is client money (held in a fiduciary capacity).

2.q: Following the United Kingdom's departure from the European Union, a question arises about the status of certain EU-derived law that was preserved in domestic law at the end of the implementation period. A party wishes to know what body of law now governs the point, given that the UK is no longer an EU member. The point turns on preserved EU-derived rules. The rule in question originated in EU law and was carried over into domestic law at the end of the implementation period, and with the UK now outside the EU the party wants to understand on what footing, if any, that preserved body of law continues to operate in the courts of England and Wales. Which of the following best describes the status of that preserved law within the domestic legal system?
o: It ceased to have any effect in domestic law immediately on the UK leaving the EU on these facts as a general rule.
It can only be applied by the Court of Justice of the European Union.
It automatically overrides any later Act of Parliament.
It continues to have effect domestically as assimilated (formerly retained) EU law, as modified by Parliament.
It continues to bind the UK courts exactly as EU law did before, without change.
2.w: On leaving the EU, a large body of EU-derived law was preserved in domestic law (originally 'retained EU law', now 'assimilated law'). It continues to have effect as part of domestic law, but is subject to amendment and repeal by Parliament and to changes in its status and interpretation made by domestic legislation.

n.0: EU-derived law was preserved domestically rather than ceasing to have effect immediately.
n.1: It is applied by domestic courts, not exclusively by the Court of Justice of the EU.
n.2: It does not automatically override later Acts of Parliament; Parliament remains sovereign.
n.4: It does not continue to bind exactly as before; its status and supremacy have been changed by domestic law.

2.q: A person is injured in an accident caused by another's negligence and wishes to bring a personal injury claim, but a considerable amount of time has now passed since the accident occurred. The potential defendant argues that the claim is now too old to be pursued and is barred by the passage of time. The injured person seeks advice on the time limit that applies to a personal injury claim in negligence and from when it runs. The claimant has only recently taken legal advice and is anxious about whether it is now too late to sue at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A personal injury claim can never be brought more than one year after the accident occurred.
A personal injury claim must always be brought within six years of the accident, without exception.
A personal injury claim may be brought at any time, because there is no time limit for such claims on these facts.
A personal injury claim must generally be brought within three years of the injury or of the claimant's knowledge of it.
A personal injury claim must be brought within twelve years, as for actions concerning deeds.
2.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the primary limitation period for a personal injury claim is three years, running from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the claimant's date of knowledge, subject to the court's discretion to extend the period.

n.0: The period is three years, not one year.
n.1: The personal injury period is three years, not the six-year period for ordinary contract/tort claims.
n.2: There is a time limit for personal injury claims; they cannot be brought at any time.
n.4: Twelve years applies to certain actions on deeds, not to personal injury claims.

2.q: A company proposes to allot new ordinary shares for cash to a new outside investor. Existing shareholders complain that they were not first offered the chance to take up the new shares in proportion to their existing holdings, which would preserve their percentage stakes. The company had not passed any resolution to disapply the relevant rights. The court considers pre-emption rights on the allotment of shares under the Companies Act 2006. The new shares were being issued for cash, and the existing members held their shares in fixed proportions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Existing shareholders generally have statutory pre-emption rights and must be offered the new shares first, unless disapplied.
Pre-emption rights apply only to public companies and never to private companies.
Pre-emption rights apply only where the new shares are being issued for non-cash consideration.
Existing shareholders never have any right to be offered new shares before outsiders.
The directors may always ignore pre-emption rights whenever they consider it commercially sensible on these facts as a general rule.
2.w: Under s.561 Companies Act 2006, where equity shares are allotted for cash, they must first be offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings (statutory pre-emption rights), unless those rights are excluded by the articles or disapplied by special resolution.

n.1: Pre-emption rights apply to private as well as public companies.
n.2: Statutory pre-emption applies to allotments for cash, not non-cash consideration.
n.3: Existing shareholders do generally have pre-emption rights.
n.4: Directors cannot simply ignore pre-emption rights; they must be disapplied or excluded.

2.q: A defendant charged with murder relies on loss of control. The prosecution argues that the defence must fail because the defendant did not react instantly to the trigger but had a short period before acting, and because they acted partly out of anger. The defence points out that the defendant did genuinely lose self-control. The court considers the requirements of the loss of control defence, including the relevance of delay and of a desire for revenge. The defendant had waited a short while, still seething, before finally confronting and killing the victim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Any delay at all between the trigger and the killing automatically defeats the defence.
The defence succeeds even where the defendant acted in a considered desire for revenge.
The defence always fails unless the loss of self-control was completely sudden and immediate on these facts as a general rule.
The loss of self-control need not be sudden, but the defence fails if the defendant acted in considered desire for revenge.
The defence is available only where the defendant acted entirely without any emotion.
2.w: Under the Coroners and Justice Act 2009, the loss of self-control need not be sudden, so some delay does not automatically defeat the defence. However, the defence does not apply if the defendant acted in a considered desire for revenge (s.54(4)).

n.0: Delay does not automatically defeat the defence.
n.1: A considered desire for revenge defeats the defence, so it does not succeed in that case.
n.2: Suddenness is not required, so the defence is not confined to instant reactions.
n.4: The defence does not require the absence of all emotion; it concerns loss of self-control.

2.q: A seller of a remote farm, which has never been used for sheep farming, tells a prospective buyer during negotiations that in the seller's view the land 'would probably support about 2,000 sheep'. The seller has no special knowledge of the land's carrying capacity and honestly holds that view, and the buyer knows the land has not previously been used in that way. The land in fact supports far fewer sheep, and the buyer claims misrepresentation. The buyer seeks advice on whether the statement was actionable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The statement is actionable, because the buyer relied on it in deciding whether to buy the farm.
The statement is likely a non-actionable statement of opinion, not a statement of fact, on these facts.
The statement is actionable, because a seller is always taken to guarantee the accuracy of their views.
The statement is an actionable misrepresentation, because any statement inducing a contract is one of fact.
The statement is an actionable misrepresentation, because it turned out to be inaccurate.
2.w: A genuine statement of opinion, honestly held by someone with no special knowledge and where both parties are equally able to judge, is not a statement of fact and is not actionable as a misrepresentation (Bisset v Wilkinson). The carrying-capacity estimate here is such an opinion.

n.0: Reliance alone does not make an honest opinion actionable if it is not a statement of fact.
n.2: A seller does not guarantee honest opinions where they have no special knowledge.
n.3: Not every inducing statement is one of fact; opinions and mere puffs are excluded.
n.4: Mere inaccuracy of an honest opinion does not convert it into an actionable misstatement of fact.

2.q: A defendant negligently injures the claimant, causing a modest wound. The claimant is then taken to hospital, where a doctor administers grossly negligent treatment that is completely outside the range of any competent care, and it is this second, egregious act which causes the claimant's much more serious final condition. The original defendant argues that the doctor's grossly negligent treatment broke the chain of causation, so that the original defendant is not responsible for the more serious harm. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The original defendant is always liable for all consequences, because nothing can break the chain of causation.
A grossly negligent intervening medical act may break the chain of causation, relieving the original defendant of liability for the later harm.
The original defendant remains liable for everything, because the claimant would not have been in hospital but for the original wound.
The chain is broken only where the claimant deliberately injured themselves after the accident.
The chain of causation is broken by any medical treatment at all, however careful, that the claimant receives.
2.w: An intervening act (novus actus interveniens) may break the chain of causation where it is sufficiently independent and unreasonable. Medical treatment usually does not break the chain, but grossly negligent treatment, so far outside competent care, can do so, relieving the original defendant of liability for the additional harm.

n.0: An intervening act can break the chain; the original defendant is not liable come what may.
n.2: 'But for' the wound is not enough; a sufficiently unreasonable intervening act can still break legal causation.
n.3: A grossly negligent third-party act, not only self-harm, can break the chain.
n.4: Ordinary or merely careless medical treatment does not break the chain; only grossly negligent treatment may.

2.q: The government proposes to take a significant action, such as entering into a treaty with another state or deploying the armed forces, relying on powers that do not derive from any statute. A commentator asks what the legal source of such powers is. The powers are non-statutory executive powers exercised in the name of the Crown. The government relies on them for foreign affairs and defence. The government is proposing to do something significant on the international and defence stage, entering a treaty or committing the armed forces, and points out that it relies for this not on any Act of Parliament but on longstanding powers exercised in the name of the Crown, prompting the question of their legal source. Which of the following best describes the source of these powers?
o: The direct authority of the electorate expressed at a general election.
The inherent legislative power of the courts to authorise executive action.
The royal prerogative, comprising residual non-statutory powers of the Crown exercised by ministers.
A general statutory power conferred on ministers by a single Act of Parliament on these facts.
The powers of the devolved legislatures acting collectively.
2.w: Actions such as making treaties, conducting foreign affairs, deploying the armed forces, and granting mercy derive from the royal prerogative: the residue of non-statutory powers historically vested in the Crown, now exercised in practice by ministers. The prerogative is subject to the courts' supervision and can be displaced by statute.

n.0: The powers derive from the Crown's prerogative, not directly from the electorate.
n.1: The courts do not confer such executive powers; they supervise their exercise.
n.3: These powers are prerogative powers, not a single general statutory power.
n.4: They are central executive prerogative powers, not powers of the devolved legislatures.

2.q: A potential applicant wishes to bring a claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, but a grant of representation to the estate was taken out some time ago, and time has been passing. The applicant is concerned about a time limit for bringing the claim. The court considers the time limit for a claim under the 1975 Act. The applicant had only recently learned of the death, with the grant taken out months earlier. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claim must be brought within six years of the date of the deceased's death.
A claim must generally be brought within six months of the grant of representation, though the court may permit a late claim.
There is no time limit at all for bringing a claim under the 1975 Act.
A claim must be brought before the grant of representation is ever taken out.
A claim may be brought at any time until the estate has been fully distributed on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
2.w: An application under the 1975 Act must generally be made within six months of the date on which the grant of representation was first taken out. The court has a discretion to allow an application to be made after that period in appropriate cases.

n.0: The period runs from the grant (six months), not six years from death.
n.2: There is a time limit; it is not open-ended.
n.3: The claim is made after the grant, within six months of it, not before it.
n.4: The general limit is six months from the grant, not merely until distribution.

2.q: A landowner, doing a friend a favour, gave the friend oral permission to keep a caravan on a corner of the landowner's field while the friend looked for somewhere permanent to live. Nothing was ever put in writing and no rent or other payment was charged. Some months later the landowner sold and transferred the whole field to a buyer, who intends to develop it. The buyer now wants the caravan removed, but the friend insists that, having been given permission to keep the caravan there, they have a right to remain which binds the new owner of the field. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The permission is an overriding interest binding the buyer because the friend is in occupation.
The permission is a restrictive covenant preventing the buyer from removing the caravan.
The permission is a bare licence, which is personal and does not bind the buyer of the land.
The permission is a lease, which gives the friend a proprietary right against the buyer.
The permission is an easement, which automatically binds the buyer as a legal interest.
2.w: A bare licence is mere permission to be on land. It is personal to the parties, creates no proprietary interest, and does not bind a purchaser of the land; the buyer can require the caravan's removal (subject to reasonable notice).

n.0: A personal licence is not an interest capable of overriding under Schedule 3, so occupation does not make it bind.
n.1: A licence is not a restrictive covenant and imposes no burden running with the land.
n.3: There is no grant of exclusive possession for a term, so it is not a lease.
n.4: Parking/keeping a caravan by permission is not an easement, and a bare licence is not a legal interest.

2.q: A person receives a jury summons and asks whether they are eligible to serve, having heard that eligibility depends on age, registration to vote and residence, subject to certain disqualifications and the right to seek excusal. The person has been summoned for jury service. They query their eligibility. Having received a summons to attend for jury service, the recipient is unsure whether they actually qualify, having gathered that it turns on matters such as age, being on the electoral register and residence, with certain people disqualified and others able to seek to be excused. Which of the following best describes eligibility for jury service?
o: Anyone of any age may be compelled to serve with no exceptions.
Only qualified lawyers are eligible to serve as jurors.
Jurors are appointed for life once they have served on one jury on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A person is generally eligible if aged 18 to 75, on the electoral register and resident as required, unless disqualified or excused.
Only property owners are eligible to serve on a jury.
2.w: To be qualified for jury service a person must generally be aged 18 to 75, be registered as a parliamentary or local government elector, and have been ordinarily resident in the UK for the required period. Certain people are disqualified (for example, due to certain criminal convictions or mental health grounds), and some may be excused or have service deferred.

n.0: There are age limits and exceptions; not everyone of any age must serve.
n.1: Jury service is not confined to qualified lawyers; ordinary citizens serve.
n.2: Jurors are not appointed for life; they serve when summoned.
n.4: Eligibility is not based on property ownership.

2.q: A settlor wishes to create a valid express private trust during their lifetime, transferring assets to trustees to hold for a group of beneficiaries. A dispute later arises as to whether a valid trust was created at all. The court examines whether the fundamental requirements for the creation of an express trust are satisfied on the facts. The settlor's adviser is asked to explain what must be established for a valid express private trust to exist. The assets were substantial, and several people claimed to be entitled under the arrangement the settlor had described. Which of the following best describes the requirements?
o: There must be a professional trustee appointed, or no valid trust can arise at all.
There must be certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter and certainty of objects.
There must simply be a signed document, whatever its contents happen to say.
There must be consideration provided by the beneficiaries to the settlor for the trust.
There must be approval of the arrangement by the court before any trust can exist.
2.w: An express private trust requires the 'three certainties' (Knight v Knight): certainty of intention to create a trust, certainty of the subject matter of the trust, and certainty of the objects (beneficiaries), together with the relevant formalities and constitution.

n.0: A professional trustee is not required for a valid trust.
n.2: A signed document is not enough; the three certainties must be present.
n.3: A trust is not a bargain; beneficiaries need give no consideration.
n.4: No prior court approval is required to create a trust.

2.q: A married couple, Mr and Mrs Hale, live together in a house which is registered in the sole name of Mr Hale. Mrs Hale made no financial contribution to the purchase and has no beneficial interest in the property, but she is concerned that Mr Hale, with whom relations have become strained, might try to sell or mortgage the home over her head without telling her. She wishes to protect her right to occupy the matrimonial home so that it is binding on any buyer or lender who deals with Mr Hale in the future. Which of the following is the correct way for her to do so?
o: By registering a notice of home rights under the Family Law Act 1996 against the title.
It cannot be protected at all, because the spouse has no beneficial interest in the home.
By relying on an overriding interest, which arises automatically from the marriage.
By registering a restriction that prevents the owning spouse from ever selling the home.
By lodging a caution, which is the only route open to a non-owning spouse.
2.w: A non-owning spouse or civil partner has statutory home rights (a right of occupation) under the Family Law Act 1996. To bind a purchaser these must be protected by entry of a notice on the register; they are not an overriding interest and marriage alone does not bind a buyer.

n.1: Home rights exist independently of any beneficial interest and can be protected.
n.2: Home rights are not overriding and do not bind a buyer automatically from the marriage.
n.3: Home rights are protected by a notice; they do not entitle the spouse to a restriction barring any sale.
n.4: Protection is by a notice of home rights, not a caution.

2.q: A trust provides for a beneficiary to receive capital 'on attaining the age of 25'. The beneficiary is currently 20 years old. A question arises about the nature of the beneficiary's interest before reaching that age, and what happens if the beneficiary were to die before 25. The gift is expressed to take effect only on the beneficiary reaching a stated age. The beneficiary has not yet reached that age. The trust document ties the gift of capital to the beneficiary reaching a particular age, the beneficiary is still some years short of it, and the family want to understand both what the beneficiary presently owns and what would happen to the entitlement were the beneficiary to die before getting there. Which of the following best describes the nature of the interest?
o: It is a contingent interest that automatically passes to the estate if the beneficiary dies at 22.
It is a vested interest that the beneficiary owns absolutely from the outset.
It is a contingent interest, which does not vest unless and until the beneficiary reaches 25.
It is no interest at all, because future interests are not recognised in trusts.
It is a vested interest defeasible only on the beneficiary's marriage.
2.w: An interest expressed to arise 'on attaining' a stated age is contingent on the beneficiary satisfying that condition. It does not vest unless and until the beneficiary reaches 25; if the beneficiary dies before then, the contingency is not met and the interest generally fails, rather than passing to the beneficiary's estate.

n.0: A contingent interest that fails does not automatically pass to the estate; the contingency was not met.
n.1: The interest is contingent, not vested absolutely from the outset.
n.3: Future (contingent) interests are recognised in trusts.
n.4: The interest is contingent on age, not a vested interest defeasible on marriage.

2.q: A solicitor is employed in the legal department of a large commercial company as an in-house solicitor, and holds a current practising certificate. A dispute arises between the company and one of its major suppliers which is likely to end up in contested court proceedings. The company wishes its own in-house solicitor to conduct that litigation on the company's behalf, so as to save the cost of instructing an external firm to do the work. The solicitor is unsure whether, as an employed solicitor rather than one in private practice, they are actually permitted to conduct litigation for their employer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An employed solicitor may act for their employer only in non-contentious matters, and never in any litigation.
An employed solicitor may conduct the litigation only if the company also instructs an external firm alongside them.
An employed solicitor may act for their employer, including conducting litigation on the employer's behalf.
An employed solicitor may conduct the litigation only after obtaining the SRA's specific prior permission to do so.
An employed solicitor may never conduct litigation, because that is reserved to solicitors in private practice.
2.w: An employed (in-house) solicitor who holds a practising certificate may provide legal services to, and act for, their employer, including exercising rights of audience and conducting litigation on the employer's behalf. Restrictions mainly concern acting for third parties, not for the employer itself.

n.0: The in-house solicitor's ability to act for the employer is not limited to non-contentious work.
n.1: There is no requirement to instruct an external firm alongside the in-house solicitor.
n.3: No specific prior SRA permission is required to act for the employer in this way.
n.4: Conducting litigation is not reserved to those in private practice; in-house solicitors may do it for their employer.

2.q: A vulnerable and frightened witness is due to give evidence at a Crown Court trial, and there is concern that giving evidence in the ordinary way, in open court in front of the defendant, would prevent them giving their best evidence. The prosecution wishes to help the witness give evidence effectively. The solicitor considers the availability of special measures for witnesses. The witness was terrified of the defendant and dreaded having to face them across the courtroom. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Special measures are available only in cases involving offences of dishonesty.
The court may direct special measures, such as a screen or a live video link, to help vulnerable or intimidated witnesses give their best evidence.
Special measures may be used only after the witness has already broken down in court.
