All witnesses must always give evidence in open court in the ordinary way, with no assistance on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Special measures are available only to the defendant and never to prosecution witnesses.
2.w: The court may grant special measures directions to assist eligible vulnerable or intimidated witnesses in giving their best evidence — for example the use of screens, giving evidence by live link, video-recorded evidence in chief, or the removal of wigs and gowns — under the Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999.

n.0: Special measures are not confined to dishonesty offences.
n.2: Special measures are arranged in advance, not only after a witness breaks down.
n.3: Not all witnesses must give evidence in the ordinary way; special measures may assist.
n.4: Special measures are for eligible witnesses generally, not only the defendant.

2.q: A firm holds confidential information from a former client that is material to a new client's matter, and there is a risk to that confidential information if it acts for the new client. The firm wishes to act for the new client and considers putting arrangements in place to protect the former client's confidential information. The firm owes a continuing duty of confidentiality to the former client. The firm wishes to act for the new client. The firm still holds confidential information from a former client that bears directly on a new client's matter, and, wanting to take on the new client without betraying the old one, it is weighing whether erecting internal safeguards would be enough to let it act consistently with its continuing duty of confidentiality. Which of the following best describes when the firm may act using an information barrier?
o: The firm may act provided it charges the new client a higher fee.
The firm may act only if effective safeguards (an information barrier) protect the confidential information and, generally, the affected clients give informed consent.
The firm may act only if the former client's matter has fully concluded, with no further safeguards needed on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The firm may act freely because the duty of confidentiality ends when the retainer ends.
The firm may never act for a new client whose matter relates to a former client.
2.w: The duty of confidentiality continues after the retainer ends. A firm must not act for a new client against a former client where it holds confidential information material to the new matter, unless effective safeguards (such as an information barrier separating those with the information) protect the confidentiality and, generally, informed consent is obtained. The former client's confidentiality outweighs the new client's interest in disclosure.

n.0: Charging a higher fee does not address the confidentiality risk.
n.2: Mere conclusion of the former matter, without safeguards, does not make it safe to act.
n.3: The duty of confidentiality does not end with the retainer; it continues.
n.4: The firm may act in some cases with proper safeguards, so 'never' is too absolute.

2.q: An elderly person with poor eyesight is asked to sign a document by someone they trust. They are told it is a minor form of one kind, when in fact it is a deed of a fundamentally different character that disposes of a valuable asset. Without reading it (being unable to do so) and relying on the misdescription, they sign. They later discover the true nature of what they signed and seek to escape it entirely. The signer was fundamentally mistaken about the very nature of the document, not merely its terms, and was not careless in the circumstances. Which of the following best describes the plea available to the signer?
o: The signer may rescind only, so a good-faith third party would still take free.
The signer has no remedy because non est factum has been abolished.
The signer may plead non est factum, so that the signature is not binding.
The signer is bound absolutely, because a signature always binds regardless of the circumstances.
The signer may rely on common mistake shared with the other party.
2.w: The plea of non est factum ('it is not my deed') may be available, exceptionally, where a signer is fundamentally mistaken as to the very nature (not merely the contents) of the document, and was not careless. If made out, the document is void, not merely voidable, so the signer is not bound. The plea is narrow and rarely succeeds.

n.0: A successful non est factum renders the document void, going further than mere rescission.
n.1: Non est factum has not been abolished; it survives as a narrow doctrine.
n.3: A signature does not always bind where non est factum is genuinely made out.
n.4: The signer's mistake is unilateral and fundamental, not a common mistake shared by both parties.

2.q: A defendant is drafting a defence in response to particulars of claim. The defence must respond to each of the claimant's allegations. The defendant fails to deal at all with one particular allegation of fact in the particulars of claim, neither admitting it, denying it, nor requiring it to be proved. The allegation was one the defence simply did not address. Working through the particulars of claim, the defence responded to most of the allegations but simply passed over one factual assertion altogether, neither accepting it, contesting it, nor putting the claimant to proof of it, and the claimant now relies on that silence. Which of the following best describes the effect of failing to deal with the allegation?
o: The court must strike out the entire defence for the omission.
The defendant is generally taken to admit the allegation not dealt with in the defence.
The allegation is automatically deemed denied because the defence was filed.
The failure has no effect provided the defence is verified by a statement of truth.
The allegation must always be proved by the claimant regardless of the defence.
2.w: Under the CPR, a defendant who fails to deal with an allegation in the defence is generally taken to admit it (subject to limited exceptions, such as where the defence sets out the nature of the case in relation to the issue). The defence should therefore state which allegations are admitted, denied, or not admitted (requiring proof).

n.0: The consequence is deemed admission of that allegation, not striking out the whole defence.
n.2: An unaddressed allegation is generally taken to be admitted, not deemed denied.
n.3: A statement of truth does not cure the failure to deal with the allegation.
n.4: Because it is taken as admitted, the claimant need not prove it.

2.q: The directors of a private company wish to call a general meeting of the members to consider a proposed ordinary resolution. They ask how much notice must be given to the members for the meeting, applying the default statutory position. The company is a private company and no shorter-notice consent has been obtained. The directors are calling a general meeting. The directors are fixing a date for a general meeting to put an ordinary resolution to the members, no one has agreed to accept the meeting on shorter notice, and they want to be sure they give the members the minimum period the default statutory rules require. Which of the following best describes the minimum notice required?
o: At least 28 clear days' notice for any general meeting.
At least 21 clear days' notice in every case without exception.
No notice is required provided a quorum happens to be present.
At least 14 clear days' notice, unless the members agree to short notice.
At least 7 clear days' notice for all private company meetings.
2.w: A general meeting of a private company may generally be called on at least 14 clear days' notice. Shorter notice is possible if agreed by a majority in number of the members holding at least the requisite percentage of the shares (90% for a private company, or higher if the articles specify). Public company AGMs require 21 days.

n.0: 28 days is not the statutory minimum for a general meeting.
n.1: 21 days is the requirement for a public company AGM, not the general private-company default.
n.2: Proper notice is required; a chance quorum does not dispense with it.
n.4: 7 days is not the default minimum notice.

2.q: A claimant wishes to challenge a public body's decision by judicial review, but some time has already passed since the decision was made, and the claimant is unsure whether they are still in time to bring the claim. A solicitor advises that judicial review has strict time requirements. The solicitor considers the time limit for bringing a claim for judicial review. The decision had been made a couple of months earlier and the claimant had been slow to act. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A claim may be brought within twelve years, as for actions concerning land.
A claim must be brought promptly and in any event within three months of the grounds arising, subject to any shorter or extended period.
A claim for judicial review may be brought at any time within six years of the decision on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A claim must be brought within 24 hours of the decision being made.
There is no time limit for bringing a claim for judicial review.
2.w: A claim for judicial review must be made promptly and in any event within three months of the date on which the grounds to make the claim first arose (with shorter periods in some contexts, such as planning). The court may extend time in limited circumstances, but delay can be fatal.

n.0: Twelve years does not apply to judicial review.
n.2: The judicial review period is three months, not six years.
n.3: The limit is three months (and promptly), not 24 hours.
n.4: There is a strict time limit for judicial review.

2.q: During an emergency, fire officers rushing to save a life carry heavy lifting equipment on an ordinary vehicle not designed for it, because no suitable vehicle is available in time. A rescuer is injured when the equipment shifts. The claimant argues the service was negligent to transport the equipment that way. In assessing breach, the court weighs the risk against the importance of the objective being pursued. The activity was undertaken to save a human life in an emergency. Which of the following best describes how the social utility of the activity affects the breach analysis?
o: The social utility of an activity is irrelevant to whether the defendant fell below the standard of care on these facts.
Any risk taken in an emergency automatically amounts to a breach of duty.
The social utility of saving life is weighed in the balance and may justify taking a risk that would otherwise be a breach.
The defendant is judged by a lower standard than ordinary care simply because it is a public service.
The only relevant factor is the seriousness of the harm, never the purpose of the activity.
2.w: Breach is assessed by weighing the magnitude of the risk (likelihood and seriousness of harm) against factors including the cost of precautions and the social utility of the defendant's conduct. Where the activity serves a valuable purpose, such as saving life in an emergency, that utility may justify running a risk that would otherwise constitute a breach.

n.0: Social utility is a recognised and relevant factor in the breach balance.
n.1: Taking a risk in an emergency is not automatically a breach; utility is weighed.
n.3: The standard remains reasonable care; the utility is weighed within it, not a lower standard.
n.4: The purpose and utility of the activity are relevant, not only the seriousness of harm.

2.q: A decorator agrees to redecorate a house for a lump sum of £5,000. The decorator completes essentially all of the work to a proper standard, but leaves a few minor defects which would cost about £150 to put right. The client, seizing on the defects, refuses to pay anything at all, arguing that the decorator has not completely performed the contract. The decorator sues for the price. The client seeks advice on whether they can withhold the whole £5,000 for these minor outstanding defects. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The client may withhold the whole price until the decorator returns and remedies every last defect.
The decorator may recover the full £5,000, and the client has no remedy for the minor defects.
The decorator may recover only if the client first agrees in writing to accept the work as done.
The decorator may recover the price less the cost of remedying the minor defects, having substantially performed.
The decorator may recover nothing at all, because the contract was not completely performed to the letter.
2.w: Where a party has substantially performed an entire obligation, subject only to minor defects, they may recover the contract price less the cost of remedying those defects (Hoenig v Isaacs). The client cannot refuse the whole price for trivial shortcomings.

n.0: The client may deduct the remedial cost but cannot withhold the entire price for minor defects.
n.1: The client is entitled to deduct the cost of the defects, so the full price is not payable.
n.2: No further written acceptance is needed once there has been substantial performance.
n.4: Substantial performance does entitle the party to payment, so recovering nothing is wrong.

2.q: After statements of case have been served, a party realises that their pleaded case needs to be changed to correct an error and to add a new allegation. The other party does not consent to the change. The party wishes to know whether, and how, they can amend their statement of case at this stage. The court considers amendments to statements of case under the Civil Procedure Rules. A key date had been pleaded wrongly and a further allegation now needed to be added to the case. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A statement of case may be amended only during the trial itself and at no other time.
A statement of case can never be amended once it has been served on the other party.
A statement of case may be amended only if the amendment reduces the value of the claim.
After service, a statement of case may be amended only with the consent of all parties or the court's permission.
A party may amend its statement of case freely at any time without consent or permission on these facts.
2.w: Under the CPR, a party may amend a statement of case at any time before it has been served without permission. Once it has been served, it may be amended only with the written consent of all the other parties or with the permission of the court.

n.0: Amendment is not confined to the trial itself.
n.1: A served statement of case can be amended, with consent or the court's permission.
n.2: Amendment is not limited to those that reduce the value of the claim.
n.4: Amendment after service is not free; consent or permission is required.

2.q: An individual is dissatisfied with a decision made by a government department about a statutory entitlement, such as a welfare benefit or tax matter, and wishes to challenge it before a specialist body rather than the ordinary courts. A colleague mentions the tribunals system. The challenge concerns a specialist administrative decision. The decision concerns a statutory entitlement of exactly the sort Parliament has assigned to specialist adjudication rather than the ordinary courts, and the individual, wanting both an initial hearing before people expert in the field and a route to challenge an adverse result, asks how the tiered system fits together. Which of the following best describes the structure of the tribunals system?
o: All such disputes are decided at first instance in the Crown Court.
The First-tier Tribunal decides such cases, with onward appeal (usually on a point of law) to the Upper Tribunal.
Tribunals have no appeal structure; their decisions are always final.
Tribunal decisions can only ever be challenged by judicial review, never by appeal on these facts as a general rule.
Such disputes must be brought in the County Court like ordinary civil claims.
2.w: Under the unified tribunals structure, specialist disputes (such as tax, social security and immigration matters) are decided at first instance in the First-tier Tribunal, with an onward right of appeal, usually on a point of law, to the Upper Tribunal, which is a superior court of record. This provides a specialist, tiered system distinct from the ordinary courts.

n.0: Such administrative disputes are not decided at first instance in the Crown Court.
n.2: There is an appeal structure; tribunal decisions are not always final.
n.3: There is a statutory right of appeal to the Upper Tribunal, not only judicial review.
n.4: These disputes go to the tribunal, not the County Court as ordinary civil claims.

2.q: A company limited by shares proposes to return value to its shareholders in a way that would reduce the capital available to meet creditors' claims. A creditor is concerned, relying on the principle that a company's share capital is a fund that must in general be maintained for the protection of creditors. The court considers the doctrine of maintenance of share capital under company law. The proposal would hand cash back to the members while leaving creditors with a thinner buffer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Share capital may be distributed to shareholders whenever the directors think it appropriate on these facts as a general rule.
A company may return its share capital to shareholders freely at any time it chooses.
Capital maintenance applies only to public companies and never to private companies.
As a general rule a company must maintain its capital and may not return it to shareholders except by permitted procedures.
There is no principle of capital maintenance in modern company law at all.
2.w: The capital maintenance doctrine provides that a company's share capital is, in general, to be maintained for the benefit of creditors, so it may not be returned to shareholders except through permitted procedures (such as a properly conducted reduction of capital, or a buyback complying with the Act).

n.0: Directors cannot simply distribute capital at will.
n.1: Capital cannot be returned freely; permitted procedures must be followed.
n.2: Capital maintenance applies to private companies too, albeit with some more flexible procedures.
n.4: Capital maintenance remains a principle of modern company law.

2.q: A 15-year-old is arrested and detained at a police station and is to be interviewed about an alleged offence. The custody officer is aware that special safeguards apply to the interviewing of juveniles and certain vulnerable suspects. The young person's solicitor asks who must be present to support the juvenile during the interview. The solicitor considers the requirement for an appropriate adult under PACE Code C. The teenager was frightened and had no adult with them when first brought into the station. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A juvenile may be interviewed alone, with no adult or solicitor present, to speed up the process on these facts.
An appropriate adult is required only for suspects aged under 10 years.
A juvenile requires only a solicitor and never any appropriate adult.
An appropriate adult replaces the need for the juvenile to have any legal advice.
A juvenile (or vulnerable suspect) must have an appropriate adult present for the interview, in addition to any solicitor.
2.w: Under PACE Code C, a juvenile (a person under 18) or a mentally vulnerable suspect must have an appropriate adult present. The appropriate adult's role is to support and advise the suspect and observe fair conduct; this is in addition to, and does not replace, the right to legal advice.

n.0: A juvenile cannot be interviewed alone without the required safeguards.
n.1: The safeguard applies to under-18s (and vulnerable adults), not only under-10s.
n.2: An appropriate adult is required in addition to a solicitor, not instead of one.
n.3: The appropriate adult does not replace the right to legal advice.

2.q: A defendant in a criminal trial declines to give evidence and argues that it is not for the defendant to prove innocence. The court must direct itself on who bears the burden of proving the elements of the offence. No statutory reverse burden applies to the offence charged. The defendant has chosen to say nothing in evidence and rests on the contention that the case against them has not been made out, so the court must be clear about which side carries the obligation to prove the elements of the offence and how the presumption of innocence operates here. Which of the following best describes where the legal burden of proof generally lies in a criminal trial?
o: The court itself bears the burden of establishing the facts.
The defendant bears the burden of proving innocence.
The burden lies on whichever party called the first witness.
The prosecution bears the burden of proving the defendant's guilt.
The burden is shared equally between prosecution and defence.
2.w: Reflecting the presumption of innocence, the legal burden of proving the elements of a criminal offence generally rests on the prosecution, which must make the tribunal sure of guilt. The defendant is not required to prove innocence, save where a statute expressly places a specific burden on the defence.

n.0: The court does not bear a burden of proof; it adjudicates.
n.1: The defendant does not generally have to prove innocence.
n.2: The burden does not depend on who called the first witness.
n.4: The burden is not shared equally; it rests on the prosecution.

2.q: A person who is not a trustee helps a trustee to commit a breach of trust, for example by helping to channel misapplied trust funds, though that person never receives the trust property for their own benefit. The beneficiaries seek to hold the helper personally liable. The claim is one of accessory liability for assisting the breach. The helper did not receive trust property beneficially. The outsider never kept any of the trust money for themselves but played an active part in moving it along and putting the breach into effect, and the beneficiaries are seeking to hold that helper personally accountable as an accessory to what the trustee did. Which of the following best describes what must be shown for dishonest assistance?
o: That the person received trust property beneficially with knowledge of the breach.
That the person was a trustee or fiduciary of the property in question.
That the person genuinely believed their conduct was honest, whatever the objective standard on these facts.
That the person dishonestly assisted in a breach of trust, dishonesty being assessed objectively by ordinary standards.
That the person was negligent in failing to detect the breach of trust.
2.w: Dishonest assistance imposes personal liability on an accessory who dishonestly assists a breach of trust, even without receiving trust property. Dishonesty is judged by the objective standards of ordinary honest people, applied to the defendant's actual knowledge of the facts; the defendant's own view that they were honest is not the test.

n.0: Beneficial receipt with knowledge is knowing receipt, a different claim.
n.1: The defendant need not be a trustee or fiduciary to be liable as an accessory.
n.2: The defendant's own belief in their honesty does not determine liability; the standard is objective.
n.4: Mere negligence is insufficient; dishonesty is required.

2.q: Ms Yates and Mr Zaman bought a house together as an unmarried couple, taking the legal title in both their names as trustees and holding the beneficial interest as tenants in common in equal shares. Their relationship has since broken down. Ms Yates has moved out and wants the house sold so that she can realise her share, which she needs for a deposit on somewhere new. Mr Zaman has remained living in the house and refuses to agree to a sale. Ms Yates applies to the court under the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 for an order for sale. Which of the following best describes the court's powers on the application?
o: The court has no power to intervene in a dispute between co-owners of land.
The court must physically partition the house and the land between the two co-owners, dividing it into separate parcels.
The court may order a sale, refuse it, or regulate occupation, weighing the statutory factors.
The court may only award financial compensation to the co-owner who wishes to sell.
The court must order an immediate sale whenever any co-owner asks for one.
2.w: Under s.14 TOLATA 1996 the court may make such order as it thinks fit relating to the trustees' functions, including ordering or refusing a sale and regulating occupation. Section 15 lists the factors to weigh (the intentions and purpose of the trust, the welfare of any minor occupier, and the interests of any secured creditor).

n.0: The court plainly has jurisdiction to resolve co-ownership disputes under s.14.
n.1: Physical partition is not the remedy the court must impose; it exercises the s.14 discretion.
n.3: The court's powers are not limited to compensation; it can order sale or regulate occupation.
n.4: A sale is not automatic; the court weighs the s.15 factors and may refuse it.

2.q: Two people own land as beneficial joint tenants. One of them dies. The survivor and the deceased's family dispute what happens to the deceased's interest, the family arguing it passes under the deceased's will. The co-owners held as joint tenants, not tenants in common, and no severance occurred. One joint tenant has died. The couple held the property as beneficial joint tenants with no severance ever having taken place, and now that one of them has died a dispute has erupted between the survivor and the deceased's relatives, who insist the deceased's share should pass under the will. Which of the following best describes the effect of the death?
o: The deceased's interest passes on the deceased's intestacy to their next of kin.
The deceased's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant by the right of survivorship.
The deceased's interest passes to the Crown as ownerless property.
The deceased's interest passes under the deceased's will to their chosen beneficiary on these facts.
The deceased's interest is divided equally between the survivor and the estate.
2.w: Under a joint tenancy the right of survivorship (jus accrescendi) applies: on the death of a joint tenant, their interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s), outside the deceased's will or intestacy. Survivorship takes precedence over any testamentary gift, so the deceased cannot leave their joint-tenancy interest by will (unless they severed it before death).

n.0: It does not pass on intestacy; survivorship takes it to the co-owner.
n.2: It passes to the surviving joint tenant, not to the Crown.
n.3: A joint tenant's interest does not pass under their will; survivorship applies.
n.4: It is not split between survivor and estate; the whole passes by survivorship.

2.q: Two parties have a contract which contains a clause providing that any dispute between them is to be referred to arbitration rather than litigated in court. One party nonetheless issues court proceedings in respect of a dispute covered by the clause, and the other party wishes to hold them to the agreement to arbitrate. The court considers the effect of an arbitration agreement when one party sues in court, under the Arbitration Act 1996. The contract clearly required disputes of this kind to be resolved by arbitration, not by litigation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court will ignore the arbitration agreement unless both parties now agree to arbitrate on these facts.
The court will strike out the claim entirely, leaving the claimant with no remedy at all.
The court will generally stay the court proceedings so the dispute can be referred to arbitration as agreed.
The arbitration clause has no effect and the court will simply hear the claim as normal.
Arbitration agreements are unlawful, so the court proceedings must always continue.
2.w: Under s.9 of the Arbitration Act 1996, where a party brings court proceedings in respect of a matter that the parties agreed to refer to arbitration, the other party may apply for a stay, and the court will stay the proceedings (unless the arbitration agreement is null, void, inoperative or incapable of being performed), so the dispute goes to arbitration.

n.0: The court gives effect to the existing agreement; fresh agreement is not required.
n.1: The claim is stayed, not struck out, leaving arbitration as the forum.
n.3: The arbitration clause is given effect; the court does not simply hear the claim.
n.4: Arbitration agreements are lawful and enforceable, not unlawful.

2.q: Between exchange and completion of a purchase of registered land, the buyer holds a contract but is not yet the registered proprietor. The buyer's solicitor is concerned to protect the buyer's interest under the contract against the risk of the seller attempting to sell or mortgage the property to someone else before completion. The solicitor considers how the buyer's contractual (estate contract) interest can be protected on the register. The seller was known to be in financial difficulty, raising a risk of a competing dealing. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer is automatically registered as proprietor on exchange, so no protection is needed.
The buyer can only protect the interest by taking physical possession of the property.
The buyer protects the interest by lodging the deposit with the Land Registry.
The buyer's contractual interest cannot be protected on the register in any way before completion.
The buyer may protect the estate contract by entering a notice against the seller's registered title.
2.w: On exchange the buyer acquires an equitable interest (an estate contract) in the land. For registered land this can be protected by entering a notice on the charges register of the seller's title, which protects the buyer's priority against a subsequent purchaser or chargee.

n.0: The buyer is not registered as proprietor on exchange; protection may be prudent.
n.1: The interest is protected by a register entry, not merely by taking possession.
n.2: Protection is by entering a notice, not by lodging the deposit at the Land Registry.
n.3: The buyer's estate contract can be protected by a notice; it is not unprotectable.

2.q: For more than 30 years the owner of a farm has grazed their sheep on a neighbouring landowner's meadow, doing so openly, as of right, and without the neighbour's permission, and the neighbour never objected at any time throughout that long period. The meadow has now been sold to a new owner, who wishes to put a stop to the grazing and argues that the farmer has no right to continue turning animals out on the land. The farmer seeks advice on the nature of any right they have acquired over the meadow, and whether it binds the new owner. Which of the following best describes it?
o: No right at all, because a right to graze can only be granted expressly by deed, on these facts.
A licence to graze, which ended automatically when the meadow changed hands.
An easement of grazing, which cannot bind a successor to the servient land.
A profit à prendre of pasture acquired by prescription, binding the new owner of the meadow.
An overriding interest in the meadow arising from the presence of the sheep.
2.w: A right to take the produce of another's land, such as grazing (pasture), is a profit à prendre. It can be acquired by long use as of right (prescription) and, once acquired as a legal profit, binds successors to the servient land.

n.0: A profit can be acquired by prescription, not only by express deed.
n.1: Use as of right is not a mere licence and does not end on a sale of the servient land.
n.2: Grazing is a right to take produce and so is a profit, not an ordinary easement, and a legal profit binds successors.
n.4: A profit is not an interest that overrides simply because animals are present; it binds as a legal profit acquired by prescription.

2.q: For more than 30 years the members of the Okafor household have fished a stretch of a neighbouring landowner's private lake, doing so openly, as of right, and without the landowner's permission, and the previous landowner never objected at any point during that period. The land around the lake has now been sold to a new owner, who has put up notices and wishes to stop the fishing altogether. The household wishes to continue fishing and seeks advice on what right, if any, they have acquired over the lake through their long and uninterrupted use, and whether that right is binding on the new owner. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A profit à prendre of fishing (piscary) acquired by prescription.
No right at all, because a right to fish can only be granted expressly by deed.
An easement of fishing, which cannot bind any successor to the servient land.
A licence to fish, which ended automatically when the lake was sold.
An overriding interest in the lake arising from the act of fishing itself.
2.w: A right to take fish from another's water is a profit à prendre (a profit of piscary). It can be acquired by long use as of right (prescription), and once acquired as a legal profit it binds successors to the servient land.

n.1: A profit can be acquired by prescription, not only by express deed.
n.2: Fishing is the taking of produce, so it is a profit, and a legal profit binds successors.
n.3: Use as of right is not a mere licence and does not end on a sale of the servient land.
n.4: The right is a profit acquired by prescription; it does not depend on overriding through occupation.

2.q: A firm is instructed to act for a private limited company on a substantial commercial matter. One of the company's directors, who happens to give the firm its day-to-day instructions on the matter, privately approaches the solicitor and asks them to structure the transaction in a particular way that would benefit that director personally, at the direct expense of the company itself. The solicitor is uneasy and is unsure to whom their professional duties are actually owed in this situation, and how they ought to respond to the director's personal request. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The client is the board and all the shareholders jointly, so the solicitor needs every shareholder's consent to each step.
The client is whichever director gives the instructions, so the solicitor must act on that director's personal wishes here.
The client is the company, a separate legal person, so the solicitor must act in its interests, not a director's personal interests.
There is no identifiable client at all, because a company cannot itself be the client of a firm of solicitors.
The client is the majority shareholder, whose personal interests the solicitor must prefer to those of the company itself.
2.w: A company is a separate legal person and is itself the client. Instructions are given through its authorised officers, but the solicitor's duties are owed to the company, not to individual directors or shareholders in their personal capacities.

n.0: The solicitor takes instructions through authorised officers and need not obtain every shareholder's consent to each step.
n.1: A director gives instructions on the company's behalf, but is not personally the client.
n.3: A company can be, and here is, the client of the solicitor.
n.4: Duties are owed to the company, not to the majority shareholder personally.

2.q: A successful non-lawyer entrepreneur wishes to invest in, and to take a substantial ownership stake in, a new business that will provide legal services directly to the public, and also to sit on its management board, working alongside the qualified solicitors who will actually carry out the legal work. The entrepreneur has been told by an acquaintance that non-lawyers are completely barred from owning any part of a legal practice in England and Wales. A solicitor is asked whether there is in fact any lawful structure through which a non-lawyer may own and help to manage a provider of legal services. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: This is permitted only if the non-lawyer first qualifies as a solicitor before taking any ownership stake.
This is permitted only where the non-lawyer holds a minority stake of no more than a fixed small percentage.
This is permitted through a licensed alternative business structure (ABS), which allows non-lawyers to own and manage it.
This is not permitted in any circumstances, because only qualified lawyers may ever own a legal services provider.
This is permitted without any regulation, because ownership of legal businesses is entirely unrestricted.
2.w: The Legal Services Act 2007 introduced alternative business structures (ABSs), which may be licensed to allow non-lawyers to own and manage bodies providing legal services, subject to approval and regulation. Non-lawyer ownership is therefore possible, but only through a licensed and regulated ABS.

n.0: The non-lawyer need not qualify as a solicitor; the ABS regime permits their involvement.
n.1: There is no fixed small percentage cap; a licensed ABS can permit substantial non-lawyer ownership.
n.3: Non-lawyer ownership is possible through a licensed ABS, so it is not barred outright.
n.4: Ownership of legal businesses is regulated, not unrestricted; a licence is required.

2.q: A judgment creditor has a money judgment that remains unpaid. The creditor learns that the debtor holds a substantial credit balance in a bank account, that is, the bank owes money to the debtor. The creditor wishes to intercept that money to satisfy the judgment. A third party (the bank) owes money to the judgment debtor. The creditor wishes to have that money paid to it instead. The creditor has discovered that, while the debtor pleads poverty, the debtor is in fact holding a healthy credit balance at its bank, so that the bank effectively owes the debtor money, and the creditor wants that money diverted to itself before the debtor can move or spend it. Which of the following best identifies the appropriate enforcement method?
o: A third party debt order requiring the bank to pay the debt to the creditor.
An order for the debtor's committal to prison for non-payment on these facts.
A charging order over the debtor's land.
A writ of control against the debtor's goods.
An attachment of earnings order against the debtor's salary.
2.w: A third party debt order (formerly garnishee order) requires a third party who owes money to the judgment debtor, such as the debtor's bank holding a credit balance, to pay that money directly to the judgment creditor to satisfy the judgment. An interim order is made first, followed by a final order after a hearing.

n.1: Committal is not the route for enforcing an ordinary money judgment of this kind.
n.2: A charging order secures against land, not a bank debt.
n.3: A writ of control enforces against goods, not money held by a third party.
n.4: Attachment of earnings targets wages from an employer, not a bank balance.

2.q: An individual carries on a business on their own account as a sole trader, without forming any company or partnership. The business runs into financial difficulty and cannot pay its trade creditors. The creditors wish to know whether they can look beyond the business assets to the individual's personal assets to satisfy the debts. The sole trader argues that only the business, and not they personally, is liable. The court considers the liability of a sole trader for business debts. The debts were considerable and the business had few assets of its own with which to meet them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The sole trader has no personal liability at all, as the business is a separate legal person.
The sole trader is liable only if they acted dishonestly in running the business.
The sole trader's liability is limited to the assets they invested in the business.
The sole trader is personally liable without limit for the debts of the business.
The sole trader is liable only up to the nominal value of any shares they hold.
2.w: A sole trader and their business are not separate legal persons. The sole trader is personally liable, without limit, for all the debts and obligations of the business, so creditors may look to the trader's personal assets.

n.0: A sole trader business is not a separate legal person; there is no limited liability.
n.1: Liability arises from the debts, not only where the trader acted dishonestly.
n.2: A sole trader's liability is not limited to what they invested.
n.4: A sole trader has no shares; liability is personal and unlimited.

2.q: A firm receives £2,000 from a client at the outset of a matter, paid in advance to cover both the firm's anticipated legal fees and potential disbursements as the work progresses. No bill has yet been delivered and no disbursements have yet been incurred. The cashier must classify the £2,000 on receipt for the purposes of the SRA Accounts Rules. The money is a general payment on account. The client handed over the money as a single general payment at the start of the retainer to keep things moving, without allocating it between fees and specific disbursements, and the cashier must classify the whole sum correctly at the point it is received rather than waiting to see how it is later spent. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the £2,000?
o: The £2,000 need not be banked until a disbursement is actually incurred.
The £2,000 may be retained in the office account until the first bill.
The whole £2,000 is office money because it will fund the firm's fees.
The whole £2,000 is client money and must be paid into the client account.
Half is office money for fees and half is client money for disbursements.
2.w: Money paid in advance generally on account of costs and disbursements, before any bill is delivered or disbursement incurred, is client money in its entirety. It must be paid promptly into the client account. It becomes office money, in whole or part, only as bills are delivered or the firm is entitled to reimbursement.

n.0: It must be banked promptly, not held unbanked until a disbursement arises.
n.1: It cannot be retained in the office account pending a bill.
n.2: None of it is office money yet, as no bill has been delivered.
n.4: There is no automatic half-and-half split; the whole sum is client money on account.

2.q: A party to a contract wishes to transfer to a third party not only the benefit of the contract (the right to receive performance) but also the burden (its own obligations to perform), so as to be released from those obligations. The other contracting party has not agreed to release the transferor. The transferor seeks to shed its own contractual obligations. The contracting party wants to offload not just the right to receive performance but its own side of the bargain, its obligations, onto a third party and walk away free of them, but the other party to the contract has never agreed to let the transferor off the hook. Which of the following best describes the position on assigning the burden of a contract?
o: Neither the benefit nor the burden of a contract can ever be transferred.
The burden of a contract can be freely assigned in the same way as the benefit on these facts as a general rule.
The burden passes automatically to anyone who receives the benefit.
The burden can be assigned provided notice is given to the other party.
The burden of a contract cannot generally be assigned without the other party's consent; only the benefit is assignable.
2.w: While the benefit of a contract can generally be assigned, the burden (a party's obligations) cannot be transferred to a third party without the other party's consent. To transfer obligations and be released, the parties must novate the contract (a tripartite agreement replacing the old contract with a new one), rather than simply assigning.

n.0: The benefit can be assigned, so it is not the case that nothing can be transferred.
n.1: The burden is not freely assignable like the benefit.
n.2: Receiving the benefit does not automatically impose the burden.
n.3: Mere notice does not transfer the burden; the other party's agreement (novation) is needed.

2.q: A firm receives money from a client on account of costs for work the firm has not yet done and for which no bill has yet been delivered. The bookkeeper must classify this money for the purposes of the SRA Accounts Rules, as it affects which account it goes into. The bookkeeper considers how money on account of costs is treated before a bill is raised. The client has paid the sum in advance to fund forthcoming work on the matter, the firm has not yet carried out that work, and no bill or other written notification of costs has been sent, so the bookkeeper must decide how to treat the payment on receipt. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Money on account of costs is always office money and goes straight into the office account on these facts.
Money on account of costs belongs to the firm immediately and may be spent at once.
Money on account of costs is treated as a gift to the firm from the client.
Money on account of costs, before a bill is delivered, is client money and must go into the client account.
Money on account of costs need not be banked at all until the bill is raised.
2.w: Money received from a client generally on account of costs for work not yet billed is client money and must be paid into the client account. It becomes office money (which may be transferred to the office account) only once the firm has delivered a bill or other written notification of costs.

n.0: It is client money until a bill is delivered, not immediately office money.
n.1: It does not belong to the firm to spend before a bill is raised.
n.2: It is the client's money on account, not a gift to the firm.
n.4: It must be banked promptly in the client account, not held unbanked.

2.q: A buyer and seller agree that, in place of the seller's original obligation to deliver goods (which the seller can no longer conveniently perform), the seller will instead pay the buyer a sum of money, and the buyer accepts this new arrangement in full satisfaction of the original obligation. The buyer provides its agreement to give up the original right in return for the new promise. The seller pays the sum. The buyer later tries to sue on the original obligation as well. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer may sue on the original obligation, because it has already received the substitute payment.
The original obligation is discharged only if the substitution was ordered by a court.
The original obligation survives, because replacing delivery with money is not permitted in law.
The original obligation is discharged by accord and satisfaction, so the buyer cannot sue on it.
The original obligation survives, because an obligation once created can never be discharged by agreement.
2.w: A contractual obligation can be discharged by agreement where there is accord (agreement to release) and satisfaction (fresh consideration for the release). Here the buyer agreed to accept a money payment in place of delivery, and that new arrangement discharges the original obligation.

n.0: Having accepted the substitute in satisfaction, the buyer cannot also enforce the original obligation.
n.1: Accord and satisfaction operates by agreement of the parties, without any court order.
n.2: Substituting a money payment for delivery, by agreement, is perfectly permissible.
n.4: Obligations can be discharged by agreement supported by consideration; they are not indelible.

2.q: On exchange of contracts incorporating the Standard Conditions of Sale, the buyer's solicitor advises the buyer about insuring the property. The buyer assumes the seller remains responsible for the property until completion. Under the Standard Conditions, risk in the property passes to the buyer on exchange. The buyer wrongly assumes the seller bears the risk until completion. Contracts have just been exchanged on the sale, the standard conditions apply, and the buyer, assuming the seller will look after the building right up to completion, is surprised when the solicitor raises the question of insurance, given how the standard conditions allocate the risk between the parties from exchange onwards. Which of the following best describes the buyer's position on insurance?
o: The property is automatically insured by the Land Registry between exchange and completion.
The buyer need not insure until completion, as the seller bears all risk until then.
Neither party need insure because the contract allocates all loss to the seller.
Insurance is unnecessary because any damage entitles the buyer to rescind automatically.
The buyer should insure the property from exchange, as risk generally passes to the buyer on exchange.
2.w: Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, risk in the property generally passes to the buyer on exchange of contracts, and the seller is not obliged to insure after exchange. The buyer should therefore insure the property from exchange (or ensure it is covered), because if it is damaged between exchange and completion the buyer generally must still complete.

n.0: The Land Registry does not insure property between exchange and completion.
n.1: The seller does not bear all risk until completion under the Standard Conditions; risk passes on exchange.
n.2: The contract does not allocate all loss to the seller; risk passes to the buyer.
n.3: Damage does not automatically entitle the buyer to rescind; the buyer generally must still complete.

2.q: During a fight, the defendant strikes the victim with a bottle, breaking the skin so that the victim bleeds, cutting through the whole skin (both the outer and inner layers). The prosecution considers a charge of unlawful wounding. The defendant intended or foresaw some harm. The injury broke the continuity of the whole skin. In the course of a brawl the defendant swung a bottle at the victim with enough force to split the skin so that blood flowed from the cut, the injury going right through both layers of skin rather than leaving a mere graze or a bruise beneath an intact surface. Which of the following best describes what amounts to a 'wound' for these offences?
o: A wound means only an injury caused by a bladed weapon.
A wound requires the victim to have been rendered unconscious.
A wound means any injury to the body, including internal bruising alone.
A wound requires the victim to suffer permanent disfigurement.
A wound requires a break in the continuity of the whole skin (both layers).
2.w: For the offences of wounding (under ss.20 and 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861), a 'wound' requires a break in the continuity of the whole skin, that is, both the outer layer (epidermis) and the inner layer (dermis). A mere graze or internal rupturing of blood vessels (bruising) is not a wound.

n.0: A wound is not confined to injuries from a bladed weapon.
n.1: Unconsciousness is not required for a wound.
n.2: Internal bruising alone, without breaking the whole skin, is not a wound.
n.3: Permanent disfigurement is not required; a break in the whole skin suffices.

2.q: A metalworking workshop operates immediately next door to Mr Barlow's house in a residential street. In recent months the workshop has begun running noisy cutting and hammering machinery late into the night, often continuing until the early hours of the morning, well beyond ordinary working hours. The noise regularly wakes Mr Barlow's household, prevents them from sleeping, and seriously disturbs their ordinary use and enjoyment of their home. Mr Barlow has complained to the workshop's owner, who refuses to change the hours, saying it is entitled to run its business on its own premises exactly as it sees fit. Which of the following best describes Mr Barlow's claim?
o: No claim, because a landowner may always use their own land as they wish.
Trespass to land, because the noise physically enters the homeowner's property.
Breach of a restrictive covenant implied into every conveyance of neighbouring land. as a general rule in most cases
Private nuisance, for unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of the home, giving rise to an injunction and damages.
Adverse possession, because the noise interferes with the homeowner's occupation.
2.w: Unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of land, such as excessive night-time noise, is an actionable private nuisance. Remedies include an injunction to restrain the nuisance and damages.

n.0: The right to use one's land is limited by the duty not to cause an actionable nuisance.
n.1: Noise is an interference with enjoyment (nuisance), not a direct physical trespass.
n.2: No restrictive covenant is implied into every conveyance; this is a nuisance claim.
n.4: Nuisance does not create or defeat title by adverse possession.

2.q: A judge is sentencing an offender for an offence for which the Sentencing Council has issued a definitive guideline setting out the approach and sentencing ranges. The judge is considering how much weight must be given to the guideline. There is nothing exceptional making the guideline inappropriate on these facts. The offence is a common one for which the Sentencing Council has published a detailed step-by-step guideline with categories and ranges, the facts fall squarely within the ordinary run of such cases, and the judge is conscious of the need to explain how far the guideline dictates the outcome. Which of the following best describes the judge's obligation in relation to the sentencing guideline?
o: The judge must follow the guideline unless satisfied it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.
The judge must apply the guideline only if the prosecution asks for it.
The judge is absolutely bound by the guideline in every case without exception on these facts as a general rule.
The judge must refer the guideline to the Court of Appeal before sentencing.
The judge may disregard the guideline entirely at personal discretion.
2.w: A court must follow any relevant sentencing guideline unless it is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. This gives the guidelines strong effect while leaving the court a limited power to depart where the interests of justice require it.

n.1: The duty to follow the guideline does not depend on a prosecution request.
n.2: The obligation is strong but not absolute; departure is possible in the interests of justice.
n.3: There is no requirement to refer the guideline to the Court of Appeal before sentencing.
n.4: The judge cannot simply disregard a relevant guideline at will.

2.q: A defendant convicted on indictment receives a sentence that the Attorney General considers to be unduly lenient, given the seriousness of the offending. The offence is one to which the relevant scheme applies. The sentence passed in the Crown Court is said to be far too low. The Attorney General wishes to have it reviewed. After a Crown Court trial the sentence handed down strikes many, including the Attorney General, as far too soft for offending of this gravity, the offence is one within the relevant scheme, and the Attorney General is looking for a way to have that lenient sentence reviewed and, if appropriate, increased. Which of the following best describes the mechanism available?
o: The sentence may be increased only if the defendant also appeals against conviction on these facts as a general rule.
There is no mechanism to challenge a sentence for being too lenient.
The Attorney General may simply increase the sentence without any court involvement.
The prosecution witnesses may appeal the sentence themselves.
The Attorney General may refer the sentence to the Court of Appeal as unduly lenient for the offences within the scheme.
2.w: Under the unduly lenient sentence scheme, the Attorney General may, for certain offences, refer a Crown Court sentence to the Court of Appeal where it appears unduly lenient. The Court of Appeal may then increase the sentence. This is separate from the defendant's own right to appeal against sentence.

n.0: An unduly lenient reference does not depend on the defendant appealing conviction.
n.1: There is a mechanism (the unduly lenient sentence scheme) to challenge over-lenient sentences.
n.2: The Attorney General cannot increase the sentence personally; it must be referred to the Court of Appeal.
n.3: Witnesses have no right to appeal the sentence.

2.q: A family lives together in a rented house which is affected by a persistent nuisance emanating from a neighbouring property. Several members of the household are troubled by it, but only one of them, the tenant, has any legal interest in the land; the others are family members and licensees living there with no proprietary interest of their own. They all wish to sue the neighbour in private nuisance. The neighbour argues that most of the household have no standing to bring such a claim. The nuisance had continued for many months and troubled the whole household throughout that period. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No one may sue in private nuisance unless they also own the neighbouring land causing it.
Any person who is in fact troubled by the interference has standing to sue in nuisance.
Only the owner of the freehold, and never a mere tenant, may sue in private nuisance.
Only a person with a proprietary interest in the affected land can generally sue in private nuisance.
Anyone who lives in the affected property may sue in private nuisance, whatever their interest.
2.w: Private nuisance protects rights in land, so generally only a person with a proprietary interest in the affected land (such as a freeholder or tenant in possession) has standing to sue. Mere occupiers without such an interest cannot bring the claim (Hunter v Canary Wharf).

n.0: The claimant need not own the offending land; they must have an interest in the affected land.
n.1: Being troubled by the interference is not enough without a proprietary interest.
n.2: A tenant in possession does have a sufficient interest to sue; it is not confined to freeholders.
n.4: Mere residence without a proprietary interest does not give standing in private nuisance.

2.q: A landlord of business premises protected by the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 wishes to oppose the tenant's application for a new tenancy, because the landlord genuinely intends to demolish and reconstruct the premises (or to occupy them for its own business). The tenancy is protected and the landlord opposes renewal. The landlord relies on a statutory ground. The tenant has applied for a new tenancy of its protected business premises, but the landlord wants to resist, saying it genuinely means to knock the building down and rebuild, or to move into the premises for its own business, and the question is on what footing the landlord may oppose renewal. Which of the following best describes the landlord's ability to oppose renewal?
o: The landlord may oppose renewal only on statutory grounds, some of which (redevelopment or own occupation) entitle the tenant to compensation.
The landlord may oppose renewal for any reason it chooses, without needing a statutory ground on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The landlord may oppose renewal only with the consent of the tenant.
The landlord may oppose renewal only by obtaining permission from the SRA.
The landlord can never oppose renewal of a protected business tenancy.
2.w: A landlord may oppose the grant of a new business tenancy only on one or more of the grounds set out in s.30(1) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, such as breaches by the tenant, suitable alternative accommodation, or the landlord's genuine intention to redevelop or to occupy the premises. Where opposition succeeds on certain 'no-fault' grounds (such as redevelopment or own occupation), the tenant is entitled to statutory compensation.

n.1: The landlord cannot oppose for any reason; a statutory ground is required.
n.2: Opposition does not depend on the tenant's consent.
n.3: SRA permission is irrelevant to opposing a business lease renewal.
n.4: The landlord can oppose on statutory grounds, so 'never' is wrong.

2.q: On an intestacy, part of the estate is to be held for the intestate's issue. One of the intestate's children has already died, leaving children of their own (the intestate's grandchildren). The estate must be divided among the issue. The family asks how the share for that branch of the family is dealt with, and whether minor beneficiaries take immediately. The court considers the statutory trusts for issue on intestacy. One of the intestate's children had died young, leaving two children of their own who survived. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The estate is divided equally per capita among all descendants of every generation at once.
The issue take per stirpes, with a deceased child's share passing to their own children, contingent on reaching 18 (or marrying earlier).
Minor grandchildren take their share outright and immediately, whatever their age.
Grandchildren can never take any share on intestacy while any child of the intestate survives.
A deceased child's share simply lapses, and the surviving children take everything between them on these facts as a general rule.
2.w: On the statutory trusts, the issue take per stirpes: the estate is divided between the branches, and the share of a child who has predeceased passes to that child's own issue equally. Interests of issue are contingent on attaining 18 (or marrying or forming a civil partnership earlier).

n.0: Division is per stirpes by branch, not per capita across all generations.
n.2: Minor beneficiaries' interests are contingent on reaching 18, not taken outright at any age.
n.3: Grandchildren take their deceased parent's share even while other children survive.
n.4: A deceased child's share does not simply lapse; it passes to their issue.

2.q: A squatter has been in adverse possession of a piece of registered land for 11 years, occupying it openly as their own throughout that period. The squatter applies under Schedule 6 to the Land Registration Act 2002 to be registered as the proprietor of the land in place of the current registered proprietor. The registered proprietor is duly notified of the application by the Land Registry and, within the time allowed for doing so, objects to it. None of the three special statutory conditions that can override such an objection applies on these facts. Which of the following best describes the likely outcome of the application?
o: The squatter is registered immediately, because a registered proprietor cannot object to such an application, on these facts.
The application is rejected permanently, because adverse possession cannot affect registered land at all.
The application is rejected initially, because the registered proprietor objected and no statutory exception applies.
The squatter must instead show 12 years' possession before any application can be made.
The application succeeds automatically, because 10 years' adverse possession of registered land gives title.
2.w: Under Schedule 6 LRA 2002 a squatter may apply after 10 years, but the registered proprietor is notified and, if they object, the application is generally rejected unless one of the three limited conditions applies. The proprietor then usually has a further period to evict or regularise.

n.0: The registered proprietor is entitled to object; the squatter is not registered as of right.
n.1: Adverse possession can affect registered land, but through the Schedule 6 notice regime.
n.3: For registered land the trigger is 10 years under Schedule 6, not 12.
n.4: Ten years' possession does not automatically give title to registered land; the proprietor can object.

2.q: Two or more defendants agree together on a course of conduct which, if carried out in accordance with their intentions, will necessarily amount to the commission of a criminal offence by one or more of them. They are charged with an inchoate offence based on their agreement, even though the substantive offence has not yet been carried out. The court considers the offence of statutory conspiracy under the Criminal Law Act 1977. The two had agreed the plan in detail, though they were arrested before anything further could be done. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Conspiracy is committed only where the defendants also took a substantial step towards the crime on these facts.
Conspiracy requires the defendants to have signed a written agreement setting out the plan.
Conspiracy is an agreement between two or more people to pursue a course of conduct that will involve an offence.
Conspiracy requires the agreed offence to have actually been carried out and completed.
Conspiracy can be committed by a single person acting entirely alone.
2.w: Under s.1 Criminal Law Act 1977, statutory conspiracy is committed where a person agrees with one or more others on a course of conduct which, if carried out as intended, will necessarily amount to or involve the commission of an offence. The agreement itself is the offence; the substantive crime need not be carried out.

n.0: Unlike attempt, conspiracy does not require a substantial step towards the crime.
n.1: No written agreement is required; the agreement may be informal.
n.3: The agreed offence need not be carried out; the agreement is the offence.
n.4: Conspiracy requires at least two people; one person alone cannot conspire.

2.q: A buyer is induced to enter a contract by the seller's misrepresentation. After discovering the truth, the buyer nevertheless proceeds to treat the contract as continuing, using the subject matter and making further payments for a considerable time without protest, before eventually seeking to unwind the contract. The buyer clearly elected to continue with the contract after learning the full facts. The buyer now seeks rescission of the contract. The buyer had every opportunity to complain once the truth came out but instead pressed on with the arrangement, drawing benefits from it and paying further instalments over many months, and only when the venture later disappointed did the buyer turn round and try to unwind the whole thing. Which of the following best explains why rescission is likely to be unavailable?
o: Rescission is unavailable because misrepresentation never gives a right to rescind.
Rescission is unavailable because only the party who made the statement may rescind.
Rescission is unavailable solely because some time has passed since the contract.
Rescission is unavailable because the buyer suffered no loss of any kind.
The right to rescind has been lost by affirmation of the contract after discovering the truth.
2.w: Rescission is an equitable remedy that may be barred, including by affirmation: where the misrepresentee, with knowledge of the truth and of the right to rescind, elects to continue with the contract, the right to rescind is lost. The buyer's continued use and payment after discovering the truth amount to affirmation, barring rescission.

n.0: Misrepresentation can give a right to rescind; the point is that the right has been lost here.
n.1: It is the misled party who may rescind; that is not the reason it is barred.
n.2: Mere lapse of time is a separate potential bar; here the clear bar is affirmation by conduct.
n.3: The bar to rescission is affirmation, not the absence of loss.

2.q: A person made a chargeable lifetime transfer into a trust and also made a potentially exempt transfer to an individual, and then died within seven years. The executors must work out how the nil rate band is applied to these lifetime transfers when computing the inheritance tax. Several lifetime transfers were made within the seven years before death. The executors must apply the cumulation principle. In the seven years before death the deceased had made a chargeable transfer into a trust and a potentially exempt gift to an individual, and the executors, now bringing those failed and chargeable transfers into account, must apply the nil rate band across them in the correct sequence. Which of the following best describes how the nil rate band is applied?
o: The nil rate band is applied to the largest transfer first, whenever it was made.
The nil rate band is applied only to the death estate and never to lifetime transfers on these facts as a general rule.
The nil rate band is shared equally between all the transfers regardless of date.
The nil rate band is applied to the transfers in chronological order, earlier transfers using it up first (cumulation).
Each lifetime transfer has its own separate full nil rate band.
2.w: Inheritance tax on lifetime transfers operates on a cumulative basis: the nil rate band is set against transfers in chronological order, so earlier transfers use it up first, and later transfers (and ultimately the death estate) have the benefit only of any remaining band. This is the principle of cumulation.

n.0: The band is applied chronologically, not to the largest transfer first.
n.1: The band is applied to lifetime transfers too, not only the death estate.
n.2: It is not shared equally regardless of date; order matters.
n.4: Each transfer does not get its own full separate band; cumulation applies.

2.q: A firm has been holding client money for a client, but the matter has now concluded, all bills have been paid, and there is no longer any proper reason for the firm to continue holding the balance. The money simply remains in the client account. The bookkeeper considers what must happen to client money once there is no longer any reason to hold it, under the SRA Accounts Rules. The transaction completed some months ago, the firm's final bill has been settled in full, and a modest balance simply remains in the client account with no outstanding disbursements or further steps for the firm to take on the client's behalf. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Client money may be transferred to the firm's office account once the matter is over.
Client money must be paid to the SRA once the matter has been completed.
Client money may be kept in the client account indefinitely after the matter has ended.
Client money must be returned to the client (or the person entitled) promptly once there is no longer any proper reason to hold it.
Client money left over automatically becomes the firm's office money at the end of the matter on these facts as a general rule.
2.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require that client money is returned promptly to the client (or other person entitled to it) as soon as there is no longer any proper reason to hold it. Leaving residual balances in the client account is a breach.

n.0: It must be returned to the client, not transferred to the office account.
n.1: It is returned to the client, not paid to the SRA.
n.2: Client money cannot be kept indefinitely after the matter ends.
n.4: Leftover client money does not become the firm's office money automatically.

2.q: A defendant fails to act to prevent harm to a victim, and the victim is injured as a result of the defendant doing nothing. In general the criminal law imposes no liability for a mere failure to act, but the prosecution argues that this defendant was under a positive duty to act in the particular circumstances. The evidence is that the defendant had voluntarily assumed responsibility for the vulnerable victim's care and then neglected them. The court considers when an omission can give rise to liability. The victim was frail and wholly dependent on the defendant, who had taken them into their own household. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Liability for an omission arises only where the defendant is a qualified medical professional on these facts as a general rule.
There can never be criminal liability for a failure to act in any circumstances whatsoever.
Liability for an omission arises whenever the defendant simply could have prevented the harm.
Liability for an omission arises only where the defendant intended the victim to die.
Liability for an omission may arise where the defendant was under a recognised duty to act, such as an assumed duty of care.
2.w: Although there is no general duty to act, criminal liability for an omission arises where the defendant is under a recognised legal duty to act — for example by contract, a special relationship, the voluntary assumption of responsibility, or creating a dangerous situation — and fails to do so (R v Stone and Dobinson; R v Miller).

n.0: Duty situations are not confined to medical professionals.
n.1: There can be liability for omissions where a duty to act exists.
n.2: Mere ability to prevent harm does not create a duty to act.
n.3: Omissions liability does not require an intention that the victim die.

2.q: A person makes what is intended to be an outright gift of registered land to a donee, but fails to complete the necessary transfer and registration formalities, so that the legal title never passes and the gift is imperfect. The donee is a volunteer. The donee argues that, because the donor plainly intended to benefit them, the court should treat the failed gift as taking effect as a declaration of trust in the donee's favour instead. The land was valuable, and the donee had spent money in the expectation that the intended gift would go through. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court will not treat a failed gift as a declaration of trust merely to give effect to the donor's intention.
The court will perfect the gift because the donee is a volunteer who relied on it.
The failed gift takes effect as a charitable trust for the donee's benefit.
The failed gift automatically creates a resulting trust in the donee's favour.
The court will always save a failed gift by treating it as a self-declaration of trust on these facts.
2.w: Equity will not perfect an imperfect gift, and it will not construe an intended outright gift as a declaration of trust simply to give effect to the donor's intention where the transfer has failed (Milroy v Lord; Jones v Lock). The court does not save the gift by reinterpreting it as a trust.

n.1: Volunteer status and reliance do not lead equity to perfect the imperfect gift.
n.2: There is no charitable element; this is a private intended gift.
n.3: A failed gift does not create a resulting trust for the intended donee.
n.4: The court does not routinely rescue failed gifts as self-declarations of trust.

2.q: A public body reaches a decision seriously affecting an individual without following a fair procedure — for example without giving the person any opportunity to put their case. The individual challenges the decision by judicial review, not on its merits but on the way it was reached. A solicitor is asked which ground of judicial review is engaged where the decision-making procedure was unfair. The solicitor considers the ground of procedural impropriety. The individual complained not about the outcome but about how unfairly the decision had been reached. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Procedural fairness applies only where the statute expressly requires a fair procedure.
The way a decision is reached is legally irrelevant, provided the outcome is reasonable on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Procedural impropriety is not a recognised ground of judicial review.
A decision can be challenged only on its substance and never on the procedure followed.
The decision may be quashed for procedural impropriety, which includes a breach of the rules of natural justice and procedural fairness.
2.w: Procedural impropriety is a recognised ground of judicial review. It includes a failure to observe the rules of natural justice and common-law procedural fairness (such as the right to a fair hearing and the rule against bias), as well as a failure to follow statutory procedural requirements.

n.0: Procedural fairness can be implied at common law, not only where the statute requires it.
n.1: The procedure followed is very relevant, not merely the outcome.
n.2: Procedural impropriety is one of the classic grounds of review.
n.3: Decisions can be challenged on procedure as well as substance.

2.q: A concern is raised that the executive might pressure judges by threatening their removal or pay if they decide cases against the government. A commentator points to constitutional protections designed to keep the judiciary independent of the other branches. The issue is the constitutional protection of judicial independence. The separation of powers is engaged. Concern is voiced that a government displeased with judgments going against it might try to lean on judges by threatening their positions or their pay, and a commentator points to the constitutional arrangements specifically designed to insulate the judiciary from that kind of executive pressure. Which of the following best describes a key protection of judicial independence?
o: Judges serve entirely at the pleasure of the government of the day.
The executive may reduce judges' salaries whenever it disapproves of their decisions on these facts as a general rule.
Senior judges have security of tenure and protected salaries, and can be removed only through strict constitutional processes.
Judicial independence has no legal or constitutional protection in the UK.
Ministers may dismiss any judge who rules against the government.
2.w: Judicial independence is protected constitutionally: senior judges hold office during good behaviour with security of tenure (removable only on an address by both Houses of Parliament), their salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund and protected from executive reduction, and the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 places a duty on ministers to uphold judicial independence.

n.0: Judges do not serve at the government's pleasure; they have security of tenure.
n.1: The executive cannot reduce judges' salaries in response to their decisions.
n.3: Judicial independence is protected by law and convention, not unprotected.
n.4: Ministers cannot dismiss judges for ruling against the government.

3.q: A debtor owes a creditor £10,000 which is due and undisputed. The creditor, wanting some payment rather than none, agrees to accept £6,000 in full and final settlement, and the debtor pays that sum. The creditor later sues for the remaining £4,000. There was no dispute about the sum owed and nothing new was given by the debtor beyond part of the existing debt. The debtor had pleaded cash-flow difficulty, the creditor reluctantly took what it could get to avoid the risk of recovering nothing at all, and the debtor gave nothing beyond a slice of the very sum already due before the creditor later changed its mind and pursued the shortfall. Which of the following best describes the creditor's ability to recover the balance?
o: The creditor cannot recover the balance, because accepting part payment always discharges the whole debt on these facts.
The creditor cannot recover the balance, because the debtor provided fresh consideration by paying early.
The creditor may recover only if the debtor acted dishonestly in negotiating the settlement.
The creditor may recover the balance only if the agreement was not put in writing.
The creditor may recover the balance, as part payment of a debt is not good consideration for a promise to forgo the rest.
