3.w: Under the rule in Pinnel's Case, affirmed in Foakes v Beer, payment of a smaller sum is not good consideration for a promise to release the balance of a larger debt. Absent fresh consideration (such as early payment, a different place, or a chattel) or an applicable estoppel, the creditor remains entitled to recover the outstanding £4,000.

n.0: Accepting part payment does not by itself discharge the whole debt.
n.1: On these facts the debtor gave nothing new; paying part of what was already due is not fresh consideration.
n.2: The rule does not turn on the debtor's honesty in negotiating.
n.3: Whether the agreement was in writing does not supply the missing consideration.

3.q: A firm holds £1,200 in the client account for a client, provided to cover an anticipated disbursement. When the disbursement is finally incurred it costs only £900, leaving £300 of the client's money in the client account with no remaining purpose on the matter. The cashier considers what should happen to the £300. The matter is otherwise concluded. The client had put the firm in funds generously to be sure the disbursement could be met, the actual cost came in lower than expected, and with the work now finished the firm is left holding money that has served its purpose and has no further role to play on the matter. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The £300 surplus may be retained by the firm against possible future costs.
The £300 surplus becomes office money once the disbursement is paid.
The £300 surplus may be kept in the client account indefinitely.
The £300 surplus may be transferred to the office account as a handling charge.
The £300 surplus is client money and must be returned to the client promptly.
3.w: The £300 not needed for the disbursement remains client money. With the matter concluded and no proper reason to hold it, the firm must return the surplus to the client promptly. It does not become office money, and cannot be retained against speculative future costs or taken as a charge.

n.0: The firm cannot retain it against possible future costs.
n.1: Paying the disbursement does not convert the surplus into office money.
n.2: It cannot be left in the client account indefinitely once there is no reason to hold it.
n.3: It cannot be taken to the office account as a handling charge.

3.q: A defended claim is for around £40,000 and is expected to be reasonably complex, with disclosure, witness evidence and possibly expert evidence, and a trial likely to last more than a day. The parties need to know the track to which such a claim is likely to be allocated. The court considers allocation between the fast track, intermediate track and multi-track under the Civil Procedure Rules. The case would need disclosure, witness statements and probably an expert on one issue. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A more complex claim of this value is likely to be allocated to the multi-track (or intermediate track).
The claim must be allocated to the small claims track because it is a money claim.
The claim will be allocated purely according to which party the court favours.
The claim will be allocated to the fast track in every case regardless of complexity or trial length.
The claim cannot be allocated to any track because its value exceeds £25,000.
3.w: Higher-value or more complex claims are allocated to the multi-track (or, within a defined value band and complexity, the intermediate track). The fast track is generally for claims up to £25,000 capable of a one-day trial with limited expert evidence; a complex £40,000 claim is beyond that.

n.1: A £40,000 complex claim is not a small claims track matter.
n.2: Allocation is by reference to value and complexity, not favouritism.
n.3: The fast track is not used regardless of complexity; complex higher-value claims go to the multi-track.
n.4: Claims over £25,000 are allocated (to the multi-track), not left unallocated.

3.q: A landowner has used a right of way over a neighbour's land openly, without permission and without force or secrecy, for well over twenty years, and now claims a legal easement by long use. The use has been as of right (without force, secrecy or permission) for the requisite period. The landowner claims a prescriptive easement. For well over twenty years the landowner has openly driven across the neighbour's land to reach their own, doing so without asking permission, without any secrecy and without force, and now, relying on that long and uninterrupted use, claims to have acquired a legal right of way. Which of the following best describes how such an easement may be acquired by prescription?
o: By long use as of right, which may be claimed under common law prescription, lost modern grant, or the Prescription Act 1832.
By a single year's use of the right of way.
By any use at all, even if it was with the owner's permission.
Only by an express deed of grant from the servient owner.
By registering the right as a company charge at Companies House on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
3.w: An easement may be acquired by prescription where the claimant has used the right 'as of right' (without force, without secrecy and without permission, nec vi, nec clam, nec precario) for the requisite long period. There are three routes: common law prescription, the doctrine of lost modern grant, and the Prescription Act 1832 (typically requiring twenty years' use).

n.1: A single year's use is far short of the period required.
n.2: Use with permission is not 'as of right' and cannot found prescription.
n.3: Prescription arises from long use, not an express deed of grant (which would be express grant, not prescription).
n.4: Registration as a company charge is irrelevant to acquiring an easement by prescription.

3.q: At a Crown Court trial the admissibility of the defendant's confession is disputed, and the judge must resolve whether it can be put before the jury before the jury hears it. The defendant's solicitor asks how the disputed admissibility is determined. The solicitor considers the procedure for determining the admissibility of a confession (the voir dire). The parties disagreed sharply over whether the jury should ever hear the disputed confession. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The confession is automatically put before the jury without any ruling on admissibility on these facts.
Admissibility is determined only after the jury has returned its verdict.
The jury decides whether the confession is admissible after hearing all the evidence.
The judge determines admissibility in a trial within a trial (voir dire) in the absence of the jury.
Admissibility is decided by the prosecution, which chooses what the jury hears.
3.w: Where the admissibility of a confession is disputed in the Crown Court, the judge determines the issue in a 'trial within a trial' (voir dire), hearing evidence and argument in the absence of the jury, and rules on admissibility before the jury hears the confession.

n.0: Disputed confessions are not automatically put to the jury without a ruling.
n.1: Admissibility is decided before, not after, the verdict.
n.2: Admissibility is a question of law for the judge, not the jury.
n.4: The prosecution does not decide admissibility; the judge does.

3.q: A firm conducting personal injury work is offered payments by a claims management company in return for the referral of personal injury clients to the firm, and considers whether it may pay or receive such referral fees. The work is a personal injury claim. Referral fees are proposed in connection with it. A claims management company offers the firm payments in exchange for steering personal injury clients its way, and the firm, doing this kind of work, must decide whether paying or pocketing such referral fees is something it is allowed to do in the personal injury context. Which of the following best describes the position on referral fees in this context?
o: Referral fees in relation to personal injury claims are prohibited, so the firm must not pay or receive them.
Referral fees are permitted in personal injury cases without any restriction.
Referral fees are always permitted provided they are disclosed to the client on these facts as a general rule.
Referral fees are permitted provided they are paid to the SRA.
Referral fees are prohibited only where the client objects to them.
3.w: Under section 56 of the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012, referral fees in relation to personal injury claims are prohibited: regulated persons must not pay or be paid a referral fee in connection with such claims. In other areas referral arrangements may be permitted subject to conduct requirements such as disclosure and independence.

n.1: Referral fees in personal injury claims are restricted (prohibited), not unrestricted.
n.2: Disclosure does not make referral fees lawful in personal injury claims; they are prohibited.
n.3: Referral fees are not made lawful by paying them to the SRA.
n.4: The prohibition applies regardless of whether the client objects.

3.q: A public body makes an important decision affecting an individual's liberty or livelihood but gives no reasons at all for its decision, leaving the individual unable to understand why the decision went against them or whether it might be challengeable. The individual argues they were entitled to reasons. A solicitor is asked whether a public body must give reasons for its decisions. The solicitor considers the duty to give reasons in public law. The individual was left completely in the dark about why the decision had gone against them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A public body is never required to give reasons for any decision it makes.
A public body must always give full written reasons for every decision, however trivial on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
There is no universal duty to give reasons, but fairness increasingly requires reasons, especially where important interests are affected.
A public body must give reasons only to those who can afford to pay for them.
Reasons are required only where the statute expressly says so and in no other case.
3.w: There is no general common-law duty to give reasons for every decision, but fairness will often require reasons, particularly where important interests (such as liberty or livelihood) are at stake or where a decision appears aberrant. Statute may also impose a duty to give reasons (R v Home Secretary, ex p Doody).

n.0: There is no blanket rule that reasons are never required.
n.1: There is no universal duty to give reasons for every trivial decision.
n.3: The duty to give reasons does not depend on payment.
n.4: Fairness can require reasons even without an express statutory duty.

3.q: A director proposes to buy a valuable property from the company (or sell a valuable property to it) where the value of the asset exceeds the higher statutory threshold and is significant relative to the company's asset value. The board asks whether the transaction can simply be approved by the directors. The counterparty is a director and the asset is a substantial non-cash asset. The company wishes to comply with the Companies Act 2006. One of the directors wants to buy a substantial property from the company at a price well above the statutory threshold and significant in the context of the company's assets, and the board is trying to establish whether it can simply sign this off itself or must put it to the members. Which of the following best describes the approval required?
o: The transaction may be approved by the board of directors alone without member involvement.
The transaction is prohibited outright and can never be carried out.
The substantial property transaction must be approved by an ordinary resolution of the members.
The transaction requires approval by special resolution of 75% of members.
The transaction requires the approval of the company's creditors.
3.w: Under ss.190-191 of the Companies Act 2006, an arrangement by which a director acquires from, or the company acquires from a director, a substantial non-cash asset (exceeding the statutory value thresholds) must be approved by an ordinary resolution of the members. Without approval the transaction is generally voidable and the director may have to account.

n.0: Board approval alone is insufficient for a substantial property transaction.
n.1: The transaction is not outright prohibited; it may proceed with member approval.
n.3: The requirement is an ordinary resolution, not a special resolution.
n.4: Creditor approval is not the applicable requirement.

3.q: A client tells a solicitor, in confidence during a meeting at the office, that they intend to carry out a serious act of violence against a named individual, giving enough detail that the solicitor forms the genuine belief that there is a real and imminent risk to that person's life. The information was plainly given in confidence, and the solicitor is acutely conscious of the strict duty of confidentiality that is ordinarily owed to a client. The solicitor now has to decide whether they may disclose what they have been told, to the police or the intended victim, in order to try to prevent the threatened harm. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may disclose the threat only after the intended victim has already come to serious harm.
The solicitor may disclose the threat only if the client first gives express permission to do so.
Confidentiality may be overridden where disclosure is necessary to prevent serious harm, such as a risk to a person's life.
The solicitor must disclose every confidence a client shares, whether or not any harm is threatened.
The duty of confidentiality is absolute, so the solicitor may not disclose the threat in any circumstances at all.
3.w: The duty of confidentiality is not absolute. Disclosure may be justified, exceptionally, where it is necessary to prevent serious harm — for example where the solicitor reasonably believes disclosure is needed to prevent death or serious physical harm to a person.

n.0: The point of the exception is to prevent the harm, not to wait until after it occurs.
n.1: The exception applies precisely because the client will not consent; consent is not required.
n.3: There is no duty to disclose ordinary confidences; the exception is narrow and harm-based.
n.4: Confidentiality is not absolute; a serious-harm exception can apply.

3.q: A defendant accepts that part of the claimant's money claim is well founded, but disputes the rest. The defendant wishes to admit the part they accept so as to narrow the issues and limit their costs exposure, while continuing to defend the balance. The claimant asks what the effect of a partial admission is. The court considers admissions under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant accepted part of the sum was plainly due but strongly disputed the rest of it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An admission by the defendant has no legal effect and can always be freely ignored.
A defendant who admits part of a claim is automatically taken to admit the whole of it on these facts.
A defendant can only ever admit the entire claim, and never just part of it.
An admission can only be made orally at the trial and never in writing beforehand.
A defendant may admit the whole or part of a claim, and the claimant may obtain judgment on the admitted part.
3.w: Under Part 14 CPR, a party may admit the whole or part of another party's case, and admissions may be made in the statements of case or in writing. Where a defendant admits part of a money claim, the claimant may enter judgment on the admitted part and continue to litigate the disputed balance.

n.0: Admissions have legal effect and can found judgment.
n.1: Admitting part does not amount to admitting the whole.
n.2: Partial admissions are permitted, not only admission of the whole claim.
n.3: Admissions can be made in writing before trial, not only orally at trial.

3.q: A borrower has repaid the mortgage loan in full slightly after the contractual redemption date stated in the mortgage. The lender argues that, the legal date for redemption having passed, the borrower has lost the right to get the property back. The borrower has repaid the debt after the legal redemption date. The borrower wishes to recover the property. The borrower has finally cleared the whole debt, but only a little after the contractual date fixed in the mortgage for redemption, and the lender is now arguing that, because that legal date has gone by, the borrower has forfeited any right to have the property back. Which of the following best describes the borrower's right to redeem?
o: The borrower loses all right to the property once the legal redemption date passes on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The borrower may redeem only with the lender's fresh consent after that date.
The property automatically becomes the lender's on the legal redemption date.
The borrower may redeem only by taking court proceedings within 24 hours.
The borrower retains an equitable right to redeem (the equity of redemption) even after the legal date for redemption has passed.
3.w: Although a mortgage historically fixed a legal date for redemption, equity recognises the borrower's continuing right to redeem after that date, the equity of redemption. On repaying the debt (with interest and costs), the borrower is entitled to have the property back and the mortgage discharged, notwithstanding that the contractual redemption date has passed.

n.0: The borrower does not lose the property merely because the legal date passed; equity allows redemption.
n.1: Redemption after the legal date does not require the lender's fresh consent.
n.2: The property does not become the lender's automatically on the legal date.
n.3: There is no 24-hour court-proceedings requirement to redeem.

3.q: A landowner sold off a plot of land and, on the sale, took from the buyer a covenant restricting building on the plot. The covenant was expressed to be for the benefit of other land; but that other land was land which the seller did not own at all and which was situated several miles away from the plot that had been sold. A successor in title now wishes to enforce the covenant against the current owner of the burdened plot, who has begun building on it. The successor seeks advice on whether the covenant is enforceable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The covenant is enforceable, because restrictive covenants always bind successors to the burdened plot. on the facts of this case
The covenant is not enforceable against the successor, because a restrictive covenant must accommodate (touch and concern) the benefited land.
The covenant is enforceable, because the burden of any covenant runs with the land in equity.
The covenant is enforceable only if it was also protected by a notice on the register.
The covenant is enforceable, because it was expressed to benefit some land, wherever situated.
3.w: For the burden of a restrictive covenant to run in equity, the covenant must accommodate (touch and concern) the benefited land — it must relate to and benefit that land, which normally requires proximity. A covenant benefiting distant, unconnected land does not satisfy this and is not enforceable against successors.

n.0: Restrictive covenants bind successors only where the running conditions, including accommodation, are satisfied.
n.2: Not every covenant burden runs in equity; the touch-and-concern requirement must be met.
n.3: Protection by notice is necessary but not sufficient; the covenant must first be one whose burden can run.
n.4: Merely being expressed to benefit some land is insufficient; the land must be accommodated.

3.q: A solicitor is faced with a difficult situation in which two of the SRA Principles pull in opposite directions. Acting in the way the client is pressing for would serve the solicitor's duty to act in the client's best interests; but doing so would at the same time undermine the solicitor's duty to uphold the rule of law and the proper administration of justice. The solicitor cannot possibly satisfy both duties at once, and must decide which of the two competing Principles should take precedence in resolving the dilemma. Which of the following best describes how a conflict between the Principles is to be resolved?
o: The Principle that best serves the public interest, especially the public interest in the proper administration of justice, takes precedence.
The most recently introduced of the conflicting Principles automatically takes precedence over the older one.
The Principle requiring the solicitor to act in the client's best interests always takes precedence over every other Principle.
Neither Principle applies once they conflict, so the solicitor is free to act however they think best.
The solicitor may simply choose whichever of the two conflicting Principles they personally consider the more important.
3.w: The SRA Principles provide that, where two or more Principles come into conflict, the one which takes precedence is the one that best serves the wider public interest, and in particular the public interest in the proper administration of justice.

n.1: Precedence does not turn on which Principle is newer.
n.2: The duty to the client does not automatically override the wider public interest Principles.
n.3: A conflict does not disapply the Principles; one of them must be given precedence on the public-interest test.
n.4: Resolution is not a matter of personal preference; the public-interest test governs.

3.q: A private company needs to take a routine management decision about its day-to-day trading operations. A shareholder argues that all such decisions must be put to the shareholders in general meeting, while the directors say that ordinary management is a matter for the board. The company's articles follow the model articles. The court considers the general division of decision-making power between the board of directors and the shareholders in general meeting. The decision concerned a routine supply contract of the kind the company entered into every week. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: All decisions of the company are for the directors alone, with no role for the shareholders on these facts as a general rule.
The directors are generally responsible for managing the company, while certain decisions are reserved to the shareholders.
Day-to-day decisions are taken by the company's creditors rather than its directors.
All decisions of the company must be taken by the shareholders in general meeting.
Every management decision must be approved by both the board and the shareholders together.
3.w: Under the model articles, the directors are responsible for the management of the company and may exercise all its powers, while certain important matters (such as altering the articles, or removing a director) are reserved to the shareholders by the Companies Act 2006 or the articles.

n.0: Some decisions are reserved to shareholders, so it is not all for the directors.
n.2: Creditors do not take the company's management decisions.
n.3: Not all decisions must go to the general meeting; day-to-day management is for the board.
n.4: Routine decisions do not require both board and shareholder approval.

3.q: After a matter concludes, a firm is left holding a residual balance of £900 for a former client whom it cannot trace despite reasonable efforts. The firm wishes to withdraw the money from the client account and pay it to charity. The residual balance exceeds £500 and the client cannot be found. The firm wants to clear the balance in a compliant way. Long after the matter ended the firm is still holding a leftover balance of £900 for a client who has vanished despite genuine efforts to trace them, and the firm would like to clear it by giving it to charity, mindful that the sum is above the level at which it could act on its own. Which of the following best describes what the firm must do under the SRA Accounts Rules for a balance of this size?
o: The firm may pay any residual balance to charity without the SRA's authority whatever its size on these facts.
The firm must obtain the SRA's prior authority before withdrawing a residual balance exceeding £500 to pay to charity.
The firm may simply transfer the balance to its own office account as unclaimed.
The firm must keep the balance in the client account indefinitely and take no step.
The firm must pay the balance to the former client's bank despite being unable to trace them.
3.w: The Accounts Rules allow residual client balances to be withdrawn and paid to charity where the firm has taken reasonable steps to return the money and keeps records. For balances of £500 or less per client matter this may be done without SRA authority; for larger balances (such as £900) the firm must obtain the SRA's prior authority before withdrawing.

n.0: Larger residual balances (over £500) require the SRA's authority; it is not unrestricted.
n.2: The firm cannot simply take the residual balance to its own office account.
n.3: Leaving it indefinitely with no step is not the compliant route.
n.4: The client cannot be traced, so payment to their bank is not possible; the charity route with SRA authority applies.

3.q: Creditors of an insolvent company seek to hold its individual shareholders personally liable for the company's debts by asking the court to disregard the company's separate legal personality — to 'pierce the corporate veil'. There is no suggestion of fraud or of the company being used as a mere facade to evade an existing legal obligation. The creditors simply argue it would be fair. The court considers when the corporate veil may be pierced. The company had been properly run and was simply the victim of a downturn in its market. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The corporate veil is pierced only rarely and in exceptional cases, not merely because it would be fair.
The corporate veil is pierced whenever a company is unable to pay its debts.
The corporate veil can never be pierced in any circumstances whatsoever.
The corporate veil is pierced whenever the court considers it would be fair to do so.
The corporate veil is pierced automatically where the company has only one shareholder on these facts.
3.w: The separate personality established in Salomon is strongly protected. The courts will pierce the corporate veil only in very limited and exceptional circumstances (for example where the company is used as a mere facade to evade an existing obligation), and not simply because it would appear fair (Prest v Petrodel; VTB Capital).

n.1: Insolvency alone is not a ground for piercing the veil.
n.2: The veil can be pierced in rare cases, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: General fairness is not enough to pierce the veil.
n.4: A single shareholder does not lead to automatic piercing (Salomon itself involved concentrated ownership).

3.q: A professional owes the victim a duty of care and, by a grossly negligent breach of that duty, causes the victim's death. The breach involved a serious failure falling far below the standard reasonably expected, and there was an obvious and serious risk of death. The defendant is charged with manslaughter, though they committed no intentional unlawful act against the victim. The court considers gross negligence manslaughter. The victim had been in the defendant's professional care and died following the defendant's serious lapse. Which of the following best describes its elements?
o: There must be proof that the defendant foresaw the victim's death as a virtual certainty.
There must be evidence that the defendant acted with a dishonest motive of some kind.
There must be an intentional unlawful criminal act directed at the victim by the defendant.
There must be a duty of care, a grossly negligent breach, an obvious risk of death, and causation of death.
There must be proof that the defendant intended to kill or cause serious harm to the victim on these facts.
3.w: Gross negligence manslaughter (R v Adomako) requires a duty of care owed to the victim, a breach of that duty, an obvious and serious risk of death, that the breach caused the death, and that the negligence was so gross as to be criminal in the jury's view.

n.0: Foresight of virtually certain death is not the test; an objective risk of death is.
n.1: A dishonest motive is not an element of the offence.
n.2: It does not require an intentional unlawful act; it rests on negligence.
n.4: It does not require intent to kill or cause serious harm.

3.q: A testator leaves a legacy in their will to a named charitable institution which, unknown to the testator, had already ceased to exist by the time the testator died, so that the specific gift cannot take effect as intended. It is established that the testator had a general charitable intention rather than an intention to benefit only that one particular institution. The executors seek advice on what happens to the failed charitable gift. The institution had merged into other bodies some years before the testator made the will in question. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The gift passes to the testator's next of kin, because the named charity no longer exists.
The gift passes to whichever charity the executors personally prefer, without any restriction on these facts.
The gift is void, because a charitable gift can never be redirected to a different charity.
The gift may be applied cy-près to another charity with similar purposes, given the general charitable intention.
The gift simply fails and falls back into the testator's residuary estate in every case.
3.w: Where a charitable gift fails at the outset (initial failure) but the testator had a general charitable intention, the doctrine of cy-près allows the property to be applied to another charitable purpose as near as possible to the original, rather than failing altogether.

n.0: It does not pass to the next of kin where cy-près applies.
n.1: Redirection is to similar charitable purposes under court/Commission scheme, not the executors' free choice.
n.2: Charitable gifts can be redirected cy-près; they are not incapable of redirection.
n.4: With a general charitable intention, the gift does not simply fail into residue.

3.q: The prosecution holds material that would normally have to be disclosed to the defence, but disclosing it would create a real risk of serious prejudice to an important public interest, such as revealing the identity of an informant or a sensitive investigative technique. The prosecution wishes to withhold the material lawfully. The material is sensitive and its disclosure could harm an important public interest. The prosecution seeks to avoid disclosing it. The prosecution is holding material that in the ordinary way it would have to hand over, but revealing it could betray the identity of an informant or expose a sensitive method, risking real harm to an important public interest, and the prosecution is anxious to keep it back without falling foul of its disclosure duties. Which of the following best describes the proper course?
o: The prosecution must apply to the court for a public interest immunity ruling on whether the material can be withheld.
The defence must consent before any material can ever be withheld.
The prosecution must always disclose the material regardless of the public interest on these facts as a general rule.
The prosecution may destroy the material so that it need not be disclosed.
The prosecution may simply decide for itself not to disclose the material.
3.w: Where disclosable material is sensitive and its disclosure would risk serious harm to an important public interest, the prosecution must not simply withhold it unilaterally; it must apply to the court for a ruling on public interest immunity. The court balances the public interest in non-disclosure against the defendant's right to a fair trial and decides what, if anything, may be withheld.

n.1: Defence consent is not the mechanism; the court rules on PII.
n.2: Not all such material must be disclosed; PII may justify withholding, subject to the court.
n.3: Destroying material would be improper and potentially an abuse of process.
n.4: The prosecution cannot decide for itself to withhold; it must seek a court ruling.

3.q: A defendant charged with murder relies on loss of control and points to a qualifying trigger. In one version of the facts the trigger is a genuine fear of serious violence from the victim; in another it is things said or done which constituted circumstances of an extremely grave character and gave the defendant a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged. The prosecution argues that the trigger relied on does not qualify. The court considers the qualifying triggers for loss of control. The defendant said the victim's conduct had left them feeling gravely and justifiably wronged in the moment. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A fear of serious violence, or grave circumstances giving a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged, can qualify.
Only a fear of serious violence can ever be a qualifying trigger; words alone never suffice on these facts.
Sexual infidelity on its own is the paradigm qualifying trigger under the Act.
Any cause whatever of the loss of self-control is a qualifying trigger under the Act.
A qualifying trigger arises only where the victim had a weapon at the time.
3.w: Under s.55 Coroners and Justice Act 2009 the qualifying triggers are a fear of serious violence from the victim against the defendant or another, or things done or said (or both) which were of an extremely grave character and gave the defendant a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged. Sexual infidelity is expressly excluded as a trigger.

n.1: Grave things said or done can qualify, so words are not always excluded.
n.2: Sexual infidelity is expressly excluded as a qualifying trigger.
n.3: Not any cause qualifies; the trigger must fall within the statutory categories.
n.4: The victim possessing a weapon is not the statutory test.

3.q: A person gives away their house to their child during their lifetime, hoping to reduce inheritance tax, but continues to live in the house rent-free until death, so that they never truly gave up the benefit of the property. On the death, the personal representatives consider the inheritance tax treatment of the earlier gift. The court considers the rules on gifts with reservation of benefit. The parent carried on living in the house exactly as before, paying nothing for the privilege. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The gift is valid for IHT provided the child pays a market rent to the donor for the property.
The gift removes the house from the estate provided the donor survived three years.
The gift is fully effective for IHT, because the house was given away during the donor's lifetime on these facts.
The house is generally treated as remaining part of the deceased's estate for IHT, as a gift with reservation of benefit.
The gift is ignored entirely, and the house passes under the donor's will as if never given.
3.w: Under the gift with reservation of benefit rules, where a person gives away property but reserves a benefit (such as continuing to live in the house rent-free), the property is generally treated as still forming part of their estate for inheritance tax purposes on death, negating the tax advantage.

n.0: Only paying a full market rent (removing the reservation) could avoid the rule; a rent-free arrangement does not.
n.1: The three/seven-year rules do not save a gift with a continuing reserved benefit.
n.2: The reservation of benefit means the gift is not effective to remove the house for IHT.
n.4: The gift is not simply ignored; it is treated as part of the estate for IHT.

3.q: A deceased's death estate exceeds the available nil rate band, and inheritance tax is payable on the excess. The executors are calculating the tax due on the chargeable estate passing on death (with no reduced-rate charity provision applying). No special reliefs or the reduced charity rate are in issue. The executors need the rate of inheritance tax on the taxable death estate. The value of the estate comfortably exceeds the nil rate band available to it, no gift to charity attracts the reduced rate and no special reliefs bite on the excess, so the executors simply need the ordinary percentage at which tax falls due on the part of the death estate that is chargeable. Which of the following best describes the rate of inheritance tax on the chargeable death estate above the nil rate band?
3.w: Inheritance tax on the chargeable death estate above the available nil rate band is generally charged at 40%. (A reduced rate of 36% applies where at least 10% of the net estate is left to charity, and lifetime chargeable transfers into trust are taxed at 20% during life, but the standard death rate is 40%.)

n.0: 45% is not the inheritance tax death rate (it echoes an income tax additional rate).
n.1: 50% is not the inheritance tax death rate.
n.3: 20% is the lifetime rate for chargeable transfers into trust, not the death rate.
n.4: 10% is the proportion of the estate to charity needed for the reduced 36% rate, not the tax rate.

3.q: A defendant deliberately attacks a victim with the specific aim of causing them really serious harm, and does in fact inflict grievous bodily harm on the victim. The prosecution charges the most serious of the non-fatal offences against the person. The distinguishing feature of that offence, compared with the lesser wounding offence, lies in the mental element the defendant must be shown to have had. The court considers the mens rea required for the offence under s.18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. The defendant had set out deliberately to cause the victim really serious and lasting harm. Which of the following best describes it?
o: It suffices that the defendant foresaw a risk of some minor harm to the victim.
The defendant must be shown to have intended to cause grievous bodily harm.
The defendant need only have applied unlawful force, with no particular intent.
The defendant must have intended to kill the victim, or the offence is not made out.
No mens rea is required, because s.18 is an offence of strict liability.
3.w: Section 18 OAPA 1861 (wounding or causing GBH with intent) is a specific intent offence: the prosecution must prove that the defendant intended to cause grievous bodily harm (or intended to resist/prevent lawful apprehension). Mere recklessness as to some harm is insufficient for s.18.

n.0: Foresight of minor harm suffices for s.20, not s.18.
n.2: Unlawful force with no particular intent does not satisfy s.18.
n.3: An intention to kill is not required; intention to cause GBH suffices.
n.4: Section 18 requires specific intent; it is not strict liability.

3.q: During a conveyancing transaction, one solicitor gives the other solicitor a professional undertaking — for example to discharge a mortgage from the completion proceeds, or to send documents after completion. The recipient relies on the undertaking to complete safely. A question arises about the status of undertakings given between solicitors in conveyancing. The solicitor considers the effect of a conveyancing undertaking. Completion could not safely take place without relying on the other side's promise to act. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A solicitor's undertaking binds only if it is also converted into a formal deed.
A solicitor's undertaking is enforceable only against the client, never the solicitor on these facts as a general rule.
A solicitor's undertaking can be withdrawn at will at any time before performance.
A solicitor's undertaking is a mere courtesy with no binding effect whatsoever.
A solicitor's undertaking is binding and enforceable, and must be performed; conveyancing relies heavily on such undertakings.
3.w: Professional undertakings are a cornerstone of conveyancing practice: they are personally binding on the solicitor who gives them, enforceable (including through the court's supervisory jurisdiction), and must be performed. This allows solicitors to complete transactions safely in reliance on each other's undertakings.

n.0: An undertaking is binding without being made a deed.
n.1: An undertaking is enforceable against the solicitor personally, not only the client.
n.2: An undertaking cannot be withdrawn at will; it must be performed or released.
n.3: An undertaking is binding, not a mere courtesy.

3.q: A defendant unlawfully kills another human being. The prosecution charges murder. There is a dispute about the mental element that must be proved, because the defendant says they never actually wanted the victim to die. The evidence is capable of showing that the defendant at least intended to cause the victim really serious harm. The court considers the mens rea required for murder. The victim died from the injuries inflicted, and the defendant admitted meaning to cause them really serious harm. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Murder requires only that the defendant was reckless as to causing some harm.
Murder requires an intention to kill, and nothing less will ever suffice.
Murder requires an intention to kill or an intention to cause grievous bodily harm.
Murder requires premeditation and careful planning of the killing in advance.
Murder requires that the defendant foresaw a risk that death might possibly occur.
3.w: The mens rea for murder is 'malice aforethought', which means an intention to kill or an intention to cause grievous bodily harm (R v Vickers; R v Cunningham). An intention to cause GBH is sufficient even if the defendant did not intend to kill.

n.0: Recklessness is insufficient for murder.
n.1: An intention to cause GBH also suffices; intention to kill is not the only route.
n.3: Premeditation is not required; intention at the time of the act suffices.
n.4: Foresight of a mere risk of death does not establish the intention required for murder.

3.q: A trustee misappropriates trust money and uses it to buy an identifiable asset in the trustee's own name, so that the original trust money can no longer be recovered as money but the asset bought with it still exists and has been kept separate. The beneficiaries wish to claim the asset itself, rather than merely suing the trustee personally, because the asset has risen in value. The beneficiaries seek advice on their proprietary remedy. The asset had since risen sharply in value, which was why the beneficiaries wanted it rather than mere compensation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The beneficiaries may claim only the original sum of money, and never any increase in value.
The beneficiaries may trace the trust money into the asset and claim it in equity.
The beneficiaries have no claim at all, because the money has changed its form.
The beneficiaries may claim the asset only if the trustee is insolvent at the time.
The beneficiaries have only a personal claim against the trustee and can never claim the asset.
3.w: Equity allows a beneficiary to trace misapplied trust money into an identifiable substitute asset and to assert a proprietary claim to that asset (or a charge over it). This can allow the beneficiaries to claim the asset and any increase in its value.

n.0: Tracing into an appreciating asset can capture the increase in value.
n.2: A change in form does not defeat tracing where the substitute is identifiable.
n.3: Tracing does not depend on the trustee's insolvency, though it is especially valuable then.
n.4: The beneficiaries are not confined to a personal claim; a proprietary tracing claim may lie.

3.q: A trustee proposes to buy, from one of the beneficiaries, that beneficiary's equitable interest under the trust. The trustee approaches the beneficiary directly and offers to purchase the interest. A question arises as to whether such a purchase by a trustee of a beneficiary's interest is permissible, and on what conditions, given the trustee's fiduciary position and the information the trustee holds about the trust. The beneficiary was keen to realise their interest quickly and the trustee knew a great deal about its value. Which of the following best describes the position under the fair-dealing rule?
o: The purchase is always valid, because a beneficiary is free to sell their own interest to anyone on these facts as a general rule.
The purchase is valid only if approved by a majority of the other beneficiaries.
The purchase is permissible only if the trustee acts fairly, makes full disclosure and takes no advantage of their position.
The purchase is valid provided the trustee simply pays whatever the beneficiary first asks.
The purchase is automatically void, because a trustee can never deal with a beneficiary at all.
3.w: Under the fair-dealing rule, a trustee may purchase a beneficiary's beneficial interest, but the transaction will be closely scrutinised and is liable to be set aside unless the trustee shows they acted honestly and fairly, made full disclosure, took no advantage of their position and gave a fair price.

n.0: The beneficiary's freedom to sell does not remove the scrutiny of dealings with their trustee.
n.1: Approval by other beneficiaries is not the governing condition of the fair-dealing rule.
n.3: Paying whatever is first asked does not satisfy the requirements of full disclosure and fairness.
n.4: The purchase is not automatically void; it is subject to the fair-dealing conditions.

3.q: A solicitor is preparing a witness statement, which is to be verified by a statement of truth, on behalf of a client in ongoing civil proceedings. The client wants the statement to include a particular assertion of fact which the solicitor already knows, from the contemporaneous documents on the file, to be untrue, and the client asks the solicitor to draft and put forward the statement in exactly that form so that it can be signed and served on the other side. The solicitor considers whether they may properly do as the client asks. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may include the assertion, provided the client is willing personally to sign the statement of truth.
The solicitor must not put forward a statement of truth containing an assertion the solicitor knows to be untrue.
The solicitor may include the assertion, provided the other side is unlikely ever to discover that it is false.
The solicitor may include the assertion, because drafting a statement is a purely mechanical task.
The solicitor may include the assertion, because the client, not the solicitor, takes responsibility for the statement.
3.w: A solicitor must not draft or put forward a statement of truth, or any document, that contains an assertion the solicitor knows to be false. To do so would be to mislead the court and to fail to act with integrity.

n.0: The client signing the statement does not cure the solicitor's knowing participation in a false statement.
n.2: The likelihood of discovery is irrelevant; advancing a knowingly false statement is improper regardless.
n.3: Drafting is not merely mechanical where the solicitor knows the content to be untrue.
n.4: The client's willingness to take responsibility does not permit the solicitor to advance what they know is false.

3.q: A defendant is being sentenced for several separate offences at the same time. The judge is considering whether the sentences should run at the same time or one after another, and must ensure the overall sentence is just and proportionate to the totality of the offending. The defendant faces sentence for multiple offences together. The court must fix the overall length. The defendant comes up for sentence on a handful of distinct offences at once, and the judge must decide whether the individual terms should sit alongside one another or stack up one after the next, while making sure the total the defendant ends up serving genuinely fits the overall seriousness of what they did. Which of the following best describes the principle the court applies?
o: Every sentence for every offence must always run consecutively without exception on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court must simply add the maximum for each offence together.
The totality principle: whether sentences run concurrently or consecutively, the overall sentence must be just and proportionate.
The court may only ever sentence for the single most serious offence.
Every sentence must always run concurrently, so only the longest is served.
3.w: When sentencing for more than one offence, the court decides whether sentences run concurrently (together) or consecutively (one after another), but must apply the totality principle: the overall sentence must be just and proportionate to the totality of the offending, and not simply the arithmetic sum of the individual sentences.

n.0: Sentences do not always run consecutively; the court has a choice, subject to totality.
n.1: The court does not simply add the maxima together; totality governs.
n.3: The court sentences for all the offences, not only the most serious one.
n.4: Sentences do not always run concurrently; consecutive sentences are permissible.

3.q: A borrower and a lender entered into a written agreement, signed by both parties, under which the borrower agreed to grant the lender a charge over the borrower's registered property as security for a loan of £120,000; and, on the strength of that agreement, the lender advanced the whole of the £120,000 to the borrower. Through an oversight on both sides, no formal legal charge was ever executed by deed. The borrower has since defaulted on the loan, and the lender is anxious to know what security, if any, it now holds over the property. Which of the following best describes the lender's security?
o: The lender has no security of any kind and is merely an unsecured creditor.
The lender automatically has a full legal charge once the loan money is advanced.
The lender has a lien over the property that arises only if it takes physical possession. in the circumstances
The lender has an equitable charge, because a specifically enforceable agreement to grant a charge takes effect in equity.
The lender has a profit à prendre over the property until the loan is repaid.
3.w: An agreement for value to grant a charge, satisfying s.2 LP(MP)A 1989 and specifically enforceable, creates an equitable charge in the lender's favour, even though no legal charge has been executed (United Bank of Kuwait v Sahib).

n.0: The lender is not left unsecured; equity recognises an equitable charge from the enforceable agreement.
n.1: Advancing the loan does not by itself create a legal charge; a deed is needed for that.
n.2: An equitable charge does not depend on the lender taking possession.
n.4: A profit à prendre is a right to take produce from land, not a form of security.

3.q: A firm is keen to attract new clients and prepares an advertising campaign to run across its website and its social media channels. The draft marketing material prominently claims that the firm has 'the highest success rate of any firm in the country' and offers every client a 'guaranteed win or your money back'. In truth the firm cannot substantiate either statement, and both of them are inaccurate and likely to mislead members of the public who read them. A partner reviewing the campaign before it goes live is concerned about whether the firm may lawfully publish these claims. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm's publicity must not be false or misleading, so the unsubstantiated claims breach the rules and must not be published.
The firm may publish the claims, provided the firm genuinely hopes that they will turn out to be true.
The firm may publish the claims, provided a disclaimer in small print appears somewhere on the website.
The firm may publish the claims, because advertising by law firms is not subject to any professional restrictions.
The firm may publish the claims, because clients are expected to treat all advertising with healthy scepticism.
3.w: The SRA Code requires that a firm's publicity is not false or misleading. Unsubstantiated or inaccurate claims of this kind are misleading and breach the rules, regardless of any disclaimer or the firm's hopes.

n.1: A hope that claims may prove true does not make publishing inaccurate claims proper.
n.2: A small-print disclaimer does not cure headline claims that are false or misleading.
n.3: Law firm advertising is subject to professional rules and must not mislead.
n.4: The rule against misleading publicity does not depend on how sceptical clients are.

3.q: Two neighbours are in dispute about the precise line of the boundary between their two registered titles, where their gardens meet. One of them argues that the red edging shown on the official title plan for the registered title fixes, precisely and conclusively, where the legal boundary runs, and that the other neighbour's fence has therefore been put up in the wrong place. The other neighbour disputes that the title plan can be relied on in that way. They seek advice on what weight the title plan actually carries in fixing the exact line of the boundary. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Boundary disputes can only be resolved by the neighbours buying out one another.
The red edging on the title plan always fixes the precise legal boundary between titles, on these facts.
The register is conclusive as to the exact boundary and cannot be questioned at all.
The title plan usually shows only general boundaries and does not fix the exact legal boundary line.
The boundary is wherever the current fence stands, regardless of the registered titles.
3.w: Under the general boundaries rule (LRA 2002), a registered title plan shows general boundaries only and does not determine the exact line, unless the boundary has been formally 'determined'. The precise line is a matter of evidence.

n.0: Boundary disputes are resolved on the evidence, not only by a buy-out.
n.1: The red edging indicates general, not exact, boundaries.
n.2: The register is not conclusive as to the exact boundary under the general boundaries rule.
n.4: A fence line does not automatically fix the legal boundary.

3.q: An elderly parent, who relies heavily on their adult child for advice and management of their financial affairs and reposes complete trust in them, transfers a valuable property to that child at a substantial undervalue, in a transaction that is not readily explicable by the ordinary relationship between them. The parent received no independent advice. The parent later wishes to set the transfer aside, arguing that it resulted from the influence the child had over them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transaction stands, because undue influence applies only between spouses, not parent and child.
The transaction may be set aside, as undue influence is presumed from the relationship and suspicious transaction.
The transaction stands, because a parent is always free to give property to their own child.
The transaction can be set aside only if the child obtained the property by a written misrepresentation.
The transaction can be set aside only if the parent proves the child made explicit threats.
3.w: Where there is a relationship of trust and confidence and a transaction that calls for explanation, undue influence is presumed and the burden shifts to the party benefiting to rebut it (e.g. by showing independent advice). Absent such rebuttal, the transaction may be set aside (Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge).

n.0: Undue influence is not confined to spouses; parent–child is a recognised relationship of influence.
n.2: Freedom to make gifts does not prevent a transaction being set aside for undue influence.
n.3: Undue influence does not depend on a written misrepresentation.
n.4: Presumed undue influence does not require proof of explicit threats.

3.q: A large, mature tree stands in Mr Sharpe's garden, close to the boundary with Ms Turner's house next door. Over several years the tree's roots have spread under the boundary and beneath Ms Turner's house, and they are now causing subsidence that has cracked the walls and damaged the foundations, requiring costly repairs. Ms Turner has asked Mr Sharpe to deal with the tree, but he has refused, saying the tree is on his own land and its natural growth is not his responsibility. Ms Turner wants both to recover for the damage and to stop further encroachment. Which of the following best describes her claim?
o: Trespass to land, which requires the tree owner to have personally entered onto the neighbour's property without any permission.
Breach of an implied easement of support owed by the tree owner.
Adverse possession, because the roots have occupied part of the neighbour's land.
No claim, because a landowner is never liable for the natural growth of trees.
Private nuisance, for which the neighbour may seek an injunction and damages for the encroaching roots.
3.w: Encroachment by tree roots that causes damage is an actionable private nuisance. The neighbour may abate the nuisance, and may seek damages for the harm and an injunction to restrain continuing encroachment.

n.0: Trespass requires a direct physical intrusion by a person or thing placed by the defendant, not natural root growth, which is dealt with in nuisance.
n.1: This is not a support easement question; the cause of action is nuisance.
n.2: Roots spreading underground do not give the tree owner title by adverse possession.
n.3: A landowner can be liable in nuisance for encroaching roots that cause damage.

3.q: A claimant lodges a claim for judicial review. Before the substantive hearing, the court must decide whether to allow the claim to proceed to a full hearing at all, applying a threshold test at an initial stage. The claim is at the initial stage of judicial review proceedings. The court must decide whether it can go forward. The claim for judicial review has only just been lodged, and before anyone reaches the merits the court must apply the initial filter that decides whether a claim of this kind is even allowed to go forward to a full hearing at all. Which of the following best describes the permission stage in judicial review?
o: The court decides the substance of the claim finally at this initial stage.
Permission is granted only where the claimant proves the case beyond reasonable doubt.
The claimant must obtain permission, granted where there is an arguable case with a realistic prospect of success.
Every judicial review claim proceeds automatically to a full hearing without any filter on these facts.
Permission depends solely on whether the defendant public body consents.
3.w: Judicial review has a permission (leave) stage acting as a filter: the claimant must obtain the court's permission to proceed, which is generally granted where the claim is arguable and has a realistic prospect of success (and the claimant has standing and is in time). Unmeritorious claims can be stopped at this stage before a full hearing.

n.0: The permission stage is a filter, not a final determination of the substance.
n.1: The threshold is arguability/realistic prospect, not proof beyond reasonable doubt.
n.3: Claims do not proceed automatically; permission is required.
n.4: Permission does not depend on the defendant's consent.

3.q: Before completion, a seller and buyer wish to enter into a binding contract for the sale of land. They want to be sure the contract is validly made so that it can be enforced. The agreement concerns the sale of an interest in land. The parties are recording their contract. Ahead of completion the seller and buyer want a binding commitment locking each of them into the sale, and, aware that agreements about land are not made like ordinary contracts, they are anxious to record their bargain in a way that the law will actually recognise and enforce. Which of the following best describes the formalities for a valid contract for the sale of land?
o: It requires no particular formality and may be inferred from conduct alone on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
It must be in writing, incorporate all the expressly agreed terms in one document, and be signed by or for both parties.
It must be made by deed, like the transfer itself.
It need only be signed by the seller, not the buyer.
It may be made orally provided the price is agreed.
3.w: Under s.2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, a contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land must be in writing, incorporate all the expressly agreed terms in one document (or, where contracts are exchanged, in each), and be signed by or on behalf of each party. Failure to comply generally renders the contract void.

n.0: A land contract requires signed writing; it cannot rest on conduct alone.
n.2: The contract need not be by deed; the deed is used for the transfer, the contract needs signed writing.
n.3: Both parties must sign, not only the seller.
n.4: An oral contract for the sale of land is not valid, even if the price is agreed.

3.q: A trustee wrongfully pays trust money into the trustee's own personal bank account, which already contains the trustee's own money, and then makes various withdrawals from the mixed account, some of which are dissipated. The beneficiaries seek to trace into what remains. The account contains a mixture of trust money and the trustee's own money. The beneficiaries wish to identify the trust's share of the balance. Instead of keeping the trust money separate, the trustee funnelled it into their own current account alongside their personal funds and then drew on the account for various purposes, some of the money simply frittered away, leaving the beneficiaries to work out how much of what is left they can claim. Which of the following best describes a rule applied when a trustee mixes trust money with their own in a bank account?
o: The trustee is generally presumed to have spent their own money first, preserving the trust money so far as possible.
The beneficiaries may claim the whole account including the trustee's own contributions.
The beneficiaries can never trace into a mixed bank account of this kind.
The balance is always divided equally between the trustee and the beneficiaries.
The trust money is always presumed to have been spent first, defeating the beneficiaries' claim on these facts.
3.w: Where a trustee mixes trust money with their own money in a bank account, equity applies rules favourable to the beneficiaries. Under the rule in Re Hallett, the trustee is generally presumed to have dissipated their own money first, so far as possible preserving the trust money in the account for the beneficiaries (subject to refinements such as Re Oatway).

n.1: The beneficiaries trace the trust's share, not the trustee's own contributions in addition.
n.2: Beneficiaries can trace into a mixed bank account using equity's rules.
n.3: The account is not simply divided equally by default; the tracing rules favour the beneficiaries.
n.4: Trust money is not presumed spent first against the beneficiaries; the opposite presumption favours them.

3.q: An elderly parent transfers a valuable property to an adult child for little or no payment. The parent had come to rely heavily on the child in all financial matters and reposed complete trust and confidence in the child, and the transaction is one that calls for explanation as it is not readily explicable by the ordinary motives of people in such a relationship. No independent advice was taken. The relationship was one of trust and confidence and the transaction is not readily explicable by ordinary motives. Which of the following best describes the parent's strongest ground to set the transfer aside?
o: Economic duress, arising from an illegitimate threat by the child.
Presumed undue influence, arising from the relationship of trust and a transaction calling for explanation.
Common mistake, because both parties misunderstood the transaction on these facts as a general rule.
Frustration, because circumstances changed after the transfer.
Breach of an implied term that gifts be fair in amount.
3.w: Presumed undue influence can arise where there is a relationship in which one party reposes trust and confidence in the other and the transaction calls for explanation (is not readily explicable by ordinary motives). Those elements raise a presumption of undue influence, which the other party may rebut, typically by showing the transferor had independent advice.

n.0: Duress requires illegitimate pressure/threats, which is not what is described.
n.2: There is no shared mistake about the transaction; the concern is influence over the parent.
n.3: Frustration concerns supervening events defeating performance, not the fairness of a gift.
n.4: There is no implied term requiring gifts to be fair; the doctrine in point is undue influence.

3.q: The Supreme Court, hearing a case, considers a legal principle established in an entirely separate earlier case decided by the Court of Appeal some years before. The Supreme Court concludes that the principle in that earlier, unrelated case was wrong and declares that it should no longer be followed. The two cases are different cases with different parties. The earlier authority arose from a completely separate dispute between different litigants years ago, the principle it laid down has troubled the courts since, and the final court has now concluded, in the course of deciding the present unrelated case, that the old principle should no longer stand. Which of the following best describes what the Supreme Court is doing to the earlier decision?
o: Affirming the earlier decision.
Overruling the earlier decision.
Quashing the earlier decision under judicial review.
Reversing the earlier decision.
Distinguishing the earlier decision.
3.w: Overruling occurs where a higher court, in a later and separate case, decides that the legal principle laid down in an earlier case was wrong and should no longer be followed. It is distinct from reversing, which is the appellate court changing the outcome of the very same case on appeal.

n.0: Affirming would uphold, not reject, the earlier decision.
n.2: Judicial review quashes administrative decisions, not the legal principle of an earlier judgment.
n.3: Reversing changes the result of the same case on appeal, not a different earlier case.
n.4: Distinguishing avoids a precedent on the facts without saying it was wrong.

3.q: A shareholder in a private company wishes to transfer their shares to a buyer. The company's articles contain provisions restricting the transfer of shares, for example giving the directors a discretion to refuse to register a transfer, or conferring pre-emption rights on existing members. The selling shareholder argues that they can simply sell to whomever they like. The court considers the effect of transfer restrictions in a private company's articles. The company was a small family business whose articles were designed to keep ownership within the family. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transfer of shares may be restricted by the company's articles, which can bind the selling shareholder.
A shareholder may transfer shares only with the approval of the company's creditors.
Shares can never be transferred at all in a private limited company.
Transfer restrictions in the articles are automatically void and of no effect.
Shares in a private company are always freely transferable regardless of the articles on these facts.
3.w: Unlike shares in a public/listed company, shares in a private company are commonly subject to transfer restrictions in the articles — such as directors' power to refuse registration or pre-emption provisions — which are valid and bind the members.

n.1: Creditor approval is not required to transfer shares.
n.2: Shares in a private company can be transferred, subject to the articles.
n.3: Transfer restrictions in the articles are valid, not automatically void.
n.4: Private company shares are not always freely transferable; the articles may restrict transfer.

3.q: A court is interpreting a statute where applying the words in their ordinary literal sense would produce a manifestly absurd result that Parliament plainly cannot have intended. The court wishes to adopt an interpretation that avoids the absurdity while remaining faithful to the statutory language so far as possible. The literal meaning is clear but the outcome would be absurd. Read in their ordinary sense the words would require an outcome so strange that Parliament can hardly have intended it, and the court is anxious to reach a sensible result without straying any further from the statutory language than the absurdity makes necessary. Which of the following best describes the interpretive approach the court is applying?
o: The literal rule, applying the ordinary meaning regardless of absurdity.
The presumption against retrospective effect of legislation.
The expressio unius principle, excluding what is not expressly mentioned.
The mischief rule, examining the common law before the statute was passed.
The golden rule, modifying the literal meaning to avoid an absurd result.
3.w: The golden rule allows the court to depart from the ordinary literal meaning of statutory words to the extent necessary to avoid a result that is absurd or repugnant, while otherwise adhering to the language. It is applied where the literal rule would produce such an absurdity.

n.0: The literal rule would apply the ordinary meaning despite the absurdity, which is what the court is avoiding.
n.1: The presumption against retrospectivity is a separate interpretive presumption.
n.2: Expressio unius is a distinct maxim about implied exclusion, not about absurd results.
n.3: The mischief rule focuses on the defect the statute addresses, not on avoiding absurdity in clear words.

3.q: A person is not formally appointed as a director of a company and is not recorded as such, but in reality either acts as a director (taking part in board decisions as though appointed) or is a person in accordance with whose directions the properly appointed directors are accustomed to act. The company's creditors argue that such a person should be subject to directors' duties and liabilities despite the absence of a formal appointment. The court considers the concepts of de facto and shadow directors. The person gave the orders and the board routinely did exactly as that person directed them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only a person formally appointed and registered as a director can ever owe directors' duties.
A shareholder automatically becomes a director simply by holding a majority of the shares.
A person may be treated as a de facto or shadow director and be subject to directors' duties despite no formal appointment.
A person who is not formally appointed can never incur any liability in relation to the company on these facts as a general rule.
Directors' duties apply only to executive directors who are also employees of the company.
3.w: The law looks at substance: a de facto director (who acts as a director though not validly appointed) and a shadow director (a person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the directors are accustomed to act) can be subject to directors' duties and liabilities despite the absence of a formal appointment.

n.0: Duties are not confined to formally appointed, registered directors.
n.1: Holding a majority of shares does not automatically make someone a director.
n.3: An unappointed person can incur liability as a de facto or shadow director.
n.4: Directors' duties are not limited to executive director-employees.

3.q: A government Bill has been passed by the House of Commons but the House of Lords repeatedly refuses to agree to it, seeking to block it. The government wishes the Bill to become law despite the Lords' opposition, relying on a statutory mechanism. The Bill has Commons support but is being blocked by the Lords. The government invokes the relevant statutory procedure. The elected government has the numbers in the Commons but the Lords keeps sending the Bill back, determined to stop it, and ministers, unwilling to let an unelected chamber thwart their programme, are looking to the statutory route that lets the Commons have its way despite the Lords. Which of the following best describes the effect of the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949?
o: The House of Lords has an absolute veto over all legislation the Commons proposes on these facts as a general rule.
The Commons can never pass legislation without the agreement of the Lords.
The Bill must be abandoned entirely if the Lords refuse to agree to it.
In defined circumstances a Bill may be presented for Royal Assent and become law without the consent of the House of Lords.
The monarch may personally override the Lords and enact the Bill by decree.
3.w: The Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 allow certain public Bills passed by the Commons to be presented for Royal Assent and become law without the consent of the House of Lords, subject to conditions and delay (and immediately for money bills). They reflect the primacy of the elected Commons over the unelected Lords.

n.0: The Lords has no absolute veto; the Parliament Acts limit its power to a delay.
n.1: The Commons can, in defined circumstances, legislate without the Lords' agreement.
n.2: The Bill need not be abandoned; the Parliament Acts provide a route around the Lords.
n.4: Legislation is enacted by Parliament with Royal Assent, not by monarchical decree.

3.q: A solicitor is instructed by an elderly client to prepare a will leaving a substantial legacy to a named intended beneficiary. The solicitor negligently delays and fails to prepare the will before the client dies, with the result that the intended beneficiary receives nothing they would otherwise have inherited. The disappointed beneficiary, who was never the solicitor's client and had no contract with the solicitor, wishes to claim their lost inheritance from the solicitor in the tort of negligence. The intended legacy was substantial, and the beneficiary had been clearly identified in the client's instructions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The beneficiary can never recover, because they had no contract with the solicitor.
The beneficiary can recover only if they can show the solicitor acted dishonestly rather than carelessly on these facts.
The beneficiary can never recover, because a solicitor owes duties only to the living client.
The disappointed beneficiary may recover, as the solicitor is treated as owing them a duty despite the lack of contract.
The beneficiary can recover only their own out-of-pocket expenses, and not the lost legacy.
3.w: In this special situation, a solicitor who negligently fails to carry out a testator's instructions may be liable to a disappointed intended beneficiary who loses their legacy, even though the beneficiary was not the client and there was no contract, because the assumption of responsibility extends to them (White v Jones).

n.0: The absence of a contract does not defeat the claim in this recognised category.
n.1: The liability is for negligence; dishonesty is not required.
n.2: The duty here extends beyond the living client to the intended beneficiary.
n.4: The recoverable loss is the lost legacy, not merely out-of-pocket expenses.

3.q: Before making their will, a testator agrees with a friend that the testator will leave property to the friend absolutely on the face of the will, but that the friend will in fact hold it on trust for a third party. The friend accepts this during the testator's lifetime. The will itself gives the property to the friend outright, with nothing on its face to indicate any trust. After the testator's death, the intended third party seeks to enforce the arrangement. The property was significant, and the friend had expressly promised the testator to carry out the arrangement. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The friend takes the property absolutely, because the will contains no mention of any trust on these facts as a general rule.
The arrangement fails, because a trust of this kind can never be enforced after death.
The arrangement is valid only if the third party gave consideration to the testator.
A fully secret trust may be enforced, as the terms were communicated to and accepted by the friend in the testator's lifetime.
The arrangement fails, because secret trusts are not recognised in English law.
3.w: A fully secret trust arises where a will leaves property to a person apparently absolutely, but the testator has communicated the terms of a trust to that person and they have accepted them during the testator's lifetime. It is then enforced against the apparent legatee (Ottaway v Norman).

n.0: The absence of any trust on the face of the will is the very hallmark of a fully secret trust.
n.1: Such arrangements can be enforced after death if the requirements are met.
n.2: Secret trusts do not depend on consideration from the beneficiary.
n.4: Secret trusts are recognised in English law.

3.q: A defendant negligently causes a minor injury to the claimant. Because the claimant happens to have an unusually thin skull, a rare medical susceptibility unknown to anyone, that minor injury triggers far more serious consequences than the same blow would have caused to an ordinary person. The defendant argues that they should only be liable for the modest harm that a normal person would have suffered, not for the exceptional harm caused by the claimant's hidden vulnerability. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant must take the claimant as they find them and is liable for the full extent of the harm.
The defendant's liability is reduced in proportion to the claimant's pre-existing vulnerability.
The defendant is liable for the full harm only if they knew about the claimant's condition beforehand.
The defendant is liable only for the harm an ordinary person without the vulnerability would have suffered.
The defendant is not liable at all, because the serious harm was caused by the claimant's own condition.
3.w: Under the 'eggshell skull' rule, a defendant must take the claimant as they find them. Provided some injury of the relevant type was foreseeable, the defendant is liable for the full extent of the harm, even though its severity was increased by the claimant's unforeseeable pre-existing susceptibility (Smith v Leech Brain).

n.1: Damages are not reduced for a pre-existing vulnerability under this rule.
n.2: Knowledge of the condition is not required for the eggshell skull rule to apply.
n.3: Liability is not limited to the harm an ordinary person would have suffered.
n.4: The claimant's own susceptibility does not relieve the defendant where some injury was foreseeable.

3.q: A contractor is engaged to perform services over a period. Part-way through, the client indicates in advance that it will not perform its side of the bargain, an anticipatory breach which the contractor could accept and terminate. The contractor, however, decides not to accept the repudiation, and instead insists on continuing to perform the whole contract itself and then claims the full contract price, even though the client made clear it did not want the services to continue.
