The client argues the contractor should simply have stopped and claimed damages. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The innocent party must always accept an anticipatory breach and can never elect to continue performing.
The innocent party loses all remedies entirely if it does not accept the repudiation immediately.
The innocent party may always complete performance and claim the full price, whatever the circumstances.
The innocent party may sometimes affirm and perform, but only with a legitimate interest in doing so.
The innocent party may continue performing only if the contract expressly permits it to do so.
3.w: Faced with anticipatory breach, the innocent party may affirm and perform, keeping the contract alive (White & Carter v McGregor). But the right to do so is limited: it may not be exercised where the party has no legitimate interest in performing rather than claiming damages, or where performance requires the other's cooperation.

n.0: The innocent party is not obliged always to accept the breach; affirmation is an option.
n.1: Failing to accept immediately does not strip the innocent party of remedies; it may affirm.
n.2: The right to complete and claim the price is not unlimited; a legitimate interest is required.
n.4: Affirmation does not depend on an express contractual permission to continue.

3.q: The High Court concludes that a provision in an Act of Parliament simply cannot be read compatibly with a Convention right, even applying the strong interpretive obligation available to it. The claimant asks the court to grant a formal remedy recognising the incompatibility. The court is satisfied the provision is incompatible. The court has already tried and failed to find any Convention-compatible reading of the words, however generously it approaches the task, and the claimant now presses for the formal step that acknowledges the clash between the statute and the Convention while leaving it to Parliament to respond. Which of the following best describes the remedy the High Court may grant, and its effect?
o: A declaration of incompatibility, which does not affect the validity or continuing operation of the provision.
An injunction preventing any public authority from ever applying the Act.
An order quashing the offending Act of Parliament with immediate effect.
A declaration of incompatibility, which automatically strikes down the provision on these facts as a general rule.
An order suspending the Act until Parliament repeals it.
3.w: Under section 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, where a court (the High Court and above) is satisfied that a provision of primary legislation is incompatible with a Convention right and cannot be read compatibly, it may make a declaration of incompatibility. This does not affect the validity or continuing operation of the provision; it is for Parliament to decide whether to change the law.

n.1: The court does not injunct all public authorities from applying primary legislation.
n.2: Courts cannot quash an Act of Parliament for incompatibility.
n.3: A declaration of incompatibility does not strike the provision down; it leaves it operative.
n.4: A declaration does not suspend the Act; the provision remains in force.

3.q: A journalist wishes to attend and report on court proceedings. A party argues the case should be heard entirely in private and never reported. The court considers the general principle that justice should be administered openly, subject to limited exceptions. The starting point is that hearings are public. The court weighs open justice against any need for privacy. A journalist wants to sit in and report on the hearing, but one of the parties is pressing for the whole case to be conducted behind closed doors and kept out of the press entirely, forcing the court to weigh the long-standing expectation that justice is done in public against any genuine need for privacy. Which of the following best describes the principle of open justice?
o: Open justice means the public may attend but reporting is always prohibited.
Only the parties, and never the public or press, may ever attend any hearing.
All court proceedings must always be held in private with no reporting permitted on these facts as a general rule.
Justice should generally be administered in public and be capable of being reported, subject to limited exceptions.
The principle of open justice has no application to civil proceedings.
3.w: Open justice is a fundamental principle: justice should generally be administered in public, hearings should usually be open to the public and press, and proceedings should be capable of being reported. There are limited exceptions (for example, to protect children, national security or genuinely confidential matters), where hearings may be in private or reporting restricted.

n.0: Open justice generally permits reporting, not a blanket prohibition on it.
n.1: The public and press may generally attend, not only the parties.
n.2: Proceedings are not always held in private; the norm is public hearings.
n.4: Open justice applies to civil as well as criminal proceedings.

3.q: A firm proposes to agree with a commercial client, in writing at the outset of the retainer, that the firm will not account to the client for interest on client money held during the matter, or will account on a specified different basis. The client is a sophisticated commercial party willing to agree this. The arrangement is recorded in a written agreement. At the very start of the retainer the firm wants to record in writing, with a commercial client well able to understand the point, that interest on any client money held will either not be paid or will be dealt with on some agreed alternative footing rather than the usual default. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules on interest?
o: The firm may vary the interest arrangement only with the SRA's approval.
The firm can never contract out of accounting for interest in any circumstances.
The firm and client may agree in writing to a different arrangement for interest, provided it is fair and the client agrees.
The firm must always pay the exact bank interest regardless of any agreement.
The firm may keep all interest without any agreement or disclosure to the client on these facts as a general rule.
3.w: The default position is that a firm must account to the client for a fair sum of interest on client money. However, the firm and client may agree a different arrangement, including that no interest (or a different amount) will be accounted for, provided this is agreed (typically in writing) and is fair, with the client having sufficient information to give informed agreement.

n.0: Varying the interest arrangement is a matter for agreement with the client, not SRA approval.
n.1: The firm can contract out by fair written agreement, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: A fair agreed arrangement can displace the default; the exact bank interest is not always payable.
n.4: The firm cannot simply keep all interest with no agreement or disclosure.

3.q: A claimant is injured by the conduct of a worker and wishes to hold the worker's employer vicariously liable. However, on examination it turns out that the worker's conduct, although careless-looking, did not actually satisfy the elements of any recognised tort at all: no duty was breached and no actionable wrong was committed by the worker. The claimant nonetheless argues that the employer should pay because it is a business and the worker was at work. The employer disputes that vicarious liability can arise. On analysis the worker had neither owed nor breached any duty of care to the claimant at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There can be no vicarious liability unless the employee has actually committed a tort.
The employer is liable because the worker was on duty when the incident happened.
The employer is liable because it is better able than the worker to meet the claim.
The employer is liable in any event, because vicarious liability does not require an underlying tort.
The employer is liable provided the worker was acting within the course of employment.
3.w: Vicarious liability is secondary liability for another's tort. It requires that the employee (or person in an analogous relationship) has actually committed a tort. If no tort was committed by the worker, there is nothing for which the employer can be held vicariously liable.

n.1: Being on duty does not create liability where no tort was committed.
n.2: The employer's greater means do not create liability absent a tort by the employee.
n.3: Vicarious liability is parasitic on an underlying tort; it does not arise without one.
n.4: Course of employment matters only once a tort by the employee is established.

3.q: Two trustees hold registered land on trust for beneficiaries and sell it to a buyer, who pays the purchase money to both trustees. The beneficiaries had equitable interests under the trust. The buyer wishes to take the land free of those beneficial interests, which should attach to the proceeds. The purchase money is paid to two trustees. The beneficiaries hold behind the trust. Two trustees holding registered land on trust for beneficiaries have sold it, taking care that the buyer paid the purchase money to both of them, and the buyer wants to be confident it takes the land clear of the beneficiaries' interests, which should instead fasten onto the sale money. Which of the following best describes the effect of overreaching?
o: Overreaching is impossible where the land is registered.
Overreaching requires payment to a single trustee only.
The buyer takes subject to the beneficial interests despite paying two trustees on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Overreaching requires the personal consent of every beneficiary to the sale.
The beneficiaries' equitable interests are overreached and transfer to the proceeds of sale, so the buyer takes free of them.
3.w: Where trustees of land sell and the purchase money is paid to at least two trustees (or a trust corporation), the beneficiaries' equitable interests are overreached: they are detached from the land and transfer to the proceeds of sale in the trustees' hands, so the buyer takes the land free of those interests, even if a beneficiary was in actual occupation.

n.0: Overreaching operates for registered land through payment to two trustees.
n.1: Overreaching requires payment to two trustees (or a trust corporation), not a single trustee.
n.2: Paying two trustees overreaches the interests, so the buyer does not take subject to them.
n.3: Overreaching does not require each beneficiary's personal consent.

3.q: A married couple die in circumstances where it is uncertain which of them died first — for example in a common accident — and the order of their deaths affects who inherits under their wills and the intestacy rules. There is no evidence to establish who survived whom. The court considers the presumption of order of death (commorientes) under the Law of Property Act 1925. The couple were found together and nothing could show which of them had died first. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Where the order of deaths is uncertain, they are presumed to have died at exactly the same instant.
Where the order of deaths is uncertain, the estates are simply pooled and divided equally.
Where the order of deaths is uncertain, the elder is presumed to have survived the younger.
Where the order of deaths is uncertain, both estates pass automatically to the Crown.
Where the order of deaths is uncertain, the younger is presumed to have survived the elder.
3.w: Under s.184 Law of Property Act 1925, where two or more people die in circumstances making it uncertain who survived whom, for the purposes of succession the deaths are presumed to have occurred in order of seniority, so the younger is presumed to have survived the elder.

n.0: They are not presumed to die simultaneously; s.184 applies the seniority presumption.
n.1: The estates are not simply pooled and divided equally.
n.2: It is the younger, not the elder, who is presumed to have survived.
n.3: The estates do not automatically pass to the Crown.

3.q: The UK Parliament proposes to legislate on a matter that is within the devolved competence of a devolved legislature, such as the Scottish Parliament. A question arises about the constitutional expectation that applies where Westminster legislates on devolved matters. A solicitor is asked about the convention governing this situation. The solicitor considers the Sewel convention. The proposed law would operate in an area normally handled by the devolved legislature. Which of the following best describes it?
o: By the Sewel convention Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without consent, but legally retains the power.
The devolved legislature can veto any UK legislation on any subject whatsoever.
The UK Parliament requires the monarch's personal consent before legislating on devolved matters.
The UK Parliament is legally prohibited from ever legislating on any devolved matter.
The Sewel convention is a legally enforceable rule that the courts will uphold with an injunction on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
3.w: By the Sewel convention, the UK Parliament will not normally legislate with regard to devolved matters without the consent of the relevant devolved legislature. However, this is a constitutional convention: the UK Parliament retains legal sovereignty to legislate, and the convention is not enforceable by the courts.

n.1: The devolved legislature cannot legally veto UK legislation.
n.2: The monarch's personal consent is not the requirement.
n.3: The UK Parliament is not legally prohibited from legislating on devolved matters.
n.4: The Sewel convention is not legally enforceable by the courts.

3.q: A party has failed to comply with a rule, practice direction or court order — for example missing a deadline — and as a result faces a sanction. The party applies for relief from the sanction so that they can continue with their case. The court must decide how to approach the application. The court considers the approach to relief from sanctions under the Civil Procedure Rules. The party had missed an important deadline and now risked losing the right to rely on its evidence. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court must always grant relief from any sanction whenever a party asks for it.
The court decides the application purely at random with no structured approach.
The court must always refuse relief from sanctions in every case without exception.
The court applies the three-stage Denton approach: seriousness of the breach, the reason for it, and all the circumstances.
The court grants relief only where the party in default pays a fixed statutory penalty on these facts as a general rule.
3.w: When considering relief from sanctions under CPR 3.9, the court applies the three-stage approach in Denton v TH White: assess the seriousness and significance of the breach; consider why the default occurred; and evaluate all the circumstances to deal with the application justly, including the need for compliance and efficient litigation.

n.0: Relief is not automatically granted on request.
n.1: The approach is structured (Denton), not random.
n.2: Relief is not automatically refused; it is assessed under Denton.
n.4: There is no fixed statutory penalty that secures relief.

3.q: A defendant is charged with gross negligence manslaughter. The defence argues that the defendant should be judged by reference to their own limited experience and personal shortcomings, rather than by any external standard, when deciding whether their conduct fell far below what was required. The prosecution says an objective standard applies. The court considers the standard by which the defendant's negligence is judged in gross negligence manslaughter. The defendant argued that their inexperience should excuse the seriousness of what they had done. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No standard of care applies, because gross negligence manslaughter is an offence of strict liability on these facts.
The defendant is judged by whether they personally realised their conduct was negligent.
The defendant is judged purely by their own subjective abilities and personal limitations.
The defendant is judged by the standard of the least experienced person in the field.
The defendant's conduct is judged against an objective standard of the reasonably competent person in their position.
3.w: Negligence in gross negligence manslaughter is assessed objectively: the defendant's conduct is measured against the standard of a reasonably competent person carrying out the relevant activity or occupying the relevant position, not by the defendant's own subjective abilities.

n.0: A standard of care applies; the offence is not one of strict liability.
n.1: The defendant's own realisation of negligence is not the test.
n.2: The test is objective, not based on the defendant's subjective abilities.
n.3: The standard is the reasonably competent person, not the least experienced.

3.q: During an internal review it becomes clear that a firm has committed a serious breach of the SRA Accounts Rules: client money has been used improperly and a significant shortfall existed on the client account for a period. The COFA is considering what, beyond correcting the position, the firm must do about the breach itself. The breach is serious rather than trivial. The improper use of client money went undetected for a period before the review uncovered it, the shortfall has now been made good from office money, and the COFA is turning to the question of what the firm must do about the breach itself beyond simply restoring the missing funds. Which of the following best describes the COFA's obligation under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The COFA must report the breach only if a client suffers a permanent loss.
The COFA need only record the breach internally and take no further step.
The COFA must report the breach to the firm's bank rather than the SRA.
The COFA must report every breach, however trivial, to the SRA immediately.
The COFA must ensure a serious breach is reported to the SRA.
3.w: The COFA must ensure the firm records breaches of the Accounts Rules and reports serious breaches to the SRA. A serious breach, such as improper use of client money causing a significant shortfall, must be reported; less serious breaches are recorded and dealt with internally but reported to the SRA on request or as part of the wider picture.

n.0: Reporting a serious breach does not depend on the client suffering permanent loss.
n.1: A serious breach cannot simply be recorded internally with no report.
n.2: The report goes to the SRA, not the bank.
n.3: Not every trivial breach must be reported immediately; seriousness is the trigger.

3.q: A testator, intending to revoke their existing will, deliberately tears it up and throws it away, doing so with the settled intention of revoking it. In another scenario the will is accidentally destroyed in a fire without any intention to revoke it. The executor asks whether the will has been revoked in each case. The court considers revocation of a will by destruction under the Wills Act 1837. In each case the will could no longer be found in the place where it had been kept. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A will can never be revoked by destruction, only by making a later will.
Any destruction of a will revokes it, whether or not the testator intended to revoke it on these facts as a general rule.
A will is revoked only if it is destroyed in the presence of two witnesses.
Intention alone revokes a will, even without any act of destruction at all.
Revocation by destruction requires both the act of destruction and the intention to revoke; accidental destruction does not revoke.
3.w: Under s.20 Wills Act 1837, a will is revoked by burning, tearing or otherwise destroying it by the testator (or by someone in their presence and at their direction), with the intention of revoking it. Both the physical act and the intention are required, so accidental destruction without intention does not revoke the will.

n.0: Revocation by destruction is a recognised method under s.20.
n.1: Destruction without the intention to revoke does not revoke the will.
n.2: Witnesses are not required for revocation by destruction.
n.3: Intention alone, without the act of destruction, does not revoke by this method.

3.q: On exchange of contracts for the sale of a property incorporating the Standard Conditions of Sale, the buyer pays a 10% deposit to the seller's solicitor. A question arises as to the capacity in which the seller's solicitor holds the deposit pending completion. The Standard Conditions of Sale apply and the deposit has been paid to the seller's solicitor. The parties want to know how the deposit is held. On exchange the buyer hands over the customary ten per cent, and the parties, having incorporated the standard conditions, want to be clear whether the seller's solicitor may release that money to the seller straight away or must instead hold it until the deal actually completes. Which of the following best describes the usual position under the Standard Conditions?
o: The seller's solicitor holds the deposit as stakeholder, releasing it only on completion.
The deposit is forfeited to the seller immediately on exchange in every case.
The deposit belongs to the buyer's solicitor until completion.
The deposit must be paid directly to the Land Registry on exchange.
The seller's solicitor holds the deposit as agent for the seller, who may use it at once.
3.w: Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, the deposit is generally held by the seller's solicitor as stakeholder, meaning it is held for both parties and released to the seller only on completion (subject to the buyer being able to use a deposit received on a related sale). Holding as agent, allowing the seller to use it before completion, is the alternative but not the default position.

n.1: The deposit is not forfeited on exchange; forfeiture arises only on the buyer's default in completing.
n.2: The deposit is held by the seller's solicitor as stakeholder, not by the buyer's solicitor.
n.3: The deposit is not paid to the Land Registry on exchange.
n.4: Holding as agent (with immediate use) is not the default under the Standard Conditions; stakeholder is.

3.q: A firm is dealing with two entirely separate clients at the same time. It needs to pay a disbursement of several hundred pounds on behalf of Client A, but the firm currently holds no money at all in the client account for Client A. It does, however, hold ample funds in the client account for a wholly unconnected Client B. A fee-earner, wanting to get the disbursement paid on time, proposes to pay it out of the client account anyway, in effect drawing on the money held for Client B, and to sort matters out later. The firm's compliance officer reviews the proposal. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The disbursement may be paid from the client account, because all client money is pooled together anyway.
A disbursement may be paid from the client account only if sufficient funds are held for that particular client.
The disbursement may be paid from the client account, provided Client B is unlikely to need the money soon.
The disbursement may be paid from the client account, provided the shortfall is made good within a month.
The disbursement may be paid from the client account, provided the sum involved is comparatively small.
3.w: Client money is held for each client separately, and a client's ledger must never become overdrawn. A payment out for a client must not exceed the funds actually held for that client, so paying Client A's disbursement from Client B's money is not permitted.

n.0: Client money is not pooled; each client's money is held and accounted for separately.
n.2: Whether Client B needs the money soon is irrelevant; using it for Client A is improper.
n.3: An intention to make good the shortfall later does not permit overdrawing a client ledger.
n.4: The size of the disbursement does not make the improper use of another client's money acceptable.

3.q: A commercial lease was granted before 1 January 1996 (an 'old' tenancy). The original tenant lawfully assigned the lease some years ago, and the current tenant has now defaulted on the rent. The landlord seeks to recover the arrears from the original tenant. The lease is an old tenancy and the original tenant assigned it before the current default. The landlord pursues the original tenant. The lease dates from well before the 1996 reforms, the person who originally took it assigned it on some years ago and has had nothing to do with the property since, yet the current tenant has now stopped paying and the landlord, looking for someone solvent to pursue, has turned its attention back to that first tenant. Which of the following best describes the original tenant's position?
o: The original tenant is liable only if they gave an authorised guarantee agreement.
The original tenant can never be pursued once a new tenant is in occupation.
The original tenant is liable only for defaults occurring within six months of the assignment on these facts as a general rule.
The original tenant was automatically released from all liability on assigning the lease.
Under privity of contract, the original tenant of an old lease generally remains liable on the covenants for the whole term.
3.w: For 'old' tenancies (granted before 1996), privity of contract means the original tenant generally remains liable on the leasehold covenants for the whole term, even after assigning, because they contracted directly with the landlord. This contrasts with 'new' tenancies under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995, where an assigning tenant is generally released (often subject to an authorised guarantee agreement).

n.0: An authorised guarantee agreement is a feature of new tenancies; old-lease liability rests on privity of contract.
n.1: On an old lease the original tenant can be pursued despite a new tenant being in occupation.
n.2: The original tenant's liability on an old lease is not limited to six months after assignment.
n.3: Automatic release on assignment applies to new tenancies, not old ones.

3.q: A supplier is owed £10,000 by a customer under a contract. The customer, who could in fact afford to pay in full, tells the supplier that they are short of money and offers to pay £6,000 'in full and final settlement' of the whole debt. The supplier, wanting at least something quickly, agrees in a telephone call to accept the £6,000 and to write off the rest. The customer pays the £6,000. Some weeks later the supplier changes their mind and sues the customer for the remaining £4,000. The customer argues that the debt was settled. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The supplier cannot recover the £4,000, because accepting part payment always discharges the whole debt.
The supplier cannot recover the £4,000, because the customer honestly said they were short of money.
The supplier may recover the £4,000 only if the original contract was made in writing.
The supplier may still recover the £4,000, as part payment is not consideration for giving up the balance.
The supplier cannot recover the £4,000, because the agreement to accept £6,000 was a binding variation.
3.w: Under the rule in Pinnel's Case, affirmed in Foakes v Beer, payment of a smaller sum is not good consideration for a promise to forgo the balance of a debt. Absent fresh consideration or an applicable estoppel, the creditor may still sue for the unpaid £4,000.

n.0: Part payment does not, by itself, discharge the whole debt.
n.1: The debtor's honest statement of shortage does not supply the missing consideration.
n.2: Whether the original contract was in writing is irrelevant to this rule.
n.4: The promise to accept less lacked consideration, so it was not a binding variation.

3.q: A company grants a charge over its assets to a lender to secure a loan. The company secretary is aware that the charge must be registered but is unsure of the deadline, and of the consequence of missing it. The charge is one that is registrable at Companies House. The secretary wishes to preserve the lender's security. The loan has been drawn down against the security of the new charge, the secretary knows some registration step is required but is hazy on the timescale, and the lender is anxious that nothing be done, or left undone, that might jeopardise the security it has bargained for. Which of the following best describes the registration requirement and the effect of failure to register in time?
o: The charge must be registered with HM Land Registry within 21 days in every case.
The charge must be registered within 21 days, but failure only results in a fine with the charge remaining fully valid on these facts as a general rule.
The charge need not be registered at all, as registration is optional.
The charge must be registered at Companies House within 21 days of creation, failing which it is void against a liquidator, administrator and creditors.
The charge must be registered within 12 months, and late registration has no consequences.
3.w: A registrable charge created by a company must be registered at Companies House within 21 days beginning with the day after its creation. If it is not, the charge is void against a liquidator, an administrator and any creditor of the company (though the debt itself remains payable and immediately becomes repayable).

n.0: Registration is at Companies House; Land Registry registration is a separate matter for land.
n.1: Failure does more than attract a fine; it renders the charge void against the specified persons.
n.2: Registration is not optional for registrable charges.
n.4: The period is 21 days, not 12 months, and failure has serious consequences.

3.q: A building contractor engages a carpenter to complete joinery work on a development for a fixed price. Part-way through, the carpenter runs into financial difficulty and warns that he may not finish on time, which would expose the contractor to heavy penalties under the main building contract. To keep the work on track, the contractor promises the carpenter an extra payment for each flat completed on time. The carpenter completes the remaining flats on time in reliance on that promise, but the contractor then refuses to pay the extra sums, saying the carpenter was only doing what he was already contractually bound to do. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The extra payment is unenforceable, because the carpenter merely performed an existing contractual duty.
The extra payment is unenforceable, because a promise to pay more for the same work is always void.
The extra payment is enforceable, but only if the carpenter first threatened to stop work altogether.
The extra payment is enforceable: completing on time gave a practical benefit and there was no duress.
The extra payment is unenforceable, because the original fixed price can never afterwards be varied.
3.w: Where a party promises extra payment to secure performance of an existing contractual duty and thereby obtains a practical benefit (such as avoiding a penalty and the trouble of finding another contractor), that can be good consideration, provided the promise was not obtained by economic duress (Williams v Roffey Bros).

n.0: Performing an existing duty can be consideration where it confers a practical benefit, as here.
n.1: A promise to pay more for existing work is not automatically void.
n.2: A threat to stop work is not required; indeed such duress would defeat the claim.
n.4: A fixed price can be varied where the variation is supported by consideration such as a practical benefit.

3.q: A student confuses the European Convention on Human Rights with European Union law, assuming both come from the same institutions. In fact the Convention is a product of a different international organisation and is enforced by a different court from the EU institutions. The Convention and EU law have distinct origins. The student seeks clarification. The student has muddled the Convention on Human Rights with the law of the European Union, assuming both flow from the same Brussels institutions, when in truth the Convention springs from a quite separate international body and is policed by a different court altogether, a confusion the tutor wants to correct. Which of the following best describes the position of the European Convention on Human Rights?
o: It is enforced by the UK Supreme Court sitting as an EU court.
It is a treaty of the Council of Europe, enforced by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, separate from the EU.
It is a piece of European Union legislation enforced by the Court of Justice of the EU on these facts as a general rule.
It is a domestic UK statute with no international dimension.
It ceased to have any effect in the UK when the UK left the European Union.
3.w: The European Convention on Human Rights is a treaty of the Council of Europe (a separate international organisation from the European Union), and alleged breaches can ultimately be taken to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. It is given effect domestically by the Human Rights Act 1998 and is entirely distinct from EU law; UK membership of the Convention was unaffected by leaving the EU.

n.0: It is enforced ultimately by the Strasbourg court, not by the UK Supreme Court acting as an EU court.
n.2: The Convention is not EU legislation and is not enforced by the Court of Justice of the EU.
n.3: It is an international treaty, not merely a domestic statute (though the HRA gives it domestic effect).
n.4: Leaving the EU did not end the UK's participation in the Convention.

3.q: A person trespasses onto industrial land by climbing over a fence, and is injured by a dangerous piece of machinery there. The occupier knew the machinery was dangerous, knew that people sometimes climbed in at that spot, and could reasonably have offered some protection against the danger, but did nothing. The trespasser sues the occupier. The occupier argues that it owes no duty at all to someone who was not permitted to be on the land. Warning signs had been torn down some time earlier, and the gap in the perimeter fencing had never been repaired. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The occupier may owe a duty to the trespasser under the 1984 Act where the statutory conditions are met.
The occupier owes a trespasser exactly the same common duty of care as it owes to lawful visitors.
The occupier owes no duty of any kind to a trespasser in any circumstances whatsoever.
The occupier owes a duty to a trespasser only if the trespasser was a child rather than an adult.
The occupier owes a duty to a trespasser only once the trespasser has actually been injured.
3.w: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, an occupier may owe a duty to a non-visitor (trespasser) where it is aware of the danger, knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the trespasser may come into its vicinity, and the risk is one against which it may reasonably be expected to offer some protection.

n.1: The 1984 Act duty is narrower than the common duty of care owed to lawful visitors.
n.2: A trespasser may be owed a duty under the 1984 Act, so 'no duty ever' is wrong.
n.3: The 1984 Act duty is not confined to child trespassers.
n.4: The duty exists on the conditions being met; it does not arise only after injury occurs.

3.q: A defendant is charged with an offence which requires proof of intention. The defendant did not act with the aim or purpose of bringing about the prohibited result, but the prohibited result was a virtually certain consequence of what they deliberately did, and the defendant appreciated that it was virtually certain. The jury has to decide whether the defendant can be found to have intended the result. The defendant's adviser considers the meaning of intention, including oblique intention. The consequence was one the defendant had clearly seen coming as all but inevitable when they acted. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant automatically intended the result simply because it was a possible consequence.
The defendant cannot have intended the result, because it was not their aim or purpose.
Intention can never be inferred and must always be admitted by the defendant.
Intention is established whenever the defendant was merely careless as to the result.
The jury may find intention where the result was virtually certain and the defendant appreciated that.
3.w: Intention includes direct intent (aim or purpose) and oblique intent: where the result was a virtually certain consequence of the defendant's actions and the defendant appreciated that this was so, the jury is entitled to find that the defendant intended the result (R v Woollin).

n.0: A merely possible consequence does not establish intention.
n.1: Intention is not confined to aim or purpose; oblique intent may suffice.
n.2: Intention can be inferred from the circumstances; it need not be admitted.
n.3: Carelessness is not intention.

3.q: A first mortgage of unregistered land was granted without the lender taking the title deeds (for example, a second charge, or a legal mortgage where deeds are held elsewhere). The lender wishes to protect its mortgage against a later buyer or lender. The mortgage is of unregistered land and is not protected by deposit of the title deeds. The lender wants its security to bind third parties. A lender advanced money on the security of unregistered land but, because the title deeds are held elsewhere, could not take them as security, and it is anxious that its charge should still bind anyone who later buys the land or lends against it rather than being quietly defeated. Which of the following best describes how the mortgage should be protected?
o: It should be protected by a notice on the seller's registered title.
It should be registered as a puisne mortgage (a land charge) against the estate owner's name.
It is automatically protected without any registration because it is a legal mortgage.
It requires no protection because mortgages always bind later buyers.
It should be protected by an official search with priority.
3.w: A legal mortgage of unregistered land that is not protected by a deposit of the title deeds (a puisne mortgage) is registrable as a land charge (Class C(i)) against the estate owner's name. If not registered, it will be void against a later purchaser of the land for value, so registration is essential to bind third parties.

n.0: A notice on a registered title is the method for registered land, not this unregistered mortgage.
n.2: A puisne mortgage is not automatically protected; it must be registered as a land charge.
n.3: An unprotected puisne mortgage can be void against a later purchaser, so protection is required.
n.4: An official search with priority is a registered-land search, not a method of protecting an unregistered mortgage.

3.q: A testator leaves a substantial part of their net estate to a registered charity, and the executors are told that this may reduce the rate of inheritance tax on the rest of the estate, not merely provide an exemption for the charitable gift itself. The charitable gift is large in proportion to the net estate. The executors are considering the reduced rate of inheritance tax. The testator directed a sizeable slice of the estate to a registered charity, and the executors have been told this may do more than exempt the charitable gift itself, potentially lowering the rate of tax on what is left, so they want to know the threshold that triggers that lower rate and what the rate becomes. Which of the following best describes when the reduced rate applies and what it is?
o: Where at least 25% of the estate passes to charity, the rate is reduced to 20%.
The reduced rate reduces the tax to 0% regardless of the size of the charitable gift.
The reduced rate applies only to lifetime gifts, never on death.
Where at least 10% of the net estate passes to charity, the rate of inheritance tax on the rest is reduced to 36%.
Where any gift at all is made to charity, the whole estate becomes exempt from inheritance tax on these facts.
3.w: Where at least 10% of a defined 'net estate' is left to charity, the rate of inheritance tax on the remainder of that component of the estate is reduced from 40% to 36%. The charitable gift itself is also exempt. This is separate from the general charity exemption, which applies to any charitable gift.

n.0: The threshold is 10% of the net estate for the reduced rate of 36%, not 25% for 20%.
n.1: The reduced rate is 36%, not 0%.
n.2: The reduced rate applies to the death estate, not only lifetime gifts.
n.4: Any charitable gift is exempt, but it does not make the whole estate exempt.

3.q: During litigation, one party proposes mediation to try to settle the dispute, but the other party refuses to engage in any form of alternative dispute resolution at all, without any adequate justification for that refusal, and the matter proceeds to a trial that might have been avoided. At the end, the court considers costs. The court considers the costs consequences of an unreasonable refusal to engage in ADR. A short mediation could well have resolved the whole dispute long before it reached trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An unreasonable refusal to engage in ADR may be penalised by the court in costs, even against an otherwise successful party.
A refusal to mediate is relevant only where the refusing party ultimately loses at trial on these facts as a general rule.
A refusal to engage in ADR can never have any effect on the court's decision about costs.
The court will always order the party who refused ADR to lose the case entirely.
Parties are compelled by law to settle every dispute through mediation before any trial.
3.w: The court expects parties to consider ADR, and an unreasonable refusal to engage in it may be reflected in the costs order, potentially depriving even a successful party of some or all of its costs (Halsey v Milton Keynes; PGF II v OMFS).

n.1: An unreasonable refusal can be penalised even where the refusing party succeeds at trial.
n.2: An unreasonable refusal to engage in ADR can affect costs.
n.3: A refusal to mediate does not automatically cause the refusing party to lose the case.
n.4: There is no absolute legal compulsion to settle every dispute by mediation.

3.q: A firm receives money from a client specifically to pay a professional disbursement, such as counsel's fee, that has already been incurred but not yet paid. The cashier is deciding whether the money is client money or may be treated as office money on receipt. The money is earmarked for a specific professional disbursement already incurred but unpaid. The cashier must classify and handle it correctly. The client has sent money specifically so that a particular professional disbursement, counsel's fee, can be settled, a fee that has already been run up but not yet paid, and the cashier must decide whether that earmarked money is the client's or can be treated as the firm's on receipt. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment?
o: It is automatically office money the moment it is received because the disbursement was already incurred on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
It need not be banked at all provided the disbursement is paid eventually.
It must be paid directly to the SRA pending payment of the disbursement.
It is client money to be paid into the client account, unless and until it is properly used to pay the disbursement or otherwise becomes office money.
It may be spent on the firm's general expenses because it relates to an incurred cost.
3.w: Money received from a client to pay a specific professional disbursement is client money and must be paid into the client account and applied to that disbursement (or otherwise dealt with under the rules). It does not automatically become office money simply because the disbursement has already been incurred; the firm must handle it as the client's money for the intended purpose.

n.0: It does not automatically become office money on receipt merely because the cost was incurred.
n.1: It must be banked promptly in the client account, not left unbanked.
n.2: It is not paid to the SRA; it is held as client money and applied to the disbursement.
n.4: It cannot be spent on the firm's general expenses.

3.q: A claimant is injured while they and the defendant are jointly engaged in committing a serious criminal offence together, the injury arising directly out of that joint criminal enterprise. The claimant then sues the defendant in negligence for the injuries suffered during the crime. The defendant argues that the court should not allow the claimant to found a claim on their own serious criminal wrongdoing. The two had planned the offence together in advance and were in the act of carrying it out when the injury occurred. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim is merely reduced for contributory negligence, but is never barred by illegality.
The claim is barred only if the claimant was convicted of the offence before suing.
The claim succeeds in full, because illegality is never a defence to a claim in negligence.
The claim succeeds, because the defendant was also involved in the same criminal enterprise on these facts.
The claim may be barred by the illegality defence, as it arises directly from the claimant's own serious criminal act.
3.w: The defence of illegality (ex turpi causa non oritur actio) may bar a claim which is founded on, or arises directly out of, the claimant's own serious criminal conduct, where allowing recovery would be contrary to public policy and the integrity of the legal system.

n.0: Illegality can bar the claim entirely, not merely reduce it.
n.1: A prior conviction is not a precondition to the illegality defence.
n.2: Illegality can be a defence in negligence; it is not always excluded.
n.3: The defendant's own involvement in the crime does not automatically defeat the illegality defence.

3.q: A judge is sentencing an offender for an offence for which the Sentencing Council has issued a definitive sentencing guideline. The judge is considering how much regard must be had to that guideline in deciding the sentence. The defendant's solicitor refers the court to the relevant guideline. The solicitor considers the status of sentencing guidelines. A definitive guideline set out the categories and ranges for exactly this kind of offence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court must follow the relevant sentencing guideline unless satisfied it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.
Sentencing guidelines apply only in the Crown Court and never in the magistrates' court on these facts as a general rule.
Sentencing guidelines fix a single mandatory sentence that the judge cannot vary at all.
Sentencing guidelines are relevant only where the offender pleads not guilty.
Sentencing guidelines are purely advisory and the court may ignore them entirely.
3.w: By statute, a court must, in sentencing an offender, follow any relevant sentencing guideline unless it is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. Guidelines set offence ranges and category starting points, within which the judge applies aggravating and mitigating factors.

n.1: Guidelines apply in the magistrates' court as well as the Crown Court.
n.2: Guidelines provide ranges and starting points, not a single immovable sentence.
n.3: Guidelines apply regardless of plea (with credit given separately for a guilty plea).
n.4: Guidelines are not merely advisory; the court must generally follow them.

3.q: A defendant admits owing the claimant a duty of care, but disputes that they fell below the required standard. The defendant is an ordinary person carrying out an everyday activity, and did what they genuinely thought was sensible at the time. The claimant argues that the defendant's honest belief that they were being careful is beside the point, and that the defendant must be judged against an objective yardstick. The court must decide the standard against which the defendant's conduct is measured. Which of the following best describes the standard of care?
o: The defendant is judged only by their own honest belief that they were acting carefully at the time.
The defendant is judged by whatever standard the defendant personally considers appropriate.
The defendant is judged against the standard of a reasonable person doing that activity, objectively assessed.
The defendant is judged against a purely subjective standard tailored to their own abilities.
The defendant is judged against the standard of the most careful and skilful person imaginable.
3.w: The standard of care in negligence is objective: the defendant is measured against the standard of the reasonable person carrying out the activity in question, not against their own honest belief or subjective view of what was careful (Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks).

n.0: The defendant's honest belief does not set the standard; it is objective.
n.1: The defendant cannot set their own standard of care.
n.3: The standard is objective, not tailored subjectively to the individual defendant's abilities.
n.4: The standard is that of the reasonable person, not perfection or the most skilful person.

3.q: During the UK's membership of the EU, a directive that had not been properly implemented into domestic law by the deadline conferred a clear, precise and unconditional right. An individual sought to rely on the directive against a state body, and separately another individual sought to rely on it against a private employer. The directive was unimplemented but sufficiently clear and unconditional. Reliance was sought against both a state body and a private party. The deadline for turning the directive into national law had passed with nothing done, yet its terms were clear and unconditional enough to be relied on, and two claimants tested it in different directions, one against an arm of the state and the other against an ordinary private employer. Which of the following best describes the direct effect of directives as it then operated?
o: A directive had direct effect only against private parties, never the state.
A directive had direct effect only once formally implemented into domestic law.
A directive could have vertical direct effect against the state, but not horizontal direct effect against a private party.
A directive always had full horizontal and vertical direct effect against anyone on these facts as a general rule.
A directive could never have any direct effect in any circumstances.
3.w: An unimplemented directive that was sufficiently clear, precise and unconditional could be relied upon by an individual against the state or an emanation of the state (vertical direct effect), but not against another private party (no horizontal direct effect). This reflected the position developed in EU law during membership.

n.0: This reverses the position: direct effect ran against the state, not private parties.
n.1: The whole point of vertical direct effect was reliance on an unimplemented directive against the state.
n.3: Directives did not have horizontal direct effect against private parties.
n.4: Sufficiently clear, unconditional directives could have vertical direct effect, so 'never' is wrong.

3.q: After standard disclosure has taken place, one party believes the other holds specific documents relevant to an issue that have not been disclosed, and which should have been. The party wishes the court to order the other side to carry out a further, targeted search and disclose those particular documents. Standard disclosure has already occurred but specific documents are said to be missing. The party seeks a targeted order. Standard disclosure has come and gone, but the party is convinced that particular documents bearing directly on a key issue exist and remain in the other side's hands undisclosed, and it wants the court to compel a further, focused search and production of exactly those documents. Which of the following best describes the appropriate application?
o: An application for specific disclosure, requiring a further search for and disclosure of identified documents or classes of document.
An application for a freezing injunction over the documents.
An application to strike out the other party's statement of case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
An application for a wasted costs order against the other side.
An application for summary judgment on the whole claim.
3.w: Where a party considers that the other's disclosure is inadequate, it may apply for specific disclosure under the CPR, seeking an order that the other party carry out a further search and disclose specified documents or classes of document. The court will make such an order where it is necessary to deal with the case justly and proportionately.

n.1: A freezing injunction preserves assets, not the disclosure of documents.
n.2: Striking out is a disproportionate response to a disclosure shortfall; specific disclosure is the targeted remedy.
n.3: A wasted costs order concerns a representative's conduct, not inadequate disclosure.
n.4: Summary judgment disposes of a claim; it is not a disclosure remedy.

3.q: A donor executes a share transfer form and hands it, together with the share certificate, to the intended donee, having done everything within the donor's own power to transfer the shares. The only outstanding step is registration of the transfer by the company, which is a matter for the company and outside the donor's control. The donor dies before registration is completed. The intended donee argues the transfer should be treated as effective in equity despite the missing registration. The shares were valuable, and the donee had already lodged the transfer with the company before the donor died. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transfer is effective at law, because handing over the certificate transfers legal title.
The transfer is wholly ineffective, because legal title had not been registered before death.
The transfer is effective only if the donee provided consideration for the shares.
The transfer may be effective in equity, because the donor did everything necessary for them to do.
The transfer is ineffective, because equity never perfects an imperfect gift in any circumstances.
3.w: Where the donor has done everything within their own power to effect the transfer, leaving only steps for a third party (such as company registration), equity may treat the transfer as effective and the donor as holding on trust pending registration (Re Rose), even though legal title has not yet passed.

n.0: Handing over the certificate does not itself transfer legal title to shares.
n.1: The gift is not necessarily defeated by the absence of registration where the donor did all they could.
n.2: The Re Rose principle does not depend on the donee providing consideration.
n.4: The Re Rose principle is a recognised qualification to 'equity will not perfect an imperfect gift'.

3.q: A public body's decision interferes with an individual's rights, and the challenge is brought in a context (such as a human rights or, historically, an EU law matter) where the court examines whether the interference was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, rather than merely whether it was rational. A solicitor is asked about the intensity of review in such contexts. The solicitor considers the principle of proportionality. The measure struck at a protected right and the court had to weigh it against the aim pursued. Which of the following best describes it?
o: In human rights (and certain other) contexts the court applies proportionality, asking whether the measure is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
Proportionality applies to every judicial review claim in exactly the same way as irrationality on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Proportionality allows the court to quash any decision the claimant considers unfair.
Proportionality has no place in UK public law in any circumstances.
Proportionality means the court simply defers entirely to the decision-maker in every case.
3.w: In cases engaging Convention rights under the Human Rights Act (and formerly in EU law contexts), the court applies a proportionality analysis: whether the objective is sufficiently important, whether the measure is rationally connected to it, whether a less intrusive measure could have been used, and whether a fair balance has been struck. This is a more intensive review than Wednesbury irrationality.

n.1: Proportionality is not the general standard for all judicial review; it applies in particular contexts.
n.2: Proportionality is not simply a test of the claimant's sense of unfairness.
n.3: Proportionality does have a role in UK public law, notably under the HRA.
n.4: Proportionality is a structured, intensive review, not complete deference.

3.q: An owner of a house wishes to raise money by borrowing against the property and grants a mortgage to a bank. The bank wants its security to be legally effective and to be protected against later buyers or lenders. The owner's solicitor advises on how a mortgage of registered land is created and protected. The client asks how the bank's mortgage takes effect as a legal charge and secures priority. The solicitor considers the creation and registration of a legal mortgage of registered land. The owner needed the loan quickly and the bank wanted watertight security over the house. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A mortgage of registered land can only ever be created by physically depositing the title deeds.
A mortgage of registered land need not be in writing and may be created orally.
A mortgage of registered land is protected only by the lender taking possession of the property.
A legal mortgage of registered land is created by a charge, which must be registered against the title to take effect as a legal charge.
A mortgage of registered land takes effect legally as soon as it is signed, with no need to register it on these facts as a general rule.
3.w: A mortgage of registered land is created by a legal charge, which is a registrable disposition. It must be completed by registration against the registered title (entry in the charges register) to take effect as a legal charge and to secure its priority; until registered it takes effect only in equity.

n.0: Deposit of deeds is not how a legal mortgage of registered land is created.
n.1: A mortgage must be by deed/charge in writing, not oral.
n.2: The charge is protected by registration, not by the lender taking possession.
n.4: A legal charge of registered land must be registered to take effect at law, not merely signed.

3.q: A defendant is charged with an offence and brought before the magistrates' court, where the question of bail arises pending the next hearing. The defendant has a settled home, a job, and no history of failing to attend court. The prosecution has not raised any strong objection. The defendant's solicitor advises on the starting point for bail. The solicitor considers the presumption in favour of bail under the Bail Act 1976. The defendant had strong community ties and had never previously failed to attend a court hearing. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Bail is entirely at the personal discretion of the police and cannot be considered by the court.
Bail can never be granted to a defendant who has been charged with any offence.
There is a presumption against bail, so a defendant must always be remanded in custody before trial on these facts.
Bail is granted only where the defendant pays a cash sum to the court in advance.
There is a general presumption in favour of bail, so bail should be granted unless a statutory ground for refusing it applies.
3.w: Under the Bail Act 1976 there is a general presumption in favour of bail for a defendant in criminal proceedings. Bail should be granted unless the court is satisfied that one of the statutory exceptions (grounds for refusing bail) applies on the facts.

n.0: The court, not only the police, considers bail; there is a legal framework.
n.1: Bail is available for charged defendants, subject to the exceptions.
n.2: The presumption is in favour of, not against, bail.
n.3: A cash payment in advance is not the basis for granting bail.

3.q: The directors of a private company with several directors wish to hold a board meeting to make a decision. They ask what is required for the board to act validly, in particular how many directors must be present and how a tie in voting is resolved, applying the model articles. The company has adopted the unamended model articles for private companies. The board wishes to take a decision at a meeting. The directors are gathering to take an important decision and want to be confident the meeting will be validly constituted, so they need to know how many of them must actually be present and what happens if the vote ends up evenly split between them. Which of the following best describes the position under the model articles?
o: The quorum is all the directors, who must decide unanimously.
The quorum is a majority of all the directors, with no casting vote available on these facts.
There is no quorum requirement for board meetings under the model articles.
The quorum for a board meeting is two directors, and the chair has a casting vote in the event of a tie.
A single director always forms a quorum and there is never a casting vote.
3.w: Under the model articles for private companies, the quorum for a directors' meeting is two (unless otherwise fixed, and subject to the special position of a sole-director company), and the chair of the meeting has a casting vote where votes are equal. This enables the board to act by a majority with a tie-breaker.

n.0: Board decisions are by majority, not unanimity, under the model articles.
n.1: The default quorum is a fixed number (two), not a majority of all directors.
n.2: The model articles do impose a quorum requirement.
n.4: The default quorum is two, and there is a casting vote, contrary to this option.

3.q: A fee-earner receives, through the post, a cheque representing completion monies which are client money held on behalf of a client. Instead of banking the cheque, the fee-earner simply leaves it sitting in the matter file for around two weeks before it is finally paid into the client account, purely because the file is busy and other work keeps taking priority over it. The money is not spent, misdirected or used by the firm at any point during that period. The firm's compliance officer later reviews the file and raises the delay. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: Client money need only ever be banked once the matter to which it relates has been fully completed and billed.
Client money may be held outside a client account indefinitely, provided that it is eventually banked at some point.
The delay is acceptable in these circumstances, because the money was not spent or misapplied during the period.
A cheque is not client money until it has actually cleared, so no accounts rule was engaged by the delay here.
Client money must be paid promptly into a client account, so leaving the cheque unbanked for around two weeks was a breach.
3.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require client money to be paid promptly into a client account. A cheque representing client money must be banked without delay; holding it for around two weeks is a breach even though the money was not misapplied.

n.0: The obligation to bank promptly does not wait until the matter completes.
n.1: Client money cannot be held outside a client account indefinitely; it must be banked promptly.
n.2: The absence of misapplication does not excuse the failure to bank the money promptly.
n.3: Money received as client money is client money on receipt; the promptness obligation is not deferred until clearance.

3.q: A person dies intestate leaving no spouse or civil partner. They are survived by various relatives, including children, parents, and siblings, and the family needs to know the order in which relatives inherit on intestacy where there is no surviving spouse. The court considers the statutory order of entitlement on intestacy in the absence of a spouse. The intestate had died suddenly with no will and a scattering of relatives of varying closeness. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The estate passes immediately to the Crown whenever there is no surviving spouse.
The estate passes to the intestate's parents first, ahead of any children of the intestate.
The estate is always shared equally among all surviving relatives regardless of their relationship on these facts as a general rule.
The estate passes to the issue first; only if there are none does it pass to parents, then siblings, and so on down the statutory order.
The estate passes to the most distant surviving relative, in reverse order of closeness.
3.w: Where there is no surviving spouse or civil partner, the estate passes under the statutory order to the issue on the statutory trusts; if there are no issue, then to parents; then to brothers and sisters of the whole blood (on statutory trusts); and so on down the prescribed order, with the Crown taking only as a last resort (bona vacantia).

n.0: The estate passes to the Crown only if no qualifying relatives exist.
n.1: Issue take before parents, not the other way round.
n.2: The estate is not shared equally among all relatives; a strict order applies.
n.4: Closer relatives take before more distant ones, not in reverse.

3.q: Shortly before completion, a buyer's solicitor carries out an official search of the register with priority against the seller's registered title. The search reveals no adverse entries. The solicitor wants to understand the effect of the priority conferred by the search. The search is an official search with priority (OS1). The solicitor is planning completion and registration. With completion imminent, the solicitor lodges the official pre-completion search against the seller's title, gets a clear result showing no adverse entries, and now wants to understand exactly what protection that clear search buys the buyer in the run-up to registering the purchase. Which of the following best describes the protection the priority search confers?
o: It transfers legal title to the buyer immediately on the date of the search on these facts as a general rule.
It confers a priority period during which the buyer's application to register is protected against later entries.
It removes the need ever to register the transfer at all.
It provides indemnity insurance against any defect in the seller's title.
It permanently prevents the seller from ever dealing with the land again.
3.w: An official search of the register with priority (OS1) gives the buyer a priority period (of 30 working days) during which the buyer's application to register the disposition takes priority over any other application, so entries made by others in that window do not affect the buyer. The buyer must complete and apply to register within the priority period.

n.0: It does not transfer legal title on the search date.
n.2: The transfer must still be registered; the search does not remove that requirement.
n.3: It is not indemnity insurance against title defects.
n.4: It does not permanently prevent the seller dealing with the land; it protects a limited priority period.

3.q: A commercial contract between two businesses of equal bargaining power contains a clause requiring the party in breach to pay a fixed sum on a particular breach. The sum was a genuine attempt to protect the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance and is not extravagant or out of all proportion to that interest. When the clause is triggered, the paying party argues that it is an unenforceable penalty and that only the actual loss should be payable. The other party relies on the clause as agreed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The clause is enforceable only if the fixed sum exactly matches the actual loss suffered.
The clause is enforceable if it protects a legitimate interest and is not out of all proportion.
The clause is automatically unenforceable, because any fixed pre-agreed sum is a penalty.
The clause is unenforceable, because businesses can never agree damages in advance.
The clause is enforceable only where the innocent party can prove it suffered no loss at all.
3.w: A pre-agreed damages clause is enforceable as liquidated damages, not a penalty, provided it does not impose a detriment out of all proportion to a legitimate interest of the innocent party in performance (Cavendish Square v Makdessi; ParkingEye v Beavis). A genuine, proportionate clause is binding.

n.0: The sum need not match the actual loss exactly; that is not the modern test.
n.2: Not every fixed pre-agreed sum is a penalty; proportionate clauses are enforceable.
n.3: Businesses can agree damages in advance through liquidated damages clauses.
n.4: Enforceability does not depend on the innocent party proving it suffered no loss.

3.q: In the course of negotiating the terms of a commercial deal for a client, a solicitor is dealing directly with the representatives on the other side of the transaction. In order to gain an advantage in the negotiation, the solicitor is sorely tempted to make a statement to the other side about the client's position and intentions which the solicitor knows perfectly well to be false, calculating that the misrepresentation will help to secure noticeably better terms for their own client. The statement would be made to the other party, and not to any court. The solicitor considers whether making it would be proper. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A solicitor may mislead the other side, provided the other side has its own solicitors to protect it.
A solicitor may mislead the other side, provided the statement is made orally rather than in writing.
A solicitor may mislead the other side, because the duty of honesty is owed only to the court, not to opponents.
A solicitor may mislead the other side, provided doing so secures a genuine advantage for their own client.
A solicitor must not mislead or attempt to mislead anyone, including third parties, in the course of practice.
3.w: The duty of honesty and the requirement not to mislead are not confined to dealings with the court. A solicitor must not mislead, or attempt to mislead, clients, the court, or third parties such as the other side in a negotiation.

n.0: The other side being represented does not license misleading them.
n.1: An oral misrepresentation is no more permissible than a written one.
n.2: The duty not to mislead extends beyond the court to third parties.
n.3: Advancing the client's interests does not permit making a statement known to be false.

3.q: A judge in the High Court is referred to a recent decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on the very point in issue. Counsel accepts the decision is not from a court in the ordinary domestic hierarchy but urges the judge to attach considerable weight to it. There is no directly binding domestic authority on the point. The overseas appeal happens to have been decided by many of the same senior judges who sit in the domestic final court, the reasoning is directly on the disputed point, and counsel is candid that it comes from outside the ordinary ladder of English courts while urging that it should still carry real weight. Which of the following best describes the status of a Privy Council decision in the courts of England and Wales?
o: It automatically overrules any conflicting House of Lords decision.
It is binding on all courts below the Supreme Court without exception.
It has no relevance whatsoever and must be ignored.
It is persuasive but not strictly binding on the domestic courts.
It binds the High Court but not the Court of Appeal.
3.w: Decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are not part of the ordinary domestic court hierarchy and are therefore persuasive rather than strictly binding on the courts of England and Wales. Given the seniority of its members, however, such decisions are usually treated as highly persuasive.

n.0: They do not automatically overrule House of Lords or Supreme Court authority.
n.1: Privy Council decisions are not strictly binding on the domestic courts.
n.2: They are relevant and often highly persuasive, so they cannot be ignored.
n.4: They are persuasive at every level, not binding on the High Court alone.

3.q: A claimant needs to serve a claim form on a defendant company. The claimant is unsure of the correct place at which a company may validly be served with a claim form under the Civil Procedure Rules, and wants to ensure service is effective so as not to jeopardise the claim. The company has a registered office. The court considers valid methods of serving a claim form on a company. The claimant wanted to be sure the company could not later say it had never been served. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claim form may be served on a company only at the home address of one of its shareholders.
A company cannot be served with a claim form at all and must instead be sued through its directors personally.
Service on a company is valid only if the claim form is served at the offices of its auditors.
A claim form may validly be served on a company by leaving it at, or posting it to, the company's registered office.
A company can only ever be served by handing the claim form personally to its managing director.
3.w: A claim form may be served on a company by various permitted methods, including leaving it at or sending it by post to the company's registered office (and, under the Companies Act, service at the registered office is a recognised method), among other permitted places of business.

n.0: A shareholder's home address is not a valid place for serving the company.
n.1: A company can be served; it need not be sued only through its directors personally.
n.2: The auditors' office is not a valid place for service on the company.
n.4: Personal service on the managing director is not the only valid method.

3.q: The owner of a dominant field enjoys a right of way, granted by deed for agricultural access, along a track over a neighbour's land. In recent months the dominant owner has occasionally led a small number of additional animals along the track on the way to market, causing only a trivial increase in the overall amount of use and no real additional wear, damage or inconvenience to the servient land. The servient owner, who has come to dislike the arrangement, wishes to treat this as an excessive use of the easement and to stop the dominant owner from using the track at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Excessive user converts the easement into a profit à prendre over the servient land.
Any change at all in the pattern of use automatically extinguishes the easement.
A minor increase in use within the nature of the easement is not actionable as excessive user.
The dominant owner must pay compensation to the servient owner for any increase in use.
The servient owner may block the way entirely because the dominant owner altered the use, on these facts.
3.w: Whether use is 'excessive' is a question of degree. A trivial or minor increase that remains within the character of the easement granted is not actionable; only use that goes materially beyond the scope of the right is restrained.

n.0: Excessive user does not transform an easement into a profit.
n.1: A minor change within the nature of the right does not extinguish the easement.
n.3: There is no general obligation to compensate for a minor increase in permitted use.
n.4: The servient owner cannot block a validly used easement for a trivial increase.

3.q: A suspect is about to be interviewed under caution at the police station. The interviewing officer administers the standard caution before questioning. The suspect's solicitor advises the suspect about the effect of the caution and the consequences of remaining silent. The offence is one where the suspect could later rely on facts in their defence. The solicitor considers the caution and the drawing of adverse inferences from silence. The suspect intended to give an account at trial and had to decide whether to answer questions now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The suspect may remain silent, but a court may draw an adverse inference if they later rely on a fact they could reasonably have mentioned when questioned.
The suspect must answer all questions put to them, or they commit a separate criminal offence.
The suspect may remain silent only if they have first been formally charged with the offence.
An adverse inference is drawn automatically from any silence, regardless of the defence later run on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The suspect's silence can never be mentioned or held against them in any way at trial.
3.w: The caution warns that the suspect need not say anything, but that it may harm their defence if they do not mention when questioned something they later rely on in court. Under s.34 Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, a court may draw such adverse inferences from a failure to mention a fact later relied on which the suspect could reasonably have been expected to mention.

n.1: Silence is not itself an offence; the consequence is a possible adverse inference.
n.2: The inference relates to pre-charge questioning under caution, not only post-charge silence.
n.3: Inferences are not automatic; they depend on the facts later relied on and reasonableness.
n.4: Silence can, in defined circumstances, lead to an adverse inference at trial.

4.q: A defendant of limited means is charged with a criminal offence and wishes to be represented, but cannot afford to pay privately for a solicitor to conduct the case in the magistrates' or Crown Court. The defendant's solicitor advises on the availability of public funding for criminal defence. The solicitor considers eligibility for a criminal legal aid representation order. The defendant was on a low income and could not begin to fund a defence privately. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Criminal legal aid is never available for the defence of a criminal charge.
Criminal legal aid is available only to defendants who intend to plead guilty.
Criminal legal aid depends on satisfying both a means test and the interests of justice (merits) test.
Criminal legal aid is available to every defendant automatically, regardless of means or the case.
Criminal legal aid depends only on the seriousness of the offence and not on the defendant's means.
4.w: Eligibility for a criminal legal aid representation order generally depends on satisfying both the means test (the defendant's financial circumstances) and the interests of justice test (factors such as risk of loss of liberty, complexity of the case, and ability to understand proceedings).

n.0: Criminal legal aid is available where the tests are satisfied.
