n.1: Legal aid is not confined to those pleading guilty.
n.3: Legal aid is not automatic for everyone; the tests must be met.
n.4: Both means and interests of justice are relevant, not only the offence's seriousness.

4.q: Having obtained a grant, personal representatives are administering the estate. They need to carry out various tasks, such as selling estate property to raise money, appropriating assets to satisfy legacies, and running the deceased's business briefly. The PRs ask about the scope of their powers to deal with the estate assets. The court considers the powers of personal representatives under the Administration of Estates Act 1925 and the Trustee Act 2000. The estate held a mix of property, investments and a small business the deceased had run. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: PRs have no powers to deal with the estate and must obtain a court order for every step.
PRs have wide statutory powers, including to sell, mortgage, appropriate and invest estate assets in the course of administration.
PRs may only distribute the estate exactly as directed and may never sell any asset.
PRs may deal with the estate only with the written consent of every beneficiary for each act on these facts as a general rule.
PRs may exercise powers only over land, and never over any other kind of estate asset.
4.w: Personal representatives have extensive statutory powers to administer the estate — including powers to sell, mortgage or lease assets, to appropriate assets towards a beneficiary's entitlement, to invest, and to postpone distribution — under the Administration of Estates Act 1925, the Trustee Act 2000 and related legislation (supplemented by the will).

n.0: PRs have wide powers and need not obtain a court order for every step.
n.2: PRs can sell assets; they are not confined to distributing them in specie.
n.3: PRs do not need every beneficiary's written consent for each act.
n.4: PRs' powers extend to all estate assets, not only land.

4.q: A defended claim has been allocated to a track, and the court must now give directions to manage the case through to trial, setting a timetable for steps such as disclosure, witness statements and expert evidence. The parties have completed and filed their directions questionnaires. A party asks about the court's role in actively managing the case. The court considers case management and the giving of directions under the Civil Procedure Rules. The parties had filed their directions questionnaires and the case now needed a timetable to trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Case management directions are given only in claims worth more than £1 million.
The court plays no active role and simply leaves the parties to run the case as they wish.
The court gives directions only if both parties jointly request a case management order.
The court fixes the trial date first and gives no other directions of any kind before trial on these facts as a general rule.
The court actively manages cases, giving directions and a timetable to bring the case to trial justly and at proportionate cost.
4.w: Active case management is a central feature of the CPR. The court gives directions and sets a timetable (often standard directions for the fast track, or bespoke directions after a case/costs management conference on the multi-track) to further the overriding objective of dealing with cases justly and at proportionate cost.

n.0: Case management applies across the tracks, not only to very high-value claims.
n.1: The court does play an active management role; it does not leave everything to the parties.
n.2: Directions are given by the court as a matter of course, not only on joint request.
n.3: The court gives a range of directions, not merely a trial date.

4.q: Rather than exercising its power of sale, a mortgagee took possession of a tenanted investment property from a defaulting borrower and began collecting the rents from the tenants itself. The borrower later challenges the way the mortgagee has handled the property while in possession, alleging that it failed to be diligent in collecting all of the rent that was due, allowed some units to stand empty, and left part of the income uncollected. The borrower seeks advice on the standard to which a mortgagee in possession is held in dealing with the income from the mortgaged property. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The mortgagee must transfer the property back to the borrower before collecting any rent.
The mortgagee may keep all the rents as compensation for the borrower's default.
The mortgagee must account strictly, including for rents it did receive and those it should have received with due diligence.
The mortgagee need only account for rents it actually chose to collect, and nothing more.
The mortgagee owes no duties at all once it has lawfully taken possession of the property. in the circumstances
4.w: A mortgagee in possession is accountable on a strict basis: it must account not only for what it actually receives but also for what it would have received but for its own default or want of due diligence (the doctrine of 'wilful default').

n.0: The mortgagee can take possession without first re-transferring the property.
n.1: Rents collected must be applied to the debt and accounted for, not simply kept.
n.3: The mortgagee must account for rents it ought to have received, not only those it collected.
n.4: Taking possession brings duties; the mortgagee is not free of obligation.

4.q: A landlord owns two adjoining industrial units. It let the first unit to a tenant under a lease that expressly permitted, and was clearly granted for, use as a restaurant, and the tenant fitted it out at considerable expense for that purpose. The landlord then carried out extensive works to the second, retained unit, installing equipment that generates fumes and vibration which make it impossible in practice to run a restaurant from the first unit. The tenant, unable to trade, seeks a remedy against the landlord for the loss of the use for which the unit was let. Which of the following best describes the tenant's claim?
o: Breach of the covenant for quiet enjoyment only, entitling the tenant to forfeit the landlord's reversion.
No claim, because a landlord owes no obligations in relation to neighbouring land it owns.
Trespass, because the landlord has physically entered the demised premises without consent.
Nuisance, which requires the landlord's activity to interfere with the tenant's personal health and comfort rather than their business use.
Derogation from grant, because the landlord has substantially deprived the tenant of the use the lease was granted for.
4.w: A landlord must not derogate from its grant: having let the unit for a particular purpose, it must not use its retained land so as to make that purpose substantially impossible. The tenant can claim for derogation from grant (and often breach of quiet enjoyment).

n.0: A tenant cannot forfeit the landlord's reversion; forfeiture is a landlord's remedy.
n.1: A landlord's use of retained land can breach the non-derogation obligation.
n.2: There is no need for physical entry to the demised premises for derogation from grant.
n.3: Derogation from grant does not require interference with health, unlike some nuisance claims.

4.q: An authorised firm is required to designate individuals with specific responsibility for compliance. One is responsible for the firm's compliance with its regulatory obligations generally, and another for compliance with the accounts rules. The firm is an authorised body and must appoint compliance officers. The roles cover general regulatory compliance and accounts compliance respectively. As an authorised body the firm has to allocate formal responsibility for compliance, one person overseeing its regulatory obligations at large and another its handling of client money, and the firm wants to identify the two designated roles the rules require it to fill. Which of the following best describes these roles?
o: The SRA appoints the firm's compliance officers on its behalf.
The firm must have a Compliance Officer for Legal Practice (COLP) and a Compliance Officer for Finance and Administration (COFA).
Compliance officers are required only for firms that are alternative business structures.
A single partner automatically holds all compliance responsibilities without formal designation on these facts as a general rule.
The firm need not appoint any compliance officers at all.
4.w: An authorised firm must have a Compliance Officer for Legal Practice (COLP), responsible for compliance with the firm's authorisation and regulatory obligations and for recording and reporting breaches, and a Compliance Officer for Finance and Administration (COFA), responsible for compliance with the SRA Accounts Rules. Both must be approved by the SRA.

n.0: The firm nominates its compliance officers (subject to SRA approval); the SRA does not appoint them.
n.2: COLP and COFA are required for authorised firms generally, not only ABSs.
n.3: The roles must be formally designated and SRA-approved, not automatically assumed.
n.4: Compliance officers are required; the firm cannot simply have none.

4.q: A charterer hires a ship under a contract containing a term that the vessel is to be 'in every way fitted for ordinary cargo service'. On delivery the vessel has some engine problems and an inefficient crew, which cause delays while repairs are carried out, but the vessel remains available for a substantial part of the charter period and can still perform the essential purpose of the contract. The charterer purports to terminate the whole charter for breach of that term. The shipowner disputes the right to terminate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The charterer may terminate only if the shipowner acted deliberately or dishonestly.
The charterer may terminate only if the contract expressly labelled the term a condition.
The charterer may never terminate, because a seaworthiness term is only ever a warranty.
Whether the charterer may terminate depends on how serious the breach and its consequences actually are.
The charterer may terminate automatically, because any breach of a seaworthiness term ends the contract.
4.w: A term of this kind is an innominate (intermediate) term. The remedy depends on the seriousness of the breach and its consequences: only if the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit of the contract may they terminate (Hong Kong Fir Shipping v Kawasaki).

n.0: The right to terminate turns on the seriousness of the breach, not the shipowner's state of mind.
n.1: The consequences-based approach applies even without an express 'condition' label.
n.2: Such a term is not automatically a mere warranty either; it depends on the breach.
n.4: An innominate term is not treated as a condition breached by any deviation.

4.q: A landowner orally declares that they hold a piece of land on trust for another person, intending to create a valid trust of the land. Nothing about the declaration is ever put into or evidenced by any signed writing. Later, a dispute arises and the beneficiary seeks to enforce the trust of the land, while the landowner denies that any enforceable trust of land was ever created because of the absence of writing. The land was valuable, and the intended beneficiary had made arrangements in the expectation of receiving it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust of land is void, because trusts of land can never be created by an individual on these facts.
The trust of land is unenforceable, because a declaration of trust of land must be evidenced in signed writing.
The trust of land is fully valid and enforceable despite the absence of any writing.
The trust of land is valid, because oral declarations of trust are always sufficient.
The trust of land is valid, provided the beneficiary has taken possession of the land.
4.w: Under s.53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925, a declaration of trust respecting land or any interest in land must be manifested and proved by some signed writing. An oral declaration of a trust of land is unenforceable (though not necessarily void) for want of the required written evidence.

n.0: Individuals can create trusts of land; the issue is the writing requirement.
n.2: A trust of land is not enforceable on an oral declaration alone; written evidence is needed.
n.3: Oral declarations are not always sufficient; land trusts require signed writing.
n.4: Taking possession does not satisfy the s.53(1)(b) writing requirement.

4.q: A public authority makes a decision that interferes with an individual's rights protected by the European Convention on Human Rights, and the individual argues that the authority acted unlawfully by breaching those rights. A solicitor is asked about the obligation of a public authority in relation to Convention rights under the Human Rights Act 1998. The solicitor considers section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The authority's decision plainly cut across a right protected under the Convention. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Convention rights are relevant only in the European Court of Human Rights and never in UK courts on these facts.
It is unlawful under s.6 HRA 1998 for a public authority to act in a way incompatible with a Convention right.
The Human Rights Act binds only private individuals and not public authorities.
Public authorities are entirely free to disregard Convention rights when making decisions.
A public authority may breach Convention rights provided it acts in good faith.
4.w: Under s.6 of the Human Rights Act 1998, it is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way which is incompatible with a Convention right, unless primary legislation requires it to do so. This allows Convention rights to be enforced against public authorities in the UK courts.

n.0: Convention rights are enforceable in the UK courts under the HRA, not only in Strasbourg.
n.2: The HRA binds public authorities, not (directly) private individuals.
n.3: Public authorities are not free to disregard Convention rights; s.6 binds them.
n.4: Good faith does not excuse acting incompatibly with a Convention right.

4.q: The windows of Mrs Tomlin's house have received daylight across a neighbouring plot, without interruption, for more than 20 years. The plot has been bought by a developer, which has begun putting up a large extension only a short distance from Mrs Tomlin's windows. When finished, the extension would substantially reduce the light to two of her main rooms, making them noticeably dark for ordinary use. Mrs Tomlin wants the offending part of the extension taken down, but the developer says that at most it should have to pay her a sum of money and can otherwise build as it likes on its own land. Mrs Tomlin seeks advice on the remedy she is most likely to obtain. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Nothing, unless Mrs Tomlin first registers the right of light as a notice on the developer's title.
An injunction requiring removal, the usual remedy for substantial interference with a right of light.
Nothing, because a right of light cannot be acquired over a neighbour's land in any circumstances.
Damages only, because an injunction can never be granted for interference with an easement of light acquired by prescription.
An order that the developer purchase Mrs Tomlin's house at its full market value.
4.w: A right of light can be acquired by long enjoyment, and substantial interference with it is usually restrained by injunction (Shelfer). Damages in lieu may be awarded in exceptional cases (Coventry v Lawrence), but the injunction is the primary remedy.

n.0: A right of light acquired by prescription does not depend on the claimant entering a notice to be enforceable.
n.2: A right of light can be acquired, commonly by prescription, so relief is available.
n.3: An injunction is the usual remedy; damages in lieu are the exception, not an absolute rule.
n.4: The court does not force the claimant to sell; it restrains or compensates the interference.

4.q: A sole executor named in a will proves the will and obtains probate, then dies before completing the administration of the estate. That executor had themselves appointed an executor of their own will who has proved it. A question arises about who is now entitled to complete the administration of the first estate. The court considers the chain of representation. The first executor had died only part-way through winding up the original estate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The executor of the last surviving executor becomes executor of the original estate by the chain of representation.
The original estate is left with no personal representative and simply cannot be administered.
The beneficiaries of the original estate automatically become its executors.
The chain of representation applies equally to administrators as it does to executors.
A fresh grant of probate to the original estate is always required, and the chain never applies on these facts.
4.w: Under the chain of representation, where a sole or last surviving executor who has proved the will dies having appointed an executor who proves their will, that executor automatically becomes executor of the original testator's estate too, and so on down the chain. The chain is broken by an intestacy or failure to appoint/prove an executor.

n.1: The original estate is not left without a PR where the chain operates.
n.2: Beneficiaries do not automatically become executors.
n.3: The chain of representation applies to executors, not administrators.
n.4: A fresh grant is not always required; the chain can continue the representation.

4.q: A consumer buys a new washing machine from a retailer. It proves faulty. The retailer is given one opportunity to repair it, but after the repair the same fault recurs within a short time, so the machine still does not conform to the contract. The consumer, having lost confidence, wants to return the machine and get money back rather than allow further attempts. The purchase is a consumer sale of goods governed by the Consumer Rights Act 2015, and a repair has already been attempted once without success. Which of the following best describes the consumer's remedy?
o: The consumer has a final right to reject and obtain a refund, which may be reduced for use in limited circumstances.
The consumer is entitled only to a further repair and never to a refund once repair has begun on these facts.
The consumer must allow the retailer unlimited further attempts to repair before any refund.
The consumer must accept a replacement and has no right to any refund at all.
The consumer may reject only within 30 days of purchase and has now lost all remedies.
4.w: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, after one repair or replacement has failed to bring the goods into conformity, the consumer has the final right to reject and obtain a refund. The refund may be reduced to reflect use in certain cases (and, outside the first six months, deductions are more readily made), but the consumer need not permit endless repair attempts.

n.1: A refund is available under the final right to reject, not only a further repair.
n.2: The consumer need not allow unlimited repair attempts; one failed attempt triggers the final right to reject.
n.3: The consumer is not obliged to accept a replacement instead of a refund at this stage.
n.4: The 30-day short-term right to reject is separate; the final right to reject arises after a failed repair.

4.q: A firm currently acts for a company on an ongoing commercial matter which is still very much live. A prospective new client then approaches the very same firm and asks it to bring an entirely unrelated contractual claim against that company. The new matter has nothing factually to do with the existing retainer, and no confidential information from the existing matter would need to be used in pursuing it. The company has neither been asked for, nor given, any consent to the firm acting against it. A fee-earner, seeing a chance to win extra work, wonders whether the firm may take on the new client and act against the company on the unrelated claim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may act against the company, provided a different fee-earner is put in charge of the new claim.
The firm may act against the company, provided the new client is charged a separate and higher fee.
The firm may freely act against the company, because the two matters are completely unrelated to each other.
The firm may act against the company, provided no confidential information from the existing matter is used.
The firm must not act against a person who is currently its own client, even on an entirely unrelated matter.
4.w: A solicitor owes a duty of loyalty to a current client. Acting against a person who is at the same time the firm's own client gives rise to a conflict and is not permitted, even where the two matters are unrelated, unless a recognised exception applies with informed consent.

n.0: Using a different fee-earner does not overcome the duty of loyalty owed to the current client.
n.1: Charging a higher fee is irrelevant to the conflict of acting against a current client.
n.2: Loyalty to a current client is engaged even where the new matter is unrelated.
n.3: The absence of shared confidential information does not cure the conflict of acting against a current client.

4.q: A person is injured by a defective product and wishes to bring a claim under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, but is unsure who can be held liable. The product was manufactured abroad, imported into the United Kingdom by an importer, and sold under a supermarket's own brand name, and the ultimate producer cannot easily be identified by the consumer. The injured person seeks advice on who may be liable for a defective product under the Act. The consumer wrote to the supermarket asking who had produced the item but received no useful reply at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Liability may fall on the producer, an own-brander who holds themselves out as producer, or the importer into the UK.
No one can be liable unless the consumer can identify the exact original producer abroad on these facts as a general rule.
Only the shop that physically sold the product to the consumer can ever be liable.
Only the individual factory worker who actually made the product can be held liable.
Liability falls only on whoever the consumer chooses to sue, regardless of their role.
4.w: Under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, those who may be liable include the producer (manufacturer), a person who holds themselves out as the producer by putting their own brand on the product ('own-brander'), and the person who imported the product into the UK. A mere supplier may be liable only if it fails to identify the producer on request.

n.1: Own-branders and importers can be liable even where the original overseas producer is not identified.
n.2: A mere retailer is generally liable only where it cannot identify the producer on request.
n.3: Liability is not limited to the individual worker who made the item.
n.4: Liability attaches to defined categories of person, not simply whoever is chosen as defendant.

4.q: A solicitor acts for Ms Bright, who is buying a house with unregistered title from Mr Coombes for £310,000. Mr Coombes is registered on the title deeds as sole legal owner, but unknown to Ms Bright he in fact holds the house on trust and there is a beneficiary entitled to a share. That beneficiary is not living in the property, and nothing in the deeds, on a reasonably careful inspection, or in Ms Bright's pre-contract enquiries suggests that anyone other than Mr Coombes has an interest. Ms Bright pays the whole price to Mr Coombes and takes a conveyance of the legal estate. Several months after completion the beneficiary comes forward and asserts that their interest binds Ms Bright. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Ms Bright takes subject to the interest, because a payment to a single owner can never overreach a beneficial interest.
Ms Bright takes subject to the interest, because the beneficiary could in principle have been discovered on enquiry.
Ms Bright takes free of the beneficial interest, as a bona fide purchaser of a legal estate for value without notice of it.
Ms Bright takes free of the interest, because beneficial interests in unregistered land are void unless registered as land charges.
Ms Bright takes subject to the interest, because a purchaser of unregistered land is always bound by beneficial interests.
4.w: A beneficial interest under a trust is not registrable as a land charge, so in unregistered land it is governed by the doctrine of notice. A bona fide purchaser of a legal estate for value without notice (actual, constructive or imputed) takes free of it. Here nothing could be discovered on reasonable enquiry, so Ms Bright had no notice.

n.0: Overreaching is not the issue here; the point is the buyer's lack of notice, which defeats the interest regardless of overreaching.
n.1: The facts show the interest could not be discovered on reasonable enquiry, so no constructive notice is fixed on Ms Bright.
n.3: The land charges regime does not apply to beneficial interests under a trust, so non-registration does not make the interest void.
n.4: A purchaser is not bound by every beneficial interest; the doctrine of notice governs interests outside the land charges system.

4.q: A defendant makes a Part 36 offer to settle a money claim, which the claimant rejects. At trial the claimant succeeds but is awarded a sum that fails to beat the defendant's Part 36 offer. The offer had been made well before trial and remained open. The claimant did not obtain a judgment more advantageous than the defendant's Part 36 offer. The defendant had put a realistic settlement figure on the table months before trial, the claimant pressed on regardless, and although the claimant did win, the sum the judge awarded came out below what the defendant had already offered to pay to end the case. Which of the following best describes the usual costs consequence?
o: The claimant recovers all of its costs as the successful party, regardless of the offer on these facts.
The claimant is usually ordered to pay the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, with interest.
Each party simply bears its own costs because the claimant won at trial.
The defendant must pay the claimant's costs throughout, the offer being irrelevant.
The claim is dismissed because the claimant failed to beat the offer.
4.w: Where a claimant fails to obtain a judgment more advantageous than a defendant's Part 36 offer, the usual order is that the claimant pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period (the date by which the offer could have been accepted), plus interest on those costs, even though the claimant technically won. This encourages reasonable settlement.

n.0: The claimant does not simply recover all its costs; the Part 36 offer shifts costs from the relevant period.
n.2: Costs do not simply lie where they fall; the Part 36 consequences apply.
n.3: The defendant does not pay the claimant's costs throughout where its offer was not beaten.
n.4: Failing to beat the offer affects costs, not the validity of the winning claim itself.

4.q: An individual (a sole trader) is unable to pay their debts as they fall due, and a creditor who is owed a sum exceeding the statutory minimum wishes to take formal insolvency proceedings against them. The debtor is an individual, not a company. A creditor seeks a court order dealing with the debtor's insolvency. The debtor runs a business as a sole trader, not through a company, and simply cannot meet the debts as they come due, so a creditor owed a sum above the statutory floor is looking to take formal insolvency proceedings that will put the debtor's assets into the hands of someone tasked with realising them for the creditors. Which of the following best describes the appropriate procedure and its effect?
o: A wrongful trading contribution order against the individual.
A members' voluntary liquidation of the individual's affairs.
A bankruptcy order, on which the debtor's estate vests in a trustee in bankruptcy to be realised for creditors.
A company voluntary arrangement binding the individual's creditors.
An administration order placing the individual under an administrator on these facts as a general rule.
4.w: An individual who cannot pay their debts may be made bankrupt: a creditor owed at least the statutory minimum (or the debtor themselves) may seek a bankruptcy order. On bankruptcy, the debtor's estate vests in a trustee in bankruptcy, who realises the assets and distributes them to creditors in the statutory order; the bankrupt is usually discharged after one year.

n.0: Wrongful trading applies to directors of insolvent companies, not to an individual sole trader's bankruptcy.
n.1: Members' voluntary liquidation applies to solvent companies, not individuals.
n.3: A CVA is a company procedure; the individual equivalent is an IVA, not what a creditor imposes here.
n.4: Administration is a corporate insolvency procedure, not applicable to an individual.

4.q: A landlord grants a new lease of premises to a tenant for a fixed term of 15 years. The tenant's solicitor must ensure that the tenant's leasehold estate is properly protected and given legal effect. The tenant asks whether the new lease needs to be registered at the Land Registry. The solicitor considers the registration of a newly granted lease. The tenant was paying a substantial premium for the new lease and wanted it properly protected. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A lease is registered only if the landlord's own title is unregistered.
Only leases granted for more than 21 years need to be registered at the Land Registry on these facts as a general rule.
A newly granted lease for a term of more than seven years must be registered with its own title at the Land Registry.
No lease ever needs to be registered at the Land Registry, whatever its length.
A newly granted 15-year lease takes effect purely orally without any registration.
4.w: The grant of a lease for a term of more than seven years is a registrable disposition (or, out of unregistered land, triggers compulsory registration). Such a lease must be registered with its own leasehold title at the Land Registry, and a note entered against the landlord's title.

n.0: Registration of a >7-year lease is required whether or not the landlord's title is registered.
n.1: The threshold is more than seven years, not 21.
n.3: Longer leases (over seven years) do require registration.
n.4: A 15-year lease must be granted by deed and registered, not made orally.

4.q: A settlor transfers property to trustees to be used to provide and maintain sports facilities primarily for the benefit of the employees of a particular company and their families. Although expressed as a purpose, the arrangement directly benefits an ascertainable group of individuals who could enforce it. The trust is for a purpose but a class of persons stands to benefit and could enforce it. The settlor's evident aim was to give the company's workforce somewhere to play sport, the individuals who would use and benefit from the facilities can readily be identified, and any of them could come to court to insist the trustees carry the arrangement out as intended. Which of the following best describes the likely validity of this arrangement?
o: It is valid only if it is expressed to last no longer than 21 years.
It may be valid because the purpose is for the benefit of ascertainable individuals who can enforce it.
It is valid only if it qualifies as a charitable trust for the advancement of amateur sport.
It is void because all purpose trusts without a charitable purpose are invalid without exception.
It is void because sports facilities can never be the subject of a trust.
4.w: Following Re Denley, a trust expressed as a purpose may be valid as a private trust where the purpose is sufficiently clear and directly or indirectly benefits ascertainable individuals who have standing to enforce it. Because identifiable people benefit and can enforce the trust, the beneficiary principle is satisfied.

n.0: Validity here rests on the ascertainable beneficiaries, not on a fixed 21-year limit (though perpetuity must still be satisfied).
n.2: The trust can be valid as a private Re Denley trust even if it is not charitable.
n.3: Not all non-charitable purpose trusts are void; Re Denley recognises those benefiting ascertainable individuals.
n.4: Sports facilities can be the subject of a valid trust.

4.q: A defendant performed the act constituting the offence while suffering a total loss of voluntary control caused by an external factor — for example a blow to the head, or a reaction to an anaesthetic — rather than by any internal disease of the mind. The defendant argues they were not acting voluntarily at all. The court considers the defence of (non-insane) automatism. The defendant had been knocked unconscious moments earlier and had no control over their movements. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Automatism requires a total loss of voluntary control caused by an external factor, negating the actus reus.
Automatism requires an internal disease of the mind and is treated as a form of insanity.
Automatism is a partial defence that merely reduces the offence to a lesser one.
Automatism applies whenever the defendant simply cannot remember committing the offence.
Automatism is available even where the defendant retained partial control over their actions on these facts.
4.w: Non-insane automatism arises where the defendant suffers a total loss of voluntary control due to an external cause (such as a blow, or an unexpected reaction to medication). It negates the voluntary act element of the actus reus and, if not self-induced, is a complete defence leading to acquittal.

n.1: An internal cause points to insane automatism (insanity), not non-insane automatism.
n.2: It is a complete defence (acquittal), not merely a partial one.
n.3: Mere loss of memory is not the same as a loss of voluntary control at the time.
n.4: Automatism requires a total, not partial, loss of voluntary control.

4.q: A carrier contracts to transport a mill owner's broken crankshaft to be copied, but is not told that the mill is standing idle and will remain so until the new shaft arrives. The carrier delays delivery, and the mill owner claims the profits lost during the extended stoppage, which were far greater than the carrier could have anticipated from the limited information given. The carrier was not made aware of the special circumstances (the idle mill) that caused the unusually large loss of profit. Which of the following best describes whether the lost profits are recoverable?
o: The lost profits are recoverable because remoteness is irrelevant in contract.
All the lost profits are recoverable, because any loss factually caused by breach is recoverable on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The lost profits are recoverable only if the carrier acted deliberately.
The unusual lost profits are irrecoverable, being neither ordinary losses nor within the carrier's contemplation from known special circumstances.
No damages of any kind are recoverable, because the loss was consequential.
4.w: Under the rule in Hadley v Baxendale, recoverable losses are those arising naturally in the ordinary course (first limb) or within the parties' reasonable contemplation from special circumstances actually communicated (second limb). As the special circumstances (the idle mill) were not made known, the unusually large lost profits were too remote to be recovered.

n.0: Remoteness is a central limit on damages in contract, not irrelevant.
n.1: Not every factually caused loss is recoverable; remoteness limits recovery.
n.2: Recoverability turns on remoteness, not on whether the breach was deliberate.
n.4: Some damages (ordinary losses) may still be recoverable; the point is the special lost profits are too remote.

4.q: A party wishes to withhold from inspection documents such as communications with third parties and internal materials which were created when litigation was in reasonable contemplation and for the dominant purpose of that litigation — for example, an investigator's report obtained to defend an anticipated claim. The other party demands disclosure of them. The court considers litigation privilege in civil proceedings. The report had been commissioned specifically to help defend the claim that was plainly on its way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: All documents connected with the dispute must always be disclosed to the other side.
Confidential documents created for the dominant purpose of litigation reasonably in contemplation are protected by litigation privilege.
Litigation privilege protects only communications directly between the lawyer and the client.
Documents created before proceedings are issued can never be privileged in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
Litigation privilege applies only to documents created after the trial has begun.
4.w: Litigation privilege protects confidential communications between a party (or their lawyer) and third parties, and documents, created when litigation was in reasonable contemplation or on foot, for the dominant purpose of that litigation. Such documents may be withheld from inspection.

n.0: Not all documents connected with the dispute must be disclosed; privilege protects some.
n.2: Litigation privilege extends to third-party communications, not only lawyer-client ones.
n.3: Documents can be privileged before proceedings are issued if litigation was in reasonable contemplation.
n.4: Litigation privilege can attach to documents created before, not only after, trial begins.

4.q: Two solicitors are ready to exchange contracts by telephone, each holding their client's signed part of the contract, with the buyer's deposit held by the buyer's solicitor. They wish to exchange in a way that creates a binding contract at the moment of the telephone call, using an established professional procedure. The solicitors are exchanging by telephone under a recognised professional protocol. They want certainty about the moment of exchange. Both solicitors are poised to exchange over the telephone, each holding their own client's signed part of the contract and the buyer's deposit held ready, and they want to use the recognised professional procedure that pins down the precise instant at which a binding contract springs into existence. Which of the following best describes the mechanism they will use?
o: Exchange by the buyer registering a notice at the Land Registry.
Exchange by simply posting the contracts to each other without more.
Exchange by completing the Land Registry transfer form TR1.
Exchange only becomes effective once completion has taken place.
Exchange under one of the Law Society formulae (for example Formula A, B or C).
4.w: Solicitors commonly exchange contracts by telephone using the Law Society formulae (Formula A where one solicitor holds both signed parts, Formula B where each holds their own client's part, and Formula C for chains). The formula records undertakings and fixes the precise moment a binding contract comes into existence on the call.

n.0: Registering a notice does not effect exchange of contracts.
n.1: Postal exchange is a different method; telephone exchange uses the Law Society formulae.
n.2: Form TR1 is the transfer deed used at completion, not the exchange mechanism.
n.3: A binding contract arises on exchange, not only on completion.

4.q: A client is simultaneously selling their existing home and buying a new one, with the sale proceeds needed to fund the purchase, and both transactions form part of a chain with other buyers and sellers. The client's solicitor must manage the timing so that the client is not left having sold their home without a new one, or vice versa. The client asks how the two transactions are coordinated. The solicitor considers the synchronisation of a related sale and purchase in a chain. The client could not afford to buy the new home without the proceeds of selling the old one. Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach?
o: The solicitor should complete the sale and purchase on entirely unrelated dates without coordination on these facts as a general rule.
The solicitor should exchange on the purchase first and worry about selling the existing home later.
The solicitor should exchange on the sale weeks before even finding a property to buy.
The solicitor should synchronise exchange (and completion) of the sale and purchase so the client is not committed to one without the other.
The solicitor should treat the two transactions as wholly independent, ignoring the chain.
4.w: Where a client's sale and purchase are dependent (a chain), the solicitor must synchronise the transactions — exchanging (and completing) on the sale and the purchase on the same day or in a coordinated sequence — so the client is never contractually bound to buy without having sold, or to sell without having secured the purchase.

n.0: Uncoordinated completion dates risk leaving the client without a home or double-committed.
n.1: Exchanging on the purchase alone risks the client being unable to fund it if the sale fails.
n.2: Exchanging on the sale before finding a purchase risks having nowhere to move to.
n.4: The chain must be managed, not ignored.

4.q: A professional trust corporation is appointed as trustee of a substantial trust and is paid for acting. It holds itself out as having specialist expertise in trust administration and investment. When a beneficiary later alleges that the trustee fell below the required standard, the trustee argues that it should be judged by the same standard as an ordinary lay person acting as trustee. The beneficiary disputes this. The court considers the standard of care applicable to a professional trustee. The corporation charged substantial fees and marketed itself widely as a specialist in trust work. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A professional trustee owes no enhanced duty, provided it charges reasonable fees.
A professional trustee is judged only by whether it acted honestly and in good faith.
A higher standard of care is expected of a professional trustee holding itself out as having special expertise.
A professional trustee is judged by exactly the same standard as an unpaid lay trustee.
A professional trustee is judged by a lower standard, because it takes on difficult trusts on these facts.
4.w: The statutory duty of care in the Trustee Act 2000 is calibrated to the trustee: a person acting as a professional trustee, or holding themselves out as having special knowledge or experience, is held to a correspondingly higher standard of care and skill than a lay trustee.

n.0: Charging reasonable fees does not remove the enhanced duty.
n.1: Honest good faith is not the measure; reasonable professional care is.
n.3: A professional trustee is not judged by the lay standard.
n.4: Professional trustees are held to a higher, not a lower, standard.

4.q: A public authority makes a decision that adversely affects an individual, who believes the decision was made unlawfully and wishes to challenge it in the courts. The individual is not seeking to appeal the merits but to challenge the legality of the decision-making. A solicitor is asked about the mechanism for challenging the lawfulness of a public body's decision. The solicitor considers the nature and scope of judicial review. The individual wanted the decision reviewed for legality, not a fresh decision on the merits of their case. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Judicial review allows the court to substitute its own decision on the merits for that of the public body.
Judicial review is an appeal on the facts against any decision the claimant dislikes.
Judicial review is available to challenge the decisions of private individuals in private disputes.
Judicial review is the court's supervisory jurisdiction to review the lawfulness of decisions of public bodies.
Judicial review allows the court to award damages as of right for any unlawful decision.
4.w: Judicial review is the process by which the courts exercise a supervisory jurisdiction over the exercise of public functions, reviewing the lawfulness (not generally the merits) of decisions, actions and omissions of public bodies against grounds such as illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety.

n.0: The court reviews legality, not the merits; it does not substitute its own decision.
n.1: It is not an appeal on the facts.
n.2: Judicial review concerns public functions, not purely private disputes.
n.4: Damages are not available as of right in judicial review.

4.q: A driver suffers a sudden and wholly unforeseeable event while driving — for example being attacked by a swarm of bees, or suffering an unexpected blackout — which causes them to lose all control of the vehicle, and the car strikes and injures a pedestrian. The driver did nothing voluntary that caused the loss of control. The prosecution nonetheless seeks to hold the driver criminally liable for the injury caused. The driver's adviser considers the requirement of voluntary conduct in the actus reus. The event was sudden and could not have been anticipated, and the driver had been driving normally until it struck. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The driver is liable, because the pedestrian was in fact injured by the driver's car.
The driver is liable, because a driver is always responsible for anything their vehicle does.
There is no liability, because the actus reus requires voluntary conduct, which was absent here.
The driver is liable, unless they can prove they had taken out motor insurance.
The driver is liable, because they were the person physically in control of the vehicle at the time.
4.w: The actus reus of an offence must generally be a voluntary act. Where the defendant's bodily movement is involuntary (automatism arising from an external cause, such as a swarm of bees or a blackout), the conduct element is not satisfied and there is no liability.

n.0: Mere causation of injury is not enough without a voluntary act.
n.1: A driver is not automatically liable for everything the vehicle does, absent voluntary conduct.
n.3: Insurance is irrelevant to criminal liability for the actus reus.
n.4: Being physically in the car does not supply a voluntary act where control was involuntarily lost.

4.q: During a case management hearing, a solicitor makes a statement of fact to the court, on the client's instructions, which the solicitor genuinely and reasonably believes to be true at the time it is made. Later that same day, on reviewing newly received documents, the solicitor discovers that the statement was in fact false, so that the court has been misled on a point that is material to the issues it must decide. When the solicitor explains this to the client, the client refuses to allow the position to be corrected, insisting that the court be left with the false impression. The solicitor considers what they must now do. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may leave the false impression uncorrected, provided the solicitor personally says nothing further about it.
The solicitor may correct the statement only if the opposing party first notices the error and raises it.
The solicitor need do nothing, because the statement was made in good faith and was believed true at the time.
The solicitor must at once disclose the client's confidential explanation to the court to put the record straight.
The solicitor must not allow the court to remain misled and, if the client will not consent to correction, must cease to act.
4.w: A solicitor who realises the court has been misled, even innocently, must not allow that state of affairs to continue. They should seek the client's consent to correct it; if the client refuses, the solicitor must cease to act, but must not disclose privileged information to the court.

n.0: Staying silent while the court remains misled is itself a breach of the duty to the court.
n.1: The duty to act does not wait until the other side happens to spot the error.
n.2: Good faith at the time does not excuse leaving the court misled once the truth is known.
n.3: The solicitor cannot disclose the client's privileged explanation to the court.

4.q: A landowner granted a neighbour a right of way over the landowner's registered land. The grant was made only in a written contract signed by both parties, and was never completed by deed as a legal easement. No notice in respect of the right was entered on the register. The landowner has since sold and transferred the registered land to a buyer for value. The neighbour wishes to continue using the right of way and asserts it against the new owner, who says they took the land free of it. The neighbour seeks advice on the nature of the right and whether it binds the buyer. Which of the following best describes it?
o: It is an equitable easement, which will only bind a buyer if it is protected by a notice on the register.
It is void, because an easement can never be created otherwise than by statute.
It is a profit à prendre, binding a buyer once the neighbour registers a caution.
It is a bare licence, which can never bind a buyer of the land in any circumstances. on these facts
It is a legal easement, which binds any buyer of the servient land automatically.
4.w: A legal easement must be granted by deed. A signed written contract to grant an easement, for value, takes effect only as an equitable easement, which in registered land binds a buyer of the servient land only if protected by a notice on the register.

n.1: Easements can be created by grant; the point is that without a deed the grant is equitable.
n.2: An easement is not a profit, and protection is by notice, not a caution.
n.3: An equitable easement is more than a bare licence and can bind if protected.
n.4: Without a deed the easement is equitable, not legal, so it does not bind automatically.

4.q: A defendant convicted and sentenced in the Crown Court considers that the sentence imposed was manifestly excessive or wrong in principle, and wishes to challenge it. The conviction itself is not challenged, only the sentence. The defendant was sentenced in the Crown Court following trial on indictment. The defendant seeks to appeal the sentence. The defendant does not quarrel with the jury's verdict but is aggrieved by the length of the sentence, considering it manifestly excessive and out of line with principle, and wants to know which court can be asked to look again at a sentence passed in the Crown Court after a trial on indictment. Which of the following best describes the route of appeal against sentence?
o: An appeal against sentence lies directly to the Supreme Court.
An appeal against sentence lies to the High Court by way of case stated only on these facts.
There is no right of appeal against a Crown Court sentence.
An appeal against sentence lies to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally with leave.
An appeal against sentence lies to the magistrates' court for rehearing.
4.w: A defendant sentenced in the Crown Court following trial on indictment may appeal against sentence to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally with leave (permission). The Court of Appeal may reduce (but not increase, on the defendant's own appeal) the sentence if it is manifestly excessive or wrong in principle.

n.0: The first appeal is to the Court of Appeal, not directly to the Supreme Court.
n.1: Case stated to the High Court applies to magistrates' and the Crown Court's appellate decisions, not a Crown Court sentence on indictment.
n.2: There is a right of appeal against sentence, generally with leave.
n.4: Appeal from the Crown Court does not go to the magistrates' court for a rehearing.

4.q: A newly formed private company limited by shares is arranging its management. The founders ask how many directors the company must have and whether a particular proposed director, a 17-year-old individual, may be appointed. The company is a private company, not a public company. The proposed director is under 18 but over 16. The founders are keeping the management lean and would like to appoint just one director, and they are also keen to bring in a capable 17-year-old family member, so they need to know both the minimum number of directors and whether someone of that age can lawfully be appointed. Which of the following best describes the requirements as to directors?
o: A private company must have at least one director, and a director must be a natural person aged at least 16, so the 17-year-old may be appointed.
A private company need not have any directors at all.
A private company must have at least two directors, so one director is never sufficient on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A director must be at least 18, so the 17-year-old cannot be appointed.
Only a public company may appoint a director under the age of 18.
4.w: A private company must have at least one director (a public company at least two), and at least one director must be a natural person. A director must be at least 16 years old. As the proposed director is 17, and a private company needs only one director, the appointment is permissible.

n.1: A company must have at least one director; it cannot have none.
n.2: A private company needs a minimum of one, not two, directors.
n.3: The minimum age for a director is 16, not 18, so a 17-year-old qualifies.
n.4: The minimum age of 16 applies generally, not only to public companies.

4.q: A defendant is charged with a minor road traffic offence which, by statute, can only be dealt with in one particular court. The defendant's solicitor explains that this type of offence is not one that can ever be sent to the Crown Court for trial by jury. The offence is of the least serious classification. The charge is a low-level motoring matter that carries only limited penalties, the client is anxious about the prospect of a jury trial, and the solicitor is explaining that for an offence of this least-serious category there is in fact only one venue in which the matter can be heard. Which of the following best describes where a summary offence is tried?
o: In the County Court sitting in its criminal jurisdiction.
In the High Court at first instance.
In the Crown Court only.
In either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court at the defendant's election.
In the magistrates' court only.
4.w: Summary offences, the least serious category of criminal offence, are tried only in the magistrates' court. There is no right to trial by jury for a summary offence, and it cannot be sent to the Crown Court for trial (though sentence may occasionally be committed there in limited circumstances).

n.0: The County Court is a civil court with no criminal trial jurisdiction.
n.1: The High Court does not try criminal offences at first instance.
n.2: Summary offences are not tried in the Crown Court.
n.3: A defendant cannot elect Crown Court trial for a summary offence.

4.q: A firm receives a single payment that comprises both client money (money on account of a disbursement not yet incurred) and office money (the firm's billed fees), paid together in one sum. The bookkeeper must decide how to deal with this mixed receipt under the SRA Accounts Rules. The bookkeeper considers the treatment of a mixed receipt. The single cheque arrives with a covering letter that does not separate the two elements, and the bookkeeper must decide how to route it so that the client's protected money is not left sitting in the office account while the firm's fees are extracted. Which of the following best describes the correct approach?
o: The client money must reach the client account promptly, for example by banking the whole sum and transferring the office money out promptly.
The client money element may be ignored because it was paid together with office money on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The mixed receipt need not be split and may be spent as the firm sees fit.
The whole receipt may simply be paid into the office account and left there.
The whole receipt may be kept in cash and allocated later whenever convenient.
4.w: Where a receipt is mixed client and office money, the firm must ensure the client money is paid promptly into the client account. In practice the whole sum may be paid into the client account and the office money element then transferred promptly to the office account (or the sum allocated appropriately), so client money is properly protected.

n.1: The client money element cannot be ignored.
n.2: The receipt must be dealt with under the rules, not spent as the firm sees fit.
n.3: The whole receipt cannot simply be left in the office account.
n.4: It cannot be kept in cash and allocated whenever convenient.

4.q: A solicitor holds confidential information about a client which, in the ordinary course, the solicitor would be strictly bound to keep secret and not to reveal to anyone. The solicitor is then served with a court order, made in entirely separate proceedings, which requires the solicitor to disclose that very information; there is no proper basis on which the order can be challenged and the information is not protected by privilege. The client does not want the information revealed at all. The solicitor must reconcile the duty of confidentiality with the terms of the court order. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The duty of confidentiality is absolute, so the solicitor must refuse to comply with the court order in every case.
The solicitor may disclose the information only after the client has had a final opportunity to remove it.
The solicitor must ignore the order, because a solicitor's duty to the client always overrides any court order.
The solicitor may comply with the order only if the client first gives express consent to the disclosure.
Confidentiality must yield where disclosure is required by law, such as under a valid court order or a statutory duty.
4.w: The professional duty of confidentiality is not absolute. It gives way where disclosure is required or permitted by law — for example under a valid court order, or a statutory obligation such as those under the anti-money-laundering regime — and the solicitor must then comply.

n.0: Confidentiality is not absolute; it yields to a legal obligation to disclose.
n.1: The client has no right to strip out the information before a required disclosure is made.
n.2: A solicitor may not simply ignore a valid court order in reliance on the duty to the client.
n.3: Compliance with a valid court order does not depend on the client's consent.

4.q: A solicitor faces a situation where acting in the client's immediate best interests would require conduct that undermines the proper administration of justice. The solicitor must decide which of the SRA Principles takes precedence, as two Principles appear to pull in different directions. The client's interests and the public interest in the administration of justice conflict. The solicitor must resolve the clash of Principles. The solicitor is caught between what the client wants and the wider demands of the justice system, with two of the SRA Principles apparently pointing in opposite directions, and needs to know which of them must give way when they cannot both be honoured at once. Which of the following best describes how the SRA Principles are prioritised?
o: Where two or more Principles conflict, the one that best serves the wider public interest (especially the rule of law and administration of justice) takes precedence.
All the Principles rank equally and a conflict between them cannot be resolved.
The solicitor may choose whichever Principle produces the best outcome for the client.
The Principle requiring the solicitor to act in the client's best interests always takes precedence over all others on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The most recently published Principle automatically overrides the earlier ones.
4.w: The SRA Principles must be complied with, but where two or more come into conflict, the Principle which takes precedence is the one that best serves the wider public interest, in particular the public interest in the proper administration of justice and upholding the rule of law. The duty to the client does not override these wider public interest duties.

n.1: The Principles are not all equal in a conflict; there is an order of priority.
n.2: The solicitor cannot simply pick the Principle best for the client.
n.3: The client's best interests do not always take precedence; wider public interest Principles prevail.
n.4: Priority does not depend on which Principle was most recently published.

4.q: A defendant appears in the magistrates' court charged with an either-way offence. Before any decision on allocation, the defendant is asked to indicate how they would plead if the matter proceeded to trial. The defendant indicates a guilty plea. The defendant has indicated a guilty plea at the plea before venue stage. The magistrates now consider what happens next. Facing an either-way charge in the magistrates' court, the defendant is asked at the outset, before any decision on where the case should be tried, to indicate the plea he would enter, and he indicates that he would plead guilty, which shapes what the magistrates do next. Which of the following best describes the effect of indicating a guilty plea at plea before venue?
o: The indication of a guilty plea is ignored and treated as a not guilty plea.
The court must acquit the defendant despite the indicated guilty plea.
The court proceeds to sentence (or commits for sentence to the Crown Court if its powers are insufficient), with no allocation or trial needed.
The court must still hold a full allocation hearing and then a trial on the merits on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court must send the case to the Crown Court for a jury to decide guilt.
4.w: At the plea before venue stage for an either-way offence, if the defendant indicates a guilty plea, the court treats the matter as a summary conviction and proceeds to sentence, or commits the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence if its own sentencing powers are insufficient. Allocation and trial only arise where a not guilty plea is indicated.

n.0: An indicated guilty plea is acted upon, not ignored.
n.1: An admitted guilty plea leads to sentence, not acquittal.
n.3: No full allocation and trial are needed once a guilty plea is indicated.
n.4: A guilty plea does not lead to a jury deciding guilt; guilt is admitted.

4.q: A default judgment has been entered against a defendant who failed to respond in time. The defendant applies to set the judgment aside, saying they have a defence with a real prospect of success, and explaining why they did not respond. There is no suggestion that the judgment was wrongly entered as a matter of procedure. The court considers the discretionary setting aside of a default judgment under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant explained they had been abroad and had not seen the claim until judgment was entered. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court must always refuse to set aside a default judgment once it has been entered.
The court must set the judgment aside automatically whenever the defendant asks it to.
The court may set the judgment aside if the defendant has a real prospect of successfully defending or there is some other good reason.
The court may set the judgment aside only if the claimant consents to that being done.
The court can set aside a default judgment only where the amount claimed exceeded £100,000 on these facts as a general rule.
4.w: Where a default judgment was regularly obtained, the court has a discretion to set it aside if the defendant has a real prospect of successfully defending the claim, or if there is some other good reason to set it aside or allow the defendant to defend (also considering promptness of the application).

n.0: The court is not bound always to refuse; it has a discretion to set aside.
n.1: Setting aside is not automatic on request; the test must be met.
n.3: The claimant's consent is not required for the court to set the judgment aside.
n.4: There is no such value threshold governing setting aside.

4.q: A woman is not present when her close family member is involved in an accident caused by the defendant's negligence, but she comes upon the immediate aftermath very shortly afterwards and, through her own unaided senses, witnesses the horrifying scene, suffering a recognised psychiatric illness as a result. She was not physically endangered herself. She was not a participant but perceived the immediate aftermath with her own senses and has a close tie to the victim. She rushed to the scene as soon as she heard, arriving within minutes to find her relative gravely injured and the aftermath still raw and untouched, and what she saw with her own eyes brought on a diagnosed psychiatric condition even though she herself was never in any physical danger. Which of the following best describes what she must establish as a secondary victim?
o: A close tie of love and affection, proximity in time and space to the event or its immediate aftermath, and perception through her own senses.
Only that the psychiatric harm to her was reasonably foreseeable, with no further requirements on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
That the defendant intended to cause her psychiatric harm.
That she was within the zone of physical danger at the time of the accident.
Only that she suffered some distress or grief as a result of the accident.
4.w: A secondary victim must satisfy the control mechanisms in Alcock: a close tie of love and affection with the primary victim, proximity in time and space to the accident or its immediate aftermath, perception of the event (or aftermath) through their own unaided senses, and a recognised psychiatric illness caused by a sudden shock. Mere grief or foreseeability alone is insufficient.

n.1: Foreseeability alone does not suffice for secondary victims; the control mechanisms must be met.
n.2: There is no requirement to prove the defendant intended psychiatric harm.
n.3: Being within the zone of danger would make her a primary victim, which she is not.
n.4: Ordinary distress or grief, short of a recognised psychiatric illness, is not enough.

4.q: A firm is reviewing its record-keeping and asks how long it must retain its accounting records, such as client ledgers, records of bills, and statements and reconciliations, once they have been created. A member of staff suggests they can be destroyed after a year to save storage. The firm holds client money in the ordinary course of its work. The firm generates a large volume of ledger cards, bills, bank statements and reconciliations each year, storage space is at a premium, and a member of staff has proposed a routine clear-out to reduce the archive, prompting the COFA to check exactly how long the accounting records must be preserved. Which of the following best describes the requirement under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: There is no minimum period for which accounting records must be kept.
The firm may destroy its accounting records after one year.
The firm must keep its accounting records for at least twelve months only.
The firm need only keep records until the next accountant's report is obtained.
The firm must keep its accounting records for at least six years.
4.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require a firm to keep, and retain for at least six years, accurate and contemporaneous accounting records showing its dealings with client money, including client ledgers, records of bills, and reconciliations. Destroying them after a year would breach the retention requirement.

n.0: There is a specific minimum retention period.
n.1: Records cannot be destroyed after only one year.
n.2: Twelve months is well short of the six-year requirement.
n.3: Retention is not tied to the next accountant's report; a minimum of six years applies.

4.q: Two business associates decided to buy a commercial investment property together, purely as a money-making venture and with no domestic or family relationship between them. For convenience the legal title was taken in the sole name of one of them, but the other associate provided half of the £400,000 purchase price from their own funds. There was no written declaration of trust, and nothing was said about how the beneficial interest would be held. The associates have now fallen out, and the one who contributed half the price wants to know what interest, if any, they have in the property. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An equal 50:50 beneficial share, applying the presumption used for a shared family home, in these circumstances.
A charge over the property for the money advanced, enforceable as a mortgage.
A beneficial share under a resulting trust, reflecting the proportion of the purchase price they provided.
No interest at all, because the legal title is in the other associate's sole name.
A licence to use the property, revocable by the legal owner at any time.
4.w: Outside the family-home context, a contribution to the purchase price of property vested in another's name gives rise to a presumed resulting trust in favour of the contributor in proportion to their contribution.

n.0: The Stack v Dowden family-home approach does not apply to an arm's-length commercial purchase.
n.1: The contribution creates a trust interest, not a mortgage charge, absent an agreement for security.
n.3: Sole legal ownership does not defeat a resulting trust arising from a purchase-price contribution.
n.4: A purchase-money contribution creates a beneficial interest, not a mere revocable licence.

4.q: A solicitor is making an urgent application to the court, without notice to the other side, for a freezing injunction over a defendant's assets before those assets can be dissipated. Because the defendant will have no opportunity to be heard before the order is made, the solicitor is aware that a special obligation attaches to the way in which the application must be presented to the judge. There are certain facts, known to the solicitor, which are distinctly unhelpful to the applicant's case, and the solicitor is tempted simply to leave those facts out of the material put before the court. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's duty?
o: The solicitor need present only the facts that support the applicant's case, as in any ordinary contested hearing.
The solicitor may omit the adverse facts, provided they would in any event have come out at a later hearing.
The solicitor must give full and frank disclosure of all material facts, including any adverse to the applicant.
The solicitor may omit the adverse facts, provided the applicant genuinely believes the injunction is justified.
The solicitor may present a one-sided case, because the defendant can always apply later to set the order aside.
4.w: On a without-notice application, the applicant's advisers owe a duty of full and frank disclosure to the court, which requires them to draw the court's attention to all material facts, including those adverse to the applicant, since the other side is not present to do so.

n.0: A without-notice application is not an ordinary contested hearing; adverse facts must be disclosed.
n.1: The duty is not excused because the facts might emerge later.
n.3: The applicant's belief in the merits does not permit withholding material adverse facts.
n.4: The availability of a later set-aside application does not justify a one-sided presentation.

4.q: A defendant is remanded in custody awaiting trial, and the defendant's solicitor is concerned about how long the defendant can be held in custody before the trial must take place. There are statutory limits designed to prevent excessive pre-trial detention. The solicitor considers custody time limits in criminal proceedings. The defendant had already spent a considerable time on remand awaiting a trial date. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Custody time limits apply only to defendants who have already been convicted.
A defendant may be held in custody before trial for a maximum of only 24 hours on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Custody time limits may never be extended in any circumstances whatsoever.
Custody time limits restrict how long a defendant may be held in custody awaiting trial, and may be extended by the court on application.
There is no limit on how long a defendant may be held in custody before trial.
4.w: Custody time limits set the maximum period a defendant may be held in custody awaiting trial (for example a set number of days in the magistrates' court or before Crown Court trial). If the limit is reached without trial, the defendant must be released on bail unless the prosecution successfully applies to extend the limit on the statutory grounds.

n.0: Custody time limits concern pre-trial (unconvicted) detention.
n.1: The limits are measured in weeks/months, not a mere 24 hours.
n.2: Custody time limits can be extended on the statutory grounds.
n.4: There are custody time limits, so detention is not unlimited.

4.q: The government seeks to introduce fees that would in practice prevent many people from bringing claims to enforce their legal rights before a tribunal, effectively denying them access to justice. A claimant challenges this by reference to a fundamental constitutional principle. A solicitor is asked which principle is engaged where access to the courts is impeded. The solicitor considers the rule of law and the right of access to justice. The proposed fees were set so high that ordinary people could not realistically bring claims. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Access to the courts is a fundamental aspect of the rule of law, and measures that unjustifiably impede it may be unlawful.
Access to the courts is a mere privilege that the government may remove at will for any reason on these facts as a general rule.
Access to justice is guaranteed only to those who can afford to pay for it in full.
The courts cannot consider any challenge to fees set by the government.
The rule of law has nothing to do with whether people can bring claims to court.
4.w: Access to the courts is a constitutional right and a fundamental element of the rule of law. Measures (such as prohibitive fees) that effectively prevent people from vindicating their legal rights may be held unlawful as an unjustified interference with that right (R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor).

n.1: Access to justice is a constitutional right, not a privilege removable at will.
n.2: Access to justice is not confined to those who can pay any fee set.
n.3: The courts can and do review measures impeding access to justice.
n.4: The rule of law is closely concerned with access to the courts.

4.q: A company has been registered and the Registrar of Companies has issued a certificate of incorporation. Some months later, a person challenges the company's existence, alleging that a technical defect in the registration documents means the company was never properly formed. The certificate of incorporation has been duly issued by the Registrar. The challenge is to the validity of the company's formation. The company has been trading for some months on the strength of its certificate when a disgruntled counterparty, looking for a way out of a deal, claims that a paperwork slip at the registration stage means the company was never validly formed in the first place. Which of the following best describes the effect of the certificate of incorporation?
o: The certificate is only provisional and may be set aside for any documentary defect.
The certificate binds only the company, not third parties dealing with it.
The certificate proves the company exists only until its first annual return is filed.
The certificate has no legal effect and the company's existence must be separately proved on these facts as a general rule.
The certificate is conclusive evidence that the requirements of registration have been complied with and the company exists.
4.w: The certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the requirements of the Companies Act 2006 as to registration have been complied with and that the company is duly registered. Once issued, the company's existence cannot be attacked on the basis of alleged defects in the registration process.

n.0: The certificate is conclusive, not merely provisional or liable to be set aside for defects.
n.1: Its conclusive effect is not confined to the company; it establishes the company's existence generally.
n.2: Its conclusive effect is not limited to the period before the first annual return.
n.3: The certificate has decisive legal effect; separate proof of existence is not needed.

4.q: A defendant commits an offence, claiming that they only did so because another person threatened them with death or serious injury unless they committed it, and a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing the defendant's characteristics might have responded in the same way, with no safe avenue of escape available. The defendant relies on duress by threats. The court considers the availability and requirements of that defence. The defendant said a gang had threatened to kill their family unless they carried out the offence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Duress by threats may be a defence to most offences, but is not available to murder or attempted murder.
Duress by threats is available only where the threat was of minor harm to the defendant.
Duress by threats is available only where the defendant had a reasonable avenue of escape but chose not to use it.
Duress by threats is a complete defence to any offence, including murder, without exception.
Duress by threats is never a defence to any criminal offence in English law.
4.w: Duress by threats requires a threat of death or serious injury which a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing the defendant's relevant characteristics could not have resisted, with no safe avenue of escape. It is a complete defence to most crimes, but is not available to murder, attempted murder (or, generally, some forms of treason).

n.1: The threat must be of death or serious injury, not minor harm.
n.2: The defence requires the absence of a safe avenue of escape, not the presence of one.
n.3: Duress is not available to murder or attempted murder.
n.4: Duress is a recognised defence to many offences.

4.q: A person forms a private limited company to run their business, becoming its sole shareholder and director, and the company is duly incorporated. The business later fails owing money to creditors, who wish to pursue the shareholder personally for the company's debts, arguing that in reality the company and the individual are one and the same. The shareholder relies on the company's separate legal personality. The court considers the effect of incorporation on liability. The individual had run the same business as a sole trader before deciding to incorporate it. Which of the following best describes the position?
