o: The shareholder is liable without limit because they are the only shareholder and director.
The company is a separate legal person, so the shareholder is generally not liable for its debts.
The company has no separate personality until it has traded for at least one full year.
The company's separate personality is ignored whenever the company cannot pay its debts.
The shareholder is always personally liable for the company's debts as its controller.
4.w: On incorporation a company becomes a separate legal person distinct from its members (Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd). The shareholders' liability is generally limited to any amount unpaid on their shares, and they are not personally liable for the company's debts, even where one person owns and runs it.

n.0: Being sole shareholder/director does not create unlimited personal liability.
n.2: Separate personality arises on incorporation, not after a year's trading.
n.3: Separate personality is not disregarded simply because the company is insolvent.
n.4: A controlling shareholder is not, for that reason, personally liable for company debts.

4.q: The owner of a house and an adjoining field had, while owning both together, regularly used a track running across the field in order to reach the house from the lane. The owner then sold the house to a buyer but kept the field for themselves. The conveyance of the house to the buyer said nothing at all about any right to use the track across the retained field. The buyer of the house now wishes to continue using the track for access, as the seller had always done, and asserts a right to do so. Which of the following best describes the basis of any such right?
o: A bare licence, personal to the buyer, which the seller may revoke at will.
An easement implied into the conveyance in the buyer's favour, for example under s.62 LPA 1925 or Wheeldon v Burrows.
A profit à prendre over the field, allowing the buyer to take produce from it.
A right arising only if the buyer later uses the track as of right for 20 years.
No right can arise, because an easement can only ever be created by an express grant in the conveyance.
4.w: On a sale of part, an easement may be implied in favour of the buyer over the retained land, for example under the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows (continuous and apparent quasi-easements necessary for reasonable enjoyment) or by s.62 LPA 1925 operating on prior use.

n.0: The buyer's right, if any, is a proprietary easement, not a revocable bare licence.
n.2: Using a track for access is an easement, not a profit to take produce.
n.3: An implied easement can arise immediately on the conveyance without 20 years' later use.
n.4: Easements can be implied on a conveyance, not only expressly granted.

4.q: A conveyance of part of a seller's land imposed a restrictive covenant on the land sold, the covenant being expressed to be 'for the benefit of the retained land' of the seller. That retained land has since been sold on to a new owner. The later conveyance of the retained land did not expressly mention the restrictive covenant or purport to assign its benefit to the new owner. The current owner of the burdened land is now acting in breach, and the new owner of the retained land nevertheless wishes to enforce the covenant against them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The benefit is likely annexed to the retained land and passes with it, so the new owner can enforce it.
Only the original covenantee may enforce the covenant, regardless of who owns the land.
The new owner can enforce it only if the benefit was expressly assigned in their conveyance.
The covenant lapsed when the retained land was sold without mentioning it.
The benefit is personal to the original seller and cannot pass to a later owner of the retained land, on these facts.
4.w: Where a covenant is expressed to benefit identified retained land, the benefit is annexed to that land (and s.78 LPA 1925 assists annexation). It then passes automatically to successors of the benefited land, who can enforce it without an express assignment.

n.1: Successors to the benefited land can enforce, not only the original covenantee.
n.2: Express assignment is unnecessary where the benefit is annexed to the land.
n.3: The covenant does not lapse merely because the benefited land is sold.
n.4: A covenant taken for the benefit of retained land is not merely personal to the seller.

4.q: An occupier is granted the right to occupy residential premises. The agreement is labelled a 'licence', but in substance the occupier has exclusive possession of the premises for a fixed term at a rent, and the owner has no genuine right to share or control occupation. The label used and the substance of the arrangement differ. The occupier has exclusive possession for a term at a rent. Although the document the parties signed is headed a licence, in reality the occupier has been given exclusive possession of the premises for a fixed period at a rent, with the owner retaining no genuine right to come and go or share the space, so substance and label appear to diverge. Which of the following best describes how the arrangement is characterised?
o: It is neither a lease nor a licence and creates no rights at all.
It is likely a lease (tenancy), because the substance (exclusive possession for a term at a rent) prevails over the label.
It is an easement over the premises.
It is a licence, because the parties labelled it a licence.
It is a freehold estate because the occupier has exclusive possession on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
4.w: Following Street v Mountford, the grant of exclusive possession of premises for a term at a rent creates a tenancy (lease), whatever label the parties use; the court looks at the substance of the arrangement, not merely its description. If the occupier truly has exclusive possession for a term, it is a lease even if called a licence.

n.0: Exclusive possession for a term at a rent does create rights (a lease).
n.2: An easement is a right over another's land, not exclusive possession of premises.
n.3: The label 'licence' does not govern where the substance is a tenancy.
n.4: Exclusive possession for a term is characteristic of a leasehold, not a freehold estate.

4.q: A court is interpreting a statutory provision that, on its ordinary meaning, would appear to conflict with a Convention right. The court is considering whether it can read the provision in a way that is compatible with the Convention right. A solicitor is asked about the interpretive obligation on the courts under the Human Rights Act 1998. The solicitor considers section 3 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The ordinary reading of the provision would have produced a clear breach of a Convention right. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Section 3 applies only to secondary legislation and never to Acts of Parliament.
So far as it is possible to do so, legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights.
The court must strike down any statute that is incompatible with a Convention right.
The court must always apply the literal meaning of a statute even if it breaches Convention rights on these facts.
The court may rewrite any statute freely to achieve any result it considers desirable.
4.w: Under s.3 of the Human Rights Act 1998, so far as it is possible to do so, primary and subordinate legislation must be read and given effect in a way that is compatible with Convention rights. This is a strong interpretive obligation, though it cannot be used to go against a fundamental feature of the legislation.

n.0: Section 3 applies to both primary and subordinate legislation.
n.2: The courts cannot strike down primary legislation; s.3 (and s.4) reflect this.
n.3: Section 3 requires a compatible reading where possible, not always the literal meaning.
n.4: Section 3 permits a strained reading where possible, but not unlimited rewriting.

4.q: A buyer purchases a building that later proves to have been negligently constructed with defective foundations. No person is injured and no other property is damaged; the only loss is the cost of repairing the defective building itself and the reduction in its value. The buyer sues the negligent builder in the tort of negligence for that cost. The loss claimed is the cost of making good the defect in the thing itself, with no personal injury or damage to other property. Which of the following best describes the recoverability of this loss in negligence?
o: It is recoverable because economic loss is freely recoverable in the tort of negligence.
It is recoverable because defective buildings are treated as physical damage to other property.
It is always recoverable in negligence as ordinary consequential loss.
It is recoverable provided the defect was merely difficult, rather than impossible, to discover on these facts.
It is generally irrecoverable in negligence, being pure economic loss in respect of a defective product or building.
4.w: The cost of repairing a defect in the product or building itself, and its diminution in value, is pure economic loss, which is generally not recoverable in the tort of negligence (Murphy v Brentwood). Such loss is usually recoverable, if at all, only in contract or under a specific assumption of responsibility, not in ordinary negligence.

n.0: Pure economic loss is generally not freely recoverable in negligence.
n.1: A defect in the thing itself is not damage to 'other property'.
n.2: This kind of loss is not treated as ordinary recoverable consequential loss in negligence.
n.3: Recoverability does not turn on how difficult the defect was to discover.

4.q: A diner eats a meal in a restaurant where payment is required on the spot before leaving. Knowing payment is expected there and then, the diner dishonestly leaves without paying and without any intention of returning to pay. Payment on the spot was required and expected for the meal supplied. The defendant left dishonestly, intending to avoid payment. The restaurant, like most, expected the bill to be settled before anyone left, the defendant knew perfectly well that payment on the spot was required, and having finished the meal they slipped out without paying and with no intention of ever coming back to make good the bill. Which of the following best identifies the offence under the Theft Act 1978?
o: Theft of the meal under the Theft Act 1968.
Fraud by false representation under the Fraud Act 2006.
No offence, because the meal had already been consumed.
Making off without payment under section 3.
Obtaining services dishonestly under the Fraud Act 2006.
4.w: Making off without payment (s.3 Theft Act 1978) is committed where a person, knowing that payment on the spot for goods supplied or services done is required or expected, dishonestly makes off without having paid as required and with intent to avoid payment. Leaving a restaurant without paying for a meal is the classic example.

n.0: The meal was supplied and consumed with payment expected on the spot; making off without payment fits better than theft here.
n.1: There need be no false representation; the offence is making off without payment.
n.2: Consuming the meal does not prevent the offence; the offence lies in making off without paying.
n.4: Obtaining services dishonestly focuses on dishonestly obtaining the service; the gist here is making off without paying for what was supplied.

4.q: A long-established factory begins to emit noise and smells that interfere with the comfort of neighbouring residents in what has always been a quiet residential area. The residents sue in private nuisance in respect of the loss of amenity, and the factory argues the interference is not unreasonable. The complaint concerns interference with comfort and enjoyment, not physical damage to the land. The character of the locality is residential. The area had always been peaceful and residential, the factory's noise and odours now intrude on the residents' day-to-day comfort at home, and the argument centres on whether an interference of that character, in a neighbourhood of this kind, crosses the line into an unreasonable one. Which of the following best describes the relevance of the locality to the claim?
o: The character of the locality is relevant only to claims for physical damage to land.
The character of the locality means an industrial user can never be liable in a residential area.
The character of the locality determines liability solely according to who was there first.
The character of the locality is relevant to whether an amenity interference is unreasonable.
The character of the locality is irrelevant to every private nuisance claim.
4.w: In private nuisance the character of the locality is relevant to whether an interference with comfort or amenity is unreasonable: what counts as a nuisance in a quiet residential area may not in an industrial one. Locality is not, however, relevant where the nuisance causes physical damage to property, which is actionable regardless of the neighbourhood.

n.0: Locality is relevant to amenity claims, not (as stated) only to physical damage claims.
n.1: An industrial user can still be liable in a residential area; locality is one factor, not a shield.
n.2: Priority in time ('coming to the nuisance') does not by itself determine liability.
n.4: Locality is relevant to amenity nuisance, so it is not irrelevant.

4.q: A tribunal or public body makes a decision based on a misunderstanding or misapplication of the law — an error of law — which affects the outcome. A claimant challenges the decision by judicial review. A solicitor is asked whether such an error is a basis for the courts to intervene, and how it relates to jurisdiction. The solicitor considers error of law as a ground of judicial review. The tribunal had plainly misunderstood the legal test it was required to apply to the case. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An error of law by a public body can never be corrected by the courts.
An error of law is generally reviewable; since Anisminic most such errors are treated as going to jurisdiction.
The courts may correct only errors of fact and never errors of law.
An error of law is reviewable only where the body admits that it made a mistake.
Errors of law are relevant only in appeals and can never be raised in judicial review on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
4.w: An error of law is a form of illegality and is generally reviewable. Following Anisminic and later authority, most errors of law made by a public body or tribunal are treated as taking it outside its jurisdiction, rendering the decision a nullity, so the courts can quash the decision.

n.0: Errors of law can be corrected by the courts.
n.2: The courts review errors of law (more readily than errors of fact).
n.3: Review does not depend on the body admitting its mistake.
n.4: Errors of law can be raised in judicial review, not only on appeal.

4.q: A person wishes to bring a claim under the Human Rights Act 1998 alleging that a public authority has acted incompatibly with their Convention rights, but a question arises about whether this particular claimant is entitled to bring such a claim. The claimant must show they are affected in the right way. A solicitor is asked who may bring a claim under the Human Rights Act 1998. The solicitor considers the victim requirement under section 7 of the Act. The claimant had to show they were personally affected by the authority's conduct. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Anyone at all may bring a Human Rights Act claim, whether or not they are affected on these facts.
Only a person who is (or would be) a victim of the unlawful act may bring a claim under the Human Rights Act.
Only the Government may bring proceedings under the Human Rights Act.
A claim may be brought only by a person who has suffered financial loss.
Human Rights Act claims may be brought only by companies and not by individuals.
4.w: Under s.7 of the Human Rights Act 1998, a person may bring proceedings against a public authority for acting incompatibly with a Convention right only if they are (or would be) a victim of the unlawful act — broadly, a person directly affected by it. This is narrower than the 'sufficient interest' test in ordinary judicial review.

n.0: The claimant must be a victim; not anyone may claim.
n.2: HRA claims are brought by victims, not the Government.
n.3: Financial loss is not the test; being a victim is.
n.4: Individuals (and in some cases organisations that are victims) may bring HRA claims.

4.q: A defendant aged 15 is charged with a very serious offence, such as a homicide or another grave crime for which a long custodial sentence is available for adults. Youths are usually dealt with in the youth court, but this offence falls within a special category. The defendant is under 18 but charged with a grave crime. The usual youth court venue is in question. The accused is only fifteen and would ordinarily have their case dealt with in the youth court, but the charge is of the gravest kind, a homicide, the sort of offence for which the adult courts hold far greater sentencing powers, which throws the usual choice of venue into doubt. Which of the following best describes where such a case may be tried?
o: The case may be sent to the Crown Court, as certain grave crimes (including homicide) fall outside the youth court's usual jurisdiction.
The case cannot be tried at all until the defendant turns 18.
The case must be tried in the adult magistrates' court.
The case must always be tried in the youth court whatever the offence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The case must be tried by a jury in the youth court.
4.w: Although defendants under 18 are generally dealt with in the youth court, certain grave crimes are exceptions. Homicide offences must be sent to the Crown Court, and other specified grave crimes (where a long sentence may be required) may be sent there, so a youth charged with such an offence can be tried in the Crown Court.

n.1: The case can be tried while the defendant is under 18; it need not wait until they are 18.
n.2: Youths are not tried in the adult magistrates' court; the alternatives are the youth court or Crown Court.
n.3: Not all youth cases stay in the youth court; grave crimes are exceptions.
n.4: The youth court does not sit with a jury; jury trial is in the Crown Court.

4.q: A firm acting for a client in a personal injury claim receives a settlement of £2,500 paid to the firm on the client's behalf. The firm considers that £500 of the sum represents costs it is entitled to, but it has not yet delivered any bill to the client for those costs. The cashier must decide how the £2,500 is classified when it is received. No bill or written notification of costs has yet been given. The settlement cheque has been paid to the firm rather than to the client directly, the client is expecting to receive the balance after the firm's charges, and the cashier is conscious that the firm cannot help itself to its costs simply because it believes it is owed them. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the receipt?
o: The whole £2,500 is office money because the firm is owed costs.
The £500 is office money and only £2,000 is client money on receipt.
The £500 may be paid straight into the office account before any bill.
The £2,500 may be split at the firm's discretion whenever convenient.
The whole £2,500 is client money and must be paid into the client account.
4.w: Money received on behalf of a client, such as damages, is client money in its entirety and must be paid into the client account. The firm cannot treat any part as office money for its costs until it has delivered a bill or other written notification of costs; only then may it transfer the billed amount to the office account.

n.0: The firm is owed costs but cannot treat the money as office money without a bill.
n.1: No part is office money yet, because no bill has been delivered.
n.2: The £500 cannot go to the office account before any bill.
n.3: The receipt is client money and must be banked as such promptly, not apportioned at will.

4.q: A defendant inflicts a non-fatal wound on a victim. Before the victim dies, an entirely free, deliberate and informed act of a third party (or of the victim), independent of the defendant's conduct, intervenes and is the immediate cause of the death. The defendant argues that this intervening act broke the chain of causation between the wound and the death. The court considers when a subsequent act will break the chain of causation. The later act was wholly independent of the defendant and was the immediate cause of the death. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The chain is broken by any subsequent event at all, however minor or foreseeable.
The chain is broken only where the defendant intended the intervening act to occur.
Nothing that happens after the defendant's act can ever break the chain of causation on these facts.
The chain can be broken only by an act of the victim, and never by a third party.
A free, deliberate and informed intervening act may break the chain of causation, relieving the defendant.
4.w: The chain of causation may be broken by a novus actus interveniens: a free, deliberate and informed act of a third party (or the victim) that is sufficiently independent of the defendant's conduct can break legal causation and relieve the defendant of responsibility for the ultimate result.

n.0: Not every subsequent event breaks the chain; it must be free, deliberate and informed (or otherwise sufficiently independent).
n.1: The defendant's intention regarding the intervening act is not the test.
n.2: Subsequent events can break the chain in appropriate circumstances.
n.3: Both third-party and victim acts can, in principle, break the chain.

4.q: A 16-year-old is charged with a criminal offence which, for an adult, would be an either-way matter, but which is not a grave crime requiring Crown Court trial. The young person's solicitor advises on which court will normally deal with a defendant of this age. The solicitor considers the jurisdiction of the youth court. The young defendant and their family wanted to know which court would hear the case. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A defendant under 18 may choose to be tried in any court they prefer.
A defendant under 18 is always sent to the Crown Court for trial whatever the offence on these facts.
A defendant under 18 is always tried in the adult magistrates' court alongside adults.
A defendant under 18 is generally dealt with in the youth court, save for certain grave or specified cases.
A defendant under 18 cannot be prosecuted for any criminal offence at all.
4.w: Defendants under 18 are generally dealt with in the youth court, a specialist part of the magistrates' court. There are exceptions where a young defendant may be sent to the Crown Court — for example homicide, certain grave crimes, or where jointly charged with an adult in some circumstances.

n.0: A young defendant does not freely choose the court; the rules on jurisdiction govern.
n.1: Under-18s are not always sent to the Crown Court.
n.2: Under-18s are dealt with in the youth court, not routinely the adult court.
n.4: Those over the age of criminal responsibility can be prosecuted.

4.q: An adult beneficiary of full capacity is absolutely entitled to the entire beneficial interest in a trust fund, with no other person having any interest in it. The trust was set up to pay the fund to the beneficiary at a later age, but the beneficiary now wishes to bring the trust to an end immediately and have the fund transferred to them straight away, against the wishes of the trustees who point to the age condition. The fund was substantial and the beneficiary had a pressing personal reason for wanting it released now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The beneficiary may require the trustees to transfer the fund and end the trust under the rule in Saunders v Vautier.
The beneficiary has no power to interfere with how the trustees choose to administer the trust.
The beneficiary may end the trust only if a court first approves the early distribution.
The beneficiary may end the trust only with the consent of the settlor who created it.
The beneficiary must wait until the stated age, because the terms of the trust are binding come what may on these facts.
4.w: Under the rule in Saunders v Vautier, a beneficiary (or beneficiaries together) who is of full age and capacity and absolutely entitled to the whole beneficial interest may direct the trustees to transfer the trust property and bring the trust to an end, overriding a mere postponement of enjoyment.

n.1: An absolutely entitled adult beneficiary can indeed call for the fund.
n.2: Court approval is not needed where a single adult is absolutely entitled.
n.3: The settlor's consent is not required to invoke Saunders v Vautier.
n.4: An age condition merely postponing enjoyment does not prevent a sole absolutely-entitled adult ending the trust.

4.q: A firm has delivered a bill to a client and, applying the money it held for the client, is entitled to £600 of costs. That £600 has therefore become office money, but it remains sitting in the general client account some time after the bill was delivered, mixed with genuine client money. The cashier queries whether this is acceptable. The money is now properly due to the firm. The bill was delivered to the client several weeks ago, the entitlement to the £600 is not in doubt, and yet the sum has never been moved across to the office account, so it continues to swell the client account balance alongside money that genuinely belongs to other clients. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The £600 may remain in the client account indefinitely once it is due to the firm.
The £600 must be paid to the SRA because it is mixed with client money.
The £600 may remain in the client account until the client next instructs the firm.
The £600 must be transferred out of the client account to the office account promptly.
The £600 need not be moved provided the client account is reconciled each month.
4.w: Once money the firm holds has become office money (here, billed costs the firm is entitled to), it should not be left in the client account. Retaining office money in the client account is itself a breach, so the firm must transfer the £600 to the office account promptly after the entitlement arises.

n.0: Office money must not be left in the client account indefinitely.
n.1: The money is the firm's; it is transferred to the office account, not paid to the SRA.
n.2: There is no basis for leaving it until the client next gives instructions.
n.4: Reconciliation does not cure the retention of office money in the client account.

4.q: Two businesses have dealt with each other regularly over several years, and on every previous occasion the seller's delivery notes have incorporated the seller's standard terms, including a limitation clause, of which the buyer has always been aware. On the latest order the goods are delivered first and the delivery note handed over only afterwards, but the course of dealing has been consistent and well known to the buyer. The parties are experienced commercial contractors with a long, consistent history of dealing on these terms. Which of the following best describes whether the limitation clause is incorporated?
o: The clause is automatically incorporated into every contract between any businesses.
The clause cannot be incorporated because it was handed over after delivery on this occasion.
The clause may be incorporated by the parties' consistent prior course of dealing.
The clause can never be incorporated unless separately signed on each occasion.
The clause is incorporated only if the buyer expressly re-agreed to it for this order.
4.w: Terms can be incorporated by a consistent and well-known course of dealing between the parties. Where experienced commercial parties have regularly contracted on the same standard terms, those terms may be incorporated into a further transaction even if, on the particular occasion, the document containing them was provided after the moment of contracting.

n.0: Terms are not automatically incorporated into every contract between businesses; a basis such as course of dealing is needed.
n.1: Late delivery of the note on one occasion does not defeat incorporation built on a consistent prior course of dealing.
n.3: A fresh signature on each occasion is not required where a course of dealing exists.
n.4: Express re-agreement for the specific order is not necessary given the established course of dealing.

4.q: A solicitor is appearing as the advocate for a client at a hearing in the county court. While preparing the night before, the solicitor becomes aware of a binding decision of a higher court which is directly relevant to the very legal issue that will be before the judge, but which is distinctly unhelpful to the client's argument and which the opposing advocate has plainly overlooked. The solicitor would much prefer to say nothing at all about it, in the hope that neither the judge nor the other side will happen to find it. The solicitor considers what their duty as an advocate actually requires. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The advocate may withhold the authority, because the duty to the client outweighs any duty to the court.
The advocate may stay silent about the authority, because it is for the other side to find and cite it.
The advocate may stay silent, provided they do not positively deny that any such authority exists.
The advocate must draw the court's attention to relevant adverse binding authority, even if it harms the client's case.
The advocate must cite the authority only if the judge specifically asks whether there is any against them.
4.w: An advocate owes a duty to the court not to mislead it, which includes a positive obligation to draw the court's attention to relevant binding authority, even where it is adverse to the client's case. The duty to the court takes precedence over the client's interests here.

n.0: The duty to the court prevails over the client's interests in this respect.
n.1: The advocate cannot leave it to the other side; the duty to cite adverse binding authority is the advocate's own.
n.2: Silence that allows the court to overlook binding authority is itself misleading.
n.4: The duty is not contingent on the judge happening to ask.

4.q: The partners in an existing firm wish to bring in a new person as a partner. There is no written partnership agreement making special provision about admitting new partners. One of the existing partners objects to the proposed new partner joining. The others argue that a simple majority should be enough to admit the newcomer. The court considers the default rule on the admission of a new partner under the Partnership Act 1890. The deceased had been an equal partner and no one had planned for what would happen on a death. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: No new partner may be introduced without the consent of all existing partners, absent contrary agreement.
A new partner may be admitted by a simple majority of the existing partners.
A new partner may be admitted only with the approval of the firm's principal creditors on these facts.
A new partner may be admitted by any single existing partner acting alone.
A new partner is admitted automatically once they contribute capital to the firm.
4.w: Under s.24(7) Partnership Act 1890, no person may be introduced as a partner without the consent of all existing partners, unless the partnership agreement provides otherwise. The objection of one partner therefore blocks the admission under the default rule.

n.1: A simple majority is not sufficient under the default rule.
n.2: Creditor approval is not the statutory requirement for admitting a partner.
n.3: A single partner cannot admit a new partner alone.
n.4: Contributing capital does not by itself make someone a partner.

4.q: A claimant considers that the defendant's defence is hopeless and has no real substance, and wishes to obtain judgment without the expense of a full trial, on the basis that the defence has no real prospect of success and there is no other reason for a trial. The claimant applies for judgment before trial. The court considers the test for summary judgment under Part 24 of the Civil Procedure Rules. The pleaded defence amounted to little more than a bare denial with nothing at all to support it. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Summary judgment is available only where the claim is worth less than £10,000.
Summary judgment may be given where a party has no real prospect of success and there is no other compelling reason for a trial.
Summary judgment must be granted whenever either party simply asks the court for it.
Summary judgment may be given only after all the witnesses have given oral evidence at trial on these facts as a general rule.
Summary judgment is available only to defendants and can never be sought by a claimant.
4.w: Under Part 24 CPR, the court may give summary judgment against a claimant or defendant on the whole claim or an issue if that party has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim, defence or issue, and there is no other compelling reason why the case or issue should be disposed of at trial.

n.0: There is no such value limit on summary judgment.
n.2: It is not granted automatically on request; the test must be satisfied.
n.3: Summary judgment is decided before trial, not after oral evidence.
n.4: Summary judgment can be sought by claimant or defendant, not only defendants.

4.q: Two lay trustees administer a trust together. They disagree about a particular decision: one trustee wishes to take a certain course, and the other does not. The first trustee purports to act alone, on the basis that a majority or even a single trustee should be able to bind the trust. A beneficiary questions whether one of two trustees can act unilaterally in this way. The trustees seek advice on how decisions must be taken where there is more than one trustee of a private trust. The proposed course would have committed a significant part of the fund to a single course of action. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Any decision is valid provided at least one trustee supports it.
Trustees of a private trust must generally act unanimously, so one trustee cannot act alone.
The trustee who was appointed first has the casting vote on any disagreement.
A single trustee may always act alone and bind the trust, whatever the others think.
Decisions are always taken by a simple majority of the trustees in every private trust.
4.w: Trustees of a private trust must generally act unanimously; decisions require the agreement of all the trustees, and one trustee cannot bind the trust by acting alone (unless the trust instrument or statute provides otherwise, as for some charitable and pension trusts where majority decisions may apply).

n.0: Support from only one trustee does not make a decision valid.
n.2: There is no casting vote for the first-appointed trustee.
n.3: A single trustee cannot generally act alone to bind a private trust.
n.4: Private trustees act unanimously, not by simple majority.

4.q: A party carrying out disclosure must look for the documents it is required to disclose. It has a very large number of documents, including archived and electronic material, and wonders how far it must go in searching for disclosable documents, and whether the duty ends once its list is served. The court considers the duty to search and the continuing nature of disclosure under the Civil Procedure Rules. The party held thousands of documents, many of them archived or held only in electronic form. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Once the list of documents is served, the duty of disclosure ends entirely.
A party must make a reasonable and proportionate search, and the duty of disclosure continues until proceedings end.
A party must search every document it holds regardless of cost or proportionality.
The duty to search applies only to paper documents and never to electronic material.
A party need not search at all and may simply disclose whatever comes easily to hand on these facts as a general rule.
4.w: A party must make a reasonable search for disclosable documents, the extent being judged by proportionality (number of documents, nature of the case, ease and cost of retrieval, significance). The duty of disclosure is continuing: documents that later come to light must be disclosed.

n.0: Disclosure is a continuing duty, not ended on service of the list.
n.2: The search must be reasonable and proportionate, not unlimited regardless of cost.
n.3: The duty extends to electronic as well as paper documents.
n.4: A party cannot simply disclose whatever is convenient; a reasonable search is required.

4.q: Personal representatives have finished paying the debts and are ready to transfer estate property to the beneficiaries entitled under the will, including transferring the deceased's house to a beneficiary. They need to know the mechanism by which estate property is vested in a beneficiary. The court considers the use of an assent in the administration of an estate. The debts had all been paid and the beneficiary was waiting to have the house put in their name. Which of the following best describes it?
o: An assent is required only for personal chattels and never for land.
Property automatically vests in beneficiaries the moment the testator dies, with no further step.
The PRs must sell all estate property and can only ever distribute cash to beneficiaries.
The PRs vest property in a beneficiary by an assent, which for land must be in writing.
Property can be transferred to a beneficiary only by a court order in every case.
4.w: When ready to distribute, personal representatives transfer estate property to the entitled beneficiary by an assent. An assent of a legal estate in land must be in writing, signed by the PRs and naming the person in whose favour it is given, in order to pass the legal estate.

n.0: An assent of land must be in writing; the requirement is not confined to chattels.
n.1: Property does not vest in beneficiaries automatically at death; the PRs must assent or transfer it.
n.2: PRs are not obliged to sell everything and distribute only cash; they may assent assets in specie.
n.4: A court order is not required for an ordinary assent.

4.q: An employee, during the working day, abandons their assigned duties entirely and goes off on a substantial personal errand of their own, wholly unconnected with their job and for their own purposes. While engaged in that purely personal venture, and far removed from anything they were employed to do, the employee negligently injures a third party. The injured party sues the employer, seeking to rely on vicarious liability. The employer argues that the employee was on a frolic of their own at the time. The personal errand had taken the employee several miles away from their assigned place of work that day. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The employer is liable, because the injury happened during the employee's normal working hours.
The employer is liable, because the employee was still technically employed at the time of the injury.
The employer is liable, because an employer is responsible for everything an employee does all day.
The employer is liable, provided the employee was using the employer's vehicle when the injury occurred on these facts.
The employer is unlikely to be liable, because the employee was on a frolic of their own outside the course of employment.
4.w: Vicarious liability arises only where the employee is acting in the course of employment. Where the employee has abandoned their duties on a purely personal venture — a 'frolic of their own' — unconnected with the job, the act falls outside the course of employment and the employer is not vicariously liable.

n.0: Merely occurring in working hours does not bring a personal frolic within the course of employment.
n.1: Still being employed does not make a personal frolic part of the course of employment.
n.2: An employer is not responsible for everything an employee does regardless of connection to the job.
n.3: Using the employer's vehicle does not, by itself, bring a personal frolic within employment.

4.q: A company makes taxable profits from its trading activities and from chargeable gains during its accounting period. A businessperson wants to understand which tax the company itself is liable to pay on those profits and gains, as distinct from taxes payable by its shareholders or employees. The court considers the tax to which a UK company is subject on its income and gains. The company had a profitable trading year and had also sold a property at a healthy gain. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A company pays capital gains tax on its trading profits at the individual rate.
A company pays corporation tax on its taxable income profits and chargeable gains.
A company pays no tax at all on its profits; only its shareholders are taxed.
A company pays income tax on its profits in exactly the same way as an individual.
A company pays only VAT and is not subject to any tax on its profits.
4.w: A UK company is chargeable to corporation tax on its taxable total profits, which comprise both its income profits (such as trading profits) and its chargeable gains, for each accounting period.

n.0: Companies pay corporation tax on gains, not capital gains tax at the individual rate.
n.2: A company is itself liable to tax on its profits.
n.3: Companies pay corporation tax, not income tax, on their profits.
n.4: A company is subject to corporation tax on profits, in addition to VAT on relevant supplies.

4.q: A tenant of commercial premises wishes to assign the lease to a buyer, and the lease contains a covenant not to assign without the landlord's consent, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. The tenant applies to the landlord for consent, but the landlord is slow to respond and appears to be withholding consent without good reason. The tenant asks about the landlord's obligations. The solicitor considers the landlord's duties on an application for consent to assign under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988. The proposed assignee was financially sound and the tenant was anxious to complete the sale. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The tenant may assign the lease freely without ever seeking the landlord's consent.
The landlord must give consent within a reasonable time except where it is reasonable to withhold it, and give written reasons for any refusal.
The landlord must always consent to any proposed assignment without exception.
The landlord has no time limit and may take as long as it wishes to consider the application.
The landlord may refuse consent for any reason at all, however arbitrary, and need not explain on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
4.w: Where a lease requires the landlord's consent to assign, not to be unreasonably withheld, the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988 imposes duties on the landlord to give consent within a reasonable time (unless it is reasonable to refuse), to give the tenant written notice of the decision, and to state reasons for any refusal, with the burden of showing reasonableness on the landlord.

n.0: The tenant must seek consent where the lease requires it.
n.2: The landlord may reasonably refuse in some cases; it need not always consent.
n.3: The 1988 Act requires a decision within a reasonable time, not unlimited delay.
n.4: The landlord cannot refuse for any arbitrary reason where consent is not to be unreasonably withheld.

4.q: A person dies without leaving a valid will, and is therefore intestate. They are survived by their spouse and by children (issue). The estate exceeds the statutory legacy figure. The family need to know how the estate is distributed between the surviving spouse and the children under the intestacy rules. The court considers the entitlement of a surviving spouse where the intestate leaves issue. The estate comfortably exceeded the fixed statutory legacy figure set for a surviving spouse. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The children take the entire estate, and the surviving spouse receives nothing at all.
The estate is divided equally between the spouse and each of the children in equal shares on these facts.
The spouse takes only the personal chattels, with everything else passing to the children.
The spouse takes the entire estate absolutely, and the children receive nothing at all.
The spouse takes the personal chattels, a statutory legacy, and half the residue, with the other half to the issue.
4.w: Under the intestacy rules, where the intestate leaves a spouse (or civil partner) and issue, the spouse takes the personal chattels, a fixed statutory legacy (with interest), and one half of the residuary estate absolutely; the other half of the residue is held on the statutory trusts for the issue.

n.0: The spouse does take a substantial entitlement; the children do not take everything.
n.1: The division is not simply equal shares among spouse and each child.
n.2: The spouse takes more than just the chattels where there is issue.
n.3: Where there is issue, the spouse does not take the whole estate.

4.q: A buyer contracts to purchase goods 'described as new' from a seller. The written contract describes the goods by that description, and the buyer relies on the description in agreeing to buy. When the goods arrive they are in fact second-hand and reconditioned, and so do not correspond with the description under which they were sold. The buyer wishes to know the basis on which it can complain, and in particular whether the description formed part of the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The description is a term of the contract, and goods sold by description must correspond with that description.
The description binds the buyer, not the seller, so the buyer must accept the goods as delivered.
The description is a mere representation, so the buyer's only possible claim is for misrepresentation.
The description has no legal effect, because descriptions of goods are always mere sales talk.
The description is a term only if the buyer inspected the goods before agreeing to buy them.
4.w: Where goods are sold by description and the buyer relies on that description, there is an implied condition that the goods will correspond with the description (s.13 Sale of Goods Act 1979). The description is a contractual term, and delivering non-conforming goods breaches it.

n.1: The description binds the seller to supply conforming goods, not the buyer to accept whatever arrives.
n.2: A description relied upon in a sale by description is a term, not merely a representation.
n.3: Contractual descriptions of goods are not merely sales talk; they have legal effect.
n.4: Correspondence with description does not depend on the buyer having inspected the goods.

4.q: An estate includes land which is to be held on trust for beneficiaries, one of whom is a minor with a life interest arising. A single individual proposes to take out the grant and act alone as the only personal representative. A question arises about the minimum number of personal representatives required in these circumstances. The court considers the number of personal representatives needed where there is a minor beneficiary or a life interest. The estate's main asset was a house held for the family, including a young grandchild. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only a trust corporation, and never individuals, may act where there is a life interest.
At least four personal representatives are always required to administer any estate.
No personal representative is needed where a minor is a beneficiary of the estate.
A single personal representative can always act alone, whatever interests arise under the estate on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Where a minority or life interest arises, at least two personal representatives (or a trust corporation) are required.
4.w: Although a sole personal representative can generally act, where there is a minority interest or a life interest arising under a will or intestacy, at least two personal representatives (or a trust corporation) are required to give a valid receipt for capital money arising from land, to protect the beneficiaries.

n.0: Two individuals can act; a trust corporation is an alternative, not the only option.
n.1: The maximum is four PRs, but two is not always required unless such interests arise.
n.2: PRs are needed to administer the estate even where a minor benefits.
n.3: A sole PR cannot give a valid receipt for capital from land where a minority or life interest arises.

4.q: A person is buying their first home and has heard that they may qualify for a reduction in the tax normally payable by buyers, while another buyer purchasing an additional residential property (on top of one they already own) may have to pay more. The client asks how stamp duty land tax varies according to the buyer's circumstances. The solicitor considers SDLT reliefs and surcharges. The client was weighing up the true cost of the purchase once the tax was taken into account. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: First-time buyers may qualify for SDLT relief, while buyers of additional residential properties may pay a higher-rate surcharge.
Buyers of additional properties are entirely exempt from SDLT on the extra property.
SDLT reliefs and surcharges depend only on whether the property is registered or unregistered.
First-time buyers always pay double the ordinary rate of SDLT on their purchase.
SDLT is a single flat amount that is identical for every buyer regardless of their circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
4.w: SDLT varies with circumstances: first-time buyers may claim first-time buyers' relief (paying reduced or no SDLT up to certain limits), whereas a buyer purchasing an additional residential property (such as a second home or buy-to-let) may be liable to the higher-rate surcharge on top of the standard rates.

n.1: Buyers of additional properties pay more (a surcharge), not nothing.
n.2: Reliefs/surcharges turn on the buyer's circumstances, not the registration status of the land.
n.3: First-time buyers receive relief, not a doubled rate.
n.4: SDLT is not a single flat amount for everyone; rates and reliefs vary.

4.q: A defendant is charged with an offence for which a statute expressly places a specific legal burden on the defendant to establish a particular defence. The defendant accepts that this reverse burden applies but disputes the standard to which the defence must be proved. A legal burden, not merely an evidential one, rests on the defendant. The statute creating the offence expressly requires the defendant, rather than the prosecution, to establish the particular matter relied on by way of defence, and while the defendant accepts that this unusual reverse burden bites, the argument now is about how convincingly the defence must be made out. Which of the following best describes the standard the defendant must meet to discharge such a burden?
o: Absolute certainty as to the defence.
The balance of probabilities.
A prima facie evidential threshold only.
So that the tribunal is sure of the defence.
Beyond reasonable doubt, as for the prosecution.
4.w: Where a statute places a legal (persuasive) burden on the defendant to prove a defence, the defendant must discharge it only on the balance of probabilities, the civil standard. The defendant is not required to prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt; that higher standard applies to the prosecution's proof of guilt.

n.0: Absolute certainty is not required.
n.2: A legal burden requires proof on the balance of probabilities, not merely raising a prima facie evidential issue.
n.3: Being 'sure' equates to the criminal standard, which the defendant need not meet.
n.4: The defendant need not prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt.

4.q: A solicitor is instructed to act for both the borrower and the lender on the grant of a mortgage over a residential property, on the footing that their interests are aligned and only the lender's standard terms are involved. During the transaction the lender gives the solicitor certain confidential instructions which, if they were disclosed to the borrower, would seriously prejudice the borrower's position, and it becomes clear that the interests of borrower and lender have begun to diverge. The solicitor realises they can no longer act fairly for both at the same time. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's position?
o: The solicitor may continue acting for both, because acting for borrower and lender together is always permitted.
The solicitor may continue for both, provided the solicitor privately decides which client's interests to prefer.
The solicitor may pass the lender's confidential instructions to the borrower to keep both clients fully informed.
The solicitor may continue for both, because a mortgage transaction cannot as a matter of law give rise to a conflict.
A conflict has arisen, with confidentiality and disclosure duties clashing, so the solicitor must stop acting for at least one.
4.w: Acting for borrower and lender is permissible only while their interests are aligned. Once a conflict arises and the duty of confidentiality to one client cannot be reconciled with the duty of disclosure to the other, the solicitor must cease acting for at least one of them.

n.0: Acting for borrower and lender is not always permitted; it depends on their interests remaining aligned.
n.1: The solicitor cannot secretly prefer one client while purporting to act for both.
n.2: The solicitor cannot disclose one client's confidential instructions to the other.
n.3: A mortgage transaction can give rise to a conflict once interests diverge.

4.q: A testator's estate turns out to be insufficient to pay all the debts and give effect to all the gifts in the will in full. Some gifts will have to be reduced or will fail. The executors must decide the order in which the different kinds of gift (specific, general/pecuniary, and residuary) are reduced to meet the shortfall. The court considers the doctrine of abatement of gifts. The debts were heavy and there was plainly not enough to satisfy every gift in full. Which of the following best describes the general order?
o: Specific gifts abate first, before any general or residuary gifts are touched.
Gifts abate in the order in which they happen to appear in the wording of the will.
General legacies abate last, after both specific and residuary gifts have been exhausted.
Residuary gifts abate first, then general (pecuniary) legacies, and specific gifts abate last.
All gifts abate equally and proportionately at the same time, whatever their type.
4.w: Where an estate is insufficient, gifts abate to meet liabilities in a set order: the residuary gift is used first, then general (pecuniary) legacies abate rateably, and specific gifts abate last (with the subject matter of specific gifts being the most protected), subject to any contrary provision in the will.

n.0: Specific gifts abate last, not first.
n.1: Abatement follows the type of gift, not the order of appearance in the will.
n.2: General legacies abate before specific gifts, not last.
n.4: Gifts do not all abate equally at once; the order depends on their type.

4.q: A commercial contract for the supply of services contains a clause purporting to exclude the supplier's liability for loss caused by its own negligence, other than death or personal injury (for example, damage to the customer's property). A dispute arises after the supplier's carelessness damages the customer's equipment, and the customer challenges the clause. The clause is contained in the supplier's written standard terms and is relied on to exclude liability for negligently caused property damage. The contract is a business-to-business contract subject to the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977. Which of the following best describes the clause's effectiveness?
o: The clause is automatically void because negligence liability can never be excluded on these facts as a general rule.
The clause is valid because reasonableness is irrelevant to property damage claims.
The clause is valid only if the customer separately insured against the loss.
The clause is automatically valid because the parties are both businesses.
The clause is effective to exclude liability for such negligence only so far as it satisfies the requirement of reasonableness.
4.w: Under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, a term excluding liability for negligence causing loss or damage other than death or personal injury is effective only in so far as it satisfies the requirement of reasonableness. Liability for negligently caused death or personal injury cannot be excluded at all, but property damage exclusions are tested for reasonableness.

n.0: Negligence liability for loss other than death/personal injury can be excluded if reasonable, so it is not always void.
n.1: Reasonableness is precisely the applicable test for excluding negligently caused property damage.
n.2: Validity turns on reasonableness under UCTA, not on whether the customer insured separately.
n.3: The clause is not automatically valid merely because both parties are businesses; reasonableness applies.

4.q: A claimant succeeds in judicial review proceedings, persuading the court that a public authority's decision was unlawful. The claimant wants the unlawful decision to be deprived of legal effect so that the matter can be reconsidered lawfully. The court is considering the appropriate remedy. The court has accepted that the authority acted unlawfully, the claimant does not want damages but wants the tainted decision stripped of legal effect so the authority can look at the matter again and decide it properly, and the court turns to which remedy achieves that. Which of the following best describes the principal remedy that sets aside an unlawful decision in judicial review?
o: A declaration of incompatibility under the Human Rights Act.
An order for specific performance of the decision.
A quashing order, which the court grants at its discretion.
An award of exemplary damages as of right.
A binding direction that the authority reach a particular outcome.
4.w: A quashing order sets aside an unlawful decision, so that it has no legal effect and the matter can, if appropriate, be reconsidered lawfully. Judicial review remedies (quashing, prohibiting and mandatory orders, declarations, injunctions) are discretionary; the court is not bound to grant a remedy even where a ground is established.

n.0: A declaration of incompatibility relates to primary legislation under the HRA, not quashing an administrative decision.
n.1: Specific performance is a private-law contractual remedy, not a judicial review remedy.
n.3: Damages are not available as of right in judicial review and require a recognised private-law cause of action.
n.4: The court generally requires reconsideration lawfully rather than dictating the substantive outcome.

4.q: One partner in a trading firm enters into a contract with a third party which is of a kind usually made by businesses of that type, and which appears to be for carrying on the firm's business in the usual way. The third party does not know of any restriction on that partner's authority. The other partners say that they had privately agreed that no partner could make such a contract without the others' consent, and so the firm is not bound. The court considers a partner's authority to bind the firm under the Partnership Act 1890. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm is bound, because the partner had apparent authority to make a contract of that kind.
The firm is bound only if the contract turned out to be profitable for the firm.
The firm is not bound, because the partners had privately restricted that partner's authority.
The firm is bound only if the third party first checked the partnership agreement.
The firm is not bound unless all the partners signed the particular contract.
4.w: Under s.5 Partnership Act 1890, the acts of a partner carrying on in the usual way business of the kind carried on by the firm bind the firm, unless the partner had no authority and the third party knew that or did not believe them to be a partner. A private restriction unknown to the third party does not affect the firm's liability.

n.1: The firm is bound regardless of whether the contract proved profitable.
n.2: A private, undisclosed restriction does not protect the firm against a third party without notice.
n.3: A third party is not required to check the partnership agreement.
n.4: All partners need not sign; one partner's usual-business act binds the firm.

4.q: On exchange of contracts for a residential purchase, the buyer is required to pay a deposit to the seller's solicitor. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale, and the buyer asks how much the deposit will usually be and on what basis the seller's solicitor holds it pending completion. The buyer is concerned about whether the money is at risk if the transaction does not complete. The solicitor considers the usual deposit and the basis on which it is held. The buyer was funding the deposit from savings and was nervous about handing the money over. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The deposit is usually 10% of the price and is generally held by the seller's solicitor as stakeholder until completion.
The deposit is held by the buyer's own solicitor and never released to the seller's side.
No deposit is ever payable on exchange of a residential conveyancing contract.
The deposit is usually the full purchase price and is paid directly to the seller personally on these facts as a general rule.
The deposit is always 50% of the price and is spent immediately by the seller.
4.w: The deposit is customarily 10% of the purchase price, payable on exchange. Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, the seller's solicitor generally holds the deposit as stakeholder, meaning it is held on behalf of both parties and released to the seller only on completion.

n.1: The deposit is held by the seller's solicitor (as stakeholder), not retained by the buyer's solicitor.
n.2: A deposit is payable on exchange; it is not the case that none is ever payable.
n.3: The deposit is not the full price, nor paid to the seller personally in the ordinary case.
n.4: The usual deposit is 10%, not 50% spent immediately.

4.q: A party argues that a previous decision of a higher court should not be treated as binding because, in reaching it, the court overlooked a relevant statutory provision that, had it been considered, would have led to a different result. The provision was in force at the time but was not cited to the court. The later court must decide how to treat that earlier decision. The overlooked provision was directly relevant and, on any view, would have pointed the earlier court towards the opposite conclusion, and the party now before the later court argues that this omission is exactly the kind of flaw that frees a court from an otherwise binding authority. Which of the following best describes the relevant exception to precedent?
o: The earlier decision is automatically overruled by the later court's disapproval.
The earlier decision becomes binding only on courts of equal standing.
The earlier decision may be treated as per incuriam and not binding.
The earlier decision is persuasive in criminal but not civil cases.
The earlier decision remains fully binding despite the oversight.
4.w: A decision reached per incuriam, that is, in ignorance or forgetfulness of a relevant statutory provision or binding authority which would have affected the result, need not be followed. It is one of the recognised exceptions allowing a court not to be bound by what would otherwise be precedent.

n.0: Disapproval alone does not automatically overrule; per incuriam is the applicable doctrine.
n.1: Per incuriam status is not limited to courts of equal standing.
n.3: The per incuriam exception is not confined to criminal cases.
n.4: An oversight of a relevant provision can render a decision per incuriam, so it is not fully binding.

4.q: A defendant is convicted in the magistrates' court. The defendant does not dispute the facts found but contends that the magistrates misapplied the law in reaching their decision, and wishes to challenge the conviction specifically on that point of law. The challenge is on a point of law only. The defendant accepts the facts as the magistrates found them and does not want the evidence heard again, but maintains that on those very facts the law did not permit a conviction, so the challenge is confined to the legal analysis the bench applied. Which of the following best describes the appropriate route of appeal from the magistrates' court?
o: Appeal directly to the Supreme Court on the point of law.
Appeal to the Crown Court for a full rehearing of the evidence.
Application to the same magistrates to reconsider their decision.
Appeal directly to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
Appeal by way of case stated to the High Court.
4.w: Where the challenge to a magistrates' court decision is on a point of law (or that they acted in excess of jurisdiction), the appropriate route is an appeal by way of case stated to the High Court (a Divisional Court of the King's Bench Division). Appeal to the Crown Court is for a rehearing, generally on fact and/or sentence.

n.0: There is no direct appeal from the magistrates' court to the Supreme Court.
n.1: An appeal to the Crown Court is a rehearing of the evidence, not the route for a pure point of law.
n.2: Asking the same magistrates to reconsider is not an appeal route on a point of law.
n.3: Appeals do not go directly from the magistrates' court to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).

4.q: Trustees of a trust wish to hand over certain administrative and investment functions to a professional agent, because they lack the time and expertise to carry out all the day-to-day management themselves. A beneficiary objects, arguing that trustees must always act personally and can never delegate any of their functions to anyone else. The trustees seek advice on whether, and how, they may delegate functions to an agent under the modern statutory framework. The day-to-day management had become time-consuming and technically demanding for the trustees involved. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Trustees may never delegate any of their functions and must always act personally in everything.
Trustees may delegate only if all the beneficiaries consent in signed writing beforehand.
Trustees may delegate every function including the distribution of the trust, without any limit.
Trustees may delegate certain functions to an agent under the Trustee Act 2000, subject to safeguards.
Trustees may delegate only to another trustee, and never to an outside professional agent.
4.w: The Trustee Act 2000 permits trustees to delegate certain of their functions (such as investment and administration) to agents, subject to safeguards including acting within the duty of care, giving any necessary policy statement, and keeping the arrangement under review. Certain core functions cannot be delegated.

n.0: The old strict rule against delegation has been relaxed by statute.
n.1: General beneficiary consent in writing is not the statutory precondition.
n.2: Some functions (such as distribution decisions) cannot be delegated, so 'every function' is wrong.
n.4: Delegation may be to an outside agent, not only to another trustee.

4.q: A firm delivers a bill to a client that includes the firm's professional fees plus VAT charged on those fees. The client pays the bill in full. The cashier is classifying the VAT element the firm has charged on its own fees, and asks whether that VAT is client money or office money for the purposes of the SRA Accounts Rules. The VAT is output tax on the firm's own services. The bill separated out the firm's professional charges and the VAT chargeable on them, the client has now settled the whole amount, and the cashier is working through which elements of the payment are the firm's own money and which, if any, must be treated as belonging to the client. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The VAT must be paid into a separate designated client account.
The VAT belongs to the client and must be returned to them.
The VAT must be held in the client account until it is paid to HMRC.
The VAT charged on the firm's own fees is office money.
The VAT charged on the firm's own fees is client money.
4.w: VAT the firm charges on its own professional fees is part of the firm's billed charges and is office money once the bill is delivered and paid. The firm accounts for that output VAT to HMRC as part of its own tax affairs; it is not client money held for the client.

n.0: It need not go into a designated client account.
n.1: It does not belong to the client to be returned; it is part of the firm's charge.
n.2: It is office money, not client money held pending payment to HMRC.
n.4: VAT on the firm's own fees is not client money.

4.q: A seller delivers goods to a buyer under a contract of sale, the property in the goods having passed to the buyer, and the buyer simply refuses to pay the agreed price of £12,000 although the goods conform to the contract in every respect. The seller does not want to claim damages for a lost bargain; it wants to recover the actual agreed price for goods the buyer now owns. The seller seeks advice on the appropriate claim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The seller may only claim damages for its loss of profit, and never the agreed price itself.
The seller may bring an action for the price of the goods, as the property in them has passed to the buyer.
The seller may claim the price only if the contract expressly said the price was payable on delivery.
The seller must first resell the goods elsewhere before it can make any claim against the buyer.
The seller may recover nothing, because the buyer's refusal to pay is not a breach of contract.
4.w: Where goods have been sold and the property in them has passed to the buyer, and the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay, the seller may maintain an action for the price under the Sale of Goods Act 1979 (s.49), rather than being confined to a damages claim.

n.0: The seller is not limited to loss-of-profit damages; it may sue for the price where property has passed.
n.2: The action for the price arises where property has passed; it is not confined to an express payment-on-delivery term.
n.3: The seller need not resell first to claim the price where property has passed.
n.4: Refusing to pay for conforming goods is a breach on which the seller can sue.

4.q: A member of the public wishes to complain about the conduct of a solicitor and separately about the conduct of a barrister, and asks which bodies are responsible for regulating each branch of the profession. The two branches of the profession have different frontline regulators. The person wants to direct each complaint correctly. The complainant has grievances about two lawyers, one a solicitor and the other a barrister, and, understanding that the two branches of the profession answer to different frontline regulators, wants to be sure each complaint is directed to the body that actually oversees that kind of lawyer. Which of the following best describes the regulation of solicitors and barristers?
o: Solicitors are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority and barristers by the Bar Standards Board.
Neither solicitors nor barristers are subject to any professional regulation on these facts as a general rule.
Both solicitors and barristers are regulated directly by the government.
Solicitors and barristers are both regulated by the Bar Council alone.
Both solicitors and barristers are regulated solely by the Law Society.
4.w: The legal profession has separate frontline regulators: solicitors are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (the regulatory arm of the Law Society), and barristers by the Bar Standards Board (the regulatory arm of the Bar Council). Both operate under the oversight of the Legal Services Board created by the Legal Services Act 2007.

n.1: Both branches are subject to professional regulation.
n.2: The professions are regulated by independent regulators, not directly by the government.
n.3: The Bar Council (through the BSB) regulates barristers, not solicitors as well.
n.4: The Law Society's regulatory functions are exercised by the SRA, and barristers are regulated by the BSB, not the Law Society.

4.q: A worker is directly involved in a serious accident at work caused by the employer's negligence. The worker is physically in the zone of danger and reasonably fears for their own safety, and although they escape physical injury they suffer a recognised psychiatric illness as a result of the terrifying event. The worker claims damages for the psychiatric injury. The employer argues that damages for psychiatric harm are subject to the strict control mechanisms that apply to bystanders. The worker had to be helped from the scene and has been unable to return to work since the incident. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: As a primary victim in the zone of physical danger, the worker can recover if some personal injury was foreseeable.
The worker must satisfy the strict secondary-victim control mechanisms before recovering anything.
The worker can recover only if the psychiatric illness was foreseeable in a person of ordinary fortitude, judged separately from physical risk.
The worker can recover only if a close relative was also injured in the same accident.
The worker cannot recover, because damages for psychiatric injury are never available without physical injury.
4.w: A primary victim — someone within the range of foreseeable physical injury — can recover for consequent psychiatric illness provided physical injury of some kind was foreseeable; it is not necessary that the psychiatric harm itself was foreseeable (Page v Smith). The strict secondary-victim controls do not apply.

n.1: The secondary-victim control mechanisms do not apply to a primary victim.
n.2: For a primary victim, foreseeability of physical injury suffices; separate foreseeability of psychiatric harm is not required.
n.3: A primary victim need not show a close relative was injured.
n.4: Psychiatric injury can be recovered even without physical injury, especially by a primary victim.

4.q: A professional owes a duty of care to the victim, breaches that duty in a grossly negligent way, and the breach causes the victim's death. The prosecution considers gross negligence manslaughter. There was a duty, a grossly negligent breach, and a resulting death. The court must identify the further element required. The professional plainly owed the victim a duty of care and breached it in a way the prosecution says was grossly negligent, and that breach led to the victim's death, so the court must pin down the further ingredient that separates a criminal killing of this kind from ordinary civil negligence. Which of the following best completes the requirements for gross negligence manslaughter?
o: The defendant must have been reckless as to causing some property damage.
The breach must have given rise to a serious and obvious risk of death, and be so bad as to be criminal.
The defendant must have intended to kill or cause serious harm to the victim on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant must have foreseen the exact manner of the victim's death.
The breach need only give rise to a risk of some minor harm.
4.w: Under Adomako, gross negligence manslaughter requires a duty of care, a breach of that duty, causation of death, a serious and obvious risk of death at the time of breach, and that the breach was so grossly negligent as to be criminal in the jury's view. A risk of merely some harm is insufficient; the risk must be of death.

n.0: Recklessness as to property damage is irrelevant to gross negligence manslaughter.
n.2: Intention to kill or cause serious harm is the mens rea of murder, not gross negligence manslaughter.
n.3: The defendant need not foresee the precise manner of death.
n.4: A risk of minor harm is not enough; the risk must be a serious and obvious risk of death.

5.q: A firm is instructed by a new client who holds a prominent public office in an overseas government, and who is therefore a politically exposed person, and whose funds for the matter are being routed to the firm through a jurisdiction that is well known to present a high risk of money laundering. The fee-earner proposes simply to carry out the firm's standard identity checks, on the basis that exactly the same procedure is applied to every single client the firm takes on. The firm's money laundering reporting officer questions whether standard checks are really sufficient in a case like this. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm need carry out no due diligence at all, because a person holding public office is inherently trustworthy.
The firm need only carry out its standard due diligence, because the same checks apply to every client alike.
The firm must carry out enhanced due diligence, because this situation presents a higher risk of money laundering.
The firm may carry out reduced due diligence, because a public official's identity is a matter of public record.
The firm may proceed without further checks, provided the client signs a declaration about the source of the funds.
5.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require enhanced due diligence in higher-risk situations, including where the client is a politically exposed person or funds involve a high-risk jurisdiction. Standard checks are not sufficient in such cases.

n.0: Holding public office is a risk factor for enhanced checks, not a reason to omit them.
n.1: Higher-risk situations require more than the standard level of due diligence.
n.3: Being a public figure does not justify reduced due diligence; the opposite applies.
n.4: A client declaration does not replace the required enhanced due diligence.

5.q: A private company limited by shares wishes to reduce its share capital to return surplus capital to shareholders. The directors ask about a procedure available to a private company that does not require a court order. The company is a private company and its directors are willing to make a statement about its solvency. The company seeks the simplest lawful route. The company is sitting on surplus capital it would like to hand back to shareholders, it is a private company whose directors are willing to vouch formally for its solvency, and it is looking for the most straightforward lawful way to reduce its capital without going to court. Which of the following best describes the available procedure?
o: A special resolution confirmed by the court in every case.
The unanimous written consent of all the company's creditors.
A special resolution supported by a solvency statement from the directors.
