An ordinary resolution alone, with no solvency statement required.
A board resolution alone, without any member involvement.
5.w: A private company limited by shares may reduce its capital by special resolution supported by a solvency statement made by the directors (Companies Act 2006, ss.641-644), without needing court confirmation. The solvency statement must be made within a short period before the resolution and filed at Companies House. Public companies must use the court route.

n.0: Court confirmation is required for public companies, but the private-company route avoids it via the solvency statement.
n.1: Creditor consent is not the mechanism; a directors' solvency statement supports the resolution.
n.3: An ordinary resolution is insufficient; a special resolution plus solvency statement is needed.
n.4: A board resolution alone cannot reduce capital.

5.q: A decision-maker reaches a decision that adversely affects an individual without giving that individual any opportunity to make representations, and where one of the decision-makers had a personal interest in the outcome. The individual seeks judicial review, complaining about the way the decision was reached rather than its substance. The complaint concerns the fairness of the process. The individual was given no chance to put their side before the decision was taken, and it later emerged that one of those deciding stood to gain personally from the result, so the challenge is directed not at the wisdom of the outcome but at the manner in which the decision was arrived at. Which of the following best identifies the ground of judicial review relied on?
o: Error of fact going to jurisdiction.
Proportionality of the resulting interference.
Irrationality in the outcome of the decision.
Illegality through misdirection as to the law.
Procedural impropriety.
5.w: Procedural impropriety covers failure to observe procedural rules and breaches of the rules of natural justice, including the right to a fair hearing (the opportunity to make representations) and the rule against bias (no personal interest in the outcome). The complaint here is squarely about the fairness of the process.

n.0: Error of fact going to jurisdiction is a distinct, narrower ground.
n.1: Proportionality assesses whether an interference is excessive, not procedural fairness.
n.2: Irrationality attacks the substance of a decision, not the fairness of the procedure.
n.3: Illegality concerns legal error or exceeding powers, not a want of fair process.

5.q: A person who believes they are dying makes a gift of an asset to another, in contemplation of their imminent death, and hands over the asset (or the means of control of it) on the condition that the gift is to take effect only if they die. They then die of the contemplated cause. The recipient claims the asset as a valid gift, although it was not left to them by will. The court considers the doctrine of donatio mortis causa (deathbed gift). The donor, gravely ill in hospital, handed over the keys and documents to the recipient. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A deathbed gift is valid only if the donor in fact recovers from their illness.
A deathbed gift takes effect immediately and unconditionally when the words are spoken on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A valid deathbed gift may take effect where it was made in contemplation of imminent death, conditional on death, with delivery of the subject matter.
A deathbed gift is valid only where it is witnessed by two independent witnesses.
A deathbed gift is never valid unless it is also set out in a properly executed will.
5.w: A donatio mortis causa is a valid gift made in contemplation of the donor's impending death, conditional upon death (so it is revocable if the donor recovers), and completed by delivery of the subject matter or the means of controlling it, taking effect on death outside the will.

n.0: The gift takes effect on death; if the donor recovers, it is revoked.
n.1: The gift is conditional on death, not immediate and unconditional.
n.3: Two witnesses are not required for a donatio mortis causa.
n.4: A donatio mortis causa does not require a will; that is its point.

5.q: A person facing a decision by a public tribunal that could deprive them of an important interest complains that they were given no proper opportunity to present their case and that the tribunal was not impartial. They wish to rely on a Convention right guaranteeing a fair hearing. The complaint concerns the fairness and impartiality of the determination of the person's civil rights. A Convention right is engaged. The individual stands to lose something important through a tribunal's determination of their civil rights, yet complains they were shut out of properly putting their case and that those deciding were not impartial, which brings into play the Convention guarantee concerned with the fairness of such hearings. Which of the following best identifies the relevant Convention right?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair trial (a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal).
Article 10, the right to freedom of expression.
Article 1 of the First Protocol, the protection of property.
Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life.
Article 3, the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment on these facts as a general rule.
5.w: Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights guarantees the right to a fair trial: in the determination of civil rights and obligations or a criminal charge, everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The complaint about a fair hearing and impartiality engages Article 6.

n.1: Article 10 concerns freedom of expression.
n.2: Article 1 of the First Protocol concerns peaceful enjoyment of possessions.
n.3: Article 8 concerns private and family life, not the fairness of a hearing.
n.4: Article 3 concerns torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, not fair hearings.

5.q: A testator made a valid will leaving their estate to various beneficiaries. Some time later the testator marries. The will was not expressed to be made in contemplation of that marriage. After the testator's death, the beneficiaries under the will and the new spouse dispute whether the will still stands. The court considers the effect of marriage on an existing will under the Wills Act 1837. The testator had married a new partner some years after first making the will. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The testator's marriage revokes the earlier will, unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage.
Marriage has no effect at all on a will made before the marriage.
Marriage suspends the will temporarily but it revives automatically on any later divorce.
Marriage revokes only the gifts to persons other than the new spouse, leaving the rest intact.
Marriage revokes the will only if the testator has children with the new spouse.
5.w: Under s.18 Wills Act 1837, a will is revoked by the testator's subsequent marriage (or civil partnership), unless it appears the will was made in expectation (contemplation) of that particular marriage and the testator intended it not to be revoked.

n.1: Marriage does have an effect: it generally revokes the earlier will.
n.2: Marriage revokes the will; it does not merely suspend it pending a divorce.
n.3: Marriage revokes the whole will, not only gifts to others.
n.4: Revocation by marriage does not depend on there being children.

5.q: A commentator observes that, in the UK constitution, law-making, the administration of government, and the resolution of legal disputes are carried out by broadly distinct institutions — Parliament, the executive, and the judiciary — with various checks between them, although the separation is not complete. A solicitor is asked to explain the constitutional principle this describes. The solicitor considers the separation of powers. The commentator was trying to make sense of how power is shared between the branches of the state. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The separation of powers means Parliament decides the outcome of individual court cases.
The separation of powers is a rule that the monarch personally exercises all three functions.
The separation of powers requires the judiciary to be controlled directly by the government of the day.
The separation of powers means that a single institution exercises all governmental functions together on these facts as a general rule.
The separation of powers distributes functions between the legislature, the executive and the judiciary, with checks and balances between them.
5.w: The separation of powers refers to the distribution of governmental functions between the legislature (which makes law), the executive (which implements it), and the judiciary (which resolves disputes and interprets the law), with checks and balances between them, although in the UK the separation is partial rather than absolute.

n.0: Parliament does not decide individual court cases; that is for the judiciary.
n.1: The monarch does not personally exercise all three functions.
n.2: Judicial independence from government is a key aspect, not government control of the judiciary.
n.3: Separation of powers means functions are distributed, not concentrated in one body.

5.q: A commercial landlord is granting a lease of commercial premises and is considering the VAT position, in particular whether VAT will be charged on the rent and on any premium. The default position for most supplies of interests in land is that they are exempt from VAT, but there is a mechanism by which the landlord can choose to charge VAT. The landlord asks about VAT on the commercial property. The solicitor considers the option to tax for VAT purposes. The landlord wanted to be able to recover the VAT it incurred on refurbishing the premises. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only residential property can ever be subject to an option to tax.
VAT is always charged at the standard rate on every supply of land, with no exemption on these facts as a general rule.
Supplies of land are generally exempt from VAT, but the owner may 'opt to tax', making its supplies standard-rated.
VAT on land is charged only where the buyer is an individual rather than a business.
Land can never be subject to VAT under any circumstances at all.
5.w: Most supplies of interests in land are exempt from VAT by default. However, the owner of commercial property can elect to 'opt to tax' (waive the exemption), which makes its supplies of that property standard-rated for VAT, allowing it to recover related input VAT. Residential property largely remains exempt.

n.0: The option to tax applies to commercial, not residential, property.
n.1: Land supplies are generally exempt by default, not always standard-rated.
n.3: The VAT position turns on the option to tax, not on whether the buyer is an individual.
n.4: Land can be subject to VAT, for example following an option to tax.

5.q: A company agrees to carry out work for a customer at an agreed price. After the contract is made, the company finds that, because of unexpected increases in the cost of materials and labour, performing the work will be far more expensive and much less profitable than it had anticipated, though the work remains entirely possible to carry out. The company argues that the contract has been frustrated by these changed economic circumstances and that it is released from its obligations. The customer disputes this. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is not frustrated; performance is merely more expensive, not radically different.
The contract is frustrated, provided the company can show the loss it will suffer is substantial.
The contract is frustrated, because performing it is now significantly less profitable than expected.
The contract is frustrated, because the company did not foresee the increase when it contracted.
The contract is frustrated, because any unexpected rise in costs discharges a contract.
5.w: Frustration requires performance to become impossible, illegal or radically different from what was undertaken. Mere increased cost, hardship or reduced profitability does not frustrate a contract (Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC), so the company remains bound.

n.1: The size of the loss does not turn mere expense into frustration.
n.2: Reduced profitability alone does not amount to frustration.
n.3: Failure to foresee a cost increase does not, by itself, frustrate the contract.
n.4: An unexpected rise in costs does not discharge a contract that remains possible to perform.

5.q: A statute is drafted in general words which, read literally, could be taken to authorise an interference with a fundamental common-law right, such as access to the courts, without expressly saying so. A court is asked to interpret the statute. A solicitor is asked about the interpretive presumption the courts apply where fundamental rights are at stake. The solicitor considers the principle of legality in statutory interpretation. The words were wide enough, on their face, to strip the person of access to the courts. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Under the principle of legality, fundamental rights are presumed not to be overridden by general words; clear express language is required.
The principle of legality means the courts must ignore fundamental rights when reading statutes on these facts as a general rule.
The courts will interpret any ambiguous statute so as to remove as many rights as possible.
General words in a statute are always read as overriding any fundamental right.
Fundamental rights can be overridden only by a decision of a government minister.
5.w: Under the principle of legality, the courts presume that Parliament does not intend to interfere with fundamental common-law rights (such as access to justice) by general or ambiguous words. Such rights can be overridden only by clear and express statutory language, so the courts read general words restrictively to protect those rights (R v Home Secretary, ex p Simms).

n.1: The principle of legality protects, rather than ignores, fundamental rights.
n.2: The courts protect rights on interpretation; they do not maximise their removal.
n.3: General words are not read as overriding fundamental rights; express words are needed.
n.4: Fundamental rights are overridden by clear statute, not a minister's decision.

5.q: A case involving an indictable offence has been sent to the Crown Court. Before trial, the court holds a hearing at which the defendant enters a plea and, if not guilty, directions are given to prepare the case for trial, including on issues, witnesses and timetabling. This is the first hearing in the Crown Court following the sending. The court manages the progress of the case. The indictable case has been sent up from the magistrates, and the Crown Court now lists the first hearing at which the defendant will be arraigned and, if the plea is not guilty, the judge will set the case on course for trial with directions on issues, witnesses and timetable. Which of the following best identifies this hearing?
o: A plea and trial preparation hearing (PTPH).
A voir dire to determine the admissibility of evidence.
An allocation hearing to decide the mode of trial.
A Newton hearing to resolve a factual dispute for sentence.
A committal for sentence hearing.
5.w: In the Crown Court, the first hearing after a case is sent is generally the plea and trial preparation hearing (PTPH), at which the defendant is arraigned (enters a plea) and, if a not guilty plea is entered, the judge gives case management directions to prepare the matter for trial.

n.1: A voir dire is a trial within a trial on admissibility, not the initial preparation hearing.
n.2: Allocation (mode of trial) occurs in the magistrates' court, not as the Crown Court's PTPH.
n.3: A Newton hearing resolves a factual dispute relevant to sentence after a guilty plea, not this preparatory hearing.
n.4: Committal for sentence is a separate process from the magistrates, not the Crown Court's PTPH.

5.q: A party needs a witness to attend trial to give evidence, but the witness is unwilling to attend voluntarily. The party wishes to compel the witness's attendance, and possibly the production of documents by that witness. The court considers the means of compelling a reluctant witness to attend and give evidence at trial. The witness had refused every request to attend court voluntarily to give their evidence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is no way to compel a reluctant witness; only willing witnesses can ever give evidence on these facts.
The party must simply ask the other side to persuade the witness to attend voluntarily.
The party may obtain a witness summons requiring the witness to attend court to give evidence or produce documents.
The party may compel attendance only by paying the witness a fee fixed by the other side.
A witness can be compelled to attend only in criminal, and never in civil, proceedings.
5.w: A party may obtain a witness summons requiring a person to attend court to give evidence and/or to produce documents. Failure to comply with a validly served witness summons can amount to a contempt of court.

n.0: Reluctant witnesses can be compelled by a witness summons.
n.1: Persuasion by the other side is not the mechanism; a summons is.
n.3: Compulsion is by summons, not by a fee set by the opposing party.
n.4: Witness summonses are available in civil proceedings.

5.q: A will leaves a legacy to a beneficiary. The will is witnessed by two people, one of whom is the spouse (married partner) of that beneficiary. The remainder of the will is validly executed. The gift is to a beneficiary whose spouse acted as one of the two witnesses. The validity of the gift, rather than of the will, is in question. The will was properly drawn up and attested by two people, but one of those two witnesses happens to be married to the very person to whom the will leaves a legacy, which puts in doubt not the validity of the will as a whole but whether that particular beneficiary may keep the gift. Which of the following best describes the effect on the gift?
o: The gift is reduced by half rather than failing entirely.
The gift to the beneficiary fails, because a gift to the spouse of an attesting witness is void.
The whole will is invalid because a beneficiary's spouse witnessed it.
The gift is valid, because the rule only affects a witness who is personally the beneficiary.
The gift is valid, because the will had a second, independent witness.
5.w: Under s.15 of the Wills Act 1837, a gift to an attesting witness, or to the spouse or civil partner of an attesting witness, is void, although the will itself remains validly executed and the witness's attestation is still effective. So the gift to this beneficiary (whose spouse witnessed the will) fails, but the will stands.

n.0: The gift fails entirely; it is not merely halved.
n.2: The will itself is not invalidated; only the gift fails.
n.3: The rule extends to the spouse or civil partner of a witness, not only the witness personally.
n.4: The presence of another witness does not save the gift under s.15.

5.q: A solicitor gives another party's solicitor a professional undertaking, in the course of a transaction, to send certain title documents once the transaction has completed. The undertaking as given does not specify any particular date, or any period, within which the documents are to be provided. After completion, the solicitor then takes no steps at all for a long period to fulfil the undertaking, taking the convenient view that, because no deadline was ever written down, there is no time by which they are actually obliged to perform it. The recipient eventually complains about the delay. The solicitor considers their obligation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Because no time was specified, the solicitor is under no obligation to perform the undertaking at any particular point.
The solicitor may choose any timescale they like, however long, since none was written into the undertaking.
The undertaking lapses automatically if it is not performed immediately upon completion of the transaction.
Where no time is specified, the undertaking must still be performed within a reasonable time.
The undertaking need only be performed if and when the recipient formally demands performance of it.
5.w: An undertaking is binding according to its terms, and where it does not specify a time for performance, the law implies that it must be carried out within a reasonable time. The absence of a stated deadline does not mean there is no obligation to perform.

n.0: The absence of a stated time does not remove the obligation; a reasonable time is implied.
n.1: The solicitor cannot take an unlimited time; performance must be within a reasonable period.
n.2: An undertaking does not lapse merely because it is not performed the instant the transaction completes.
n.4: Performance is not contingent on a formal demand by the recipient.

5.q: The members of a solvent company decide voluntarily to bring the company to an end and wind it up, and the directors are able to make a statutory declaration of solvency. In a different scenario, an insolvent company is wound up voluntarily with the creditors taking control of the process. A businessperson wants to understand the difference between the two kinds of voluntary liquidation. The court considers members' and creditors' voluntary liquidation under the Insolvency Act 1986. In one case the directors could confirm the company could pay its debts in full within twelve months. Which of the following best describes the distinction?
o: A members' voluntary liquidation is for a solvent company with a declaration of solvency; a creditors' voluntary liquidation is for an insolvent one.
There is no difference; both types are used only for insolvent companies.
A members' voluntary liquidation is used only for insolvent companies with no assets on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Both types can only ever be commenced by a petition presented by a creditor.
A creditors' voluntary liquidation requires an order of the court in every case.
5.w: A members' voluntary liquidation is available where the company is solvent and the directors make a statutory declaration of solvency; a creditors' voluntary liquidation applies where the company is insolvent, so the creditors have the principal say in the conduct of the liquidation.

n.1: There is a clear difference based on solvency.
n.2: A members' voluntary liquidation is for solvent, not insolvent, companies.
n.3: Voluntary liquidations are commenced by resolution, not a creditor's petition.
n.4: A creditors' voluntary liquidation does not require a court order (unlike compulsory winding up).

5.q: A settlor creates a discretionary trust under which trustees have discretion to distribute a fund among a wide class described as the settlor's 'relatives and dependants'. No beneficiary is entitled to any share unless and until the trustees exercise their discretion in their favour. A question arises as to the test for certainty of objects that applies to this discretionary trust, and whether the class is sufficiently certain for the trust to be valid. The class was potentially very large, and the trustees wanted to know whether they could validly administer it. Which of the following best describes the applicable test?
o: The trust is valid only if the trustees distribute equally among every member of the class.
The trust is valid only if the class contains no more than a fixed maximum number of people on these facts.
The trust is valid if it can be said with certainty whether any given person is or is not a member of the class.
The trust is valid only if a complete list of every possible beneficiary can be compiled.
The trust is valid only if all the beneficiaries can be personally identified in advance.
5.w: For a discretionary trust, certainty of objects is governed by the 'is or is not' (given postulant) test: the trust is valid if it can be said with certainty whether any given individual is or is not a member of the class (McPhail v Doulton). A complete list is not required.

n.0: Equal distribution is not required; the trustees have a discretion.
n.1: There is no fixed numerical cap on the size of the class.
n.3: The complete-list test applies to fixed trusts, not discretionary trusts.
n.4: Advance identification of all beneficiaries is not required for a discretionary trust.

5.q: A defendant, with a view to gain for themselves or intending to cause loss to another, makes an unwarranted demand of the victim, reinforcing the demand with menaces — for example threatening to reveal damaging information unless the victim pays money. The demand is not one the defendant reasonably believes they have proper grounds to make in that way. The defendant is charged under the Theft Act 1968. The court considers the offence of blackmail. The defendant threatened to expose an embarrassing secret unless the victim paid over a large sum of money. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Blackmail requires the victim to have actually paid the money that was demanded.
Blackmail requires the defendant to have used physical violence against the victim.
Blackmail is committed only where the information threatened to be revealed was false on these facts.
Blackmail is committed by any demand for money, whether or not menaces were used.
Blackmail is making an unwarranted demand with menaces, with a view to gain or intent to cause loss.
5.w: Under s.21 Theft Act 1968, blackmail is committed where a person, with a view to gain for themselves or another or with intent to cause loss to another, makes an unwarranted demand with menaces. A demand is unwarranted unless the defendant believes they have reasonable grounds for it and that the use of the menaces is a proper means of reinforcing it.

n.0: The offence is complete on the demand; the victim need not have paid.
n.1: Physical violence is not required; menaces suffice.
n.2: The truth or falsity of the information threatened is not the test.
n.3: Menaces are essential; a bare demand is not blackmail.

5.q: A buyer intends to rely on the physical condition of the property when deciding whether to proceed and at what price. The buyer's solicitor advises the buyer about protecting themselves against the risk of hidden physical problems with the building. The property is an older house. The solicitor considers the buyer's protection regarding the physical state of the property. The house was over a hundred years old and the buyer had not yet had it inspected. Which of the following best describes the appropriate advice?
o: The buyer may rely entirely on the seller's estate agent's description of the property's condition on these facts.
The buyer need not obtain any survey, because the seller guarantees the condition of the property.
The buyer is fully protected by the local land charges search against physical defects.
The buyer should obtain an appropriate survey of the property, as the seller is not obliged to disclose physical defects.
The buyer's solicitor's investigation of title will reveal all physical defects in the building.
5.w: Because caveat emptor applies to the physical condition of the property, the buyer should commission an appropriate survey (its level depending on the property's age and type) to identify physical defects. The seller is not obliged to volunteer them, and title investigation and searches do not reveal building condition.

n.0: The estate agent's description is not a reliable substitute for a survey.
n.1: The seller does not guarantee the property's condition.
n.2: The local land charges search does not reveal physical defects.
n.4: Investigation of title concerns ownership and burdens, not the physical state of the building.

5.q: A defendant commits an offence after their drink was secretly spiked by someone else, so that they became intoxicated without knowing it and against their will. As a result of this involuntary intoxication they did not form the mens rea for the offence. The defendant relies on the involuntary nature of the intoxication. The court considers the effect of involuntary intoxication on criminal liability. Someone had secretly added a strong drug to the defendant's soft drink earlier that evening. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Involuntary intoxication may be a defence if, because of it, the defendant did not form the required mens rea.
Involuntary intoxication is treated in exactly the same way as voluntary intoxication.
Involuntary intoxication is never a defence, because the defendant still committed the act.
Involuntary intoxication is a defence only to offences of basic intent, and never specific intent on these facts.
Involuntary intoxication is a complete defence even where the defendant did form the mens rea.
5.w: Involuntary intoxication (for example a spiked drink) may be a defence where, because of it, the defendant did not form the mens rea of the offence. However, if the defendant did form the necessary mens rea despite the intoxication, the involuntary intoxication provides no defence (R v Kingston).

n.1: Involuntary intoxication is treated more favourably than voluntary intoxication.
n.2: It can be a defence where mens rea was not formed, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: It is not limited to basic intent offences in the way voluntary intoxication is.
n.4: If the mens rea was formed, intoxication (even involuntary) is no defence.

5.q: A property is subject to a first registered charge in favour of Bank A and a later, second, registered charge in favour of Bank B. Bank A's charge secures an initial loan and, by its express terms, also secures any further advances that Bank A may later choose to make to the same borrower. Bank A now wishes to make a further advance to the borrower and to have that further advance rank ahead of Bank B's second charge in order of priority. Bank A seeks advice on whether, and in what circumstances, it can achieve priority for the further advance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Bank B's charge is void, because a property can carry only one registered charge at a time.
Bank A always ranks first for all sums, regardless of when advances were made or notice received.
The two charges rank equally and share the proceeds of sale rateably in all cases.
Bank B always ranks first for everything it is owed, because its own charge was registered before Bank A made the further advance.
Bank A's further advance may still rank ahead of Bank B where the tacking rules under the LRA 2002 are satisfied.
5.w: Priority of registered charges generally follows the order of registration, but a prior chargee may 'tack' further advances so they rank with its original charge in defined circumstances under s.49 LRA 2002 (for example where it had no notice of the subsequent charge, or was obliged to make the advance).

n.0: A property can carry more than one registered charge; the later charge is not void.
n.1: The first chargee does not automatically rank first for further advances in all cases; tacking is subject to conditions.
n.2: Registered charges do not simply share rateably; they rank by priority.
n.3: A prior chargee can, within the tacking rules, gain priority for a further advance over an intervening charge.

5.q: A party failed to include an important document in its disclosure list and did not permit inspection of it, whether through oversight or otherwise. At trial that party now wishes to rely on the document to support its case. The other party objects that the document was never disclosed. The court considers the consequence of failing to disclose a document under the Civil Procedure Rules. The document had simply been overlooked when the party prepared and served its disclosure list. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A party may always rely on any document at trial, whether or not it was ever disclosed on these facts as a general rule.
The document is automatically admitted, and the other party must simply deal with it.
A party may not rely at trial on a document it failed to disclose or allow inspection of, without the court's permission.
The party may rely on the undisclosed document only if it helps the other side's case.
Failure to disclose a document has no consequence of any kind at trial.
5.w: Under the CPR, a party may not rely on any document which it failed to disclose or in respect of which it failed to permit inspection, unless the court gives permission. This encourages proper compliance with disclosure obligations.

n.0: Undisclosed documents cannot be relied on as of right; permission is needed.
n.1: An undisclosed document is not automatically admitted for the defaulting party.
n.3: The restriction is not limited by whether the document helps the other side.
n.4: Non-disclosure does have consequences for the ability to rely on the document.

5.q: Owing to an error made by the Land Registry when titles in the area were first registered, a strip of land that in fact belongs to Mr Vaughan's registered title was mistakenly included within the registered title of his neighbour, Ms Ward. Relying on her title, Ms Ward has since fenced the strip into her garden and treated it as her own. Mr Vaughan has now discovered the mistake and wishes both to have the register corrected so that the strip is shown as his, and to be compensated for any loss he has suffered as a result. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The true owner must claim in the tort of deceit against the Land Registry for the error.
The register may be altered to correct the mistake. on the facts of this case
The true owner's only remedy is to buy the strip back from the neighbour at market value.
The neighbour keeps the strip automatically, because the register is conclusive as to ownership.
The register can never be altered once a title has been registered, whatever the mistake.
5.w: The register can be altered to correct a mistake (rectification where it prejudices a registered proprietor in possession). Where a person suffers loss by reason of a mistake in the register or its rectification, a statutory indemnity may be payable under the LRA 2002.

n.0: The route is statutory alteration plus indemnity, not a deceit claim against the registry.
n.2: The remedy is correction of the register, not a forced purchase by the true owner.
n.3: Registration is not indefeasible against a mistake; the register can be rectified.
n.4: The register is not immutable; the LRA 2002 provides for alteration and rectification of mistakes.

5.q: A person attends a police station voluntarily to help with an investigation, having not been arrested. They are asked questions and become concerned about their status and whether they are free to leave. The person's solicitor advises them about the position of a voluntary attender at the police station. The solicitor considers the rights of a person attending the police station voluntarily. The person had come in of their own accord and was growing uneasy about whether they could go. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A voluntary attender may never leave once questioning has begun.
A voluntary attender need not be cautioned before being questioned about an offence.
A voluntary attender has no right to legal advice because they have not been arrested.
A voluntary attender is automatically detained and loses all rights on entering the police station on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A voluntary attender is free to leave at any time unless arrested, and is still entitled to free legal advice and to be cautioned before questioning about an offence.
5.w: A person who attends the police station voluntarily and has not been arrested is free to leave at will unless and until they are arrested. They remain entitled to free and independent legal advice, and must be cautioned before being questioned about an offence.

n.0: A voluntary attender may leave unless arrested.
n.1: A caution is still required before questioning about an offence.
n.2: A voluntary attender is entitled to free legal advice.
n.3: A voluntary attender is not automatically detained on entering.

5.q: Shortly before its insolvent liquidation, a company made a payment to one particular unsecured creditor which had the effect of putting that creditor in a better position, in the insolvency, than they would otherwise have been, and the company was influenced by a desire to produce that effect. The liquidator wishes to challenge the payment. The court considers the power to set aside a preference under the Insolvency Act 1986. The favoured creditor was a company connected to one of the directors of the failing business. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The liquidator may challenge the payment only if it was made after the winding up order.
A preference can be challenged only where it was made to a secured rather than unsecured creditor on these facts as a general rule.
Any payment to a creditor before liquidation is automatically valid and cannot be challenged.
The liquidator may challenge the payment as a preference where the company was influenced by a desire to prefer the creditor.
The liquidator may challenge the payment only if the creditor knew the company was insolvent.
5.w: Under s.239 Insolvency Act 1986, a liquidator or administrator may apply to set aside a preference — where, within the relevant time before insolvency, the company did something that put a creditor in a better position on insolvency and was influenced by a desire to produce that effect (desire being presumed for connected persons).

n.0: The relevant conduct occurs before, not after, the winding up order.
n.1: Preferences can be challenged whether the creditor was secured or unsecured.
n.2: Pre-liquidation payments are not automatically immune from challenge.
n.4: The test focuses on the company's desire to prefer, not the creditor's knowledge.

5.q: A worker develops a lung condition caused by inhaling dust at work. Some of the dust exposure was due to the employer's negligence (the 'guilty' dust) and some was innocent exposure that could not have been avoided. Medical evidence shows the disease was caused by the cumulative effect of all the dust, and that the guilty dust made a material contribution to the total. The condition is a 'divisible' one, worsened cumulatively by the total dust inhaled. Over the years the worker breathed in dust from the factory air, some of it the product of the employer's failure to provide proper extraction and some of it exposure that no reasonable precaution could have prevented, and the medical evidence links the disease to the combined burden of all the dust inhaled. Which of the following best describes the basis on which the employer may be liable?
o: The employer's liability depends solely on the 'but for' test being satisfied on the balance of probabilities.
The employer escapes liability because the innocent dust also contributed to the harm.
The employer is liable because the guilty dust made a material contribution to the cumulative harm.
The employer is liable in full only if the guilty dust alone would have caused the disease.
The employer is liable only if it can be shown which single particle of dust caused the disease.
5.w: Where a condition results from the cumulative effect of tortious and non-tortious exposure and the tortious exposure made a material (more than negligible) contribution to the harm, the defendant is liable (Bonnington Castings). The claimant need not prove that the guilty exposure alone would have caused the disease, nor satisfy a strict 'but for' test in these cumulative-cause cases.

n.0: In cumulative-cause cases material contribution, not strict 'but for', is the applicable test.
n.1: The presence of innocent exposure does not defeat liability where guilty exposure materially contributed.
n.3: It is enough that the guilty dust materially contributed; it need not alone have caused the disease.
n.4: The claimant need not identify the precise particle responsible.

5.q: A patient attends a doctor with symptoms, and the doctor negligently fails to diagnose a serious illness. By the time the illness is correctly diagnosed, the patient's chance of a successful recovery has fallen, but even with prompt correct diagnosis the patient would, on the balance of probabilities, more likely than not have suffered the same poor outcome anyway. The patient claims damages for the reduced chance of recovery caused by the delay. The doctor argues that causation is not made out on the ordinary balance of probabilities. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim succeeds, because the doctor's negligence undoubtedly worsened the patient's position.
The claim fails only if the patient made a full recovery despite the delay in diagnosis.
The claim is likely to fail, because loss of a less-than-even chance of recovery is generally not recoverable.
The claim succeeds automatically, because the doctor admitted failing to diagnose the illness.
The claim succeeds, because any reduction in the chance of recovery is always compensable in full on these facts.
5.w: In clinical negligence, the claimant must generally prove on the balance of probabilities that the negligence caused the adverse outcome. Where the lost chance of recovery was less than even, the courts have generally refused to allow recovery for the reduced chance itself (Gregg v Scott).

n.0: Worsening the position is not enough without proving causation on the balance of probabilities.
n.1: The difficulty is the standard of proof of causation, not whether the patient recovered.
n.3: An admission of failure to diagnose does not establish causation of the outcome.
n.4: A reduction in a less-than-even chance is not generally compensable, so recovery is not automatic.

5.q: A company was formed by two people on the basis of mutual trust to run a business together as quasi-partners, both participating in management. One has now been excluded from all management by the other, and although the company is solvent, the relationship of trust and confidence underlying it has irretrievably broken down. The excluded member wants the company brought to an end. The company is solvent but the basis on which it was formed has collapsed. The two set the company up as equals, each expecting to have a hand in running it, but one has now shut the other out of management entirely, and although the business is perfectly solvent the personal trust the venture depended on has completely collapsed. Which of the following best describes the remedy available?
o: A claim for wrongful trading against the controlling member.
A petition to wind up the company on the just and equitable ground under section 122(1)(g).
A derivative claim on behalf of the company against the excluded member.
An application to have the company administratively dissolved by the Registrar.
A petition to wind up the company on the ground that it is unable to pay its debts.
5.w: Where a solvent company was formed as a quasi-partnership on a basis of mutual trust and participation, and that relationship has broken down (for example by exclusion from management), a member may petition to wind up the company on the just and equitable ground under s.122(1)(g) of the Insolvency Act 1986.

n.0: Wrongful trading concerns insolvent trading, not this quasi-partnership breakdown.
n.2: A derivative claim enforces the company's cause of action, not the exclusion complaint.
n.3: Administrative dissolution by the Registrar does not address the members' dispute.
n.4: Inability to pay debts is not the ground here; the company is solvent.

5.q: On completion of a sale, the contract for sale and the transfer deed contain overlapping provisions, and a question arises about whether the buyer can still rely on the terms of the contract after completion, or whether those terms are subsumed into the transfer. Some contractual obligations were intended to continue after completion. The buyer asks about the effect of completion on the contract terms. The solicitor considers the doctrine of merger on completion. Some obligations in the contract had been intended to carry on being enforceable after completion. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Contract terms generally merge in the transfer on completion, except those the parties intend to survive completion.
The contract is automatically rescinded on completion, extinguishing every obligation.
The transfer deed has no effect, and only the contract governs the parties after completion on these facts.
All contract terms always survive completion in full and can be relied on indefinitely.
Completion has no effect at all on the enforceability of the contract terms.
5.w: Under the doctrine of merger, on completion the terms of the contract generally merge in the transfer deed, so that the buyer's rights derive from the transfer. However, contractual obligations not covered by the transfer, and terms expressed to survive completion (non-merger provisions), continue to be enforceable.

n.1: Completion does not automatically rescind the contract; merger applies to its terms.
n.2: The transfer deed is effective; it is what conveys the estate.
n.3: Not all contract terms survive; many merge in the transfer.
n.4: Completion does affect the contract terms through merger.

5.q: A suspect is detained at a police station and wants a family member to be told where they are, being anxious that relatives will not know what has happened to them. The suspect asks the custody officer whether they have any right to have someone informed of their arrest and detention. The solicitor considers the right to have someone informed under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The suspect had young children at home and was desperate for their family to know where they were. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The suspect may have someone informed only if they pay a fee for the call on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The suspect has a right to have someone told of their arrest, though it may be delayed for serious offences.
The suspect has no right to have anyone informed of their arrest at all.
The suspect may only have someone informed after they have been charged.
The police must contact the suspect's employer, but never a family member.
5.w: Under s.56 PACE 1984, a detained person has the right, if they request it, to have one friend, relative or other person told of their arrest and where they are being held. This right may be delayed (not denied) for up to 36 hours in limited circumstances where an indictable offence is involved and authorised by a senior officer.

n.0: No fee is required to exercise the right.
n.2: There is a right to have someone informed.
n.3: The right arises on detention, not only after charge.
n.4: The suspect chooses who is informed; it is not the employer only.

5.q: A solicitor is defending a client on a criminal charge that is due to go to trial. In a private conference the client admits to the solicitor that they did in fact commit the offence, but instructs the solicitor that they nonetheless wish to plead not guilty and to require the prosecution to prove its case against them at trial. The client does not ask the solicitor to put forward any positive account of innocence, but simply to hold the prosecution to proof. The solicitor considers carefully what they may and may not properly do at the trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may continue only if the client agrees to plead guilty to the offence charged.
The solicitor may put the prosecution to proof, but must not advance a positive case of innocence known to be false.
The solicitor must disclose the client's admission of guilt to the court before the trial begins.
The solicitor must refuse to act at all, because a client who has admitted guilt cannot plead not guilty.
The solicitor may run any defence the client wishes, including asserting facts the solicitor knows to be untrue.
5.w: A defendant who admits guilt to their solicitor may still require the prosecution to prove its case, and the solicitor may test and challenge the prosecution evidence. The solicitor must not, however, assert a positive case they know to be false or call the client to give evidence of innocence.

n.0: The client is entitled to require proof, so continuing does not depend on a guilty plea.
n.2: The solicitor must not disclose the client's privileged admission to the court.
n.3: An admission to the solicitor does not prevent a not-guilty plea putting the prosecution to proof.
n.4: The solicitor may not advance facts they know to be untrue, whatever the client wishes.

5.q: A house is held by two trustees, Mr Price and Mrs Quinn, on trust for several adult beneficiaries in defined shares. One of those beneficiaries lives in the house and has a beneficial interest under the trust. A buyer agrees to purchase the house from the trustees and, on completion, pays the whole of the purchase price to Mr Price and Mrs Quinn together as the two trustees. After completion, the beneficiary who lives in the house refuses to leave, claiming that, because she was in occupation and had a beneficial interest, her interest binds the buyer and entitles her to remain. The buyer seeks advice. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer takes subject to the interests, because a buyer of a trust property is always bound by them.
The buyer takes subject to the occupier's interest, because actual occupation always binds a buyer.
The buyer takes free only if the occupying beneficiary consented in writing to the sale.
The buyer takes free of the beneficial interests. on the facts of this case
The buyer takes free only if the beneficial interests were protected by a notice on the register.
5.w: Payment of capital money to at least two trustees (or a trust corporation) overreaches the beneficiaries' interests, which are swept off the land onto the proceeds of sale. The buyer therefore takes free, even of an occupier's interest (City of London BS v Flegg).

n.0: A buyer is not automatically bound; overreaching is the mechanism that frees the title.
n.1: Actual occupation does not save an interest that has been overreached by proper payment to two trustees.
n.2: The occupier's written consent is not required where the interest is overreached by two-trustee payment.
n.4: Overreaching operates regardless of any notice; a notice is neither needed nor effective against it.

5.q: A borrower already has a first mortgage over their property in favour of Bank A, and now wishes to borrow further from Bank B, which will take a second charge over the same property. Both charges are registered. The borrower defaults, and the property is sold, but the proceeds are insufficient to pay both lenders in full. The lenders dispute priority. The solicitor considers the priority of two registered charges over the same property. Both banks had lent substantial sums and the sale proceeds would not cover them both. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The later charge always takes priority over the earlier charge in every case.
Registered charges generally rank in the order in which they are entered on the register, so the earlier-registered charge has priority.
The two charges always share the proceeds equally, whatever the order of registration.
A second charge can never validly be created over a property that already has a first charge on these facts as a general rule.
Priority between charges depends solely on which lender advanced the larger sum.
5.w: The priority of registered charges over the same registered estate is generally determined by the order in which they are entered on the register. So a first registered charge (Bank A) ranks ahead of a later registered charge (Bank B), and is paid first from the proceeds of sale.

n.0: The later charge does not automatically take priority.
n.2: The charges do not share equally; registration order governs priority.
n.3: A second charge can validly be created behind a first charge.
n.4: Priority is by registration order, not the size of the advance.

5.q: A court is interpreting a statute that could, on one reading, operate to impose criminal liability without any fault, or to apply to events before it came into force. The court applies established presumptions of statutory interpretation unless the statute clearly displaces them. The statute is silent or ambiguous on these points. The court applies interpretive presumptions. The wording could be read either to punish a person who had no idea they were doing anything wrong, or to reach back and catch things done before the Act existed, and the court, finding the statute unclear on both points, turns to the settled presumptions that fill such gaps unless Parliament has plainly displaced them. Which of the following best describes how such presumptions operate?
o: The court ignores all presumptions and applies only the literal words.
The court presumes that statutes always bind the Crown automatically.
The court presumes that all statutes operate retrospectively unless stated otherwise on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court presumes that criminal offences never require any mental element.
The court presumes, unless clear words show otherwise, against retrospective effect and in favour of requiring mens rea for criminal offences.
5.w: Courts apply certain presumptions when construing statutes, rebuttable by clear words: for example, a presumption against retrospective operation, a presumption that mens rea is required for criminal offences, a presumption against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts, and a presumption that statute does not bind the Crown. These guide interpretation where the statute is unclear.

n.0: The court does apply presumptions; it does not ignore them entirely.
n.1: The presumption is that statute does not bind the Crown, not that it always does.
n.2: The presumption is against, not in favour of, retrospective operation.
n.3: The presumption is that criminal offences do require mens rea, not that they never do.

5.q: A small company is heavily dependent on a supplier and is contractually entitled to delivery of components at an agreed price. Knowing the company will be ruined if supply stops, the supplier refuses to deliver unless the company agrees on the spot to pay a much higher price, giving the company no realistic practical alternative but to agree in order to survive. The company agrees under protest and later refuses to pay the increase. The supplier sues for the higher price, and the company argues the variation is not binding. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The variation is binding, because the company agreed to the new price rather than terminating.
The variation is binding, because the company continued to accept deliveries at the higher price.
The variation is void, because a price can never lawfully be changed once a contract is agreed.
The variation is binding, because economic pressure in commercial dealings is never unlawful.
The variation is voidable for economic duress, as illegitimate pressure left no real choice.
5.w: Economic duress makes a contract or variation voidable where illegitimate pressure (such as a threatened breach) is applied which leaves the victim no reasonable practical alternative but to agree (Atlas Express v Kafco; Pao On). Agreeing under protest to avoid ruin is a classic case.

n.0: Agreeing rather than terminating does not validate a variation extracted by duress.
n.1: Continued acceptance under the same coercion does not cure the duress or affirm the variation.
n.2: Prices can lawfully be varied by agreement; the vice here is the duress, not variation itself.
n.3: Illegitimate commercial pressure can amount to duress; it is not always lawful.

5.q: An elderly client comes to a solicitor to give instructions about disposing of their property during their lifetime, but attends the meeting accompanied throughout by a much younger relative who happens to stand to benefit very substantially from the arrangement the client is proposing. During the meeting the relative does almost all of the talking, repeatedly answers questions on the client's behalf, and appears distinctly anxious to ensure that the client is never left alone with the solicitor at any point. The solicitor becomes concerned that the client's instructions may not genuinely be their own. Which of the following best describes how the solicitor should proceed?
o: The solicitor should ask the relative to confirm in writing that the instructions represent the client's wishes.
The solicitor may simply take the instructions as relayed by the relative, since the relative knows the client's wishes.
The solicitor may proceed without further enquiry, provided the client nods in agreement with what is said.
The solicitor must refuse to act altogether whenever a client attends with a relative who will benefit.
The solicitor should see the client alone, to satisfy themselves that the instructions are genuinely the client's own free wishes.
5.w: Where there is a risk that a client is being influenced by a third party, particularly one who stands to benefit, the solicitor should take instructions from the client alone and in private, so as to satisfy themselves that the instructions are genuinely those of the client and freely given.

n.0: Written confirmation from the benefiting relative does not establish the client's free will.
n.1: The solicitor must not simply rely on the benefiting relative to relay the client's wishes.
n.2: A nod of agreement in the relative's presence does not resolve the concern about influence.
n.3: An outright refusal to act is not required; seeing the client alone is the appropriate step.

5.q: A defendant makes a formal offer to settle the claim, complying with the requirements of Part 36 of the Civil Procedure Rules. The claimant does not accept it, proceeds to trial, and fails to obtain a judgment more advantageous than the defendant's offer. The parties dispute the costs consequences. The defendant made the offer well before trial and it remained open. The court considers the costs consequences of a Part 36 offer that the claimant fails to beat. The defendant had put forward a realistic settlement figure that the claimant had gambled on beating at trial. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claimant automatically loses the entire claim for having rejected the offer.
There are no costs consequences at all, because a Part 36 offer is only an informal negotiation on these facts.
The claimant will usually pay the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, plus interest, unless unjust.
The defendant must pay all of the claimant's costs, because the claimant still won some money.
The costs consequences apply only if the offer was made in the last week before trial.
5.w: Where a claimant fails to obtain a judgment more advantageous than a defendant's Part 36 offer, the usual costs consequence is that the claimant pays the defendant's costs from the expiry of the relevant period, together with interest on those costs, unless the court considers it unjust.

n.0: Failing to beat the offer affects costs, not the claimant's substantive success on the claim.
n.1: Part 36 has defined costs consequences; it is not merely informal negotiation.
n.3: The defendant does not pay all the claimant's costs where the offer was not beaten.
n.4: The consequences do not depend on the offer being made only in the final week.

5.q: A settlor establishes a trust fund to relieve poverty among a defined group of poor people. A question arises about the requirement of public benefit, because the class of potential beneficiaries is relatively narrow and, in the ordinary way, a charitable trust must benefit a sufficient section of the public rather than a small private group. The trustees seek advice on whether the trust can be charitable despite the narrowness of the class it benefits. The defined group was small and known to the settlor, which is what prompted the concern about public benefit. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust is charitable only if the poor beneficiaries are complete strangers to the settlor on these facts.
The trust cannot be charitable, because it benefits too small a class of people.
The trust cannot be charitable, because relief of poverty is not a charitable purpose.
The trust is charitable only if it benefits the whole of the general public without limit.
Trusts for the relief of poverty are treated more generously, so a narrower class may still be charitable.
5.w: Relief of poverty is a recognised charitable purpose, and the public benefit requirement is applied more leniently to poverty trusts, so a comparatively narrow class (even, historically, poor relations or poor employees) may still qualify as charitable.

n.0: There is no requirement that the poor beneficiaries be strangers to the settlor.
n.1: Poverty trusts are not defeated merely by a relatively narrow class.
n.2: Relief of poverty is a charitable purpose.
n.3: A charitable trust need not benefit the entire public without limit.

5.q: A defendant deliberately attacks the victim, intending to cause them really serious harm, and inflicts a grievous injury. The prosecution considers the most serious non-fatal offence against the person. The defendant acted with intent to cause really serious harm and caused grievous bodily harm. The issue is the required mental element for the gravest offence. The attack was deliberate and targeted, the defendant meaning to inflict really serious injury on the victim rather than merely to frighten or to cause a minor hurt, and a grievous injury duly resulted, so the prosecution is aiming at the most serious of the non-fatal offences against the person. Which of the following best describes the mens rea for the offence under section 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861?
o: The defendant must intend to kill the victim.
It suffices that the defendant was negligent as to causing harm.
It suffices that the defendant foresaw some harm might result.
The defendant must intend to cause grievous bodily harm (or intend to resist or prevent lawful apprehension).
The defendant need have no particular state of mind, as the offence is one of strict liability on these facts.
5.w: Section 18 (wounding or causing grievous bodily harm with intent) is a specific intent offence: the prosecution must prove the defendant intended to cause grievous bodily harm (or intended to resist or prevent lawful apprehension). Mere foresight of some harm suffices only for the lesser s.20 offence, not for s.18.

n.0: An intention to kill is the mens rea for murder/attempted murder, not what s.18 requires.
n.1: Negligence is insufficient for s.18.
n.2: Foreseeing some harm is the mens rea for s.20, not the intent required for s.18.
n.4: Section 18 requires a specific intent; it is not a strict liability offence.

5.q: A buyer of registered land has completed the purchase by deed of transfer and paid the price, but has not yet applied to register the transfer at the Land Registry. The buyer believes that, having completed, they are already the legal owner. The transfer is a registrable disposition of registered land that has not yet been registered. The buyer assumes legal ownership passed on completion. Completion has taken place, the deed of transfer has been signed and the money has changed hands, and the buyer, assuming that is the end of the matter, has not yet lodged any application at the Land Registry, believing the legal estate already sits with them by virtue of completion alone. Which of the following best describes the effect of registration on a registrable disposition?
o: Registration is required only for first registration of unregistered land.
Legal title passes on completion of the deed, and registration is merely optional.
The disposition does not operate at law until the registration requirements are met.
Legal title passes only when the purchase money is paid, regardless of registration.
The transfer is void unless registered within seven days of completion.
5.w: Under s.27 of the Land Registration Act 2002, a registrable disposition of a registered estate (such as a transfer, or the grant of a legal charge or a lease over seven years) does not operate at law until the relevant registration requirements are met. Until registration, the buyer holds only an equitable interest, so registration is essential, not optional.

n.0: Registration of dispositions is required for dealings with already-registered land too, not only first registration.
n.1: Legal title does not pass on completion alone for registered land; registration is required and not optional.
n.3: Payment of the money does not pass legal title without registration.
n.4: The transfer is not void if not registered within seven days; but it does not operate at law until registered.

5.q: Mrs Pryce fell into arrears on the mortgage over her home, and the lender exercised its power of sale. Wanting a quick sale, the lender put the property on the market for only a few days, did not obtain a proper valuation, and sold it to a company connected with the lender for £250,000, a figure well below the £310,000 that a proper marketing campaign would realistically have achieved. Mrs Pryce, who is left owing the shortfall on her loan, complains that the property was effectively given away and that the sale price was far too low. She seeks advice on the lender's duty and any remedy she may have. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The sale is automatically void, and the property must be returned to the borrower free of the mortgage.
The lender must take reasonable care to obtain the proper price, and any shortfall sounds in damages.
The borrower's only remedy is to repay the connected buyer and recover the property by way of redemption.
The lender owes no duty at all as to the price once the borrower has defaulted, so there is no remedy.
The lender need only act in good faith, so the price actually obtained is legally irrelevant.
5.w: A mortgagee exercising its power of sale must act in good faith and take reasonable care to obtain the true market value at the time of sale (Cuckmere Brick v Mutual Finance). A sale at an undervalue, particularly to a connected party, can found a claim in damages for the difference.

n.0: The sale to a purchaser is not usually set aside; the remedy is damages, so the sale is not automatically void.
n.2: Once the power of sale is validly exercised the equity of redemption is overreached, so redemption is not the remedy.
n.3: Default does not free the lender of any duty as to price; it must take reasonable care to obtain the proper value.
n.4: Good faith is necessary but not sufficient; there is a distinct duty of reasonable care as to price.

5.q: A seller sends an offer to a buyer by email. The buyer sends an email accepting the offer, but owing to a problem on the buyer's own mail server the acceptance is not received by the seller until the following day, by which time the seller has sold the goods elsewhere. The buyer argues acceptance was complete when the email was sent. The communication was by an effectively instantaneous method. The buyer was keen to secure the goods and believed the deal was done the instant the reply was sent, the seller heard nothing that day and, treating the offer as still open, sold to another customer, and only afterwards did the delayed message finally surface on the seller's system. Which of the following best describes when the acceptance took effect?
o: When the buyer first decided to accept the offer, regardless of communication.
When the buyer clicked send, because acceptance is always effective on despatch on these facts as a general rule.
When the acceptance was actually received by the seller, as the postal rule does not apply to instantaneous communications.
When the seller chose to open and read the email, whenever that occurred.
Never, because acceptance by email is not recognised in contract law.
5.w: The postal rule (acceptance effective on posting) is an exception confined to non-instantaneous methods such as post. For instantaneous or effectively instantaneous communications such as email, the general rule applies: acceptance takes effect when and where it is received by the offeror. As it was received after the goods were sold, no contract was formed in time.

n.0: An uncommunicated intention to accept is not an effective acceptance.
n.1: The despatch rule is the postal-rule exception; it does not apply to instantaneous communications.
n.3: Receipt (arrival), not the moment the offeror chooses to read it, is generally the relevant point.
n.4: Acceptance by email is perfectly capable of forming a contract.

5.q: Two parties to a commercial contract have agreed that any dispute will be referred to a private tribunal whose decision they will accept as final. A dispute arises, it is referred, and the tribunal issues its decision. One party now wonders whether the decision can simply be ignored. The parties agreed to this process in their contract. Their contract contained a clause committing any dispute to a private determination whose outcome they promised to treat as final, the process has now run its course and produced a result, and the party who came off worse is testing whether that result carries any real legal force. Which of the following best describes the effect of an arbitration award?
o: The award is merely advisory and neither party is obliged to comply.
The award takes effect only if later approved by a judge at trial.
The award can be freely disregarded because arbitration is informal.
The award binds only the party that referred the dispute.
The award is binding on the parties and can be enforced through the courts.
5.w: Arbitration produces a binding award. Where parties agree to arbitrate, the arbitrator's award is final and binding on them and can be enforced through the courts, with only limited grounds for challenge. This distinguishes arbitration from facilitative processes such as mediation, which do not impose a binding outcome.

n.0: An arbitration award is binding, not merely advisory.
n.1: The award is binding without needing subsequent approval by a judge at trial.
n.2: An award cannot be freely disregarded; it is enforceable despite arbitration's flexibility.
n.3: The award binds both parties, not only the party that referred the dispute.

5.q: In 2016 a landlord granted a 10-year commercial lease of office premises. Some years into the term, with the landlord's written consent, the tenant assigned the lease to an assignee; and, as a lawful condition of giving that consent, the landlord required the outgoing tenant to enter into an authorised guarantee agreement (AGA) guaranteeing the assignee's performance of the covenants. The assignee has since fallen several months into arrears with the rent, and the landlord wishes to recover the unpaid sums. The landlord seeks advice on which party or parties it can pursue for the arrears. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The assignee alone, because the outgoing tenant gave no continuing liability.
Any former tenant in the chain, as all remain liable for the life of the lease.
The outgoing tenant alone, under the principle of privity of contract.
The assignee as current tenant, and the outgoing tenant under its AGA.
Only the landlord's managing agent, who approved the assignment.
5.w: Under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995, on a lawful assignment of a post-1995 lease the outgoing tenant is released from the tenant covenants, but may be required to guarantee the immediate assignee by an AGA. So the landlord can pursue the current tenant (assignee) and the outgoing tenant under its AGA, but not earlier tenants.

n.0: The outgoing tenant remains liable under its AGA for the assignee, so it is not the assignee alone.
n.1: Former tenants are released under the 1995 Act; the old privity-of-contract liability for the life of the lease does not apply.
n.2: For post-1995 leases the outgoing tenant is released on assignment, subject only to any AGA.
n.4: An agent authorising the assignment does not become liable for the rent.

5.q: A tenant of commercial premises has, on more than one occasion, sublet part of the premises without the landlord's consent, in breach of a covenant in the lease prohibiting subletting without consent. The breaches do not concern the payment of rent. The landlord, having lost patience, now wishes to forfeit the lease and recover possession of the premises because of the unauthorised subletting. Before the landlord can lawfully proceed to forfeit the lease for a breach of this kind, there is a step that the law requires the landlord to take first. Which of the following is that step?
o: Simply re-enter the premises, because no notice is required for any type of breach.
Give the tenant six months to buy the freehold before forfeiture can proceed.
Apply to the Land Registry to remove the tenant's lease from the register.
Obtain a court order authorising the landlord to end the lease before taking any step, in these circumstances.
Serve a notice under s.146 LPA 1925 specifying the breach and, if remediable, requiring it to be remedied.
5.w: For a breach other than non-payment of rent, forfeiture requires the landlord first to serve a s.146 notice specifying the breach and, where the breach is capable of remedy, requiring the tenant to remedy it and (usually) pay compensation, before proceeding to forfeit.

n.0: A s.146 notice is required for non-rent breaches; re-entry without it is not permitted.
n.1: There is no right for the tenant to buy the freehold as a precondition of forfeiture.
n.2: Forfeiture is not carried out by an application to the Land Registry.
n.3: No separate court authorisation to end the lease is needed before serving the s.146 notice.

5.q: A private client is dissatisfied with the service they have received from their solicitor on a matter and makes a formal, written complaint to the firm about it. The firm investigates the complaint fully under its own internal complaints procedure and sends the client a detailed final written response, but the client remains unhappy with both the way the matter was handled and the outcome of the complaint itself. The client now asks the solicitor what further avenue is open to them to have their complaint about the firm's service considered independently by someone outside the firm. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The client must complain directly to the Solicitors Regulation Authority, which resolves all client service complaints.
The client has no further route available, because the firm's final response on the complaint is conclusive.
The client must be informed of their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman, and of the time limits for doing so.
The client may only escalate the matter if the amount in dispute exceeds a fixed financial threshold set by the firm.
The client's only remaining option is to bring a claim in the civil courts against the firm for its poor service.
5.w: Firms must operate a complaints procedure and inform clients, in writing at the outset and again if a complaint is not resolved, of their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman (which handles service complaints) and of the applicable time limits for doing so.

n.0: The SRA regulates conduct; service complaints go to the Legal Ombudsman, not the SRA.
n.1: The firm's final response is not the end of the road; the client may go to the Legal Ombudsman.
n.3: Access to the Legal Ombudsman is not gated behind a firm-set financial threshold.
n.4: Litigation is not the only route; the Legal Ombudsman deals with service complaints.

5.q: An enabling Act provides that regulations made under it will not come into force unless and until they have been approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament. The minister prepares regulations and must secure a positive vote before they can take effect. Parliament's active approval is required. The Act makes clear that the minister cannot simply lay the instrument and let it take effect; instead nothing happens until each House has actively voted its approval, reflecting a deliberate choice by Parliament to keep a tighter grip on this particular power. Which of the following best describes the parliamentary control procedure applicable to these regulations?
o: The negative resolution procedure.
A procedure requiring no parliamentary involvement at all.
The procedure for granting Royal Assent to Bills.
The procedure for issuing a declaration of incompatibility.
The affirmative resolution procedure.
5.w: Under the affirmative resolution procedure, a statutory instrument requires the positive approval of Parliament, by a resolution of each House (or, for some financial matters, the Commons), before it can come into force or continue in force. It involves a higher level of scrutiny than the negative procedure.

n.0: The negative procedure requires no positive vote; the instrument stands unless annulled.
n.1: This procedure does involve Parliament; approval is expressly required.
n.2: Royal Assent concerns primary legislation, not delegated legislation.
n.3: A declaration of incompatibility is a court remedy under the HRA, not a legislative procedure.

5.q: Trustees are choosing investments for a trust fund. They are considering putting the entire fund into a single high-risk asset. A beneficiary questions whether the trustees are approaching the investment decision correctly under the Trustee Act 2000. The trustees have a general power of investment but must apply the statutory criteria. They are considering concentrating the whole fund in one asset. Tempted by the prospect of a large return, the trustees are contemplating sinking the whole fund into one speculative asset, and a beneficiary who has got wind of the plan wants to know what factors the trustees are actually obliged to weigh before committing the fund in that way. Which of the following best describes the standard investment criteria the trustees must apply?
o: The personal investment preferences of the trustees themselves.
The suitability of investments to the trust and the need for diversification of investments so far as appropriate.
The requirement to invest only in government-backed securities.
The maximisation of returns regardless of risk to the trust fund.
The need to obtain the prior approval of the court for each investment on these facts as a general rule.
5.w: Under s.4 of the Trustee Act 2000, in exercising the power of investment trustees must have regard to the standard investment criteria: the suitability of the proposed investment to the trust (including the suitability of that kind of investment and of the particular investment), and the need for diversification of investments in so far as is appropriate to the circumstances of the trust.

n.0: The criteria are objective statutory factors, not the trustees' personal preferences.
n.2: Trustees have a wide power of investment; they are not confined to government securities.
