n.3: Trustees must consider risk and suitability, not maximise return regardless of risk.
n.4: Court approval is not required for each investment under the standard criteria.

5.q: A partnership carries on a trade and makes profits, which are shared among the partners in the agreed proportions. The partners want to understand how those trading profits are taxed, and in particular whether the partnership itself is taxed as a separate entity or whether the partners are taxed individually on their shares. The court considers the taxation of the profits of a general partnership. The firm had several partners who each drew a share of the profits at the end of the year. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only the senior partner is taxed on the whole of the partnership's profits.
The partnership is taxed as a single entity, and the partners pay no tax at all.
The partnership is tax-transparent, so each partner is charged to income tax on their share of the profits.
The partnership's profits are entirely free of tax in the hands of the partners on these facts as a general rule.
The partnership pays corporation tax on its profits as if it were a company.
5.w: A general partnership is tax-transparent: it is not itself a separate taxable entity for income tax. Instead, each partner is assessed to income tax (and pays national insurance) on their share of the partnership's trading profits.

n.0: All partners are taxed on their respective shares, not only the senior partner.
n.1: The partners are taxed on their shares; the profits are not tax-free at partnership level with no partner tax.
n.3: Partnership profits are taxable in the partners' hands, not tax-free.
n.4: A general partnership does not pay corporation tax; that applies to companies.

5.q: A person has clearly been wronged (for example, their goods have been misappropriated online) but does not know the identity of the wrongdoer. A third party, who became innocently mixed up in the wrongdoing, holds information that would reveal the wrongdoer's identity. The applicant seeks an order compelling that third party to disclose the information so that proceedings can be brought. The third party is innocent but holds identifying information. The applicant needs that information to sue. The applicant has plainly been wronged but has no idea who is behind it, while a third party, itself blameless, became caught up in the events and holds the very information that would unmask the wrongdoer, and the applicant needs a way to prise that information loose so it can sue. Which of the following best identifies the order sought?
o: A charging order over the third party's property.
A third party debt order against the innocent party.
A freezing injunction against the innocent third party's assets on these facts as a general rule.
A wasted costs order against the third party.
A Norwich Pharmacal order requiring the third party to disclose information identifying the wrongdoer.
5.w: A Norwich Pharmacal order may be granted against a third party who, though perhaps innocent, has become mixed up in another's wrongdoing and holds information (such as the identity of a wrongdoer) necessary to enable the applicant to bring a claim. It compels disclosure of that information, typically with the applicant paying the third party's reasonable costs.

n.0: A charging order is an enforcement method against property, not a disclosure order.
n.1: A third party debt order enforces a money judgment, not disclosure of a wrongdoer's identity.
n.2: A freezing injunction preserves assets; it does not compel identifying information.
n.3: A wasted costs order concerns a legal representative's conduct, not third-party disclosure.

5.q: A business owner signs a written contract to buy an automatic vending machine, without reading it. The document she signs contains, in ordinary print, a clause excluding the seller's liability for the machine's failure to perform. The machine proves seriously defective, and when the buyer complains the seller relies on the exclusion clause. The buyer argues that she should not be bound by the clause because she never actually read it before signing. She seeks advice on whether the clause was incorporated into the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The clause is incorporated only if the seller expressly drew the buyer's attention to it before signing.
The clause is not incorporated, because the buyer did not in fact read it before signing the document.
The clause is incorporated, because a party who signs a contractual document is generally bound by its terms.
The clause is not incorporated, because an exclusion clause can never be included in a signed contract.
The clause is not incorporated, because the buyer was a business rather than a consumer.
5.w: A person who signs a contractual document is bound by its terms whether or not they have read them, in the absence of misrepresentation (L'Estrange v Graucob). The signed exclusion clause is therefore incorporated, subject to any statutory controls on its effectiveness.

n.0: With a signed document, special notice of the clause is not required for incorporation.
n.1: Failing to read a signed document does not prevent its terms binding the signatory.
n.3: Exclusion clauses can be, and often are, included in signed contracts.
n.4: The signature rule applies to businesses as well; the buyer's status does not defeat incorporation.

5.q: A person who is not a trustee dishonestly helps a trustee to commit a breach of trust, for example by knowingly assisting in the improper transfer or laundering of misapplied trust funds, although that person never receives any of the trust property for their own benefit. A beneficiary wishes to hold the assistant personally liable for the loss caused by the breach. The assistant argues that, since they never received any trust property, they cannot be liable. The assistant had helped route the misapplied funds through several accounts to disguise their origin. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The assistant is liable only where the trustee who committed the breach cannot be found on these facts as a general rule.
The assistant can never be liable, because they did not receive any trust property.
The assistant is liable only if they acted carelessly rather than dishonestly.
The assistant may be personally liable for dishonest assistance in a breach of trust, though they received no property.
The assistant is liable only if they were themselves appointed as a trustee.
5.w: A person who dishonestly assists in a breach of trust is personally liable to account for the resulting loss as an accessory, even though they never received any trust property. The touchstone is dishonesty judged by the objective standard (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan; Ivey v Genting).

n.0: Liability does not depend on the primary trustee being untraceable.
n.1: Receipt of property is not required for accessory (dishonest assistance) liability.
n.2: The basis of liability is dishonesty, not mere carelessness.
n.4: The assistant need not be a trustee to be liable.

5.q: A person took out a life assurance policy and, during their lifetime, wrote the policy in trust for their children, so that the policy proceeds are held on trust for the children rather than forming part of the person's own estate. On the person's death, a question arises about how the policy proceeds are dealt with. The court considers the treatment of a life policy written in trust. The policy had been set up years ago specifically to provide for the children on death. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The policy proceeds pass on intestacy regardless of the terms of the trust.
The policy proceeds can only ever be paid to the deceased's surviving spouse.
The policy proceeds pass to the beneficiaries under the trust, outside the estate and generally free of the deceased's IHT.
The policy proceeds pass to the personal representatives to be used to pay the estate's debts on these facts as a general rule.
The policy proceeds always form part of the deceased's estate and pass under the will.
5.w: Where a life policy is written in trust, the policy proceeds do not form part of the deceased's estate; they pass directly to the beneficiaries under the trust, outside the will and intestacy, and are generally outside the deceased's estate for inheritance tax purposes.

n.0: The proceeds pass under the trust, not on intestacy.
n.1: The beneficiaries are those named in the trust, not necessarily the spouse.
n.3: The proceeds pass to the trust beneficiaries, not to the PRs for debts.
n.4: A policy in trust does not form part of the estate or pass under the will.

5.q: Trustees of a substantial trust fund wish to invest the trust money. They are considering putting the entire fund into a single asset. A beneficiary questions whether the trustees are entitled to invest as they propose, and whether there are statutory criteria they must apply when exercising their power of investment. The trustees seek advice on the scope of their power of investment and the criteria that govern how it must be exercised. The fund was large and the beneficiaries' financial security depended heavily on how it was invested. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Trustees have a wide power of investment but must apply the standard investment criteria of suitability and diversification.
Trustees must always place the entire fund into a single asset for simplicity.
Trustees may only ever invest trust money in government bonds and nothing else.
Trustees may not invest trust money at all without first obtaining a court order.
Trustees may invest the fund in any way they personally please, with no criteria to apply on these facts as a general rule.
5.w: Under the Trustee Act 2000, trustees have a general power to invest as if absolutely entitled, but in exercising it they must have regard to the standard investment criteria — the suitability of investments and the need for diversification appropriate to the trust.

n.1: Diversification points against putting the whole fund into a single asset.
n.2: Trustees are no longer confined to a narrow list such as government bonds.
n.3: A court order is not generally required before trustees may invest.
n.4: The power of investment is not unfettered; the statutory criteria must be applied.

5.q: A prospective client of modest means wishes to bring a personal injury claim which the solicitor, after an initial assessment, considers has strong prospects of success. The client explains frankly that they simply cannot afford to pay the firm's fees on a private, hourly-rate basis as the case proceeds through the courts, and asks whether there is any lawful way in which the firm can act for them so that the firm's fee depends instead on the outcome of the claim. The solicitor considers the various funding options that are lawfully available for a claim of this kind. Which of the following best states the position?
o: The solicitor may enter a conditional fee agreement, which is lawful for such a claim if the statutory requirements are met.
The solicitor must act free of charge, because a client who cannot pay privately is entitled to free representation.
The solicitor may act only if the client first obtains legal aid, which is available for all personal injury claims.
The solicitor cannot lawfully offer any arrangement under which the firm's fee depends upon the outcome of the case.
The solicitor may agree to buy the client's claim outright and keep whatever damages are ultimately recovered in it.
5.w: Conditional fee agreements ('no win, no fee') are lawful for claims of this kind under the Courts and Legal Services Act 1990 (as amended), subject to statutory requirements on form and success-fee caps. Buying the claim outright would be champertous and is not permitted.

n.1: There is no rule requiring a solicitor to act free of charge for a client who cannot pay privately.
n.2: Legal aid is not generally available for personal injury claims, so this is not a precondition to acting.
n.3: Outcome-dependent fees are permitted through CFAs (and DBAs in some cases); they are not prohibited.
n.4: A solicitor may not purchase the client's cause of action and take the damages; that is champerty.

5.q: A person books and pays for a package holiday which is described as offering particular facilities and enjoyment. The holiday turns out to be a great disappointment, falling far short of what was promised, and the traveller suffers distress and loss of enjoyment as a result, though little in the way of financial loss. The traveller claims damages for the disappointment and loss of enjoyment. The tour operator argues that damages for distress can never be awarded in contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Damages for distress are available in every contract wherever the claimant feels upset by a breach.
Damages for distress are available only if the traveller also suffered physical injury on the holiday.
Damages for distress and loss of enjoyment may be awarded, as an important object of this contract was enjoyment.
Damages are limited strictly to a refund of the price the traveller paid for the holiday.
Damages for distress and loss of enjoyment can never be awarded for any breach of contract.
5.w: Although damages for distress are generally not recoverable in contract, an exception applies where an important object of the contract was to provide pleasure, relaxation or peace of mind, such as a holiday. Damages for disappointment and loss of enjoyment may then be awarded (Jarvis v Swans Tours).

n.0: Distress damages are the exception, not available in every contract merely because a party is upset.
n.1: Physical injury is not a precondition to distress damages in an enjoyment contract.
n.3: The traveller is not confined to a refund; loss of enjoyment is compensable in such contracts.
n.4: Distress damages are not wholly barred in contract; the enjoyment exception applies here.

5.q: A solicitor learns, in confidence from a client, information suggesting that a third party is at risk of serious physical harm. The solicitor is bound by the duty of confidentiality but is considering whether disclosure may exceptionally be justified to prevent that harm. The information was received in confidence. There is a risk of serious harm to another. In confidence, the client has let slip information suggesting that someone else faces a real risk of serious physical harm, and the solicitor, bound as a rule to keep the client's confidences, is wrestling with whether this is one of the rare situations in which disclosure can be justified. Which of the following best describes when confidentiality may be overridden here?
o: Confidentiality may be overridden whenever the solicitor personally thinks it would be convenient on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Confidentiality may be overridden where disclosure is justified to prevent serious physical or mental harm, or is otherwise permitted or required by law.
Confidentiality can never be overridden in any circumstances whatsoever.
Confidentiality may be overridden only with the client's express consent in every case.
Confidentiality automatically ends as soon as any third party is mentioned.
5.w: The duty of confidentiality is fundamental but not absolute. It may be overridden in limited circumstances, including where disclosure is required or permitted by law, or where the solicitor reasonably believes disclosure is necessary to prevent the client or a third party committing a serious criminal offence or causing serious physical or mental harm. Disclosure should be limited to what is necessary.

n.0: Mere convenience does not justify breaching confidentiality.
n.2: Confidentiality can be overridden in limited circumstances, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: The harm and legal exceptions do not depend on the client's consent.
n.4: Confidentiality is not lost merely because a third party is mentioned.

5.q: A person has been arrested and is being held at a police station. Before being interviewed, they ask whether they are entitled to speak to a solicitor, and whether they will have to pay for legal advice at the police station. They have limited means. The solicitor considers the detained suspect's right to legal advice under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The suspect was worried about the cost, having very little money, and unsure of their rights. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The suspect may consult a solicitor only after the police interview has finished.
The suspect has a right to free and independent legal advice, which can be exercised at any time while in detention.
The suspect has no right to legal advice until they have been formally charged.
The suspect is entitled to legal advice only if the offence is triable on indictment on these facts as a general rule.
The suspect must pay privately for any legal advice received at the police station.
5.w: Under PACE 1984 (s.58) and Code C, a person held in custody is entitled, if they request it, to consult a solicitor privately at any time, and free and independent legal advice is available at the police station regardless of means.

n.0: The suspect can consult a solicitor before and during interview, not only after.
n.2: The right to advice arises during detention, not only after charge.
n.3: The right is not limited to indictable offences.
n.4: Police station advice is free; the suspect does not have to pay privately.

5.q: A solicitor receives a cheque for £1,500 of client money but, wishing to smooth the firm's own cash position, deliberately holds it for four days before paying it into the client account, even though it could have been banked at once. The delay is a conscious choice rather than an administrative oversight. The COFA reviews the incident. The COFA considers its seriousness under the SRA Accounts Rules. The solicitor could have banked the cheque the same day but chose not to, using the firm's temporary hold on the money to ease its own cash position, and the COFA is weighing how seriously the rules treat a delay that was a conscious decision rather than a mere oversight. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The delay is acceptable provided no client suffers actual financial loss.
The delay is a matter for the firm's internal policy and not the rules.
Deliberately delaying the banking of client money is a serious breach of the rules.
A delay of only four days is never a breach of the rules.
The delay is acceptable because the money was eventually banked in full.
5.w: Client money must be paid promptly into the client account. A deliberate decision to withhold client money from the client account to benefit the firm's cash flow is a serious breach, and the deliberate nature aggravates it; it may also raise integrity concerns, regardless of whether the money is later banked in full or a client suffers loss.

n.0: Breach does not depend on a client suffering actual loss.
n.1: Prompt banking is a rule requirement, not merely internal policy.
n.3: A short delay can still breach the promptness requirement, especially if deliberate.
n.4: Eventual banking does not excuse a deliberate failure to bank promptly.

5.q: A person dies leaving a substantial legacy to a registered charity. The personal representatives are considering the inheritance tax treatment of the gift to the charity, and whether leaving a large proportion to charity affects the rate of tax on the rest of the estate. The court considers the charity exemption and the reduced rate of inheritance tax. A large slice of the estate had been left to a well-known national charity. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Gifts to charity are exempt only up to the amount of the nil rate band.
Gifts to charity are exempt from inheritance tax, and leaving at least 10% of the net estate to charity can reduce the rate on the rest to 36%.
Gifts to charity are exempt only where the charity is based within the United Kingdom and nowhere else on these facts as a general rule.
There is no inheritance tax advantage of any kind in leaving money to charity.
Gifts to charity are taxed at the full 40% rate like any other legacy.
5.w: Gifts to qualifying charities are exempt from inheritance tax. In addition, where at least 10% of the net estate is left to charity, the rate of IHT on the remainder of the chargeable estate is reduced from 40% to 36%.

n.0: The charity exemption is not capped at the nil rate band.
n.2: The exemption is not limited only to UK-only charities in the way stated.
n.3: There are clear IHT advantages to charitable giving.
n.4: Charitable gifts are exempt, not taxed at 40%.

5.q: A suspect who is detained at a police station has a mental health condition that makes them vulnerable, and the custody officer must ensure appropriate safeguards are in place for the interview and detention. The suspect's solicitor is concerned that the suspect understands what is happening and is treated fairly. The solicitor considers the safeguards for a vulnerable adult suspect under PACE Code C. The suspect struggled to follow what was being said and became distressed during the process. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A vulnerable adult suspect is treated in exactly the same way as any other adult, with no extra safeguards on these facts as a general rule.
A vulnerable adult suspect requires safeguards only if charged with a serious offence.
A vulnerable adult suspect loses the right to legal advice because of their condition.
A vulnerable adult suspect may not be interviewed at all in any circumstances.
A vulnerable adult suspect must have an appropriate adult present and be afforded additional safeguards during detention and interview.
5.w: Under PACE Code C, a suspect who is mentally vulnerable or has a mental disorder must be treated as a vulnerable person, requiring an appropriate adult to be present for interview and other key steps, along with additional safeguards to ensure they understand their position and are treated fairly.

n.0: Vulnerable adults receive additional safeguards, not identical treatment.
n.1: The safeguards apply regardless of the seriousness of the offence.
n.2: Vulnerability does not remove the right to legal advice; it adds safeguards.
n.3: A vulnerable adult can be interviewed with the proper safeguards.

5.q: At the end of a short interim hearing lasting less than a day, the court makes a costs order and must decide how the amount of costs is to be quantified. The receiving party has filed a statement of costs. One party argues the costs should be quantified there and then, while the other says a separate detailed process is required. The court considers summary and detailed assessment of costs under the Civil Procedure Rules. The hearing had taken only a couple of hours and the winning party had filed a schedule of its costs. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Costs of a short interim hearing can only ever be assessed months later at a separate hearing on these facts as a general rule.
All costs must always be quantified by a later detailed assessment, never summarily.
The amount of costs is always fixed by a statutory scale regardless of the work done.
The court will generally assess the costs of a short hearing summarily there and then, rather than by a later detailed assessment.
The court has no power to quantify costs at the end of a hearing at all.
5.w: The court will normally make a summary assessment of costs at the conclusion of a fast-track trial or of any other hearing lasting not more than a day, quantifying the costs immediately (often from the parties' statements of costs), rather than directing a later detailed assessment.

n.0: Summary assessment allows immediate quantification, not only a later separate hearing.
n.1: Short-hearing costs are usually assessed summarily, not always by detailed assessment.
n.2: Costs are assessed by reference to the work done, not a fixed scale in the ordinary case.
n.4: The court can and does quantify costs at the end of a hearing.

5.q: A claimant suffers a leg injury caused by the defendant's negligence, leaving the claimant with a permanent limp and reduced earning capacity. Before trial, the same leg is seriously injured again in an entirely separate incident, which would in any event have caused the same disability. The defendant argues that the second injury reduces the damages payable for the first. The first tortfeasor's negligence caused an injury whose effects were later overtaken by a separate tortious injury. The first accident left the claimant with a permanent limp and a settled reduction in earning capacity, and then, entirely by chance and through a wholly unconnected wrongdoer, the very same leg was badly hurt again before the case came to trial, prompting the first defendant to argue its own responsibility had shrunk. Which of the following best describes the effect on the first defendant's liability?
o: The first defendant's liability ends completely at the moment the second injury occurs.
The first defendant is liable only for losses arising after the second injury, not before.
The first defendant remains liable for the continuing effects of the original injury despite the later separate injury.
The first defendant becomes jointly liable with the person who caused the second injury for everything on these facts.
The second injury automatically extinguishes all damages for the first injury from the outset.
5.w: Where a claimant's tortious injury is later overtaken by a second, separate tortious injury producing the same disability, the first tortfeasor remains liable for the continuing loss caused by the original injury (Baker v Willoughby). The later tort does not wipe out the first defendant's responsibility for the damage it caused.

n.0: The first defendant's liability does not cease when the second injury occurs.
n.1: The first defendant remains liable for the ongoing effects, including after the second injury.
n.3: The first defendant is not made jointly liable for the separate second tort.
n.4: The second injury does not extinguish damages for the first from the outset.

5.q: A company is unable to pay its debts as they fall due, and a creditor who is owed a substantial undisputed sum wishes to take formal insolvency action to have the company wound up by the court and its assets realised and distributed. The creditor asks on what basis a company may be compulsorily wound up. The court considers compulsory winding up under the Insolvency Act 1986. The debt was long overdue and the company had ignored a formal statutory demand for payment. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A company can never be wound up against the wishes of its shareholders.
A creditor may petition for the company to be compulsorily wound up on the ground that it is unable to pay its debts.
Only the company's own directors may ever apply to have the company wound up.
Compulsory winding up is available only where the company has acted fraudulently.
A creditor may wind up the company only if owed more than half of the company's total debts on these facts.
5.w: Under the Insolvency Act 1986, a company may be wound up by the court on a petition (often by a creditor) on grounds including that the company is unable to pay its debts (inability being demonstrated, for example, by an unsatisfied statutory demand or unpaid judgment).

n.0: A company can be wound up against shareholders' wishes, e.g. on a creditor's petition.
n.2: Creditors, not only directors, may petition to wind up a company.
n.3: Inability to pay debts, not fraud, is the usual ground.
n.4: There is no rule that the creditor must be owed more than half the total debts.

5.q: A claimant has obtained a money judgment against a defendant who does not pay voluntarily. The claimant wishes to enforce the judgment against the defendant's assets or income. They ask what methods of enforcement are available to recover the judgment debt. The court considers the enforcement of a money judgment under the Civil Procedure Rules and related legislation. The defendant had the means to pay but was simply refusing to satisfy the judgment debt. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claimant must start a fresh claim from the beginning in order to recover the judgment debt.
The only way to enforce a money judgment is to have the defendant imprisoned for non-payment.
The claimant may choose from several methods, such as taking control of goods, a charging order, a third party debt order or attachment of earnings.
A judgment creditor has no means of enforcing a judgment if the defendant simply refuses to pay on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Enforcement is available only where the judgment debt exceeds £50,000.
5.w: A judgment creditor has a range of enforcement methods, including a writ or warrant of control (taking control of goods), a charging order over the debtor's property, a third party debt order (against sums owed to the debtor, e.g. in a bank account), and attachment of earnings, choosing the method best suited to the debtor's circumstances.

n.0: A fresh claim is not required; enforcement proceeds on the existing judgment.
n.1: Imprisonment is not the ordinary method of enforcing a civil money judgment.
n.3: There are effective enforcement methods; the creditor is not without remedy.
n.4: Enforcement is not restricted to debts over £50,000.

5.q: A public body made a clear and unambiguous promise to an individual that they would receive a particular substantive benefit, and the individual relied on that promise, but the body now seeks to go back on it. The individual argues they are entitled to the benefit itself, not merely to a fair procedure. A solicitor is asked whether a public body can be held to a substantive promise. The solicitor considers substantive legitimate expectation. The individual had reorganised their affairs in reliance on the promised benefit. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A public body is always bound to honour every promise it ever makes, without exception.
A public body may resile from any promise simply because circumstances have changed at all.
Substantive legitimate expectation applies only to promises made in writing under seal.
In limited circumstances a clear promise may give rise to a substantive legitimate expectation, and resiling from it may be an abuse of power.
A substantive legitimate expectation can never be enforced against a public body in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule.
5.w: In limited circumstances the courts recognise a substantive legitimate expectation: where a public body has made a clear, unambiguous promise of a substantive benefit on which a person has relied, resiling from it may be so unfair as to amount to an abuse of power, and the court may hold the body to the promise unless there is a sufficient overriding public interest (R v North and East Devon HA, ex p Coughlan).

n.0: A public body is not bound to honour every promise regardless of the public interest.
n.1: A body may resile only where justified by an overriding public interest, not for any change at all.
n.2: There is no requirement that the promise be under seal.
n.4: Substantive legitimate expectation can be enforced in limited circumstances.

5.q: A settlor transfers property to trustees on an express trust which then fails, or which disposes of only part of the beneficial interest so that a surplus remains undisposed of after the trust purposes have been carried out. There is no provision in the trust instrument dealing with what should happen to the undisposed-of beneficial interest. The question arises as to where the beneficial interest in the surplus goes. A significant sum was left over once the express purposes had been fully carried out by the trustees. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The undisposed-of beneficial interest is shared equally among all the original beneficiaries.
The undisposed-of beneficial interest is applied by the trustees to any purpose they choose.
The undisposed-of beneficial interest passes automatically to the Crown as ownerless property on these facts.
The undisposed-of beneficial interest results back to the settlor (or their estate) on an automatic resulting trust.
The undisposed-of beneficial interest passes to the trustees beneficially as a windfall.
5.w: Where an express trust fails or does not exhaust the beneficial interest, the undisposed-of interest is held on an automatic resulting trust for the settlor (or their estate), because the settlor did not effectively dispose of that part of the beneficial interest.

n.0: It results to the settlor, not shared among beneficiaries who were not given it.
n.1: Trustees cannot apply the surplus to purposes of their own choosing.
n.2: The surplus goes back to the settlor, not to the Crown as bona vacantia in the ordinary case.
n.4: Trustees do not take the surplus beneficially; they hold on resulting trust.

5.q: A defendant is attacked and uses force to defend themselves. In deciding whether the defendant has a defence, the court must consider both what the defendant believed the circumstances to be and whether the force used was proportionate. The defendant honestly believed force was necessary to defend themselves. The issue is the amount of force used. Set upon without warning, the defendant hit back to protect themselves, honestly convinced that force was needed to fend off the attack, and the court, accepting that belief, must now judge whether the amount of force the defendant actually used can be justified in the situation as they saw it. Which of the following best describes the test for the degree of force in self-defence?
o: The defendant must always retreat before any force can be justified.
The force is reasonable only if it caused no injury to the attacker.
The force is judged solely by what a trained expert would have done.
Any degree of force at all is permitted once the defendant is attacked on these facts.
The force must be reasonable in the circumstances as the defendant honestly believed them to be.
5.w: In self-defence, the defendant is judged on the facts as they honestly believed them to be (even if mistaken), and the force used must be reasonable (proportionate) in those circumstances. There is no absolute duty to retreat, and a pre-emptive strike may be lawful; grossly disproportionate force is not reasonable (with a modified test in householder cases).

n.0: There is no absolute duty to retreat before using force.
n.1: Reasonableness does not require that no injury be caused to the attacker.
n.2: The test is what was reasonable in the circumstances, not what a trained expert would do.
n.3: Not any degree of force is permitted; it must be reasonable/proportionate.

5.q: A director allowed the company to keep trading and incurring credit at a time when they knew, or ought to have concluded, that there was no reasonable prospect that the company would avoid going into insolvent liquidation, and did not take every step to minimise loss to creditors. On the company's insolvent liquidation, the liquidator seeks to make the director personally contribute to the company's assets. The court considers wrongful trading under the Insolvency Act 1986. The company had gone on ordering supplies long after rescue had become plainly hopeless. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The director can only be liable if the liquidator proves the director acted dishonestly on these facts as a general rule.
The director is liable only if they personally guaranteed the company's debts.
The director may be ordered to contribute to the company's assets for wrongful trading, without proof of dishonesty.
Wrongful trading applies only to the debts the director personally incurred.
A director can never be made personally liable for the debts of a limited company.
5.w: Under s.214 Insolvency Act 1986, a director may be ordered to contribute to the company's assets where, before the insolvent liquidation, they knew or ought to have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation and did not take every step to minimise loss to creditors. Dishonesty need not be shown.

n.0: Wrongful trading does not require proof of dishonesty (unlike fraudulent trading).
n.1: Liability does not depend on a personal guarantee.
n.3: The contribution is not limited to debts the director personally incurred.
n.4: Directors can be made personally liable in insolvency, e.g. for wrongful trading.

5.q: Following a person's arrest, the police wish to search the arrested person and, in some circumstances, the premises where they were arrested or which they occupy, for evidence relating to the offence. The suspect's solicitor considers the extent of the police powers of search that arise on and after arrest. The solicitor considers the search powers under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The police believed evidence of the offence might be found on the suspect or at their home. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The police may search any premises anywhere in the country without any limit or condition on these facts as a general rule.
The police may never search an arrested person or any premises in any circumstances.
The police may search only if the arrested person expressly agrees to the search.
The police may search premises only after obtaining a conviction against the suspect.
The police have statutory powers, subject to conditions, to search an arrested person and certain premises for evidence.
5.w: PACE 1984 confers powers, subject to conditions, to search an arrested person (s.32) for evidence or items that might assist escape or cause harm, to enter and search premises where the person was when or immediately before arrest (s.32), and to search premises occupied or controlled by a person under arrest for an indictable offence (s.18), among other search powers.

n.0: Search powers are subject to conditions and limits, not unlimited.
n.1: The police do have search powers on and after arrest.
n.2: A lawful search does not depend on the arrested person's agreement.
n.3: Search powers arise on arrest/investigation, not only after conviction.

5.q: During their lifetime, a person makes an outright gift of a large sum of money to their adult child. The donor survives for several years after making the gift. The personal representatives, after the donor's later death, must consider the inheritance tax treatment of that lifetime gift to an individual. The court considers potentially exempt transfers (PETs) for inheritance tax. The gift had been a generous one made to help the child buy their first home. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A lifetime gift to an individual is a potentially exempt transfer, becoming fully exempt if the donor survives seven years.
A lifetime gift to an individual is never subject to inheritance tax in any circumstances.
A lifetime gift to an individual becomes exempt only if the donor survives for three years.
A lifetime gift to an individual is always immediately chargeable to inheritance tax when made on these facts as a general rule.
A lifetime gift to an individual is exempt only up to the amount of the annual exemption.
5.w: An outright lifetime gift to another individual is a potentially exempt transfer (PET). It is not charged to IHT when made, and becomes wholly exempt if the donor survives seven years; if the donor dies within seven years, it becomes chargeable (with taper relief potentially reducing the tax after three years).

n.1: A PET can become chargeable if the donor dies within seven years.
n.2: The survival period is seven years, not three.
n.3: A PET is not immediately chargeable when made.
n.4: A PET is not limited to the annual exemption; the seven-year rule governs its exemption.

5.q: A claimant argues that the defendant should be liable in negligence for failing to act — for a pure omission — where the defendant simply stood by and did nothing while the claimant came to harm, even though the defendant could easily have intervened to help. There was no special relationship between them, the defendant did not create the danger, and the defendant had assumed no responsibility for the claimant. The claimant says the defendant should have acted as any decent person would. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is liability because a bystander always owes a legal duty to rescue those in peril.
There is generally no liability in negligence for a pure omission to act, absent a recognised exception.
There is liability whenever the defendant could easily have prevented the harm but chose not to.
There is always liability for failing to help another person who is in danger.
There is liability because failing to act is treated in law exactly like a positive act of harm.
5.w: The common law generally imposes no liability in negligence for a pure omission — a mere failure to confer a benefit or to rescue — absent a recognised basis for a duty, such as a special relationship, assumption of responsibility, control, or the defendant having created the danger.

n.0: A bystander does not generally owe a legal duty to rescue.
n.2: Ease of prevention alone does not create a duty to act.
n.3: There is no general duty to help; liability for omissions is exceptional.
n.4: The law distinguishes omissions from positive acts; they are not treated identically.

5.q: A defendant enters a building as a trespasser without, at that point, any particular criminal intent. Having got inside, however, the defendant then steals property, or attempts to steal, or inflicts grievous bodily harm on someone within. The defendant is charged with burglary based on what they did after entering. The court considers the form of burglary under the Theft Act 1968 that turns on the defendant's conduct after entry. Once inside, the defendant helped themselves to items and struggled with an occupant who disturbed them. Which of the following best describes this form of the offence?
o: This is burglary only where the defendant entered a commercial rather than residential building on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
This is burglary only if the defendant was carrying a weapon when they entered the building.
Under s.9(1)(b), burglary is committed where, having entered as a trespasser, the defendant steals or attempts to steal or inflicts or attempts GBH.
This is burglary only if the defendant also caused damage to the building on entry.
This cannot be burglary, because the defendant had no criminal intent at the moment of entry.
5.w: Under s.9(1)(b) Theft Act 1968, a person is guilty of burglary if, having entered a building (or part) as a trespasser, they steal or attempt to steal anything, or inflict or attempt to inflict grievous bodily harm. The relevant intent need only be formed after entry.

n.0: The offence is not confined to commercial buildings.
n.1: Carrying a weapon relates to aggravated burglary, not this offence.
n.3: Damage on entry is not required for s.9(1)(b).
n.4: Section 9(1)(b) does not require the intent at entry; conduct after entry suffices.

5.q: A client instructs a firm on the all-cash purchase of an expensive property and, when asked to do so, is able to prove their identity without any difficulty at all. However, the very large sum of money being used to fund the purchase appears wholly out of keeping with what little the firm knows of the client's apparently modest means, and the client becomes noticeably evasive whenever the subject of where the money has actually come from is gently raised. The fee-earner is satisfied as to identity and is minded to proceed on that basis alone. Which of the following best describes what the firm must do?
o: The firm may proceed, provided the purchase price is paid to the firm by way of a bank transfer.
The firm may proceed, because the source of a client's funds is never any concern of the solicitor.
The firm may proceed, because a client who can prove their identity is presumed to be acting honestly.
The firm need do nothing further, because verifying the client's identity is all that the Regulations ever require.
The firm must obtain evidence of the source of the funds, and not simply rely on having verified the client's identity.
5.w: Customer due diligence is risk-sensitive and, where the circumstances suggest a higher risk, extends beyond identity to scrutinising and obtaining evidence of the source of the client's funds. Unexplained wealth inconsistent with the client's profile is a classic warning sign requiring further enquiry.

n.0: Payment by bank transfer does not answer the concern about where the money originated.
n.1: The source of funds is very much the solicitor's concern under the money laundering regime.
n.2: Proving identity does not displace the need to scrutinise suspicious funding.
n.3: Verifying identity is not the whole of due diligence; source of funds must be addressed where risk arises.

5.q: A dispute arises about a well-established practice by which those in government behave in a particular way — for example that the monarch acts on ministerial advice — even though no statute or case requires it, and a party argues this practice is legally enforceable in the courts. A solicitor is asked about the status of such non-legal but binding constitutional practices. The solicitor considers constitutional conventions. The practice had been observed for generations, yet was written down in no statute at all. Which of the following best describes them?
o: Constitutional conventions have no significance and are freely ignored without any consequence on these facts.
Constitutional conventions can be enforced by the courts through an award of damages.
Constitutional conventions are rules of EU law binding on the UK institutions.
Constitutional conventions are binding practices of the constitution but are not legally enforceable in the courts.
Constitutional conventions are statutes that can be directly enforced by the courts.
5.w: Constitutional conventions are non-legal rules of constitutional behaviour that are regarded as binding in practice by those who operate the constitution (for example, that the monarch assents to bills passed by Parliament), but they are not laws and are not directly enforceable by the courts.

n.0: Conventions are significant and generally observed, not freely ignored.
n.1: Breach of a convention does not sound in damages in the courts.
n.2: Conventions are domestic constitutional practices, not rules of EU law.
n.4: Conventions are not statutes and are not directly enforceable in the courts.

5.q: A cricket club has played on its ground for decades. On a rare occasion a ball is hit out of the ground, over a high fence, and injures a passer-by, something that has happened only a handful of times in many years. The passer-by sues the club in negligence. The likelihood of a ball escaping and causing injury was very small, and the club had taken sensible precautions such as a high boundary fence. The risk that materialised was small and infrequent. Which of the following best describes whether the club is likely to be in breach?
o: The club is unlikely to be in breach, as the low probability of harm meant reasonable care did not require more.
The club is in breach because any foreseeable risk, however small, must always be eliminated on these facts.
The club is in breach because sporting clubs are strictly liable for injuries to passers-by.
The club is automatically in breach because injury in fact occurred to the passer-by.
The club is in breach because it should have ceased playing cricket altogether.
5.w: Whether there is a breach depends on what the reasonable person would do in response to the risk. Where the likelihood of harm is very small and reasonable precautions have been taken, the reasonable person may not be required to do more, and there is no breach, even though harm has in fact occurred on a rare occasion.

n.1: Not every foreseeable risk must be eliminated; the probability and cost of precautions are weighed.
n.2: There is no strict liability here; the question is whether reasonable care was taken.
n.3: The occurrence of harm does not automatically establish breach.
n.4: Reasonable care did not require abandoning the activity altogether given the small risk.

5.q: Rather than holding a client's substantial sum in the pooled general client account, a firm opens a separate designated deposit account in the firm's name for that particular client, into which the money is paid and on which the bank pays interest. The client asks who is entitled to the interest that the designated account earns. The account holds only this client's money. The firm decided that the size of the sum and the length of time it would be held justified a separate account rather than pooling it with other clients' funds, and the client, aware that interest rates make the sum meaningful, now wants to know precisely how the interest on that dedicated account is to be dealt with. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The interest belongs to the firm because the account is in the firm's name.
The interest is shared equally between the firm and the client.
All the interest actually earned on the designated deposit account belongs to that client.
The firm keeps the interest and pays the client only a fair sum from office money.
The interest must be paid to the SRA because it arises on a designated account.
5.w: Where client money is held in a separate designated deposit account holding only that client's money, the interest the account actually earns belongs to that client and must be accounted for to them in full. This differs from a general client account, where the firm keeps the bank interest but must account to the client for a fair sum.

n.0: The account being in the firm's name does not make the interest the firm's.
n.1: The interest is not shared; it all belongs to the client.
n.3: The 'fair sum from office money' approach applies to a general client account, not a designated deposit account.
n.4: The interest belongs to the client, not the SRA.

5.q: A firm receives £5,000 from a client on account of anticipated legal fees, for which no bill has yet been delivered, so the money is client money and is paid into the general client account. The firm operates a conventional double-entry bookkeeping system with a cash account (client side) and a client ledger for each client. The bookkeeper is asked to record the receipt correctly in the firm's accounts. The firm's client ledger for this client currently shows a nil balance, the cheque has cleared into the general client account at the bank, and the cashier is entering the transaction into the accounting system, mindful that every entry must have an equal and opposite counter-entry to keep the records in balance. Which of the following best describes the double-entry required to record this receipt?
o: Credit the client cash account and credit the client's ledger, with no debit entry.
Record the receipt on the office side only, as the money will later fund the firm's fees.
Debit the office cash account and credit the client's ledger on the office side.
Debit the client's ledger and credit the client cash account, both on the client side.
Debit the client cash account and credit the client's ledger, both on the client side.
5.w: A receipt of client money increases the client bank balance and creates a liability to the client. In double entry that is recorded by debiting the client cash account (money in) and crediting the client's ledger account (the firm owes it to the client), both entries on the client side.

n.0: Every entry needs an equal and opposite entry; two credits do not balance.
n.1: Money received on account before a bill is client money and is recorded on the client side.
n.2: Client money is recorded on the client side, not the office side.
n.3: This reverses the entries; a receipt is a debit to cash, not a credit.

5.q: A court must interpret a statutory provision whose words, given their ordinary grammatical meaning, produce a clear result. One party argues the court should simply apply the words as written, even though the outcome is not the one that party would prefer. The words are not ambiguous and the result is not absurd. The dispute turns entirely on a single subsection whose wording, read naturally, admits of only one meaning, and the party disadvantaged by that meaning is pressing the court to look behind the words, while the opponent insists the court should simply take the provision as it stands. Which of the following best describes the approach the court is being invited to take?
o: The mischief rule, focusing on the gap the statute aimed to remedy.
The golden rule, modifying the words to avoid an absurd result.
The ejusdem generis rule, limiting general words by a preceding list.
The literal rule, giving the words their ordinary and natural meaning.
The purposive approach, giving effect to the statute's broader aims.
5.w: The literal rule requires the court to give the words of a statute their ordinary, plain and natural meaning, applying them even if the result seems harsh, provided the words are clear and unambiguous. The other approaches only come into play where the literal meaning is ambiguous or produces absurdity.

n.0: The mischief rule looks beyond the words to the defect being remedied, not the plain meaning.
n.1: The golden rule departs from the literal meaning to avoid absurdity, which is not the case here.
n.2: Ejusdem generis is a specific aid for general words following a list, not the approach described.
n.4: The purposive approach looks to the statute's aims rather than simply applying clear words.

5.q: A firm holds money for several different clients in its general client account. The bookkeeper is asked whether money held for one client can be used to make a payment on behalf of a different client, on the basis that all the money is in the same bank account. The bookkeeper considers whether client money may be used across different clients under the SRA Accounts Rules. All the clients' funds sit together in the firm's general client account at the bank, and a fee-earner suggests that, because the pooled balance is more than enough overall, a payment for one client could be met even though little is held for that particular client. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Money held for one client must not be used for another client; each client's money is accounted for separately.
Money held for one client may be used for another provided it is replaced within a week.
Money in the general client account may be used freely for any client, as it is all pooled together.
Money held for one client may be used for another if the two clients are related.
Money held for one client may be used for another with the firm's own authorisation.
5.w: Although client money for different clients may be held in one general client account, the firm must account for each client's money separately (through client ledgers) and must not use one client's money for the benefit of another. Doing so is a breach of the SRA Accounts Rules.

n.1: Replacing it quickly does not make using another client's money permissible.
n.2: Money in the general client account is not a free pool; it is held for individual clients.
n.3: The clients being related does not permit it.
n.4: The firm cannot authorise using one client's money for another.

5.q: A developer laid out an estate of similar houses, dividing the land into plots and selling each plot subject to identical covenants restricting use to a single private dwelling. The developer's clear and common intention, understood by all the buyers when they bought, was that the plots should be mutually bound by, and mutually able to enforce, the covenants against one another. One current owner is now acting in breach of the covenant, and another owner within the estate, who bought a different plot from the developer, wishes to enforce the covenant against them. Which of the following best describes the basis on which they can do so?
o: The covenants are unenforceable, because identical covenants on many plots cancel each other out.
The owner can enforce it only against the original buyer of the offending plot, not a successor.
The owner cannot enforce it, because only the developer who imposed the covenants can enforce them.
The owner can enforce it under a building scheme. in the absence of any contrary agreement
The owner can enforce it only if the benefit was expressly assigned to them in their conveyance.
5.w: Where the conditions for a building (or letting) scheme are met, the covenants are mutually enforceable between the owners of plots within the scheme, so any plot owner can enforce against any other, including successors (Elliston v Reacher).

n.0: Identical covenants across plots are the hallmark of a scheme, not a reason they fail.
n.1: Scheme covenants bind and benefit successors, not just original buyers.
n.2: Under a building scheme, enforcement is not confined to the developer.
n.4: A building scheme provides mutual enforceability without needing express assignment.

5.q: In March last year a property developer, Hartwell Developments Ltd, agreed to let a neighbouring occupier, Mr Okafor, use a plot at the edge of one of its building sites. The arrangement was recorded in a document signed by both of them. It was expressed to give Mr Okafor 'the right to occupy the plot for as long as he wishes', with no fixed end date and no provision allowing either party to bring it to an end. Hartwell Developments Ltd intended the right to take effect as a legal estate that would bind any future owner of the site. A trainee solicitor is asked to advise whether that is possible under the Law of Property Act 1925. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: It cannot be a legal estate, because a legal estate must first be substantively registered before it can exist.
It can be a legal estate, because a right to occupy for an uncertain period is a term of years absolute.
It can be a legal estate, because the developer intends the right to bind the land permanently and indefinitely.
It can be a legal estate, because any interest in land will become legal once it is granted to the neighbour by deed.
It cannot be a legal estate, as only a fee simple absolute in possession or a term of years absolute is legal.
5.w: Section 1(1) LPA 1925 recognises only two legal estates: a fee simple absolute in possession and a term of years absolute. A right for an uncertain or indefinite period is neither, so it cannot exist as a legal estate (at most it takes effect in equity).

n.0: Registration affects how a legal estate is dealt with, but it is s.1(1) that limits which estates can be legal at all.
n.1: A term of years absolute requires a certain maximum duration; a right lasting 'as long as he wishes' lacks that certainty.
n.2: Intention to bind the land does not create a legal estate outside the two categories fixed by s.1(1).
n.3: Creation by deed is a formality; it cannot turn an interest that is not one of the two permitted estates into a legal estate.

5.q: A student is surprised to learn that the United Kingdom does not have a single document setting out its constitution, and asks a solicitor to explain where the rules of the UK constitution are actually found. The rules come from a variety of sources rather than one codified text. The solicitor considers the sources and nature of the UK constitution. The student had expected a single document like the constitutions of many other countries. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The UK has no constitution of any kind, written or unwritten.
The UK constitution consists solely of Acts of the European Union.
The UK constitution is contained entirely in a single codified written document on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The UK constitution is made up only of decisions of the monarch.
The UK has an uncodified constitution drawn from statutes, case law, conventions and other sources, rather than a single written document.
5.w: The UK constitution is uncodified: rather than a single written document, it is found in a range of sources including Acts of Parliament, case law (common law), constitutional conventions, the royal prerogative, and works of authority. It is often described as 'unwritten' in the sense of not being codified.

n.0: The UK does have a constitution, albeit uncodified.
n.1: The constitution is not made up solely of EU law.
n.2: The UK constitution is not contained in a single codified document.
n.3: The constitution is not simply the monarch's decisions.

5.q: Two parties contract for the sale of a specific cargo of goods which, unknown to either of them, had already ceased to exist at the time the contract was made, having perished before the agreement. Neither party was at fault, and both genuinely believed the goods still existed and could be sold and bought. When the true position emerges, a dispute arises as to the status of the contract. The buyer seeks advice on the effect of the parties' shared mistaken belief about the existence of the goods. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is voidable at the seller's option, because only the seller bears the risk of the goods.
The contract is void for common mistake, because the subject matter did not exist when it was made.
The contract is valid and the buyer must pay, because both parties acted entirely in good faith.
The contract is valid, because a mistake shared by both parties can never affect a contract.
The contract is void only if the seller expressly promised that the goods still existed.
5.w: Where both parties enter a contract under a shared fundamental mistake as to the existence of the subject matter (res extincta) — the goods having already perished — the contract is void for common mistake (Couturier v Hastie; and see s.6 Sale of Goods Act 1979).

n.0: The contract is void, not merely voidable at one party's option.
n.2: Good faith does not save a contract for the sale of goods that no longer existed.
n.3: A sufficiently fundamental common mistake does affect the contract, rendering it void.
n.4: The contract is void for the mistake itself; it does not turn on an express promise of existence.

5.q: A defendant is charged with theft and the only issue is dishonesty. The defendant claims they believed that what they did was in accordance with ordinary standards, and that they should be judged by their own view of honesty. The prosecution says a different, largely objective, test applies. The court must direct itself on the correct approach to dishonesty in the criminal law following recent authority. The defendant insisted their conduct was normal in their line of work and so could not be dishonest. Which of the following best describes the test for dishonesty?
o: The court decides what the defendant actually believed as to the facts, then applies the objective standard of ordinary decent people.
The defendant is dishonest whenever they took property belonging to someone else.
Dishonesty is judged purely by the defendant's own personal standards of honesty.
The defendant is dishonest only if they personally realised that ordinary people would regard their conduct as dishonest on these facts.
Dishonesty requires proof that the defendant intended to make a permanent gain for themselves.
5.w: Following Ivey v Genting Casinos (applied in criminal law in R v Barton and Booth), the court first ascertains the defendant's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts, then decides whether their conduct was dishonest by the objective standards of ordinary decent people. There is no separate requirement that the defendant appreciated others would regard it as dishonest.

n.1: Taking another's property is not automatically dishonest.
n.2: Dishonesty is not judged purely by the defendant's own standards.
n.3: The old second (subjective) limb of Ghosh no longer applies.
n.4: Dishonesty does not require an intention to make a permanent gain.

5.q: A firm's cashier is about to make a payment from the general client account that would take the overall balance on the client bank account itself into debit (overdrawn), not merely one client's ledger. The cashier queries whether this is permitted. The proposed payment would overdraw the client bank account as a whole. The firm operates a general client account. A payment is queued up that, once it goes out, would take not just one client's ledger but the whole client bank account below zero, and the cashier pauses, unsure whether letting the client account itself slip into an overdrawn position is something the rules will tolerate. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The client account may be overdrawn with the bank's consent to an overdraft facility.
The client account may be overdrawn provided it is brought back into credit within a month.
There is no restriction on the client account being overdrawn.
The client account may be overdrawn if the firm's office account is in credit.
The client account must not be overdrawn; a payment that would overdraw it must not be made.
5.w: A firm must not make a payment from a client account if it would result in the client account being overdrawn. Client money must always be available, and overdrawing the client account (or an individual client's ledger) would mean paying out money the firm does not hold for clients, which breaches the SRA Accounts Rules.

n.0: An agreed bank overdraft facility does not make overdrawing the client account permissible.
n.1: Restoring the position within a month does not permit overdrawing the client account.
n.2: There is a clear rule against overdrawing the client account.
n.3: The state of the office account does not license overdrawing the client account.

5.q: A buyer's solicitor is considering additional pre-contract searches beyond the standard ones, depending on the location and nature of the property. The property is near a river and in an area historically used for industry, so there is concern about the risk of flooding and of land contamination. The solicitor considers which search addresses these particular environmental risks. The house stood close to a river and on the site of a long-closed industrial works. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A bankruptcy search against the seller reveals the property's flood risk.
The local land charges search is the only search that reveals contamination and flood risk.
A Land Registry official copy reveals whether the land is contaminated or at risk of flooding.
An environmental search reveals risks such as land contamination and flooding affecting the property.
Environmental risks cannot be investigated before exchange of contracts.
5.w: An environmental search reports on environmental risks affecting the property, including whether the land is or may be contaminated (and the risk of liability under the contaminated land regime) and the risk of flooding, drawing on databases of past land uses and flood data.

n.0: A bankruptcy search concerns insolvency, not flood risk.
n.1: The local land charges search does not provide the detailed environmental risk data.
n.2: Official copies of the register do not report contamination or flood risk.
n.4: Environmental risks can be investigated pre-exchange via an environmental search.

5.q: Two parties make a contract which contains an express term stating that a named third party is entitled to enforce a particular benefit conferred on them by the contract, and the third party is expressly identified by name. The promisor then fails to confer that benefit, and the named third party wishes to enforce the term directly against the promisor. The promisor argues that, as the third party is not a party to the contract, they cannot sue on it. The third party seeks advice under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The third party may enforce the term only after first joining the original promisee to the claim.
The third party can never enforce the term, because only the original contracting parties can sue.
The third party may enforce the term only if the promisor agrees to let them do so.
The third party may enforce the term only if they provided consideration for the promise.
The third party may enforce the term, as the contract expressly provides that they may do so.
5.w: Under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, a third party may enforce a term of a contract if the contract expressly provides that they may, or if the term purports to confer a benefit on them (and it is not shown the parties did not intend it to be enforceable). Here the contract expressly so provides.

n.0: The third party need not join the promisee to enforce a right conferred under the Act.
n.1: The 1999 Act allows a qualifying third party to enforce; enforcement is not limited to the original parties.
n.2: Enforcement does not require the promisor's separate agreement once the Act is satisfied.
n.3: A third party enforcing under the Act need not have provided consideration.

5.q: A developer built a small single-storey extension in clear breach of a restrictive covenant benefiting a neighbouring house. The breach causes the benefited neighbour only modest harm to their outlook, which can readily be valued in money, and taking the extension down again would be highly wasteful and expensive, out of all proportion to that limited harm. The neighbour has applied promptly to the court for an injunction requiring the extension to be demolished. The developer accepts that there has been a breach, but argues that a modest money payment would fully compensate the neighbour and that ordering demolition would be oppressive. Which of the following best describes the likely outcome of the application?
o: The court must always grant an injunction to enforce a restrictive covenant, whatever the effect.
The court may award damages in lieu of an injunction, given the small and quantifiable nature of the harm.
The neighbour has no remedy of any kind at all, because a restrictive covenant cannot be enforced once the breach is already complete.
The court will order the developer to buy out the neighbour's land at a price it fixes.
Damages are never available for breach of a restrictive covenant; only an injunction lies.
5.w: Although an injunction is the usual remedy, the court has a discretion to award damages in lieu (in equity) where the injury is small, capable of being estimated in money and adequately compensated by a small payment, and an injunction would be oppressive (Shelfer; Coventry v Lawrence).

n.0: An injunction is not automatic; the court may award damages in lieu in an appropriate case.
n.2: A completed breach does not bar a remedy; damages in lieu remain available.
n.3: The court does not force the neighbour to sell their land to the wrongdoer.
n.4: Damages in lieu of an injunction can be awarded for breach of a restrictive covenant.

5.q: A defendant's factory lawfully carries on an activity expressly authorised by statute, and does so without negligence and strictly within the terms of that statutory authority. An inevitable consequence of carrying on the authorised activity in the manner permitted is some escape or interference affecting neighbouring land, which would otherwise be actionable. A neighbour sues in nuisance and under Rylands v Fletcher. The defendant relies on the fact that the activity was authorised by, and conducted in accordance with, statute. The statute set out in detail how the activity was to be carried on, and the factory had followed it exactly. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant is liable because statutory authority protects only public bodies, never private businesses.
The defendant remains fully liable, because carrying on any activity that harms a neighbour is always actionable on these facts.
The defendant is liable unless the neighbour consented in writing to the activity beforehand.
Statutory authority is never a defence to a claim in nuisance or under Rylands v Fletcher.
Statutory authority may provide a defence where the harm is an inevitable consequence of the authorised activity done without negligence.
5.w: Where a defendant acts under statutory authority and the interference or escape is an inevitable consequence of doing the authorised thing in the authorised manner, without negligence, statutory authority can provide a defence to nuisance and to a claim under Rylands v Fletcher.

n.0: The defence is not confined to public bodies; it turns on acting under statutory authority.
n.1: Not all harm to a neighbour is actionable; a valid statutory-authority defence may apply.
n.2: The defence does not depend on the neighbour's prior written consent.
n.3: Statutory authority can be a defence to these claims in appropriate circumstances.

5.q: In a criminal trial, the defendant wishes to raise a particular defence. The judge must decide who bears the burden of putting enough evidence of the defence before the court to make it a live issue, as opposed to the ultimate burden of disproving it. A distinction is drawn between raising an issue and proving it. The defence must first be sufficiently raised. The defendant wants to run a particular defence, and the judge has to separate two different questions, first whether enough evidence has been put forward to make that defence a live issue at all, and second who must ultimately prove or disprove it once it is in play. Which of the following best describes the evidential burden as distinct from the legal burden?
o: The evidential burden is the burden of adducing enough evidence to raise an issue, while the legal burden is the burden of proving it.
The evidential and legal burdens are the same thing under a different name.
The evidential burden is irrelevant once a plea of not guilty is entered.
The evidential burden always rests on the defendant for every element of the offence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The evidential burden requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of the whole case.
5.w: The evidential burden is the burden of adducing sufficient evidence to raise an issue for the tribunal to consider (for example, enough evidence of self-defence to make it live). The legal (persuasive) burden is the burden of actually proving the issue to the required standard. For many defences the defendant bears the evidential burden, but the prosecution then bears the legal burden of disproving the defence.

n.1: The two burdens are distinct: raising an issue versus proving it.
n.2: The evidential burden remains relevant to which issues are live at trial.
n.3: The evidential burden does not rest on the defendant for every element; the prosecution proves the offence.
n.4: The evidential burden is about raising an issue, not proving the whole case to the criminal standard.

6.q: A settlor tells the intended beneficiary that they are giving them property on trust, but never actually transfers the legal title of the property to the intended trustees, and does everything as a gratuitous arrangement for which the beneficiary gives nothing in return. The trust is therefore never completely constituted by a transfer of the property. The intended beneficiary, a volunteer, seeks to compel the settlor to perfect the arrangement. The property remained registered in the settlor's sole name throughout, and no deed of transfer was ever executed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust is incompletely constituted, and equity will not assist a volunteer to perfect it.
The court will compel the settlor to transfer the property to complete the trust.
The trust is fully constituted, because the settlor announced an intention to create it.
The trust is valid, because the beneficiary relied on the settlor's statement.
The trust is valid, because consideration is never required to create a trust.
6.w: A trust must be completely constituted by vesting the trust property in the trustees (or a valid self-declaration of trust). Where it is not, and the intended beneficiary is a volunteer, equity will not perfect an imperfect gift or assist a volunteer to compel constitution (Milroy v Lord).

n.1: Equity will not compel the settlor to complete an imperfect gift for a volunteer.
n.2: An announced intention does not constitute the trust without vesting the property.
n.3: Reliance alone does not constitute the trust here.
n.4: Though consideration is not needed to create a trust, a volunteer cannot compel constitution of an incomplete one.

6.q: A neighbour, purely out of spite following a disagreement, deliberately sets out to disturb the claimant by banging on the party wall and making loud noises whenever the claimant is trying to give music lessons, doing so with the specific intention of ruining the claimant's peaceful enjoyment of their home. The activity would perhaps be tolerable if done innocently, but it is done maliciously to annoy. The claimant sues in private nuisance and the defendant argues that noise-making on one's own property can never be a nuisance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The claim fails, because music lessons are themselves a sensitive and non-ordinary use of land.
Malice is entirely irrelevant in nuisance, so the defendant's motive makes no difference at all on these facts.
The defendant's malice is relevant and may make an otherwise borderline interference an actionable nuisance.
There can be no nuisance, because making noise on one's own property is always lawful.
The claim succeeds only if the noise caused physical damage to the claimant's property.
6.w: Malice is a relevant factor in assessing the reasonableness of an interference in private nuisance. Conduct done deliberately to annoy a neighbour may be an actionable nuisance even where the same activity, done innocently, might not be (Christie v Davey).

n.0: Giving music lessons at home is an ordinary use; the vice is the malicious interference.
n.1: Malice is relevant to reasonableness in nuisance, not irrelevant.
n.3: Making noise on one's own land can be a nuisance, especially where done maliciously.
n.4: Nuisance covers interference with enjoyment; physical damage is not required.

6.q: Two teenagers of the same age are playing together with plastic rulers when one ruler snaps and a fragment injures the other's eye. The injured teenager sues the other in negligence. The defendant is a child, and the question arises as to the standard of care by which a child defendant's conduct is to be judged when deciding whether they were negligent. The claimant argues the defendant should be judged like an adult. Both children were of exactly the same age and were playing together in the ordinary way that children of that age do. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A child is judged by exactly the same standard of care as a reasonable adult would meet.
A child is judged by the standard of a reasonable child of the same age, not by the adult standard.
A child is judged purely by their own individual level of maturity and understanding.
