A child is judged by the standard of the most careful child that could be imagined.
A child can never be liable in negligence, whatever the child's age or conduct.
6.w: Where the defendant is a child, the standard of care is that of a reasonable and careful child of the defendant's age, not the adult standard (Mullin v Richards). The test remains objective, but calibrated to the defendant's age.

n.0: A child is not held to the full adult standard of care.
n.2: The standard is objective for a child of that age, not the child's own subjective maturity.
n.3: The standard is the reasonable child of that age, not the most careful child imaginable.
n.4: Children can be liable in negligence if they fall below the standard of a reasonable child of their age.

6.q: Parliament has passed a statute that comprehensively regulates a particular area which was previously governed by the royal prerogative. The government seeks to rely on the prerogative to act in a way inconsistent with the statutory scheme. The statute now covers the same ground as the former prerogative. The government prefers to use the prerogative. Parliament has since enacted a detailed statutory scheme covering exactly the territory the prerogative once occupied, but the government, finding the statute inconvenient, wants to fall back on the old prerogative power to act in a way the statute would not permit, forcing the question of which source of power now governs. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The statute is invalid because it interferes with the royal prerogative.
The prerogative always prevails over any inconsistent Act of Parliament.
The government may freely choose between the statute and the prerogative on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Where statute covers the same ground, the government must act under the statute, and the prerogative is displaced to that extent.
The prerogative can be used to suspend the operation of the statute.
6.w: Where a statute regulates an area formerly governed by the prerogative, the executive must act under the statute; the prerogative is displaced or goes into abeyance to the extent of the statutory scheme (Attorney General v De Keyser's Royal Hotel; Fire Brigades Union). The prerogative cannot be used to circumvent or frustrate the will of Parliament expressed in the statute.

n.0: The statute is valid; Parliament may legislate over prerogative areas.
n.1: The prerogative does not prevail over statute; statute displaces the prerogative.
n.2: The government cannot freely choose the prerogative where statute covers the ground.
n.4: The prerogative cannot be used to suspend a statute's operation.

6.q: A party needs the court to make an order during the course of proceedings, before trial — for example an order about disclosure or an extension of time. They must make an interim application to the court. The party is unsure of the basic procedure for making such an application and what must accompany it. The court considers the procedure for interim applications under the Civil Procedure Rules. The order sought was needed well before trial to keep the case moving to the court's timetable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The party must file an application notice, usually supported by evidence, and serve it on the other party.
Interim orders can only ever be obtained at the final trial and never beforehand.
Interim applications require no notice to the other side in any circumstances at all.
Only the claimant, and never the defendant, may make an interim application to the court on these facts.
A party may obtain any interim order simply by telephoning the court informally.
6.w: An interim application is generally made by filing an application notice (Form N244) setting out what order is sought and why, usually supported by evidence, and serving it on the respondent. Some applications may be made without notice where justified, but notice is the norm.

n.1: Interim orders are available before trial, not only at trial.
n.2: Notice to the other side is the norm, with without-notice applications being exceptional.
n.3: Either party may make an interim application, not only the claimant.
n.4: An informal phone call is not the proper procedure for an interim application.

6.q: Entrepreneurs wish to incorporate a private company limited by shares and ask what must be delivered to the Registrar of Companies to bring the company into existence. They intend to adopt the default constitution unless they provide their own. The company is to be a new private company limited by shares. The founders want to know what registration requires. The founders have settled on a private company limited by shares, are content to fall back on the default constitution unless they supply their own, and simply want to know what package of documents and information actually has to reach the Registrar before the company legally comes into being. Which of the following best describes what must be delivered to Companies House to form the company?
o: Nothing formal, as a company comes into existence simply by the founders trading together on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A court order approving the formation of the company.
Only a single signed partnership agreement between the founders.
Only the company's first set of annual accounts.
An application to register with the required documents, details and fee, following which a certificate of incorporation is issued.
6.w: To form a company, an application for registration must be delivered to the Registrar with the required documents and information, including a memorandum of association, the proposed articles (or reliance on the model articles), a statement of capital, proposed officers and registered office, and the fee. The Registrar then issues a certificate of incorporation.

n.0: A company does not arise merely from trading together; registration is required.
n.1: No court order is needed to incorporate a company.
n.2: A partnership agreement does not form a company.
n.3: First accounts are not what brings a company into existence.

6.q: A claimant and their solicitor agree that, instead of charging on the usual basis, the solicitor's fee will be a percentage of the damages actually recovered if the claim succeeds, and nothing by way of that fee if it does not. The fee is a share of the sums recovered. The arrangement is a form of contingency funding. Rather than bill in the ordinary way, the solicitor offers to take, as the fee, an agreed slice of whatever damages the client actually recovers, so that the firm shares in the winnings if the claim succeeds and takes nothing by way of that fee if it does not. Which of the following best identifies this arrangement?
o: An after-the-event insurance policy covering the opponent's costs.
A fixed fee payable in advance whatever the outcome.
A conditional fee agreement charging the normal fees plus a capped success fee on these facts.
A damages-based agreement, under which the lawyer's fee is a percentage of the damages recovered.
A legal aid arrangement funded from central government.
6.w: A damages-based agreement (DBA) is a form of contingency fee arrangement under which the lawyer's fee is calculated as an agreed percentage of the financial benefit (damages) recovered by the client, subject to statutory caps, and is payable only on success. It differs from a conditional fee agreement, where the fee is the normal fee plus a success fee.

n.0: After-the-event insurance covers costs risk; it is not the fee arrangement described.
n.1: A DBA is contingent on success and linked to damages, not a fixed advance fee.
n.2: A conditional fee agreement charges normal fees plus a success fee, not a percentage of damages.
n.4: A DBA is private funding, not legal aid.

6.q: A person buys a house next to an existing workshop and then sues the workshop owner in private nuisance for noise that the workshop has been generating in the same way for many years, from before the claimant arrived. The workshop owner argues that the claimant 'came to the nuisance' and so cannot complain. The activity pre-dated the claimant's arrival but the claimant's use of the land is otherwise ordinary. The workshop had been operating in exactly the same way for many years before the claimant ever moved in next door, and the owner's central point is that the claimant knowingly bought a house beside a working workshop and cannot now be heard to complain about the very activity that was always there. Which of the following best describes the effect of the claimant having come to the nuisance?
o: It is a complete defence that the claimant came to the nuisance.
It is generally no defence that the claimant came to the nuisance.
It prevents any remedy but allows the claimant to recover nominal damages only.
It is a defence because an established activity acquires immunity from any later neighbour.
It is a defence only if the activity had continued for more than five years.
6.w: It is generally no defence to a claim in private nuisance that the claimant came to the nuisance, that is, acquired or began using their land after the defendant's activity had begun. The defendant cannot rely on the prior existence of the activity to defeat the claim, though the claimant's use of land and locality remain relevant to reasonableness.

n.0: Coming to the nuisance is not a complete defence.
n.2: The claimant is not limited to nominal damages merely for having come to the nuisance.
n.3: An established activity does not acquire general immunity against later neighbours by mere continuation.
n.4: There is no rule making it a defence after a fixed period such as five years (contrast prescription's twenty years).

6.q: A defendant commits a criminal act — an unlawful assault — which, although not intended to kill or cause serious harm, is objectively dangerous in the sense that a sober and reasonable person would recognise it as carrying some risk of harm, and that act in fact causes the victim's death. The defendant is charged with manslaughter. The court considers the elements of unlawful act (constructive) manslaughter. The single blow the defendant struck unexpectedly proved fatal when the victim fell and hit their head. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defendant is guilty only if a reasonable person would have foreseen a risk of death specifically.
The defendant is guilty only if the unlawful act was a civil wrong rather than a crime.
The defendant cannot be guilty, because they never intended to kill or cause serious harm.
The defendant is guilty of murder, because the unlawful act resulted in death.
The defendant may be guilty of unlawful act manslaughter, as a dangerous criminal act caused the death.
6.w: Unlawful act manslaughter requires an intentional criminal act which is objectively dangerous (a sober and reasonable person would recognise a risk of some harm) and which causes death. The defendant need not intend death or serious harm, nor foresee the risk (R v Church; DPP v Newbury).

n.0: The dangerousness test requires foresight of some harm, not specifically death.
n.1: The base act must be a crime, not merely a civil wrong.
n.2: Absence of intent to kill or cause serious harm does not preclude this form of manslaughter.
n.3: Without intent to kill or cause GBH it is manslaughter, not murder.

6.q: A firm has carried out work for a client and wishes to take payment of its fees from money it holds for that client in the client account. The bookkeeper is asked what must happen before the firm can transfer money from the client account to the office account in respect of its costs. The bookkeeper considers the transfer of costs from client to office account under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm has completed a discrete piece of work and wishes to be paid for it from the money it already holds for the client in the client account, and the bookkeeper needs to know what step must come first before that money can move to the office account. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may transfer money for its costs at any time, before or without any bill.
The firm may transfer its costs only with the prior written approval of the SRA.
The firm may transfer its costs provided the amount taken is reasonable, without a bill on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The firm may never transfer client money to the office account for its own costs.
The firm may transfer money for its costs from client to office account only after a bill or written notification of costs has been given to the client.
6.w: Money held for a client becomes office money, capable of transfer to the office account for the firm's costs, only once the firm has delivered a bill of costs or other written notification of the costs incurred. Only then, and only up to the amount notified, may the transfer be made.

n.0: A transfer for costs cannot be made before or without a bill.
n.1: SRA approval is not required for a proper costs transfer.
n.2: Reasonableness of the amount does not dispense with the need for a bill.
n.3: The firm can take its properly billed costs from client money, so 'never' is wrong.

6.q: The police wish to interview a suspect about an offence and later rely on what is said as evidence. The suspect's solicitor is advising on how interviews must be conducted and recorded, and when questioning must stop. The suspect is detained at the police station. The solicitor considers the conduct of police interviews under PACE and the Codes of Practice. The police wanted the suspect's answers to stand up as evidence if the matter went to court. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Interviews must generally be recorded and conducted under caution, and questioning must cease once there is sufficient evidence to charge.
Interviews need not be recorded and may be conducted informally without any caution.
Interviews may be conducted only in writing and never by audio recording.
The police may continue interviewing a suspect indefinitely even after deciding to charge them.
The police may interview a suspect who has asked for a solicitor before the solicitor arrives, without restriction on these facts.
6.w: Under PACE and the Codes, a suspect must be cautioned before questioning about an offence, interviews at the police station must generally be audio-recorded, and questioning must cease once the officer believes there is sufficient evidence for a realistic prospect of conviction and the suspect has been given the opportunity to give their account.

n.1: Interviews must be recorded and conducted under caution, not informally.
n.2: Interviews are audio-recorded, not only in writing.
n.3: Questioning must stop once there is sufficient evidence to charge.
n.4: Interviewing before a requested solicitor arrives is restricted, not unrestricted.

6.q: A settlor creates a trust of a fund to be used to maintain a specific animal belonging to the settlor, and for the upkeep of a particular tomb, for as long as the law allows. There are no human beneficiaries to enforce the trust, and the purpose is not charitable. The settlor's adviser considers whether such a non-charitable purpose trust can nonetheless be valid, given the general rule that private purpose trusts are void for want of a beneficiary. The settlor left detailed directions about how the particular animal and the tomb were each to be looked after. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Such trusts are valid only if they are for the public benefit like a charitable trust.
Such trusts are always void, because there are no beneficiaries who can enforce them.
Such trusts are always valid, because a settlor may create a trust for any purpose at all on these facts.
Such trusts are valid only if a charity agrees to take responsibility for enforcing them.
Such trusts may be valid as recognised anomalous exceptions, but only if they satisfy the perpetuity rules.
6.w: Although non-charitable purpose trusts are generally void for lack of a beneficiary, there are recognised anomalous exceptions — including trusts for specific animals and for the maintenance of particular graves or monuments — which may be valid provided they comply with the perpetuity rules (Re Endacott; Re Dean).

n.0: These exceptions do not require public benefit; that is the charitable route.
n.1: These recognised exceptions are not always void.
n.2: A settlor cannot create a valid private trust for any purpose whatever.
n.3: A charity's willingness to enforce is not the basis of these exceptions.

6.q: A firm receives £600 from a client specifically to pay a search fee that the firm has already incurred but not yet paid to the search provider. Instead of ensuring the money is used for that purpose, the cashier posts the £600 to the office account and the search fee remains unpaid for some time. The COFA reviews the entry. The money was provided for a specific disbursement. The client handed over the money for the express purpose of clearing a search fee the firm had already run up on the matter, but instead of that money reaching the provider the fee stayed outstanding while the receipt sat in the office account, and the COFA is examining how the sum should have been handled. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The money need not be applied to the search fee at all, as the firm chooses how to use it on these facts.
The money may be used for the firm's general expenses until the fee falls due.
The money should be held as client money and used to pay the disbursement, or the disbursement paid promptly.
The money may remain in the office account indefinitely once the fee is eventually paid.
The money is office money the moment it is received for a disbursement already incurred.
6.w: Money received from a client to meet a specific disbursement is client money and must be dealt with accordingly: held in the client account and applied to the disbursement, or used to pay the disbursement promptly. Posting it to the office account and leaving the disbursement unpaid misapplies the client's money and breaches the rules.

n.0: The firm cannot treat it as free to use as it chooses; it is earmarked client money.
n.1: It must not be used for the firm's general expenses.
n.3: It cannot remain in the office account indefinitely.
n.4: It does not automatically become office money simply because the disbursement was already incurred; it is the client's money for that purpose.

6.q: A defendant pleads guilty to an offence, but the defence and prosecution disagree about the factual basis of the plea — the defendant admits the offence but on a significantly less serious version of the facts than the prosecution alleges, and the difference would materially affect sentence. The court must resolve the dispute before sentencing. The solicitor considers how such a factual dispute after a guilty plea is resolved. The two sides put forward sharply different accounts of how the offence had been committed. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The guilty plea is automatically withdrawn whenever the facts are disputed.
The court must simply accept the prosecution's version of the facts without any hearing.
The dispute is resolved by a full jury trial of the whole offence again.
The court may hold a Newton hearing to determine the disputed facts before sentencing.
The court must sentence on the defence version of the facts in every case.
6.w: Where a defendant pleads guilty but there is a significant dispute about the factual basis that would affect sentence, the court may hold a Newton hearing: the judge hears evidence and determines the disputed facts (to the criminal standard) before proceeding to sentence on the facts as found.

n.0: The guilty plea stands; the facts are resolved by a Newton hearing.
n.1: The court does not simply accept the prosecution's version without resolving the dispute.
n.2: A Newton hearing, not a full jury trial, resolves the factual dispute after a guilty plea.
n.4: The court does not automatically adopt the defence version.

6.q: An Act of Parliament contains a provision empowering a minister, by secondary legislation, to amend or repeal provisions of primary legislation, including the Act itself. A commentator is concerned about the breadth of such a power. A solicitor is asked to explain what such a provision is and its constitutional significance. The solicitor considers so-called Henry VIII powers. The provision let a minister rewrite primary legislation by order, which troubled the commentator. Which of the following best describes them?
o: A Henry VIII power is a provision that abolishes the monarchy.
A Henry VIII power allows the courts to strike down Acts of Parliament.
A Henry VIII power lets secondary legislation amend or repeal primary legislation, and is construed strictly.
A Henry VIII power is a type of prerogative power exercised personally by the monarch on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A Henry VIII power is a rule that prevents any amendment of legislation whatsoever.
6.w: A 'Henry VIII power' is a provision in an Act that authorises the amendment or repeal of primary legislation by means of secondary (delegated) legislation. Such powers are constitutionally significant because they allow the executive to change primary law, and the courts construe them strictly.

n.0: A Henry VIII power does not abolish the monarchy.
n.1: It does not give the courts power to strike down Acts.
n.3: It is a statutory delegated power, not a personal prerogative of the monarch.
n.4: It permits, rather than prevents, amendment of legislation.

6.q: A seller offers to sell a piece of machinery to a buyer for £20,000. The buyer writes back saying that they will pay £18,000 for it. The seller replies that they are not prepared to reduce the price and hears nothing further for a few days. The buyer then writes again, saying that on reflection they accept the original price of £20,000 after all, and asserts that there is now a binding contract at that figure. The seller, who has in the meantime found another purchaser, denies that any contract exists. The buyer seeks advice. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer's counter-offer merely paused the original offer, which revived once the seller rejected it.
A binding contract arose at £18,000, because the seller failed to reject that figure quickly enough.
The counter-offer of £18,000 destroyed the original offer, which the buyer could no longer accept.
The original offer of £20,000 remained open, so the buyer's later acceptance created a binding contract.
A binding contract arose at £20,000, because the buyer eventually agreed to the seller's original price.
6.w: A counter-offer rejects and destroys the original offer, which cannot then be accepted later (Hyde v Wrench). By offering £18,000 the buyer rejected the £20,000 offer, so their subsequent purported acceptance of £20,000 was itself only a new offer, which the seller was free to decline.

n.0: A counter-offer destroys the original offer; it does not merely suspend it.
n.1: The seller's silence did not create a contract at the counter-offer figure.
n.3: The original offer did not remain open once it had been met by a counter-offer.
n.4: By the time the buyer agreed to £20,000, that offer had already been destroyed by the counter-offer.

6.q: A court reviewing a public authority's decision that interferes with a Convention right must decide how intensively to scrutinise it. Counsel argues that mere Wednesbury unreasonableness is not the right test where a Convention right is engaged, and that a more structured and intensive assessment applies. A Convention right is engaged by the interference. The intensity of review is in issue. The decision under challenge bites directly on a Convention right, and the claimant argues that the old, deferential unreasonableness standard is simply not searching enough in such a case, pressing the court to subject the interference to a more structured and demanding form of scrutiny. Which of the following best describes the applicable standard?
o: No review at all, because interference with rights is a matter for the executive on these facts.
A review confined to whether the decision-maker acted in good faith.
Only traditional Wednesbury unreasonableness, with no more intensive scrutiny.
Proportionality, a more intensive and structured review than traditional Wednesbury unreasonableness.
A pure merits review in which the court substitutes its own decision as of right.
6.w: Where a Convention right is engaged, the court applies a proportionality assessment, which is more intensive and structured than traditional Wednesbury review. It considers whether the objective is sufficiently important, whether the measure is rationally connected to it, whether a less intrusive measure could have been used, and whether a fair balance has been struck.

n.0: There is review; interference with rights is not immune from scrutiny.
n.1: Review is not confined to good faith; proportionality is a structured, substantive test.
n.2: Traditional Wednesbury is not the applicable standard where a Convention right is engaged.
n.4: Proportionality is not a pure merits review; the court does not simply substitute its own view as of right.

6.q: A company wishes to raise capital by allotting new shares to an outside investor. The directors need to know whether they have authority to allot the shares and whether any shareholder approval is required, given the constitution and the Companies Act 2006. The company has more than one class of shares and the articles do not give the directors general authority to allot. The court considers the requirements for a valid allotment of shares. The company had ordinary and preference shares, and the board had no standing allotment authority. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Only the shareholders, and never the directors, may ever allot new shares in the company.
The directors may always allot new shares freely, without any authority or shareholder involvement on these facts.
An allotment of shares requires the prior approval of the company's creditors.
An allotment is valid only if the new investor is an existing member of the company.
The directors need authority to allot, which may require shareholder approval where the articles do not confer it.
6.w: Directors may only allot shares if authorised to do so — by the articles or by ordinary resolution of the members — except that directors of a private company with only one class of shares may generally allot without further authority unless the articles restrict it. Where such authority is absent, shareholder approval is required.

n.0: Directors can allot where duly authorised; it is not reserved solely to shareholders.
n.1: Directors cannot always allot freely; authority is required.
n.2: Creditor approval is not required for an allotment.
n.3: Shares can be allotted to new investors, not only existing members.

6.q: A company has more than one class of shares, and the rights attached to one class (for example preference shares) are to be altered in a way that affects that class specifically. The holders of the affected class are concerned that their special rights could be changed without their agreement. The court considers the protection given to a class of shareholders when their class rights are to be varied under the Companies Act 2006. The preference shareholders feared that their fixed dividend rights were about to be watered down. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Class rights may be varied by an ordinary resolution of the company as a whole.
Class rights may generally be varied only with the consent of the required proportion of that class of shareholders.
Class rights may be varied only with the unanimous consent of every shareholder in the company on these facts.
Class rights may be varied by the directors alone whenever they consider it appropriate.
Class rights can never be varied once they have been attached to a class of shares.
6.w: The rights attached to a class of shares may be varied only in accordance with the variation of class rights procedure — generally requiring the consent in writing of holders of at least three-quarters in nominal value of the class, or a special resolution passed at a separate class meeting — protecting the affected class.

n.0: An ordinary resolution of the whole company is not sufficient to vary a class's rights.
n.2: Unanimity of every shareholder is not required; the class consent threshold governs.
n.3: Directors cannot vary class rights alone.
n.4: Class rights can be varied through the proper procedure; they are not immutable.

6.q: Part-way through a straightforward matter, a solicitor becomes frustrated with a client who is slow to respond to requests for information, and decides that they would simply rather not continue acting for that client. There is no conflict of interest, the client is fully up to date with the firm's bills, and there is nothing at all improper about the instructions the client has given; the solicitor has just lost enthusiasm for the work. The solicitor proposes to stop acting straight away, without any notice, leaving the client to find another firm. The solicitor asks whether they may terminate the retainer in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may only cease acting where there is good reason to do so and on giving the client reasonable notice.
The solicitor may never cease acting once instructed, and must see every matter through to its conclusion.
The solicitor may cease acting at any time and for any reason, as a retainer is terminable instantly at will.
The solicitor may cease acting immediately, provided the client is sent a final bill for the work done so far.
The solicitor may cease acting without notice, provided another firm has already agreed to take the matter on.
6.w: A solicitor may only stop acting for a client where there is good reason to do so and on reasonable notice, so as not to leave the client's interests unprotected. Mere reluctance to continue, without good reason or notice, does not justify terminating the retainer.

n.1: A solicitor is not bound to continue in every case; they may cease acting for good reason on notice.
n.2: A retainer is not terminable instantly at will for any reason; good reason and reasonable notice are required.
n.3: Sending a final bill does not, by itself, satisfy the requirements of good reason and reasonable notice.
n.4: Another firm's willingness to take over does not dispense with the need for good reason and proper notice.

6.q: Two people take a transfer of land to hold as joint tenants. For a joint tenancy of the legal (and beneficial) estate to exist, four characteristics must be present in their ownership. The co-owners hold together rather than in distinct shares. The question concerns the requirements for a joint tenancy. The two co-owners have taken a transfer of the property intending to hold it together as joint tenants rather than in distinct shares, and, to be sure a joint tenancy has genuinely arisen, they want to know the set of conditions their co-ownership must satisfy. Which of the following best describes the 'four unities' required for a joint tenancy?
o: Unity of price, purpose, place and person.
Unity of registration, occupation, payment and intention.
Unity of possession, interest, title and time.
Unity of survivorship, severance, shares and sale.
Unity of possession alone, the other unities being irrelevant.
6.w: A joint tenancy requires the four unities: unity of possession (each is entitled to possession of the whole), unity of interest (their interests are identical in nature, extent and duration), unity of title (they derive title from the same document or act), and unity of time (their interests vest at the same time). A tenancy in common requires only unity of possession.

n.0: 'Price, purpose, place and person' are not the four unities.
n.1: 'Registration, occupation, payment and intention' are not the four unities.
n.3: 'Survivorship, severance, shares and sale' are not the four unities.
n.4: A joint tenancy needs all four unities, not just unity of possession.

6.q: In the course of a hard-fought piece of civil litigation, a solicitor repeatedly misses court-imposed deadlines and turns up to hearings without having prepared properly, causing several hearings to be adjourned and putting the opposing party to significant additional and entirely unnecessary legal costs. The opposing party is understandably aggrieved by all this and applies to the court for an order that the solicitor personally, rather than the solicitor's own client, should bear the extra costs that the solicitor's conduct has caused. The court considers the application. Which of the following best describes the court's power?
o: The court has no power to order a solicitor personally to pay costs, which can only ever fall on the litigant client.
The court may order the solicitor to pay costs only where the solicitor is shown to have acted dishonestly.
The court may order the solicitor to pay costs only if the client first formally complains about the solicitor's conduct.
The court may make a wasted costs order against the solicitor personally for their improper, unreasonable or negligent conduct.
The court may penalise the solicitor only by reporting the matter to the SRA, and not by any order for costs.
6.w: Under the court's wasted costs jurisdiction, a legal representative may be ordered to pay costs personally where those costs have been caused by the representative's improper, unreasonable or negligent act or omission. Dishonesty is not required.

n.0: The court can order a legal representative personally to pay wasted costs; the liability is not confined to the client.
n.1: Improper, unreasonable or negligent conduct suffices; dishonesty need not be shown.
n.2: A wasted costs order does not depend on a prior complaint by the client.
n.4: A wasted costs order is itself a costs sanction, separate from any regulatory referral.

6.q: A testator has a valid will, and later wishes to make some changes to it without making an entirely new will. They execute a separate document, properly signed and witnessed, which amends certain provisions of the existing will while leaving the rest in place. The executor asks about the status and effect of this supplementary document. The court considers codicils and their effect on a will. The testator wanted only to tweak a couple of legacies rather than rewrite the whole will. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A codicil is a supplementary testamentary document that amends the will and, on execution, republishes it as at the codicil's date.
A codicil can only reduce gifts in a will and can never add new ones.
A codicil has no legal effect unless it is written on the same piece of paper as the will on these facts as a general rule.
A codicil need not be signed or witnessed, unlike a will.
A codicil automatically revokes the entire existing will and replaces it in full.
6.w: A codicil is a testamentary document, executed with the same formalities as a will, which adds to, varies or partially revokes an existing will. It leaves the rest of the will in force, and on execution it 'republishes' the will as at the date of the codicil.

n.1: A codicil can add, vary or revoke provisions, not only reduce gifts.
n.2: A codicil need not be on the same paper as the will.
n.3: A codicil must be executed with will formalities (signed and witnessed).
n.4: A codicil amends rather than automatically revokes the whole will.

6.q: A person has died leaving a valid will which appoints a named executor who is willing and able to act. The executor needs formal authority to deal with the deceased's assets, such as to sell property and collect in bank accounts. The executor asks what document confers that authority where there is a valid will and a willing executor. The court considers the appropriate grant of representation in these circumstances. The executor was ready and willing to act and needed authority to sell the deceased's house. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The executor obtains a grant of probate, which confirms their authority to administer the estate under the will.
The executor needs no grant at all and may deal with every asset without any authority on these facts.
The executor obtains letters of administration with the will annexed.
The executor must apply to the Court of Protection for authority to act.
The executor obtains letters of administration, as used where there is no valid will.
6.w: Where the deceased left a valid will appointing an executor who is willing and able to act, the appropriate grant is a grant of probate, which confirms the executor's authority (deriving from the will) to administer the estate.

n.1: A grant is generally needed to deal with many assets; the executor cannot ignore it.
n.2: Letters of administration with the will annexed are used where there is a will but no proving executor.
n.3: The Court of Protection deals with living persons lacking capacity, not deceased estates.
n.4: Letters of administration are for cases without a proving executor, e.g. intestacy.

6.q: A dispute arises about the relationship between an Act of Parliament and a rule of the common law developed by the courts. The Act, validly passed, contains a clear provision that is inconsistent with the pre-existing common law rule. A party argues the court should prefer the common law. The Act is clear and unambiguous. The judge-made rule had governed this area for many years until Parliament legislated, and the statute now says something plainly at odds with it, leaving the court to decide which source of law must give way where a clear statute and an established common law rule cannot both stand. Which of the following best describes the position under the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty?
o: The common law rule prevails because it is older and judge-made.
The Act of Parliament prevails over the inconsistent common law rule.
The Act is invalid because it conflicts with the common law.
The two rules apply equally and the party may select either.
The court may choose whichever rule it considers fairer.
6.w: Under the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty, Parliament is the supreme law-making body. A clear and valid Act of Parliament prevails over any inconsistent rule of the common law; the courts give effect to the statute. The common law can be overridden or altered by statute.

n.0: The common law does not prevail over a clear inconsistent statute merely because it is older.
n.2: An Act is not invalid for conflicting with the common law; statute overrides common law.
n.3: The rules do not apply equally; the statute takes precedence.
n.4: The court must give effect to the statute, not simply choose the rule it prefers.

6.q: A claimant suffers personal injuries in an accident caused by the defendant's negligence and wishes to bring a claim. A significant period has passed since the accident, and the claimant is unsure whether they are still in time. They need to know the limitation period that applies specifically to a personal injury claim and the date from which it runs. The court considers the limitation period for personal injury claims under the Limitation Act 1980. The claimant had spent a long time recovering from the injuries before turning to legal action. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A personal injury claim must always be brought within one year of the accident occurring on these facts as a general rule.
A personal injury claim must generally be brought within three years of the injury or of the claimant's date of knowledge.
A personal injury claim must be brought within six years of the date of the accident.
A personal injury claim may be brought at any time, as there is no limitation period.
A personal injury claim must be brought within twelve years of the date of the accident.
6.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the limitation period for a personal injury claim is three years, running from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the claimant's date of knowledge, subject to the court's discretion to disapply the period.

n.0: The period is three years, not one year.
n.2: Six years is the ordinary contract/tort period, not the personal injury period.
n.3: There is a limitation period for personal injury claims.
n.4: Twelve years does not apply to personal injury claims.

6.q: A trustee of a trust is also a director of a company, and an opportunity arises in which the trustee's personal interests, or the interests of the company, come into conflict with the interests of the trust and its beneficiaries. The trustee proceeds to act in the matter without the authority of the trust instrument, the beneficiaries or the court. A beneficiary complains that the trustee has breached a fundamental fiduciary obligation. The opportunity was potentially very profitable, both for the company and for the trustee personally. Which of the following best describes the rule the trustee has broken?
o: A trustee may prefer their own interests provided the trust suffers no measurable loss.
A trustee owes no fiduciary duties at all where they are also a company director.
A trustee must not place themselves in a position where their duty and their interest conflict, without authority.
A trustee may act despite a conflict provided they act in what they think is good faith.
A trustee is free to act in any matter, even where their interest conflicts with the trust's on these facts.
6.w: A core fiduciary duty of a trustee is the no-conflict rule: a trustee must not, without authority, place themselves in a position where their personal interest (or a duty to another) conflicts, or may conflict, with their duty to the trust and its beneficiaries.

n.0: The no-conflict rule applies regardless of whether loss results.
n.1: Being a company director does not remove the trustee's fiduciary duties.
n.3: Good faith does not authorise acting in a position of conflict.
n.4: A trustee is not free to act where their interest conflicts with the trust's.

6.q: A client needs an advocate to conduct a trial in the Crown Court. The client is aware that both solicitors and barristers exist but is unclear about who may appear as an advocate in the higher courts. The client asks about rights of audience. The matter will be heard in the Crown Court. The client has been told that lawyers in England and Wales come in more than one kind and is unsure whether the person who advises on a case is necessarily the same person who can stand up and argue it in the higher courts, so wants the position on who may act as an advocate spelt out. Which of the following best describes the position on rights of audience in the higher courts?
o: Only solicitors may appear as advocates in the higher courts.
Only barristers may ever appear as advocates in any court in England and Wales.
Barristers have rights of audience in the higher courts, and solicitors may obtain higher rights as solicitor advocates.
Neither solicitors nor barristers may appear; only the client may address the court on these facts as a general rule.
Rights of audience in the higher courts are granted only by the Supreme Court.
6.w: Barristers traditionally have full rights of audience in all courts, including the higher courts. Solicitors have rights of audience in the lower courts and may obtain higher rights of audience, qualifying as solicitor advocates able to appear in the higher courts. Rights of audience are regulated by the approved regulators.

n.0: Rights of audience in the higher courts are not confined to solicitors.
n.1: Solicitors can obtain higher rights of audience, so advocacy is not confined to barristers.
n.3: Qualified advocates, not only the client, may address the court.
n.4: Rights of audience are granted through the regulatory framework, not by the Supreme Court.

6.q: A solicitor negligently fails to issue a client's personal injury claim before the limitation period expires, with the result that the client's otherwise strong claim becomes statute-barred and worthless. The client sues the solicitor. The solicitor accepts the mistake but argues that, because the client never actually obtained any judgment in the original claim, the client cannot show they have suffered any recoverable loss. The client seeks advice on the basis of a claim against the solicitor. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor is liable only in contract, and the client can recover nothing in the tort of negligence.
The solicitor is liable only if the client can now still bring the original claim despite the limitation bar.
The solicitor has no liability, because the client never obtained a judgment in the original claim.
The solicitor is liable in professional negligence for the value of the lost, time-barred claim.
The solicitor has no liability, because missing a limitation date is never regarded as negligent.
6.w: A solicitor owes their client a duty to exercise reasonable care and skill. Allowing a good claim to become statute-barred is a breach, and the client's recoverable loss is assessed by reference to the value of the claim that has been lost (its prospects and likely value).

n.0: The client may sue in tort as well as contract for the solicitor's negligence.
n.1: The loss arises precisely because the original claim is now barred; that is the damage.
n.2: The lost claim is the recoverable loss; a prior judgment is not required.
n.4: Missing a limitation date through carelessness is a classic example of negligence.

6.q: A firm's cashier prepares the periodic client account reconciliation, comparing the bank statement, the client cash account and the total of the client ledger balances. A junior member of staff asks whether the cashier can simply file the completed reconciliation once it balances, or whether anyone else must review it. The firm is an authorised body. The firm wants to be confident its client money controls are robust and that responsibility for oversight does not rest solely with the person who compiles the figures, so the question of who must review and approve each completed reconciliation has become a live governance point in the review. Which of the following best describes the requirement about approving the reconciliation under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The reconciliation must be approved by the firm's external accountant each time.
The reconciliation must be signed off by the COFA or a manager of the firm.
The reconciliation may be filed by the cashier alone once it balances.
The reconciliation must be sent to the SRA for approval each time.
The reconciliation must be signed off by the client whose money is held.
6.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require that each client account reconciliation is signed off by the COFA or a manager of the firm. This provides independent oversight of client money, so that discrepancies are identified and investigated by someone with responsibility, rather than the reconciliation resting solely with the person who prepared it.

n.0: The external accountant reports periodically but need not approve each reconciliation.
n.2: The reconciliation cannot simply be filed by the cashier who prepared it.
n.3: Reconciliations are not routinely sent to the SRA for approval.
n.4: The client does not sign off the firm's internal reconciliation.

6.q: A firm needs to pay a Land Registry fee of £300 on a client's behalf. To avoid delay, the firm pays the £300 from its office account before it has received any money from the client to cover it. The firm later expects to be reimbursed for the disbursement. The cashier considers how this is treated under the SRA Accounts Rules. The fee was payable to a third party to progress the registration without delay, the client had not yet put the firm in funds for it, and the firm chose to advance the cost itself, meaning the cashier must decide how the payment and its later recovery are correctly recorded. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment?
o: The firm must treat the £300 as client money even though it came from the office account.
The firm may recover the £300 from client money without ever notifying the client of the cost on these facts as a general rule.
The firm may pay the disbursement from office money and later recover it from the client by a bill or from client money held.
The firm must never pay a client's disbursement from office money in any circumstances.
The firm may reimburse itself from another client's money in the client account.
6.w: A firm may meet a client's disbursement out of its own office money if it wishes, effectively advancing the cost. It then recovers the sum from the client, either by including it in a bill or by reimbursing itself from client money held for that client once available, with the disbursement properly notified to the client.

n.0: Money paid out of the office account is office money, not client money.
n.1: The disbursement must be properly notified to and recoverable from the client, not taken silently.
n.3: Paying a disbursement from office money is permitted, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: Another client's money cannot be used to reimburse the firm.

6.q: By a deed, a landowner granted the owner of the neighbouring house 'a right of way on foot' over a lane running across the landowner's field. For years the neighbour used the lane only to walk to and from the road. The neighbour has now built a garage beside the house and wishes to drive cars along the lane to reach it, which would involve regular vehicular use of the lane. The landowner objects that the grant was for access on foot only, while the neighbour argues that a right of way permits any reasonable means of access. Which of the following best describes the neighbour's rights?
o: The right is limited to access on foot, and driving vehicles falls outside the express grant.
The right extends to any reasonable use, including vehicular access to the garage.
The right is void for uncertainty, because it did not specify the type of vehicles allowed.
The right entitles the neighbour to vehicular access, provided it does not increase the burden.
The right automatically expands to vehicular use once the dominant land is developed.
6.w: An express easement is construed by its grant. A right of way 'on foot' is confined to pedestrian access; using it for vehicles exceeds the grant and is actionable, regardless of later development of the dominant land.

n.1: An express easement does not confer all reasonable uses; it is limited to what was granted.
n.2: A pedestrian right of way is certain; it is simply limited to access on foot.
n.3: The test is the scope of the grant, not merely whether the burden increases.
n.4: Development of the dominant land does not automatically enlarge the scope of an express right.

6.q: When rebuilding a garden wall along the boundary with the neighbouring registered property, Mr Croft built the new wall several feet over the boundary, so that it now stands on a strip of his neighbour Ms Dalby's registered land. The wall has been up for only a few months. Ms Dalby wants the wall taken down and the strip restored to her, but Mr Croft argues that she has suffered no real financial loss and that, at most, she should be paid a small sum and leave the wall where it is. Ms Dalby seeks advice on the most appropriate remedy. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: An injunction requiring removal of the encroaching wall, with damages in lieu available at the court's discretion.
Nothing, because the neighbour acquired title to the strip by adverse possession the very moment the encroaching wall was built.
Damages only, because an injunction is never available for a boundary encroachment.
Nothing, unless the claimant can prove a specific financial loss caused by the wall.
An order transferring the encroached strip to the neighbour on payment of its market value.
6.w: An encroachment is a continuing trespass to land. The primary remedy is an injunction to remove it, though the court has a discretion to award damages in lieu (Jaggard v Sawyer). Trespass is actionable without proof of loss.

n.1: Adverse possession requires long possession and, for registered land, the LRA 2002 procedure; it is not instant.
n.2: An injunction is available and usual for encroachment; damages are not the only remedy.
n.3: Trespass is actionable per se, so the claim does not depend on proving financial loss.
n.4: The court does not force the claimant to sell the strip to the trespasser.

6.q: A party is dissatisfied with a first-instance decision and wishes to challenge it in a higher court. They believe they can appeal automatically as of right, simply because they disagree with the outcome. They ask about the requirements for bringing an appeal and the grounds on which an appeal may succeed. The court considers appeals in civil proceedings under the Civil Procedure Rules. The party felt the judge had misapplied the law and wanted the decision overturned on appeal. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Permission to appeal is generally required, and an appeal succeeds only if the decision was wrong or unjust due to serious procedural irregularity.
An appeal will succeed whenever the appeal court would itself have reached a different view.
There is no right of appeal against any first-instance decision in civil proceedings.
A party may appeal automatically as of right simply because they disagree with the decision.
An appeal is a complete re-hearing at which fresh evidence is always heard as a matter of course on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
6.w: Permission to appeal is generally required (from the lower court or the appeal court), granted where there is a real prospect of success or some other compelling reason. An appeal is usually a review, not a re-hearing, and will be allowed only where the decision was wrong, or unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity.

n.1: Mere disagreement or that the appeal court might differ is not the test; the decision must be wrong or unjust.
n.2: There is a route of appeal, subject to permission.
n.3: There is no automatic right of appeal merely on disagreement; permission is generally needed.
n.4: An appeal is usually a review, not a full re-hearing with fresh evidence as of right.

6.q: Parliament has conferred power on a minister to make regulations by statutory instrument. The relevant Act provides that such regulations are to be laid before Parliament and will become law unless either House passes a resolution to annul them within the prescribed period. No positive vote of approval is required. The minister makes regulations accordingly. The Act allows the minister to legislate by statutory instrument and sets the terms on which Parliament will scrutinise the result, providing that the instrument stands as law once laid unless one of the Houses moves within the prescribed period to strike it down, without any need for a positive vote. Which of the following best describes the parliamentary control procedure being used?
o: The super-affirmative resolution procedure.
A hybrid instrument procedure.
The affirmative resolution procedure.
The negative resolution procedure.
The Royal Assent procedure for primary legislation.
6.w: Under the negative resolution procedure, a statutory instrument is laid before Parliament and becomes (or remains) law unless it is annulled by a resolution of either House within the prescribed period (commonly 40 sitting days). No affirmative vote of approval is needed; the instrument takes effect unless objected to.

n.0: The super-affirmative procedure involves enhanced scrutiny beyond a simple approval vote.
n.1: A hybrid instrument procedure applies to instruments affecting particular private interests differently.
n.2: The affirmative procedure requires a positive vote of approval, which is not the case here.
n.4: Royal Assent is part of the process for primary legislation, not delegated legislation.

6.q: A trespasser climbs over a fence onto industrial premises at night and is injured by a dangerous piece of machinery. The occupier knew the machinery was dangerous, knew that people sometimes climbed in at that point, and could readily have offered some protection against the risk. The injured person was not a lawful visitor. The occupier was aware of the danger and of the likelihood of trespassers coming into its vicinity. There had been previous incidents of people getting into the yard at that spot, the machine was left accessible and unguarded, and the occupier was well aware both of how dangerous it was and that intruders were apt to come near it, yet took no steps to fence it off or warn. Which of the following best describes when the occupier owes a duty to the trespasser under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984?
o: A duty arises where the occupier is aware of the danger, knows a trespasser may come, and it is reasonable to offer protection.
The occupier owes a trespasser exactly the same common duty of care as a lawful visitor on these facts as a general rule.
A duty arises automatically whenever any trespasser is injured on the premises.
A duty arises only if the occupier deliberately intended to injure the trespasser.
No duty is ever owed to a trespasser, whatever the occupier knew or could have done.
6.w: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, an occupier owes a duty to a non-visitor if it is aware of the danger (or has reasonable grounds to believe it exists), knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the trespasser may come into its vicinity, and the risk is one against which, in all the circumstances, it may reasonably be expected to offer some protection. Those conditions are satisfied here.

n.1: The duty owed to trespassers is narrower than the common duty owed to lawful visitors.
n.2: The duty does not arise automatically on any injury; the statutory conditions must be met.
n.3: The duty does not require an intention to injure; it turns on knowledge and reasonableness.
n.4: A duty can be owed to trespassers under the 1984 Act, so 'never' is wrong.

6.q: A defendant made a confession to the police, but the defence alleges that it was obtained by oppression, or in circumstances likely to render it unreliable. The prosecution wishes to rely on the confession at trial. The defendant's solicitor seeks to have the confession ruled inadmissible. The solicitor considers the exclusion of a confession under section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The defendant said the confession had been beaten out of them during a long, aggressive interview. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The defence must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the confession was unreliable on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A confession is always admissible once it has been made, however it was obtained.
The court must exclude the confession if it may have been obtained by oppression or be unreliable, unless the prosecution disproves this.
A confession can be excluded only if the police acted in bad faith deliberately.
The court may exclude a confession only if the defendant later pleads not guilty.
6.w: Under s.76 PACE 1984, where it is represented that a confession was or may have been obtained by oppression, or in consequence of anything said or done likely to render it unreliable, the court must not allow it to be given in evidence unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that it was not so obtained.

n.0: The prosecution must prove the confession was not so obtained; the burden is not on the defence.
n.1: A confession is not always admissible; s.76 provides for exclusion.
n.3: Exclusion does not require deliberate bad faith; unreliability suffices.
n.4: Exclusion under s.76 does not depend on the plea.

6.q: A supplier and a manufacturer enter a contract under which the manufacturer is to deliver goods and be paid in monthly instalments as each batch is delivered and accepted, each delivery being separately priced. After several batches have been delivered, paid for and accepted without complaint, a dispute arises over one later batch. The manufacturer argues that, because the contract is a single overall agreement, any problem with one batch entitles it to be paid for none of them. The supplier disputes this analysis of the contract. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The obligations are likely divisible, so payment is earned batch by batch as each delivery is completed.
The contract is entire, so the manufacturer must repay everything already received for earlier batches.
The contract is divisible only if it expressly uses the word 'severable' in its wording.
The obligations are entire, because any contract for a series of deliveries is treated as a single whole.
The contract is entire, so no payment at all is earned unless every batch is delivered without any issue.
6.w: Where a contract provides for separate deliveries to be separately priced and paid for as they are made, the obligations are divisible (severable). Payment is earned for each completed and accepted delivery, and a problem with one instalment does not defeat payment for the others.

n.1: Divisible obligations already earned do not have to be repaid because of a later dispute.
n.2: Divisibility depends on the structure of the obligations, not on using the word 'severable'.
n.3: A series of separately priced deliveries is not automatically treated as a single entire obligation.
n.4: The contract is not entire; separately priced deliveries make the obligations divisible.

6.q: A document drawn up between a landlord and a tenant purports to grant the tenant a lease of shop premises 'for the duration of the war', and fixes no other date, event or maximum period by reference to which the term is to come to an end. A rent is reserved and paid monthly, and the tenant has gone into occupation and traded from the premises. A dispute has now arisen between the parties over the status of the arrangement, and in particular whether a valid lease for a term of years was ever created by a grant framed in this open-ended way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A valid lease arises, because the end of the war provides a sufficiently certain end date.
No valid term of years arises, because a lease must have a certain maximum duration.
A fee simple arises, because an uncertain lease is automatically upgraded to freehold.
An easement arises, giving the tenant a right to occupy until the war ends.
A valid lease arises, because the parties clearly intended a tenancy to exist between them.
6.w: A lease must have a certain maximum duration, ascertainable at the outset. A term 'for the duration of the war' is uncertain and does not create a valid term of years (Lace v Chantler; Prudential Assurance v London Residuary Body), although a periodic tenancy may arise from entry and payment of rent.

n.0: The end of the war is not ascertainable in advance, so the term is uncertain.
n.2: An uncertain lease is not converted into a freehold estate.
n.3: A right to exclusive possession for a term is a lease question, not an easement.
n.4: Intention to create a tenancy cannot cure the lack of certainty of maximum duration.

6.q: A company stores a large quantity of a hazardous liquid in tanks on its industrial site as part of a non-ordinary use of the land. Through no negligence on its part, the liquid escapes and floods neighbouring land, causing damage of a kind that was a foreseeable consequence of such an escape. The neighbour sues under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher. The company brought and accumulated the substance for its own purposes in a non-natural use of the land, and it escaped. Which of the following best sets out what the claimant must establish under that rule?
o: That the defendant was negligent in allowing the dangerous thing to escape.
That the dangerous thing was naturally present on the land before it escaped.
That the defendant intended the dangerous thing to escape onto the neighbour's land on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
That the defendant brought and accumulated a dangerous thing in a non-natural use of land, which escaped and caused foreseeable damage.
That the escape caused only pure economic loss to the neighbour.
6.w: Under Rylands v Fletcher (a form of strict liability), the claimant must show the defendant brought onto and accumulated on its land a thing likely to do mischief if it escaped, in a non-natural (extraordinary) use of the land, that the thing escaped, and that damage of a foreseeable type resulted. Negligence and intention need not be proved.

n.0: Negligence need not be proved; liability under the rule is strict.
n.1: The thing must be brought onto the land, not naturally present; natural accumulations are excluded.
n.2: Intention to cause the escape is not required.
n.4: The rule addresses property/physical damage from escape, not pure economic loss.

6.q: A contract contains an exclusion clause which is worded in a way that is genuinely ambiguous: on one reading it excludes liability for a particular kind of loss, and on another reading it does not. The party who drafted the clause, and who now seeks to rely on it to avoid liability, argues for the wider reading that would defeat the claim against it. The other party argues for the narrower reading. The court must decide how to resolve the ambiguity in the clause. Which of the following best describes the approach the court will take?
o: The court will simply strike the ambiguous clause out of the contract altogether.
The court will ask the drafting party what it intended the clause to mean and adopt that meaning.
Any ambiguity in the clause is construed in favour of the party seeking to rely on it.
The court will always adopt whichever reading gives the clause the widest possible effect.
Any ambiguity in the clause is construed against the party seeking to rely on it.
6.w: Under the contra proferentem principle, an ambiguous exclusion or limitation clause is construed against the party who put it forward and seeks to rely on it, so the narrower interpretation that preserves liability is generally preferred where the wording is genuinely unclear.

n.0: The court construes the clause; it does not simply delete it for ambiguity.
n.1: The drafting party's subjective account of intention does not govern the construction.
n.2: Ambiguity is resolved against, not in favour of, the party relying on the clause.
n.3: The court does not automatically give an ambiguous exclusion its widest effect.

6.q: A contract for the sale of a residential property requires the seller to give the buyer vacant possession on completion. Shortly before completion, the buyer's solicitor is concerned that other people may be living at the property who could remain after completion. The contract requires vacant possession on completion. The buyer's solicitor is checking the position on occupiers. The contract obliges the seller to hand the property over with vacant possession, but the buyer's solicitor has picked up hints that other people may be living there, and is anxious to establish exactly what the seller must deliver and why the presence of any occupier could matter to the buyer. Which of the following best describes what vacant possession requires and why the occupier check matters?
o: The seller must give up the property empty of people, possessions and legal occupiers, so occupiers with rights must be dealt with before completion.
Vacant possession requires only that the furniture be removed, not the people.
Occupiers are irrelevant because their rights end automatically on completion.
Vacant possession merely requires the seller to hand over the keys, whoever is living there on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Vacant possession is satisfied so long as the seller personally has moved out.
6.w: An obligation to give vacant possession requires the seller to hand over the property free of people, chattels and any legal right of occupation, so that the buyer can take actual, unimpeded possession on completion. Occupiers with interests could be overriding interests binding the buyer, so the solicitor must ensure any such occupiers are dealt with (for example, by obtaining releases) before completion.

n.1: Vacant possession requires the removal of people and their right to occupy, not merely furniture.
n.2: Occupiers' rights do not automatically end on completion; they may bind the buyer.
n.3: Vacant possession is more than handing over keys; the property must be free of occupiers and possessions.
n.4: It is not enough that the seller alone has moved out if others with rights remain.

6.q: A buyer's solicitor is checking the seller's capacity to sell, because the property is not being sold by a single individual absolute owner but by two co-owners holding on trust, one of whom has since died. The solicitor is concerned to ensure the buyer takes free of any beneficial interests. The solicitor considers how a buyer takes free of the beneficial interests of co-owners. The property had been in the joint names of a couple, one of whom had recently died. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer can never take free of the beneficial interests of co-owners in any circumstances.
The buyer must obtain the written consent of every beneficiary before completing the purchase.
The buyer takes free of beneficial interests automatically, whoever the money is paid to.
The buyer takes free of beneficial interests only if the purchase price is paid to a single surviving co-owner on these facts as a general rule.
The buyer should ensure the purchase money is paid to at least two trustees (or a trust corporation) so that beneficial interests are overreached.
6.w: Where land is held on a trust of land by co-owners, a buyer overreaches the beneficiaries' interests (which are swept off the land onto the proceeds) by paying the purchase money to at least two trustees or a trust corporation. Where one of two co-owners has died, a second trustee may need to be appointed to achieve overreaching.

n.0: The buyer can take free by overreaching through payment to two trustees.
n.1: Overreaching, not each beneficiary's written consent, is the mechanism.
n.2: Overreaching is not automatic regardless of who is paid; two trustees are required.
n.3: Payment to a single surviving co-owner does not overreach beneficial interests behind a trust.

6.q: A defendant of limited means is charged with a criminal offence and wishes to know whether they can obtain publicly funded legal representation. Their solicitor explains that eligibility depends on more than just the defendant's financial position. The defendant faces criminal proceedings. The defendant has very little income but the solicitor is careful to explain that a grant of public funding does not turn on finances alone, since the seriousness of the charge, the risk to the defendant's liberty and the complexity of the case all feed into a separate assessment that must also be satisfied. Which of the following best describes the basis on which criminal legal aid is granted?
o: It is granted automatically to every defendant regardless of circumstances.
It is available only after the defendant has been convicted.
It depends on both a means test and an interests of justice test.
It depends only on whether the offence is triable in the Crown Court.
It depends solely on the defendant's income, with no other requirement.
6.w: Criminal legal aid for representation is generally subject to two requirements: a means test (assessing the defendant's financial resources) and an interests of justice test (considering, for example, whether the defendant risks loss of liberty, the complexity of the case, and the ability to understand proceedings). Both must be satisfied.

n.0: Legal aid is not granted automatically to every defendant.
n.1: Legal aid is to fund representation during proceedings, not only after conviction.
n.3: Eligibility is not determined only by whether the offence is Crown Court triable.
n.4: Income alone is not the sole criterion; the interests of justice test also applies.

6.q: A defendant approaches a victim, uses force by pushing them, and at that moment and in order to do so takes the victim's bag. The prosecution charges robbery. Force was used on the victim at the time of the theft and in order to steal. The theft (appropriation) accompanied the use of force. The defendant came up to the victim in the street, shoved them hard, and in the very act of doing so snatched the bag from their grasp, the push being used precisely so that the defendant could get hold of the property and make off with it. Which of the following best describes the key requirements distinguishing robbery from theft?
o: Robbery requires the use of a weapon during the theft.
Robbery is theft where the defendant uses or threatens force on a person immediately before or at the time of stealing, and in order to steal.
Robbery requires entry into a building as a trespasser.
Robbery requires that the victim suffer actual bodily harm.
Robbery is committed only where force is used after the theft is complete on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
6.w: Robbery (s.8 Theft Act 1968) is committed where a person steals and, immediately before or at the time of doing so and in order to steal, uses force on any person or puts or seeks to put any person in fear of being then and there subjected to force. All the elements of theft must be present, plus the force element used for the purpose of stealing.

n.0: A weapon is not required for robbery; any force (or threat of force) suffices.
n.2: Entry as a trespasser to a building is an element of burglary, not robbery.
n.3: Actual bodily harm is not required; even a small amount of force can suffice.
n.4: The force must be used before or at the time of stealing and in order to steal, not merely afterwards.

6.q: A claimant, having started proceedings, decides that they no longer wish to pursue the claim and want to bring it to an end. They are aware that stopping a claim can have costs consequences. The claimant asks how a claim is brought to an end by the claimant's own choice, and what the usual costs consequence is. The court considers discontinuance of a claim under the Civil Procedure Rules. The claimant had lost confidence in the claim and wanted to stop before incurring further costs. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claimant who discontinues never has to pay any of the defendant's costs at all.
A claim can only be brought to an end by a full trial and judgment on the merits.
A claimant may discontinue only with the permission of the defendant in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A claimant may generally discontinue by filing and serving a notice, and will usually be liable for the defendant's costs to that date.
A claimant can never discontinue a claim once proceedings have been started.
6.w: Under Part 38 CPR, a claimant may generally discontinue all or part of a claim at any time by filing and serving a notice of discontinuance (permission being needed only in certain cases). The usual costs consequence is that the discontinuing claimant is liable for the defendant's costs up to discontinuance.

n.0: Discontinuance usually carries liability for the defendant's costs.
n.1: A claim can be ended by discontinuance, not only by trial and judgment.
n.2: The defendant's permission is not generally required to discontinue.
n.4: A claimant can discontinue; it is not impossible once proceedings start.

6.q: A tenant of premises has committed a breach of a covenant in the lease (other than non-payment of rent), and the landlord wishes to forfeit the lease and recover possession. Before taking steps to forfeit, the landlord's solicitor advises that a particular statutory notice must first be served on the tenant. The tenant asks what the landlord must do before forfeiting for such a breach. The solicitor considers the procedure for forfeiture for breach of a non-rent covenant. The tenant had altered the premises in serious breach of covenant and refused to put matters right. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The landlord may forfeit immediately for any breach without giving the tenant any notice at all on these facts as a general rule.
The landlord may forfeit only by physically evicting the tenant without any legal process.
The landlord must first serve a notice under s.146 Law of Property Act 1925 specifying the breach and allowing time to remedy it.
The landlord must obtain the tenant's written consent before forfeiting the lease.
The landlord must apply to the Land Registry to cancel the tenant's leasehold title.
6.w: To forfeit a lease for breach of a covenant other than payment of rent, the landlord must first serve a notice under s.146 Law of Property Act 1925 specifying the breach, requiring it to be remedied (if capable of remedy) and, where appropriate, requiring compensation, giving the tenant a reasonable time to comply before forfeiture is pursued (and the tenant may seek relief).

n.0: A s.146 notice is required first; the landlord cannot forfeit immediately without notice for a non-rent breach.
n.1: Forfeiture must follow the proper legal process, not self-help eviction of residential tenants.
n.3: The tenant's written consent is not the requirement; a s.146 notice is.
n.4: Forfeiture is not effected by cancelling the leasehold title at the Land Registry.

6.q: A defendant is to stand trial, and the prosecution holds material gathered during the investigation which it does not intend to use as evidence, some of which might undermine the prosecution case or assist the defence. The defendant's solicitor wants to ensure this material is disclosed. The solicitor considers the prosecution's duty of disclosure of unused material under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996. Some of the material the police had gathered plainly pointed away from the defendant's guilt. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The prosecution has no duty to disclose anything to the defence at any stage.
The prosecution must disclose unused material only after the trial has concluded.
The prosecution must disclose unused material that might reasonably undermine its case or assist the defence.
The prosecution must disclose only material that strengthens the prosecution case.
The prosecution need only disclose the evidence it intends to rely on and nothing else on these facts.
6.w: Under the CPIA 1996, the prosecution is under a duty to disclose to the defence any material in its possession which has not been used as evidence and which might reasonably be considered capable of undermining the prosecution case or of assisting the defence case.

n.0: There is a statutory duty of disclosure to the defence.
n.1: Disclosure is made before trial to allow a fair trial, not after it.
n.3: The duty concerns material undermining the prosecution or assisting the defence, not material that strengthens the prosecution.
n.4: Disclosure extends to relevant unused material, not just the used evidence.

6.q: A firm is asked to act for both the seller and the buyer in the same conveyancing transaction.
