The firm considers whether it may act for both parties given their opposing interests in the transaction. The two clients are on opposite sides of the same transaction. Their interests conflict. The firm is asked to handle the same conveyancing transaction for both the seller and the buyer at once, two clients whose interests in the deal are directly opposed, and it must decide whether it can properly act for both of them or whether the conflict rules stand in the way. Which of the following best describes the firm's position?
o: The firm may act for both only if neither party is legally represented elsewhere.
There is a conflict of interest, so the firm generally must not act for both, unless a recognised exception with safeguards applies.
The firm may act for both provided it charges only one set of fees.
The firm may always act for both buyer and seller to save costs.
The firm may act for both because conveyancing is administrative rather than adversarial on these facts as a general rule.
6.w: Acting for both the seller and buyer in the same transaction generally involves a conflict of interest, because their interests conflict, so the firm must not act for both unless one of the conflict exceptions applies (substantially common interest or competing for the same objective) with the required safeguards, including informed consent. Even then, acting must be reasonable.

n.0: Whether the parties are represented elsewhere does not, by itself, permit acting for both.
n.2: Charging a single fee does not resolve the conflict of interest.
n.3: The firm cannot always act for both merely to save costs; a conflict generally prevents it.
n.4: Conveyancing can involve genuinely conflicting interests; it is not merely administrative.

6.q: A purchaser of registered land buys for valuable consideration and completes the registrable disposition by registration. Before the purchase there was a third-party interest that was not protected by any notice or restriction on the register and was not an overriding interest. The buyer took a registered disposition for value; the third-party interest was unprotected. The buyer wants to know the effect on that interest. The buyer is paying full market value and will complete the transfer by registration, and it has emerged that a third party held some interest in the land beforehand which was never entered on the register and does not fall within any category of overriding interest, so the buyer wants to know where that leaves it. Which of the following best describes the position under the Land Registration Act 2002?
o: The unprotected interest is converted into an overriding interest on completion.
The buyer takes subject to every prior interest whether protected or not.
The unprotected interest automatically binds the buyer regardless of registration on these facts.
The registered disposition for value postpones (takes priority over) the unprotected interest.
Priority is decided solely by which interest was created first in time.
6.w: Under s.29 of the Land Registration Act 2002, on the registration of a registrable disposition made for valuable consideration, the priority of any interest affecting the estate is postponed to the disposition unless it was protected (by notice or as an overriding interest) at the time of registration. So an unprotected, non-overriding interest is postponed to the buyer.

n.0: An unprotected interest is not converted into an overriding interest by completion.
n.1: The buyer for value does not take subject to unprotected interests that are not overriding.
n.2: An unprotected, non-overriding interest does not automatically bind the buyer for value.
n.4: For registered dispositions for value, the s.29 priority rule, not simply first in time, governs.

6.q: A firm concluded a client's matter some time ago and rendered its final bill, which the client duly paid in full. A modest balance of the client's own money nonetheless remains sitting in the firm's client account, and there is now no outstanding work, unpaid disbursement or any other proper reason for the firm to continue holding on to it. The money simply stays in the client account, month after month, without ever being dealt with. The firm's compliance officer reviews the client ledger and raises the outstanding balance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may simply transfer the residual balance to its own office account to tidy up the ledger.
The firm must return the residual balance to the client promptly once there is no longer any proper reason to hold it.
The firm may retain the balance permanently, provided it pays the client a small amount of interest.
The firm may keep the residual balance in its client account indefinitely, as it belongs to the client anyway.
The firm need only return the balance if and when the former client actually asks for it back.
6.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require client money to be returned promptly to the client (or the person entitled to it) as soon as there is no longer any proper reason to hold it. Leaving residual balances sitting in the client account indefinitely is a breach.

n.0: The residual balance is the client's money and must not be moved into office account.
n.2: Paying some interest does not entitle the firm to keep money it has no reason to hold.
n.3: The money cannot simply be left in the client account indefinitely; it must be returned promptly.
n.4: The duty to return does not wait for the former client to ask.

6.q: A defendant is to be tried summarily in the magistrates' court for an either-way offence that the magistrates have agreed to keep. On conviction, the magistrates consider the sentence, and the question arises of the maximum custodial sentence the magistrates' court can impose for a single either-way offence. The trial is summary in the magistrates' court. The court is considering its sentencing powers. Having tried and convicted the defendant of an either-way offence it agreed to keep, the magistrates now turn to sentence and confront the fact that the offending looks serious, prompting the bench to check the ceiling on the custodial term they are actually permitted to pass for a single such offence. Which of the following best describes the magistrates' sentencing powers?
o: The magistrates' court may impose up to 10 years' custody for an either-way offence.
The magistrates' court must always commit every convicted defendant to the Crown Court on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The magistrates' court has a limited maximum custodial sentence and must commit to the Crown Court for sentence if greater punishment is needed.
The magistrates' court may impose any length of custodial sentence, including life.
The magistrates' court has no power to impose any custodial sentence at all.
6.w: The magistrates' court's custodial sentencing powers are capped (limited to a statutory maximum per offence, historically six months for a single either-way offence, with a higher aggregate for two). Where the court considers its powers insufficient to reflect the seriousness of the offending, it may commit the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence.

n.0: The cap is far below 10 years for an either-way offence.
n.1: Not every convicted defendant is committed; only where the magistrates' powers are insufficient.
n.3: The magistrates cannot impose any length of sentence, let alone life.
n.4: The magistrates do have power to impose custodial sentences, subject to the cap.

6.q: A member of a company wishes to enforce a provision in the company's articles of association, arguing that the articles create binding legal obligations between the member and the company (and between members). Another member disputes that the articles have contractual effect at all. The provision in question concerns membership rights. The court considers the legal effect of a company's articles of association under the Companies Act 2006. The provision the member relied on concerned their rights as a shareholder in the company. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The articles bind the directors personally but never the members of the company.
The articles are enforceable only by the company, and never by an individual member.
The articles bind only those members who were shareholders when the company was first formed on these facts.
The articles are merely internal guidance with no binding legal effect on anyone.
The articles form a statutory contract between the company and its members, and between the members themselves.
6.w: Under s.33 Companies Act 2006, the provisions of a company's constitution bind the company and its members to the same extent as if there were covenants on the part of the company and each member to observe them. The articles thus take effect as a statutory contract, enforceable in respect of membership rights.

n.0: The statutory contract binds the members, not only the directors.
n.1: Members can enforce membership rights under the articles, not only the company.
n.2: The contract binds current members, not only original ones.
n.3: The articles are not mere guidance; they have binding contractual effect.

6.q: During negotiations to buy a horse from his nephew, a man writes to the nephew saying that, if he hears nothing more, he will consider the horse to be his at a stated price. The nephew does not reply to that letter, but privately tells an auctioneer to keep the horse out of a forthcoming sale because he intends to sell it to his uncle. The auctioneer mistakenly sells the horse anyway, and the uncle claims that a binding contract to buy the horse had already been formed with his nephew by the time of the sale. The uncle seeks advice on whether that is correct. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is a contract, because the uncle validly stipulated that silence would count as acceptance.
There is a contract, because the nephew's silence amounted to acceptance of the uncle's offer.
There is a contract, because the nephew's instruction to the auctioneer was itself the acceptance.
There is no contract, because an offer to buy a horse must always be made in writing signed by both.
There is no contract, because silence cannot be imposed on the nephew as a mode of acceptance.
6.w: An offeror cannot stipulate that the offeree's silence will constitute acceptance; acceptance must generally be communicated (Felthouse v Bindley). The nephew's uncommunicated intention did not create a contract, so no binding agreement had been formed when the horse was sold.

n.0: An offeror cannot validly impose silence as a mode of acceptance on the offeree.
n.1: Silence does not amount to acceptance, even where the offeror purports to treat it as such.
n.2: The nephew's private instruction to the auctioneer was not communicated to the uncle as an acceptance.
n.3: There is no rule requiring a contract for the sale of a horse to be in signed writing.

6.q: A landlord granted a 20-year headlease of a commercial building. The head tenant later breached a covenant in the headlease, and the landlord has now forfeited the headlease for that breach. A sub-tenant, who occupies the second floor of the building under a sub-lease granted out of the headlease, was in no way responsible for the head tenant's breach and has always complied with its own obligations. The forfeiture of the headlease would ordinarily bring the sub-lease to an end as well, leaving the innocent sub-tenant without any premises from which to run its business. The sub-tenant wishes to protect its position and remain in occupation of its part. Which of the following best describes the sub-tenant's position?
o: The sub-tenant has no remedy, because forfeiture of the headlease automatically ends all sub-leases with no relief.
The sub-tenant may prevent the forfeiture of the headlease altogether by paying the head-rent.
The sub-tenant may apply for relief from forfeiture and, if granted, be vested with a new lease of their part.
The sub-tenant may only claim damages from their immediate landlord and cannot keep possession.
The sub-tenant becomes the freeholder's direct tenant automatically on the same terms.
6.w: Forfeiture of a headlease destroys sub-leases derived from it, but a sub-tenant (or mortgagee) may apply for relief under s.146(4) LPA 1925. The court may vest a new lease of the sub-tenant's part in them, usually for no longer than the original sub-term.

n.0: Relief is available to sub-tenants under s.146(4); forfeiture is not the automatic end of their rights.
n.1: A sub-tenant cannot simply prevent forfeiture of the headlease by paying the head-rent.
n.3: Relief can restore possession by a new lease, so the sub-tenant is not confined to damages.
n.4: There is no automatic direct tenancy with the freeholder on forfeiture.

6.q: A solicitor becomes aware of facts which they reasonably believe are capable of amounting to a serious breach of the SRA's regulatory requirements by another solicitor within the same firm, involving the deliberate misuse of money held in the client account. The solicitor is reluctant to become involved, hoping that the firm will quietly deal with the matter internally without any outside scrutiny, and is genuinely unsure whether they are obliged to take the matter beyond the firm at all. The solicitor considers what the regulatory framework requires of them in these circumstances. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor need do nothing, because reporting the conduct of a colleague is always a purely voluntary matter.
The solicitor may stay silent, provided they personally had no involvement in the misuse of the client money.
The solicitor must report the matter to the SRA, as there is a duty to report facts capable of amounting to a serious breach.
The solicitor may wait indefinitely to see whether the firm chooses to deal with the matter internally first.
The solicitor must report the matter only to the firm's managers, and never directly to the regulator itself.
6.w: The SRA Code requires a solicitor to report promptly to the SRA (or another approved regulator) any facts or matters they reasonably believe are capable of amounting to a serious breach of the regulatory arrangements, including breaches by others.

n.0: Reporting a serious breach is a duty, not a purely voluntary matter.
n.1: The duty to report does not depend on the solicitor having been personally involved.
n.3: The obligation is to report promptly, not to wait indefinitely for the firm to act.
n.4: The duty is to report to the SRA, not merely to raise it internally with managers.

6.q: A defendant commits an offence not because a person expressly ordered them to, but because the objective circumstances they faced threatened death or serious injury, leaving them no reasonable alternative but to break the law — for example driving dangerously to escape an imminent threat. The defendant relies on a defence closely related to duress by threats. The court considers the defence of duress of circumstances. The defendant drove dangerously only to escape a group who were chasing them and threatening violence. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Duress of circumstances applies only where the defendant sought and obtained police assistance first on these facts.
Duress of circumstances applies only where the danger was to the defendant's property.
Duress of circumstances may excuse an offence where objective circumstances of danger left no reasonable alternative.
There is no such defence; only an express threat from another person can ever excuse an offence.
Duress of circumstances is a complete defence to every offence, including murder.
6.w: Duress of circumstances operates on similar principles to duress by threats, but the compulsion arises from the objective circumstances of danger (threatening death or serious injury) rather than an express threat to commit a particular offence. Like duress by threats, it is not available to murder or attempted murder.

n.0: There is no requirement to have obtained police assistance first.
n.1: The danger must be to the person (death or serious injury), not merely property.
n.3: The defence exists and is not confined to express threats from a person.
n.4: It is not available to murder or attempted murder.

6.q: A squatter acquired a strip of unregistered land by 12 years' adverse possession, with the effect that the paper owner's title to the strip was extinguished under the Limitation Act 1980. Throughout that period the strip had been subject to a legal right of way benefiting a neighbouring property, which had been created by deed many years before the squatter arrived. The owner of the neighbouring property wishes to continue using the right of way over the strip, but the squatter argues that their adverse possession has swept away all earlier rights over the land. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The squatter takes the land free of the easement, because adverse possession clears all prior rights.
The easement is automatically extinguished after 12 years, along with the paper owner's title.
The squatter takes the land subject to the existing legal easement.
The squatter takes free of the easement unless the neighbour objected during the 12 years.
The neighbour must re-grant the right of way to the squatter for it to continue.
6.w: Adverse possession extinguishes the dispossessed paper owner's title, but the squatter takes the land subject to third-party proprietary rights such as an existing legal easement. The neighbour's right of way is not defeated by the squatter's possession of the servient strip.

n.0: Adverse possession does not sweep away third-party rights like easements; it defeats only the paper owner's title.
n.1: The easement is not extinguished merely because the servient owner's title is.
n.3: The neighbour need not have objected; their easement survives regardless.
n.4: No re-grant is needed; the legal easement continues to bind the land.

6.q: A party wishes to rely on expert evidence, for example a surveyor's or medical opinion, to support its case. It intends simply to instruct an expert and produce the report at trial. The other party objects that expert evidence cannot be used without the court's involvement. The court considers the control of expert evidence under the Civil Procedure Rules. The issue turned on technical matters on which only a qualified expert could properly assist. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Expert evidence may be relied on only with the court's permission, and the expert's overriding duty is to the court.
Expert evidence may be given only by an expert employed full-time by the court itself on these facts as a general rule.
An expert's duty is owed solely to the party who instructs and pays them.
Expert evidence is never admissible in civil proceedings under any circumstances.
A party may freely rely on any expert evidence it wishes without any court permission.
6.w: Expert evidence is restricted to that which is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings, and no party may call an expert or put in an expert's report without the court's permission. The expert owes an overriding duty to help the court, which prevails over any duty to the instructing party.

n.1: Experts are instructed by the parties (or jointly), not employed by the court.
n.2: The expert's overriding duty is to the court, not solely to the instructing party.
n.3: Expert evidence is admissible with permission, not never.
n.4: Expert evidence requires the court's permission; it cannot be used freely.

6.q: Two testators, a couple, make wills in agreed, mirror terms, and expressly agree with each other that neither will alter their will after the first of them dies, intending the survivor to be bound. After the first dies leaving their estate accordingly, the survivor then makes a new will departing from the agreement. The disappointed beneficiaries under the original arrangement seek a remedy. The court considers the doctrine of mutual wills. They had promised each other faithfully that the survivor would leave everything as agreed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The agreement is enforceable only if it was made in a formal deed separate from the wills.
The survivor is completely free to change their will, and the agreement has no effect at all.
The survivor's later will is automatically void, because mirror wills can never be changed.
The doctrine applies only where the two wills were contained in a single document.
Equity may impose a constructive trust binding the survivor to the agreed terms, despite the later will.
6.w: Where two people make mutual wills on the basis of a binding agreement not to revoke them, and one dies having kept to the agreement, equity may impose a constructive trust on the survivor's estate to give effect to the agreed dispositions, notwithstanding that the survivor later makes a different will.

n.0: A separate formal deed is not required; the binding agreement is the key.
n.1: Mutual wills can bind the survivor; the agreement is not without effect.
n.2: The later will is not automatically void; equity imposes a constructive trust instead.
n.3: The doctrine does not require the wills to be in a single document.

6.q: A defendant deliberately sets fire to a building, and does so either intending to endanger the life of another or being reckless as to whether the lives of others would be endangered by the fire. Damage by fire results. The defendant is charged with the aggravated form of criminal damage. The court considers arson being aggravated criminal damage endangering life under the Criminal Damage Act 1971. The fire spread quickly through the occupied building while several people were still inside at the time. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The offence is the same as basic criminal damage, with no additional element required.
The aggravated offence is committed where the damage is by fire and life is intended or recklessly endangered.
The offence requires the defendant to have intended to destroy the whole building completely on these facts.
The offence is committed only where the property destroyed belonged to another person.
The offence is committed only where a person was actually killed by the fire.
6.w: Under s.1(2) and s.1(3) Criminal Damage Act 1971, where criminal damage is caused by fire it is charged as arson, and it is aggravated where the defendant intends by the destruction/damage to endanger life, or is reckless as to whether life would be endangered. The aggravated offence can be committed even in respect of the defendant's own property.

n.0: The aggravated offence has the additional life-endangerment element.
n.2: Total destruction of the building is not required.
n.3: The aggravated offence can apply even to the defendant's own property, so ownership by another is not essential.
n.4: Actual death is not required; endangerment (intended or reckless) suffices.

6.q: For more than ten years a landowner has occupied a narrow strip of land on the wrong side of a boundary fence, in the genuine and reasonable belief that the strip formed part of their own registered title. The land on both sides is registered. The true registered proprietor of the strip has recently commissioned a survey, noticed the position, and objects to the landowner's continued occupation. The landowner has nonetheless applied to the Land Registry to be registered as proprietor of the strip on the basis of their long occupation. Which of the following best describes the landowner's prospects on that application?
o: The application succeeds automatically, because ten years' occupation always confers title.
The application must fail, because any objection by the registered proprietor always defeats it, on these facts.
The applicant must show 12 years' possession before any application can be considered.
The application must fail, because adverse possession cannot ever apply to registered land.
The application may still succeed under the reasonable-belief-of-boundary condition, despite the objection.
6.w: Although a registered proprietor's objection usually defeats a Schedule 6 application, one of the three exceptions is that the applicant reasonably believed the land belonged to them for ten years and it adjoins their own land. On these facts that condition may be satisfied.

n.0: Ten years' occupation does not confer title automatically; the conditions must be met.
n.1: An objection does not always defeat the application; the boundary condition is an exception.
n.2: For registered land the relevant period under Schedule 6 is ten years, not twelve.
n.3: Adverse possession can apply to registered land under the Schedule 6 regime.

6.q: A defendant takes another person's property intending to keep it, use it up, or otherwise treat it as their own to dispose of, so that the owner will not get it back in any meaningful form. In another version of the facts, the defendant borrows the property intending genuinely to return it in the same state very shortly. A dispute arises about the intention to permanently deprive. The court considers s.6 of the Theft Act 1968. The defendant had used the item up entirely, leaving nothing of value to return to the owner. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Treating property as one's own to dispose of regardless of the owner's rights can amount to intention permanently to deprive.
A genuine intention to return the very same property shortly can still be intention permanently to deprive on these facts.
Intention permanently to deprive is irrelevant to theft and need not be proved at all.
There is always an intention permanently to deprive whenever property is taken, even briefly.
Intention permanently to deprive requires the defendant to destroy the property completely.
6.w: Under s.6 Theft Act 1968, a person may have the intention permanently to deprive if they intend to treat the property as their own to dispose of regardless of the owner's rights. A genuine intention to return the very same property intact, by contrast, negates that intention.

n.1: A genuine intention to return the property shortly negates the required intention.
n.2: Intention permanently to deprive is an essential element of theft.
n.3: A brief taking with intention to return does not, in itself, show intention permanently to deprive.
n.4: Destruction is not required; treating the property as one's own to dispose of suffices.

6.q: An individual in financial difficulty wishes to avoid the consequences of bankruptcy by reaching a formal, binding arrangement with their creditors to pay part of what is owed over time, supervised by an insolvency practitioner. The debtor is an individual seeking an alternative to bankruptcy. The arrangement would bind creditors once approved. Anxious to keep clear of the stigma and consequences of being made bankrupt, the individual wants instead to put a formal proposal to their creditors to pay off part of what is owed over time under an insolvency practitioner's supervision, in a way that will bind the creditors once the necessary majority approves it. Which of the following best identifies the procedure?
o: A company voluntary arrangement, which is the correct procedure for an individual on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A creditors' voluntary liquidation of the individual.
An administration, placing the individual under an administrator.
An individual voluntary arrangement (IVA), supervised by an insolvency practitioner and binding creditors if approved by the requisite majority.
A bankruptcy order, which is the only option available to an insolvent individual.
6.w: An individual voluntary arrangement (IVA) allows an insolvent individual to propose a binding arrangement to their creditors, typically to pay part of their debts over a period, supervised by an insolvency practitioner. If approved by at least 75% in value of creditors voting, it binds all unsecured creditors and enables the debtor to avoid bankruptcy.

n.0: A CVA is the company procedure; the individual equivalent is an IVA.
n.1: Creditors' voluntary liquidation applies to companies, not individuals.
n.2: Administration is a corporate procedure, not for individuals.
n.4: Bankruptcy is not the only option; an IVA is an alternative.

6.q: A defendant is charged with an either-way offence. At the allocation hearing the magistrates decide that the case is suitable for summary trial and are willing to keep it. The defendant, however, would prefer to be tried by a jury. The magistrates have accepted jurisdiction. The magistrates have indicated they are prepared to keep the case and deal with it themselves, but the client, distrustful of summary justice for the allegation faced, would rather put the matter before a jury of ordinary citizens, and wants to know whether that choice remains available. Which of the following best describes the defendant's position on the venue for trial?
o: The defendant may choose the High Court instead of either court.
The defendant may only be tried in the Crown Court if the prosecution agrees.
The defendant may elect to be tried in the Crown Court by a jury.
The defendant must be tried in the magistrates' court once they accept jurisdiction.
The defendant has no say; the magistrates' decision on venue is final.
6.w: For an either-way offence, even where the magistrates accept jurisdiction and are content to try the case summarily, the defendant retains the right to elect trial on indictment in the Crown Court before a jury. The defendant's election overrides the magistrates' willingness to keep the case.

n.0: The High Court is not an option for trial of the offence.
n.1: The defendant's right to elect Crown Court trial does not depend on the prosecution's agreement.
n.3: The defendant is not compelled to accept summary trial once magistrates accept jurisdiction.
n.4: The defendant does have a say; the election is the defendant's, not the magistrates'.

6.q: A firm needs to make a payment out of the client account on behalf of a client — for example to pay a disbursement or to return money to the client. The bookkeeper is asked when withdrawals from the client account are permitted under the SRA Accounts Rules. The payment relates to the client for whom the money is held. The bookkeeper considers the permitted withdrawals from a client account. The firm holds a credit balance for the client on that matter, the intended payment is a disbursement due to be met from those funds, and the bookkeeper wants to confirm the circumstances in which money may properly leave the client account. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Client money may be withdrawn only for the purpose it is held, on the client instructions or as permitted, and only up to funds held for that client.
Client money may never be withdrawn from the client account for any reason at all.
Client money may be withdrawn freely provided the total client account balance stays positive on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Client money may be withdrawn from the client account for any purpose the firm chooses.
Client money may be withdrawn only after the SRA has approved each individual payment.
6.w: Under the SRA Accounts Rules, client money may be withdrawn from the client account only for the purpose for which it is being held, following the client's instructions or as otherwise permitted by the rules, and only to the extent of the money held for that particular client (so as not to overdraw the client's ledger).

n.1: Client money can be withdrawn for proper purposes; it is not frozen entirely.
n.2: A positive overall balance does not permit overdrawing an individual client's ledger.
n.3: Withdrawals cannot be for any purpose the firm chooses.
n.4: Routine withdrawals do not need individual SRA approval.

6.q: A firm is approached by two entirely separate would-be buyers who each, quite independently of the other, want the firm to act for them in trying to buy the very same house, which has only just come onto the market and is expected to attract several competing offers. Each buyer wants the firm's help to secure the property ahead of the other, and their interests in doing so are directly and obviously opposed. A fee-earner, seeing the prospect of two fees rather than one, wonders whether the firm can simply act for both buyers at the same time. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may act for both buyers, because whichever of them succeeds will be perfectly satisfied with the outcome.
The firm may act for both buyers, provided each buyer instructs a different fee-earner within the firm.
The firm may act for both buyers, provided it does not tell either of them the amount the other is offering.
There is a conflict, as the buyers compete for the same property, so the firm should not act for both.
The firm may act for both buyers, because acting on a house purchase is only routine conveyancing work.
6.w: Two clients competing to buy the same property have directly conflicting interests, so there is a conflict of interest. The firm should not act for both unless a recognised exception applies with informed consent and safeguards; merely withholding information or using separate fee-earners does not cure it.

n.0: The eventual satisfaction of the winner does not remove the conflict at the time of acting.
n.1: Using different fee-earners in the same firm does not, by itself, cure a conflict between the clients.
n.2: Withholding each buyer's offer from the other does not resolve the underlying conflict.
n.4: The competing bids create a genuine conflict; this is not merely routine work.

6.q: A claimant makes a Part 36 offer to settle, which the defendant rejects. At trial the claimant obtains a judgment that is at least as advantageous as its own Part 36 offer. The offer complied with the requirements of Part 36 and the relevant period had expired. The claimant equalled or bettered its own Part 36 offer at trial. The claimant had made a properly formulated offer to settle that the defendant turned down, the case went the distance, and at trial the claimant did at least as well as, if not better than, the figure it had proposed in that offer. Which of the following best describes the enhanced consequences that usually follow for the claimant?
o: The claimant recovers nothing extra because the defendant was entitled to reject the offer on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The claimant must pay the defendant's costs for having gone to trial.
The claimant's enhanced entitlement depends on the defendant having made its own offer.
The claimant simply recovers its costs on the standard basis with no enhancement.
The claimant is usually entitled to indemnity costs and enhanced interest from the end of the relevant period, plus an additional amount.
6.w: Where a claimant obtains a judgment at least as advantageous as its own Part 36 offer, the court will usually order enhanced consequences: interest on the sum awarded at an enhanced rate, costs on the indemnity basis (with enhanced interest on costs), and an additional amount (a percentage uplift subject to a cap), unless it is unjust to do so.

n.0: Beating one's own Part 36 offer does bring extra entitlements, contrary to this option.
n.1: The claimant does not pay the defendant's costs where it beat its own offer.
n.2: The enhanced consequences do not depend on the defendant having made an offer.
n.3: The consequences are enhanced (indemnity costs and interest), not merely standard-basis costs.

6.q: A solicitor is acting for both the buyer and the buyer's mortgage lender in a purchase, as is commonly permitted where their interests are not in conflict. After investigating title, the solicitor must confirm to the lender that the property is good security for the loan. The solicitor acts for both buyer and lender, whose interests currently coincide. The solicitor is reporting to the lender before completion. The same solicitor is acting for the buyer and for the mortgage lender, whose interests presently pull in the same direction, and having investigated the title the solicitor must now give the lender the formal confirmation it needs about the property before the advance is released for completion. Which of the following best describes what the solicitor provides to the lender?
o: A guarantee that the borrower will repay the mortgage in full.
A valuation of the property in place of any confirmation about the title.
A certificate of title confirming that the title is good and marketable and the property is suitable security.
An undertaking to indemnify the lender against any fall in the property's value.
A report on title addressed only to the buyer, with nothing provided to the lender on these facts as a general rule.
6.w: Where a solicitor acts for both buyer and lender, the solicitor gives the lender a certificate of title confirming that the title is good and marketable and that the property provides adequate security for the advance, in the standard form required by the lender. This is distinct from a valuation and does not guarantee repayment or property values.

n.0: The solicitor does not guarantee the borrower's repayment.
n.1: A valuation is separate; the lender needs confirmation about the title via the certificate.
n.3: The solicitor does not indemnify the lender against falls in value.
n.4: The lender requires its own certificate of title; a report to the buyer alone is insufficient.

6.q: A person dishonestly obtains a service for which payment is, or would be, required, without paying for it, knowing that payment is expected, and intending to avoid paying. For example, they use a subscription service by dishonest means having decided never to pay. The service was one made available on the basis it would be paid for. The defendant obtained it dishonestly, intending not to pay. The defendant helped themselves to a service that is only ever provided on the footing that it will be paid for, using dishonest means to get it while having decided from the outset that they would never actually pay the charge that everyone knows attaches to it. Which of the following best identifies the offence under the Fraud Act 2006?
o: Obtaining services dishonestly under section 11.
Fraud by false representation under section 2.
Theft of the service under the Theft Act 1968.
No offence, because services cannot be stolen.
Making off without payment under the Theft Act 1978.
6.w: Section 11 of the Fraud Act 2006 creates the offence of obtaining services dishonestly: obtaining services for which payment is required, by a dishonest act, knowing they are or might be chargeable and intending not to pay (or not to pay in full). Unlike the s.1 fraud offences, it is result-based (the services must actually be obtained).

n.1: Section 2 covers dishonest false representations; s.11 specifically covers obtaining services.
n.2: Services are not 'property' capable of being stolen under the Theft Act 1968.
n.3: Obtaining services dishonestly is an offence under s.11, so 'no offence' is wrong.
n.4: Making off without payment applies where payment on the spot is expected for goods/services already supplied and the defendant departs; s.11 fits obtaining the service dishonestly.

6.q: A settlor wishes to create a trust of land and proposes to appoint six individuals as trustees so that decisions can be shared widely. A solicitor advises that there is a statutory limit on the number of trustees who may hold legal title to land. The trust property consists of land held on trust. The settlor wants as many trustees as possible. The settlor is enthusiastic about spreading responsibility as widely as possible and has drawn up a list of six proposed trustees, but the solicitor warns that the law will not let all of them hold the legal estate in the land, whatever the settlor's wishes. Which of the following best describes the position on the number of trustees of land?
o: The maximum number of trustees of land is two in every case.
There is no limit on the number of trustees who may hold legal title to land on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A trust of land must always have exactly three trustees.
The limit on trustees of land applies only to charitable trusts.
The number of trustees of land is limited to a maximum of four, being the first four named who are able and willing to act.
6.w: Where land is held on trust, the number of trustees is limited to a maximum of four; if more are named, the first four named who are able and willing to act take the legal estate. This contrasts with trusts of pure personalty, where there is no statutory maximum number of trustees.

n.0: The maximum is four, not two.
n.1: There is a statutory maximum of four for trustees of land.
n.2: There is no fixed requirement of exactly three trustees.
n.3: The four-trustee limit for land is not confined to charitable trusts.

6.q: An adult who lacks the mental capacity to make a valid will has assets that would, on intestacy, pass in a way that does not reflect their known wishes or best interests. A relative wishes a will to be made on the person's behalf. The person cannot make a valid will themselves due to lack of capacity. A will reflecting their best interests is desired. The person's condition means they can no longer understand what making a will involves, yet the way their property would devolve on intestacy would cut across what everyone knows they would have wanted, and a relative is asking how, if at all, a will reflecting the person's best interests might still be made. Which of the following best describes how a will may be made for such a person?
o: No will can ever be made for a person who lacks testamentary capacity.
A relative may simply sign a will on the person's behalf without any court involvement on these facts.
The Court of Protection may authorise a statutory will to be made on behalf of the person who lacks capacity.
The intestacy rules must always apply, as a will is impossible in this situation.
The person's attorney under a lasting power of attorney may make a will for them.
6.w: Where a person lacks testamentary capacity, the Court of Protection may, under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, authorise the execution of a statutory will on their behalf, making provision in their best interests. This is distinct from an ordinary will and requires the court's involvement.

n.0: A statutory will can be made, so it is not true that no will is ever possible.
n.1: A relative cannot simply sign a will for the person without court authority.
n.3: Intestacy is not inevitable; a statutory will can be authorised.
n.4: An attorney under an LPA cannot make a will for the donor; that requires the Court of Protection.

6.q: A solicitor is instructed to recover a substantial unpaid commercial debt for a client. In order to increase the pressure on the debtor to pay up quickly, the solicitor proposes writing to the debtor to say that, unless the outstanding sum is paid in full within seven days, the client will report the debtor to the police for fraud. The alleged fraud is wholly unconnected with the recovery of the debt and would be raised only as a lever to force a settlement of the civil dispute. The solicitor asks a colleague whether this course of action is proper. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor must not do this, as it is improper to threaten criminal proceedings merely to gain an advantage in a civil matter.
The solicitor may do this, because any lawful pressure that helps to recover the client's money is entirely permitted.
The solicitor may do this, because reporting a suspected crime to the police is always in the wider public interest.
The solicitor may do this, provided the alleged fraud is something that the client genuinely and reasonably suspects.
The solicitor may do this only if counsel first advises that making the threat is reasonable in the circumstances.
6.w: It is a breach of professional conduct to use, or threaten to use, criminal or regulatory proceedings solely to obtain an advantage in a civil dispute. This amounts to taking unfair advantage and does not serve the proper administration of justice.

n.1: Not all pressure is legitimate; threatening criminal action as leverage in a civil matter is improper.
n.2: The threat here is made to gain civil advantage, not out of a genuine public-interest report.
n.3: A genuine suspicion does not make it proper to deploy the threat as leverage in the civil dispute.
n.4: Counsel's approval cannot make an improper threat proper.

6.q: Two friends, Ms Hollis and Ms Iqbal, bought a house together several years ago. They hold the legal estate on trust for themselves, and in equity they hold as beneficial joint tenants, so that on the death of either the survivor would take the whole by survivorship. Following a disagreement, Ms Hollis decides she no longer wishes to share ownership in that way. She signs a written notice stating that she wishes to sever the joint tenancy with immediate effect, and posts it to Ms Iqbal at the house, where it is duly delivered. Ms Iqbal does not agree to the change. Which of the following best describes the effect of the notice?
o: It has no effect, because a joint tenancy can be severed only by the agreement of all of the joint tenants.
It ends the co-ownership altogether, so the property is then owned solely by the severing friend.
It has no effect, because severance of a joint tenancy must be made by deed rather than by written notice.
It severs both the legal and the beneficial joint tenancy, so each of the friends holds a distinct legal share.
It severs the beneficial joint tenancy, so the friends hold the equitable interest as tenants in common.
6.w: A written notice under s.36(2) LPA 1925 severs the joint tenancy in equity, converting the beneficial interest into a tenancy in common in equal shares. The notice takes effect when delivered and does not require the other joint tenant's agreement. The legal estate cannot be severed and remains held on a joint tenancy.

n.0: Section 36(2) allows unilateral severance by written notice; the agreement of all is only one of several methods.
n.1: Severance changes how the beneficial interest is held; it does not extinguish the other co-owner's share.
n.2: Written notice is itself a valid method of severance; no deed is required.
n.3: The legal estate cannot be held as a tenancy in common and is not severed; only the equitable joint tenancy is affected.

6.q: Trustees who have no particular expertise in investment matters are about to exercise their power to invest a large trust fund across a range of assets. They are considering simply making the investment decisions themselves, on the basis of their own general knowledge, without taking any external input. A beneficiary asks whether the trustees are required to take advice before investing. The trustees seek guidance on their obligations under the Trustee Act 2000. The sums to be invested were considerable and the range of possible investments was wide and complex. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustees may invest only through a stockbroker who takes over the decision entirely.
The trustees must ordinarily obtain and consider proper advice before exercising the power of investment.
The trustees must always follow whatever advice they receive without any independent thought on these facts.
The trustees never need to take any advice, because the decision is entirely theirs to make.
The trustees must obtain the consent of every beneficiary before making any investment.
6.w: Under the Trustee Act 2000, before exercising the power of investment (and when reviewing investments) trustees must obtain and consider proper advice about how the power should be exercised, having regard to the standard investment criteria, unless it is reasonably concluded that advice is unnecessary.

n.0: Taking advice does not require handing the decision entirely to a broker.
n.2: They must consider advice, but they are not bound to follow it blindly.
n.3: Trustees generally must take proper advice; it is not simply their own decision.
n.4: Beneficiary consent to each investment is not required.

6.q: A discretionary trust exists under which trustees may distribute income among a class of potential beneficiaries. One member of the class, before any distribution has been made to them, purports to deal with their supposed 'share' as though they already owned a defined part of the fund. A dispute arises about the nature of that member's interest. No distribution has yet been made in that member's favour. The member has run into financial difficulty and is trying to raise money against what they assume is their entitlement, but the trustees have made no decision in their favour, and the other potential beneficiaries dispute that this member owns anything they can deal with at all. Which of the following best describes the interest of an object of a discretionary trust before any distribution?
o: The object has no proprietary interest in any particular part of the fund, only a hope of being selected.
The object holds the legal title to a proportionate part of the trust property.
The object may compel the trustees to pay them an equal share on demand.
The object owns a fixed and defined share of the fund from the outset.
The object's interest vests automatically after a fixed period regardless of selection on these facts.
6.w: An object of a discretionary trust has no proprietary interest in any specific part of the fund unless and until the trustees exercise their discretion in that object's favour. Before then the object has only a hope (a mere expectancy) of benefiting, and cannot claim a defined share or compel payment.

n.1: The object holds no legal title to any part of the trust property.
n.2: The object cannot compel an equal payment on demand.
n.3: The object does not own a fixed share before any distribution.
n.4: The interest does not vest automatically after a period; it depends on the trustees' selection.

6.q: A claimant wishes to bring judicial review proceedings against a body, but a question arises about whether that body's decision is capable of being judicially reviewed at all, given the nature of the body and the function it was performing. The body performs a public function under statutory powers. A solicitor is asked when a body's decision is amenable to judicial review. The solicitor considers amenability to judicial review. The body was not a government department but was carrying out functions of a plainly public character. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A decision is amenable to judicial review where the body is exercising a public function, whether or not it is a governmental body.
Only decisions of central government departments can ever be judicially reviewed.
Any decision by any person or body at all can be judicially reviewed, including purely private ones on these facts as a general rule.
Amenability depends solely on whether the body describes itself as a public authority.
A decision can be judicially reviewed only where the claimant has a contract with the body.
6.w: Judicial review is available in respect of the exercise of public functions. What matters is the nature of the function rather than merely the identity of the body, so even a non-governmental body may be amenable to judicial review when exercising a public function; purely private or contractual functions are generally not.

n.1: Amenability is not confined to central government departments.
n.2: Purely private functions are generally not amenable to judicial review.
n.3: It is the nature of the function, not the body's self-description, that governs.
n.4: A contract with the body is not the test; the public nature of the function is.

6.q: A testator's will leaves a substantial gift to their spouse and appoints the spouse as executor. The couple later divorce (the marriage is dissolved), but the testator never changes the will before dying. The former spouse claims the gift and the right to act as executor. The court considers the effect of divorce on gifts and appointments in an existing will under the Wills Act 1837. The couple had gone through a bitter divorce a year or so before the testator died. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The divorce has no effect at all on the will and its provisions remain fully in force.
The former spouse takes the gift and acts as executor exactly as if the divorce had not happened.
The former spouse still acts as executor but loses only the gift left to them.
The whole will is revoked automatically by the divorce, so the testator dies intestate.
The former spouse is treated as having died before the testator, so the gift and appointment to them fail.
6.w: Under s.18A Wills Act 1837, where a marriage is dissolved or annulled after the will, any appointment of the former spouse as executor and any gift to the former spouse take effect as if the former spouse had died on the date the marriage ended (the rest of the will remaining valid).

n.0: Divorce does affect the will's provisions for the former spouse.
n.1: The former spouse does not take the gift or act as executor as before.
n.2: Both the gift and the executor appointment to the ex-spouse are affected, not just the gift.
n.3: Divorce does not revoke the whole will; only the provisions for the ex-spouse are affected.

6.q: On the agreed completion date, the buyer's solicitor fails to complete the purchase because the buyer's funds are not ready, and the seller wishes to force the issue. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale, under which time is not automatically of the essence for completion. The seller asks how they can make time of the essence and put pressure on the buyer to complete. The solicitor considers the service of a notice to complete. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The seller may serve a notice to complete, making time of the essence and requiring completion within the notice period.
The seller may treat the contract as automatically discharged the instant completion does not occur on these facts.
The seller must apply to the court for an order compelling completion before taking any other step.
The seller can do nothing at all and must simply wait indefinitely for the buyer to complete.
The seller may immediately rescind and keep the deposit the moment completion is a day late.
6.w: Where completion does not take place on the agreed date and time is not of the essence, the innocent party may serve a notice to complete under the Standard Conditions of Sale, which makes time of the essence and requires completion within the notice period (usually 10 working days); failure to comply then allows the innocent party to pursue their remedies.

n.1: The contract is not automatically discharged the instant completion is missed.
n.2: A notice to complete, not necessarily a court application, is the usual first step.
n.3: The seller has a remedy (a notice to complete); it need not wait indefinitely.
n.4: The seller cannot rescind and keep the deposit immediately for a short delay where time is not of the essence.

6.q: A member of the armed forces, while in actual military service on operations, expresses their testamentary wishes informally, without the usual formalities of writing, signature and two witnesses. They later die. A question arises whether these informal wishes can take effect as a will. The person was in actual military service when the wishes were expressed. The usual Wills Act formalities were not observed. The service member spoke their wishes plainly to comrades while deployed on active operations, with no opportunity to sit down and prepare a formal signed and witnessed document, and after their death the family want to know whether those informally expressed wishes can govern the estate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The wishes take effect only as a lifetime gift, not as a will.
The wishes are effective only if later reduced to a signed and witnessed document.
The wishes are wholly ineffective, because no will can ever dispense with the statutory formalities on these facts.
The wishes are valid only if a commanding officer countersigned them.
A privileged will may be valid despite the lack of formalities, because the testator was in actual military service.
6.w: A privileged will may be made by a soldier in actual military service (and by certain seamen), without the usual formalities: it may be informal, even oral, and can dispose of the testator's estate. This is an exception to the Wills Act formalities, reflecting the position of those on active service.

n.0: A privileged will operates as a will, not merely as a lifetime gift.
n.1: A privileged will need not later be reduced to signed, witnessed writing.
n.2: The formalities can be dispensed with for a privileged will, so the wishes are not automatically ineffective.
n.3: No countersignature by a commanding officer is required for a privileged will.

6.q: A seller during negotiations makes an accurate statement of fact to the buyer, but before the contract is signed the position changes so that the statement, though true when made, has become false by the time of contracting. The seller becomes aware of the change but says nothing to the buyer, who enters the contract still relying on the original statement. When the buyer discovers the true position, they claim misrepresentation. The seller argues that the statement was true when it was originally made. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There may be an actionable misrepresentation, as a statement that becomes false before contracting must be corrected.
There is a misrepresentation only if the change of circumstances was caused by the seller's own act.
There is a misrepresentation only if the buyer expressly asked the seller to confirm the statement again.
There is no misrepresentation, because a seller is never under any duty to update earlier statements.
There is no misrepresentation, because the statement was entirely true at the time it was first made.
6.w: A representation is treated as continuing until the contract is made. If a statement, true when made, becomes false before contracting and the representor knows this, they must correct it; failing to do so can be an actionable misrepresentation (With v O'Flanagan).

n.1: The duty to correct does not depend on the seller having caused the change of circumstances.
n.2: The duty to correct arises whether or not the buyer asks for reconfirmation.
n.3: There is a duty to correct a continuing representation that has become false before contracting.
n.4: Truth at the time of making does not excuse failing to correct a statement that later becomes false.

6.q: An individual who runs a business through a company sells a business asset, or their shares, and makes a gain. Separately, a company disposes of a capital asset and makes a gain. The individual wants to understand the difference in how the gain is taxed depending on whether it is made by an individual or by a company. The court considers the taxation of capital gains for individuals and companies. The disposals produced substantial gains, and the taxpayers wanted to know their tax exposure. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Gains made by individuals are taxed as trading income under corporation tax rules.
Only companies, and never individuals, are ever charged to tax on capital gains.
Both individuals and companies pay capital gains tax on their gains in exactly the same way on these facts as a general rule.
Neither individuals nor companies pay any tax on gains from disposing of assets.
An individual's chargeable gains are subject to capital gains tax, while a company's gains are charged to corporation tax.
6.w: An individual who makes a chargeable gain on the disposal of an asset is subject to capital gains tax (subject to reliefs and the annual exempt amount), whereas a company's chargeable gains are brought into its corporation tax computation and taxed as part of its total profits.

n.0: Individuals' gains are charged to CGT, not corporation tax.
n.1: Individuals are also chargeable on gains, via CGT.
n.2: Individuals pay CGT while companies pay corporation tax on gains; they are not identical.
n.3: Gains are taxable, not free of tax.

6.q: A buyer, Mr Naylor, purchased a registered freehold property for £500,000. Some years earlier the land had been made subject to a restrictive covenant, in favour of a neighbouring owner, prohibiting any use other than as a private dwelling. That covenant had never been protected by the entry of a notice on the register of the property's title. Mr Naylor, who knew nothing of the covenant, completed the purchase and was registered as proprietor. He has now opened a shop on the ground floor. The neighbouring owner, who has the benefit of the covenant, seeks to enforce it against Mr Naylor and stop the commercial use. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The covenant does not bind the new owner: an unprotected covenant loses priority to a buyer for value.
The covenant binds the new owner, because opening a shop is a serious breach of its terms.
The covenant binds the new owner, because restrictive covenants automatically run with the land in equity.
The covenant does not bind, because the burden of a covenant can never pass to a successor in title.
The covenant binds the new owner, because it was created before the new owner bought the land.
6.w: In registered land a restrictive covenant must be protected by a notice to bind a later purchaser. An unprotected covenant is postponed to a registered disposition made for valuable consideration (s.29 LRA 2002), so it does not bind the buyer (though it may still bind the original covenantor personally).

n.1: The seriousness of the breach does not make an unprotected covenant enforceable against a purchaser.
n.2: The burden can run in equity, but only if protected; without a notice it loses priority to a buyer for value.
n.3: The burden of a restrictive covenant can pass in equity (Tulk v Moxhay); it fails here only for want of protection.
n.4: Priority in registered land turns on protection by notice, not merely on when the covenant was created.

6.q: A director makes a decision on behalf of the company. In doing so, the director focuses only on short-term profit and ignores relevant matters such as the likely long-term consequences, the interests of employees, and the company's reputation, when they should have acted in the way they considered, in good faith, most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole. A shareholder alleges a breach of duty. The court considers which duty is engaged under the Companies Act 2006. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The duty to act within the company's constitution and for proper purposes only (s.171) on these facts.
The duty not to accept benefits from third parties by reason of the office (s.176).
The duty to act in good faith to promote the success of the company for the members as a whole (s.172).
The duty to exercise independent judgement when acting for the company (s.173).
The duty to declare an interest in an existing transaction with the company (s.182).
6.w: Under s.172 Companies Act 2006, a director must act in the way they consider, in good faith, would be most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, having regard to factors including long-term consequences, employees, and the company's reputation.

n.0: Section 171 concerns constitutional limits and proper purposes.
n.1: Section 176 concerns benefits from third parties.
n.3: Section 173 concerns independent judgement, a distinct duty.
n.4: Section 182 concerns declaring interests in existing transactions.

6.q: A firm has finished acting for a client on a matter and has delivered its bill, but the client has failed to pay the firm's proper costs despite reminders. The client now demands that the firm immediately hand over the entire file of papers relating to the matter, which remains in the firm's possession, so that the client can take the matter elsewhere. The firm has done nothing wrong in the conduct of the matter and its fees are properly due and owing. The firm considers whether it may hold on to the papers until it is paid. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may keep the papers only if the client agreed, in writing at the outset, to such an arrangement.
The firm has no right to keep any papers, but may instead simply sue the client for the unpaid fees.
The firm must hand over all of the papers at once, because a client is always entitled to their file on demand.
The firm may exercise a retaining lien over the client's papers until its proper outstanding fees are paid.
The firm may keep the papers permanently, whether or not the client ever pays the outstanding fees.
6.w: A solicitor generally has a common-law retaining lien over a client's papers and property in the firm's possession as security for the firm's properly incurred and unpaid costs. The lien must not be exercised inconsistently with the solicitor's other duties, but it does entitle the firm to withhold the papers pending payment.

n.0: The retaining lien arises at common law and does not depend on a prior written agreement.
n.1: Suing for the fees is an additional remedy; it does not mean the firm has no lien over the papers.
n.2: A client is not automatically entitled to the file on demand where proper fees remain unpaid.
n.4: The lien secures payment; it is not a right to keep the papers permanently regardless of payment.

6.q: A commercial buyer tells a machinery seller, before contracting, that it needs a compressor capable of running continuously in a dusty foundry environment, and relies on the seller to select a suitable model. The seller, who deals in such equipment, supplies a compressor that is of good general quality but cannot cope with continuous dusty operation and fails within weeks. The buyer, a business, made its particular purpose known and relied on the seller's skill and judgement. The sale is a commercial sale of goods governed by the Sale of Goods Act 1979. Which of the following best describes the buyer's strongest implied-term claim?
o: Breach of the implied term that the goods be reasonably fit for the particular purpose made known.
No implied term applies, because the buyer inspected nothing before purchase.
Breach of the implied term that the goods correspond with their description only.
Breach of an implied term that the goods be of the very highest quality obtainable.
No implied term applies, because fitness for purpose is never implied in commercial sales.
6.w: Under s.14(3) of the Sale of Goods Act 1979, where the buyer expressly or impliedly makes known a particular purpose, and reasonably relies on the seller's skill and judgement, there is an implied term that the goods are reasonably fit for that purpose. The compressor's inability to perform the disclosed continuous dusty operation breaches that term.

n.1: Fitness for a particular purpose does not depend on the buyer having inspected the goods.
n.2: Correspondence with description (s.13) is a different term; the issue here is fitness for the disclosed purpose.
n.3: The implied standard is reasonable fitness/satisfactory quality, not the very highest quality obtainable.
n.4: Fitness for purpose is implied in commercial sales where the s.14(3) conditions are met.

6.q: A defendant is charged with an offence that can only be dealt with in the magistrates' court, being a relatively minor matter such as a low-level public order or driving offence. The defendant's solicitor explains where such a case will be heard and by whom it will be tried. The solicitor considers the trial of a summary-only offence. The matter was a minor one that the police had charged as a straightforward summary offence. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A summary-only offence can be tried in any court the defendant selects.
A summary-only offence cannot be tried at all and must be discontinued.
A summary-only offence must always be sent to the Crown Court for trial on indictment.
A summary-only offence may be tried in the Crown Court before a jury at the defendant's choice on these facts.
A summary-only offence is tried in the magistrates' court, with no right to trial by jury in the Crown Court.
6.w: A summary-only offence is triable only in the magistrates' court (before a bench of magistrates or a district judge). There is no right to elect Crown Court trial by jury for a summary-only offence.

n.0: The defendant cannot select any court for a summary-only offence.
n.1: Summary-only offences are tried in the magistrates' court, not discontinued.
n.2: Summary-only offences are not sent to the Crown Court for jury trial.
n.3: There is no right to jury trial for a summary-only offence.

6.q: A public body has, by a clear promise or an established practice, led an individual to expect that a particular procedure (such as consultation) will be followed before a decision is made, but the body then departs from that procedure without good reason. The individual challenges the decision. A solicitor is asked about the individual's ability to hold the body to the expected procedure. The solicitor considers procedural legitimate expectation. The body had always consulted before such decisions, and people had come to rely on that. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A public body may always depart from any promise or practice it has established, without any consequence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A clear promise or established practice may give rise to a legitimate expectation that a procedure will be followed, which the body cannot depart from unfairly.
Legitimate expectation requires the individual to have paid the public body for the expectation.
A public body's past promises are never relevant to the lawfulness of its decisions.
Legitimate expectation applies only where the individual has a contract with the public body.
6.w: Where a public body, by a clear and unambiguous representation or an established practice, creates a legitimate expectation that a particular procedure (such as consultation) will be followed, it may be procedurally unfair to depart from that expectation without good reason, giving rise to a ground of review.

n.0: A body cannot always resile from a promise or practice without consequence.
n.2: It does not depend on payment.
n.3: A body's representations and practices can be relevant to the lawfulness of its decisions.
n.4: Legitimate expectation does not require a contract.

6.q: In litigation against the government, a party seeks disclosure of documents, but the government resists on the ground that disclosing them would cause real harm to an important public interest, such as national security. A solicitor is asked about the basis on which the government may seek to withhold relevant documents from disclosure in the public interest. The solicitor considers public interest immunity. The documents were plainly relevant, but the government said releasing them would harm the public interest. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Public interest immunity is decided solely by the government minister with no role for the court on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Public interest immunity may allow documents to be withheld where the public interest in non-disclosure outweighs disclosure.
Relevant documents can never be withheld from disclosure on any public interest ground.
Public interest immunity applies only to documents held by private companies.
The government may withhold any document it wishes simply by asserting it is confidential.
6.w: Public interest immunity may justify withholding otherwise disclosable documents where the public interest in withholding them (for example national security or the proper functioning of the public service) outweighs the public interest in disclosure. The court, not the government alone, weighs the competing interests and decides.

n.0: The court, not solely the minister, decides PII.
n.2: Documents can be withheld on PII grounds where justified.
n.3: PII concerns public interest documents, typically held by public bodies, not only private companies.
n.4: A mere assertion of confidentiality is not enough; the court balances the interests.

6.q: During negotiations, a seller makes a statement to the buyer that is literally true but tells only half the story, creating a misleading overall impression because the seller does not reveal an important qualifying fact. The buyer, relying on the misleading impression created, enters the contract and later suffers loss when the full picture emerges. The seller argues that, because everything actually said was true, there can be no misrepresentation. The buyer seeks advice on whether a misrepresentation claim can succeed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A claim can succeed only if the seller was under a fiduciary duty to the buyer.
There can be no misrepresentation, because everything the seller actually stated was literally true.
A claim can succeed only if the buyer specifically asked the seller about the qualifying fact.
A half-truth that creates a misleading overall impression can amount to an actionable misrepresentation.
There can be no misrepresentation, because a seller is never obliged to volunteer any information at all.
6.w: Although silence generally does not amount to misrepresentation, a statement which is literally true but misleading because it is only a half-truth can be an actionable misrepresentation, since the overall impression conveyed is false (Dimmock v Hallett; With v O'Flanagan principle).

n.0: No fiduciary duty is needed; the misleading statement itself founds the claim.
n.1: Literal truth of the words does not save a statement that is misleading as a half-truth.
n.2: A misleading half-truth is actionable whether or not the buyer asked about the missing fact.
n.4: The claim does not rest on a general duty to volunteer information, but on the misleading half-truth given.

7.q: The prosecution wishes to adduce evidence of the defendant's previous convictions for similar offences, to show that the defendant has a propensity to commit offences of the kind charged, making it more likely they committed this one. The evidence is of the defendant's bad character. The prosecution relies on a statutory gateway. The prosecution wants the jury to hear that the defendant has a string of previous convictions for offences just like the one now charged, arguing that this shows a tendency to behave in the way alleged and makes guilt more likely, and it must bring the material within the statutory scheme governing such evidence. Which of the following best describes the basis for admitting such evidence?
o: It may be admitted only after the defendant has been convicted.
Evidence of a defendant's bad character is never admissible in any circumstances on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
It may be admitted automatically without reference to any gateway or safeguard.
It may be admitted through the gateway allowing relevant evidence of the defendant's propensity to commit offences of the kind charged.
It may be admitted only if the defendant consents to its use.
7.w: Under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, evidence of a defendant's bad character is admissible only through one of the statutory gateways. One gateway admits evidence relevant to an important matter in issue between the defendant and prosecution, which can include propensity to commit offences of the kind charged; the court may still exclude it if admission would be unfair.

n.0: Such evidence may be admitted at trial, not only after conviction.
n.1: Bad character evidence can be admissible through a gateway, so 'never' is wrong.
n.2: Admission is through gateways with safeguards, not automatic.
n.4: The defendant's consent is not required for a prosecution gateway to apply.

7.q: Two people agree together on a course of conduct that will, if carried out as intended, necessarily amount to the commission of a criminal offence by one or more of them. They intend the agreement to be carried out. No steps beyond the agreement have yet been taken. The parties have agreed on a course of conduct amounting to an offence. The two of them sat down and agreed on a plan which, if carried through as they meant it to be, could only be achieved by committing a criminal offence, and although they fully intended to go ahead, nothing had yet been done to put the plan into effect beyond the agreement itself. Which of the following best describes the offence of statutory conspiracy?
o: Conspiracy requires the parties to have used threats against each other.
Conspiracy can be committed by a single person acting alone.
Conspiracy requires an act that is more than merely preparatory to the offence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
An agreement between two or more people to pursue a course of conduct that will necessarily involve an offence, intending it be carried out.
Conspiracy requires that the substantive offence actually be committed.
7.w: Statutory conspiracy (Criminal Law Act 1977) is committed where a person agrees with one or more others on a course of conduct that, if carried out in accordance with their intentions, will necessarily amount to or involve the commission of an offence. The offence is complete on the agreement; the substantive offence need not be carried out.

n.0: Threats between the parties are not an element of conspiracy.
n.1: Conspiracy requires at least two people; one person alone cannot conspire.
n.2: An act more than merely preparatory is the actus reus of an attempt, not conspiracy.
n.4: The substantive offence need not actually be committed; the agreement is the offence.

7.q: A defendant of previous good character, with no relevant convictions, stands trial. The defence wishes the jury to be told that the defendant's good character is relevant to how they should assess the case. The defendant's solicitor considers the direction the judge should give about the defendant's good character. The solicitor considers the good character direction in a Crown Court trial. The defendant had never been in trouble before and had an unblemished record over many years. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The judge must ignore the defendant's good character entirely and give no direction about it on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The judge should direct the jury that the defendant's good character is relevant to their credibility and to the likelihood of their having offended.
Good character is relevant only to sentence and never to the jury's consideration of guilt.
The judge must direct the jury that good character proves the defendant is innocent.
Good character can be considered only if the prosecution agrees that it is relevant.
7.w: Where a defendant is of good character, the judge should generally give a good character direction, telling the jury that this is relevant to the defendant's credibility (the first limb) and to the likelihood of their having committed the offence (the second, propensity limb), so that the jury may take it into account in the defendant's favour.
