n.0: Good character is relevant to the jury's assessment; it is not ignored.
n.2: Good character is relevant to guilt (credibility and propensity), not only sentence.
n.3: Good character does not prove innocence; it is a factor in the defendant's favour.
n.4: The direction does not depend on the prosecution agreeing to relevance.

7.q: A consumer buys a new washing machine from a retailer. Ten days after delivery, the machine develops a serious fault which means it does not work properly and is not of satisfactory quality. The consumer returns to the retailer and says that they no longer want the machine and want their money back straight away, rather than a repair or replacement. The retailer says the consumer is only entitled to a repair. The consumer seeks advice on their rights under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The consumer may reject the goods only if the retailer is first given a chance to repair them.
The consumer may reject the goods only within 14 days of delivery, and that period has now expired.
The consumer's only entitlement is to a repair or replacement, and never to a refund of the price.
The consumer has no rights at all, because the machine worked when it was first delivered.
The consumer has the short-term right to reject and get a refund, the fault appearing within 30 days.
7.w: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, goods must be of satisfactory quality, and the consumer has a short-term right to reject faulty goods and obtain a refund if they do so within 30 days of ownership passing. The consumer here is within that period.

n.0: The short-term right to reject does not require giving the retailer a chance to repair first.
n.1: The short-term right to reject lasts 30 days, not 14, so it has not expired.
n.2: The consumer is not confined to repair or replacement; the short-term right to reject gives a refund.
n.3: Later failure to meet satisfactory quality still gives rights, even if the machine initially worked.

7.q: A defendant who has spent a period in custody on remand awaiting trial is sentenced to imprisonment. The defendant asks whether the time already spent in custody before sentence counts towards the sentence to be served. The defendant was remanded in custody before conviction and sentence. A custodial sentence is now imposed. By the time sentence is passed the defendant has already spent a good stretch behind bars on remand while awaiting trial, and they naturally want to know whether that period already served counts towards the prison term the judge is now imposing or whether it simply falls away. Which of the following best describes how the remand time is treated?
o: Time on remand counts only if the judge expressly orders it in each case.
Time spent in custody on remand generally counts automatically towards the custodial sentence.
Time on remand can only be credited if the defendant applies to the Court of Appeal.
Time spent on remand is always ignored and never counts towards the sentence.
Time on remand doubles the credit given for a guilty plea.
7.w: Time spent in custody on remand before sentence generally counts automatically towards a custodial sentence: the days are administratively credited against the term to be served, so the defendant is not required to serve that time again. This is distinct from any separate reduction for a guilty plea.

n.0: Crediting is generally automatic and does not require an express order in each case.
n.2: No application to the Court of Appeal is needed for remand time to count.
n.3: Remand time is not ignored; it generally counts towards the sentence.
n.4: Remand time is credited against the sentence; it does not double the guilty-plea discount.

7.q: A person dies leaving an estate whose value is well above the tax-free threshold. The personal representatives must work out the inheritance tax payable on the death estate. They understand that a certain amount of the estate is taxed at a nil rate before tax is charged on the excess. The PRs ask about the basic operation of the nil rate band. The court considers the charge to inheritance tax on death and the nil rate band. The estate was worth well over a million pounds and the family faced a large tax bill. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Inheritance tax is charged only on the part of the estate below the nil rate band.
Inheritance tax is charged on the whole estate at 40% with no tax-free amount at all on these facts.
Inheritance tax is charged on the death estate above the available nil rate band, broadly at 40% on the excess.
Inheritance tax is never payable on a deceased person's estate in any circumstances.
Inheritance tax is charged at a flat 20% on the entire value of every estate.
7.w: On death, inheritance tax is charged on the value of the death estate. A nil rate band (a threshold) is taxed at 0%, and the value of the estate above the available nil rate band is charged to IHT, broadly at 40% (subject to reliefs and exemptions).

n.0: Tax is charged on the excess above the nil rate band, not the part below it.
n.1: There is a nil rate band, so not the whole estate is taxed.
n.3: IHT can be payable on estates above the threshold.
n.4: The death rate is broadly 40% on the excess, not a flat 20% on everything.

7.q: A firm receives £2,000 of client money but, through a posting error, the cashier pays it into the firm's office account instead of the client account. The mistake comes to light during the next reconciliation, by which time the money has been sitting in the office account for a period. The firm wants to put matters right. The money is undoubtedly client money. The receipt was correctly identified as client money at the outset, but a keying error sent it to the wrong ledger and the wrong bank account, and it was only when the balances were checked that the misplacement came to light, leaving the firm to decide how quickly and by what route to put it right. Which of the following best describes the correct action under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm may leave the money in the office account until the matter concludes on these facts.
The firm must report the error to the police before correcting it.
The firm may leave the money in the office account as the error was innocent.
The firm must transfer the money into the client account promptly on discovering the error.
The firm need do nothing provided the office account is never overdrawn.
7.w: Client money paid into the office account in error must be transferred into the client account promptly once the error is discovered, so that the client money is properly protected. The mistake is a breach that must be corrected without delay, and recorded; an innocent cause does not excuse leaving the money misplaced.

n.0: It cannot be left in the office account until the matter concludes.
n.1: Police reporting is not the prescribed step; prompt correction is.
n.2: An innocent error does not permit leaving client money in the office account.
n.4: The breach must be corrected regardless of whether the office account stays in credit.

7.q: A defendant, intending to steal from a particular safe, does everything necessary to open it, but unknown to them the safe is completely empty, so no theft could in fact be completed. The defendant is charged with attempted theft, and argues that as there was nothing to steal, they cannot be guilty. The defendant intended to steal and did acts more than merely preparatory. The offence was factually impossible to complete. The defendant had cased the target, brought the tools, and got as far as opening the safe fully intending to help themselves to the contents, only to find it standing completely empty, so that however hard they had tried there was in fact nothing there to be stolen. Which of the following best describes the position on attempts?
o: The defendant cannot be guilty, because the offence was impossible to complete.
The defendant is guilty only if they later succeed in a further attempt.
The defendant cannot be guilty unless property was actually taken.
The defendant may still be guilty of attempt, as factual impossibility is no defence.
The defendant is guilty of the full offence of theft despite the empty safe.
7.w: Under s.1(2) of the Criminal Attempts Act 1981, a person may be guilty of attempting to commit an offence even though the facts are such that the commission of the offence is impossible. So a defendant who intends to steal and does an act more than merely preparatory can be guilty of attempted theft even though the safe was empty.

n.0: Factual impossibility does not prevent liability for the attempt.
n.1: Liability for the attempt arises now; it does not depend on a later successful attempt.
n.2: Actual taking would be the full offence; the attempt does not require it.
n.4: The full offence is not committed where nothing is taken; the liability is for the attempt.

7.q: A general partnership has no written partnership agreement dealing with what happens on the death or bankruptcy of a partner. One of the partners then dies. The surviving partners assumed the firm would simply carry on unchanged, but a question arises as to the effect of the death on the partnership itself under the default statutory rules. The court considers the position under the Partnership Act 1890 in the absence of any contrary agreement. The supplier had dealt with the firm for years and simply carried on invoicing it just as before. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The death of a partner has no legal effect on the partnership in any circumstances.
The partnership is dissolved only if a majority of the surviving partners vote for it.
Subject to any agreement, the partnership is dissolved by the death of a partner.
The partnership is dissolved only where the deceased partner held a majority share.
The partnership always continues automatically, regardless of a partner's death.
7.w: Under s.33 Partnership Act 1890, subject to any agreement between the partners, a partnership is dissolved by the death or bankruptcy of any partner. A well-drafted partnership agreement usually displaces this default by providing for continuation.

n.0: Death does have a legal effect under the default statutory rule.
n.1: No vote of the survivors is required under the default rule.
n.3: Dissolution is not confined to death of a majority-share partner.
n.4: The firm does not automatically continue in the absence of contrary agreement; death dissolves it.

7.q: A trustee mixes trust money with their own in a bank account, spends the balance down to a low point (below the amount of trust money), and then later pays in fresh money of their own from an unconnected source. The beneficiaries seek to claim the later deposits as trust money. The account balance had dropped below the level of trust money before the new, unconnected deposits were made. After paying in the trust money the trustee ran the mixed account almost dry, so that at one point the balance fell well below the sum taken from the trust, and only afterwards did the trustee top it up again with money of their own from a wholly separate source. Which of the following best describes the position under the lowest intermediate balance rule?
o: The trust may claim the highest balance the account ever reached at any time.
The trust claim cannot exceed the lowest intermediate balance, so later unconnected deposits are not automatically trust money.
The trust may always claim the full amount originally paid in, regardless of intervening withdrawals on these facts.
The trust may claim all later deposits because any money in the account belongs to the trust.
The trust loses all claim to the account the moment any withdrawal is made.
7.w: Under the lowest intermediate balance rule, the beneficiaries' traceable claim to a mixed account cannot exceed the lowest balance to which the account fell after the trust money was paid in. Later deposits from an unconnected source are not treated as trust money, absent an intention to make good the trust, so the claim is capped at that lowest intermediate balance.

n.0: The claim is limited by the lowest, not the highest, balance reached.
n.2: The claim is capped at the lowest intermediate balance, not the full amount originally paid in.
n.3: Later unconnected deposits do not automatically become trust money.
n.4: A withdrawal does not necessarily destroy the entire claim; the claim survives up to the lowest balance.

7.q: A long leaseholder of a flat, having held the lease for some years, wishes to obtain greater security by extending the term of their lease, or by joining with other leaseholders to acquire the freehold of the building. The leaseholder asks whether the law gives long residential leaseholders any such rights against the landlord. The solicitor considers leasehold enfranchisement and lease extension rights. The leaseholder had a long lease but was worried about its diminishing value as the years passed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Long leaseholders have no rights at all to extend their lease or acquire the freehold.
Only commercial leaseholders, and never residential ones, have any enfranchisement rights.
A leaseholder may extend the lease only by paying the landlord whatever sum the landlord demands on these facts as a general rule.
A leaseholder can acquire the freehold only if the landlord freely chooses to sell it.
Qualifying long residential leaseholders have statutory rights to extend their lease or (collectively for flats) to acquire the freehold.
7.w: Statute gives qualifying long residential leaseholders important rights: a leaseholder of a flat may claim an individual lease extension, and leaseholders of flats may collectively enfranchise (acquire the freehold of their building); leaseholders of houses have their own enfranchisement rights. The price is determined by statutory valuation, not simply the landlord's demand.

n.0: Long residential leaseholders do have statutory enfranchisement/extension rights.
n.1: These rights are for residential, not commercial, leaseholders.
n.2: The price is set by statutory valuation, not an arbitrary landlord demand.
n.3: Enfranchisement does not depend solely on the landlord choosing to sell.

7.q: Several professionals wish to carry on business together with limited liability but with the internal flexibility of a partnership. They form a limited liability partnership and register it. A creditor of the LLP, unpaid on a debt, seeks to make the individual members personally liable for the LLP's debts as if they were ordinary partners. The business is a duly registered LLP and the debt is that of the LLP itself. The professionals deliberately chose the LLP structure precisely to shield themselves from personal exposure while keeping a partnership-style internal arrangement, and the disappointed creditor is now testing whether it can look past that structure to the individuals behind it for payment of the debt. Which of the following best describes the members' liability?
o: The members are personally liable because an LLP has no separate legal personality.
The members are generally not personally liable for the LLP's debts, as the LLP is a separate legal person with limited liability.
The members are jointly liable without limit for the LLP's debts like ordinary partners on these facts as a general rule.
The members are liable in full unless the LLP has at least four designated members.
The members are liable only up to the amount of profits they have drawn.
7.w: An LLP is a body corporate with separate legal personality, and its members generally have limited liability: the LLP itself is liable for its debts, not the members personally, save in exceptional cases (such as personal wrongdoing or clawback on insolvency). The creditor's claim lies against the LLP, not the members personally.

n.0: An LLP does have separate legal personality.
n.2: LLP members are not jointly liable without limit like ordinary partners.
n.3: Limited liability does not depend on having four designated members (an LLP needs at least two designated members, a different point).
n.4: Liability is not simply capped at profits drawn; the LLP itself bears the debt.

7.q: A solicitor, acting entirely outside their professional practice and in their private life, is convicted of a serious criminal offence of dishonesty which involved deceiving other people over a sustained period for their own personal financial gain. The conduct had nothing directly to do with any client of the firm, or with the solicitor's day-to-day work. The solicitor now argues that, because the whole matter arose purely in their private life and away from the office, it is simply no concern of the SRA and cannot amount to any breach of their professional obligations. A colleague is asked whether that argument is correct. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The SRA has no interest in a solicitor's private life, so purely private conduct can never be a breach.
Private conduct is relevant only where the solicitor is actually sent to prison for the offence.
Private conduct can be acted on only if a client happens to complain about it to the SRA.
Private conduct is a matter for the police alone and is never within the SRA's remit.
Conduct outside practice can breach the duty to uphold public trust in the profession and lead to regulatory action.
7.w: The SRA Principles require solicitors to act in a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the profession and in legal services. Serious misconduct, including dishonesty, in a solicitor's private life can undermine that trust and so fall within the regulator's remit.

n.0: Private conduct is not beyond the SRA's reach where it affects public trust in the profession.
n.1: Regulatory action does not depend on the solicitor receiving a custodial sentence.
n.2: The SRA can act on serious private misconduct whether or not a client complains.
n.3: Criminal liability and professional regulation operate in parallel; both can apply.

7.q: A defendant charged with murder raises diminished responsibility, seeking to reduce the offence to manslaughter. A question arises at trial about who has to prove the elements of the partial defence, and to what standard, given that the prosecution ordinarily bears the burden of proving guilt. The court considers the burden and standard of proof for diminished responsibility. Two psychiatrists gave differing evidence about the extent of the impairment the defendant had suffered. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Neither party bears any burden, because the judge decides the issue without proof.
The prosecution must disprove diminished responsibility beyond reasonable doubt.
The defence need only raise diminished responsibility, and the prosecution must then disprove it.
The defence must prove diminished responsibility on the balance of probabilities.
The defence must prove diminished responsibility beyond reasonable doubt.
7.w: Diminished responsibility is one of the exceptional situations where a legal burden rests on the defence: the defendant must prove the elements of the partial defence on the balance of probabilities.

n.0: There is a burden of proof; the judge does not simply decide without it.
n.1: The prosecution does not bear the burden of disproving diminished responsibility.
n.2: For diminished responsibility the defence bears a legal, not merely evidential, burden.
n.4: The defence standard is the balance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt.

7.q: A defendant unlawfully strikes a victim, and the blow causes the victim to suffer injuries that are more than merely transient and trifling — for example significant bruising, a black eye and a temporary loss of consciousness — although the injuries are not life-threatening or permanent. The defendant is charged with an offence under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 reflecting this level of harm. The court considers which offence is appropriate for actual bodily harm. The victim needed to rest for several days and had a badly swollen and painful face afterwards. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: This can only be common assault, however serious the injuries the victim suffered.
This is an offence only if the defendant specifically intended to cause actual bodily harm on these facts as a general rule.
No offence is committed unless the injuries are permanent or life-threatening.
This may amount to assault occasioning actual bodily harm under s.47, requiring the mens rea for the assault or battery.
This must be grievous bodily harm with intent under s.18 in every case of injury.
7.w: Assault occasioning actual bodily harm (s.47 OAPA 1861) requires an assault or battery that causes actual bodily harm (harm more than transient and trifling). The mens rea is only that required for the underlying assault or battery; no additional intent as to the harm is needed.

n.0: Injury beyond the transient and trifling takes this above common assault.
n.1: No additional intent as to the ABH is required beyond the assault/battery mens rea.
n.2: ABH does not require permanent or life-threatening injury.
n.4: Section 18 requires intent to cause GBH; that is not established merely by ABH-level injury.

7.q: A local authority, which is a public body exercising statutory functions, makes a decision affecting an individual in a way that interferes with that individual's Convention rights. The authority is not required by any incompatible primary legislation to act as it did. The individual considers challenging the authority's conduct. The authority exercised a statutory function in the way it chose, not because any Act compelled that particular course, and the individual affected wants to know whether the way the authority acted can be said to be unlawful given the body's public character and its obligations under the Act. Which of the following best describes the position under section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998?
o: Only central government, not local authorities, is bound by Convention rights.
It is unlawful for the public authority to act incompatibly with a Convention right.
A public authority may act incompatibly provided it later apologises.
A public authority is free to act incompatibly with Convention rights if it chooses.
Convention rights bind private individuals in the same way as public authorities.
7.w: Section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 makes it unlawful for a public authority to act in a way that is incompatible with a Convention right, unless primary legislation requires it to act that way. A local authority exercising statutory functions is a public authority for this purpose.

n.0: Local authorities, not just central government, are public authorities bound by section 6.
n.2: A later apology does not make the incompatible act lawful.
n.3: A public authority is not free to breach Convention rights at will.
n.4: The Act principally binds public authorities, not private individuals directly.

7.q: A privately funded defendant is acquitted at trial after incurring legal costs in defending the proceedings. The defendant asks whether they can recover any of their costs. The defendant was not legally aided and has been acquitted. The defendant wishes to recover defence costs. Having paid privately to defend himself, the defendant has been cleared at trial and is now considerably out of pocket for his legal costs, so he is asking whether, having been acquitted, he can get any of that expenditure back and, if so, from where. Which of the following best describes the position on a defendant's costs order?
o: The acquitted defendant may recover costs only from the individual prosecutor personally on these facts as a general rule.
The acquitted defendant must apply to the Court of Appeal to recover any costs.
The court may make a defendant's costs order for reasonable costs from central funds, though the amount recoverable may be capped.
The acquitted defendant automatically recovers all costs in full without limit.
An acquitted defendant can never recover any of their defence costs.
7.w: An acquitted defendant may be awarded a defendant's costs order, allowing recovery of some or all reasonable costs incurred, generally payable out of central funds. However, recovery for privately funded defendants is subject to caps (often at legal aid rates), so the full costs incurred may not be recovered.

n.0: A defendant's costs order is generally paid from central funds, not by the prosecutor personally.
n.1: The trial court can make the order; an application to the Court of Appeal is not required.
n.3: Recovery is not automatic and unlimited; caps commonly apply.
n.4: An acquitted defendant can, in appropriate cases, recover costs, so 'never' is wrong.

7.q: A solicitor is acting for a client in financial remedy proceedings following a divorce. During a conference the client admits, in strict confidence, that they hold substantial assets in an undisclosed offshore bank account which they have deliberately kept out of the figures filed with the court, and firmly instructs the solicitor to say nothing whatever about those assets and to proceed on the basis of the figures already before the court. The solicitor knows that the court is being asked to decide the case on the footing that those figures are complete and accurate. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's duty under the SRA Standards and Regulations?
o: The duty of confidentiality entitles the solicitor to disregard the undisclosed assets entirely and simply carry on.
The solicitor must immediately report the client to the police for the non-disclosure of the offshore assets.
The solicitor may rely on the client's instructions and present the case exactly as the client wishes it to be put.
The solicitor must follow the client's instructions in full, including the instruction not to disclose the assets.
The solicitor must not knowingly mislead the court and must cease to act if the client refuses to correct the position.
7.w: A solicitor must not knowingly or recklessly mislead the court. In financial remedy proceedings there is a duty of full and frank disclosure, so the solicitor cannot advance a case they know to be materially incomplete, and must cease acting if the client refuses to put the position right.

n.0: Confidentiality does not permit the solicitor to continue advancing a knowingly incomplete case.
n.1: An immediate report to the police is not the primary professional duty here; the duty is not to mislead the court and to cease acting if necessary.
n.2: The client's instructions cannot require the solicitor to mislead the court.
n.3: A solicitor must not follow an instruction that would result in the court being misled.

7.q: A trustee, faced with a difficult decision about how to exercise a discretionary power under the trust, is unsure whether the course they propose is proper and is worried about being personally liable if it later turns out to be wrong. Rather than simply going ahead and risking a breach, the trustee wants to protect their position by obtaining guidance before acting. The trustee seeks advice on what they can do to obtain protection when genuinely in doubt about the exercise of a power. The decision was finely balanced and the trustee did not want to expose themselves to a later claim. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustee has no option but to act on their own judgement and simply hope it is correct.
The trustee may act however they wish, because a trustee is never liable for an honest decision on these facts.
The trustee may resign, and doing so automatically discharges all past and future liability.
The trustee may apply to the court for directions and will be protected if they act in accordance with them.
The trustee must always obtain the consent of all the beneficiaries before exercising any power.
7.w: A trustee who is genuinely in doubt about how to exercise a power or administer the trust may apply to the court for directions. If the trustee then acts in accordance with the court's directions, they are protected from a subsequent allegation of breach in respect of that action.

n.0: The trustee is not forced to act on their own judgement; they may seek court directions.
n.1: An honest decision does not automatically shield a trustee from liability.
n.2: Resignation does not discharge a trustee from liability for past breaches.
n.4: Unanimous beneficiary consent is not required to exercise a power, nor is it the protective route here.

7.q: The solicitors acting for a buyer and a seller in a residential transaction are preparing the contract and, as is usual in conveyancing practice, propose to base it on a widely used standard set of contractual terms rather than drafting every provision from scratch, adapting them with any special conditions the transaction requires. The buyer asks what these standard terms are and their role in the contract. The solicitor considers the use of the Standard Conditions of Sale in a residential conveyancing contract. The solicitors wanted a reliable, well-understood framework rather than reinventing every clause. Which of the following best describes their role?
o: The Standard Conditions of Sale replace the need for any written contract between the parties.
The Standard Conditions of Sale are commonly incorporated as the contract's general terms, supplemented by special conditions for the particular deal.
The Standard Conditions of Sale apply only to commercial property and never to residential sales.
The Standard Conditions of Sale are drafted afresh by the parties for every individual transaction.
The Standard Conditions of Sale are imposed by statute and cannot be varied by the parties in any way on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
7.w: Residential conveyancing contracts commonly incorporate the Standard Conditions of Sale as their general terms (with the Standard Commercial Property Conditions used for commercial deals). These standard terms are then adapted and supplemented by special conditions tailored to the particular transaction.

n.0: They form part of, rather than replace, the written contract.
n.2: The residential Standard Conditions of Sale are for residential deals (commercial deals use the SCPC).
n.3: They are pre-drafted standard terms, not written afresh each time.
n.4: The Standard Conditions are contractual terms the parties adopt and can vary, not statutory rules.

7.q: A claimant brings a personal injury claim funded in the usual way, and is concerned that, if the claim fails, they will be ordered to pay the defendant's costs and be financially ruined. The claimant has heard that a special costs regime applies to personal injury claims which limits their exposure to the defendant's costs. The court considers qualified one-way costs shifting (QOCS) in personal injury litigation. The claimant was of modest means and was anxious about the risk of a large adverse costs order. Which of the following best describes it?
o: QOCS means the defendant can never recover any costs from anyone in any circumstances.
Under QOCS, a losing personal injury claimant must always pay the defendant's costs in full.
Under QOCS, an unsuccessful personal injury claimant is generally protected from paying the defendant's costs, subject to exceptions.
QOCS applies to all civil claims of every kind, not only personal injury claims.
QOCS requires the claimant to pay the defendant's costs only if the claim was worth over £25,000 on these facts as a general rule.
7.w: Qualified one-way costs shifting (QOCS) generally protects an unsuccessful claimant in a personal injury claim from having to pay the successful defendant's costs, subject to exceptions (such as fundamental dishonesty, claims struck out, or costs offset against damages/Part 36).

n.0: QOCS is qualified, with exceptions; it is not an absolute bar on any recovery.
n.1: QOCS protects the losing claimant; it does not require them to pay in full.
n.3: QOCS is specific to personal injury claims, not all civil claims.
n.4: QOCS protection does not turn on the claim exceeding £25,000.

7.q: Trustees are about to distribute the trust fund but are concerned that there may be beneficiaries or claimants of whom they are not currently aware, and they do not want to be personally liable if an unknown claimant later comes forward after the distribution. They wish to protect themselves before distributing. The trustees seek advice on a statutory step they can take to guard against personal liability to unknown claimants. The estate was complex, with dealings going back many years and records that were far from complete. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustees are automatically protected against all unknown claimants without taking any step.
The trustees can only protect themselves by obtaining the consent of every possible claimant first on these facts.
The trustees may advertise for claimants under s.27 Trustee Act 1925 to protect themselves before distributing.
The trustees may distribute free of any liability provided they act honestly and in good faith.
The trustees have no way to protect themselves and must simply distribute and hope for the best.
7.w: Under s.27 of the Trustee Act 1925, trustees may give statutory notice by advertisement for claimants, and, having waited the required period, may then distribute the estate/trust fund without being personally liable to claimants of whom they had no notice at the time of distribution.

n.0: Trustees are not automatically protected without taking the statutory step.
n.1: Obtaining every possible claimant's consent is not the mechanism; advertisement is.
n.3: Honest good faith alone does not give the s.27 protection.
n.4: There is a protective step available; trustees are not left with no protection.

7.q: A lender advances money to a company for a specific, identified purpose (to pay a particular class of the company's creditors), on terms that the money is to be used only for that purpose and not mixed with the company's general funds. Before the purpose can be carried out, the company becomes insolvent. The lender argues that the money did not become part of the company's general assets available to all creditors, but was held on trust. The money was paid into a separate account and was never mixed with the company's ordinary trading funds. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The money may be held on a Quistclose-type trust for the lender, as it was advanced for a specific purpose that failed.
The money is held on a charitable trust because it was to pay creditors.
The money automatically belongs to the company's general creditors on its insolvency.
The money is the company's absolutely, because a loan always transfers full ownership.
The money is held on trust only if the loan agreement expressly created a trust in those words on these facts.
7.w: Where money is lent for a specific, exclusive purpose and is not to be at the borrower's free disposal, a Quistclose trust may arise: the money is held on trust for that purpose, and if the purpose fails, it results to the lender rather than falling into the general estate (Barclays Bank v Quistclose; Twinsectra v Yardley).

n.1: There is no charitable element; it is a private purpose loan.
n.2: Such money does not necessarily fall to the general creditors; a trust may protect it.
n.3: A purpose-restricted loan does not transfer full beneficial ownership to the borrower.
n.4: The trust can arise from the purpose restriction without the word 'trust' being used.

7.q: One of two beneficial joint tenants wishes to bring the joint tenancy to an end and hold as tenants in common, so that their share can pass under their will. They are considering the ways in which a beneficial joint tenancy may be severed during their lifetime. The co-owners currently hold as beneficial joint tenants. One wishes to sever. One of the beneficial joint tenants no longer wants the survivorship rule to apply to their share, preferring that it pass under their will as a distinct share, and is asking what steps are open to them, during their lifetime, to turn the joint tenancy into a tenancy in common. Which of the following best describes how severance may be effected?
o: Only by obtaining a court order in every case.
Only with the consent of all the other joint tenants in writing.
Only on the death of one of the joint tenants.
By written notice to the other joint tenant(s), or by an act operating on one's own share, mutual agreement, or a course of dealing.
Severance of a beneficial joint tenancy is not possible during the joint tenants' lifetimes on these facts as a general rule.
7.w: A beneficial joint tenancy may be severed during the joint tenants' lives in several ways: by giving written notice of severance to the other joint tenant(s) under s.36(2) of the Law of Property Act 1925, or by one of the methods in Williams v Hensman, namely an act of a joint tenant operating on their own share (such as selling or mortgaging it), mutual agreement, or a course of dealing. Severance creates a tenancy in common.

n.0: A court order is not required; written notice or the Williams v Hensman methods suffice.
n.1: Written notice under s.36(2) does not require the others' consent.
n.2: Severance occurs during life; death triggers survivorship, not severance.
n.4: Severance is possible during the joint tenants' lifetimes.

7.q: A public body reaches a decision that, although within its legal powers and taken by a fair procedure, is so extreme that no reasonable authority properly directing itself could ever have arrived at it. A claimant seeks judicial review, focusing on the quality of the decision itself rather than the procedure. The decision defies logic and accepted standards. There is no complaint that the body lacked the power or that the procedure was unfair; the objection is to the decision itself, which the claimant says is so far removed from anything a sensible authority could have decided that it cannot be allowed to stand on review. Which of the following best identifies the ground of judicial review relied on?
o: Procedural impropriety through a breach of natural justice.
Breach of a substantive legitimate expectation.
Failure to give reasons for the decision.
Irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness).
Illegality through acting outside statutory powers.
7.w: Irrationality, or Wednesbury unreasonableness, is a ground of judicial review that applies where a decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority, properly directing itself, could have made it. It targets the substance or quality of the decision rather than the legality of the power or the fairness of the procedure.

n.0: Procedural impropriety concerns unfair procedure, which is not the focus here.
n.1: Legitimate expectation involves reliance on a promise or practice, not extreme unreasonableness.
n.2: Failure to give reasons is a distinct procedural complaint, not irrationality.
n.4: Illegality concerns exceeding or misusing legal powers, not the extreme quality of a lawful-powered decision.

7.q: A party dissatisfied with a decision of the First-tier Tribunal on a specialist matter wishes to challenge it. They are told there is a specialist appellate tribunal that hears such appeals, generally on a point of law, and which is itself a superior court of record. The challenge is from the First-tier Tribunal. An onward appeal route exists. Unhappy with how the First-tier Tribunal decided their specialist matter, the party wants to take the point higher, and is told that a dedicated appellate tribunal, itself a superior court of record, exists to hear such appeals, generally confined to questions of law. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The First-tier Tribunal's decisions can only ever be challenged by judicial review on these facts as a general rule.
Appeals from the First-tier Tribunal lie directly to the Supreme Court.
Appeals from the First-tier Tribunal lie to the Crown Court.
There is no route of appeal from the First-tier Tribunal at all.
An appeal generally lies, usually on a point of law, to the Upper Tribunal, with a further onward route in appropriate cases.
7.w: Within the unified tribunals structure, an appeal from the First-tier Tribunal generally lies, usually on a point of law and often with permission, to the Upper Tribunal, which is a superior court of record. From the Upper Tribunal a further appeal may lie to the Court of Appeal in appropriate cases.

n.0: There is a statutory appeal route to the Upper Tribunal, not only judicial review.
n.1: Appeals go to the Upper Tribunal, not directly to the Supreme Court.
n.2: Appeals do not lie to the Crown Court, which is a criminal court.
n.3: There is a route of appeal from the First-tier Tribunal, so 'no route' is wrong.

7.q: A developer sells part of their land and imposes a restrictive covenant on the buyer not to build on the land sold, to protect the developer's retained land. The land is later sold on to a new owner who wishes to build. The covenant is restrictive (negative) and was intended to benefit the retained land. The burdened land has changed hands. When selling off part of the land the developer made the buyer promise not to build on it, so as to protect the land the developer kept, and now that the burdened plot has passed into new hands the new owner wants to build, raising the question whether that negative promise still binds them. Which of the following best describes when the burden of the restrictive covenant runs to bind the new owner in equity?
o: The burden runs in equity under Tulk v Moxhay if the covenant is restrictive, touches and concerns the land, and there is notice.
The burden binds the new owner only if they paid less than market value.
The burden runs only if the new owner personally re-covenants with the developer on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The burden of a restrictive covenant never binds a successor to the land.
The burden runs at law automatically like any positive obligation.
7.w: Under Tulk v Moxhay, the burden of a restrictive covenant can run in equity to bind successors where the covenant is negative (restrictive) in substance, it touches and concerns (benefits) the covenantee's retained land, the parties intended the burden to run, and the successor has notice (in registered land, protected by a notice on the register). Positive covenants do not run in this way.

n.1: Being bound does not depend on paying below market value; notice is the relevant factor.
n.2: A fresh covenant by the new owner is a separate device; Tulk v Moxhay makes the original burden run in equity.
n.3: The burden of a restrictive covenant can bind successors in equity; it is positive covenants that do not run.
n.4: The burden does not run at law like a positive obligation; it runs in equity under Tulk v Moxhay.

7.q: A defendant carries out a series of acts against a victim as part of one connected episode: at the point when the defendant had the guilty mind (mens rea), the act that actually caused the prohibited result had not yet been completed, and by the time the fatal act occurred the defendant may have believed the victim was already dead. The defence argues that the guilty act and the guilty mind did not exactly coincide in time. The court considers the coincidence of actus reus and mens rea. The whole episode unfolded over a short, continuous period as part of a single connected course of events. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The coincidence requirement does not apply to offences against the person at all.
The defendant is liable only if the victim in fact died at the exact moment of the guilty mind.
The defendant is automatically liable regardless of whether the mens rea ever existed at all.
The defendant may be liable where the acts form one continuing transaction during which the mens rea was present.
The defendant cannot be liable unless the guilty act and guilty mind coincided at one precise instant.
7.w: Although actus reus and mens rea must coincide, the courts treat a series of connected acts as one continuing transaction. If the defendant had the mens rea at some point during that transaction, the coincidence requirement is satisfied even if the fatal act occurred later (Thabo Meli v R; R v Church).

n.0: The coincidence principle applies to offences against the person too.
n.1: Liability does not depend on death occurring at the precise moment of the guilty mind.
n.2: Liability still requires that mens rea existed during the transaction.
n.4: Exact instantaneous coincidence is not required; a continuing transaction suffices.

7.q: An individual sells the whole of their trading business, which they have owned and run for many years, and makes a substantial chargeable gain on the disposal of the business assets. They ask their adviser whether any relief may reduce the rate of capital gains tax on the qualifying gain. The disposal is of a business the individual has owned and operated for the requisite period. The individual seeks to reduce the CGT payable on the qualifying gain. Having built up and run the business over many years, the individual is now selling it outright and stands to make a large gain on the business assets, and is asking whether any relief exists that could bring down the capital gains tax rate on the part of the gain that qualifies. Which of the following best describes a relief that may apply?
o: The gain is treated as trading income subject to income tax and national insurance on these facts as a general rule.
The gain is automatically exempt from capital gains tax with no conditions.
The gain is charged to corporation tax rather than capital gains tax.
Business Asset Disposal Relief may apply, reducing the rate of capital gains tax on qualifying gains up to a lifetime limit.
No relief of any kind is available on the disposal of a business.
7.w: Business Asset Disposal Relief (formerly Entrepreneurs' Relief) may reduce the rate of capital gains tax on qualifying gains from the disposal of all or part of a trading business (or qualifying shares), subject to conditions including a minimum ownership period, up to a lifetime limit on qualifying gains. It reduces the CGT rate rather than exempting the gain entirely.

n.0: The gain is a capital gain, not trading income subject to income tax and NICs.
n.1: The gain is not automatically exempt; relief has conditions and a lifetime limit.
n.2: An individual's gain is charged to capital gains tax, not corporation tax.
n.4: Reliefs such as Business Asset Disposal Relief are available on qualifying business disposals.

7.q: A will leaves a general pecuniary legacy of a fixed sum of money to a beneficiary, without specifying when it is to be paid. The executors do not pay it until well over a year after the death. The beneficiary asks whether they are entitled to interest on the delayed legacy, and from when. The legacy is a general pecuniary legacy with no special payment date. Payment was delayed beyond a year from death. The will left a fixed cash sum to the beneficiary but said nothing about when it should be paid, and the executors did not in fact pay it until well over a year had gone by, prompting the beneficiary to ask whether interest is due on the delayed legacy and, if so, from what date it starts to run. Which of the following best describes the position on interest?
o: Interest generally runs on a general pecuniary legacy from the first anniversary of death (the end of the executor's year).
Interest runs only from the date the beneficiary first demands payment.
No interest is ever payable on a pecuniary legacy however long payment is delayed on these facts as a general rule.
Interest runs from the date the grant of probate is issued.
Interest runs on the legacy from the date of death in every case.
7.w: A general pecuniary legacy that is not paid within the executor's year generally carries interest from the first anniversary of the death (the date by which it ought to have been paid), at the rate applicable to legacies, unless the will provides otherwise or an exception applies (such as a legacy to a minor child of the testator, which may carry interest from death).

n.1: Interest does not depend on the beneficiary demanding payment.
n.2: Interest can be payable if the legacy is paid late, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Interest runs from the first anniversary of death, not the date of the grant.
n.4: Interest on a general legacy generally runs from the end of the executor's year, not from death.

7.q: A person dies owning their home, which they leave to their children (direct descendants). The personal representatives are considering whether an additional inheritance tax allowance, beyond the ordinary nil rate band, is available because the home is passing to descendants. The court considers the residence nil rate band. The family home was worth a substantial sum and was being left to the deceased's two children. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The residence nil rate band applies to any gift of any property to anyone at all.
The residence nil rate band exempts the whole of the home from inheritance tax in every case on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
An additional residence nil rate band may be available where a home is left to direct descendants, subject to conditions and a taper for large estates.
The residence nil rate band is available only where the home is left to a spouse.
There is no additional allowance for a home; only the ordinary nil rate band applies.
7.w: The residence nil rate band is an additional nil rate band available, subject to conditions, where a residence (or its value) is left to direct descendants. It is subject to a maximum amount and is tapered away for estates above a high value threshold.

n.0: The RNRB applies to a residence left to descendants, not any gift to anyone.
n.1: It is a capped additional band, not a complete exemption of the whole home.
n.3: It applies where the home passes to descendants, not (for the RNRB) to a spouse.
n.4: There is an additional residence nil rate band beyond the ordinary NRB.

7.q: A firm acting for a client in a transaction receives £1,000 from a third party, the money being intended for the client in connection with the matter the firm is handling. The cashier is unsure how to classify money that has come from someone other than the firm's own client, and whether the usual client account protections apply to it. The money relates to the firm's delivery of regulated services. The payment arrived from someone other than the firm's own client but was clearly earmarked for the client in connection with the matter the firm is handling, and the cashier is unsure whether money that did not come from the client still attracts the full protection of the client account rules. Which of the following best describes the treatment of the £1,000 under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The £1,000 is office money because it came from a third party.
The £1,000 is client money and must be paid into the client account.
The £1,000 must be returned to the third party regardless of the client's interest.
The £1,000 may be held in cash outside any account as third-party money.
The £1,000 falls outside the rules because the payer is not the firm's client.
7.w: Client money includes money held or received for a third party in the course of delivering regulated services, not only money received from the firm's own client. Money received from a third party for the client is client money and must be paid into the client account and dealt with in accordance with the rules.

n.0: Money from a third party for the client is client money, not office money.
n.2: It is held for the client's benefit and dealt with under the rules, not automatically returned to the payer.
n.3: It cannot be held in cash outside a client account.
n.4: The rules apply to money held for third parties too, not only the firm's client.

7.q: In negotiations for a business contract, one party makes a statement of fact to the other which turns out to be false, and which induced the contract. The statement was not made dishonestly, but the maker had no reasonable grounds for believing it was true. The innocent party has suffered loss and wishes to claim damages. The party who made the statement argues that, since they were not fraudulent, no damages can be claimed against them. The innocent party seeks advice under the Misrepresentation Act 1967. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Damages are available under s.2(1) unless the maker proves a reasonable belief in the statement's truth.
No damages are available at all, because the maker of the statement was not fraudulent.
Damages are available only if the innocent party has already rescinded the whole contract.
Damages are available only where the statement later became an express term of the contract.
Damages are available only if the innocent party first proves the maker was negligent.
7.w: Under section 2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act 1967, once a misrepresentation inducing the contract is shown, the representor is liable in damages unless they prove they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe, the statement was true. The burden of disproving negligence lies on the representor.

n.1: Damages are available under s.2(1) even without fraud.
n.2: Damages under s.2(1) do not depend on the contract first having been rescinded.
n.3: A s.2(1) claim does not require the statement to have become a contractual term.
n.4: The claimant need not prove negligence; the representor must disprove it.

7.q: A squatter has been in open adverse possession of a plot of registered land for 15 years. The registered proprietor has taken no steps during that time to remove the squatter or to assert any claim to the land. The squatter argues that, because more than the old 12-year limitation period has now passed, the registered proprietor's title has automatically been extinguished in the squatter's favour and the land has become theirs without more. The squatter seeks advice on their true position under the current law governing adverse possession of registered land. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The proprietor's title was extinguished but the squatter must pay compensation to be registered.
The squatter became the registered proprietor automatically after 10 years of possession.
The registered proprietor's title was automatically extinguished after 12 years, as with unregistered land, as a matter of general law.
The registered proprietor's title is not automatically extinguished; the squatter must use the LRA 2002 procedure to be registered.
Adverse possession has no application at all to registered land in any circumstances.
7.w: For registered land the automatic extinguishment rule does not apply. Time does not bar the registered proprietor; instead the squatter must apply under Schedule 6 LRA 2002 (after 10 years), and the proprietor can object, so title is not lost by mere lapse of time.

n.0: There is no scheme of paying compensation to be registered; the proprietor's objection generally defeats the application.
n.1: There is no automatic registration of the squatter after 10 years; an application and the Schedule 6 process are needed.
n.2: Registered land is not subject to the 12-year automatic extinguishment of unregistered land.
n.4: Adverse possession does apply to registered land, but under the Schedule 6 regime.

7.q: A husband, about to go to work abroad for an extended period, promises his wife that he will pay her a monthly allowance of £200 while he is away. The couple are on good terms at the time and nothing is written down or formalised. Some months later the marriage breaks down, the husband stops the payments, and the wife sues him to enforce the promise of the monthly allowance, arguing that it was a clear agreement supported by their relationship. The husband denies that the arrangement was ever legally binding. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is a binding contract, because the wife plainly relied on the promise of the allowance.
There is a binding contract, because any clear promise of money between spouses is legally enforceable.
There is no binding contract: domestic arrangements are presumed to lack intention to create legal relations.
There is no binding contract, because a promise between spouses can never be legally enforceable.
There is a binding contract, because the promise concerned a specific sum payable each month.
7.w: Agreements made between spouses in a domestic or social context are presumed not to be intended to create legal relations (Balfour v Balfour). On these facts that presumption is not rebutted, so the promise of the allowance is not an enforceable contract.

n.0: Reliance alone does not rebut the presumption against intention in a domestic arrangement.
n.1: Not every promise of money between spouses is enforceable; the domestic presumption applies.
n.3: Spousal promises can be enforceable where intention is shown, so 'never' is too absolute.
n.4: Specifying a monthly sum does not, by itself, rebut the presumption against legal intention.

7.q: A person hires a room overlooking a route, at a high price, for the specific purpose, known to both parties, of watching a royal procession that is due to pass by on a particular day. The procession is then cancelled because of the monarch's illness, although the room itself remains perfectly usable and the view unobstructed. The room owner sues for the agreed hire charge, and the hirer refuses to pay, arguing that the whole purpose of the contract has been destroyed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract stands, because frustration can never apply merely because an event is cancelled.
The contract is frustrated only if the room could not physically be entered on the day.
The contract stands and the hirer must pay, because the room remained available to be used.
The contract is likely frustrated: the cancelled procession destroyed its common foundation.
The hirer must pay, because watching the procession was only the hirer's private motive.
7.w: Where the occurrence of a particular event is the common foundation of the contract, known to both parties, its cancellation may frustrate the contract even though performance remains physically possible (Krell v Henry). The procession's cancellation destroyed the shared purpose of hiring the room.

n.0: Cancellation of the very event that is the contract's foundation can frustrate it.
n.1: Frustration here does not turn on physical inability to enter the room.
n.2: Continued availability of the room does not save the contract where its shared purpose has gone.
n.4: The purpose was not a mere private motive; it was the common basis of the contract known to both.

7.q: A strong swimmer is walking past a lake when they see a stranger, with whom they have no relationship and for whom they have no responsibility, struggling in the water. The swimmer could easily have effected a rescue at no risk but chooses to walk on, and the stranger drowns. The stranger's family wish to sue the swimmer in negligence for failing to act. The swimmer did nothing to create the danger and had assumed no responsibility for the stranger's safety. Which of the following best describes the swimmer's liability in negligence for the pure omission to act?
o: There is liability because everyone owes a general legal duty to rescue strangers in peril.
There is generally no liability for a pure failure to act absent a recognised duty to act.
There is liability because failing to rescue is always treated the same as causing the harm.
There is liability because the swimmer's skill created a special duty to all swimmers in difficulty.
There is automatic liability whenever a person could easily have prevented harm to another.
7.w: The common law generally imposes no liability for pure omissions: a person is not ordinarily liable for merely failing to confer a benefit or prevent harm to another. A duty to act arises only in recognised situations, such as where the defendant created the danger, assumed responsibility, or had control over the claimant or a third party. None applies here.

n.0: English law imposes no general duty to rescue a stranger in peril.
n.2: A pure omission is not equated with positively causing the harm absent a duty to act.
n.3: Merely being a capable swimmer does not create a special duty to those in difficulty.
n.4: Ease of prevention does not by itself create a duty to act.

7.q: A client with a strong but by no means certain civil claim asks a solicitor how the litigation might be funded and what the financial risks of bringing it will actually be. The solicitor discusses entering into a conditional fee agreement, but says nothing at all about what will happen to costs if the claim fails, and in particular never mentions that the client could be ordered to pay the opponent's legal costs, or that insurance against that very risk is available to buy. The client later loses at trial and is shocked to be facing the opponent's costs. Which of the following best describes the solicitor's regulatory position?
o: The solicitor breached only the rules on client money by failing to warn about the opponent's costs.
The solicitor acted properly, because the risk of paying an opponent's costs is common knowledge among litigants.
The solicitor acted properly, because a solicitor need only ever explain the firm's own fees to the client.
The solicitor breached the duty to explain the funding options and the risk of paying the opponent's costs on losing.
The solicitor did nothing wrong, because the risk of an adverse costs order only arises after trial in any event.
7.w: To act in the client's best interests and give the best possible information, the solicitor must explain the available funding options and the associated risks, including the possibility of an adverse costs order if the claim fails and the availability of insurance against that risk.

n.0: The failing concerns funding and costs information, not the client money rules.
n.1: The solicitor cannot assume the client already understands the adverse costs risk.
n.2: The duty to inform is not limited to the firm's own fees; it includes the risk of paying the opponent's costs.
n.4: The client needs to understand the adverse costs risk before deciding to litigate, not only after trial.

7.q: A director of a company, who is held out by the company as having authority to make contracts of a particular kind, enters into such a contract with a third party. In fact the board had not actually authorised this particular contract, but the third party did not know that and reasonably relied on the director's apparent authority. The company now denies it is bound. The court considers whether the company is bound by the acts of a person with ostensible (apparent) authority. The third party had dealt with the company through this director on several previous occasions. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The company is never bound by a director acting without actual authority in any circumstances.
The company is never bound unless the board expressly authorised the specific contract in advance on these facts.
The company is bound where it held the director out as having authority and the third party reasonably relied on it.
The company is bound only if the third party inspected the company's internal board minutes.
The company is bound only where the contract turned out to be beneficial to the company.
7.w: A company may be bound by the acts of an agent with ostensible (apparent) authority: where the company, by its conduct, represents that the person has authority, and a third party reasonably relies on that representation, the company is bound even without actual authority (Freeman & Lockyer; and statutory protections also assist third parties).

n.0: A company can be bound by ostensible authority despite the absence of actual authority.
n.1: Express prior authorisation is not always required; ostensible authority can bind the company.
n.3: A third party is not required to inspect internal board minutes.
n.4: The company is bound regardless of whether the contract benefited it.

7.q: A defendant applies to have the claimant's statement of case struck out, arguing that it discloses no reasonable grounds for bringing the claim, or is an abuse of the court's process. The claimant resists, saying the court has no power to end a claim without a trial. The court considers its power to strike out a statement of case under Part 3.4 of the Civil Procedure Rules. The particulars as drafted set out no facts capable of amounting to any recognised cause of action. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court must strike out any claim that a defendant asks it to strike out.
The court has no power to strike out a statement of case in any circumstances at all on these facts.
The court may strike out a statement of case that discloses no reasonable grounds or is an abuse of process.
The court may strike out a claim only where the claimant consents to the strike out.
The court may strike out a statement of case only after the trial has concluded.
7.w: Under CPR 3.4, the court may strike out a statement of case (or part of it) if it discloses no reasonable grounds for bringing or defending the claim, is an abuse of the court's process, or if there has been a failure to comply with a rule, practice direction or court order.

n.0: Strike out is discretionary and requires the grounds to be met, not automatic on request.
n.1: The court does have a strike-out power.
n.3: Strike out does not require the claimant's consent.
n.4: Strike out is a pre-trial (or interim) remedy, not confined to after trial.

7.q: A settlor transfers a fund to trustees to be applied for a stated purpose, and claims that the trust is a valid charitable trust so that it does not need identifiable beneficiaries and can last indefinitely. The purpose is said to benefit the community. When the status of the trust is challenged, the court must decide whether it qualifies as charitable. The settlor's adviser is asked to explain the essential requirements a trust must meet to be charitable. The fund was substantial and the settlor wanted the arrangement to endure well beyond an ordinary lifetime. Which of the following best describes the requirements?
o: It must benefit the settlor's own family and friends as its primary object.
It must have identifiable individual beneficiaries who can enforce it in court on these facts.
It must be registered as a company before it can be treated as charitable.
It must simply be intended by the settlor to do some good in the world.
It must be for a recognised charitable purpose, for the public benefit, and exclusively charitable.
7.w: To be charitable, a trust must be for a purpose within the descriptions of charitable purposes in the Charities Act 2011, must be for the public benefit, and must be exclusively charitable. Charitable trusts are an exception to the beneficiary principle and are enforced by the Attorney General/Charity Commission.

n.0: A trust primarily for the settlor's family and friends is not charitable.
n.1: Charitable trusts need no identifiable individual beneficiaries; that is the point of the exception.
n.2: Incorporation as a company is not required for a charitable trust.
n.3: A general intention to do good is not enough; the purpose must be legally charitable.

7.q: A public authority interferes with a right such as the right to respect for private and family life, which is a qualified Convention right that may be interfered with only where the interference is justified. The claimant argues the interference was not justified. A solicitor is asked about how interference with a qualified Convention right is assessed. The solicitor considers the structure of qualified Convention rights (such as Articles 8 to 11). The authority had interfered with the person's private life and had to justify doing so. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Interference with a qualified right is permitted only if it is in accordance with the law, pursues a legitimate aim, and is necessary and proportionate.
Qualified rights may be interfered with only where the individual consents in writing.
Interference with a qualified right requires no justification of any kind.
A public authority may interfere with a qualified right for any reason it considers convenient on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Qualified Convention rights are absolute and can never be interfered with in any circumstances.
7.w: Qualified Convention rights (such as Articles 8 to 11) may be interfered with, but only where the interference is in accordance with the law, pursues one of the legitimate aims specified in the article, and is necessary in a democratic society — that is, a proportionate response to a pressing social need.

n.1: Justification is by the legal/legitimate-aim/proportionality test, not the individual's written consent.
n.2: Interference with a qualified right does require justification.
n.3: Interference cannot be for any convenient reason; it must be justified.
n.4: Qualified rights are not absolute; that describes rights like Article 3.

7.q: A defendant carried out an activity that created only a very small risk of harm, where the cost and difficulty of eliminating that small risk entirely would have been very high, and where the activity itself had significant social utility. An accident nonetheless occurred and the claimant was injured. The claimant argues the defendant should have taken every possible precaution regardless of cost. The court must weigh the relevant factors in deciding whether the defendant breached the standard of care. Which of the following best describes how breach is assessed?
o: Breach weighs the likelihood and seriousness of harm against the cost of precautions and utility.
The defendant is in breach unless they eliminated every conceivable risk, whatever the cost.
Breach depends only on whether harm was in fact caused to the claimant.
Breach is assessed purely by asking whether the defendant could have afforded better precautions.
The defendant is never in breach so long as the activity had some social utility of any kind.
7.w: Whether the standard of care has been breached involves balancing the magnitude of the risk (likelihood and seriousness of harm) against the cost and practicability of precautions and the social utility of the defendant's activity (Bolton v Stone; Watt v Hertfordshire).

n.1: A defendant need not eliminate every conceivable risk regardless of cost; the test is a balance.
n.2: The occurrence of harm does not by itself establish breach.
n.3: Affordability alone is not the test; the full balancing of factors applies.
n.4: Social utility is one factor in the balance, not a complete answer to any risk.

7.q: A firm is asked to act for two clients on the same transaction: a group of investors who together wish to buy and then jointly develop a single commercial property, all of them pursuing exactly the same commercial objective and wanting the deal structured in the same way. There is nonetheless a technical conflict of interest between them, because their individual positions are not quite identical. The clients all want the one firm to act for the whole group in order to save time and cost, and are content to be told how their information will be handled. The firm considers whether it may act. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may act provided it simply charges each investor a separate fee for the work done.
The firm may never act for two clients where any conflict of interest exists between them, whatever the circumstances.
The firm may act only if the SRA gives its prior approval to the joint retainer between the investors.
The firm may act only under the substantially-common-interest exception, with informed consent and appropriate safeguards.
The firm may act for the group without any consent, because the investors all want the same outcome.
7.w: Although there is a conflict, the SRA Code permits acting where the clients have a substantially common interest in relation to the matter, provided each gives informed consent (generally in writing) and appropriate safeguards are put in place. It is not an absolute bar.

n.0: Charging separate fees does not address the conflict; informed consent and safeguards do.
n.1: A conflict is not an absolute bar; the substantially-common-interest exception can apply.
n.2: There is no requirement for prior SRA approval of such a retainer.
n.4: A shared desired outcome does not remove the need for informed consent and safeguards.

7.q: A widow dies. Her late husband died some years earlier leaving his entire estate to her, so that none of his nil rate band was used on his death. The personal representatives of the widow's estate wish to know whether the husband's unused nil rate band can be used against the widow's estate. The court considers the transferable nil rate band between spouses. The husband's whole estate had passed to his wife, using none of his own allowance. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transferable nil rate band is available only where the spouses had made mirror wills.
The survivor's estate can only ever use a single nil rate band, whatever happened on the first death on these facts.
The first spouse's unused nil rate band is simply lost and can never be used again.
The nil rate band can be transferred only between parents and children, not between spouses.
The unused proportion of the first spouse's nil rate band may be transferred and claimed against the survivor's estate.
7.w: Where a spouse or civil partner dies without using all of their nil rate band (for example because their estate passed exempt to the survivor), the unused proportion can be transferred to and claimed on the death of the survivor, potentially giving the survivor's estate up to two nil rate bands.

n.0: The transfer does not depend on mirror wills having been made.
n.1: The survivor's estate may use more than a single nil rate band via the transfer.
n.2: The unused nil rate band is not lost; it can be transferred.
n.3: The transferable nil rate band operates between spouses/civil partners, not parent to child.

7.q: A company markets a health product with a widely published advertisement promising to pay £100 to any purchaser who uses the product correctly and still catches influenza, and stating that it has deposited a sum with its bank to show its sincerity. A customer buys the product, uses it exactly as directed, and nevertheless catches influenza. When the customer claims the £100, the company argues that the advertisement was mere sales talk, that the customer never communicated any acceptance to the company, and that there was therefore no binding contract. The customer seeks advice on whether they are entitled to the £100. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A contract formed when the customer performed the act; acceptance need not be separately communicated.
There is no contract, because the deposit with the bank was not a genuine offer to the public.
There is no contract, because an advertisement of this kind can never amount to a binding offer.
There is no contract, because the customer never notified the company that they accepted the offer.
There is a contract, but only if the customer had told the company in advance that they would use the product.
7.w: A unilateral offer, made to the world and intended to be acted upon, is accepted by performing the required act, and full performance dispenses with the need to communicate acceptance in advance (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co). Using the product as directed formed a binding contract.

n.1: The deposit reinforced, rather than negated, the intention to be bound by the promise.
n.2: An advertisement can amount to a binding unilateral offer where it shows an intention to be bound.
n.3: For a unilateral offer, performance is acceptance; separate communication is not required.
n.4: Advance notification of intention to perform is not required for acceptance of a unilateral offer.

7.q: A bank agreed to lend Mr Bianchi £180,000 against his registered freehold shop as security. Mr Bianchi signed a document intended to create a legal charge over the shop in the bank's favour, and the loan was advanced to him in full. Owing to an oversight at the bank, the document was signed but never validly executed as a deed. Mr Bianchi has now defaulted on the loan, and a dispute has arisen about the bank's rights over the shop. The bank is concerned that, because the charge was not made by deed, it may have no security at all. Which of the following best describes the bank's position?
o: The bank has an equitable charge, as a valid agreement for value to grant a charge can take effect in equity.
The bank has a fully legal mortgage, because signing the document is enough to create one.
The bank has no security of any kind and ranks only as an unsecured creditor for the debt.
The bank has a profit a prendre over the land until the loan has been repaid in full.
The bank acquires a fully legal mortgage as soon as it takes possession of the property from the borrower in person.
7.w: A legal mortgage or charge must be made by deed (s.52 LPA 1925). Without a valid deed there is no legal charge, but a written agreement for value to grant a charge can be specifically enforceable and take effect as an equitable charge (United Bank of Kuwait v Sahib).

n.1: A legal charge requires a validly executed deed, which is missing, so it is not a legal mortgage.
n.2: The bank is not left wholly unsecured; equity can recognise an equitable charge from the agreement.
n.3: A profit a prendre is a right to take produce from land; it is not a form of security for a loan.
n.4: Taking possession does not convert a defective charge into a legal mortgage.

7.q: A testator's will makes a specific gift of 'my shares in ABC Ltd' to a named beneficiary. Before the testator dies, however, the testator sold all of those shares and no longer owns any shares in ABC Ltd at the date of death, and the will was not updated. The beneficiary claims the value of the shares, or other assets in substitution. The court considers the doctrine of ademption. The testator had sold the shareholding to fund their retirement and never replaced it. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The executors must buy equivalent shares so that the beneficiary receives the gift in specie.
The gift takes effect over whatever the testator bought with the proceeds of sale.
The gift is unaffected, because a specific gift can never fail once it is written in the will.
The specific gift adeems and fails, because the subject matter no longer forms part of the estate at death.
The beneficiary is entitled to the cash value of the shares out of the general estate instead on these facts.
7.w: A specific gift adeems (fails) if the specific asset given no longer forms part of the testator's estate at the date of death — for example because it has been sold or otherwise disposed of. The beneficiary receives nothing in its place, absent a contrary provision.

n.0: The executors are not required to buy replacement shares.
n.1: The gift does not automatically attach to substituted assets.
