n.2: A specific gift can fail by ademption despite being written in the will.
n.4: The beneficiary is not entitled to the cash value out of the general estate.

7.q: A later general statute contains general words that, read literally, might be taken to repeal or override an earlier statute of major constitutional importance, but the later Act does not expressly address that earlier statute. A party argues the earlier constitutional statute has been impliedly repealed. The earlier statute is a 'constitutional' statute. The later Act uses only general words. A later Act framed in broad general terms could, if read at face value, be said to sweep away part of an earlier statute of real constitutional weight, even though the later Act never mentions it, and a party is arguing that the earlier measure has simply been repealed by implication. Which of the following best describes the position under the doctrine concerning constitutional statutes?
o: Constitutional statutes override all later Acts regardless of Parliament's intention.
Constitutional statutes are not subject to implied repeal and can be repealed only by clear express words or unavoidable implication.
Constitutional statutes can never be repealed or amended by Parliament at all.
Constitutional statutes lose all effect as soon as any later statute is passed.
Constitutional statutes are repealed by any later inconsistent statute in the ordinary way on these facts as a general rule.
7.w: Following Thoburn v Sunderland City Council, certain 'constitutional' statutes are not subject to the doctrine of implied repeal: they can be repealed or amended only by express words in a later statute, or by words so specific that the inference of an intention to repeal is irresistible. General words in a later Act will not impliedly repeal them.

n.0: Constitutional statutes do not override later Acts regardless of intention; express repeal is possible.
n.2: Parliament can repeal constitutional statutes by clear express words, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: They do not lose effect automatically on any later statute; express repeal is required.
n.4: Constitutional statutes are protected from implied repeal, unlike ordinary statutes.

7.q: A defendant is on trial in the Crown Court, and a question arises about the respective functions of the judge and the jury in reaching a verdict — in particular who decides questions of law and who decides questions of fact. The defendant's solicitor explains the division of roles at a Crown Court trial. The solicitor considers the roles of judge and jury in the Crown Court. The defendant wanted to understand who would actually decide whether they were guilty. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The jury decides all questions of law, and the judge decides all questions of fact.
The jury and the judge decide the verdict jointly by a majority of all of them together on these facts.
The judge decides questions of law and directs the jury, while the jury decides the facts and returns the verdict.
The prosecution decides questions of law, and the jury simply confirms the verdict.
The judge alone decides both the law and the facts, and there is no jury.
7.w: In the Crown Court there is a division of function: the judge decides questions of law (such as admissibility of evidence), manages the trial and directs the jury on the law, while the jury is the tribunal of fact, deciding the facts and returning the verdict of guilty or not guilty.

n.0: The jury decides facts, not questions of law.
n.1: The verdict is the jury's, reached separately from the judge.
n.3: Questions of law are for the judge, not the prosecution.
n.4: Crown Court trials are decided with a jury as the tribunal of fact.

7.q: A firm delivered a bill to a client for £1,000 and duly transferred that sum from client money to the office account. The client queries the charges, and the firm agrees to reduce (abate) its bill to £700, accepting it over-charged by £300. At the point of the reduction the firm still holds other client money for this client. The firm considers how to deal with the £300. The firm had already moved the billed amount across to its office account in the ordinary way, but the client's complaint about the level of the charges has been upheld to the extent of £300, and the firm must now work out the accounts consequences of having taken money it has agreed it should not have charged. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The £300 may be retained by the firm as a contribution to its costs.
The £300 need not be repaid because the client agreed to continue instructing the firm on these facts.
The £300 remains office money because it was validly billed at the time.
The £300 over-charged is client money again and must be returned to the client or the client account.
The £300 may be kept in the office account until the client requests repayment.
7.w: When a firm abates (reduces) a bill after transferring the billed sum to the office account, the amount of the reduction was never properly the firm's money. The over-charged £300 must be treated as client money once more and repaid to the client, or returned to the client account, promptly.

n.0: The firm cannot retain the over-charged amount as a contribution to costs.
n.1: Continued instructions do not entitle the firm to keep the over-charge.
n.2: The reduction means the £300 was not validly the firm's after all.
n.4: It must be repaid promptly, not held pending a request.

7.q: A court finds that a provision in an Act of Parliament is incompatible with a Convention right, and it is not possible to read the provision compatibly under the interpretive obligation. The court cannot invalidate the Act. A solicitor is asked what the higher courts can do where primary legislation is found incompatible with a Convention right. The solicitor considers section 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998. No compatible reading of the statute was possible, however hard the court tried. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court must simply ignore the Act and decide the case as if it did not exist.
A higher court may make a declaration of incompatibility, which does not affect the validity of the Act but signals the incompatibility to Parliament.
The court may strike down and invalidate the incompatible Act of Parliament.
The court may amend the Act itself to remove the incompatibility.
The court can do nothing at all where primary legislation is incompatible with a Convention right on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
7.w: Under s.4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, where a higher court is satisfied that a provision of primary legislation is incompatible with a Convention right and cannot be read compatibly, it may make a declaration of incompatibility. This does not affect the validity or continuing operation of the Act, but signals to Parliament that it may wish to amend the law.

n.0: The court does not ignore the Act; it applies it but may declare incompatibility.
n.2: The court cannot strike down or invalidate the Act.
n.3: The court does not itself amend the Act; that is for Parliament.
n.4: The court can make a declaration of incompatibility, so it is not powerless.

7.q: An offender is convicted of an offence that is serious enough to pass the community sentence threshold but does not require custody. The court wishes to impose a sentence in the community with requirements tailored to the offending and the offender. The defendant's solicitor advises on this kind of sentence. The solicitor considers community orders for adult offenders. The offence crossed the threshold for a community penalty but plainly did not require prison. Which of the following best describes them?
o: A community order may be imposed only on offenders who plead not guilty.
A community order allows the court to impose one or more requirements, such as unpaid work, a curfew or rehabilitation activity.
A community order can consist only of a fine and nothing else.
A community order requires the offender's employer to supervise them at work on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A community order is simply another name for an immediate prison sentence.
7.w: A community order enables the court to impose one or more requirements on the offender — for example an unpaid work requirement, a curfew, a rehabilitation activity requirement, a programme, or an exclusion — tailored to the offence and the offender, as an alternative to custody where the community threshold is met.

n.0: A community order is available regardless of plea.
n.2: A community order comprises requirements, not only a fine.
n.3: Supervision is by the probation service, not the offender's employer.
n.4: A community order is served in the community, not in prison.

7.q: A registered proprietor discovers that the register contains a mistake which understates the extent of the land included in their registered title, so that a strip that should form part of their title is not shown as belonging to them and appears in a neighbour's title instead. The proprietor is not in possession of the disputed strip. They wish to have the register put right so that it accurately reflects the true extent of their title. The proprietor seeks advice on whether, and by what means, the position can be corrected. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The register may be altered to correct the mistake. on these facts
Alteration is available only where the mistake benefits a squatter in adverse possession.
The proprietor must instead claim damages, as the register itself cannot be changed.
The register can never be altered once a title has first been registered.
Alteration is impossible unless every affected party first agrees to it in writing.
7.w: The register can be altered to correct a mistake. Where alteration would prejudice a registered proprietor in possession there are restrictions (it is then 'rectification'); but where the proprietor is not in possession, correction is more freely available under the LRA 2002.

n.1: Alteration to correct mistakes is not confined to adverse-possession cases.
n.2: The remedy is correction of the register, with indemnity for loss, not merely damages in place of it.
n.3: The register is not immutable; the LRA 2002 provides for alteration to correct mistakes.
n.4: Unanimous written consent is not a precondition to alteration.

7.q: A tenant took an assignment of a commercial lease that was granted in 2010 (a 'new' tenancy for the purposes of the relevant legislation). After the assignment, the assignee tenant fails to pay the rent, and the landlord considers who is liable. The lease covenants bind the current tenant while they hold the lease. The landlord asks about the assignee's liability for the lease covenants. The solicitor considers the liability of an assignee of a new tenancy under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995. The assignee had taken over a lease with many years still to run and substantial rent obligations. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The assignee is never liable for any of the lease covenants after taking the assignment.
The assignee, as the current tenant, is bound by the tenant covenants of the lease while it holds the lease (privity of estate).
Only the original tenant remains liable for the covenants, whoever currently holds the lease on these facts as a general rule.
The assignee is liable only for covenants it expressly agrees to in a separate document.
The landlord can enforce the covenants only against the freeholder, not the tenant.
7.w: Under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995, for a 'new' tenancy (granted on or after 1 January 1996) the tenant covenants pass to the assignee, who is bound by them while they hold the lease (privity of estate). The outgoing tenant is generally released on a lawful assignment, subject to any AGA.

n.0: The current assignee tenant is bound by the tenant covenants while it holds the lease.
n.2: For a new tenancy the original tenant is generally released on assignment, so it is not solely liable.
n.3: The assignee is bound by the lease covenants generally, not only those separately agreed.
n.4: The landlord enforces tenant covenants against the tenant, not the freeholder.

7.q: An employee, in the course of doing their job for their employer, negligently injures a member of the public. The injured claimant wishes to sue the employer rather than the employee, because the employer is better able to meet a claim. The employer argues that it should not be responsible for the wrongdoing of another person and that only the employee who actually caused the injury should be liable. The claimant seeks advice on the basis on which the employer may be held responsible. The employee was carrying out an ordinary task assigned to them when the injury to the claimant occurred. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The employer is liable only if the employee cannot afford to pay the claim themselves.
The employer is liable only where it personally instructed the employee to commit the tort.
The employer is liable only where the employee is an independent contractor rather than a true employee.
The employer may be vicariously liable for a tort committed by an employee acting in the course of employment.
The employer can never be liable for a tort committed by its employee against a third party.
7.w: An employer is vicariously liable for torts committed by an employee acting in the course of their employment. This is a form of strict, secondary liability that does not require the employer itself to have been at fault.

n.0: Vicarious liability does not depend on the employee's inability to pay.
n.1: The employer need not have instructed the tort; course of employment suffices.
n.2: Vicarious liability arises for employees; it does not generally apply to independent contractors.
n.4: Employers are routinely liable for employees' torts through vicarious liability.

7.q: A potential claimant wishes to sue for breach of a simple contract that occurred some years ago. Before advising on the merits, the solicitor must consider whether the claim can still be brought in time, given the statutory limitation rules. The claim is founded on a simple contract. The alleged breach happened several years ago, the prospective claimant has only recently decided to pursue it, and before spending time on the merits the solicitor must work out whether the passage of time has already barred the claim under the statutory limitation regime for this kind of action. Which of the following best describes the ordinary limitation period for a claim in simple contract?
o: Twelve years from the date the contract was signed.
There is no limitation period for contract claims.
One year from the date the claimant discovered the breach.
Three years from the date of the breach in every case.
Six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued.
7.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the ordinary limitation period for an action founded on a simple contract is six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued (generally the date of breach). Different periods apply to certain claims, such as personal injury (three years) and specialties/deeds (twelve years).

n.0: Twelve years applies to specialties (contracts by deed), not simple contracts, and runs from accrual not signing.
n.1: There is a limitation period for contract claims.
n.2: One year is not the general contractual limitation period.
n.3: Three years is the usual period for personal injury claims, not simple contract.

7.q: A will contains a gift described in words that are ambiguous or unclear, and the executors must work out what the testator meant, for example which of two possible people or assets was intended. They wish to know how the court approaches the interpretation of the words used in a will. The court considers the interpretation (construction) of wills, including the 'armchair' principle. The wording could point to either of two people the testator had known by the same name. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court refuses to interpret any will that contains an ambiguous or unclear expression.
The court interprets the will solely by reference to what the beneficiaries say the testator meant on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court ignores the words of the will entirely and simply gives effect to what seems fair.
The court must always give the words their most literal meaning, whatever the resulting absurdity.
The court seeks the testator's intention from the words used, read in light of the surrounding circumstances known to the testator (the armchair principle).
7.w: In construing a will the court seeks the testator's intention as expressed in the words used, read in their ordinary sense but in the light of the circumstances known to the testator when the will was made (placing itself in the testator's 'armchair'). Extrinsic evidence is admissible in limited circumstances under s.21 AJA 1982.

n.0: The court does interpret ambiguous wills rather than refusing to do so.
n.1: Interpretation is not governed by the beneficiaries' assertions of intention.
n.2: The court does not ignore the words and simply do what seems fair.
n.3: The court avoids an absurd literal reading where the context shows another meaning.

7.q: A sole adult beneficiary is absolutely entitled to the whole of a trust fund under a trust that was intended to continue until the beneficiary reached a later age. The beneficiary, now of full age and mentally capable, wishes to bring the trust to an end and have the property transferred to them at once, despite the settlor's contrary wishes. The beneficiary is of full age, capacity, and absolutely entitled to the entire beneficial interest. The settlor had intended the fund to be kept back until the beneficiary was considerably older, but the beneficiary is now an adult of full capacity, solely and absolutely entitled to everything in the fund, and wants it handed over immediately rather than waiting as the settlor wished. Which of the following best describes the beneficiary's ability to end the trust?
o: The beneficiary cannot end the trust because the settlor's stated intention is binding on these facts as a general rule.
The beneficiary must wait until the age specified by the settlor in every case.
The beneficiary may require the trustees to transfer the property and end the trust under the rule in Saunders v Vautier.
The beneficiary may end the trust only after obtaining the court's approval.
The beneficiary may end the trust only with the consent of the settlor.
7.w: Under the rule in Saunders v Vautier, a beneficiary who is of full age and capacity and absolutely entitled to the entire beneficial interest (or all such beneficiaries acting together) may direct the trustees to transfer the trust property and bring the trust to an end, notwithstanding the settlor's contrary intention or a specified later age.

n.0: The settlor's stated intention does not prevent a sui juris, absolutely entitled beneficiary ending the trust.
n.1: The beneficiary need not wait for the settlor's specified age if absolutely entitled and sui juris.
n.3: Court approval is not required where the Saunders v Vautier conditions are met.
n.4: The settlor's consent is not required.

7.q: A defendant is tried on indictment in the Crown Court before a judge and jury and is convicted. The defendant believes there were serious errors in the judge's directions to the jury and wishes to challenge the conviction. The trial took place in the Crown Court. The defendant was tried before a judge and jury on a serious charge, was convicted, and complains that the summing-up misdirected the jury on the law, and is now taking advice on the court to which such a challenge to a conviction returned by a jury must be directed. Which of the following best identifies the court to which an appeal against conviction on indictment ordinarily lies?
o: The High Court, by way of case stated.
The magistrates' court, exercising a supervisory role.
The Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
The Crown Court, before a different judge.
The Supreme Court, as the first appeal court.
7.w: A defendant convicted on indictment in the Crown Court appeals against conviction (and/or sentence) to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), generally with leave. Appeal by way of case stated to the High Court is available from the magistrates' court and from the Crown Court in its appellate capacity, not from trial on indictment.

n.0: Case stated to the High Court is not the route for a conviction on indictment.
n.1: The magistrates' court has no supervisory role over Crown Court convictions.
n.3: The appeal does not go to another Crown Court judge.
n.4: The Supreme Court is not the first appeal court from the Crown Court.

7.q: A buyer has completed the purchase of a residential property for a price above the relevant threshold. The buyer's solicitor must deal with the tax payable on the purchase and file the necessary return with HMRC within the statutory time limit, or penalties will arise. The buyer asks about the tax on the purchase and the deadline. The solicitor considers stamp duty land tax on the acquisition of land in England. The price was well above the tax threshold and the deadline for filing was fast approaching. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Stamp duty land tax is payable by the seller out of the sale proceeds, not by the buyer.
Stamp duty land tax is payable by the buyer, and an SDLT return must generally be filed within 14 days of completion.
The SDLT return may be filed at any time within six years of completion without penalty.
No tax is ever payable on the purchase of residential property in England.
Stamp duty land tax is payable only where the buyer is a company and never an individual on these facts as a general rule.
7.w: Stamp duty land tax (SDLT) on the acquisition of land in England is payable by the buyer. The buyer's solicitor must submit an SDLT return and pay the tax due generally within 14 days of the effective date (usually completion), with penalties and interest for late filing or payment.

n.0: SDLT is payable by the buyer, not the seller.
n.2: The return must be filed within 14 days, not any time within six years.
n.3: SDLT can be payable on residential purchases above the threshold.
n.4: SDLT applies to individuals as well as companies.

7.q: A person who is not a solicitor, and who holds no professional authorisation of any kind, sets up a business offering, for a fee, to conduct litigation on behalf of members of the public in the county court and to stand up and address the court on their behalf at hearings. They genuinely believe that, because the market for legal services is open to competition, anyone at all is free to offer these services. A qualified solicitor is asked whether these particular activities may lawfully be carried on by an unauthorised person in this way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Conducting litigation and exercising rights of audience are reserved legal activities that may only be carried on by an authorised person.
Only exercising rights of audience is restricted; conducting litigation may be carried on by any person for reward.
These activities may be carried on by anyone, provided no fee above a fixed statutory maximum is charged for them.
These activities may be carried on by anyone, provided the client is told in writing that the provider is not a solicitor.
Anyone may conduct litigation and exercise rights of audience, because no legal activity is restricted to authorised persons.
7.w: Under the Legal Services Act 2007, certain activities are 'reserved legal activities' — including the exercise of a right of audience and the conduct of litigation — which may only be carried on by a person authorised to do so; doing so while unauthorised is a criminal offence.

n.1: Both the conduct of litigation and rights of audience are reserved, not just rights of audience.
n.2: There is no fee ceiling that permits an unauthorised person to carry on reserved activities.
n.3: A disclosure that the provider is not a solicitor does not permit carrying on a reserved activity.
n.4: Some legal activities are reserved and restricted to authorised persons.

7.q: Before completing a purchase, the buyer's solicitor wishes to check whether the seller is subject to any bankruptcy proceedings that could affect their ability to deal with the property, particularly where a mortgage lender is also being acted for. The solicitor considers which search is made to check the insolvency position of an individual seller or borrower. A lender was funding the purchase and wanted to be sure the borrower was not insolvent. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A drainage and water search reveals the seller's insolvency position on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The Land Registry title plan reveals the seller's bankruptcy status.
A local land charges search reveals whether the seller is bankrupt.
There is no way to check whether an individual seller is bankrupt.
A bankruptcy search (Form K16 at the Land Charges Department) is made against the individual to check for insolvency entries.
7.w: A bankruptcy search (Form K16) is made at the Land Charges Department against the name of an individual (for example a borrower, on behalf of a lender) to reveal any bankruptcy petitions or orders that would affect the person's capacity to deal with the property.

n.0: A drainage and water search does not reveal insolvency.
n.1: The title plan does not show bankruptcy status.
n.2: The local land charges search does not reveal an individual's bankruptcy.
n.3: Insolvency can be checked by a bankruptcy search.

7.q: A seller of registered land, Delia, entered into an estate contract in January agreeing to sell the land to a first buyer. The first buyer paid a deposit but did not protect the estate contract by entering a notice against the title on the register. In March, before the sale to the first buyer had been completed, Delia transferred the same land to a second buyer for valuable consideration, and the second buyer was duly registered as the new proprietor. The first buyer has now discovered the second sale and asserts the estate contract against the second buyer. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The second buyer is bound, because a prior estate contract always binds a later purchaser of the land.
The second buyer takes free only if the first buyer was not in occupation of the land.
The second buyer is bound if the first buyer can show the second buyer ought to have discovered the contract. on these facts
The second buyer takes free of the estate contract, because an unprotected interest is postponed to a registered disposition for value.
The first buyer prevails, because the estate contract was created before the second sale.
7.w: On a registered disposition for valuable consideration, priority is governed by s.29 LRA 2002: interests not protected by an entry on the register (and not overriding) are postponed to the disposition. An unprotected estate contract of vacant land therefore does not bind the registered second buyer.

n.0: A prior estate contract does not automatically bind a later registered purchaser for value.
n.1: Occupation could raise an overriding interest, but on these facts the unprotected contract is postponed; occupation is not stated.
n.2: Notice is generally irrelevant in registered land; priority turns on protection and the s.29 rules.
n.4: Mere priority in time does not preserve an unprotected interest against a registered disposition for value.

7.q: In the course of acting on a residential property purchase, a solicitor becomes genuinely suspicious that the money the client is using to fund the transaction represents the proceeds of crime. The client is pressing hard for the purchase to complete as quickly as possible and is impatient at any suggestion of delay. The solicitor is conscious of the various obligations imposed on them by the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and wants to be clear about how they must act before taking any further step in the matter. Which of the following best describes what the solicitor must do?
o: Take no action at all unless and until the sum involved exceeds a fixed statutory reporting threshold amount.
Make a suspicious activity report to the NCA, do not proceed without consent, and avoid tipping off the client.
Proceed with the purchase as normal, because legal professional privilege prevents any disclosure to the authorities.
Immediately tell the client of the suspicion, so that the client has a chance to explain the source of the funds.
Simply return the funds to the client and close the file, without taking any other step in relation to the matter.
7.w: Under POCA 2002, a person who suspects money laundering must make a suspicious activity report to the NCA, obtain appropriate consent before proceeding, and must avoid tipping off. Privilege does not protect communications made to further a criminal purpose.

n.0: There is no minimum threshold that removes the reporting obligation once suspicion is formed.
n.2: Privilege does not extend to the iniquity here and does not permit the solicitor to proceed regardless.
n.3: Telling the client of the suspicion risks the criminal offence of tipping off.
n.4: Simply returning the funds and closing the file does not discharge the reporting duty and may itself tip off the client.

7.q: A firm needs to pay a disbursement (such as a court fee or expert's fee) on behalf of a client, and the bookkeeper must decide whether it can be paid from the client account and how it is recorded. The firm holds sufficient money for that client. The bookkeeper considers the payment of disbursements from the client account under the SRA Accounts Rules. The disbursement is a court issue fee that must be paid to progress the client's claim, the firm holds ample funds for this client in the client account, and the bookkeeper wants to confirm whether the payment can properly be met from those client funds. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A disbursement may be paid from the client account without recording it in the ledgers.
A disbursement may be paid from the client account only if sufficient client money is held for that particular client.
A disbursement may be paid from money held for a different client if convenient.
A disbursement may never be paid from the client account and must always come from office money on these facts.
A disbursement may be paid from the client account even if no money is held for that client.
7.w: A disbursement may be paid out of the client account on a client's behalf only where sufficient client money is held for that client (so that the client's ledger is not overdrawn). Otherwise it must be met from office money, and the payment must be properly recorded in the accounts.

n.0: All payments must be recorded in the ledgers.
n.2: Another client's money must not be used to pay the disbursement.
n.3: Disbursements can be paid from client money where held, so 'never' is wrong.
n.4: A disbursement cannot be paid from the client account if no money is held for that client.

7.q: During litigation, one party's legal representative causes significant unnecessary costs to be incurred by the other side through an improper, unreasonable or negligent act or omission in the conduct of the proceedings. The innocent party seeks an order that the costs so wasted be paid by the representative personally, rather than by the client. The wasted costs were caused by the representative's own conduct. The innocent party seeks a remedy against the representative directly. The wasted expense flowed not from anything the client did but from the representative's own improper and unreasonable handling of the case, and the party left out of pocket wants to recover those costs from the lawyer personally rather than pursuing a client who was not really at fault. Which of the following best identifies the order available?
o: A summary judgment against the legal representative.
An order for indemnity costs against the represented client on these facts.
A charging order over the representative's assets.
A third party debt order against the representative's firm.
A wasted costs order requiring the legal representative to meet the costs personally.
7.w: A wasted costs order may be made against a legal representative personally where costs have been incurred as a result of any improper, unreasonable or negligent act or omission by the representative (or which it is unreasonable to expect the client to pay). It is directed at the representative, not the client, and requires a causal link to the wasted costs.

n.0: Summary judgment disposes of a claim without trial; it is not the remedy for wasted costs.
n.1: An order against the client does not address the representative's own conduct.
n.2: A charging order is an enforcement method, not the remedy for a representative's misconduct.
n.3: A third party debt order enforces a money judgment against a debt owed to the debtor, not this situation.

7.q: A firm arranges for a client's money in a transaction to be held not by the firm but through a third-party managed account operated by a regulated payment provider, so that payments in and out are handled by that provider rather than through the firm's own client account. The bookkeeper asks how money handled in this way is treated under the SRA Accounts Rules. The firm never itself holds or receives the money. Under the arrangement the payment provider receives the funds and makes payments on the agreed terms, the firm gives instructions but never itself receives or controls the money, and the bookkeeper wants to understand how, if at all, this money features in the firm's own client account obligations. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Money held through a compliant third-party managed account is not client money held by the firm.
The firm must still pay the money into its own client account before it can be used.
Use of a third-party managed account is prohibited under the SRA Accounts Rules.
The firm must reconcile the third-party managed account as if it were its own client account.
The firm must treat the money as office money because a payment provider holds it.
7.w: The Accounts Rules permit a firm to use a third-party managed account (TPMA). Because the firm does not itself hold or receive the money, it is not client money held by the firm, and the usual client account obligations (such as reconciliations) do not apply to it, though the firm must take steps to satisfy itself the arrangement is appropriate and inform the client.

n.1: The point of a TPMA is that the money is not routed through the firm's own client account.
n.2: TPMAs are expressly permitted, not prohibited.
n.3: Because the money is not the firm's client money, the firm does not reconcile the TPMA as its own client account.
n.4: Money in a TPMA is not office money.

7.q: A claimant wishes to sue in relation to statements made by a Member of Parliament during a debate in Parliament, and to have the court examine and rule on what was said in parliamentary proceedings. A solicitor is asked whether the courts can inquire into things said and done in Parliament. The issue concerns the protection given to parliamentary proceedings. The solicitor considers parliamentary privilege. The words complained of had been spoken by the member during a heated parliamentary debate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The courts may freely examine and rule on anything said during proceedings in Parliament.
Parliamentary privilege means the courts must decide all disputes about parliamentary procedure on these facts as a general rule.
Members of Parliament have no protection at all for what they say in debates.
Parliamentary proceedings are protected by parliamentary privilege and generally cannot be questioned or impeached in the courts.
Parliamentary privilege prevents Parliament itself from discussing any legal matter.
7.w: Under parliamentary privilege (reflected in Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689), the freedom of speech and proceedings in Parliament may not be impeached or questioned in any court. The courts will not generally inquire into or adjudicate on what is said or done in the course of parliamentary proceedings.

n.0: The courts cannot freely examine parliamentary proceedings; privilege protects them.
n.1: Privilege keeps such matters out of the courts, rather than requiring the courts to police procedure.
n.2: MPs have significant protection (privilege) for what they say in debate.
n.4: Privilege protects Parliament's proceedings; it does not stop Parliament debating matters.

7.q: A claimant applies for an interim injunction to restrain the defendant pending trial. The court is satisfied there is a serious question to be tried. It must now decide whether to grant the injunction, considering whether damages would be an adequate remedy for either side and where the least risk of injustice lies. There is a serious issue to be tried and the court is applying the American Cyanamid guidelines. The court is prepared to accept that the claim is not fanciful and raises a genuine issue fit for trial, and now has to work through the remaining stages of the established interim-injunction guidelines before deciding whether restraining the defendant in the meantime is the right course. Which of the following best describes the next stage of the court's analysis?
o: Whether the claimant is more likely than not to win at the eventual trial on these facts as a general rule.
Whether the claim has been allocated to the multi-track.
Whether the defendant consents to the injunction being granted.
Whether damages would be an adequate remedy and, if not clearly so, where the balance of convenience lies.
Whether the claimant can prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
7.w: Under the American Cyanamid guidelines, once a serious question to be tried is shown, the court asks whether damages would be an adequate remedy for the claimant (if so, an injunction is usually refused) and for the defendant if enjoined. If damages are not an adequate remedy for either or both, the court decides where the balance of convenience lies, often preserving the status quo.

n.0: The court does not, at the interim stage, decide who is likely to win at trial on the merits.
n.1: Track allocation is not part of the American Cyanamid test.
n.2: The defendant's consent is not the test; the court applies the guidelines.
n.4: The criminal standard of proof has no application to an interim injunction.

7.q: A rogue, pretending in writing to be a wealthy and creditworthy individual whose identity actually exists, induces a seller to contract at a distance and to part with goods on credit, the seller intending to deal only with that named, reputable person and not with the rogue. The rogue disappears and the goods end up with an innocent third party. Identity, not merely creditworthiness, was crucial to the seller, and the dealing was in writing rather than face to face. The seller intended to contract only with the specifically identified person. Which of the following best describes the effect on the contract with the rogue?
o: The contract is fully valid, because a mistake as to the other party's identity never matters.
The contract is voidable only, so a third party who buys in good faith always gets good title on these facts.
The contract may be void for unilateral mistake as to identity, so no title passes to the rogue or the third party.
The contract is valid because identity is only ever relevant in face-to-face dealings.
The contract is void for common mistake shared by both seller and rogue.
7.w: Where parties deal at a distance in writing and the seller intended to contract only with a specifically identified, existing third person (identity being material), a unilateral mistake as to identity can render the contract void, so no title passes to the rogue or on to a later buyer. This contrasts with face-to-face dealings, where the contract is usually only voidable.

n.0: A mistake as to identity can matter where identity is crucial and the dealing is at a distance.
n.1: If the contract is void (not merely voidable), even a good-faith third party gets no title.
n.3: Identity can be material in written dealings at a distance, not only face to face.
n.4: The mistake is unilateral (only the seller is mistaken), not a common mistake shared by both.

7.q: A business occupier of premises to which paying visitors come displays a prominent notice at the entrance which purports to exclude all of its liability for personal injury caused by the negligence of the occupier or its staff. A visitor is injured through the occupier's negligence and, when they claim, the occupier relies on the exclusion notice to defeat the claim for the physical injury. The visitor seeks advice on whether the occupier can exclude liability for their personal injury in this way. The visitor had paid an entrance fee and had no realistic opportunity to negotiate the terms of entry. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The occupier can exclude liability for personal injury provided the notice is large and clearly displayed.
The occupier cannot exclude liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence, as statute prohibits it.
The occupier can exclude all liability by a clear notice, because visitors are taken to accept its terms.
The occupier can exclude liability for personal injury provided the visitor had paid to enter the premises.
The occupier can exclude liability for personal injury unless the visitor is a consumer rather than a business.
7.w: An occupier's ability to exclude the common duty of care is constrained by statute. Under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (business liability) and the Consumer Rights Act 2015 (for consumers), liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence cannot be excluded or restricted at all.

n.0: Size and prominence of the notice do not overcome the statutory prohibition.
n.2: A clear notice cannot exclude liability for negligently caused personal injury.
n.3: Payment to enter does not permit excluding liability for personal injury.
n.4: The bar on excluding personal-injury liability protects consumers and applies to business visitors under UCTA too.

7.q: A solicitor acts for Mr Frost, who is buying a registered house from Ms Gill. Mr Frost knows that a lodger occupies one of the upstairs rooms. Before completion, Mr Frost's solicitor asks Ms Gill, but does not ask the lodger, whether anyone other than the seller has any interest in the house. Ms Gill replies that no one else has any interest. In fact the lodger has a beneficial interest in the house and remains in actual occupation. After completion the lodger asserts that interest against Mr Frost, who says he cannot be bound because he was told there was no other interest. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer is bound, because inquiry must be made of the occupier, not merely the seller.
The buyer is not bound, because the buyer already knew that the lodger was living in the property.
The buyer is bound only if the lodger's interest was entered as a notice on the register.
The buyer is not bound, because the seller was asked and stated that no one else had an interest.
The buyer is not bound, because a lodger can never have an interest capable of overriding.
7.w: Under Schedule 3 paragraph 2 LRA 2002, the interest of a person in actual occupation overrides. The exception for failure to disclose applies only where inquiry was made of the person entitled to the interest. Inquiry of the seller alone does not trigger it, so the lodger's interest binds Mr Frost.

n.1: The buyer's knowledge does not defeat the interest; if anything, it reinforces that the buyer is bound.
n.2: Actual occupation makes the interest override without any need for a notice on the register.
n.3: The seller's denial is irrelevant; the relevant inquiry must be made of the occupier who holds the interest.
n.4: An occupier such as a lodger can hold a beneficial interest capable of overriding through actual occupation.

7.q: A promoter, acting to set up a company that has not yet been incorporated, enters into a contract 'on behalf of' the intended company with a supplier, before the company legally exists. After incorporation the company does not adopt or ratify the contract, and the supplier is not paid. The supplier seeks to recover from the promoter personally. The promoter argues that they contracted only as agent for the company. The court considers liability on a pre-incorporation contract under the Companies Act 2006. The promoter had signed the order in the company's name weeks before it was actually formed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The supplier's only remedy is against the company, which must ratify the contract.
The promoter is personally liable on the pre-incorporation contract, subject to any agreement to the contrary.
The promoter is liable only if they expressly guaranteed the contract in writing.
The company is automatically liable on the contract once it is later incorporated.
Neither the promoter nor the company is ever liable on a pre-incorporation contract on these facts.
7.w: Under s.51 Companies Act 2006, a contract purporting to be made by or on behalf of a company before it is formed takes effect as one made with the person purporting to act for the company, who is personally liable on it, subject to any agreement to the contrary. The company cannot be bound by a contract made before it existed unless it makes a new contract after incorporation.

n.0: A company cannot ratify a contract made before it existed; a fresh contract is needed.
n.2: Personal liability under s.51 does not depend on an express written guarantee.
n.3: The company is not automatically bound; it did not exist when the contract was made.
n.4: The promoter is generally liable, so it is not the case that no one is.

7.q: An owner of land enjoys, by permission, a right to use a driveway over adjoining land also owned by the same seller. The seller then sells the benefited land to a buyer by conveyance, without expressly mentioning the driveway right, which was in use at the time. A right in use at the time of the conveyance was not expressly granted. The conveyance is silent about the right. When the two plots were in common ownership the buyer's plot was enjoyed with the informal use of a driveway across the retained land, and when the seller later conveyed the benefited plot without mentioning that right, which was in use at the time, the buyer wants to know whether a legal easement passed anyway. Which of the following best describes how a legal easement may nonetheless arise on the conveyance?
o: An easement arises only if the buyer pays an additional sum for it.
The right is automatically extinguished by the conveyance.
Section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 may operate to convert the right into a legal easement passing with the conveyance.
An easement can arise only by twenty years' prescription.
No easement can ever arise unless expressly granted in the conveyance on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
7.w: Section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 implies into a conveyance of land all rights, privileges and easements enjoyed with the land, and can operate to upgrade a permission or informal right (such as use of a driveway) into a full legal easement passing to the buyer, even though the conveyance does not expressly mention it, where the conditions are met.

n.0: No additional payment is required for s.62 to operate.
n.1: The right is not extinguished; s.62 can carry it forward as an easement.
n.3: Prescription is one route, but s.62 provides another without needing twenty years' use.
n.4: An easement can arise without express grant, for example via s.62.

7.q: A campaigning organisation, which is not itself directly affected by a public body's decision but has a genuine concern about the issue, wishes to bring judicial review proceedings challenging that decision. The public body argues the organisation has no right to bring the claim. A solicitor is asked whether the claimant is entitled to bring judicial review. The solicitor considers the requirement of standing in judicial review. The organisation had genuine expertise and a real concern about the lawfulness of the decision. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The claimant must have a sufficient interest in the matter, which can include a suitably concerned campaign group in appropriate cases.
Standing in judicial review depends solely on whether the claimant can afford the court fees.
A campaign group can never have standing to bring judicial review under any circumstances.
Only a person directly and personally affected in their private rights can ever bring judicial review on these facts as a general rule.
Anyone at all may bring judicial review, with no requirement of any interest in the matter.
7.w: To bring judicial review a claimant must have a 'sufficient interest' in the matter to which the claim relates. This is applied flexibly and, depending on the context, a public-interest group or campaigning body with genuine expertise and concern may be found to have sufficient interest to bring a claim.

n.1: Standing depends on sufficient interest, not the ability to pay fees.
n.2: Campaign groups can, in appropriate cases, have standing.
n.3: Standing is not confined to those personally affected in their private rights.
n.4: There is a requirement of sufficient interest; not anyone may bring a claim.

7.q: Contracts have been exchanged for the purchase of a house, with completion due in a few weeks. Between exchange and completion, before the buyer has taken possession, the property is seriously damaged by fire through no fault of either party. The buyer assumes the seller bears the loss until completion. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale. The solicitor considers where the risk in the property lies between exchange and completion, and the buyer's insurance position. The buyer had not yet arranged buildings insurance, assuming the seller remained responsible. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Risk is shared equally between buyer and seller between exchange and completion in every case.
Risk remains with the seller until completion, so the buyer need not insure until completion day on these facts.
Risk generally passes to the buyer on exchange, so the buyer should insure the property from exchange of contracts.
Risk passes to the buyer only once the buyer has physically moved into the property.
Risk never passes to the buyer at all, and the seller must always bear any damage.
7.w: Under the Standard Conditions of Sale, the risk in the property generally passes to the buyer on exchange of contracts. The buyer is therefore well advised to insure the property from exchange (and lenders typically require it), since damage occurring before completion is generally the buyer's risk.

n.0: Risk is not shared equally; it generally passes to the buyer on exchange.
n.1: Risk does not remain with the seller until completion under the standard position.
n.3: Risk passes on exchange, not on taking physical possession.
n.4: Risk does pass to the buyer on exchange under the SCS.

7.q: A court is exercising its powers and interpreting the Civil Procedure Rules in a case, and the parties disagree about how a particular procedural provision should be applied. One party urges the court to have regard to the fundamental purpose that underpins the entire body of rules. The court considers the overriding objective of the Civil Procedure Rules. The dispute over the rule would affect how much time and cost the whole case would consume. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The overriding objective is to make litigation as slow and thorough as possible.
The overriding objective is to maximise the costs recovered by the successful party on these facts.
The overriding objective is to ensure that the claimant always wins the case.
The overriding objective applies only to multi-track claims and no others.
The overriding objective is to enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost.
7.w: The overriding objective in CPR 1.1 is to enable the court to deal with cases justly and at proportionate cost, which includes ensuring the parties are on an equal footing, saving expense, dealing with cases proportionately, expeditiously and fairly, and allotting an appropriate share of the court's resources.

n.0: It seeks expeditious, proportionate handling, not slowness.
n.1: It aims at proportionate cost, not maximising costs recovery.
n.2: The objective is even-handed justice, not that the claimant always wins.
n.3: The overriding objective governs all cases, not only the multi-track.

7.q: An organisation engages an individual whose relationship with it, although not a formal contract of employment, is akin to employment: the individual is integrated into the organisation's activities and works on its behalf rather than running an independent business of their own. The individual commits a tort connected with that work, and the claimant seeks to hold the organisation vicariously liable. The relationship is closely analogous to employment rather than that of an independent contractor. The individual wore the organisation's uniform, was told what to do and how to do it, and was in practice absorbed into the organisation's operation rather than trading independently on their own account, so the question is whether that relationship is close enough to employment to carry vicarious liability. Which of the following best describes when vicarious liability may arise from such a relationship?
o: Vicarious liability arises only where there is a formal written contract of employment.
Vicarious liability may arise where the relationship is akin to employment, even without a formal contract of employment.
Vicarious liability arises automatically for anyone doing any work for the organisation.
Vicarious liability arises for the acts of any independent contractor engaged by the organisation on these facts.
Vicarious liability can never arise unless the wrongdoer is a direct employee.
7.w: Vicarious liability requires a relationship of employment or one 'akin to employment'. Where a person is integrated into the defendant's organisation and works on its behalf rather than running their own independent business, the relationship may be sufficiently analogous to employment to found vicarious liability, even without a formal employment contract. True independent contractors generally fall outside it.

n.0: A formal written contract of employment is not essential; an akin-to-employment relationship suffices.
n.2: It does not arise automatically for anyone doing any work; the relationship must be employment or akin to it.
n.3: Vicarious liability does not generally arise for the acts of a genuine independent contractor.
n.4: It can arise for relationships akin to employment, not only for direct employees.

7.q: A consumer is injured by a defective product and also suffers damage to a private item of property worth several hundred pounds, as well as damage to the defective product itself. The consumer claims under the Consumer Protection Act 1987. The private property damaged was for the consumer's own private use and its value exceeds the statutory threshold. The consumer wants to know what losses are recoverable under the Act. The fire not only injured the consumer but also ruined a valuable personal possession kept nearby and destroyed the appliance itself, and the consumer is trying to work out which of these various heads of loss the statutory product-liability regime will actually allow to be recovered. Which of the following best describes the damage recoverable under the Consumer Protection Act 1987?
o: Damage to any property, including business property and the defective product itself.
Only the cost of replacing the defective product, and nothing else.
Death or personal injury, and damage to private property above the statutory threshold, but not the defective product itself.
Only death or personal injury, with no recovery for any property damage at all.
Any and all financial losses flowing from the defect, including the cost of the product itself on these facts as a general rule.
7.w: The Consumer Protection Act 1987 allows recovery for death or personal injury, and for damage to private (non-business) property exceeding the statutory threshold (£275). It does not allow recovery for damage to the defective product itself, nor for pure economic loss; those must be pursued, if at all, in contract or ordinary negligence.

n.0: Business property and the product itself are excluded, so 'any property' is wrong.
n.1: Recovery is not limited to replacing the product; personal injury and qualifying property damage are covered.
n.3: Property damage (to qualifying private property) is recoverable, not only personal injury.
n.4: The cost of the defective product itself is not recoverable under the Act.

7.q: A claimant obtains a High Court money judgment for a substantial sum, which the defendant does not pay for a considerable period. The claimant wishes to recover interest for the period during which the judgment remained unpaid, in addition to the judgment sum itself. The judgment debt has remained outstanding since it was entered. The claimant seeks interest on the unpaid judgment debt. The defendant has left the substantial judgment sum unpaid for a long time, and the claimant, conscious that the money has been kept from it throughout that period, wants to recover interest for the delay in addition to the principal amount the court originally ordered. Which of the following best describes the position on interest on the judgment debt?
o: Interest accrues at whatever rate the claimant chooses to charge.
Interest accrues only from the date enforcement proceedings are commenced on these facts.
Interest accrues only if the original contract provided for it.
Interest generally runs on the outstanding judgment debt at the statutory rate until it is paid.
No interest can ever accrue on a judgment debt after judgment is entered.
7.w: A money judgment debt generally carries interest at the statutory rate (currently 8% under the Judgments Act 1838 for High Court judgments, with similar provision for qualifying County Court judgments) from the date of judgment until payment. This is distinct from any interest awarded on the substantive claim up to judgment.

n.0: The rate is the statutory rate, not one the claimant chooses.
n.1: Interest runs from the date of judgment, not only from commencement of enforcement.
n.2: Statutory judgment interest does not depend on the original contract providing for interest.
n.4: Interest does continue to accrue on an unpaid judgment debt after judgment.

7.q: A prospective client who is profoundly deaf contacts a firm and asks it to arrange a British Sign Language interpreter for their first appointment, so that they can understand the advice and give proper instructions. The fee-earner is reluctant, regarding the request as inconvenient and an unwelcome additional cost to the firm, and wonders whether the firm can instead simply insist that the client bring along a friend or relative to interpret, or else decline to take the client on at all. The firm seeks advice on its obligations towards this prospective client. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may decline to act for the client, because a firm is free to choose its clients for any reason it likes.
The firm must not discriminate and must make reasonable adjustments, such as arranging an interpreter.
The firm need only make adjustments if the client can show that the disability was caused by another's fault.
The firm may insist that the client bring their own interpreter, as the cost of adjustments always falls on the client.
The firm has no obligations until a retainer is formally agreed, so it need do nothing for a prospective client.
7.w: Under the Equality Act 2010 and the SRA's requirements, a firm must not unlawfully discriminate and must make reasonable adjustments for disabled clients, which can include arranging and paying for measures such as a sign language interpreter.

n.0: A firm's freedom to choose clients does not extend to unlawful discrimination on protected grounds.
n.2: The duty does not depend on how or why the client came to be disabled.
n.3: The duty to make reasonable adjustments means the cost cannot simply be shifted onto the disabled client.
n.4: Obligations not to discriminate and to make adjustments apply to prospective clients, not just existing ones.

7.q: A government minister makes a decision that goes beyond the powers actually conferred on the minister by the enabling Act of Parliament, purporting to do something the statute does not authorise. A person affected seeks to challenge the decision in judicial review proceedings. The decision exceeds the statutory power. The enabling Act set out in some detail what the minister could and could not do, the step actually taken falls outside that grant of power, and the person affected is framing the challenge around the fact that the minister simply had no authority to do what was done. Which of the following best identifies the ground of judicial review being relied on?
o: Procedural impropriety.
Proportionality of the interference.
Illegality.
Irrationality.
Legitimate expectation arising from a promise.
7.w: Illegality as a ground of judicial review arises where a decision-maker acts outside the powers conferred on it, misdirects itself in law, or fails to give effect to the law. Acting beyond the powers conferred by the enabling Act (ultra vires) is a classic instance of illegality.

n.0: Procedural impropriety concerns unfair procedure or breach of natural justice, not acting ultra vires.
n.1: Proportionality assesses whether an interference is excessive, not whether the power existed.
n.3: Irrationality concerns a decision so unreasonable no reasonable authority could reach it, not exceeding powers.
n.4: Legitimate expectation involves reliance on a promise or practice, which is not what is described.

7.q: A wife agreed to charge the family home, which she co-owns with her husband, to a bank as security for the debts of her husband's struggling business. She entered into the charge only after her husband pressured her and seriously misled her about the nature and extent of what she was signing, and she received no independent legal advice about the transaction. The business has since failed, and the bank, which took no steps to ensure that she understood the transaction or obtained advice, now seeks to enforce the charge and take possession of the home. The wife seeks advice on her position against the bank. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The charge may be set aside against her. as a general rule in most cases
The lender's position is unaffected, because undue influence is only relevant between the spouses.
The charge is automatically void, because a spouse can never validly charge a jointly owned home.
The charge binds her only for half of the debt, reflecting her share of the home.
The charge is fully enforceable against her, because she signed the security documents.
7.w: Where a person offers their home as surety for another's debts in a non-commercial relationship, the lender is put on inquiry as to undue influence. If it fails to take reasonable steps (such as ensuring she received independent advice), the charge may be set aside as against her (RBS v Etridge).

n.1: Undue influence affects the lender where it was put on inquiry and did nothing.
n.2: Such a charge is not automatically void; it may be set aside in the circumstances described.
n.3: If set aside for undue influence, the charge fails against her, not merely as to half.
n.4: Her signature does not save the charge where the lender was on notice and took no steps.

7.q: Two businesses sign a short document recording that they will work together on a project, and that they will 'negotiate in good faith and agree the price and detailed terms at a later date'. No price, quantity or key terms are in fact ever settled between them. When a dispute arises, one party tries to enforce the document as a binding contract, arguing that the parties clearly intended to be bound to work together. The other says that, because the essential terms were left to be agreed in the future, there is nothing the court can enforce. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: There is a binding contract, and the court will simply fix a reasonable price and terms for the parties.
There is a binding contract, because the parties plainly intended to be legally bound to one another.
There is a binding contract, because putting the arrangement in a signed document makes it certain enough.
There is no binding contract, because an agreement to agree essential terms in the future is too uncertain to enforce.
There is a binding contract, because a duty to negotiate in good faith is fully enforceable in English law.
7.w: An agreement which leaves essential terms, such as price, to be agreed in the future is generally too uncertain to be an enforceable contract, and an agreement to negotiate in good faith is not enforceable in English law (Walford v Miles). There is therefore no binding contract.

n.0: The court will not write the contract for the parties by fixing terms they never agreed.
n.1: An intention to be bound cannot cure the fatal uncertainty of leaving essential terms unagreed.
n.2: Recording an incomplete agreement in signed form does not make its missing essential terms certain.
n.4: English law does not recognise an enforceable bare duty to negotiate in good faith.

7.q: A general partnership has no written agreement dealing with how profits and losses are to be shared, or whether any partner is entitled to a salary. One partner contributed far more capital than the others and worked longer hours, and argues they should therefore receive a larger share of the profits and a salary for their extra work. The court considers how profits and losses are shared, and whether a partner is entitled to a salary, under the default rules of the Partnership Act 1890. The firm had traded successfully for several years without ever agreeing anything in writing. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: In the absence of agreement, partners share profits and losses equally and are not entitled to a salary.
Profits are shared in proportion to the capital each partner contributed to the firm.
The partner who works the longest hours is automatically entitled to a salary.
Profits are shared equally, but losses fall only on the partner who caused them.
The partner with the largest capital contribution is entitled to the largest share of profits.
7.w: Under s.24 Partnership Act 1890, in the absence of contrary agreement, partners share equally in the capital and profits of the business and must contribute equally to losses, and no partner is entitled to a salary for acting in the partnership business.

n.1: Profits are shared equally by default, not in proportion to capital.
n.2: There is no default entitlement to a salary for working longer hours.
n.3: Losses are shared equally, not borne only by the partner who caused them.
n.4: A larger capital contribution does not, by default, give a larger profit share.

7.q: A defendant honestly but mistakenly believes they are about to be attacked, and uses force in response that would have been reasonable had the situation been as they believed. In fact there was no real threat at all; the belief was genuine but wrong, and (in this scenario) was not caused by the defendant's voluntary intoxication. The defendant relies on self-defence. The court considers the effect of a mistaken belief on self-defence. In the dark the defendant genuinely thought the approaching figure was about to attack them. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A mistaken belief can never be relied on, so the defence fails whenever the belief was wrong.
The defendant is judged only on the facts as they actually were, ignoring their honest belief.
The defendant may rely on the mistaken belief only if the mistake was a reasonable one to make.
The defendant may rely on the mistaken belief only where it was caused by voluntary intoxication.
The defendant is judged on the facts as they honestly believed them, even if the belief was mistaken.
7.w: For self-defence, the reasonableness of the force is judged on the facts as the defendant honestly believed them to be, even if that belief was mistaken; the belief need not be reasonable (though its reasonableness is relevant to whether it was genuinely held). A mistaken belief induced by voluntary intoxication, however, cannot be relied on.

n.0: A mistaken belief can be relied on; the defence does not automatically fail.
n.1: The defendant is judged on the facts as believed, not only as they actually were.
n.2: The mistake need not be reasonable, only genuinely held.
n.3: A drunken mistaken belief cannot be relied on, so this is the opposite of the rule.

7.q: A director has breached a duty to the company, but the breach is one the company is willing to overlook. The company proposes to ratify the director's conduct by resolution of the members, and a question arises about whose votes may count. The director in question is also a member and controls a substantial shareholding. The company proposes to ratify the breach. The board would rather draw a line under the director's breach than pursue it, and proposes to have the members approve what happened, but the director concerned also holds a large block of shares, which raises the question of whose votes may properly be counted in any such approval. Which of the following best describes the requirement for a valid ratification?
o: Ratification requires the unanimous consent of every member including the director on these facts as a general rule.
A breach of duty by a director can never be ratified by the members.
Ratification requires a special resolution with the director's votes fully counted.
Ratification is by ordinary resolution, but the votes of the director (and connected members) are disregarded.
Ratification may be effected by the board of directors alone.
7.w: Under s.239 of the Companies Act 2006, a director's conduct amounting to a breach of duty may be ratified by ordinary resolution of the members, but the votes of the director (if a member) and any member connected with them are disregarded in determining whether the resolution is passed. This prevents the wrongdoer approving their own breach.

n.0: Ratification does not require unanimity; an ordinary resolution (excluding the wrongdoer's votes) suffices.
n.1: Many breaches of duty can be ratified by the members, so 'never' is wrong.
n.2: An ordinary resolution suffices, and crucially the director's votes are not counted.
n.4: The board alone cannot ratify a breach of duty owed to the company.

7.q: In the course of administering a deceased's estate, a solicitor is asked by the executors to advise on and arrange the sale of a portfolio of shares held by the estate and to reinvest the proceeds in specific named financial products chosen by the beneficiaries. This work would involve carrying on activities that are regulated under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, and the firm itself is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. The solicitor wants to know on what basis, if any, the firm may lawfully carry out this investment work for the estate. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm may carry out the work simply because it is being done in the course of administering an estate.
The firm may do such work only if authorised, or the activity is exempt as incidental to its legal services.
The firm may never carry out any activity that is regulated under the Act in any circumstances whatsoever.
The firm may carry out any financial services work it wishes, because solicitors are wholly outside the scope of the Act.
The firm may carry out the work, provided the client signs a written waiver of the statutory protections involved.
7.w: Carrying on a regulated activity under FSMA 2000 requires FCA authorisation, unless it is an exempt regulated activity carried on incidentally to the provision of legal services and supervised by the SRA under Part XX. Estate administration does not automatically bring the work outside the regime.

n.0: Doing the work within an estate does not, by itself, make it exempt from the regime.
n.2: Firms can carry on some regulated activities through the exempt regime, so 'never' is wrong.
n.3: Solicitors are not outside FSMA; they must be authorised or fall within the exempt regime.
n.4: A client waiver cannot displace the statutory authorisation requirements.

7.q: A statute contains a clause purporting to prevent any court from questioning or reviewing decisions of a particular tribunal, appearing to exclude judicial review entirely. A claimant nonetheless seeks to challenge a decision of that tribunal that was made without jurisdiction. A solicitor is asked about the effect of such an ouster clause. The solicitor considers the approach of the courts to ouster clauses. The tribunal had made a fundamental error, yet the statute seemed to shut out any challenge. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The courts will always give an ouster clause its widest possible meaning.
Ouster clauses are automatically void and have no effect whatsoever on the courts.
The courts construe ouster clauses very narrowly and a decision made outside jurisdiction may still be reviewable.
An ouster clause completely and effectively excludes judicial review in all circumstances on these facts.
Ouster clauses can be relied on only by private bodies, never by public ones.
7.w: The courts construe ouster clauses very restrictively, in accordance with the principle that access to judicial review will not be excluded except by the clearest words. In Anisminic, a clause purporting to oust review did not protect a decision that was a nullity for error of law/excess of jurisdiction.

n.0: The courts construe such clauses narrowly, not widely.
n.1: Ouster clauses are not automatically void, but are narrowly construed.
n.3: Ouster clauses are not treated as wholly effective to exclude review.
n.4: Ouster clauses concern public law decisions, not a private/public distinction of this kind.

8.q: A landlord and a tenant entered into a written agreement, signed by both and complying with the formalities for a contract for the disposition of an interest in land, for the grant of a seven-year lease of business premises at a stated rent. On the strength of that agreement the tenant went into possession of the premises and has paid the agreed rent ever since. No lease was ever completed by deed as the agreement had envisaged. A dispute has now arisen between them, and it has become important to determine whether the tenant holds a lease for the full seven-year term or merely some lesser interest. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The tenant has no interest of any kind, because a seven-year lease must be by deed to exist.
The tenant has an equitable lease, because equity treats a specifically enforceable agreement for a lease as a lease.
The tenant has a legal seven-year lease, because taking possession dispenses with the need for a deed. on these facts
The tenant has a mere licence, revocable by the landlord on reasonable notice.
The tenant has only a periodic tenancy at law and no rights under the seven-year agreement.
8.w: A seven-year lease requires a deed to be legal, but a specifically enforceable written agreement for the lease takes effect as an equitable lease (Walsh v Lonsdale), so the tenant holds on the agreed terms in equity.

n.0: Absence of a deed does not leave the tenant with no interest; equity recognises the agreement.
n.2: Taking possession does not create a legal seven-year lease without a deed.
n.3: An enforceable agreement for a lease is more than a revocable licence.
n.4: The agreement gives an equitable lease on its terms, not merely an implied periodic tenancy.

8.q: A consumer buys a household appliance which, because of a manufacturing defect present when it left the factory, catches fire and injures the consumer and damages their other property. The consumer wishes to claim compensation for the personal injury and property damage caused by the defective product, but is worried about having to prove exactly how the manufacturer was careless. The consumer seeks advice on a claim under the Consumer Protection Act 1987. The appliance was only a few months old and had been used entirely in the ordinary domestic way. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The producer is liable only where the defect caused financial loss rather than physical harm.
The producer may be strictly liable for damage caused by a defective product, without proof of negligence.
The consumer must prove the manufacturer was negligent before any claim can succeed at all.
The consumer has no claim, because liability for products arises only in contract with the seller.
The producer is liable only if the consumer bought the product directly from the producer.
8.w: Under the Consumer Protection Act 1987, a producer is strictly liable for damage caused by a defect in their product, so the injured person need not prove negligence. A product is defective if its safety is not such as persons generally are entitled to expect.

n.0: The Act covers death, personal injury and certain property damage, not just financial loss.
n.2: The Act imposes strict liability, so negligence need not be proved.
n.3: The claim under the Act is not confined to those in a contract with the seller.
n.4: Liability does not require the claimant to have bought the product from the producer.

8.q: A bill has been passed by the House of Commons but the House of Lords is refusing to agree to it, and the Government wishes to know whether the bill can nonetheless become law without the Lords' consent. A solicitor is asked about the respective roles of the two Houses and the mechanism that can allow the Commons to prevail. The solicitor considers the role of the House of Lords and the Parliament Acts. The Lords kept sending the bill back and the Government was anxious to get it onto the statute book. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The Lords is mainly a revising chamber; under the Parliament Acts the Commons can sometimes legislate without its consent.
The House of Commons can never pass any legislation without the agreement of the Lords.
The House of Lords is the elected chamber and the Commons is the appointed one.
The House of Lords has an absolute veto over all legislation, which can never be overridden on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The House of Lords alone can make law without any involvement of the House of Commons.
8.w: The House of Lords is principally a revising chamber that scrutinises and can delay legislation.
