Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, in defined circumstances a bill may be presented for royal assent and become law without the consent of the House of Lords, so the elected Commons can ultimately prevail.

n.1: The Commons can, via the Parliament Acts, legislate without the Lords in defined cases.
n.2: The Commons is the elected chamber; the Lords is largely appointed.
n.3: The Lords does not have an absolute, unoverridable veto.
n.4: The Lords cannot make law alone without the Commons.

8.q: A defendant accumulates a hazardous substance on its land in a non-natural use. The substance escapes and damages a neighbour's property, but the escape was caused entirely by the deliberate, unforeseeable act of a trespassing stranger over whom the defendant had no control and whose conduct it could not have anticipated. The neighbour sues under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher. The escape resulted solely from the unforeseeable act of a third-party stranger. The defendant had contained the substance carefully, but an intruder with no connection to the defendant deliberately interfered with the tanks in a way the defendant could not have foreseen or guarded against, and it was that stranger's act alone that brought about the escape onto neighbouring land. Which of the following best describes the defendant's position?
o: The defendant is liable because only an act of God can ever provide a defence.
The defendant is liable unless it can prove the stranger was insolvent.
The defendant is strictly liable regardless of who caused the escape.
The defendant may rely on the defence of act of a stranger to escape liability.
The defendant is liable because the act of a stranger is never a defence under the rule.
8.w: Liability under Rylands v Fletcher is strict but not absolute. Recognised defences include the act of an unforeseeable stranger: where the escape is caused by the deliberate and unforeseeable act of a third party over whom the defendant has no control, the defendant is not liable. Other defences include act of God, the claimant's own default, consent and statutory authority.

n.0: Act of God is not the only defence; act of a stranger is also recognised.
n.1: The defence does not depend on the stranger's solvency.
n.2: Liability is strict but subject to defences, so it is not regardless of who caused the escape.
n.4: The act of a stranger is a recognised defence, contrary to this option.

8.q: A will leaves property to a named person 'to hold on trust for the purposes I have communicated to them', so that the existence of a trust is disclosed on the face of the will, but the actual beneficiaries and terms are not. The testator had told that person the terms of the trust before executing the will, and the person accepted them at that time. After death, a question arises as to whether this half-secret trust is enforceable. The property was substantial, and the trustee had written down the terms the testator gave before the will was signed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trust fails, because a trust that is mentioned in a will can never be a secret trust.
The named person takes the property beneficially, because the terms were not set out in the will on these facts.
The trust fails, because half-secret trusts are not recognised in English law.
The half-secret trust may be enforced, as the terms were communicated and accepted before or at the time the will was made.
The trust is valid only if the terms were communicated after the will had been executed.
8.w: A half-secret trust is disclosed on the face of the will but its terms are not. It may be enforced where the terms were communicated to, and accepted by, the trustee before or at the time the will was executed (Blackwell v Blackwell). Communication after the will is generally too late.

n.0: A trust mentioned in a will is precisely a half-secret trust.
n.1: The person does not take beneficially; the will shows they hold on trust.
n.2: Half-secret trusts are recognised in English law.
n.4: For half-secret trusts communication must be before or at the time of the will, not after.

8.q: A defendant's case has been sent to the Crown Court for trial, and following prosecution disclosure the defence must set out the nature of its case in a formal document. The defendant's solicitor advises on the obligation to serve this document and the consequences of not doing so. The solicitor considers the defence statement under the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996. The case had been sent up for trial and the prosecution had already served its disclosure. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A defence statement is required only where the defendant intends to plead guilty.
The defence statement must set out all the evidence the defence will call, word for word.
In the Crown Court the defence must serve a defence statement, and adverse inferences may follow from failing to do so.
A defence statement is required only in the magistrates' court and never in the Crown Court on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The defence never has to reveal any part of its case before the trial begins.
8.w: Following prosecution disclosure, the defendant in Crown Court proceedings must serve a defence statement setting out the nature of the defence, the matters of fact on which issue is taken with the prosecution, and any points of law relied on. Failure to serve one, or inconsistency with the defence run, may permit adverse comment or inferences.

n.0: A defence statement is relevant to contested (not guilty-plea) cases.
n.1: It sets out the nature of the defence, not every word of the evidence.
n.3: It is compulsory in the Crown Court (and voluntary in the magistrates' court).
n.4: The defence must reveal the nature of its case via the defence statement in the Crown Court.

8.q: A testator prepares a document intended to be their will. A dispute later arises about whether it was validly executed as a will. The document is in writing and was signed by the testator, but there is a question about the involvement of witnesses at the time of signing. The executor needs to know the formal requirements for a valid will. The court considers the formalities for a valid will under the Wills Act 1837. The document had been prepared at home and the family disagreed about who had actually been present. Which of the following best describes them?
o: The will must be registered at a government registry before it can take effect as valid.
The will is valid provided it is typed and signed, whether or not anyone witnessed the signature.
The will must be signed by the testator before a single independent witness, such as a solicitor.
The will need only be in the testator's own handwriting, with no requirement for any witnesses at all on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The will must be in writing, signed by the testator, whose signature is made or acknowledged before two witnesses present at the same time, who then sign.
8.w: Under s.9 Wills Act 1837, a valid will must be in writing and signed by the testator (or by someone in their presence and at their direction), the testator must intend by the signature to give effect to the will, and the signature must be made or acknowledged in the presence of two or more witnesses present at the same time, who each then sign (or acknowledge) in the testator's presence.

n.0: There is no requirement to register a will for it to be valid.
n.1: Witnessing is required; a typed and signed document alone is not enough.
n.2: A single witness is not sufficient; two witnesses are required.
n.3: Two witnesses are generally required; a handwritten will is not exempt from that.

8.q: Immediately after granting a legal mortgage over their home to a bank, the borrower fell into arrears with the monthly mortgage payments. The bank wishes to take possession of the property with a view to selling it. The borrower argues that the bank has no right to possession unless and until it first obtains a court order establishing that the borrower is in default, and that the right to possession cannot arise merely from the grant of the mortgage itself. The bank seeks advice on the nature and timing of its right to possession of the mortgaged home. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A legal mortgagee may never take possession of a mortgaged dwelling in any circumstances.
A legal mortgagee has no right to possession until the borrower has defaulted for at least six months. in the absence of any contrary agreement
A legal mortgagee has a right to possession that arises as soon as the mortgage is made, subject to statutory and equitable restrictions for dwellings.
A legal mortgagee acquires a right to possession only after exercising its power of sale.
A legal mortgagee must first obtain the borrower's written consent before taking possession.
8.w: A legal mortgagee's right to possession arises from the grant of the mortgage itself, 'before the ink is dry' (Four-Maids v Dudley Marshall). In practice, for a dwelling the right is subject to statutory controls (s.36 Administration of Justice Act 1970) allowing the court to postpone possession where the borrower can remedy the default.

n.0: A mortgagee can take possession of a dwelling, subject to the AJA 1970 protections.
n.1: The right to possession does not depend on a fixed period of default.
n.3: The right to possession is independent of, and precedes, exercise of the power of sale.
n.4: The borrower's consent is not required for a legal mortgagee to seek possession.

8.q: A civil claim is decided at trial, and one party is largely successful while the other loses. The successful party seeks an order that the losing party pay its costs. The losing party argues that each side should simply bear its own costs. The court considers the general rule on the incidence of costs following trial under the Civil Procedure Rules. The successful party had run the case efficiently and now wanted its legal costs paid by the loser. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The general rule is that the unsuccessful party pays the successful party's costs, though the court has a discretion.
The court has no power to make any order about costs after a trial.
Costs are always split equally between the parties regardless of who won.
Each party always bears its own costs, whatever the outcome of the trial.
The successful party always pays the unsuccessful party's costs as a matter of course on these facts as a general rule.
8.w: The general rule under CPR 44 is that the unsuccessful party will be ordered to pay the costs of the successful party ('costs follow the event'), although the court retains a broad discretion and may make a different order having regard to conduct, partial success and other factors.

n.1: The court does have power to make costs orders.
n.2: Costs are not automatically split equally.
n.3: Parties do not always bear their own costs; the loser usually pays.
n.4: It is the unsuccessful party who usually pays, not the successful one.

8.q: A defendant approaches the victim in the street and, in order to steal the victim's bag, threatens the victim with immediate force unless they hand it over, and then takes the bag. The force or threat is used at the time of, and in order to carry out, the stealing. The defendant is charged with an offence more serious than simple theft. The court considers the offence of robbery under the Theft Act 1968. The victim, badly frightened, let go of the bag rather than risk being attacked in the street. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Robbery is committed whenever force is used, even if no theft is involved at all.
Robbery requires the force to be used only after the property has already been taken away on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Robbery is theft where the defendant uses force, or threatens force, immediately before or at the time of stealing and in order to steal.
Robbery requires the victim to have suffered actual physical injury during the incident.
Robbery is simply any theft committed in a public place such as the street.
8.w: Under s.8 Theft Act 1968, robbery is committed where a person steals and, immediately before or at the time of doing so and in order to do so, uses force on any person or puts or seeks to put any person in fear of being then and there subjected to force.

n.0: There must be a theft; force alone without stealing is not robbery.
n.1: The force must be immediately before or at the time of stealing and in order to steal.
n.3: Actual injury is not required; a threat of force suffices.
n.4: Robbery is not simply theft in a public place; force or threat of force is essential.

8.q: A person has an estate contract (a contract to buy registered land) and wishes to protect it against the possibility that the seller might sell to someone else before completion, so that a later buyer would be bound by it. The interest is a third-party interest in registered land that the holder wishes to protect on the register. The holder wants a later purchaser to be bound. Some weeks will pass between contract and completion, during which the buyer worries the seller could be tempted to sell the same land to a higher bidder, and the buyer wants to put something on the register now so that any later purchaser would take the land bound by the buyer's contract. Which of the following best describes the appropriate method of protection?
o: Doing nothing, as estate contracts bind later buyers automatically.
Applying for first registration of the seller's title.
Lodging a caution against first registration of the land.
Entering a restriction that prevents any dealing with the land at all.
Entering a notice on the register in respect of the estate contract.
8.w: A third-party interest such as an estate contract is protected in registered land by entering a notice on the charges register. A notice preserves the priority of the interest so that a later registered disposition takes subject to it. A restriction, by contrast, regulates whether and how a disposition may be registered (for example, requiring a certificate), rather than protecting the priority of a burden.

n.0: Estate contracts do not automatically bind later buyers of registered land; protection is needed.
n.1: First registration relates to bringing unregistered land onto the register, not protecting this interest.
n.2: A caution against first registration applies to unregistered land, not registered land.
n.3: A restriction controls how dispositions may be registered; it does not itself protect the priority of a burden like an estate contract.

8.q: A defendant has been convicted and the court must decide on sentence. The judge is considering the purposes that sentencing is intended to serve when deciding how to deal with the offender. The defendant's solicitor makes submissions in mitigation. The solicitor considers the statutory purposes of sentencing for adult offenders. The offence was moderately serious and the court had a wide range of sentencing options open to it. Which of the following best describes them?
o: The sole purpose of sentencing is to raise revenue for the state through fines.
Sentencing has no defined purposes and is entirely at the whim of the individual judge.
The only purpose of sentencing is to punish the offender as severely as possible.
Sentencing purposes include punishment, reduction of crime (including deterrence), reform and rehabilitation, protection of the public, and reparation.
The only purpose of sentencing is to compensate the offender for the inconvenience of prosecution on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
8.w: The statutory purposes of sentencing for adults include the punishment of offenders, the reduction of crime (including by deterrence), the reform and rehabilitation of offenders, the protection of the public, and the making of reparation by offenders to persons affected by their offences.

n.0: Raising revenue is not the purpose of sentencing.
n.1: There are defined statutory purposes, not unfettered whim.
n.2: Maximum severity is not the sole purpose; several purposes apply.
n.4: Sentencing is not to compensate the offender.

8.q: A solicitor is asked to act for both the buyer and the buyer's mortgage lender in a residential purchase, on the basis that their interests in obtaining good title are the same. During the transaction the solicitor becomes aware of something about the property or the borrower that the lender would want to know but the buyer would prefer to keep from the lender. The solicitor considers their position when acting for both buyer and lender. The borrower had asked the solicitor to keep a particular matter from the lender's knowledge. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The solicitor may always act for both, and may keep the borrower's confidences from the lender whatever happens on these facts as a general rule.
The solicitor may act for both, but need not disclose anything material to the lender at all.
The solicitor may never act for both a buyer and a lender in the same transaction.
The solicitor may act for both while their interests coincide, but must cease to act if an actual conflict arises that cannot be reconciled.
The solicitor must always prefer the lender's interests over those of the buyer client.
8.w: A solicitor may usually act for both buyer and lender in a standard residential purchase because their interests coincide, but must not continue if a conflict of interest arises between them (for example information material to the lender that the buyer will not allow to be disclosed); the solicitor would then have to cease acting for one or both.

n.0: The solicitor cannot simply withhold material information from the lender client while continuing to act for both.
n.1: The solicitor cannot act for the lender while concealing material information from it.
n.2: Acting for both is permissible where interests coincide; it is not always prohibited.
n.4: The solicitor owes duties to both clients and must not simply prefer the lender.

8.q: A claimant issues a claim form but does not include the full particulars of claim within it, intending to serve them separately. The claimant wants to understand what the particulars of claim must contain and by when they must be served, so that the defendant knows the case they have to meet. The court considers the requirements for particulars of claim under the Civil Procedure Rules. The defendant needed to understand precisely what factual case they were being asked to meet. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The particulars of claim are optional and need never be served on the defendant at all.
The particulars of claim may be served at any time before the trial, however late.
The particulars of claim must set out all the evidence and legal argument the claimant will rely on at trial on these facts.
The particulars must set out a concise statement of the facts relied on and be served with or shortly after the claim form.
The particulars of claim need only state the amount of money the claimant wants to recover.
8.w: The particulars of claim must contain a concise statement of the facts on which the claimant relies (and certain specific matters where relevant). They must be contained in or served with the claim form, or served within 14 days after service of the claim form (and within the claim form's validity period).

n.0: Particulars of claim are required, not optional.
n.1: They cannot be served at any time before trial; there are time limits.
n.2: They state the facts relied on, not all the evidence and legal argument.
n.4: The particulars must set out the material facts, not merely the sum claimed.

8.q: A suspect is being detained at a police station in connection with an indictable offence. The standard maximum period of detention without charge is approaching, but the police wish to detain the suspect for longer to continue their investigation. The offence is indictable and the initial detention limit is nearly reached. The police seek to extend detention lawfully. The investigation is not complete and the police are keen to hold the suspect longer, but the clock on the ordinary detention limit for the indictable matter is running down, so the custody team needs to know who can authorise further detention and how far it can lawfully be stretched. Which of the following best describes how detention without charge may be extended beyond the initial limit?
o: Detention without charge can never exceed the initial 24 hours in any circumstances.
A superintendent may authorise up to 36 hours, and a magistrates' court may extend detention up to a maximum of 96 hours.
Only the Crown Court may authorise any extension of detention without charge.
Detention may be extended to any length simply on the authority of the investigating officer on these facts as a general rule.
A custody officer alone may extend detention indefinitely as needed.
8.w: Under PACE, the basic limit on detention without charge is 24 hours. For an indictable offence, a superintendent (or above) may authorise continued detention up to 36 hours, and a magistrates' court may issue and extend a warrant of further detention, up to an overall maximum of 96 hours from the relevant time, after which the suspect must be charged or released.

n.0: Detention can exceed 24 hours for indictable offences via the extension procedures.
n.2: Extensions are authorised by a superintendent and then the magistrates' court, not the Crown Court.
n.3: The investigating officer cannot extend detention to any length at will.
n.4: A custody officer cannot extend detention indefinitely; the statutory scheme and time limits apply.

8.q: A creditor is owed money under a contract (a chose in action) and wishes to transfer the benefit of that debt to a third party, so that the third party can enforce it and sue for it in their own name. The creditor wants to make a legal (statutory) assignment of the debt. The right assigned is a purely contractual benefit. The creditor is owed a debt under a contract and wants to hand the benefit of that debt over to a third party outright, so that the third party can chase and sue for it in its own name, and is trying to make the transfer as a full legal assignment rather than merely an equitable one. Which of the following best describes the requirements for a valid legal assignment under section 136 of the Law of Property Act 1925?
o: No formality is required; a legal assignment can be inferred from conduct on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The assignment must be absolute, in writing signed by the assignor, and express written notice must be given to the debtor.
The assignment may be made orally provided the debtor is aware of it.
The assignment requires the debtor's consent before it can take effect.
The assignment must be made by deed and registered at Companies House.
8.w: For a legal (statutory) assignment of a chose in action under s.136 of the Law of Property Act 1925, the assignment must be absolute (not by way of charge only), in writing signed by the assignor, and express notice in writing must be given to the debtor. The assignee can then sue in their own name. An assignment not meeting these requirements may still take effect in equity.

n.0: A legal assignment requires the statutory formalities; it is not inferred from conduct.
n.2: An oral assignment does not satisfy s.136; writing and written notice are required.
n.3: The debtor's consent is not required to assign the benefit (the burden is different).
n.4: A deed and Companies House registration are not the s.136 requirements.

8.q: A company goes into liquidation with limited assets and many claimants, including a bank with a fixed charge, a lender with a floating charge, employees owed wages, the liquidator's own fees, unsecured trade creditors, and the shareholders. The liquidator must distribute the available funds in the correct statutory order of priority. The court considers the order in which claims are paid in a corporate liquidation. The available funds fell far short of the total claims, so the order of payment would be decisive. Which of the following best describes the general order of priority?
o: Unsecured creditors are always paid in full before any secured creditor receives anything.
Shareholders are paid first, followed by unsecured creditors and only then secured creditors on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Fixed charge holders, then liquidation expenses, then preferential creditors, then floating charge holders, then unsecured creditors, then shareholders.
All creditors and shareholders are simply paid an equal share of whatever assets remain.
The order of payment is decided entirely at the liquidator's personal discretion.
8.w: In a liquidation the general order is broadly: fixed charge creditors (from their charged asset), then the costs/expenses of the liquidation, then preferential creditors (e.g. some employee claims), then the prescribed part and floating charge creditors, then unsecured creditors, and finally any surplus to shareholders.

n.0: Secured creditors generally rank ahead of unsecured creditors, not behind.
n.1: Shareholders are paid last, not first.
n.3: Assets are not simply shared equally among all; priority applies.
n.4: The order is fixed by statute, not left to the liquidator's discretion.

8.q: A claimant suffers a novel type of loss in circumstances that do not fall within any previously recognised category in which a duty of care has been held to exist. The claimant argues that the defendant should nonetheless owe them a duty of care in the tort of negligence. The court must decide whether to recognise a duty of care in this new situation, and considers the established approach to determining whether a duty arises in a case of this kind. Which of the following best describes the test the court applies?
o: The court imposes a duty of care in every case in which the claimant has in fact suffered a loss.
The court asks whether harm was foreseeable, proximity exists, and a duty is fair, just and reasonable.
The court refuses a duty of care in any situation that is not already an established category.
The court imposes a duty of care only where the defendant and claimant had a contract between them.
The court imposes a duty of care whenever the defendant could afford to pay compensation.
8.w: In a novel situation, the court decides whether to recognise a duty of care using the threefold approach derived from Caparo v Dickman: reasonable foreseeability of harm, a relationship of proximity, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty, developed incrementally by analogy with established cases.

n.0: A duty does not arise merely because loss was suffered; the threefold test must be satisfied.
n.2: Novel duties can be recognised incrementally; the law is not frozen to existing categories.
n.3: A contract is not required for a duty of care in negligence.
n.4: The defendant's ability to pay is irrelevant to whether a duty of care exists.

8.q: A private company wishes to pass members' decisions without holding a physical meeting, using the written resolution procedure. The directors ask what majorities are needed to pass, by written resolution, a decision that would ordinarily require an ordinary resolution, and one that would ordinarily require a special resolution. The company is a private company using written resolutions. The decisions correspond to ordinary and special resolutions respectively. Rather than convening a meeting, the company intends to put decisions to the members in writing, and the directors want to be clear about the level of support required to carry, by that route, both a run-of-the-mill decision and one of the more important kind that would normally need a special resolution. Which of the following best describes the required majorities?
o: A written ordinary resolution needs a simple majority, and a written special resolution at least 75%, of eligible members votes.
Written resolutions require only a simple majority whatever the type of decision.
A written ordinary resolution needs 75% and a written special resolution needs 90% on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Written resolutions can only ever be passed unanimously by all eligible members.
Both written ordinary and special resolutions require unanimity of all members.
8.w: For written resolutions of a private company, an ordinary resolution is passed by members representing a simple majority of the total voting rights of eligible members, and a special resolution by members representing not less than 75% of those voting rights. The thresholds mirror the votes needed at a meeting, but are measured against eligible members' total voting rights.

n.1: Special resolutions require 75%, so a simple majority is not enough for all decisions.
n.2: The thresholds are simple majority and 75%, not 75% and 90%.
n.3: Written resolutions need not be unanimous; the ordinary/special thresholds apply.
n.4: Written resolutions do not require unanimity of all members.

8.q: A partner instructs a cashier to transfer £3,000 from the general client account into the office account, describing it as an advance against fees the firm expects to bill later. No bill or written notification of costs has been delivered for that sum, and the money is currently held for a client. The cashier is uneasy about carrying out the instruction. The cashier considers the position under the SRA Accounts Rules. The partner is under pressure to improve the firm's month-end figures and has framed the movement as a routine advance, but the cashier knows no bill has gone out for the sum and that the money still belongs to a client, and must decide whether it is proper to act on the instruction. Which of the following best describes the correct response?
o: The cashier may make the transfer because the firm expects to bill the fees later.
The cashier may make the transfer provided it is reversed within five weeks.
The cashier should not make the transfer, as taking the money without a bill would breach the rules.
The cashier must carry out any transfer a partner instructs without question.
The cashier may make the transfer if the partner confirms the instruction in writing on these facts.
8.w: Client money may become office money capable of transfer only once a bill or written notification of costs has been delivered. Transferring client money to the office account as an unbilled 'advance' against future fees would be an improper withdrawal in breach of the Accounts Rules, so the cashier should not make the transfer merely on the partner's say-so.

n.0: An expectation of billing later does not make the money office money now.
n.1: Reversing it later does not make an improper withdrawal permissible.
n.3: A partner's instruction does not authorise a transfer that breaches the rules.
n.4: A written instruction does not cure the absence of a bill.

8.q: A defendant (or the prosecution) considers that the magistrates' court made an error of law or acted in excess of jurisdiction in reaching its decision, and wishes to challenge the decision on that legal basis rather than by a rehearing of the facts. The solicitor considers the route for challenging a magistrates' court decision on a point of law. The defendant argued the magistrates had misdirected themselves on the meaning of the offence. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A point of law can be challenged only by the prosecution and never by the defence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A point of law can only ever be challenged by a full rehearing in the Crown Court.
A point of law is challenged by appealing directly to the Court of Appeal.
The decision may be challenged by appeal to the High Court by way of case stated, or by judicial review, on a point of law or jurisdiction.
There is no way to challenge a magistrates' court decision on a point of law.
8.w: Where a magistrates' court decision is challenged on the ground that it was wrong in law or in excess of jurisdiction, the challenge is made to the High Court (Divisional Court) by way of appeal by case stated, or by judicial review, rather than by the factual rehearing available in the Crown Court.

n.0: Case stated is available to either party, not only the prosecution.
n.1: A point of law goes to the High Court by case stated/judicial review, not a Crown Court rehearing.
n.2: The route is to the High Court, not directly to the Court of Appeal.
n.4: There is a route to challenge on a point of law.

8.q: Three friends own a house together as beneficial joint tenants. One of the three, without telling the other two, grants a mortgage over their own beneficial interest in the house to a lender as security for a personal loan. That friend has now died. The two surviving friends assume that, under the right of survivorship, the deceased's interest in the house simply passes to them by operation of law and that the lender's mortgage falls away with the death. The question arises how the deceased friend's beneficial interest in the house is now held and dealt with. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The whole beneficial ownership passed to the lender on the grant of the mortgage.
Nothing changed, so the deceased's share passes by survivorship to the other two friends. in the circumstances
The mortgage is void, because a joint tenant cannot deal with their share at all.
The joint tenancy continued and the lender's charge simply disappeared on the death.
Mortgaging the share severed that friend's joint tenancy, so their share is held in common and passes under their estate.
8.w: A joint tenant who deals with their own equitable share — for example by mortgaging it — severs the joint tenancy as to that share, converting it into a tenancy in common. Survivorship no longer applies to it, so on death it passes under the deceased's estate (subject to the mortgage).

n.0: Mortgaging one share does not transfer the whole beneficial ownership to the lender.
n.1: Survivorship does not operate on a share that has been severed by the owner dealing with it.
n.2: A joint tenant can deal with their own share; doing so severs the joint tenancy.
n.3: The lender's charge over the severed share survives the death; it does not disappear.

8.q: On completion of the purchase of registered land, legal ownership is to be transferred from the seller to the buyer. The buyer's solicitor prepares the document that will transfer the legal estate, to be executed by the seller (and, where relevant, the buyer). The buyer asks what form this document takes and how it must be executed to be effective. The solicitor considers the transfer deed used to transfer registered land. The buyer needed to become the registered owner and take good legal title to the house. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The transfer of legal ownership requires no document at all once the price is paid on these facts.
The transfer is effective as soon as it is signed, whether or not it is witnessed.
The transfer is made by the buyer alone, and the seller need not execute anything.
The transfer is made by deed (e.g. Form TR1), which must be signed as a deed, witnessed, and delivered.
The transfer of registered land may be made by a simple unsigned written note.
8.w: The legal estate in land is transferred by deed. In registered conveyancing this is usually a Land Registry transfer (Form TR1), which must be executed as a deed — signed by the transferor (and transferee where it contains their covenants), witnessed, and delivered — and then submitted to the Land Registry to register the buyer.

n.0: A deed of transfer is required; payment alone does not pass legal title.
n.1: Execution as a deed requires witnessing, not merely signature.
n.2: The transfer is executed by the transferor (seller), not the buyer alone.
n.4: A transfer of a legal estate cannot be made by a mere unsigned note.

8.q: For more than 25 years Mrs Kelso, the owner of a house, has walked every day across an adjoining field to reach a lane, using a well-worn path. She has never asked permission to do so, and neither the previous owners of the field nor anyone else has ever objected or tried to stop her. The field has recently been sold to Mr Lang, who has now put up a fence blocking the path and has told Mrs Kelso that she has no right to cross his land. Mrs Kelso seeks advice on whether she can continue to use the path to reach the lane. Which of the following best describes her position?
o: She has no right at all, because a right of way over open land can only ever arise by necessity.
She has a personal licence only, which was personal to the old owner and ended when the field was sold.
She has an overriding interest in the field that binds the new owner however the use first began.
She has an easement, but only if it had been expressly granted to her by deed at some earlier time.
She may have acquired an easement by prescription, from using the way as of right for over 20 years.
8.w: Long use of a right of way as of right (without force, secrecy or permission) for at least 20 years can give rise to an easement by prescription. Once acquired as a legal easement, it binds a successor to the servient land such as Mr Lang.

n.0: Necessity is a separate, narrow route; it is not the only way to acquire a right of way.
n.1: Nothing indicates the use was permissive; use as of right is the basis for prescription, not a mere licence.
n.2: A right of way is an easement; it is not an interest that overrides through occupation of the servient land.
n.3: Express grant by deed is one way to create an easement, but prescription creates one without any deed.

8.q: A 17-year-old who has recently started an apprenticeship and lives independently buys a quantity of ordinary work clothing and basic tools from a supplier on credit, all of which are genuinely required for the apprenticeship and are suitable to the young person's actual needs and situation. The young person then refuses to pay for the goods, arguing that, because they are a minor, the contract cannot be enforced against them at all. The supplier seeks advice on whether it can recover payment for the clothing and tools. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The contract is unenforceable, because contracts with minors are valid only if approved by a parent.
The contract is enforceable against the minor, because the goods were necessaries suitable to their condition and needs.
The contract is entirely unenforceable, because no contract with a minor can ever be enforced against them.
The contract is enforceable only for the tools, because clothing can never count as a necessary.
The contract is enforceable, because a minor who is working is treated in all respects as an adult.
8.w: Although contracts with minors are generally unenforceable against them, a minor is bound to pay a reasonable price for necessaries — goods suitable to the minor's condition in life and actual requirements — as well as for beneficial contracts of service such as apprenticeships. The goods here are necessaries.

n.0: Parental approval is not the test; the goods being necessaries is what makes the contract enforceable.
n.2: Contracts with minors are not all unenforceable; those for necessaries bind the minor.
n.3: Clothing suitable to the minor's needs can be a necessary; it is not excluded as a category.
n.4: A working minor is not treated as an adult across the board; the necessaries rule is the relevant exception.

8.q: A trustee wishes to buy an asset which forms part of the trust property, paying what they say is a fair market price for it. The purchase is not authorised by the trust instrument, the beneficiaries or the court. A beneficiary later objects to the trustee having bought trust property, even though the price paid was fair. The trustee argues that, as the price was fair and honestly arrived at, the sale to themselves should stand. The asset was an attractive one that the trustee had long wanted to acquire for their own portfolio. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The purchase is valid, because a trustee is always free to buy trust property.
The purchase is voidable by the beneficiaries under the self-dealing rule, regardless of the fairness of the price.
The purchase is valid, provided the trustee genuinely believed the price to be fair.
The purchase is void only if the trustee paid less than the market value of the asset on these facts as a general rule.
The purchase is valid and unimpeachable, because the trustee paid a fair market price.
8.w: Under the self-dealing rule, a trustee who purchases trust property may have the transaction set aside (it is voidable) at the instance of a beneficiary, however fair the price and however honest the trustee, unless the purchase was authorised. The rule is strict and applies irrespective of fairness.

n.0: A trustee is not free to buy trust property without authority.
n.2: The trustee's honest belief in fairness does not validate the purchase.
n.3: The rule applies regardless of whether the price was below market value.
n.4: A fair price does not save a self-dealing purchase from being voidable.

8.q: A firm has carried out full customer due diligence on a client at the very start of a transaction that falls within the money laundering regime, obtaining and carefully recording evidence of the client's identity and of the source of the funds being used. The transaction then completes without incident and the file is closed. A fee-earner, tidying up the office and short of storage space, proposes to destroy all of the due diligence records straight away, on the basis that the matter is now completely finished. The firm's money laundering reporting officer intervenes. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm need not keep any due diligence records at all once identity has originally been verified.
The firm must keep the due diligence records for about five years after the relationship ends.
The firm need keep the records only until the client's next matter, whenever that happens to be.
The firm may destroy the due diligence records immediately, because the transaction has now completed.
The firm must keep the records permanently and may never destroy them under any circumstances.
8.w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require firms to keep records of the customer due diligence carried out, and of the transaction, for a prescribed period (broadly five years) after the business relationship ends or the transaction is completed, so records must not be destroyed immediately.

n.0: Records of the due diligence must be kept, not merely the fact that identity was once checked.
n.2: Retention is measured by the prescribed period, not by whenever the client next instructs the firm.
n.3: Completion of the transaction does not permit immediate destruction of the records.
n.4: Permanent retention is not required; the obligation is to keep them for the prescribed period.

8.q: Facing a temporary shortage in the office account, a solicitor uses £2,000 of client money from the client account to pay the firm's rent, intending to replace the money a week later, which the firm does. No client authorised the use of their money for this purpose. The COFA discovers what has happened. The COFA considers the position under the SRA Accounts Rules. The office account was temporarily short of funds when the rent fell due, the solicitor dipped into the client account to cover it and topped the client account back up a week later, and the COFA must assess whether the temporary and fully-reimbursed nature of the borrowing makes any difference. Which of the following best describes it?
o: There is no breach provided no individual client's ledger went into debit on these facts.
There is no breach because the money was replaced within a week.
Using client money to meet the firm's expenses is a serious breach even if it is replaced.
The use is acceptable if the firm records its reason on the file.
The use is acceptable because it was a short-term, temporary measure.
8.w: Client money may only be used for the purpose for which it is held. Using it to meet the firm's own expenses, such as rent, is an improper withdrawal and a serious breach of the Accounts Rules — potentially raising integrity issues — even where the firm intends to and does replace the money shortly afterwards.

n.0: The breach lies in the improper use, not only in whether a ledger went into debit.
n.1: Replacing the money does not undo the breach of misusing client money.
n.3: Recording a reason does not authorise using client money for the firm's expenses.
n.4: Being short-term or temporary does not make misuse of client money acceptable.

8.q: A defendant is charged with attempting to commit an offence. The prosecution can show that the defendant did an act more than merely preparatory, but there is a dispute about the mental element required for the attempt. The defence argues that recklessness as to the consequences should be enough, while the prosecution says a higher mental element is needed. The court considers the mens rea of a criminal attempt. The defendant argued that they had only been reckless, not that they had actually intended the result. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The defendant must intend to bring about the consequences required for the full offence.
The defendant need only be reckless as to the consequences of their conduct.
The mens rea for an attempt is always lower than for the completed offence.
The defendant need have no mens rea at all, because the offence was not completed.
The defendant must merely have foreseen that the offence might possibly occur.
8.w: The mens rea of attempt generally requires an intention to commit the full offence; the defendant must intend to bring about the consequences that are the elements of the completed offence (for example, for attempted murder, an intention to kill). Recklessness as to the result is generally insufficient.

n.1: Recklessness as to the consequences is generally insufficient for attempt.
n.2: The mens rea for an attempt can be higher (e.g. attempted murder requires intent to kill), not always lower.
n.3: An attempt does require mens rea, notwithstanding non-completion.
n.4: Mere foresight of possibility is not the required intention.

8.q: A testator's will leaves a gift to a named charity. By the time the testator dies, that charity has ceased to exist as a separate body, having merged with or transferred its assets to a successor charity carrying on the same charitable work. The executors must decide what happens to the gift. The court considers the effect of a gift to a charity that has ceased to exist in its original form. The charity's work was still being carried on, now under the banner of a larger organisation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The executors may keep the gift for the estate's own general purposes.
The gift is void and the money passes to the Crown as ownerless property.
The gift may pass to the successor charity carrying on the work, or be applied cy-pres, rather than simply failing.
The gift automatically lapses and falls into residue in every case.
The gift passes to the testator's next of kin because the charity no longer exists on these facts as a general rule.
8.w: Where a charitable gift is made and the named charity has ceased to exist but its work continues (for example through a successor or merged charity), the gift can often be given effect to that successor, or applied cy-pres to a similar charitable purpose, particularly where a general charitable intention is shown, rather than lapsing.

n.0: The executors cannot simply keep the gift for the estate.
n.1: It does not pass to the Crown as bona vacantia in these circumstances.
n.3: A charitable gift does not automatically lapse where the work continues; cy-pres or a successor may take it.
n.4: It does not necessarily pass to the next of kin.

8.q: Ms Everett holds a flat under a long lease that requires her to pay an annual service charge to the landlord, which is meant to fund the cleaning, lighting and maintenance of the common parts of the building. For the past year the landlord has largely failed to provide those services: the common parts have been left dirty, and the lighting has often not worked. Ms Everett is angry about this and has refused to pay the latest service charge at all, taking the view that, because the landlord has not provided the services, she owes nothing. She seeks advice on her position. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The tenant is automatically released from the service charge because the landlord has not performed its side.
The tenant may withhold the service charge indefinitely until every service has been provided in full.
The tenant must pay the charge and has no remedy of any kind for the landlord's failure to provide services.
The tenant owes nothing, because covenants in a lease are always mutually dependent on one another.
The tenant remains liable to pay, but may claim, or sometimes set off, for the landlord's failure to provide the services.
8.w: Leasehold covenants are generally independent, so the landlord's failure to provide services does not by itself discharge the tenant's covenant to pay. The tenant's route is a claim for breach (and, where the conditions are met, equitable set-off); service charges are also controlled for reasonableness by s.19 Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.

n.0: Covenants are not automatically discharged by the other party's breach; the obligation to pay continues.
n.1: Simply withholding the charge indefinitely is not permitted and risks the tenant's own breach.
n.2: The tenant is not without a remedy; she can sue for the breach and may have statutory protection on reasonableness.
n.3: Lease covenants are generally independent, not mutually dependent, so non-provision does not cancel the charge.

8.q: An Act of Parliament has received Royal Assent, but a person wishes to know when its provisions actually take legal effect, as the Act itself contains a section dealing with when it is to come into force. The Act has been passed but its operative date is in question. The Act contains provision about commencement. The Act has cleared all its stages and received Royal Assent, but a party needs to know from what moment its provisions actually bite, and, noticing that the Act itself contains a section dealing with commencement, wants to understand the default position and how it can be varied. Which of the following best describes when an Act's provisions come into force?
o: Only after a further vote of both Houses of Parliament following Royal Assent on these facts.
On Royal Assent, unless the Act provides for a different commencement date or for commencement by order.
Only when a court first applies the Act in a decided case.
Always immediately on Royal Assent, regardless of any provision in the Act.
Only once the Act has been in existence for at least one year.
8.w: An Act comes into force on the date of Royal Assent unless the Act itself provides otherwise. Many Acts specify a later commencement date, or provide that some or all provisions come into force on a day appointed by a minister through a commencement order (a statutory instrument), so different parts may come into force at different times.

n.0: No further parliamentary vote is needed after Royal Assent for the Act to commence.
n.2: An Act's force does not depend on a court first applying it.
n.3: Commencement can be deferred by the Act; it is not always immediate on Royal Assent.
n.4: There is no rule requiring a year to pass before an Act can take effect.

8.q: A settlor establishes a trust that pursues a mixture of aims, some charitable and some that are not charitable at all, and the trust funds may be applied to either kind of purpose at the trustees' discretion. The trust seeks recognition as a charity. The funds could lawfully be applied to non-charitable as well as charitable purposes. The trust deed lists a range of aims side by side, some plainly charitable and others not charitable at all, and leaves the trustees free to spend the fund on either sort, so the question is whether an arrangement drawn so widely can attract charitable status and its advantages. Which of the following best describes the effect on the trust's charitable status?
o: The trust is charitable so long as the non-charitable purposes are lawful.
The trust is charitable because it pursues at least one charitable purpose.
The trust is not charitable because it is not established exclusively for charitable purposes.
The trust is charitable provided most of the funds are in fact used for charity.
The trust is charitable if the trustees promise to prefer the charitable purposes on these facts.
8.w: To be charitable a trust must be established exclusively for charitable purposes. Where trust funds may be applied to non-charitable as well as charitable purposes, the trust is not exclusively charitable and generally fails to qualify as a charity, even if some of the purposes are charitable.

n.0: Lawfulness of the non-charitable purposes does not make the trust exclusively charitable.
n.1: Pursuing one charitable purpose does not cure the presence of permitted non-charitable purposes.
n.3: It is not enough that most funds are in fact used for charity; the purposes must be exclusively charitable.
n.4: A promise to prefer charity does not satisfy the exclusivity requirement.

8.q: A deceased owned shares in an unquoted trading company and business assets used in a trading business they carried on. The executors are considering whether relief may reduce the value of these business assets for inheritance tax purposes. The assets are relevant business property held for the requisite period. The executors are computing the inheritance tax on the estate. Among the deceased's assets are shares in an unquoted trading company and equipment used in a business the deceased ran, all held for long enough to qualify, and the executors want to know whether a relief exists that could strip out much or all of the value of those business assets before tax is charged. Which of the following best describes the relief that may apply to the business assets?
o: Business property relief may reduce the value transferred, potentially by up to 100% for qualifying business property.
No relief is available for business assets under any circumstances.
Business assets are always charged to inheritance tax at double the normal rate on these facts as a general rule.
The business assets are entirely exempt from inheritance tax in every case.
Relief applies only if the business assets are sold before death.
8.w: Business property relief can reduce the value transferred of qualifying relevant business property (such as an interest in an unincorporated business or unquoted trading company shares) held for the requisite period, at rates of up to 100% (or 50% for some assets), subject to conditions and exclusions (for example, businesses that are wholly or mainly investment).

n.1: Relief is available for qualifying business property, so 'no relief' is wrong.
n.2: Business assets are not charged at double the normal rate.
n.3: Business property is not automatically wholly exempt; relief depends on conditions and rates.
n.4: Relief applies to qualifying property held at death, not only to assets sold beforehand.

8.q: A firm holds client money for many different clients in its general client account. The bookkeeper is setting up the accounting records and wants to ensure that the firm can, at any time, show how much is held for each individual client and on what matter. The firm must keep records of its dealings with client money. Many clients' funds are pooled in one bank account. The firm handles matters for dozens of clients whose money all sits in the one general client account at the bank, and the bookkeeper wants the system built so that, if asked at any moment, the firm can say precisely how much of that pooled balance belongs to a given client on a given matter. Which of the following best describes the record-keeping requirement under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: The firm need only record the total balance held across all clients.
The firm need not keep ledgers provided the bank statement is retained.
The firm must keep a separate client ledger for each client, identifying the client and the matter and showing a running balance.
The firm may record client money only once a year in its annual accounts.
The firm may keep a single combined ledger for all clients with no individual breakdown on these facts as a general rule.
8.w: The SRA Accounts Rules require accurate, contemporaneous records, including a separate client ledger account for each client (and matter), recording all receipts and payments of that client's money and showing a current balance. This enables the firm to demonstrate at any time how much it holds for each client, even though the money is pooled in one bank account.

n.0: Recording only the total across all clients does not meet the requirement for individual ledgers.
n.1: Retaining the bank statement does not replace the requirement to keep client ledgers.
n.3: Records must be contemporaneous, not compiled only once a year.
n.4: A single combined ledger with no individual client breakdown is not sufficient.

8.q: An employee is given a job that involves interacting with members of the public on the employer's behalf. In the course of carrying out that role, the employee commits a serious wrongful act against a customer which is closely connected with the duties the employee was employed to perform, even though the act was itself a gross abuse of the employee's position. The victim sues the employer. The employer argues that a deliberate wrongful act by the employee cannot possibly be within the course of employment. The employee had been placed in a position of trust and authority over the very customer who was harmed. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The employer may still be vicariously liable if the wrongful act was closely connected with the employee's duties.
The employer is liable only for careless acts by employees, and never for intentional ones on these facts.
The employer is never liable for a deliberate or criminal wrongful act by an employee.
The employer is liable for any act at all committed by an employee at any time or place.
The employer is liable only where it expressly authorised the wrongful act in question.
8.w: An employer may be vicariously liable even for an employee's intentional or criminal wrongdoing where there is a sufficiently close connection between the wrongful act and the acts the employee was authorised to do, such that it is fair to impose liability (Lister v Hesley Hall; Mohamud).

n.1: Vicarious liability is not limited to careless acts.
n.2: Deliberate or criminal acts can fall within vicarious liability under the close-connection test.
n.3: Not every act by an employee attracts liability; a close connection with the employment is needed.
n.4: Express authorisation of the wrong is not required.

8.q: A testator's will leaves a legacy to a named friend. The friend dies before the testator, and is not related to the testator. The will contains no substitution provision saying who should take if the friend predeceases. After the testator's death, the executors must decide what happens to the gift. The friend left children of their own. The court considers the doctrine of lapse. The friend had been named for a modest legacy and had no family connection to the testator. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The gift is simply void and the whole will fails as a result.
The gift takes effect in favour of the friend's estate as though the friend had survived.
The gift is held on trust indefinitely until the friend's estate can claim it.
The gift passes automatically to the deceased friend's own children instead.
The gift lapses because the beneficiary predeceased the testator, and it falls into residue.
8.w: Under the doctrine of lapse, a gift to a beneficiary who predeceases the testator generally fails (lapses). Unless there is a substitution clause or a statutory exception applies, the lapsed gift falls into residue (or, if it is the residuary gift, passes on intestacy).

n.0: The lapse of one gift does not make the whole will fail.
n.1: A lapsed legacy falls into residue, not the friend's estate.
n.2: The gift does not vest in the friend's estate; it lapses.
n.3: The gift does not automatically pass to the friend's children (no statutory exception applies to a mere friend).

8.q: A party wishes to rely at trial on a statement made out of court by a person who will not be called as a witness, in order to prove the truth of what was stated — in other words, hearsay evidence. The other party argues that hearsay is simply inadmissible in civil proceedings. The court considers the admissibility of hearsay evidence in civil cases under the Civil Evidence Act 1995. The person who made the statement was abroad and could not be called to give evidence in person. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Hearsay evidence is admissible only where the maker of the statement has died.
Hearsay evidence is entirely inadmissible in civil proceedings in every case.
Hearsay evidence is admissible only in criminal, and never in civil, proceedings.
Hearsay evidence, if admitted, must always be treated as conclusive proof of the facts stated on these facts as a general rule.
Hearsay evidence is generally admissible in civil proceedings, subject to notice requirements and its weight being assessed.
8.w: Under the Civil Evidence Act 1995, evidence is not to be excluded in civil proceedings solely on the ground that it is hearsay. Such evidence is generally admissible, subject to notice requirements, with the court assessing the weight to be given to it.

n.0: Admissibility does not depend on the maker having died.
n.1: Hearsay is not inadmissible in civil proceedings.
n.2: Civil hearsay is admissible under the 1995 Act; the criminal rules differ.
n.3: Hearsay is not conclusive; its weight is assessed by the court.

8.q: When selling off part of their garden, an owner extracted from the buyer a covenant to contribute to the cost of maintaining a private road shared by both plots. That buyer has since sold their plot on to a successor in title. The successor now regularly uses the shared road but refuses to pay any contribution towards its upkeep, arguing that the obligation to pay was personal to the original buyer and did not pass to them on the sale. The owner of the retained land, faced with mounting repair bills, seeks advice on whether the maintenance obligation can be enforced against the successor. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The obligation binds the successor, because positive and restrictive covenants are treated identically. on the facts of this case
The obligation is not directly enforceable against the successor, because the burden of a positive covenant does not run with freehold land.
The obligation binds the successor, because the burden of any freehold covenant runs with the land.
The obligation is void, because covenants to pay money can never be created over land.
The obligation binds the successor, because it was protected by a notice on the register.
8.w: The burden of a positive covenant (here, to pay towards upkeep) does not run with freehold land at law or in equity (Rhone v Stephens). It cannot be enforced directly against a successor, though indirect devices (such as a chain of indemnity covenants or the benefit-and-burden principle) may assist.

n.0: Positive and restrictive covenants are treated differently as to whether the burden runs.
n.2: Only the burden of restrictive covenants can run in equity; positive burdens do not run.
n.3: Covenants to pay money are valid; the difficulty is enforcing the burden against a successor.
n.4: Entry of a notice cannot make a positive burden run where the law does not allow it.

8.q: Two defendants set out together to commit a robbery. During it, one of them (the principal) inflicts serious harm on the victim. The prosecution seeks to hold the second defendant liable as an accessory to that further offence. The second defendant assisted or encouraged the principal in the venture. The issue is the mental element required of the accessory. The two set off together on the robbery, and in the middle of it the one who confronted the victim went further and inflicted serious injury, leaving the prosecution to work out on what mental footing the companion who merely helped and encouraged can be fixed with responsibility for that further violence. Which of the following best describes the mental element for secondary (accessorial) liability following the current law?
o: The accessory is liable on a strict liability basis regardless of their state of mind.
The accessory must intend to assist or encourage the principal to commit the offence, with intention as to the essential matters, foresight being evidence of intent.
Mere foresight that the principal might commit the offence is automatically sufficient for liability on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The accessory is liable only if they physically carried out the offence themselves.
The accessory must have intended to kill the victim in every case.
8.w: Following R v Jogee, an accessory is liable where they assist or encourage the principal intending to do so and intending that the principal commit the offence (including any required mental element). Foresight that the principal might commit the offence is evidence from which intention may be inferred, but is not, by itself, the test for liability.

n.0: Secondary liability is fault-based, not strict.
n.2: Mere foresight is only evidence of intent, not automatically sufficient (correcting the former joint-enterprise approach).
n.3: An accessory need not personally carry out the offence; assisting or encouraging suffices.
n.4: An intention to kill is not required for accessorial liability to offences other than those needing that intent.

8.q: A defendant kills the victim while having lost their self-control as a result of a qualifying trigger, in circumstances where a person of the defendant's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint, might have reacted in a similar way. The defendant is charged with murder but seeks to reduce the offence to manslaughter. The court considers the partial defence of loss of control under the Coroners and Justice Act 2009. The defendant had snapped after a sustained and frightening confrontation with the victim that evening. Which of the following best describes its effect?
o: If established, loss of control is a partial defence reducing murder to voluntary manslaughter.
If established, loss of control is a complete defence resulting in an acquittal.
Loss of control reduces murder to a lesser non-fatal offence against the person.
Loss of control has no effect on liability, because provocation was abolished with no replacement.
Loss of control applies only where the defendant also lacked the mens rea for murder.
8.w: Loss of control (ss.54-55 Coroners and Justice Act 2009) is a partial defence to murder only. If the defendant lost self-control due to a qualifying trigger and a normal person might have acted similarly, the conviction is reduced from murder to voluntary manslaughter.

n.1: It is a partial defence, not a complete one; it does not lead to acquittal.
n.2: It reduces murder to manslaughter, not to a non-fatal offence.
n.3: Provocation was replaced by the statutory loss of control defence.
n.4: It presupposes the mens rea for murder is present but partially excuses it.

8.q: An elderly testator makes a will, and after their death a disappointed relative challenges it on the ground that the testator lacked the mental capacity to make a will at the time. The court must decide whether the testator had the requisite testamentary capacity when the will was made. The relative points to the testator's age and some confusion. The court considers the test for testamentary capacity. The relative pointed to episodes of confusion in the months before the will was signed. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The testator must have a perfect memory and full physical health when making the will.
The testator need only be able to sign their name at the time the will is executed.
The testator must obtain a doctor's certificate of capacity, or the will is automatically void on these facts as a general rule.
The testator must understand the nature of making a will, the extent of their property, and the claims to which they ought to give effect.
The testator must simply be over the age of eighteen at the time the will is made.
8.w: Under the test in Banks v Goodfellow, a testator has testamentary capacity if they understand the nature of the act of making a will and its effects, understand the extent of the property being disposed of, and can comprehend and appreciate the claims to which they ought to give effect, with no disorder of the mind perverting their judgement.

n.0: Perfect memory and full physical health are not required.
n.1: Ability to sign is not enough; the testator must have the requisite understanding.
n.2: A doctor's certificate is prudent (the golden rule) but not a legal precondition to validity.
n.4: Being over eighteen is necessary but not sufficient; the Banks v Goodfellow test must be met.

8.q: A claimant succeeds in a personal injury claim in negligence, having suffered a serious physical injury, considerable pain, a long period off work with lost earnings, and various out-of-pocket expenses for treatment and care. The claimant wishes to understand what the damages award is intended to include. The defendant accepts liability but disputes some heads of loss. The claimant seeks advice on the general nature of the damages recoverable for a personal injury of this kind. The claimant was off work for many months and incurred significant costs for treatment and rehabilitation. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Damages cover only pain and suffering, and never any award for lost earnings or expenses.
Damages are limited to a fixed statutory sum that is the same for every personal injury claim on these facts as a general rule.
Damages are payable only where the injury has left the claimant permanently disabled.
Damages cover only the claimant's actual financial losses, and nothing for pain or suffering.
Damages cover both general damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and special damages for quantifiable financial losses.
8.w: Damages for personal injury comprise general damages (non-pecuniary loss such as pain, suffering and loss of amenity, and future losses that cannot be precisely calculated) and special damages (pecuniary losses accrued to trial, such as lost earnings and expenses that can be quantified).

n.0: Damages include lost earnings and expenses as well as pain and suffering.
n.1: There is no single fixed statutory sum; damages are assessed on the facts.
n.2: Damages are not confined to cases of permanent disability.
n.3: Damages include non-pecuniary loss such as pain and suffering, not only financial loss.

8.q: A plot of land is subject to an old restrictive covenant that limits its use to residential purposes only. Over the years, however, the surrounding neighbourhood has changed completely and is now wholly commercial in character, so that the covenant has become obsolete and no longer secures any real practical benefit to the land it was originally meant to protect. The owner of the plot wishes to use it for commercial purposes and wants the covenant formally removed or modified so that it no longer stands in the way of that use. Which of the following is the correct route to achieve that?
o: Bring a claim in the county court for damages in place of the covenant.
Apply to the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) under s.84 LPA 1925 to discharge or modify the covenant.
Apply to the Land Registry to delete the covenant from the register as of right.
Simply ignore the covenant, because a covenant automatically ends once the area changes character, on these facts.
Obtain the consent of the original covenantee, who alone can release the covenant.
8.w: A person interested in freehold land affected by a restrictive covenant may apply to the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) under s.84 LPA 1925 to discharge or modify it, for example where it is obsolete or no longer secures any practical benefit.

n.0: A damages claim does not remove the covenant; discharge is via s.84.
n.2: The Land Registry does not delete covenants as of right on the owner's say-so.
n.3: A covenant does not automatically end because the neighbourhood changes; a discharge must be obtained.
n.4: The original covenantee is often not the current beneficiary; the statutory route is the Upper Tribunal.

8.q: A trust holds capital for a beneficiary who will become absolutely entitled to it in the future. Before that time arrives, the beneficiary has a pressing need for a capital sum, for example to help them buy a home or start a business. The trustees would like to advance part of the capital to the beneficiary now, ahead of the date of entitlement, but are unsure whether they have power to do so. The trustees seek advice on their statutory power to apply capital early for the beneficiary's benefit. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The trustees may advance capital freely for any purpose, whether or not it benefits the beneficiary.
The trustees may never advance capital before the beneficiary becomes absolutely entitled to it.
The trustees have a statutory power of advancement to pay or apply capital early for the beneficiary's benefit.
The trustees may advance capital only with the consent of every other beneficiary of the trust.
The trustees may advance capital only if a court authorises the payment in advance.
8.w: Under s.32 of the Trustee Act 1925, trustees have a statutory power of advancement to pay or apply capital for the advancement or benefit of a beneficiary before they become absolutely entitled, subject to conditions and to any modification in the trust instrument.

n.0: Advancement must be for the beneficiary's benefit, not for any purpose at all.
n.1: Early advancement of capital is possible under the statutory power.
n.3: The consent of every other beneficiary is not the general statutory precondition.
n.4: Court authorisation is not generally required to exercise s.32.

8.q: A carrier is engaged to deliver a broken mill shaft to be used as a pattern for a replacement, and delays delivery. Unknown to the carrier, the mill is entirely stopped for want of the shaft, and the delay causes the mill owner substantial loss of profits during the extra downtime. The mill owner claims those lost profits from the carrier. The carrier did not know, and was not told, that the mill would be wholly idle until the shaft was returned. The mill owner seeks advice on whether the lost profits are recoverable. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The lost profits are never recoverable, because loss of profit can never be claimed for late delivery.
The lost profits are always recoverable in full, however unusual or unforeseeable the loss.
The lost profits are recoverable simply because they were in fact caused by the carrier's delay.
The lost profits are recoverable only if within the parties' reasonable contemplation when contracting.
The lost profits are recoverable only if the carrier acted deliberately rather than carelessly.
8.w: Under the remoteness rule in Hadley v Baxendale, losses are recoverable only if they arise naturally from the breach, or were within the reasonable contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting. Unusual losses (here, total stoppage) are recoverable only if the special circumstances were communicated.

n.0: Loss of profit can be recoverable if within reasonable contemplation, so 'never' is wrong.
n.1: Damages are limited by remoteness; not all losses, however unforeseeable, are recoverable.
n.2: Mere factual causation is not enough; the loss must also not be too remote.
n.4: Remoteness, not the defendant's state of mind, governs recoverability here.

8.q: A trustee has committed a technical breach of trust which has caused loss, but the trustee acted honestly throughout, took what they reasonably believed to be a proper course, and the breach arose from an understandable mistake rather than any want of probity. The trustee asks the court to relieve them from personal liability for the breach in these circumstances. The beneficiaries argue that any breach must result in liability. The court considers its power to relieve a trustee from liability. The loss was significant, but the trustee had genuinely tried to do the right thing throughout. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The court may relieve the trustee from liability if they acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused.
The court has no power to relieve a trustee from liability for any breach of trust whatsoever on these facts.
The court may relieve the trustee only if the beneficiaries all consent to the relief.
The court must relieve any trustee who simply asserts that they acted in good faith.
The court may relieve the trustee only where the breach caused no loss to the trust at all.
8.w: Under s.61 of the Trustee Act 1925, the court has a discretion to relieve a trustee, wholly or partly, from personal liability for a breach of trust if it appears that the trustee acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused for the breach and for omitting to obtain directions.

n.1: The court does have a statutory power to relieve trustees in appropriate cases.
n.2: Beneficiary consent is not a precondition to s.61 relief.
n.3: Relief is discretionary and requires honesty and reasonableness, not a bare assertion of good faith.
n.4: Relief is available even where loss was caused, provided the statutory conditions are met.

8.q: A public body decides to carry out a consultation before making a policy decision, and an affected group argues that the consultation was so inadequate — for example giving no real information and no genuine opportunity to respond — that it was unlawful. A solicitor is asked about the standard a lawful consultation must meet. The solicitor considers the requirements of a fair consultation. The consultation had been rushed, with little information given and no real time to respond. Which of the following best describes them?
o: A consultation may be conducted in any way the body pleases, however inadequate.
A consultation is required to reach the outcome that the majority of consultees prefer on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A lawful consultation must be at a formative stage, give sufficient information and time, and the responses must be conscientiously taken into account.
There is no requirement to consider the responses received to a consultation.
A consultation is lawful provided at least one person is asked for their view.
