8.w: Where a public body consults (whether by choice or by legal duty), the consultation must be fair: undertaken when proposals are still at a formative stage, giving sufficient reasons and information to permit intelligent consideration and response, allowing adequate time, and the product of the consultation must be conscientiously taken into account (the Gunning/Sedley criteria).

n.0: A consultation cannot be conducted in any inadequate way; it must be fair.
n.1: The body need not simply adopt the majority view, but must genuinely consider responses.
n.3: Responses must be conscientiously considered.
n.4: Asking one person is not a fair consultation.

8.q: A solicitor is representing a client in ongoing court proceedings. The client instructs the solicitor to take a particular step which would clearly advance the client's immediate interests in the case, but which the solicitor knows would have the effect of misleading the court about a matter that is material to the issues it has to decide. The client is adamant that their own interests must come first, and insists that the solicitor is simply there to do the client's bidding whatever it may be. The solicitor must decide how to resolve the clash between the duty owed to the client and the duty owed to the court. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The duty to the client always comes first, because the client is the person the solicitor is retained to serve.
The solicitor may prefer the client's interests, provided the court does not actually discover that it was misled.
The duty to the court applies only to barristers acting as advocates, and not to solicitors at all.
The solicitor may simply choose whichever of the two duties seems more convenient in the circumstances.
Where the duties conflict, the duty to the court and the administration of justice takes precedence over the client's wishes.
8.w: A solicitor owes duties both to the client and to the court, but these are not equal. Where they conflict, the duty to the court and to the proper administration of justice prevails, so the solicitor must not take a step that would mislead the court, whatever the client instructs.

n.0: The duty to the client does not always come first; it yields to the duty to the court.
n.1: Whether the court discovers the deception is irrelevant; misleading it is impermissible.
n.2: The duty to the court applies to solicitors as well as barristers.
n.3: The resolution is not a matter of convenience; the court duty governs.

8.q: During negotiations for the sale of a restaurant, the seller tells the buyer that the premises are let to a tenant who is 'a most desirable tenant', when in fact the seller knows the tenant is heavily in arrears with the rent and unreliable. The buyer, relying on that statement, agrees to buy the restaurant. Shortly after completion the true position about the tenant emerges, and the buyer wishes to unwind the transaction. The buyer seeks advice on the primary remedy available for the seller's false pre-contract statement. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The buyer's only possible remedy is to claim damages, and rescission is never available for misrepresentation.
The buyer may rescind the contract, because the seller made an actionable misrepresentation that induced it.
The buyer may rescind only if the statement was also written into the contract as an express term.
The buyer has no remedy, because the statement was made before the contract and so has no effect.
The buyer has no remedy, because a statement about a tenant is only ever a matter of opinion.
8.w: An actionable misrepresentation is an unambiguous false statement of fact made by one party which induces the other to enter the contract. Its primary remedy is rescission, setting the contract aside, and damages may also be available depending on the type of misrepresentation.

n.0: Rescission is the primary remedy for misrepresentation; damages are additional, not the only option.
n.2: Misrepresentation does not require the statement to have become an express contractual term.
n.3: A pre-contract inducing statement is precisely what founds a misrepresentation claim.
n.4: The statement was one of fact that the seller knew to be untrue, not mere opinion.

8.q: A firm delivers a bill to a client for £2,000. In error, the client pays £2,200, £200 more than the amount billed. The firm identifies the overpayment when the receipt is processed. The client did not intend the extra £200 to be held on account of any future work. The cashier considers how the £200 overpayment should be treated under the SRA Accounts Rules. The client's payment plainly exceeded the sum demanded in the bill, there is nothing in the correspondence to suggest the extra was meant as money on account of any further work, and the cashier wants to deal with the surplus correctly rather than leaving it to swell the firm's income. Which of the following best describes the correct treatment of the £200?
o: The £200 may be transferred to another client whose ledger is short.
The £200 may be kept in the office account until the client asks for it.
The £200 may be retained by the firm as a goodwill credit.
The £200 is office money because it was paid together with the firm's fees.
The £200 is client money and must be returned to the client promptly.
8.w: Only the £2,000 matching the bill is office money. The £200 overpaid does not belong to the firm; it is client money. The firm must pay it into the client account and return it to the client promptly, since there is no proper reason to hold it, rather than retaining it or leaving it in the office account.

n.0: It cannot be applied to another client's shortfall.
n.1: It must not be held in the office account awaiting a request; it is client money to be returned promptly.
n.2: The firm cannot keep the overpayment as a goodwill credit.
n.3: Being paid with the fees does not make the overpayment office money.

8.q: A buyer's solicitor wishes to find out whether the property is connected to mains water and drainage, whether the public sewer runs within its boundaries, and who is responsible for the water and sewerage services. The solicitor considers which pre-contract search provides this drainage and water information. The property was in a rural area and the buyer was unsure whether it was on mains drainage at all. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Drainage and water information cannot be obtained before completion of the purchase.
The local land charges search alone provides all drainage and water connection information.
A drainage and water search (CON29DW) provides information about mains water and sewerage connections.
The buyer must physically dig up the garden to establish the drainage position.
A bankruptcy search reveals whether the property is connected to mains drainage.
8.w: A drainage and water search (CON29DW) is made with the relevant water and sewerage undertaker and reveals whether the property is connected to mains water and to the public sewer, the location of public sewers, and who is responsible for the services.

n.0: Drainage and water information is obtained pre-contract via the CON29DW search.
n.1: The local land charges search does not cover drainage and water connections in this way.
n.3: A formal search, not excavation, provides the information.
n.4: A bankruptcy search concerns insolvency, not drainage.

8.q: A company has granted a floating charge over its assets to a lender. While the company continues to trade normally, it deals freely with the assets within the class covered by the charge. On the company's default and the occurrence of a specified event, the floating charge is said to 'crystallise'. The lender wishes to understand the effect of crystallisation on the charge. The court considers the crystallisation of a floating charge. The company had defaulted on the loan and had then ceased trading altogether soon afterwards. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Crystallisation releases the assets entirely, leaving the lender with no security over them.
Crystallisation converts the floating charge into an unsecured personal claim against the directors.
Crystallisation transfers ownership of the charged assets outright to the lender at once.
On crystallisation the floating charge attaches to the assets then within the class, becoming in effect a fixed charge over them.
Crystallisation has no effect, because a floating charge always operates as a fixed charge from the outset on these facts.
8.w: A floating charge crystallises on the occurrence of certain events (such as the company's liquidation, appointment of a receiver, cessation of business, or a specified crystallising event). On crystallisation it ceases to float and attaches to the assets then within the charged class, taking effect much like a fixed charge over them.

n.0: Crystallisation fixes the charge on the assets; it does not release them.
n.1: Crystallisation strengthens the security over the assets; it is not a mere personal claim against directors.
n.2: Crystallisation does not transfer outright ownership to the lender.
n.4: A floating charge does not operate as a fixed charge from the outset; crystallisation changes its nature.

8.q: In a civil claim for breach of contract, the judge must decide whether the claimant has proved the disputed facts on which the claim depends. Counsel asks the judge to direct themselves as to the standard the claimant must meet before the facts can be found in the claimant's favour. This is a civil, not a criminal, matter. The parties give directly conflicting accounts of what was agreed and whether the goods conformed, there is no independent documentary tie-breaker, and the judge must be clear about how convinced the court needs to be before treating the claimant's version of the disputed facts as established. Which of the following best describes the standard of proof the claimant must satisfy?
o: Absolute certainty on the evidence.
The balance of probabilities.
Clear and convincing evidence to a near certainty.
Beyond reasonable doubt.
A prima facie case only.
8.w: The standard of proof in civil proceedings is the balance of probabilities: the party bearing the burden must show that the fact in issue is more likely than not to be true. This is a lower standard than the criminal standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.

n.0: Absolute certainty is not required in civil (or indeed criminal) proceedings.
n.2: English civil law does not use a distinct 'clear and convincing' near-certainty standard.
n.3: Beyond reasonable doubt is the criminal standard, not the civil standard.
n.4: Establishing a prima facie case is not the ultimate standard for proving the claim.

8.q: At trial the prosecution seeks to rely on evidence that the defence says was obtained unfairly — for example evidence obtained following serious breaches of PACE or its Codes — such that admitting it would adversely affect the fairness of the proceedings. The defendant's solicitor applies to have the evidence excluded. The solicitor considers the court's discretion to exclude evidence under section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The evidence had been obtained after serious breaches of the codes governing police conduct. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The court must admit all evidence the prosecution wishes to rely on, whatever its effect on fairness on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may exclude evidence only where it was obtained by torture and in no other case.
The court may exclude evidence only if the defendant did not have a solicitor present.
The court may exclude prosecution evidence whose admission would so unfairly affect the proceedings that it ought not to be admitted.
The court has no power to exclude any evidence in criminal proceedings.
8.w: Under s.78 PACE 1984, the court has a discretion to refuse to allow evidence on which the prosecution proposes to rely if it appears that, having regard to all the circumstances (including how the evidence was obtained), its admission would have such an adverse effect on the fairness of the proceedings that it ought not to be admitted.

n.0: The court can exclude unfairly obtained prosecution evidence under s.78.
n.1: Section 78 is not limited to evidence obtained by torture.
n.2: Exclusion is not confined to cases where no solicitor was present.
n.4: The court does have powers to exclude evidence (ss.76 and 78).

8.q: A solicitor is explaining the historical relationship between EU law and domestic law during the period of the UK's membership of the European Union, and how conflicts between the two were resolved at that time. A student asks how the courts dealt with a UK statute that conflicted with directly effective EU law while the UK was a member. The solicitor considers the supremacy of EU law as it operated during membership. The student was trying to grasp how conflicts were handled back when the UK was still a member. Which of the following best describes it?
o: During membership, directly effective EU law took precedence over conflicting domestic law, which the courts would disapply.
During membership, the monarch personally decided whether EU or domestic law applied on these facts as a general rule.
During membership, domestic statutes always prevailed over any conflicting EU law.
EU law never had any effect in the UK even during the period of membership.
During membership, conflicts were resolved by a public vote in each case.
8.w: During the UK's membership of the EU, by virtue of the European Communities Act 1972 and cases such as Factortame, directly effective EU law took precedence over conflicting domestic legislation, and the courts would disapply the conflicting domestic provision. This relationship ended on the UK's withdrawal.

n.1: The monarch did not personally resolve such conflicts.
n.2: Domestic statutes did not always prevail over EU law during membership.
n.3: EU law did have effect in the UK during membership.
n.4: Conflicts were resolved by the supremacy principle, not a public vote.

8.q: A firm undertaking publicly funded work receives a payment from the Legal Aid Agency in respect of the firm's costs on a matter. The cashier is used to the rule that money received for the firm's costs is client money until a bill is delivered, and asks whether this Legal Aid Agency payment must go into the client account or may be paid into the office account. The payment is for the firm's own costs. The firm does a good deal of publicly funded work and receives regular payments from the Legal Aid Agency covering its costs on such matters, and the cashier wants to apply the correct treatment to this receipt rather than assuming it must follow the ordinary route for money received in respect of costs. Which of the following best describes the position under the SRA Accounts Rules?
o: Payments from the Legal Aid Agency for the firm's costs may be paid into the office account.
The payment must be split equally between the client and office accounts.
The payment must be held in cash until the matter is finally assessed.
The payment must be paid into a separate designated deposit account for the client.
The payment must always be paid into the client account like any other receipt.
8.w: The SRA Accounts Rules make specific provision for legal aid work: payments received from the Legal Aid Agency for the firm's costs may be paid into the office account, even though they include sums that would otherwise be client money, reflecting the way legal aid funding operates. The firm must still deal with any client money element appropriately.

n.1: There is no automatic equal split rule for such payments.
n.2: The payment is not held in cash pending assessment.
n.3: A designated deposit account is not required for a Legal Aid Agency costs payment.
n.4: Legal aid payments for costs need not be routed through the client account like ordinary receipts.

8.q: A director of a company simply does whatever a dominant shareholder tells them to do, mechanically following instructions and abdicating any personal assessment of what is best for the company, rather than forming and exercising their own view on the decisions before the board. A shareholder complains that the director has failed in a general duty owed to the company. The court considers which of the directors' general duties under the Companies Act 2006 is most directly engaged. The director never questioned the instructions and simply rubber-stamped whatever they were told. Which of the following best describes it?
o: The duty to avoid conflicts of interest with the company (s.175).
The duty to declare an interest in a proposed transaction with the company (s.177).
The duty to act within the company's constitution and for proper purposes (s.171).
The duty to exercise independent judgement in the performance of the role (s.173).
The duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the role (s.174).
8.w: Under s.173 Companies Act 2006, a director must exercise independent judgement. Blindly following the instructions of another and abdicating their own judgement breaches this duty (subject to the ability to act under agreements duly entered into by the company or the constitution).

n.0: Section 175 concerns conflicts of interest.
n.1: Section 177 concerns declaring interests in transactions.
n.2: Section 171 concerns acting within powers.
n.4: Section 174 concerns competence and care, not independence of judgement.

8.q: A court is faced with a statutory provision that is genuinely ambiguous. Counsel wishes to refer the court to a clear statement made by the responsible minister during the Parliamentary debates on the Bill, as recorded in Hansard, to help resolve the ambiguity. The statement is clear and was made by the promoter of the Bill. The provision is capable of bearing two quite different meanings, neither obviously right, and counsel has located a passage in the official record of the Parliamentary debates in which the responsible minister explained precisely what the clause was meant to do, and wishes to rely on it. Which of the following best describes when the court may have regard to such Parliamentary material?
o: Only where both Houses of Parliament formally consent to its use.
Never, because reference to Parliamentary debates is always prohibited on these facts as a general rule.
In every case, as a routine first step in interpreting any statute.
Where the legislation is ambiguous or obscure, and the statement relied on is a clear ministerial statement.
Only in criminal cases and never in civil proceedings.
8.w: Under Pepper v Hart, a court may refer to Hansard as an aid to interpretation where the legislation is ambiguous, obscure or leads to absurdity, where the material relied on consists of a clear statement by the minister or promoter of the Bill, and where that statement is itself clear. It is not a routine or unrestricted practice.

n.0: Formal consent of both Houses is not required.
n.1: It is not always prohibited; Pepper v Hart created a limited exception.
n.2: Reference to Hansard is not a routine first step; the conditions must be met.
n.4: The principle is not confined to criminal cases.

8.q: A tenant occupies commercial premises for the purposes of its business under a lease that has not been excluded from statutory protection. As the contractual term approaches its end, the tenant is concerned about whether it can be required to leave. The tenancy is a business tenancy to which the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 applies. The tenant occupies for business purposes. The tenant runs its business from the premises under a lease that was never contracted out of the statutory protection, and as the fixed term nears its end the tenant is worried about whether the landlord can simply require it to pack up and leave once the contractual term expires. Which of the following best describes the tenant's position on security of tenure?
o: The tenant's rights depend entirely on whatever the lease says, with no statutory protection on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The tenant may remain indefinitely and the landlord can never recover the premises.
The tenancy ends automatically on the contractual term date and the tenant must leave.
The tenant has security of tenure only if the premises are residential.
The tenancy does not end automatically; the tenant has security of tenure and a right to apply for a new tenancy, resisted only on statutory grounds.
8.w: Under Part II of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954, a tenant occupying premises for the purposes of a business has security of tenure: the tenancy does not determine automatically at the end of the contractual term but continues until ended by a statutory procedure, and the tenant has the right to apply for a new tenancy. The landlord can oppose renewal only on one of the statutory grounds. Parties may contract out by the prescribed procedure before the lease is granted.

n.0: There is statutory protection under the 1954 Act, not merely whatever the lease says.
n.1: The landlord can recover possession on statutory grounds, so the tenant cannot always remain.
n.2: A protected business tenancy does not end automatically at the term date.
n.3: The 1954 Act protects business, not residential, tenancies.

8.q: A solicitor is asked to deal with funds and becomes aware that the money is, or is likely to be, the proceeds of crime, and considers doing an act that would help another retain or use those proceeds. The solicitor is concerned about committing a substantive money laundering offence. The money appears to be criminal property. The solicitor is considering the principal offences. The solicitor has become aware that the money they are being asked to deal with is very likely the proceeds of crime, and is contemplating steps that would help someone else hold onto or use it, which brings squarely into view the substantive money laundering offences rather than merely the duty to report. Which of the following best describes the principal money laundering offences under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002?
o: Money laundering offences apply only to banks, never to solicitors.
The only offence is failing to submit an annual compliance return.
An offence is committed only where the sums involved exceed a fixed statutory threshold on these facts as a general rule.
Concealing, arranging, and acquiring/using/possessing criminal property are the principal offences under sections 327 to 329.
There are no substantive money laundering offences, only a duty to report.
8.w: The Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 creates the principal money laundering offences: concealing, disguising, converting, transferring or removing criminal property (s.327); entering into or becoming concerned in an arrangement facilitating the acquisition, retention, use or control of criminal property by another (s.328); and acquiring, using or possessing criminal property (s.329). These apply to solicitors as to others.

n.0: The offences apply to solicitors, not only banks.
n.1: The offences are not limited to failing to file a compliance return.
n.2: There is no general de minimis threshold for the principal offences.
n.4: There are substantive offences, not merely a reporting duty.

8.q: A defendant inflicts an injury on a victim, and the victim later dies. The defence argues that the defendant's act did not cause the death, because other factors also contributed. To establish causation, the prosecution must show both that the death would not have occurred without the defendant's act and that the act was a legally sufficient cause. The court considers the requirements for establishing causation in a result crime. Several factors had been present, and the defence pointed to each of them as a possible alternative cause. Which of the following best describes what the prosecution must prove?
o: Causation is established automatically once the defendant is shown to have acted unlawfully.
The defendant's act must be both a factual ('but for') cause and an operating and substantial legal cause of the result.
The prosecution need only show that the result would not have occurred but for the act, and nothing more on these facts.
The prosecution need only show that the defendant intended the result to occur.
It is enough that the defendant's act was one of many factors that happened to be present.
8.w: To establish causation the prosecution must prove factual causation (the result would not have occurred but for the defendant's act) and legal causation (the act was an operating and substantial cause of the result, more than minimal, and not overtaken by an intervening act).

n.0: Unlawfulness of the act does not by itself establish causation.
n.2: Factual causation alone is insufficient; legal causation is also required.
n.3: Intention goes to mens rea, not to whether the act caused the result.
n.4: Mere presence among many factors is not enough; the act must be a substantial operating cause.

8.q: A claimant wishes to bring a claim for breach of contract, and separately is considering a claim in the tort of negligence (not involving personal injury). Time has been passing since the events in question, and the claimant is worried the claims may be too old to bring. They need to know the primary limitation period for these claims and from when it runs. The court considers the limitation periods under the Limitation Act 1980. The events giving rise to both potential claims had occurred a number of years ago now. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The limitation period for both claims is twelve years from the date of the events complained of on these facts.
The limitation period for both claims is three years from the date the cause of action accrued.
The limitation period is one year for contract and six years for negligence claims.
The primary limitation period for both breach of contract and non-personal-injury negligence is six years from accrual.
There is no limitation period for contract or tort claims, which may be brought at any time.
8.w: Under the Limitation Act 1980, the primary limitation period for a simple contract claim and for a tort claim (other than personal injury) is six years from the date the cause of action accrued (for contract, breach; for tort, when damage is suffered).

n.0: Twelve years applies to actions on a deed (specialty), not simple contract/ordinary tort.
n.1: Three years is the personal injury period, not the ordinary contract/tort period.
n.2: Both contract and this tort claim carry a six-year period, not one year for contract.
n.4: There is a limitation period; claims cannot be brought at any time.

8.q: A claimant succeeds in a judicial review claim, having shown that a public body's decision was unlawful, and wishes to know what the court can actually order as a result — for example to undo the unlawful decision or to compel the body to act. A solicitor is asked about the remedies available in judicial review. The solicitor considers the remedies in a judicial review claim. The claimant wanted the unlawful decision undone and the body compelled to think again. Which of the following best describes them?
o: The court may grant remedies such as a quashing order, a prohibiting order, a mandatory order, a declaration or an injunction, at its discretion.
The only remedy available in judicial review is an award of damages to the claimant.
The court has no power to grant any remedy in judicial review proceedings.
The court must always quash the decision automatically once any unlawfulness is shown on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
The court may only advise the public body and can make no binding order at all.
8.w: The remedies available in judicial review include a quashing order (to set aside the decision), a prohibiting order, a mandatory order (to compel action), a declaration, and an injunction. These remedies are discretionary, so the court may decline relief (for example for delay or where it would make no difference).

n.1: Damages are not the primary remedy in judicial review and are limited.
n.2: The court does have remedial powers in judicial review.
n.3: Remedies are discretionary; quashing is not automatic.
n.4: The court can make binding orders, not merely advise.

8.q: A testator's will names a sole executor who is a child aged 15 at the date of the testator's death. A grant of probate is needed to administer the estate promptly, but the named executor is a minor. The only named executor has not yet reached 18. A grant is required without delay. The will names just one executor, but that person is only fifteen years old at the date of death, and the estate needs administering without waiting years, so the question is how a grant can be obtained when the sole named executor has not yet come of age. Which of the following best describes the position on the grant?
o: The minor's parents automatically become the executors in the minor's place permanently on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A minor cannot take a grant while under 18; a grant may be taken by others on the minor's behalf, with the minor's own right reserved.
The estate cannot be administered at all until the minor turns 18.
The 15-year-old may take the grant of probate immediately as the named executor.
The will is invalid because it names a minor as executor.
8.w: A minor cannot take a grant of probate while under 18. Where the only executor is a minor, a grant (for example letters of administration with will annexed for the minor's use and benefit) may be taken by others, such as the minor's parents or guardians, with the minor's own right to a grant reserved until they reach 18.

n.0: Those who act do so for the minor's use, with the minor's right reserved, not as permanent executors displacing the minor.
n.2: Administration need not wait until the minor turns 18; others may act meanwhile.
n.3: A 15-year-old cannot take the grant while a minor.
n.4: Naming a minor as executor does not invalidate the will.

8.q: Two people are buying a property together and intend that, if one dies, their share should pass under their will rather than automatically to the survivor. They wish to hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common. The buyers want to hold as tenants in common and to alert future dealings to the trust. The conveyancer is completing the transfer and Land Registry forms. The two purchasers want to make sure that if one of them dies their share goes under their will and not automatically to the other, so they are buying as tenants in common, and the conveyancer must reflect that choice on the register so future dealings account for the trust behind the legal title. Which of the following best describes what should be done on the register to reflect this?
o: A Form A restriction should be entered, reflecting that the survivor cannot give a valid receipt for capital money alone.
Nothing need be done, as co-owners always hold as beneficial joint tenants.
The property must be registered with two separate title numbers, one per owner.
The legal estate should be transferred into the name of one owner only.
A notice should be entered protecting each owner's beneficial share as a burden on these facts as a general rule.
8.w: Where co-owners hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common, a Form A restriction is entered on the proprietorship register. It reflects that a sole surviving registered proprietor cannot give a valid receipt for capital money (so a second trustee is needed to overreach), signalling that the survivorship rule does not apply to the beneficial interests.

n.1: Co-owners do not always hold as beneficial joint tenants; they may choose a tenancy in common.
n.2: Co-owned property has a single title; it is not split into separate titles per owner.
n.3: The legal estate is held jointly by the co-owners as trustees, not in one name only.
n.4: Beneficial shares under a trust of land are not protected by a notice; a restriction is used.

8.q: A textile manufacturer agrees to buy a large quantity of cloth from a wholesaler 'by sample', a small swatch having been shown and approved at the time of contracting. When the bulk is delivered, it matches the swatch in colour but, unlike the sample, contains a hidden weaving defect that a reasonable examination of the sample would not have revealed, making the bulk unusable. The contract was expressly a sale by sample under the Sale of Goods Act 1979. The bulk differs from the sample in a way not apparent on reasonable examination of the sample. Which of the following best describes the buyer's position?
o: The buyer may claim for breach of the implied term that the bulk correspond with the sample in quality.
The buyer has no claim, because a sale by sample implies no terms about the bulk.
The buyer has no claim, because inspection of a sample always waives all later complaints on these facts.
The buyer may claim only if the bulk also failed to match the sample in colour.
The buyer may claim only if the wholesaler expressly guaranteed the bulk in writing.
8.w: On a sale by sample under s.15 of the Sale of Goods Act 1979, there are implied terms that the bulk will correspond with the sample in quality and that the goods will be free from any defect making quality unsatisfactory that would not be apparent on reasonable examination of the sample. The hidden weaving defect breaches those implied terms.

n.1: A sale by sample does imply terms linking the bulk to the sample.
n.2: Examining a sample does not waive complaints about defects not reasonably apparent from the sample.
n.3: The correspondence term covers quality, not only colour, so a quality defect suffices.
n.4: The implied terms arise by statute and do not depend on an express written guarantee.

8.q: A firm is approached by a prospective new client who wishes to instruct it to bring a claim against a company which was, until quite recently, itself a client of the same firm on a closely related matter. From having acted for that former client, the firm still holds confidential information about the former client's affairs which is material to the new client's proposed claim and would be of real tactical value in pursuing it. The former client has not consented to the firm acting against it, and no measures have been put in place to protect its confidential information. The firm considers whether it may take on the new instruction. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The firm must not act against the former client where it holds confidential information material to the new matter.
The firm may act, provided the fee-earner who acted for the former client is different from the one now instructed.
The firm may act, provided it promises the new client that it will not actually use the confidential information it holds.
The firm may act in any event, because a former client has no say in who the firm chooses to act for later.
The firm may act freely against the former client, because the duty of confidentiality ended when that retainer concluded.
8.w: The SRA Code prohibits acting for a client against a former client where the firm holds confidential information from the former retainer that is material to the new matter, unless the former client gives informed consent or effective safeguards (such as information barriers) protect that information.

n.1: Simply using a different fee-earner is not, by itself, an effective safeguard within the same firm.
n.2: A mere promise not to use the information does not satisfy the requirement for consent or effective safeguards.
n.3: The former client's interest in its confidential information does constrain who the firm may act against.
n.4: Confidentiality survives the end of the retainer, so it does not free the firm to act against the former client.

8.q: A landlord agreed to let a flat to a tenant for a fixed term of two years, at the full market rent of £1,200 a month, with no premium or fine taken, the tenancy to take effect in possession immediately. Instead of using a deed, the parties simply recorded the letting in a written tenancy agreement, which each of them signed. A dispute has since arisen between them about the tenant's rights, and the tenant needs to know whether they hold a valid legal lease of the flat, given that no deed was ever executed to create it. Which of the following best describes the status of the lease?
o: It is a valid legal lease, because a lease for three years or less at a market rent may be created without a deed.
It is void, because every lease must be created by deed to have any effect.
It is a mere licence, because it was not made by deed.
It is valid only if the tenant also registers it as a notice against the landlord's title.
It is only an equitable lease, because it was not completed by registration at the Land Registry. on these facts
8.w: A lease for a term not exceeding three years, taking effect in possession at the best rent reasonably obtainable without a fine, is an exception to the deed requirement (s.54(2) LPA 1925) and can be a legal lease even if made only in writing or orally.

n.1: Not every lease needs a deed; short leases within s.54(2) are excepted.
n.2: A validly granted short legal lease is not a mere licence.
n.3: A short legal lease within s.54(2) does not require a notice to be valid.
n.4: The lease is legal under the short-lease exception, not merely equitable, and short legal leases are not registrable dispositions.

8.q: A solicitor is asked to act for both the buyer and the seller in the same residential conveyancing transaction. The two parties have agreed a price directly between themselves and wish to save money by instructing a single solicitor to handle the whole matter for them. They are not related or otherwise connected in any way, they have been negotiating at arm's length, and each of them plainly has their own distinct interests in the price, the contract terms and the timing of the sale and completion. The solicitor asks whether it is proper to act for both parties to this transaction. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The solicitor may act for both, provided the agreed price is confirmed to be a fair market value.
The solicitor may always act for both buyer and seller, because a conveyancing sale involves only routine paperwork.
There is a conflict, so the solicitor should not act for both buyer and seller on the same sale unless a narrow exception applies.
The solicitor may act for both, provided the buyer and seller each pay half of the solicitor's fee.
The solicitor may act for both, because the parties have already agreed the price between themselves.
8.w: Acting for both buyer and seller in the same transaction gives rise to a conflict of interest, because their interests in the price and terms differ. The solicitor should not act for both unless one of the limited exceptions (such as a substantially common interest) applies with appropriate safeguards.

n.0: A fair price does not cure the conflict inherent in acting for both sides.
n.1: Conveyancing is not merely routine; buyer and seller have opposing interests in the deal.
n.3: Splitting the fee does not remove the conflict between the parties' interests.
n.4: Agreeing the price between themselves does not eliminate the conflict over the terms and conduct of the sale.

8.q: In the course of ongoing litigation, the opposing party's solicitors write to demand disclosure of the written legal advice which a solicitor had earlier given to their own client about the merits and weaknesses of the client's case. That advice was given confidentially, in writing, for the sole purpose of advising the client on the very dispute now before the court. The client is anxious that the advice should not be handed over to the other side, and the solicitor must explain the legal basis on which it can properly be withheld. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: The advice must be disclosed, because there is no protection for communications passing between a solicitor and a client.
The advice must be disclosed, because the professional duty of confidentiality never applies once litigation has begun.
The advice may be withheld only if the solicitor personally objects to disclosing their own work to opponents.
The advice is protected by legal professional privilege, which belongs to the client.
The advice may be withheld only until the opposing party offers to keep it confidential in return.
8.w: Confidential communications between a solicitor and client made for the purpose of giving or receiving legal advice attract legal professional privilege. The privilege belongs to the client and cannot be overridden by an opponent without the client's waiver.

n.0: Solicitor–client advice communications are protected, so they are not disclosable as of course.
n.1: Privilege is not lost simply because litigation has commenced.
n.2: The protection is the client's privilege, not a matter of the solicitor's personal objection.
n.4: Withholding does not depend on the opponent agreeing to keep the advice confidential.

8.q: A government department makes a serious policy failure, and there is public debate about who should answer to Parliament for the conduct of the department and its ministers. A solicitor is asked to explain the constitutional convention that governs ministers' accountability to Parliament for their departments and their own conduct. The solicitor considers ministerial responsibility. The failure had caused a public outcry and questions about who should answer for it. Which of the following best describes it?
o: Ministers are accountable only to the civil servants who work in their departments.
Ministerial responsibility is a statutory rule enforceable in the courts by damages on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Ministers are accountable only to the monarch and never to Parliament.
Ministers have no responsibility to anyone for the conduct of their departments.
By convention, ministers are individually and collectively responsible and accountable to Parliament for their conduct and their departments.
8.w: By constitutional convention, ministers are accountable to Parliament: individual ministerial responsibility makes a minister answerable for their own conduct and the running of their department, and collective ministerial responsibility binds the government to support agreed policy publicly. These are conventions, not legally enforceable rules.

n.0: Ministers answer to Parliament, not merely to their civil servants.
n.1: Ministerial responsibility is a convention, not a statutory rule enforced by damages.
n.2: Ministers are accountable to Parliament, not only to the monarch.
n.3: Ministers do bear responsibility for their departments by convention.

8.q: A director of a company has been involved in the management of several companies that have become insolvent, and their conduct as a director makes them unfit to be concerned in the management of a company. A regulator considers seeking an order to prevent the director from acting as a director in future. The court considers the disqualification of directors under the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986. Several of the director's previous companies had collapsed leaving substantial unpaid debts. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Disqualification is automatic for any director whose company becomes insolvent.
A director can never be prevented from acting as a director of any company in the future on these facts.
A director may be disqualified only if they have been convicted of a criminal offence.
The court may disqualify a director from acting as a director for a period where their conduct makes them unfit.
Only the company's shareholders, and never the court, can disqualify a director.
8.w: Under the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986, the court may make a disqualification order (for a period up to 15 years) against a person whose conduct as a director makes them unfit to be concerned in the management of a company, among other grounds.

n.0: Disqualification is not automatic on insolvency; unfit conduct must be shown.
n.1: Directors can be disqualified in appropriate cases; it is not impossible.
n.2: Disqualification for unfitness does not require a criminal conviction.
n.4: Disqualification is ordered by the court, not by shareholders.

8.q: A solicitor who holds a current practising certificate is asked to administer an oath and take a sworn statement. In one situation the person swearing the statement is a stranger who has simply come in off the street for that purpose; in another, the person is the solicitor's own client, and the statement is to be used in the very matter in which the solicitor is acting for that client. The solicitor is unsure in which of these situations it is proper for them to administer the oath. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A solicitor may administer oaths only for their own clients, and never for members of the public.
A solicitor may administer oaths, but not in a matter in which they are acting for a party.
A solicitor may administer oaths in any matter, including one in which they act, without any restriction.
A solicitor may never administer oaths at all, because that function is reserved exclusively to the courts.
A solicitor may administer oaths only if separately appointed as a notary public to do so.
8.w: The administration of oaths is a reserved legal activity which solicitors holding a practising certificate are authorised to carry out. However, to preserve independence, a solicitor must not administer an oath or take a statement in a matter in which they, or their firm, are acting for a party.

n.0: The function is not limited to the solicitor's own clients; the restriction is the opposite way round.
n.2: A solicitor must not administer the oath in a matter in which they are acting, so it is not unrestricted.
n.3: Administering oaths is not reserved to the courts; solicitors may do it.
n.4: A solicitor need not be a notary public to administer oaths.

8.q: A public body with a discretionary power adopts a rigid policy under which it will always decide cases in a particular way, and refuses even to consider whether an individual case might justify a different outcome, effectively shutting its mind to the exercise of discretion. A claimant challenges this. A solicitor is asked which ground of judicial review is engaged. The solicitor considers the fettering of discretion as a ground of review. The body announced it would refuse every application of this kind without exception. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A body may fetter its discretion provided it acts in good faith throughout.
A body unlawfully fetters its discretion if it applies a rigid policy without being willing to consider exceptions.
A body is never permitted to have any policy at all when exercising a discretion.
A body may always apply a fixed policy and refuse to consider any individual circumstances on these facts.
The way a body exercises a discretion can never be judicially reviewed.
8.w: A body with a discretion may adopt a policy to guide the exercise of that discretion, but it must not fetter its discretion by applying the policy so rigidly that it refuses to consider whether an individual case justifies departing from it. Doing so is a form of illegality.

n.0: Acting in good faith does not cure an unlawful fetter on discretion.
n.2: A body may have a policy, so long as it does not apply it rigidly; the issue is fettering.
n.3: A body cannot apply a fixed policy while refusing to consider individual circumstances.
n.4: The exercise of discretion is reviewable.

8.q: A local authority is already under a public duty to provide a certain level of policing at a venue. The venue owner promises to pay the authority a sum in return for the authority providing exactly that level of policing, and no more, that it is already obliged by law to provide. A dispute arises over whether the venue owner must pay. The authority did no more than its existing public duty required. The venue owner wanted a visible police presence for its own commercial reasons and offered to pay for it, but what it was promised in return was no more than the level of policing the force was already legally obliged to provide to the public in any event, with nothing extra laid on. Which of the following best describes the enforceability of the promise to pay?
o: The promise is unenforceable, as performing an existing public duty is not good consideration.
The promise is unenforceable, because public authorities can never enter into contracts.
The promise is enforceable, because the venue owner received a practical benefit in every case.
The promise is enforceable, because any performance by a public body is automatically good consideration.
The promise is unenforceable, because contracts with public bodies require statutory authority in writing.
8.w: Merely performing an existing public duty, without exceeding it, is not good consideration for a promise of payment. Had the authority provided policing over and above its existing duty, that extra provision would be good consideration; but doing only what the law already requires provides nothing new to support the promise.

n.1: Public authorities can and do enter into enforceable contracts.
n.2: There is no relevant 'practical benefit' where the body does only what it was already bound to do.
n.3: Performance by a public body is not automatically good consideration if it merely fulfils an existing duty.
n.4: The problem is the absence of consideration, not a formality about statutory authority in writing.

8.q: A trustee wrongfully mixes trust money with the trustee's own money in a single bank account, and then makes various withdrawals and payments out of the mixed account, some for the trustee's own purposes. The beneficiaries wish to trace the trust money in the account and to do so on the basis most favourable to them, taking advantage of the equitable rules that apply where a wrongdoing trustee has mixed trust funds with their own. The account had seen many payments in and out, making it hard to say whose money funded which withdrawal. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Equity applies rules favourable to the beneficiaries, generally treating the trustee as spending their own money first.
The mixed money is simply divided equally between the trustee and the beneficiaries in every case.
The beneficiaries may trace only if the trustee kept a precise record of every transaction.
The beneficiaries lose all rights to trace as soon as trust money is mixed with the trustee's own money on these facts.
The trustee is presumed to have spent the beneficiaries' money first, defeating the tracing claim.
8.w: Where a trustee wrongfully mixes trust money with their own, equity resolves difficulties in the beneficiaries' favour: the trustee is generally presumed to spend their own money first (Re Hallett), but the beneficiaries may instead claim a purchased asset where that is more advantageous (Re Oatway).

n.1: The mixed fund is not simply split equally; the tracing rules favour the beneficiaries.
n.2: Tracing does not require the trustee to have kept precise records.
n.3: Mixing does not destroy the right to trace; equity assists the innocent beneficiaries.
n.4: The presumption operates against the wrongdoing trustee, not against the beneficiaries.

8.q: A company carries out an activity that affects a large section of the local community: it causes obstruction and noxious fumes affecting a whole neighbourhood of residents and road users, rather than just one landowner. One resident suffers particular, additional damage over and above the general inconvenience shared by everyone else in the area. That resident wishes to bring a civil claim arising out of the situation. The resident seeks advice on the basis of a claim in public nuisance. The obstruction lasted for weeks and affected residents, shopkeepers and road users right across the area. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: Public nuisance is purely a criminal matter, and no individual can ever bring a civil claim for it on these facts as a general rule.
An individual may sue in public nuisance only if they have suffered special damage beyond that suffered by the public generally.
The resident may sue only if they also have a proprietary interest in affected land.
The resident may sue only if the company intended to harm the local community.
Any member of the affected public may bring a civil claim in public nuisance without more.
8.w: Public nuisance is an act affecting a class of the public. An individual can bring a civil claim in public nuisance only where they have suffered special (particular) damage over and above that suffered by the public at large.

n.0: Public nuisance, though a crime, can also found a civil claim where there is special damage.
n.2: A proprietary interest in land is required for private nuisance, not for a public nuisance special-damage claim.
n.3: Intention to harm is not required for public nuisance.
n.4: An ordinary member of the affected public cannot sue without showing special damage.

8.q: A court is interpreting domestic legislation and adopts an approach that seeks to give effect to the underlying purpose and objectives of the legislation as a whole, rather than being confined strictly to the ordinary meaning of individual words. This broad, purpose-driven method is increasingly favoured in modern statutory interpretation. The court looks to the aim behind the legislation. Rather than dwelling on the precise meaning of isolated words, the court stands back and asks what the legislation as a whole was trying to achieve, treating that overall objective as the key to resolving the interpretive question before it. Which of the following best describes this approach?
o: The literal rule applied strictly to individual words.
The purposive approach to statutory interpretation.
The rule against double jeopardy in criminal proceedings.
The rule that penal statutes are construed narrowly.
The doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty.
8.w: The purposive approach interprets legislation so as to give effect to the purpose or object underlying it, looking at the statute as a whole and its aims rather than being restricted to the literal meaning of isolated words. It is the approach most commonly associated with modern interpretation.

n.0: The literal rule is the opposite: it confines the court to the ordinary meaning of the words.
n.2: Double jeopardy is a criminal-law principle, not a method of statutory interpretation.
n.3: Narrow construction of penal statutes is a specific presumption, not this general purposive method.
n.4: Parliamentary sovereignty concerns Parliament's law-making supremacy, not an interpretive approach.

8.q: A suspect detained for an indictable offence asks to consult a solicitor. The police wish to delay access to legal advice because they believe allowing it immediately would lead to interference with evidence connected with the offence. The offence is indictable and the police rely on specified statutory grounds. The suspect has requested legal advice. The suspect, held for a serious indictable offence, has asked to speak to a solicitor, but the investigating team fears that letting that happen straight away could tip off associates or lead to evidence being tampered with, and they want to know whether, and how far, that fundamental right can be held back. Which of the following best describes the police power to delay access to legal advice?
o: Access may be delayed only for an indictable offence, on the authority of a superintendent, for up to 36 hours, on specified grounds.
Access to legal advice can never be delayed under any circumstances.
Access to legal advice may be delayed at the discretion of any officer for any offence on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Access may be delayed only with the consent of the suspect's chosen solicitor.
Access may be delayed indefinitely until the investigation is complete.
8.w: The right to legal advice is fundamental, but access may exceptionally be delayed where the detainee is held for an indictable offence, a superintendent (or above) authorises the delay, and there are reasonable grounds to believe that immediate access would, for example, lead to interference with evidence or harm to others. The maximum delay is 36 hours.

n.1: Access can be delayed in exceptional, tightly defined circumstances, so 'never' is wrong.
n.2: Delay is not at the discretion of any officer for any offence; strict conditions apply.
n.3: The solicitor's consent is not the basis for delaying access.
n.4: Delay is capped (36 hours), not available indefinitely.

8.q: A claimant is preparing to issue a money claim and must decide in which court to start proceedings, choosing between the County Court and the High Court. The claim is a relatively modest money claim, well below the threshold at which High Court proceedings would be appropriate, and does not raise any special complexity or importance. The court considers the allocation of claims between the County Court and the High Court. The sum in dispute was a few thousand pounds owed under a single unpaid invoice. Which of the following best describes the position for a straightforward money claim of modest value?
o: A claimant may only ever start a money claim in the High Court, never the County Court.
The choice of court is irrelevant, because the two courts are identical in every respect on these facts.
A modest money claim must be started in the Supreme Court in the first instance.
All money claims, whatever their value, must be started in the High Court.
A straightforward money claim of relatively low value should generally be started in the County Court.
8.w: Lower-value and straightforward money claims are generally started in the County Court. Only higher-value claims (broadly those exceeding the relevant threshold) or those of particular complexity, importance or specialist nature should be commenced in the High Court.

n.0: Money claims can be, and usually are, started in the County Court.
n.1: The two courts differ in the value and type of work they handle.
n.2: First-instance claims are not started in the Supreme Court.
n.3: Not all money claims must go to the High Court; modest ones go to the County Court.

8.q: A businessperson is deciding whether to incorporate as a private limited company or a public limited company, and wants to understand a key legal difference between them. In particular, they have heard that only one of these types of company is permitted to offer its shares to the public at large. They also understand there are differences in minimum share capital requirements. The court considers a fundamental distinction between private and public companies under the Companies Act 2006. The businessperson planned eventually to raise capital from outside investors to grow the company. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A public company may offer its shares to the public and must meet a minimum share capital requirement, unlike a private company.
A private company may offer its shares to the public, but a public company may not on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
Only a private company is a separate legal person; a public company is not.
There is no legal difference between private and public companies under the Act.
A public company cannot have limited liability, whereas a private company can.
8.w: A key distinction is that a public limited company may offer its shares to the public and must have an allotted share capital of at least the statutory minimum (£50,000, a quarter paid up) and a trading certificate before trading, whereas a private company must not offer its shares to the public.

n.1: It is the public company, not the private company, that may offer shares to the public.
n.2: Both private and public companies are separate legal persons.
n.3: There are significant legal differences between the two types.
n.4: Both private and public companies can be limited by shares.

8.q: A claimant wishes to challenge a public authority's decision by judicial review. Some months have passed since the decision was made, and the defendant argues the claim is too late. The claimant asks about the time within which a judicial review claim must be brought. The grounds arose when the decision was made. The decision under attack was taken and communicated to the claimant some months ago, the claimant took time to gather evidence and seek advice before acting, and the defendant now says that even if there is a good point on the merits the challenge has simply been left too late to proceed. Which of the following best describes the time limit for bringing a claim for judicial review?
o: The claim must be brought within twelve months of the grounds arising.
The claim must be filed promptly and in any event within three months of the grounds arising.
The claim must be brought within twenty-one days of the decision without exception.
There is no time limit for bringing judicial review proceedings.
The claim may be brought at any time within six years of the decision.
8.w: A claim for judicial review must be filed promptly, and in any event not later than three months after the grounds to make the claim first arose. The requirement of promptness means a claim may be too late even within the three months, though the court has a limited discretion to extend time.

n.0: Twelve months is longer than the three-month limit.
n.2: The general time limit is three months (with a promptness requirement), not a fixed 21 days.
n.3: There is a time limit; judicial review cannot be brought at any time.
n.4: The six-year limitation period applies to certain contract and tort claims, not judicial review.

8.q: Ms Jarvis holds a flat under a seven-year lease. The lease contains a covenant by the landlord to keep the roof and exterior of the building in repair. Over the winter the roof falls into serious disrepair and rainwater repeatedly enters the flat, damaging Ms Jarvis's furniture and decorations. She has told the landlord about the problem in writing on several occasions and given access, but the landlord has refused to carry out any repairs. Ms Jarvis wishes to know what she can do to make the landlord repair the roof and to recover for the damage she has already suffered. Which of the following best describes the remedy most likely available to her?
o: Forfeiture of the lease, which is the tenant's only remedy against a landlord in breach of covenant.
Damages for breach of the repairing covenant, and possibly specific performance to compel the repairs.
An indefinite withholding of rent, which automatically discharges the landlord's repairing covenant.
No remedy, because a landlord's repairing obligations cease to be enforceable once the lease is granted.
A declaration that a constructive trust of the reversion has arisen in the tenant's favour.
8.w: A landlord's repairing covenant is enforceable by the tenant. The usual remedy is damages for breach, and specific performance may be ordered against a landlord to compel the repairs (s.17 Landlord and Tenant Act 1985).

n.0: Forfeiture is a landlord's remedy for a tenant's breach; it is not the tenant's remedy against the landlord.
n.2: Any rent set-off is limited and does not discharge the landlord's covenant; simply withholding rent risks the tenant's own breach.
n.3: Covenants in a lease remain enforceable between landlord and tenant throughout the term.
n.4: A constructive trust of the reversion is irrelevant; this is an ordinary leasehold covenant claim.

8.q: A multi-track claim reaches the disclosure stage, and the court makes an order for standard disclosure. A party is unsure which documents they are required to disclose, believing they need only produce the documents that support their own case. The other party says the obligation is wider than that. The court considers the scope of standard disclosure under the Civil Procedure Rules. There were documents that helped the other side which the party would have preferred not to reveal. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A party need only disclose the documents that support its own case, and no others.
A party must disclose every document it has ever created, whether or not relevant on these facts as a general rule in the circumstances.
A party must disclose only the documents the other side specifically asks to see.
Standard disclosure requires a party to disclose documents relied on and those adversely affecting or supporting any party's case.
There is no obligation to disclose any documents to the other side before trial.
8.w: Standard disclosure requires a party to disclose the documents on which it relies, and the documents which adversely affect its own case, adversely affect another party's case, or support another party's case (as well as documents required by a relevant practice direction), following a reasonable search.

n.0: Disclosure is not confined to documents that support one's own case.
n.1: It is limited to relevant documents within the standard disclosure categories, not everything ever created.
n.2: Standard disclosure is not confined to documents specifically requested.
n.4: There is an obligation to give disclosure where ordered.

8.q: Two companies, A and B, make a contract under which A promises B that A will pay a sum of money to C, a third party who is not a party to the contract and who has given no consideration. The contract does not mention the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 or purport to give C any right to enforce it; it is simply an arrangement between A and B. A fails to pay C, and C wishes to sue A directly for the money. C seeks advice on whether it can enforce the promise. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: C can enforce the contract, because C is the person who was actually meant to receive the money.
C can enforce the contract, provided C later gives some consideration to A for the promise.
C can always enforce any contract that mentions C or is intended to benefit C in some way.
C can enforce the contract, because privity of contract has been entirely abolished in English law.
C generally cannot enforce the contract, because C is not a party to it and the doctrine of privity applies.
8.w: Under the doctrine of privity, only a party to a contract can generally enforce it. C is not a party and, absent an applicable exception (such as the contract satisfying the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, which is not engaged here), C cannot enforce A's promise.

n.0: Being the intended recipient of the money does not overcome privity by itself.
n.1: Later providing consideration does not make a non-party able to sue on the contract.
n.2: Merely mentioning or benefiting C does not, without more, give C an enforceable right.
n.3: Privity has not been abolished; it has been modified by statute in defined circumstances.

8.q: A client with quite limited funds asks a solicitor to help with just one discrete part of a dispute — reviewing and advising on a single settlement offer that has been made — rather than taking on the conduct of the whole matter, which the client intends otherwise to handle themselves. The solicitor is perfectly willing to provide this limited, 'unbundled' service, but is unsure how to do so properly, and in particular what duties they will still owe to the client when acting only on part of the matter. Which of the following best describes the position?
o: A limited-scope retainer is permitted, but only if the client agrees never to complain about the service.
A limited-scope retainer relieves the solicitor of any professional duties at all in relation to the work done.
A limited-scope retainer is permitted, provided its limits are made clear and the agreed work is done competently.
A limited-scope retainer is permitted only where the client has been refused help by every other firm first.
A solicitor may never act on only part of a matter, and must always take on the client's whole dispute.
8.w: Acting on a limited or 'unbundled' basis is permissible. The solicitor must make the scope and limits of the retainer clear to the client, and must still act competently and in the client's best interests in carrying out the agreed, limited work.

n.0: The client cannot be required to give up the right to complain as a condition of a limited retainer.
n.1: A limited retainer narrows the scope of the work, but does not remove professional duties within that scope.
n.3: There is no requirement that the client be turned away elsewhere before a limited retainer can be offered.
n.4: A solicitor may act on part of a matter; there is no rule requiring conduct of the whole dispute.

8.q: Two commercial parties in dispute wish to resolve matters without a trial. They agree to appoint a neutral third party to help them communicate and negotiate towards their own settlement, but who will not impose any decision on them. The client asks how this form of dispute resolution works. The neutral will not decide the dispute. Both businesses want to preserve their commercial relationship and avoid the cost and publicity of a trial, they have identified an independent person acceptable to both to help them talk the matter through, and it is understood from the outset that this person will not hand down any decision. Which of the following best describes this form of alternative dispute resolution?
o: Adjudication, in which a court officer issues a final judgment.
Litigation, in which a judge determines the dispute at trial.
A reference to the Court of Justice of the European Union.
Mediation, in which a neutral facilitator helps the parties reach their own settlement.
Arbitration, in which the neutral imposes a binding decision on the parties.
8.w: Mediation is a form of alternative dispute resolution in which an independent, neutral mediator facilitates negotiation between the parties to help them reach their own voluntary settlement. The mediator does not decide the dispute or impose any outcome; any settlement is agreed by the parties themselves.

n.0: Adjudication (in this sense) involves an imposed decision, unlike facilitative mediation.
n.1: Litigation involves a judge determining the dispute, not a facilitator.
n.2: A reference to the Court of Justice concerns EU law questions, not this settlement process.
n.4: Arbitration involves the neutral imposing a binding decision, which is expressly not the case here.

8.q: The shareholders of a company wish to remove a director from office before the end of their term, against the director's wishes, and the articles do not provide any special procedure. The shareholders want to know how, and by what majority, they can lawfully remove the director under the Companies Act 2006, and what procedural protections apply. The court considers the statutory power to remove a director. The director had a service contract, and the shareholders were determined to remove them regardless. Which of the following best describes it?
o: A director can be removed only by a special resolution passed by a 75% majority.
A director cannot be removed before the end of their term in any circumstances.
The members may remove a director by ordinary resolution, but special notice of the resolution is required (s.168).
A director may be removed by a simple decision of the other directors on the board.
A director can only ever be removed by a unanimous decision of all the shareholders on these facts as a general rule.
8.w: Under s.168 Companies Act 2006, a company may by ordinary resolution (a simple majority) remove a director before the end of their term, notwithstanding anything in any agreement, but special notice of the resolution is required and the director has the right to make representations.

n.0: A special (75%) resolution is not required; an ordinary resolution suffices.
n.1: A director can be removed before the end of their term under s.168.
n.3: Removal under s.168 is by the members, not by the other directors alone.
n.4: Unanimity is not required; an ordinary resolution suffices (with special notice).

8.q: A defendant persuades a vulnerable person to make them a substantial gift of money, which the donor, though perhaps unwise, was legally capable of making, so that ownership validly passes to the defendant. The prosecution alleges theft, arguing the defendant acted dishonestly in accepting the gift. Ownership of the money validly passed to the defendant by gift. The issue is whether accepting a valid gift can be an appropriation. The defendant cultivated the friendship of a lonely and vulnerable individual and steered them into handing over a large sum as an outright gift, a gift the donor had the legal capacity to make so that ownership genuinely passed, and the prosecution says the defendant's conduct in taking it was dishonest. Which of the following best describes the position on theft?
o: Theft is impossible because the donor consented to the transfer.
There can be no theft because a valid gift transfers full ownership to the defendant.
There can be no appropriation unless the property was taken without the owner's consent on these facts as a general rule.
The defendant is liable only in the civil courts for undue influence.
There can be an appropriation even where ownership passes by a valid gift, so theft may be committed if the taking was dishonest.
8.w: Following R v Hinks, an appropriation can occur even where the defendant receives property as an indefeasible gift and ownership validly passes. Appropriation is the assumption of the rights of an owner and does not require the absence of consent, so accepting even a valid gift dishonestly can amount to theft.

n.0: The donor's consent does not prevent theft where the other elements, including dishonesty, are present.
n.1: A valid gift does not preclude theft; there can still be an appropriation.
n.2: Appropriation does not require the absence of consent (Gomez, Hinks).
n.3: Criminal liability for theft can arise in addition to any civil remedy.
